The announcement of the fate of Rynders and his men caused horror among Captain Horn's companions. Captain Horn stated that there was no chance of being rescued by a passing vessel or escaping overland. Captain Horn intended to take four black men with him on a boat to seek help. Captain Horn planned to provision the boat and rig it for sailing down the coast.

The captain found gold bars while digging in a location he described. He took a yellow object from his pocket that was shaped like a rough prism. The captain expressed confidence that the object was gold and demonstrated its shine. Mrs. Cliff questioned the ownership of the discovered gold. She concluded that the gold should not belong to the current government of Peru or the indigenous people. Miss Markham stated that the gold belongs to Captain Horn since he discovered it. Mrs. Cliff argued against informing the Peruvian government about the gold.

The shops of Paris were open to Edna, who enjoyed bargaining and accumulating furnishings for her house in Plainton. Mrs. Cliff intended to build a large addition to her house in Plainton and did not rely on Captain Horn's expedition for her plans. Mrs. Cliff possessed a sufficient fortune for the life she desired in her native town and was waiting to return to make it known. Mrs. Cliff planned to send remittances to a charitable association in Peru for the benefit of the native Peruvians. Edna received no news from Captain Horn during the Christmas holidays and into January, despite her hopes for a letter. Edna arranged for a commercial agency to telegraph her when the Miranda arrived in any French port, but no message was received. Edna and her party traveled to Italy, where they were accompanied by Professor Barré, and she continued to expect a message from Captain Horn.

Miss Panney believes that Miriam will eventually like Dora. Miss Panney plans to send the Dranes away from Cobhurst once Miriam and Dora become friends. Miss Panney considers herself experienced and capable of influencing others. Cicely calls for Miriam to get dinner, unaware of Miss Panney's visit. Miss Panney expresses a desire to get to know Cicely and her mother better. Miss Panney finds Ralph to be a pleasant and interesting person. Miss Panney contemplates a plan for Dora and Miriam to go away together to strengthen their bond.

Lawrence found himself in a position of not knowing what to say regarding a past affair. Annie expressed a desire to discuss a specific part of the affair mentioned in a letter. Lawrence agreed to tell Annie the whole affair if she had any feelings about it. Annie suggested they take a walk, but Lawrence declined due to pain in his ankle. Annie felt commiseration for Lawrence's ankle and insisted he should not walk until he is well. Lawrence shared the entire history of his affair with Miss March with Annie. Annie expressed her opinion that Lawrence was never really in love with Miss March.

Matthias delayed moving into the new house until spring due to cold weather. Judith's arrival was anticipated as beneficial for her long-term stay. Matthias expressed dissatisfaction with Judith's everyday clothing choices. Matthias compared Judith's clothing to that of Dorcas Stone, who comes from a wealthier background. The narrator believed Matthias was developing an interest in Judith. Matthias was seen as a practical man looking for a suitable mistress for Cobhurst. Judith refused to wear her teaberry gown until she moved to Cobhurst.

The woman wished to be in the location where Captain Horn might arrive after his adventure. She did not want to be informed about his arrival in France or America. She believed Captain Horn was likely to succeed in his endeavors. Captain Horn had sent remittances to support Edna, Ralph, and Mrs. Cliff. The remittances were divided into three quarters for Edna and Ralph, and one quarter for Mrs. Cliff. Edna planned to go to Europe to experience a life of freedom and opportunity. She was disappointed by Captain Horn's unqualified agreement to her plans to go to France.

Mrs Null arrived at the parlor after dismissing her driver and waited for one to two hours. Letty, the attendant, mentioned that Mrs Null's mistress was away but expected back soon. Mrs Null had supper alone and went to bed in the chamber prepared by Letty. Mrs Null came out on the porch the next morning wearing a hat with red flowers and a short jacket. A dog approached Mrs Null on the porch after she called to him. Mrs Null instructed Plez to call her if anyone arrived while she planned to go to Pine Top Hill to read. Mrs Null had been at the estate for two days and appeared to be benefiting from her stay.

Miss Panney suggests that Mrs. Drane is attempting to secure a marriage for her daughter, Miss Cicely Drane, with Mr. Haverley. La Fleur expresses skepticism about the implications of Miss Panney's words regarding Mrs. Drane. Miss Panney claims that Mr. Haverley is already set to marry Miss Dora Bannister, who is of higher social standing and wealth. Miss Panney advises La Fleur to keep the information about Mr. Haverley's engagement to Miss Bannister confidential. Miriam enters the kitchen and introduces herself to La Fleur, who has not met her before. Miss Panney introduces La Fleur as a celebrated chef who cooks for Dr. Tolbridge. La Fleur expresses her desire to pay respects to Miss Haverley during her visit.

Miss Panney expressed dissatisfaction with the bathing-master for not having boats outside the breakers for swimmers in distress. The bathing-master explained that having boats would encourage swimmers to venture beyond the breakers. Miss Panney insisted that more boats should be available during bathing hours to assist exhausted swimmers. The bathing-master stated that he was following orders from the hotel proprietors regarding the boats. Following Miss Panney's complaints, two or three boats were made available outside the breakers during bathing hours for the remainder of the season. Miss Panney delayed leaving Barport to avoid appearing as if she was following the Bannisters. Upon visiting Thorbury, Miss Panney learned from Phoebe that conditions at Cobhurst were poor and that Mike was struggling.

Edna was in the center of events, prepared for news and arrivals. The party did not return to the Hotel Boileau. Edna believed she had a better understanding of the Continental lifestyle than when she arrived from America. Captain Horn had requested Edna to consider the money he sent her as income rather than property. Edna struggled with this request due to her practical mindset and concerns about her financial future. The party established themselves at a grand hotel, which impressed Ralph. Mrs. Cliff expressed dissatisfaction with her restrictions and her financial situation.

Shirley calculated and fired at a man on the vessel, who then fell backward. The captain ordered his men to rest on their oars to wait for the other man to show himself. The captain decided it was too dangerous to approach the vessel without knowing the other man's position. A man appeared on the deck of the schooner, holding a struggling pair of legs. The man on deck threw another man overboard and then waved his hands above his head. Inkspot prepared a line to throw to the boat, and the crew quickly boarded the vessel. The captain ordered the crew to get up sail and take the schooner inside the headland for safe anchorage.

The captain joined two ladies and a boy on the plateau to deliver bad news. Mrs. Cliff suggested that Ralph could catch fish to help with their food supply. The captain informed the group about the Rackbirds, causing distress among them. Mrs. Cliff proposed leaving the area immediately, but the captain disagreed. The captain instructed the group to quickly enter a narrow passage for safety. Miss Markham expressed concern for Mrs. Cliff's fear and sought reassurance from the captain. The captain indicated that their hope for escape depended on the return of Mr. Rynders.

The captain wrote about gold bars weighing over a million dollars. The narrator is uncertain about their share of the gold and their future plans. Edna advises the narrator not to calculate what may come to them. The narrator is not of age and Edna is their guardian. The captain stored guano-bags and packed gold bars in boxes in Mexico. The gold bars are being sent to a safe-deposit bank, a mint in San Francisco, and other locations. The gold bars are cast in a novel form and are pure gold, with no markings indicating their origin.

Mr Brandon announced to Colonel Macon that he is to be married. Colonel Macon expressed disbelief and anguish at the news of the marriage. Mr Brandon explained that he felt bound to marry Mrs Keswick due to a letter she had written. Mrs Keswick had threatened Mr Brandon with a prosecution for breach of promise. The marriage between Mr Brandon and Mrs Keswick was set for the eighth of January. Mrs Keswick took charge of all wedding arrangements and correspondence. Miss Peyton was unable to attend the wedding due to responsibilities at home.

The protagonist found the captain's wife, who had deceived him. The protagonist was insulted by an old negro who was once a slave in the Rackbirds' camp in Peru. The protagonist intended to punish the negro but did not plan to kill him. The protagonist admitted to being disorderly and acknowledged his case as a great misdemeanor. The protagonist informed the magistrate that Captain Horn would likely arrive in Paris and should be arrested. The police of Paris awaited the arrival of Captain Horn with interest. Miss Markham, known as a friend of a member of the American legation, was connected to Captain Horn.

Lawrence and Annie sat together in the parlor while Mrs Keswick went to Aunt Patsy's cabin. Old Aunt Patsy died in church. Annie expressed relief that they did not speak to Aunt Patsy about the stolen shoes. Lawrence believed Aunt Patsy's death occurred before they left the church. Letty told Annie that Aunt Patsy thought Lawrence was Mr Null. Aunt Patsy believed she could die happy after seeing Annie with Lawrence.

The main responsibility is to keep two negroes and any visitors away from the mound. The characters are advised to prevent anyone from exploring the cave and to restrict the negroes from accessing water from the stream. If the captain does not return, the characters are instructed to be vigilant about the gold and to carry away as much as possible without revealing it. Ralph expresses his commitment to watch over the negroes and any other visitors. Mrs. Cliff attempts to understand the matrimonial customs of Cheditafa and Maka, but struggles with the language barrier. Cheditafa is determined to perform the marriage ceremony for Captain Horn and feels pride in his role. The wedding ceremony takes place in the afternoon on a plateau in front of a stone face, with Cheditafa dressed in his best clothes.

The captain felt unease about the disappearance of the lake as it could allow the Rackbirds easier access to the cavern. The captain left Mok on guard and instructed him to give an alarm if he heard any sounds. The captain took a nap in the evening to prepare for the early dawn watch. Miss Markham was the only person awake while the others, including Maka, were suspected to be sleeping. The captain considered the possibility of fighting the Rackbirds in the chamber rather than the passage. The captain's hope for safety relied on the early return of Rynders and his men. Daylight arrived without any sign of an attack from the Rackbirds.

The captain felt a sense of relief after a dangerous situation had passed. Cheditafa informed the captain that there were no wild beasts in the area. The captain dropped his gun and expressed his belief that they were out of danger. Ralph suggested that they should display their flag to signal their location. The captain decided to explore the empty bed of the lake for clues about its disappearance. The captain discovered a machine at the bottom of the lake, which he initially thought was made of wood. The machine included a large cylinder and a circular aperture that resembled a valve.

Miss Panney enjoyed the company of clergymen and physicians but preferred lawyers. Miss Panney believed that law is fixed and settled, unlike medicine and theology. Miss Panney's first real friend was her legal guardian, old Mr. Bannister of Thorbury. Thomas Bannister succeeded his father and was Miss Panney's legal friend for many years. Herbert Bannister, the grandson of Mr. Bannister, is now the legal counsel for Miss Panney. Miss Panney had a surprising amount of legal business despite not being considered wealthy. Cobhurst is an estate near Witton farm that has been uninhabited for nearly a year.

The plan proposed by Cardatas was seen as their only hope of success. Burke suggested that they must get into the rear of the enemy by creeping along the sand. The men showed little discipline and did not respect Burke as a commander. Captain Horn ordered a volley of shots over the heads of the enemy instead of directly wounding them. Sanchez led a charge toward the line of bags, mistakenly believing they were equally armed. Captain Horn's men were equipped with repeating rifles, which gave them an advantage. Before reaching the boats, four of the fleeing enemy fell to gunfire from Captain Horn's men.

Mr Null is addressed regarding his duty. The speaker has not seen her husband for over twelve years. The husband is engaged to Mr Brandon's niece. Aunt Keswick is mentioned as having a negative opinion of the niece. The speaker expresses a desire to befriend Junius and inform him about Mr Croft. Old Mr Brandon is described as the only ordinary Christian the speaker has met. Roberta sits on the porch on a bright and sunny morning, reflecting on her situation.

The protagonist sees a woman who is young, tall, thin, and wearing a faded blue flannel suit and a straw hat. Ralph meets Captain Horn and begins to appreciate his worthiness to possess a ship-load of gold and his sister Edna. Ralph had previously doubted Captain Horn's suitability but changes his mind after observing him with Edna. Mrs. Cliff is startled by Captain Horn's appearance but reassures herself about the fixed compact with Edna. Captain Horn is uplifted by the condition of his three companions from the wreck and desert. Cheditafa and Mok, two Africans, are summoned by Captain Horn and are initially perceived as attendants of a foreign potentate. Cheditafa presents a large gold ring to Edna and Captain Horn, indicating his concerns about the marriage ceremony he performed.

The professor ensured that the guards accompanying him spoke only French. Banker confirmed that the captain of the bandits he served was a Spaniard named Raminez. The professor identified Raminez as the captain of the Rackbirds, a band that operated on the coast of Peru. The professor had previously discussed the Rackbirds and their camp with Ralph. There had been inquiries regarding the second son of Señor Blanquotè of Granada, who was known to have lived a wild life in America as Raminez. The professor proved that Raminez was actually Tomaso Blanquotè and that he was the legal heir to the Blanquotè estates. In July, the captain and Edna returned to Paris after traveling in England.

The character Edna experiences uncertainty regarding her relationship with Captain Horn. Edna believes that a marriage ceremony performed by a black man from Africa is as binding as a solemn engagement. Cheditafa has taken his responsibilities seriously since the incident with the Rackbird. Mok has developed irregular habits during Ralph's absence. Cheditafa goes out to search for Mok on the evening Ralph is expected from Brussels. Mr. Banker observes Cheditafa leaving the hotel and recognizes him. Banker follows Cheditafa with the intention of observing Mok's behavior.

The bathing-master tied a life-line around his waist and entered the surf to rescue swimmers. The men who brought the life-line did not uncoil it or take it out of the box. The life-boat was launched by a party of men, but it capsized due to an incoming wave. The bathing-master supported a helpless form while swimming toward the shore. Miss Panney experienced intense agitation and dread regarding the situation. Several doctors arrived to assist the two lifeless figures brought to shore. Miss Panney observed a group of men attempting to revive a man lying on the sand.

Miss Roberta accepted an offer from Junius Keswick. Aunt Judy expressed satisfaction that her property would remain in the family. Junius Keswick borrowed a horse and rode away early in the morning. Junius Keswick was anxious about his aunt's house and the situation at Midbranch. Mr Brandon visited the widow Keswick and found her charming. Mr Brandon informed Junius that Aunt Judy wished to arrange a match between him and his cousin. Aunt Judy engaged Mr Brandon to help bring about a divorce for her cousin.

Annie expressed a desire to read aloud to Lawrence. Lawrence offered Annie a chair, but she preferred to sit on the door-step. Annie began reading the first chapter of a book after recalling Mr. Croft's preference for starting at the beginning. Lawrence observed Annie while she read and reflected on her appearance. Annie read three chapters before leaving to check on dinner preparations. Lawrence requested more sheets of paper from Mrs. Null after using up his supply. Annie planned to read to Lawrence again before dinner after running an errand.

Old Butterwood suffered from various kinds of rheumatism and had passed away a few months before the story begins. Mike, a colored man with Irish ancestry, is the caretaker of Cobhurst and lives in the gardener's house. Mike is often questioned about the new owner of Cobhurst, Mr. Haverley, but he knows very little about him. Mr. Haverley is expected to arrive at Cobhurst on the fourth of April and is a young, unmarried man and a second nephew to old Butterwood. Miss Panney has more information about Mr. Haverley and believes Dr. Tolbridge could provide additional details. On the third of April, Mr. Ralph Haverley and his sister Miriam are packing in a New York boarding-house. Miriam expresses her excitement about going home and not returning to school.

The narrator has a plan to retrieve more gold from a mound. The narrator believes they need a crew to help transport the gold. The narrator considers buying a small vessel to carry the gold to Paris. The narrator trusts four black men for honesty but feels they are insufficient for the crew. The narrator thinks Shirley and Burke are reliable men to assist in the treasure retrieval. Ralph expresses frustration at being excluded from the treasure retrieval adventure. Ralph's sister argues that Captain Horn should not involve Ralph in a dangerous adventure.

Master Junius informed Uncle Isham that he would not ask him any more questions. Master Junius visited Aunt Patsy and gave her money before announcing his departure. Master Junius told Uncle Isham, Letty, and Plez that he was going away to stay. Master Junius left behind a sealed letter directed to the mistress of the house. Two women approached the outer gate, one in a carriage and the other on foot. The woman on foot, wearing a purple sun-bonnet, observed the carriage with surprise and indignation. The carriage driver left the gate open upon entering and later returned to close it.

The old gentleman went to the desk on the first day of the month to review uncalled-for letters. Miss Harriet informed Mrs. Keswick that there were no letters for her that day. Mrs. Keswick expressed that she did not expect any letters. Miss Harriet suggested to Mrs. Keswick that it was time for her to return home. Mrs. Keswick indicated that she would not return home as long as another lady was staying there. Mrs. Keswick stated that her family knows her whereabouts and that she will inform them when she chooses. Miss Harriet reminded Mrs. Keswick that she is welcome to stay regardless of her board payment.

Phoebe intended to ask the minister to write a letter to Miss Panney but lacked information and funds. Phoebe claimed that Mr. Hav'ley and Miss Drane were to be married in the fall and would move to the wife's mother's home. Miss Panney expressed disbelief in Phoebe's statements and accused her of lying. Phoebe suggested that Mr. Hav'ley and Miss Drane might already be married and were waiting for the Tolbridges to return to send out wedding cards. Miss Panney doubted Phoebe's credibility and believed she had not gone to Cobhurst. Miss Panney later found Dora alone and inquired about news from Cobhurst. Dora stated she had heard nothing from Cobhurst and expressed reluctance to visit until Miriam came to see her.

Captain Horn has a letter and a message for Edna. Captain Horn cannot give Edna the letter and message in public. Captain Horn instructs Edna to meet him at the Gardens of the Tuileries. Edna leaves her carriage and walks in the Gardens of the Tuileries. Edna meets Banker in the Gardens, who has the letter from Captain Horn. Banker informs Edna that Captain Horn has had recent success but must remain discreet. Banker states that he undertook the risky job of delivering the letter to Edna in private.

Lawrence and Annie are in a secluded location that Annie finds peaceful, contrasting with the tumult of a church. Annie expresses that she initially enjoyed the excitement of the church but later felt oppressed by it. Lawrence believes that solitude would typically lower Annie's spirits, but she insists she is not alone. Lawrence realizes that Annie loves him when he looks into her eyes. Lawrence embraces Annie and assures her that she will never be alone. A sorrel horse, uninterested in the emotional exchange, begins to move forward. Lawrence attempts to control the horse but struggles to reach the reins, prompting Annie to warn him against jumping out.

Aunt Patsy's soul departed from her body without attracting attention. Lawrence and Miss Annie left the church together after feeling uncomfortable. Mr. Croft and Miss Annie got into a spring-wagon after leaving the church. Miss Annie mentioned that dinner would be late due to Letty's involvement with the Jerusalem Jumpers. Lawrence and Miss Annie decided to take a drive through the woods. The road through the woods was sandy with occasional tree roots and low-hanging branches. The woods were quiet, with little sound except for the crunching of wheels and their voices.

The landlord rang a bell at his table, prompting Mok to sing. Mok only knew one song, an African hymn taught to him by Cheditafa. Mok's performance electrified the audience, leading them to laugh and applaud. A man named Banker, a former member of the Rackbirds, entered the Black Cat during Mok's performance. Banker was an American who had previously been a gold-digger and gambler in California. Banker had escaped to Panama before eventually reaching Paris, where he felt unwanted. Banker recognized Mok as a former slave and was astonished to see him performing in Paris.

The woman observed a man on a boat from the sandy beach, noting his long hair, beard, and battered felt hat. Captain Horn entered Edna's salon and initially did not recognize her due to her changed appearance. Edna was dressed in a dark-blue flannel suit and an old straw hat with a faded ribbon. Captain Horn was a tall gentleman in a dark suit and light-colored overcoat, with a gloved hand and a hat in the other. Edna and Captain Horn shook hands as they had previously communicated. Edna expressed her joy at seeing Captain Horn again after months of separation. Captain Horn asked Edna about Ralph, Mrs. Cliff, and events since he left San Francisco.

Lawrence felt that a young woman had truthfully divined the motives of another young woman. Annie suggested that Lawrence should not write to Miss March and should tear up the letter. Annie advised Lawrence to write a note to Miss March accepting her previous statement as a conclusive answer. Lawrence and Annie discussed informing Aunt Keswick about their engagement. Annie proposed a plan to explain her use of the name Mrs Null and their engagement to Aunt Keswick. Mrs Keswick interrupted their conversation, stating that they need not tell her anything as it was already known.

A portion of the water from the vessel had run out, but it was expected to return with the rising tide. Bags were arranged on the beach in a long mound, approximately three feet high and four rows wide at the bottom. The captain supervised the arrangement of the bags to resemble the dunes of sand behind them. The captain considered concealing the bags by covering them with sand, aided by prevailing western winds. Provisions, water, and other valuable items were taken from the brig and carried to shore. Two tents were constructed from sails and spars for the party on the beach. The _Arato_ sailed southward after changing its course from Callao, with Cardatas as the first mate.

Edna has been living quietly and cheerfully during her residence in San Francisco. She has engaged in various activities such as reading, visiting theatres and concerts, and shopping. Edna has refrained from making plans and has put her past life behind her. She believes that her marriage is just the beginning of a new existence. Edna is confident that Captain Horn will return and inform her of his success or failure. Ralph inquires about a letter from Captain Horn that Edna received. Ralph expresses concern about the time since he last heard from Captain Horn.

Ralph expressed a desire to take action if Edna's previous marriage was denied. Edna indicated she did not intend to take any immediate action regarding her marital status. Ralph acknowledged the previous marriage as a solemn engagement, regardless of its legal status. Edna's mother-in-law, Mrs. Cliff, ceased her opposition to Edna's decision. Mrs. Cliff suggested that Edna should prepare for questions about her marital status from friends. Edna mentioned her past connections and prosperity, indicating she had friends in Paris.

The doctor was initially hesitant to respond to a message regarding Miss Panney. The boy delivered a message stating that Miss Panney was unwell and needed the doctor immediately. Mrs. Tolbridge expressed concern about the doctor's well-being and questioned the urgency of the situation with Miss Panney. The doctor acknowledged that Miss Panney often called him for false alarms but felt it was better to check on her during the day. Mrs. Tolbridge insisted that the doctor should not go to see Miss Panney and offered to go herself. Mrs. Tolbridge planned to take a cart to visit Miss Panney and stated she would inform the doctor if it was serious. The doctor had been working extensively and was advised by Mrs. Tolbridge to rest instead of making the trip.

Junius and Croft walk to an arbor by the garden to discuss private matters. Junius lived with his aunt after his parents died when he was young. Croft intends to propose marriage to Miss March. Mr. Brandon, the guardian of Miss March, requested Croft to cease his visits. Mr. Brandon expressed a desire for Miss March to marry Junius. Croft plans to propose to Miss March regardless of family arrangements. Croft seeks Junius's assistance in obtaining an interview with Miss March.

Miriam was past her bedtime and had not yet been awakened by Dora. Dora was content with the current circumstances and did not want to change them. Dora suggested walking down to the road to wait for the doctor. Upon returning to the porch, Ralph and Dora found that Miriam was not there. Dora deduced that Miriam had gone to bed without realizing she was not alone. Ralph felt mortified about the situation regarding Miss Bannister. Dora expressed her enjoyment of Miriam's unconventional behavior and planned to sleep in her room.

The narrator saw Miss Drane in the street while arriving in town yesterday. Miss Drane is described as pretty and well-dressed. Mrs. Tolbridge stated that Miss Drane's handwriting is more important than her appearance. The Dranes left Mrs. Brinkly's residence yesterday afternoon. The Dranes have moved to Cobhurst to board during the hot weather. La Fleur, the cook, was instrumental in the decision for the Dranes to leave Mrs. Brinkly's. The doctor supported the move to Cobhurst by speaking to the Haverleys about it.

Mrs. Keswick believes her son Junius has a scheme regarding Mr. Brandon's niece. Mrs. Keswick received a letter from Junius indicating his intention to visit. Mrs. Keswick suspected a plot involving Roberta March upon her arrival. An old negro woman identified Roberta March as the daughter of Mrs. Keswick's younger sister. Mrs. Keswick has not seen Roberta since she was eight years old. Mrs. Keswick intended to raise Roberta as her own child and name her Keswick. Roberta is currently married, which complicates Mrs. Keswick's plans for her and Junius.

Roberta March is in a strange humor and appears to wish to punish her lover. Lawrence is concerned about a man who has called upon him in an unusual location. Lawrence has a portion of his funds invested in a business concern. A man sitting on the porch identifies himself as an anti-detective. The anti-detective organization aims to protect individuals from being pursued by detectives. The organization informs clients about impending actions against them and offers strategies for evasion. The anti-detective services include mailing letters from different locations to mislead detectives.

Professor Barré was accused by Banker of being a leader of a band of robbers. The magistrate reacted with anger to Banker's accusations against Professor Barré. Captain Horn suggested that the matter regarding Banker's accusations was settled. Banker threatened Professor Barré while being removed from the room by policemen. Captain Horn expressed gratitude to Professor Barré for his influence with the magistrate. Captain Horn married Edna at the legation shortly after leaving the police station. The bridal party planned to return to the Hotel Grenade before departing for Calais.

Miss Panney was washing the breakfast dishes. Dora and Miriam were picking berries in the garden. Ralph Haverley arrived at the back door driving a brown horse and a loose-jointed wagon. Dora welcomed Ralph with a smile when he arrived. Ralph mentioned he was concerned about the new cook leaving before he returned. Miriam instructed Ralph to bring a bag of flour into the pantry. Miss Panney observed the interactions between the characters with a smile.

The captain stated that Maka could inform a prisoner that they forgave him. The prisoner identified himself as Anton Garta and was examined about the schooner _Arato_. Garta had been part of the crew of the _Arato_ and was previously unemployed. The crew believed they were going to Callao for a cargo and were unaware of the guns on board until at sea. Señor Nunez and the captain informed the crew they were pursuing a treasure ship commanded by a Yankee captain. The crew agreed to work for ten more days after being promised rewards by Señor Nunez. Garta expressed that he would not have joined the _Arato_ if he had known its true purpose.

Phoebe is Mike's wife and is currently at the house to prepare a meal. The dining-room has a large table arranged for eight people. Ralph and Miriam are the only two adults present at the table. The supper includes beefsteak, an omelet, hot rolls, fried potatoes, coffee, tea, and preserved fruit. Dr. Tolbridge visits Ralph and Miriam shortly after they begin their meal. Dr. Tolbridge introduces himself and expresses a desire to join Ralph and Miriam for supper. Phoebe initially prepared the meal based on her assumptions about the size of Ralph and Miriam's family.

Matthias built a house and a barn on the farm over the course of five years. Matthias lived with his Aunt Pacewalk while constructing the estate. Matthias named the finished estate Cobhurst and planned to live there in the fall. Judith expressed a desire to dress better for her potential role at Cobhurst. Judith and a friend, Dorcas Stone, gathered teaberries to fund the material for a new gown. Judith and another friend made the gown themselves after gathering enough teaberries. Judith decided not to wear the gown until she went to Cobhurst.

The Californian government offered a reward to a group of sailors. Captain Horn refused to negotiate with the group, asserting that the Californian government had no claim on him. Captain Horn's vessel was wrecked, but he claimed that he and his crew could take care of themselves. Cardatas attempted to shoot Captain Horn but was shot by Shirley before he could do so. The attacking party retreated after losing their leader, Cardatas. The crew of the _Miranda_ was well-armed and entrenched, surprising the men from the _Arato_. Nunez recognized the seriousness of the situation after the initial attack failed.

Keswick visited Lawrence to inquire about his ankle and general comfort. Lawrence did not correct Keswick's incorrect statement about Miss March. Lawrence believed that informing Keswick about Miss March accepting him could be dangerous. Lawrence spent the evening writing a letter, which he ultimately tore up and burned. The next day was bright and clear, with a temperature of seventy degrees by ten o'clock. Lawrence moved his chair and table to the open doorway to enjoy the view. Miss Annie visited Lawrence to bring him a book she had finished reading.

Mrs. Keswick's breakfast hour is variable. Breakfast may be delayed due to Mrs. Keswick's irregular habits or because the bread has not risen. Lawrence Croft arrived at the Keswick house and found it deserted at around eight o'clock. Croft stepped into a small flower garden and walked along a board walk. Croft intended to get an interview with Miss March and planned to inform his rival about the outcome. Mrs. Keswick's niece was cutting geraniums and chrysanthemums in the garden. The niece expressed disinterest in Croft's presence and refused to share her maiden name.

Mrs. Drane and her daughter are residents of Thorbury. Mrs. Drane's daughter is assisting Dr. Tolbridge with literary work. Ralph offered to show Mrs. Drane and her daughter the barn. Miriam agreed to assist Ralph in escorting Mrs. Drane and her daughter. Cicely expressed her lack of knowledge about barns and country life. Miriam noted that hens do not always lay their eggs in the henhouse. Miriam reflected on her brother's gentlemanly demeanor after the visit.

The work of removing gold from the hold began immediately. The captain decided to land the treasure as quickly as possible to avoid losing it to the sea. The captain and the men carried the bags high up on the beach to protect them from tide or surf. The bags were arranged in a line along the sand for easier handling later. The crew worked continuously until dark, only stopping for necessary eating and drinking. By the third day, every bag had been taken out of the hold and counted by the captain. Attempts to pump out water from the hold were largely ineffective due to the brig's position.

Miss Panney believes it is the duty of every young woman to get married. Miss Panney encourages Dora to marry Ralph Haverley. Dora expresses her reluctance to pursue Ralph Haverley. Miss Panney suggests that Ralph Haverley may have intended to visit Barport. Dora reflects on her feelings about Ralph Haverley and the possibility of other men. Dora receives a note from Miriam Haverley. Dora offers Miss Panney a ride to Cobhurst.

Ralph called out for his sister, Miriam, while in the barn. Dora suggested they go to the upper floor of the barn to find Miriam. The upper floor of the barn contained haymows and had an open door leading to a landscape. Dora expressed that it would be nice for Miriam to sit and enjoy the view from the barn. Ralph doubted that Miriam would be content to sit still and watch. Dora felt a sense of ease standing with Ralph, despite their recent acquaintance. Miss Bannister expressed a desire for Miriam to visit her in Thorbury.

The man found on the Peruvian coast was lying on his back with a bundle that was very heavy. The bundle contained about a peck of little hunks of gold. The body was identified as that of an English sailor, but there were no clear identifying features. The only items found on the body were an old knife and a dozen matches wrapped in an envelope addressed to A. McLeish, Callao, Peru. Burke wanted to search for more gold, but Shirley disagreed due to the dangerous conditions. They decided to return to the mountains with the gold and provisions, leaving their guns behind. After three days of travel, they reached a village where they found few people due to fear among the locals.

A lady wished to see Croft and was disappointed not to see him the previous day. Keswick informed Croft about the lady's wishes but did not know her reasons for wanting to meet. Lawrence received a letter from Mr Candy's cashier, stating that she would provide information about Keswick. Lawrence was pleased to receive the letter and planned to inform his agent that her services were no longer needed. Keswick confirmed to Lawrence that he was once engaged to Miss March and hoped to renew the engagement. Lawrence realized that Miss March was free and decided to visit her that morning. Croft noted the change in Lawrence's demeanor after discussing Miss March.

Aunt Patsy was buried the day after her death. Mrs. Keswick and Annie attended the ceremonies in the cabin but did not go to the burial. Two old women from the congregation finished Aunt Patsy's crazy quilt before her burial. Aunt Patsy's body was kept above ground longer than usual due to her age and the number of people who wanted to pay their respects. Mrs. Keswick resumed her usual manner of speaking after returning from Aunt Patsy's cabin. Mrs. Keswick did not express any contrition for her previous behavior towards Annie and Lawrence. Mrs. Keswick referred to Annie as 'the late Mrs. Null' as a form of sarcasm.

The captain expressed concern about the safety of Rynders and his men. Miss Markham conveyed the captain's intentions to Mrs. Cliff, who expressed faith in his abilities. Three wild beasts approached the beach, armed with guns and knives. The wild beasts discovered tracks of two men, which made them cautious. Maka, an African, fell asleep on the rocky ground after being awake for over twenty hours. Mok, another African, remained alert and fearful of the Rackbirds while crouched by the lake. Captain Horn was asleep with his guns beside him, while Ralph took his turn on watch.

Miss Panney was preparing for a drive and call. Miss Panney intended to go to Cobhurst but was concerned about what to say to Ralph regarding a telegram. Miss Panney felt it was important not to provoke Ralph into opposition. Dora informed Miss Panney that Ralph is engaged to Miss Drane. Miss Panney reacted strongly to the news of Ralph's engagement. Miss Panney abruptly left the carriage to return to the Witton house.

Ralph and Miriam are traveling to a new home. The road to their destination is rough and has been affected by heavy rains. Miriam expresses relief that their new home is not a cottage. Upon arrival, they are greeted by a colored woman holding a lamp. The woman offers them a choice of rooms and informs them that supper will be ready. Ralph and Miriam find the interior of the house to be spacious and unfamiliar. They decide to prioritize having supper before exploring their new home further.

Miss Panney suggests that the doctor should consider supporting a girl and her mother for a short period. The doctor expresses concern about the financial implications of Miss Panney's suggestion. Miriam and her brother Ralph discuss the work they have been doing while Dora Bannister was present. Miriam feels that her work has not been straightforward due to Dora's presence. Miriam has raspberries that she is unsure how to use. Miriam tries on Judith Pacewalk's teaberry gown for the first time. The teaberry gown is too large and long for Miriam.

Miss Panney expressed concern about La Fleur potentially leaving Dr. Tolbridge. Dr. Tolbridge stated that La Fleur has not asked for higher wages. La Fleur previously worked for the Dranes, who can no longer afford to employ her. La Fleur is in a doleful mood after hearing about the Dranes' financial difficulties. La Fleur intends to leave Dr. Tolbridge to serve the Dranes without asking for wages. Miss Panney plans to visit Dr. Tolbridge's house the following afternoon to discuss the situation. Dr. Tolbridge believes there is nothing that can be done to improve the Dranes' circumstances.

Miriam is looking for a first-class colored cook. Mike suggests his sister, Seraphina Paddock, as a suitable cook. Seraphina is currently keeping house and taking in washing in Bridgeport. Miriam expresses interest in having Seraphina come to work for her. Mike warns that Seraphina is particular about moving and settling in new places. Miriam reassures Mike that everything is fixed and settled at her location. Mike speculates about potential changes in the household that could affect Seraphina's decision.

The captain wanted to have a companion who was not given to suspicions and resentments. The captain believed he might find the mound empty and wished for support in that case. Shirley had not seen the great stone face before and was interested in examining it. The captain and Shirley entered the great cave of the lake after lighting a lantern. The captain found the lid of the mound as he had left it and began to open it. Shirley became pale and began to swear after looking into the mound. The captain helped Shirley to the ground and offered him a drink from a whiskey flask.

Keswick did not want to be at the house while Roberta was with Mr. Croft and chose to walk in the woods instead. Lawrence felt it was unfair to leave Keswick at the gate while he went to the house alone. Keswick objected to seeing Roberta and Croft together and wanted to avoid the appearance of bringing Croft to the house. Peggy informed Keswick that Roberta was ill and that Robert had gone to see old Miss Keswick. Keswick expressed concern that something strange must have happened since Roberta was ill and Robert had left. Mr. Croft decided it would be improper to go to the house after hearing about Roberta's condition and chose to return to the Springs. Peggy rushed ahead to the house, excitedly announcing that Junius was coming alone and that she had sent the other man away.

Lawrence visited Mrs Keswick's house in mid-December. Mrs Keswick was in good humor after posting a letter to Mr Brandon. Lawrence and Mrs Keswick were warmly greeted when they met. Annie expressed curiosity about her future living situation with Lawrence. Lawrence proposed a plan to wander the world for a year or two before settling down. Annie's response to Lawrence's proposal was quick and affirmative. The marriage of Junius Keswick and Roberta March was scheduled for January 15.

Maka was troubled by the scarcity of water and could not sleep. Maka believed there might be a stream on the other side of a ridge to the south. Maka left the camp early to search for water along the beach. Maka encountered another African man who he recognized as a fellow slave. The other man informed Maka that there was a stream a mile farther up the bay. The stream was located near a spot with five or six huts inhabited by dangerous men. Maka reported the information he learned from the other man to the captain.

Lawrence Croft was confined in a building in Mrs. Keswick's yard. The weather during Lawrence's confinement was cloudy and rainy. Mrs. Keswick briefly visited Lawrence before leaving in a covered spring wagon. Mrs. Null sent a bundle of old novels to Lawrence, which he found uninteresting. A hired barouche arrived at the yard, driven by a colored man. Junius Keswick arrived at the building with a valise and a key. Junius expressed concern for Lawrence's injury and discussed the situation regarding their stay.

La Fleur expressed satisfaction with her current living situation, despite it being different from her past experiences. La Fleur is considering leaving her current position to assist the Drane family, whom she is attached to. Miss Panney advised La Fleur against leaving Dr. Tolbridge, suggesting it would be a mistake. La Fleur stated that no one else would help the Drane family for free, which is her intention. Miss Panney suggested that it might be better for the Drane family to be helped in a way that allows them to support themselves. Miss Cicely Drane is attempting to find a teaching position to support herself and her mother. Miss Panney plans to help Miss Drane find a teaching position.

Edna mentioned a mound covered by a lake that may relate to ancient Peruvian history. The Spaniards, led by Pizarro, sought the treasures of the Incas during their conquest of Peru. The Incas attempted to hide their treasures from the Spaniards by creating a mound at the bottom of a drained lake near Cuzco. Miss Markham stated that the mound they discovered is not the same as the one mentioned in the tradition but could still contain hidden treasures. The captain expressed excitement about the possibility of treasure being hidden in the mound covered by water. Edna claimed to have seen gold when looking into the hole of the mound. The group decided to examine the mound the following day and agreed to calm their minds before doing so.

The captain discovered a stone mound that he believes is the tomb of an ancient South American king. Ralph called out to the captain while he was in the cave. The captain extinguished his lantern before meeting Ralph at the lake. Mrs. Cliff expressed a desire to sleep outside instead of returning to the caves. The captain intends to return to the caves despite Mrs. Cliff's fears. Miss Markham, who has studied South American history, doubts that ancient inhabitants buried their kings in stone tombs. Ralph is eager to explore the stone mound and open it.

Miriam attempted to make tarts for Ralph but was dissatisfied with the results. Miriam used self-raising flour in her tart recipe, which did not yield the desired outcome. Ralph encouraged Miriam to try the tarts despite her negative opinion about them. Ralph provided instructions on how to eat the tarts, which he found delicious. Miriam acknowledged that the tarts were not traditional tarts and would have been better if made by Dora Bannister. Cicely Drane was employed as Dr. Tolbridge's secretary and was working on a manuscript. Cicely focused on her task despite the presence of flowers in the garden outside.

The _Miranda_ made progress and sighted land less than two days after changing course. Captain Horn hoped to double a headland a couple of miles away and beach the vessel. The crew, including Captain Horn, Burke, Shirley, and three negroes, desired to keep the vessel afloat until reaching land. The _Miranda_ passed the southern point of the headland and sailed into a little bay. The crew headed toward a beach with every sail set and the vessel on a flood-tide. The _Miranda_ grounded on the shore of a desolate Patagonian island. Burke questioned the captain about the next steps after reaching the shore.

Mrs. Null is responsible for managing the farm while her mistress is away. Uncle Isham indicates that the land should be ploughed for wheat. Mrs. Null expresses concern about planting wheat due to competition from Western farms. Mrs. Null suggests that the field could be better used for pickles instead of wheat. Uncle Isham lives alone in a small tenement near the barn and chicken house. Letty and her son, Plez, occupy a cabin not far from the house. Uncle Isham visits Letty in the evening with a log of hickory wood.

Ralph came up from the cornfield by the woods toward the barn and pasture fields. Ralph met Mrs. Drane and La Fleur, who had just come downstairs. La Fleur used to be the cook for Mrs. Drane's household. Mrs. Drane informed Ralph that La Fleur wanted to call on his cook, Molly Tooney. Molly Tooney was in the kitchen paring potatoes when La Fleur entered. La Fleur introduced herself and expressed interest in the cooking of the current household. La Fleur offered to teach Molly Tooney how to make coffee properly.

Mrs Null enjoys the view from a hill named after pines. Mrs Null expresses a desire to talk with Freddy about their wedding tour. Mrs Null and Freddy have not communicated during their three nights and two days of travel. Mrs Null is waiting for a mistress to return and is aware that others find it peculiar. Mrs Null and Freddy are traveling without informing Mr Croft of their whereabouts. Mrs Null hopes to find Junius Keswick before Mr Croft does. Uncle Isham informs Mrs Null that the farm is not being prepared for wheat due to the absence of the mistress.

Inkspot was unable to communicate the name of the vessel on which the bags had been loaded. The sailors mentioned the name _Miranda_, which is a brig that operates on the coast. Inkspot reacted excitedly upon hearing the name _Miranda_ and referred to Captain Horn. Cardatas identified that Inkspot was trying to say Cap'n Horn of the brig _Miranda_. A sailor noted that Cap'n Horn is a Yankee skipper from California who had sailed from the port. Nunez searched a Mexican newspaper for information about the _Miranda_ and found that it had cleared from Acapulco on September 16. Cardatas learned that the _Miranda_ had anchored in the harbor three days prior and had left shortly after.

Edna received a letter from Captain Horn, dated at Marseilles. The letter was delivered to Edna by a messenger from Wraxton, Fuguet & Co. The letter was addressed to 'Mrs. Philip Horn'. Captain Horn's letter contained a long account of events after he left Valparaiso. Edna found the content of the letter uninteresting and insufficient for her emotional needs. Captain Horn did not address Edna as 'My dear Wife' in the letter. Captain Horn mentioned difficulties regarding his vessel, the _Arato_, and its cargo.

The protagonist decides to admit defeat and retreat from his previous positions. He plans to confess his feelings to Roberta and explain his actions. Peggy observes the protagonist's return with surprise and disgust. Peggy dislikes Mr. Croft, viewing him as an interloper in a potential marriage. Lawrence ties his horse and enters the house after returning. He mistakenly addresses Mrs. Keswick's niece as Miss Annie. Mrs. Keswick's niece requests to be called Mrs. Null and expresses her desire to remain in the house.

The Peruvian government and the natives are not expected to cause any trouble regarding the treasure. The treasure's existence and rights to it are unknown to the natives until informed. An agent will be sent to Peru to handle the matter. The captain has claimed twenty percent of the treasure for himself and others involved. The twenty percent will be divided among all individuals associated with the _Castor_ wreck. Mrs. Cliff expresses disappointment over the small percentage she may receive. The captain states he will divide the retained sum fairly and is open to appeals from those dissatisfied.

Lawrence followed the old lady's suggestion to take a path through the flower-garden and over the fields into the woods. He discarded his cigar and hurried through the house and flower-garden to reach a pasture-field. The pasture-field sloped down to a stream and then ascended to the edge of the woods. Lawrence saw Roberta in a light-colored dress with a red scarf inside the edge of the woods. He intended to confess everything to Roberta and hoped to win her over. Lawrence fell into the stream after stepping on a plank that turned beneath him, resulting in a painful ankle injury. He called for Uncle Isham to help him after realizing he could not walk to the woods due to his injury.

Lawrence decided to write a letter to Miss March after receiving a message from her. He felt it was necessary to communicate with her without delay. Lawrence was uncertain about the tone of his letter due to the circumstances of his acceptance. He was concerned that expressing caution in his letter could provoke Roberta March's resentment. Miss Annie arrived with Mrs. Keswick and informed Lawrence that Roberta had agreed to let him stay as a boarder. Lawrence expressed gratitude to Miss Annie for her assistance in managing the situation. Miss Annie mentioned that Lawrence would have company from Uncle Isham, Aunt Keswick, and occasionally her.

Mr Brandon plans to visit a clergyman and friends at his house. Mr Brandon expresses a desire to start immediately for New York with the old woman. Colonel Macon suggests that a letter would frighten the old woman and prompt her to leave her house. Mr Brandon decides to write a carefully constructed letter to Mrs Keswick proposing an immediate wedding. Mr Brandon proposes that the marriage ceremony take place in Richmond in a week. Colonel Macon approves of the letter written by Mr Brandon. Mr Brandon and Colonel Macon travel to Richmond two days after sending the letter.

Miriam expressed that it would be nice to get a new man to help them. The doctor was surprised by Miriam's request regarding Mike, the current man-of-all-work. Mike has been in charge since Mr. Butterwood began traveling for his rheumatism. The doctor advised Miriam and Ralph to keep Mike as he is considered trustworthy and useful. Miriam mentioned that she did not connect their home with a shabby person like Mike. Ralph expressed satisfaction with the doctor as a neighbor. Phoebe informed them that she had made a fire in the parlor.

The captain wrote that he might need to go to Berlin and could not say if he would travel to London. Mrs. Cliff waited for Edna to call her and eventually rushed into the salon where Edna was alone. Edna confirmed to Mrs. Cliff that the captain was well and in Marseilles. Edna read the captain's letter aloud to Mrs. Cliff, omitting certain passages. Mrs. Cliff expressed excitement about the captain having the gold before fainting. After recovering, Mrs. Cliff suggested they could speak openly about the situation. Edna insisted they could not speak about the captain's affairs until he arrived.

Five black men lived in a cave on a rock that could only be reached by a ladder. The men were originally from Guiana and had been brought to the isthmus about a year prior by two men who promised them work. The men were made actual slaves and worked for their captors in harsh conditions. Eight men had come down from the isthmus, but three had been killed at various times. The men were employed in cooking and carrying goods, and they were kept in the cave except when called for work. One man escaped from captivity, fearing for his life due to a threat from a member of the captors. The captors were referred to as the Rackbirds by the escaped man.

Mahs' Robert is set to marry, and a character expresses indifference about it. The Widow Keswick is content while driving home, reflecting on her situation. Peggy cannot live with Mahs' Junius and Miss Rob in New York due to their plans and her unsuitability as a maid. Peggy has a belief in her ability to influence others' lives through her thoughts and desires. Junius Keswick prefers farming over practicing law, which he only does out of obligation. Junius and Roberta plan to live at Midbranch and spend winters in New York. Mr. Brandon agrees to attend the wedding and considers spending several months in New York.

Mrs. Cliff subscribed one dollar to a cause, which was the maximum amount she felt comfortable giving. Mrs. Cliff expressed a desire for fresh cream and butter from her own cow after seeing the empty cow-stable. Mrs. Cliff retained her phaeton and considered repurchasing her horse. Mrs. Cliff occasionally made expenditures that surprised Willy Croup, as Betty had returned home. Mrs. Cliff received a letter from Edna about the captain's safe arrival in Acapulco with guano and gold. The letter included a draft that caused Mrs. Cliff to feel overwhelmed and emotional. Mrs. Cliff was advised to open a bank account in Boston but feared it would become known in Plainton.

The captain considered how to leave the caves without indicating they had been inhabited. He decided against removing all evidence of habitation from the caves. The captain gathered old rope from a vessel belonging to the Rackbirds to make oakum. He packed the crevices around the lid of the cave with oakum to prevent water from entering. The captain found the lever that controlled the outlet of water from the cave. He attempted to raise the lever to stop the water from flowing outside, but found it difficult to move.

The captain attempted to move bags in the darkness but found it futile. He had a lantern but believed it would be of little service. Upon reaching the old bed of the lake, he found it completely dry. The captain expressed joy at the discovery and reflected on his previous concerns. He decided to improve the pier built for guano landing and worked on it thoroughly. After completing work on the pier, he bailed out and repaired a leaky lighter. The _Finland_ arrived the next morning, and the guano was transferred to the ship.

Miriam plans to finish her education at home with Ralph as her teacher. Ralph Haverley is a young man under thirty with brown hair and bright eyes. Ralph had to work to support himself and his sister after the death of their parents. Ralph struggled for eight years in various occupations before securing a well-paid position in a mercantile house. Ralph dreams of a home for himself and Miriam, ideally in the suburbs, but considers city living for safety. Ralph learns late that he has inherited the estate of Cobhurst from his mother's uncle. The inheritance was based on the belief that Ralph was the only blood relation making progress in life.

Mister Michaels is at de Springs with his mud-colored horse. Mahs' Junius and Mister Crof' are in the buggy. Miss Roberta instructs Peggy to tell Mister Crof' that she is not well and cannot see him. Peggy observes that only Mister Crof' is in the buggy now. Peggy speculates that Mahs' Junius may have taken a shortcut and could arrive first. Mister Crof' is waiting at the road gate for someone to open it. Keswick has alighted to walk while Lawrence waits for him.

Mike informed that the boss is in the big meadow helping with hay. Mike mentioned that they could not find extra help due to the busy season. Dora decided to wait for Herbert instead of accompanying him to see Mr. Haverley. Dora planned to ask Phoebe about the young lady's whereabouts. Dora observed various items in the hall, including a straw hat and gloves. Dora noted the presence of a powder-horn, shot-flask, and a fowling-piece. Dora considered it manly for a young man to work in the hay-field if necessary.

Andy considers himself a good judge of scenery and knows the easiest roads for his horse. The ladies are enjoying a summer afternoon while traveling leisurely. Andy provides information about the inhabitants of the dwellings they pass. Miss Panney is an old lady living at the Witton place, known for her extensive knowledge of people. Andy recounts an experience with Miss Panney regarding his sick horse. Miss Panney offered to let Andy use her horse when she saw him with his sick horse. Cicely mentions that Miss Panney was the first to visit Mrs. Brinkly about rooms for them.

Captain Horn brought eight canvas bags of gold from the caves each day and buried them in the sand under his tent. After a month without seeing a sail, Captain Horn became increasingly cautious and monitored the ocean while walking the beach. Captain Horn expressed concerns about the possibility of never being rescued and the potential for starvation. He had previously informed Edna in a letter that she should not expect to hear from him for a long time. The Chilian schooner arrived ten days overdue, with only the captain and his mate on board. Captain Horn was pleased to see Maka, who expressed concern about his eating habits. Captain Horn was angry to learn that the Chilian captain had not brought a full cargo of bags of guano due to delays.

Mrs. Drane is engaged in sewing. The doctor has a kind feeling for Mrs. Drane and is focused on his own household. Mrs. Tolbridge believes inviting guests would require giving up having friends for the summer. The doctor suggests the Haverley family could take in Mrs. Drane for the summer. Mrs. Tolbridge expresses concern about the Haverley daughter being unable to commute daily for work. The doctor proposes that the work could be done at the Haverleys' house instead of his office. Mrs. Tolbridge thinks the Haverleys may not favor the idea of taking in Mrs. Drane.

Captain Horn presents a marriage proposal to Edna Markham as a business arrangement. The marriage is intended to secure a fortune for Edna and others in case of Captain Horn's non-return. Edna expresses concern about the possibility of Captain Horn returning safely. Captain Horn insists that the marriage plan is based solely on the assumption of his non-return. Edna refuses to disregard the possibility of Captain Horn's return. Edna ultimately agrees to the marriage proposal on a business basis. The agreement is made to secure a claim to treasure found in a cave.

Miss Annie is concerned about events occurring while Junius is away in Washington. Miss Roberta retired early to her room after a long drive. Annie visited Roberta's room to share a secret about her marital status. Annie revealed that she is not Mrs. Null and that Mr. Null is a fictional character. Annie married Freddy Null in New York for protection but found it necessary to maintain the pretense. Annie expressed concern that her aunt wants to force her into a marriage with Junius. Annie feels she cannot stay in the house if her aunt attempts to arrange a marriage with Junius.

Mrs. Tolbridge did not order coffee for the luncheon because she does not take it in the middle of the day. The luncheon was prepared by Mrs. Tolbridge's new cook, Jane La Fleur, not Kipper. Jane La Fleur is the widow of two chefs and has experience in Italian and French cooking. Mrs. Tolbridge engaged Jane La Fleur after receiving a satisfactory letter from a family she worked for in Pennsylvania. Jane La Fleur prefers to be addressed by her last name or as 'madam' by the family and servants. Jane La Fleur stated that she would be content with the salary Mrs. Tolbridge paid her last cook. Jane La Fleur expressed a preference not to work for tradesmen.

Captain Horn cut pieces of cloth more than a foot square. He prepared five bundles of gold bars weighing twelve or fifteen pounds each. Captain Horn packed the gold bundles into bags of guano that he had bought in bulk. He believed that the additional weight of the gold would not be noticed by stevedores. The task of packing the gold was unpleasant due to the strong ammoniacal odor of the guano. Captain Horn made six bundles of gold on a later trip to the caves. He aimed to finish his task before the schooner returned in about a month.

Cicely was frightened and could not sleep after receiving news that affected her deeply. Ralph Haverley returned from a moonlight walk feeling happy and planned to take action the next day. Ralph received a letter from Miriam that detailed a drowning accident and mentioned Mrs. Bannister's reaction. Mrs. Bannister declared she could not go into the ocean again after the incident and decided to return home. Ralph searched for Cicely after reading the letter but found her absent from breakfast. La Fleur, the cook, asked Ralph to deliver a message to Cicely regarding gathering lettuce and parsley. Ralph found Cicely in the garden and informed her that Miriam and others were coming home that day.

Patsy died believing Lawrence was a bone-dust peddler. Annie expressed relief that they helped Patsy die happy. Lawrence stated he would take the place of Mr. Null but would not have his attributes. Annie credited Freddy Null for the opportunities she had. Lawrence and Annie planned to inform Aunt Keswick about their engagement and the truth about Mr. Null. Aunt Keswick believed Lawrence was in love with Miss March. Lawrence resolved to ensure nothing would interfere with his love for Annie.

The principal subject of conversation is the speaker's situation regarding marriage. The speaker's aunt has selected a person for her to marry. Freddy Null provides protection to the speaker from her aunt's matrimonial schemes. The speaker believes it is important for her aunt to think she is married. The speaker previously held the position of cashier in the Information Shop but gave it up. The speaker has no plans to return to New York at this time. The speaker feels that staying with her aunt is beneficial as long as she has Freddy Null's protection.

The narrator refrains from reporting an incident involving Inkspot, a fellow-African. The _Arato_ sailed up the South Atlantic, navigating skillfully through various weather conditions. The schooner sometimes encountered large merchant-steamers traveling between Europe and South America. Shirley questions Captain Horn about the morality of taking gold on board the vessel. Captain Horn believes the gold originally belonged to the Incas of Peru and was hidden to protect it from the Spaniards. Horn states that informing the government about the gold would result in it going to the descendants of the original owners. Captain Horn intends to have the ownership of the gold decided by fair and competent authorities.

Annie considered the altered state of affairs and saw both advantages and disappointments. Lawrence Croft was considered a good match for Annie based on her inquiries about Roberta March. Mr. Brandon declared that Junius would be master of the large estate at Midbranch if he married Roberta. Annie experienced a mix of emotions regarding Mr. Brandon's success and her own failure. Lawrence announced that his ankle was well enough for him to go to New York for his affairs. Mrs. Keswick planned to start for Midbranch early the next morning and mentioned the possibility of staying overnight. Junius had developed a dislike for Mr. Croft, which complicated the relationship between him, Lawrence, and Annie.

Ralph Haverley decided to abandon mercantile life to manage a farm. Ralph aimed to conclude his business affairs by the beginning of April. Miriam Haverley had vague and chaotic anticipations about Cobhurst. Ralph and Miriam arrived at the station in Thorbury in the afternoon. Mike, the man in charge of Cobhurst, greeted Ralph and Miriam at the station. Ralph and Miriam arranged for their luggage to be transported to Cobhurst the next day. Miriam expressed a desire to hire a new person to manage Cobhurst.

Edna and Mrs. Cliff agree to stay while the captain takes Ralph to see something. Mrs. Cliff expresses concern about being left alone as the sun sets. The captain decides that everyone should go together to see the site. The group encounters difficulty climbing over a wall and navigating the lake basin. They reach a stone mound in a cave, which Ralph compares to a new hemisphere. The captain and Ralph discover a square slab on top of the mound that appears to be movable. The captain identifies a resin-like substance around the edges of the slab, indicating it can be lifted.

Mr Croft rode up to meet Mr Brandon at the point where the roads met. Mr Brandon inquired about his niece, Miss March, and confirmed she was in good health. Mr Brandon suggested they dismount and rest on a log by the roadside. Lawrence confirmed that his visit to Mr Brandon's house was intended for Miss March and involved matrimonial overtures. Mr Brandon informed Lawrence that Miss March and Mr Junius Keswick's engagement was only conditionally broken off. Mr Brandon stated that the opposition to the union of Miss March and Mr Keswick was about to be removed. Lawrence expressed that the matter should be left to Miss March to decide.

Inkspot had prior experience with whiskey before working for the Rackbirds. Mr. Burke went ashore, likely in search of whiskey, and returned without anyone knowing his whereabouts. Inkspot planned to go ashore the next night to hunt for whiskey but the _Miranda_ did not remain in the cove. The _Miranda_ later anchored in the harbor of Valparaiso, prompting Inkspot to attempt to go ashore for whiskey. Inkspot swam to a deserted pier in Valparaiso and then entered the town. Inkspot found a shop that sold whiskey and consumed multiple glasses before running out of money. Inkspot was considered the most intelligent negro among the captain's crew, with some knowledge of English and Spanish.

Ralph went to the woodhouse to gather wood for the cook. Dora observed Ralph returning with an arm-load of small sticks. Ralph expressed doubt about the new cook's ability to perform hard work. Miriam indicated that they would need to see what the new cook could do. Ralph's sister informed him that the new cook is accustomed to eating with the family. Ralph opposed the idea of the cook eating at their table. Miriam argued that the cook is respectable and should not be treated as a common servant.

The book 'The Girl at Cobhurst' was written by Frank R. Stockton and published in 1898. The contents of the book include thirty-nine chapters, each with a distinct title. Dr. Tolbridge is a leading physician in and around Thorbury. Mrs. Tolbridge is younger than Dr. Tolbridge and has a high opinion of him. The Tolbridge family consists of Dr. Tolbridge, Mrs. Tolbridge, and their fourteen-year-old son who is away at school. Miss Panney sends for Dr. Tolbridge through a boy messenger.

Captain Horn attempted to lift a stone slab with a handle but could not initially do so. Ralph held a lantern while looking into the opening created by the lifted slab. Edna climbed the mound and knelt beside Ralph to look into the opening. Mrs. Cliff inquired about what the group was observing. Edna whispered to Mrs. Cliff that she believed they had found gold. Edna fainted after expressing her belief about the gold. Captain Horn decided to cover the opening quickly and urged the group to leave the area.

La Fleur was sitting on a bench under a tree by the mansion of Cobhurst. A boy arrived in a trotting-wagon to deliver a telegram for Mr. Haverley. La Fleur informed the boy that Mr. Haverley was not at home. The boy stated that there was a delivery charge of seventy-five cents for the telegram. La Fleur opened the telegram to read its contents and found it puzzling. The telegram was signed by R. Panney, whom La Fleur suspected to be a tricky old woman. Phoebe arrived at the mansion and expressed her exhaustion from walking a long distance.

Invitations to the wedding ceremony were sent to the old friends of the Widow Keswick and Mr Brandon, but no one outside of Richmond was invited. The Widow Keswick wore her best bonnet and a travelling suit for the ceremony. Mr Brandon felt pride and attempted to maintain a strong demeanor despite his circumstances. Mrs Keswick desired a simple wedding without bridesmaids, groomsmen, flowers, or a breakfast. The church was filled with elderly acquaintances of the couple during the wedding. During the marriage service, Mr Brandon's response to the clergyman was weak and despondent, while Mrs Keswick loudly refused to marry him. Mrs Keswick left the church after declaring that their account was balanced and took a streetcar to the train for her home.

The owners of the _Arato_ will be compensated for the use of their schooner. Inkspot experienced vivid dreams while in the Straits. Garta was found drinking liquor in the forecastle. Inkspot had previously disliked Garta due to past mistreatment. Garta threatened Inkspot after discovering he knew about the liquor. Captain Horn was off the convict settlement of Punta Arenas. A search for Garta was ordered by Captain Horn, but he could not be found.

The captain attempted to lift a great lever that had likely been raised by a dozen slaves. It took the captain over an hour to elevate the lever to its upright position. After raising the lever, the captain checked other caves to ensure everything was in order. The captain returned to the lake cave and found it dry with no sound of running water. The captain speculated that an outside reservoir might fill before water entered the cave. The captain felt a sense of fear at the thought of the lake cave filling with water and causing a flood. The captain moved his trunk to a higher ground to protect it from potential flooding.

Three mules and a horse were attached to the fence in front of the post-office. Wesley Green, a negro man, brought the mail from Pocohontas, a railway station twenty miles away, twice a week. The postmistress, Miss Harriet Corvey, sat on the floor of the post-office while a semicircle of men and boys gathered around her. Old Madison Chalkley, the biggest and most venerable citizen, never received letters except for 'The Southern Baptist Recorder' on Saturdays. Colonel Iston, a tall, lean gentleman, had received only one letter in the last fifteen years, which was mistakenly addressed to someone else. Miss Harriet would open the mail in public and call out the names of the recipients, drawing the attention of everyone present. Registered letters created considerable sensation in the post-office, and Miss Harriet would wait for the recipient to arrive and sign for them.

Phoebe was sent by Miss Panney to look after Mike. Miss Panney is currently at the seashore with the Bannisters and Miss Miriam. Phoebe believes Miss Panney is more interested in Mr. Hav'ley and Miss Dora Bannister than in Mike. La Fleur offers Phoebe tea and a meat pie, which pleases Phoebe. Miss Panney wanted Phoebe to observe if Mr. Hav'ley and Miss Drane were falling in love. La Fleur doubts that there is any romantic interest between Mr. Hav'ley and Miss Drane. La Fleur replaces a telegram in its envelope after Phoebe and Mike leave to discuss their affairs.

Miss Panney visited the kitchen to speak with Molly about the social relations between the Haverleys and the Dranes. Molly expressed frustration about La Fleur, the cook, coming to instruct her on cooking for the Dranes. La Fleur arrived at the kitchen to inquire about Mrs. Drane, assuming there was company due to Miss Panney's phaeton outside. Miss Panney and La Fleur discussed La Fleur's continued interest in the Dranes and her dedication to planning meals for them. La Fleur indicated that the Dranes had not mentioned any plans to leave their current location. Miss Panney advised La Fleur to help the Dranes understand the social implications of their living situation. La Fleur believed that the Dranes were well-suited to their current location and saw no reason for them to leave.

The captain intends to charge a price for his services related to the treasure. The captain has already taken some payment and plans to receive more. The captain will divide the treasure among the party according to a fair scale. Mr. Shirley is curious about his share of the cargo and is told he can expect about four bags of anthracite coal. The letter from Captain Horn to Edna is located in a cottage in Sidmouth, Devonshire. The letter was handed to the first mate of a British steamer in Valparaiso for delivery to the post-office. The sailor who was supposed to deliver the letter spent the silver coin intended for postage.

Miss Panney was driven to the Witton house, which was a mile and a half out of the direct road. Miss Panney expressed her support for Ralph, stating he has pluck and is a country man. Ralph indicated he could not afford to farm the place as it ought to be farmed. The doctor expressed concern that Ralph might become a mere farm laborer and jeopardize his sister's education. Miriam asked Ralph specific questions about their new home, including the comfort of his bed and the number of horses. Ralph confirmed they had four horses, which excited Miriam. Miriam later inquired if one of the horses could be ridden by a lady.

The captain expressed uncertainty about the value of a cubic foot of gold. The captain planned to investigate a tomb or storehouse after sending the men to find driftwood. Edna suggested to Mrs. Cliff that they should distract themselves from the captain's investigation. Mrs. Cliff reflected on the Incas and their treasures, questioning the purpose of the caverns. Edna and Mrs. Cliff discussed their feelings about potentially becoming millionaires. Ralph and the captain returned to Edna and Mrs. Cliff after their investigation. The captain reported finding a significant amount of gold in the mound.

Isham tells a story about a cullud angel and a gate that closes after six o'clock. Eliza asks Isham what the cullud angel does after the gate closes. Isham speculates that the debbil comes at night and takes the cullud angel away. Lawrence Croft decides to stay in the neighborhood of Howlett's until he talks with Mrs Null. Lawrence accepts an invitation to spend the night at the Keswick house. Lawrence wakes up early to try to speak with Mrs Null before the family is awake. Mrs Keswick discusses the locust tree by the porch with Lawrence and considers having it cut down.

Miss Cicely Drane is a small person nearing her twenty-second year. She has handsome gray eyes, brown hair, and a pleasing face. An hour had passed since she began writing on a page of the doctor's manuscript. Miss Drane asked Dr. Tolbridge about a part of the manuscript that she found confusing. Dr. Tolbridge admitted he could not decipher his own writing from two years ago. Cicely Drane expressed concern about the slow pace of her work on the manuscript. Dr. Tolbridge mentioned that their cook, La Fleur, had spoken to him about Miss Drane's living conditions.

Burke is expected to arrive before the speaker is ready to sail. The speaker must attend to the shipping of treasure stored in the City of Mexico. The speaker plans to convert the treasure into coin or bonds before departure. Edna has decided to write to Captain Horn and Mrs. Cliff. Edna plans to go to France to meet Captain Horn upon his arrival. Edna and Ralph will start East as soon as Captain Horn sails. Cheditafa and Mok will accompany Edna and Ralph to France.

An eminent cook was preparing a dinner for the Dranes without consulting the mistress or master of the house. Miriam felt saddened by her inability to oppose the cook's decisions regarding the meal. Ralph arrived from Thorbury with a mail-bag containing a letter from Dora. Miriam expressed her desire to visit the sea after reading Dora's letter. The Cobhurst family quickly prepared for Miriam's journey, focusing on her outfit. Miriam decided to write to Miss Pender to arrange her travel to Barport. Miss Pender successfully shipped Miriam to Barport during the vacation period.

Banker believes he was deceived by his former captain, Raminez. Raminez has a distinctive eyebrow shape that Banker associates with his family background. Raminez's family has connections to the Darcias of Granada. Raminez changed his name after moving to America and engaged in discreditable actions. Banker received a visit from Professor Barré, who was accompanied by two guards. During the visit, Professor Barré confronted Banker about a previous charge made against him. Banker expressed a willingness to retract his accusations and requested assistance from Barré.
