Cheditafa recognized Banker immediately after he removed his disguise. Cheditafa experienced intense fear and resignation as he faced Banker. Banker verbally tormented Cheditafa before attempting to stab him. The setting was a rainy and dark evening in a nearly deserted street. Mok was returning from the Black Cat after drinking two glasses of beer. Mok noticed Cheditafa on his knees and Banker preparing to stab him. Mok intervened by seizing Banker's arm to prevent the attack.

Mr Brandon and Colonel Macon were sitting by the fire after dinner, smoking pipes and drinking egg-nogg. A servant brought a note for Mr Brandon from the Widow Keswick. Mr Brandon expressed anger upon reading the address of the note. Colonel Macon encouraged Mr Brandon to read the note aloud. The note suggested a triple wedding involving Mr Brandon and the Widow Keswick. Mr Brandon reacted by crumpling the note and throwing it into the fire. Colonel Macon advised Mr Brandon on how to confront the Widow Keswick.

Mr Keswick went to Washington unexpectedly. Junius informed the family that he would be in Washington by the first of the week. Mr Croft believed there would be a small company present. Roberta asked Mr Croft if he was invited. Mrs Keswick had renewed her invitation to Mr Croft at the Springs. Miss Annie found Mrs Keswick in the garden regarding a bed of turnips. Mrs Keswick expressed reluctance to greet Miss March due to past grievances.

The three-masted schooner _Castor_ was struck by a tornado off the coast of Peru in 1884. The _Castor_ was commanded by Captain Philip Horn, an experienced navigator aged about thirty-five. The vessel was carrying three passengers: Mrs. William Cliff, Miss Edna Markham, and her brother Ralph. The storm left the _Castor_ a wreck, with broken masts and a shattered rudder-post, causing it to take on water. After the storm, the crew and passengers managed to use two boats to evacuate the ship. One boat was found floating and was used to rescue a capsized boat, which was then righted and bailed out. The evacuation included provisions, water, valuables, clothing, and other items.

Mr. Brandon suddenly regained consciousness and stepped back, nearly falling into the fireplace. The Widow Keswick spoke to Mr. Brandon about their past courtship and her feelings for him. Mr. Brandon expressed disbelief at the Widow Keswick's claims about their past relationship. The Widow Keswick insisted that their feelings could transcend time and previous marriages. She recalled specific memories from their youth, including details about their appearances and a white dress she wore. Mr. Brandon showed signs of distress and attempted to leave the conversation. The Widow Keswick presented a breastpin to Mr. Brandon, reminding him of their past and urging him to express his feelings.

Miss Panney calculated the cost of a family lunch for two people, estimating it at two dollars and a half. Miss Panney expressed her views on the construction of meeting-houses by Methodists during the meal. Mrs. Tolbridge stated that she had no involvement in the plans for the new Methodist church. Miss Panney noted that the salad served was worth three dollars. The final course of the luncheon featured a dessert with strawberries and creamy frost. Miss Panney estimated the total cost of the meal to be at least five dollars. Mrs. Tolbridge confirmed that there would be no more food served after the dessert.

Lawrence Croft proposed marriage to Miss March. Mr Brandon requested Lawrence not to visit his house. Lawrence agreed not to visit Midbranch as requested by Mr Brandon. Lawrence felt anger and indignation towards Mr Brandon's request. Lawrence intended to declare his feelings to Miss March despite the request. Mr Brandon had never forbidden anyone to visit Midbranch before. Lawrence preferred to speak to Miss March in person rather than through a letter.

Mrs Keswick does not mention Mr Null and believes he should stay away. Mrs Keswick intends to find out the legal requirements for desertion. Mr Brandon has promised to assist Mrs Keswick with her plans. Mrs Null and Miss March are described as good friends. Mrs Keswick expresses frustration with young women and their behavior. Lawrence is waiting for the weather to clear to speak with Miss March. Lawrence reflects on his unsuccessful love affair with Miss March.

Ralph informed an old lady about Miriam's good fortune and his own situation with Mrs. Drane and her daughter. Miss Panney inquired if Mrs. Drane had left her daughter alone at Cobhurst. Mrs. Drane confirmed that her daughter Cicely was at Cobhurst but was not alone, as La Fleur was with her. Miss Panney observed Ralph and Mrs. Drane before leaving them. Miss Panney expressed frustration with herself and later found humor in the situation. Miss Panney planned to make Ralph visit Barport to influence his fate. Miss Panney took an unusually long time to eat her meal at a confectionery shop.

Philip Horn requests that Mrs. Cliff stay in San Francisco until further arrangements are made. Philip Horn instructs that one fourth of all moneys he sends should be given to Mrs. Cliff. Mrs. Cliff expresses shock at the tone of Philip Horn's letter to Edna. Ralph expresses concern about sailors exploring the lake basin and plans to smash a lantern to deter them. Edna's brother gathers her belongings and instructs her to prepare to leave the caves. Ralph advises Edna to take her time in getting ready to ensure all sailors have left before they do.

Mrs Null stated that her father and Aunt Keswick were on bad terms. Mrs Null's husband did not accompany her on her visit. Aunt Keswick suggested that Mrs Null should marry Junius and take over the farm. Mrs Null mentioned that Mr Null was an obstacle to her marrying Junius. Mr Brandon indicated that Aunt Keswick might want to have Mrs Null's marriage set aside. Mrs Null expressed strong attachment to her husband and denied any differences between them. Mr Brandon advised Mrs Null to keep their conversation confidential from her aunt.

Garta was believed to have slipped into the water and swum for Punta Arenas. Burke suggested that Garta may have been a former resident of Punta Arenas. Captain Horn set the course of the _Arato_ to the northeast and would not stop at Rio Janeiro. Captain Horn planned to sail to France with a cargo of gold. Maka observed Inkspot attempting to force open a locker on the _Arato_ with a hatchet. Inkspot found a nearly empty bottle of liquor in the locker he opened. Inkspot claimed he discovered the locker by smelling the whiskey through the boards.

Miss Panney ordered a phaeton and a roan mare to drive herself to Thorbury. Miss Panney expressed her interest in the young people at Cobhurst. Mrs. Tolbridge mentioned that it is too soon to consider a wife for a young man. Miss Panney advised Mrs. Tolbridge to find a better cook for her husband. Miss Panney suggested that Mrs. Tolbridge should look for a cook in the city. Miss Panney visited the Bannister household after leaving Mrs. Tolbridge. Miss Panney met with Miss Dora Bannister during her visit.

The old man expresses surprise about a visitor. Letty decides to avoid Aunt Patsy's house for a few days. The old man believes Miss Annie is glad to have her husband back. Aunt Patsy reveals that Miss Annie's husband is disliked by an elderly woman. Aunt Patsy plans to warn the elderly woman against harming Miss Annie's husband. Uncle Isham expresses concern about Aunt Patsy's intentions. Uncle Isham recounts a parable about a colored angel at the gates of heaven.

Miss March heard a gentleman shouting and came out of the woods. Lawrence was sitting on the grass with one hand on his ankle. Lawrence warned Miss March about the unsafe plank while she approached. Peggy assured Miss March that the plank was safe after testing it. Lawrence stated that he sprained his ankle while crossing the stream. Miss March offered to help Lawrence, but he declined assistance. Mrs. Keswick prepared to care for Lawrence after hearing about his injury.

Mr. Croft has expressed doubts about his suitability for a woman he is interested in. Lawrence believes that the woman will not view Mr. Croft's doubts negatively if presented correctly. Junius agrees to present Lawrence's statement accurately and without personal interpretation. Mrs. Keswick is awake and curious about the conversation between Junius and Lawrence. Annie Peyton hopes that Junius will leave the office before losing his temper. Roberta March is waiting for Junius to exit the office and believes she is the subject of their discussion. Junius exits the office calmly, which reassures one of the women watching.

Mike stated that his farm does not have sheep and is a ramshackle farm. La Fleur inferred that Mr. Haverley's farm is profitable. La Fleur described the farm as having a grand barn and broad acres. Mike confirmed that the estate extends further than what La Fleur can see. La Fleur expressed her gladness that Mrs. and Miss Drane are living at the farm. La Fleur offered to ensure that a doctor is sent if either Mrs. or Miss Drane falls ill. La Fleur expressed satisfaction with her thoughts about Mr. Haverley and the estate.

Burke walked forward in a straight line from the mound to the entrance of the passageway leading to the outer caves. Burke entered the passage and walked to the door of the room previously occupied by Captain Horn. Burke turned right and walked about ten feet to the middle apartment before returning to his original line of march. Burke reached the large cave, which was impeded by fallen rocks, making progress difficult. Burke observed that the southeast corner of the cave appeared more regular and almost right-angled. Burke discovered a rectangular space in the eastern wall and believed it concealed a handle for a trap-door. Upon returning to the mound, Burke found that the ladder he had left was missing.

A small schooner was manned by a Chilian captain, a mate, and four men. The schooner carried Captain Horn, his four negroes, and three hundred and thirty bags of guano. Captain Horn intended to establish a depot on the desert coast for storing guano. The little bay that had been the harbor of the Rackbirds was chosen by Captain Horn for landing the guano. Captain Horn brought timber to build a small pier and a lighter for transporting cargo. The crew began building the pier early the next morning after the schooner anchored. Captain Horn arranged the bags of guano in a way that allowed for easy access and created a small fort for defense.

Miriam was irritated by references to Dora. Mike was interviewed about his foreign maintenance. Mike stated that he had never received food from anyone because he did not need it. Mike mentioned that the doctor's cook gave him a pie out of gratitude for cooking advice. Miriam expressed concern that Molly did not provide enough food for Mike. Mike advised Miriam not to speak to Molly about his food situation. Miriam found Mike's manner of speaking interesting.

Ralph expressed a desire to visit Dora more than the dog. Dora appreciated Ralph's inclination to disregard social customs. Dora and Ralph arrived late to the parlor, impacting the perceptions of Mrs. and Miss Drane. Herbert Bannister engaged Ralph in conversation, leaving Dora to talk with Cicely Drane. Dora felt her spirits decline while conversing with Cicely Drane. Dora reflected on her feelings for Ralph Haverley, concluding that she loved him. Dora was concerned about Cicely Drane's presence and potential influence on Ralph.

The larger boat was equipped with six oars and had seven men, including mate Rynders, selected for the voyage. Captain Horn's camp consisted of himself, two ladies, a boy named Ralph, three sailors, and a native African named Maka. Maka was a cook who had been captured from a slave ship and had previously lived in British Guiana before moving to Panama. Captain Horn retained three sailors for their intelligence and reliability in emergencies. Captain Horn and the Englishman Davis climbed rocky hills to gain a better view of the ocean but found their main objective out of reach. The coastal area to the north appeared to be a flat desert with no signs of habitation. Captain Horn decided to make his camp as comfortable as possible while waiting for the return of his mate.

The captain brought down the lantern. Shirley expressed a desire to leave the cave and get into fresh air. The captain assisted Shirley, who appeared to be in a weakened state. The captain asked Maka to help get Shirley outside into the open air. Maka trembled upon seeing Shirley's condition but complied with the captain's request. Shirley stated he would take charge of the ship and assist with carrying duties but did not want to return to the cave. The captain reflected on Shirley's reaction to the sight of gold in the cave.

The captain consistently distributed gold from the mound regardless of who was relieved or what arrangements were made. The operations were conducted openly, with no attempt at secrecy, and the lid of the mound was not replaced after they left. Bags of gold were placed on the pier until they were taken to the vessel, where they replaced a proportionate amount of ballast. The negroes spoke and understood a little English and were uncertain about the contents of the bags. The captain believed that the negroes would be more likely to attempt theft after the treasure was secured and the ship had sailed. Maka informed the captain that the stones in the bags were causing him discomfort, and the captain explained that they were lumps of gold. Consultations were held to find a quicker method of transporting the gold, leading to a new plan involving the brig anchoring near the caves.

Dr. Tolbridge expressed concern about Miss Panney's state of mind after a disagreement regarding the Dranes' removal. Mrs. Tolbridge decided to keep her room for herself instead of giving it to Cicely Drane. Miss Panney visited Dora Bannister's house and exhibited unusual behavior, including staring and suddenly kissing Dora. Dora Bannister noted that Miss Panney seemed to be in a troubled state but was not angry with her. Mrs. Tolbridge was not optimistic about Dr. Tolbridge's ability to pacify Miss Panney. Dora Bannister expressed a desire to meet Miss Drane, the doctor's secretary, whom she had heard much about.

Captain and Shirley were startled by a deep groan from Maka, who was sitting on the sand and claimed to be sick. Maka expressed fear about going into the cave, which the captain reassured him about. The next day, the work of removing treasure from the caves to the vessel Miranda began. The Miranda was anchored near a little pier, and Shirley stayed on board with one negro while the captain and Burke took three others to the caves. The captain conversed freely about the treasure with Burke, who was eager to see it. The captain and Burke prepared bags of gold by placing bars into coffee-bags and tying them securely. Shirley decided to accompany the captain on the next trip to the cave, replacing Maka with another negro.

Shirley and Burke traveled to Callao and inquired about A. McLeish, but no one knew him. They went to Lima, sold some gold pieces, and pounded them to disguise their original shape. Shirley and Burke traveled to San Francisco on the first vessel that sailed. They estimated the gold they had was worth about twelve thousand dollars. Shirley and Burke considered sharing the treasure with others from the _Castor_ who might be in need. Burke left the decision about the treasure to Shirley to visit his sister in St. Louis. Shirley believed that if they found McLeish's heirs, the money would belong to them, but they also thought they deserved a share for their efforts.

The captain took a ring from Cheditafa and placed it on Edna's fourth finger. Cheditafa expressed satisfaction after placing the ring on Edna's finger. Mrs. Cliff commented on Cheditafa's goodness and noted that Edna would still be married the next day. The captain shared his story, which included details about treasure that Edna had not heard before. The captain discussed the ownership of the treasure and the legal rights associated with it. The captain's visit to London involved consultations with three leading lawyers regarding the treasure. The captain believes he is entitled to remuneration for the discovery of the treasure.

Mike assists Mrs. Flower regularly with household tasks. Cicely and Ralph spend more time together due to Miriam's absence. Mrs. Drane has difficulty changing her morning habits. Cicely feels she should regret Miriam's absence but does not. Ralph finds he can cope well without Miriam. Cicely takes care of the animals and plants that Miriam managed. Miss Panney plans to visit Mrs. Brinkly and Cobhurst to check on Ralph.

Ralph and Dora observed a sleeping girl who appeared tired. Ralph mentioned that the girl had been working since early in the morning. Dora expressed that the girl had the right to sleep and suggested not to disturb her. Dora planned to cover the girl with a lap robe to prevent her from getting cold. Dora and Ralph walked outside to enjoy the moonlight while discussing their fondness for the girl. Dora shared her background of losing her parents early and her independence in caring for her brother. Dora expressed her enjoyment of country life and her eagerness to help prepare breakfast.

The captain found a short black wooden pipe while searching for items to put out of sight. The captain speculated that the pipe may have belonged to a sailor from the _Mary Bartlett_. The captain entered the caves and noticed his rough pallet was left in disorder. The captain observed that the cave of the lake was drier than before, with few pools of water having evaporated. The captain discovered an old tin cup on the ground and planned to take it back with him. The captain found several pieces of gold and a small candle-end while exploring the cave. The captain noticed burnt wooden matches scattered on the ground as he approached the mound.

Miriam expressed interest in having the Dranes visit Cobhurst. Ralph considered it fortunate if Dora Bannister and her family had sought accommodations at Cobhurst instead of the Dranes. Miriam indicated she would like the ladies to come to their home. Ralph agreed to have the Dranes visit Cobhurst. The doctor was pleased with the outcome of his mission regarding the visit. Mrs. Tolbridge suggested visiting Mrs. Drane immediately to discuss the arrangements. The doctor considered informing Miss Panney about the plans before the Dranes left their current accommodations.

Dora spoke to the dog named Congo and expressed her expectations of him. Ralph did not notice Congo's absence until the next morning. Ralph considered whether to search for Congo himself or send Mike. Cicely advised Ralph against sending for Mike and suggested that Miss Bannister could return the dog herself. Miss Panney took a dose of medicine prescribed by Dr. Tolbridge after parting from Dora Bannister. Miss Panney stayed in bed until three o'clock the next afternoon, which concerned the Wittons. Miss Panney refused Mrs. Witton's offers of help and insisted on getting up.

Lawrence Croft wore a light overcoat during his afternoon walks in New York. Lawrence Croft believed the weather in Virginia was pleasant during the autumn season. Roberta March planned to stay with her Uncle Brandon for at least a month longer due to her father's trip to Texas. Lawrence Croft was attempting to study the character of Junius Keswick but felt he was making no progress. Lawrence Croft considered visiting Virginia after learning about Roberta March's extended stay. Lawrence Croft decided to visit the mountains of North Carolina, planning to stop at Midbranch. The man at the Green Sulphur Springs was surprised by Lawrence Croft's arrival and request for board.

Miss Panney arrived at Cobhurst before the doctor reached his patient's house. Mrs. Drane and Miriam had driven to Thorbury. Mr. Haverley was on the property and could be easily found. Ralph expressed his intention to marry Miss Drane. Miss Panney questioned Ralph about his feelings and the suitability of Miss Drane. Ralph affirmed that Miss Drane was the right choice for him. Miss Panney intended to visit Miss Drane to get to know her better.

Mr. Brandon addressed the gentleman as 'Junius.' Lawrence observed that the gentleman was taller than Croft and not as correctly dressed. Lawrence felt perturbed and believed there was a mistake regarding an engagement. Lawrence experienced emotions of grief, chagrin, and rage at not having won Roberta. Roberta asked Lawrence if he was leaving the next day. Lawrence expressed his dislike for autumn and preferred to see things dead. Lawrence planned to return the next morning for a walk in the woods with Roberta.

Lawrence was surprised to find that no one knew much about Mr Junius Keswick or his current whereabouts. Mr Junius Keswick had been a resident of New York when his engagement was in force. Mr Croft entered an apothecary's shop to consult a directory. The clerk informed Mr Croft that the shop did not have a directory but directed him to a nearby shop with a green door. The shop with the green door offered access to a city directory for a fee. Lawrence inquired about the name 'Junius Keswick' while looking through the directory. The directory did not list Junius Keswick, but the shopkeeper suggested checking previous years' directories.

The seaman planned to send a letter to Paris for tuppence ha'penny. The letter was placed in the pocket of his pea-jacket, which had a ripped bottom. The letter remained in the pocket until the seaman reached England and visited his family in Sidmouth. The seaman's mother found the letter in the pea-jacket and sewed on two buttons. The negro Mok was at the beer-shop called the 'Black Cat' enjoying beer and food. Mok was under strict orders from his young master, Ralph, to not go out alone. Mok did not understand French and had limited English but enjoyed the atmosphere at the beer-shop.

The jeweller believed that pieces of gold were used as currency in California. Nunez decided to provide capital to fit out the schooner _Arato_ for a trip. The schooner _Arato_ cleared from Valparaiso for Callao in ballast with a crew of ten men and a passenger named Nunez. The _Arato_ changed its course southward after leaving the harbor. The brig _Miranda_ had good winds and fair weather for ten days after leaving Valparaiso. After ten days, the _Miranda_ encountered head winds and bad weather, leading to leaks in the vessel. The crew of the _Miranda_ worked at the pumps but found that water was gaining in the hold.

Cheditafa served as the body-servant to Mrs. Horn and felt a strong sense of responsibility for her well-being. Cheditafa had officiated the wedding of Captain Horn and Edna Markham but did not disclose this information due to warnings from Mrs. Cliff. Mrs. Cliff advised Cheditafa that the marriage of a Christian by a heathen could lead to trouble unless he could prove his right to perform the ceremony. Mok, another servant, could not speak English but understood some spoken language and was quick to learn through non-verbal cues. Ralph took Mok as a valet, and Mok became increasingly useful to him, often expressing a desire to serve. Mok was fond of fine clothes and appeared to have more importance than Cheditafa at times. Mok demonstrated intelligence and agility, which helped him avoid impositions from other servants.

The protagonist experiences a state of exalted mental action influenced by recollections and whiskey. He expresses scorn for a man who highly values a piece of gold and reacts with laughter when pointing to it. The protagonist becomes excited and asks about 'Cap' 'Or,' which confuses the four men present. The four men, intrigued by the protagonist's background, invite him to sit and offer him a drink. The drink helps the protagonist express himself better through gestures and single words. The men believe the protagonist has been on a ship carrying bags of gold and that he left it to get refreshments. They conclude that the ship likely came from California and is bound for Paris, but they cannot determine where it was loaded with gold.

The man in the slouch-hat had significant experience in avoiding arrest. A group of people, including two gendarmes, pursued the man in the slouch-hat. A man in a white cap joined the chase but quickly lost interest and left. Edna felt faint and troubled after hearing Cheditafa shout 'Rackbird.' Cheditafa reassured Edna by recounting his meeting with the Rackbird. Cheditafa identified the captain of the band as Raminez, whom he had known in Panama. Edna concluded that Captain Horn was not involved with the letter intended for her.

Miriam was found alone on the front piazza, training vines on the pillars. Miriam was dressed as a woman, differing from her previous youthful costume. The old lady believed that Miriam was becoming the head of the house. Miriam stated that Molly Tooney had left of her own accord and was glad to be rid of her. Miriam expressed a desire for Cicely to stay, stating that the doctor had more work for her. Miss Panney recognized that her plans needed to change due to Miriam's attachment to Cicely. Miss Panney viewed the Drane girl as an obstacle to her matchmaking plans.

A fire broke out among the green vines, which could not be extinguished. Miss Markham expressed concern about the fire ruining the beautiful vines. The captain stated that they could not waste water on the fire and that it would not reach their tent. Ralph toasted a ship's biscuit over the embers when a portion of the burning vines fell, revealing a large stone face. The stone face was approximately eight feet above the ground and extended at least that distance up the cliff. The captain identified the stone face as a piece of sculpture likely created by the original natives. The discovery of the stone face excited the party, who speculated about its origins.

Lawrence requested all the information the man possessed immediately. The man indicated that Candy, who is in charge of Croft's job, is becoming more involved in detective work. Candy has taken up Lawrence's affair seriously after discovering that Croft had assigned someone else to the case. The man stated that Lawrence has two sets of detectives pursuing him, with the first to find him standing to gain financially. The man could not provide the current location of Candy's detectives due to being far from the New York office. The man was traveling to Mobile and stopped in Virginia to attend to Lawrence's business. Lawrence revealed that he is Mr. Croft and is not pursuing Mr. Keswick, contradicting the man's assumptions.

Mrs. McLeish was informed that her son is dead. The traveller told Mrs. McLeish that she would receive one hundred and four pounds a year from her son. The amount translates to two pounds a week for the rest of her life. The traveller explained that her son had died in South America. Shirley and Burke discovered Mrs. McLeish's address while searching for heirs of the Castor's crew. They arranged for an annuity for Mrs. McLeish using gold found with her son's body. As of November 1, eight pounds was due to Mrs. McLeish from the annuity.

Miss Dora is experiencing a transition from a youthful mentality to a more mature intellect. Dr. Tolbridge believes that Miss Dora's current mental state is a temporary phase. Miss Dora feels humiliated and believes her mental sufferings are not fanciful. Dr. Tolbridge assures Miss Dora that she will develop a stronger mind within three weeks. Miss Dora expresses a desire to pay for the consultation herself. Dr. Tolbridge states that he does not charge money for his advice and prefers to receive kittens instead. Miss Dora offers to give Dr. Tolbridge an Angora kitten.

The cavern contains a pool of water that is a foot or more in depth. The cavern turns to the left and is wider and has a higher roof in that section. A large dome-like structure, approximately ten feet high, is located at the bottom of the basin. The structure is believed to be made of stone and shows signs of masonry joints. The captain retrieves a lantern to examine the dome more closely. The dome is described as a half sphere of masonry with a smooth surface and two lines of protuberances. The captain concludes that the cave is man-made and was designed to conceal the water and the stone mound.

Captain Horn expressed a desire to buy a steamer to expedite his journey to France. Captain Horn regretted that the _Miranda_ was not a steamer, which would have made travel faster. Captain Horn estimated that he needed to sail about three thousand miles in the Pacific Ocean and two thousand miles in the Atlantic before reaching Rio Janeiro. Captain Horn decided to send a letter to Edna to inform her of his journey and alleviate any concerns. Captain Horn planned to stop at Valparaiso to send his letter ashore. A British steamer was anchored near the _Miranda_ when Captain Horn arrived off Valparaiso. Shirley reported that the first mate of the British steamer would take charge of Captain Horn's letter.

Miss Annie did not show grief or wear mourning after a death, which others attributed to customs learned in the North. Lawrence advised Annie to write to her cousin Junius about their engagement without mentioning the death. Annie's letter to Junius was posted at the railroad station after Lawrence drove her there. The family mail arrived bi-weekly at Howlett's, and Mrs. Keswick expected a letter from Miss March. Plez returned from Howlett's with letters, including one for Mrs. Keswick from Junius and another for Annie. Junius expressed surprise at Annie's use of a married title and felt she should have informed her relatives of the truth. Junius congratulated Annie on her engagement to Mr. Croft and mentioned his own renewed engagement to Miss March.

The narrator is preparing a teaberry gown for Cicely, who is now the head of the house. The narrator plans to invest Cicely with the gown the day after her wedding trip. La Fleur offers to organize a luncheon for the investiture ceremony. The Investiture Luncheon is attended by the Tolbridges and Miss Panney. Cicely wears the teaberry gown during the luncheon. Miss Panney visits Mr. Herbert Bannister to alter her will. Miss Panney intends to leave her property to Mr. Haverley, whom she considers as a grandson.

Maka and the other negroes were disappointed that the captain did not take them north from Callao. The captain lost his ship and needed to make money before returning home. The captain of the schooner was willing to start the next day due to favorable wind conditions. Captain Horn was concerned about the crew wandering into the surrounding country if they were delayed in the cove. Captain Horn had made plans to keep the men occupied in case they had to stay longer in the cove. After the schooner departed, Captain Horn felt a sense of desertion as he walked toward the caves. Captain Horn was displeased that the crew left utensils outside the caves instead of storing them properly.

Miriam Haverley is a young girl about fourteen years old. Miriam has large blue eyes and light brown hair in a long plait. Miriam is wearing a plum-colored silk gown that is worn, torn, and stained. Miriam is holding a large glass bottle with a rubber tube and bulbous mouthpiece. Miriam has been making bread and is trying to clean dough off her hands. Phoebe, who usually helps Miriam, has been away for nearly a week. Miriam has adopted a weak calf that she feeds from the bottle.

Miss Roberta and Junius were in the parlor, both wanting to speak first. Miss Roberta asked why Junius and Mr. Croft were together and where they had been. Junius stated that he and Mr. Croft had come from the Green Sulphur Springs. Miss Roberta expressed her mortification at the situation and stated she wished Mr. Croft had come of his own accord. Junius inquired about his Aunt Keswick's health and Mr. Brandon's visit, to which Miss Roberta replied that she was neither ill nor dead and that Mr. Brandon went on business. Peggy informed Aunt Judy about Miss Roberta having two suitors, Junius and Mr. Croft. Peggy recounted an incident where she interrupted a potential fight between Junius and Mr. Croft.

Edna is determined to support the captain and not criticize his performance. Edna watches the captain's boat until it disappears from view. Mrs. Cliff congratulates Edna on her good fortune. Ralph has been a faithful guardian of the captain's treasure. Edna resumes her role as a teacher, instructing Ralph in mathematics using sand for diagrams. Mrs. Cliff engages in missionary work with Mok and Cheditafa to alleviate her boredom. Mrs. Cliff is concerned that converting Cheditafa could invalidate the marriage ceremony between him and Edna.

Maka was running, followed by another man who was not one of the sailors. Ralph called to Maka, causing the second figure to stop and turn. Maka seized the second man by the arm, indicating he was not pursuing him. The second man was also an African, resembling Maka closely. The captain returned to the camp-ground as the two negroes arrived. The strange negro exhibited wild terror upon seeing the captain and fled into a cleft in the rock. Ralph and the captain followed the cries into a narrow passage that led to an open space.

The characters are preparing to leave a location after tying up bags. The captain and Burke discuss the value of gold and the importance of not revealing its origin. Burke expresses curiosity about the possibility of hidden treasures beneath a mound. The captain decides against searching for additional treasures, believing they have enough. Burke deserts the ship at midnight, using a line to reach the water unnoticed. After reaching the shore, Burke gathers tools including a lantern, hammer, and cold-chisel.

Miss Edna Markham of New York took apartments at the Hotel Boileau. Mrs. Cliff expressed a desire to return to Plainton when another ship started from France. The members of the party aimed to see and enjoy the wonders of Paris together. Mrs. Cliff appreciated art but preferred not to revisit galleries after seeing them once. Ralph was under the charge of a tutor named Professor Barré, who took a great interest in him. Edna received social invitations through the influence of Mrs. Sylvester, the wife of the American secretary of legation. Mrs. Cliff preferred to wait until her return to Plainton before engaging in further social activities.

Dora has seen the new residents of Cobhurst only briefly at the station. Miss Panney describes young Mr. Haverley as handsome, well educated, and spirited. Dora's brother, Herbert, is currently away and will not return for a week. Miss Panney suggests that Dora and Mrs. Bannister should visit the sister of the new residents. Dora expresses concern that the young lady in Cobhurst may feel lonely in her new home. Dora visits Mrs. Tolbridge to inquire about a kitten she gave to Dr. Tolbridge. Mrs. Tolbridge is writing an advertisement to find a cook and plans to visit the city to meet potential candidates.

Miriam is younger than the narrator but appears to be maturing quickly. The narrator has a favorable opinion of Ralph Haverley. Miss Panney wrote a letter to Dora Bannister expressing mild reproaches for her departure from Thorbury without notice. Miss Panney suggested that Dora invite Miriam Haverley to visit her at the seashore. Dora is fond of Miriam and is pleased with the idea of her visiting during the seaside stay. Dora consulted with Mrs. Bannister about inviting Miriam, who supported the idea. Miriam was not in good spirits and felt that La Fleur was not influenced by her clothing.

Maka stated that Cheditafa does not want a boy as a boss. The captain asserted that he has the authority to decide whether Cheditafa stays or goes. Maka expressed a preference for an older woman as a boss over a younger one. The captain was amused by Maka's comments about leadership. Maka warned that without a boss, chaos could ensue and outsiders might take advantage. Maka claimed that Cheditafa could marry the captain and Mrs. Cliff before the captain leaves. Mrs. Cliff approached the captain to discuss matters, interrupting his conversation with Maka.

The captain is preparing a boat for a voyage. Ralph expresses a desire to accompany the captain but is told he must stay with his sister and Mrs. Cliff. Ralph believes Captain Horn is a brave man but also a tyrant. Edna disagrees with Ralph and supports Captain Horn's leadership. The boat is provisioned for a long voyage, but the captain hopes to make it short. Mrs. Cliff expresses concern about being left behind and the potential dangers of the captain's voyage. Maka asks the captain who will be in charge when he leaves.

Mrs. Cliff expresses concern about keeping herself sealed and locked up. Edna reassures Mrs. Cliff that they will hear from the captain soon. Mrs. Cliff is troubled by the captain's need to make arrangements and travel to various locations. Edna writes to Ralph, urging him to come to Paris as soon as possible. Edna reflects on her feelings of loneliness and anxiety regarding the captain's return. Edna contemplates the implications of the captain's potential ownership of valuable cargo. Edna believes the captain's greatest anxiety is related to her perception of their past agreement.

Cicely plans to ask Miriam for driving lessons. Ralph claims to be a better teacher than Miriam. Ralph offers to take Cicely out for a driving lesson the next day. Cicely expresses interest in driving Mrs. Browning up a hill for a sunset view. Ralph decides to let Mrs. Browning go home by herself instead of tying her to a fence. Ralph reflects on how little he has missed his sister Miriam. Cicely and Ralph pick goldenrod on their way back to the house.

Miriam expresses the opinion that there is excessive discussion about eating. La Fleur, the cook, believes that cooking is an important intellectual pursuit. La Fleur recounts her experience working for Lady Hartleberry, who disapproved of elaborate dishes. Lady Hartleberry required her servants to report their church attendance. La Fleur was able to attend church at her discretion without Lady Hartleberry's knowledge. When the family went to Scotland, a piper was sent to check on church attendance. Miriam is working on altering Judith Pacewalk's teaberry gown for Cicely.

Miriam and Dora were in a barn with a calf that appeared to be lifeless. Miriam stated that Dr. Tolbridge diagnosed the calf with infantile ophthalmia and believed it could be cured. Miriam and Dora attempted to feed the calf using a bottle, despite concerns about the bottle leaking. The calf began to show signs of life by sucking the milk from the bottle. Miriam expressed delight as the calf was able to hold up its head after feeding. Dora became interested in the calf's welfare and suggested waiting to see if it wanted more milk. The girls heard heavy footsteps approaching the barn, causing Dora to drop the bottle and step away.

Ralph informed others that the narrow passage led to Mrs. Horn's apartment. Mrs. Cliff believed the caves were used for religious purposes and that the stone face was an ancient idol. Edna waited behind a stone barrier for Ralph's summons while packing her belongings. Ralph told Mrs. Cliff and Edna that if anything was lost, it should be charged to him. Ralph expressed a desire to stay and guard the treasure until the captain arrived. Edna opposed Ralph's idea of staying behind, stating that the captain would have instructed him to do so if he wanted it. One hour later, Edna and Mrs. Cliff watched the plateau of the great stone face sink into the horizon from the deck of the Mary Bartlett.

The boat is hauled up on shore. Miss Markham expresses concern that the Rackbirds killed three sailors. The captain believes the Rackbirds may have attacked the sailors after they survived a shipwreck. Miss Markham has a pistol that she offers to the captain. The captain instructs Miss Markham to keep her brother and Mrs. Cliff safe in the middle room. The captain has examined the cavern and identified two possible entry points for intruders. The captain plans to keep Maka on guard and station another African on a ledge for warning.

Miss Panney stands when talking to a lady and waives class privileges to request the cook, La Fleur, to sit. La Fleur smiles in response to Miss Panney's request and acknowledges the privilege. Miss Panney expresses her appreciation for La Fleur's cooking and inquires about a specific recipe. La Fleur explains that her recipe for raspberry-flavored ice was invented by her first husband, Tolati. Miss Panney has experience with various cuisines and acknowledges La Fleur's skill in cooking. La Fleur believes that French cooking is the best and expresses pride in her countrymen's work. Miss Panney states that Dr. Tolbridge's health depends on La Fleur's cooking and acknowledges her efforts.

The narrative takes place two months after Edna and her party left New York. They are staying at the Hotel Boileau in Paris, which is located near the Boulevard des Italiens. The Hotel Boileau offers private apartments, a private table, and service from their own staff in addition to hotel staff. Edna Markham is the principal member of the party in Paris, a change from her previous identity as Mrs. Philip Horn in San Francisco. Edna has concerns about her marital status with Captain Philip Horn based on the tone of his letters. In Paris, Edna feels it is inappropriate to present herself as Mrs. Horn due to the uncertainty of her relationship with Captain Horn. Edna's friends in Paris are primarily Americans, including an old schoolmate who is married to a secretary of the American legation.

The captain expressed concern about the potential return of Rynders and the presence of jaguars. The captain and Ralph decided to occupy a suite of rooms that were dry and airy. Miss Markham was disappointed after exploring the three stone rooms, finding no signs of architectural adornment or religious significance. Mrs. Cliff preferred to sleep in the open air rather than in the stone rooms. The captain informed his party about the fate he feared had overtaken three sailors, which changed their opinion about the lodgings. The party made the two rooms as comfortable as possible with available materials and slept there that night. The captain felt secure with a barricade made from four oars and his guns positioned at the narrow passage.

Uncle Isham's loyalty to the widow Keswick is based on his regard for her character. Uncle Isham is troubled when others interfere with his efforts to maintain the widow Keswick's reputation. Lawrence requested Letty to ask Mrs Null to speak with him. Lawrence's ankle has been hurting, but he has been using lotion left by Mrs Keswick. Miss Annie believes Roberta was angry with her cousin Junius after a conversation they had. Lawrence denies sending Junius to propose to Roberta on his behalf. Miss Annie states that Mrs Keswick does not take further interest in Lawrence.

Miss Annie discussed her reading with Lawrence and offered to send him more books through Uncle Isham. Lawrence expressed concern about the chilly weather affecting Miss March if she were present. Mrs Keswick visited Lawrence and proposed bringing Miss March to him for a game of whist after supper. Lawrence expressed gratitude to Mrs Keswick for her matchmaking efforts. Lawrence anticipated a pleasant supper and the chance to see Miss March during the whist game. Lawrence's plans for the whist game were disrupted, and he suspected Miss March's reluctance was the cause. The weather in Southern Virginia was gray and rainy the day after Lawrence's injury.

Peggy was instructed to shout outside her master's door until he took notice. Mrs. Keswick's horse was harnessed and she was ready to go home, but she wanted to see Mr. Brandon again. Mr. Brandon saw the spring-wagon and remembered that Mrs. Keswick intended to stay only one night. Mrs. Keswick expressed concern for Mr. Brandon's health and suggested she might stay to take care of him. Mrs. Keswick assured Mr. Brandon that she would return and urged the servants to take care of him. Mr. Brandon did not accompany Mrs. Keswick as she left his house in the spring-wagon. After Mrs. Keswick departed, Mr. Brandon expressed his feelings about her leaving.

The _Arato_ was not as good a sea-boat in a storm as the _Miranda_. Cardatas was more cautious and prudent than Captain Horn would have been. Cardatas steered well out from the coast, lengthening his course. Cardatas believed he could overtake the _Miranda_ before she reached the Straits. Nunez was despondent about finding the _Miranda_ after the storm. The _Arato_ did not make good sailing on her southeastern course. Cardatas observed a strange light on the port bow that he could not identify.

The captain stationed Maka to watch for dangerous creatures while he and Ralph investigated a cleft. The passage they entered was about two feet wide, with a lower floor and a roof a few feet above their heads. The passage was man-made and led to a dimly lit area with an open doorway. Inside the first chamber, which was about fifteen feet square, there was a jagged opening in the roof allowing light in. The captain and Ralph discovered another chamber larger than the first, with high walls and an open roof. The captain noted that the location provided safety from wild beasts and a place to wait for assistance. They had enough supplies for about a week, but their water supply was limited and could run out in a day.

Molly claims she is not the worst cook, referencing a previous cook named Phoebe. La Fleur asserts that Mr. Haverley is a gentleman despite his work on the farm. Molly mentions that there is another servant named Mike who helps her. La Fleur expresses disdain for tradespeople and distinguishes them from gentleman farmers. Mike confirms that he has been informed about La Fleur by Mr. Griffing. La Fleur claims to have lived with high families but denies cooking for Queen Victoria. Mike describes the farm as being over a hundred acres but not particularly large or small.

The captain observed a vessel making straight for land. Shirley noted that the vessel must have seen their fire from the previous night. The vessel was identified as a long green schooner with all sails set. The schooner dropped anchor and began lowering two boats. The captain suspected that the approaching boats might be manned by Rackbirds seeking vengeance. The captain instructed his companions to get their rifles in preparation for a potential confrontation. The black men were frightened and believed the approaching boats posed a threat.

Miss Bannister was not at home when Ralph and Miriam visited Cobhurst. Miss Bannister went to the city to help Mrs. Tolbridge find a new cook. Miss Panney expressed interest in Miriam during Ralph and Miriam's visit. Miriam requested to be called by her first name instead of Miss Haverley. Miss Panney described Miss Bannister as charming, pretty, and well-educated. Miss Panney noted that Miriam was younger than she initially thought. Mrs. Tolbridge reported a discouraging experience in her search for a new cook.

Mrs Keswick observed Lawrence and Annie conversing in the yard. Annie read a letter from Lawrence before they entered the arbor together. Mrs Keswick eavesdropped on their conversation about Lawrence's love for Miss March and Annie's situation with Mr Null and Mr Croft. Mrs Keswick confronted Lawrence and Annie with intense anger. Annie reacted to Mrs Keswick's outburst by turning pale and then clinging to Lawrence. Mrs Keswick accused Lawrence of deceiving her and interfering with her plans. Lawrence attempted to explain himself but was not listened to by Mrs Keswick.

Miss Panney studied anatomy using bones marked in ink with their names. Reuben, Mathias' brother, was a scientific man who used the skeleton for study. Miss Panney mentioned that the garret contains family relics and records that have not been touched for fifty years. The house is considered haunted, particularly the garret, according to Miss Panney. Phoebe delivered a note from Miriam to Ralph regarding her exploration of the house. The doctor reported that Miriam was fine, but he was not feeling well. The doctor noted that Miriam is a Nonconformist and had a long conversation with her.

Aunt Patsy is an elderly woman who has lived a long life. Mrs Null decided to visit Aunt Patsy after hearing she was alive. Plez, a maid, offered to guide Mrs Null to Aunt Patsy's house, but she declined. Aunt Patsy was found sitting in a low chair by the window, working on a quilt. Aunt Patsy's great-granddaughter was present, attempting to start a fire in the fireplace. Aunt Patsy expressed concern about finishing her quilt before she dies. Mrs Null promised to bring Aunt Patsy something nice to eat during her visit.

Maka was lying on his face at the edge of a precipice, yelling for help. The captain pulled Maka and another man up to safety. The captain was wet after the strange man he rescued stumbled against him. Ralph and the captain discovered a lake at their feet, which they initially mistook for air. The lake was about a hundred feet wide and had a cavernous roof above it. Ralph drank from the lake and expressed relief at finding water. Maka urged the captain to listen to him after the discovery of the lake.

Lawrence Croft provided his card to a cashier and requested that Mr. Candy be hurried. Lawrence Croft comes from an old family but is the most important remaining member. Lawrence's current purpose is to marry Roberta March. Lawrence became impatient after five days without hearing from Mr. Candy. The cashier informed Lawrence that Mr. Candy traced a gentleman to Niagara Falls. Lawrence decided to let the matter continue and requested updates from Mr. Candy. The cashier and a boy discussed Mr. Candy's lack of progress on Lawrence's inquiry.

Nunez and Cardatas discussed their concerns about supporting a negro. Cardatas suggested that they could go to Rio to meet the brig and speak with her captain. Nunez expressed doubt about the feasibility of going to Rio. Cardatas proposed that they could pursue the brig in the Straits of Magellan. Cardatas mentioned that he owns a small share in the schooner _Arato_, which could be used for the pursuit. Nunez traveled to Santiago to inquire about a piece of gold he possessed. The jeweller confirmed that he had previously bought four pieces of gold from Lima, originally from California.

Miss Panney believes it is too costly to keep a hack waiting. Miss Panney suggests that Phoebe observe Miss Drane's work status. Miss Drane is described as needing to earn her own living. Phoebe expresses the opinion that Mr. Hav'ley should get married. Miss Panney dismisses the idea of Miss Drane being suitable for Mr. Hav'ley. Miss Panney intends to write a letter to a friend in Barport. Miss Panney leaves Thorbury the next morning without seeing Phoebe.

Miss Panney and the doctor are discussing their efforts to help Miss Drane. Miss Panney believes it is better to work for Miss Drane in Thorbury rather than elsewhere. The doctor is expecting a patient and wishes to exhaust their efforts in Thorbury quickly. Miss Panney is aware that immediate teaching positions are rarely available in summer. Susan Clopsey is mentioned as a potential patient who has money and health issues. Miss Panney suggests that the doctor employ the Drane girl to copy his manuscript. The doctor has a manuscript titled 'Diagnosis of Sympathy' that he has not had time to copy.

Mrs. Cliff expresses a desire to discuss a matter related to the treasure before the captain's expedition. The captain has considered the implications of the treasure should he not return from his expedition. Mrs. Cliff believes that those who have shared in the expedition should also share in the treasure. The captain intends to manage the treasure in his own way and avoid disputes over it. The captain has drawn up a will leaving all his property to Mrs. Cliff, Miss Markham, and Ralph. The captain does not want his distant relatives to have any claim to his property. The captain has written private directions regarding the disposal of the treasure.

Edna expresses that she wants Captain Horn. Mrs. Cliff expresses disappointment in Captain Horn. A sailor is reported missing after going ashore. Ralph confirms that all men were counted when returning to the ship. A sailor swims nearly a mile to reach the beach after falling overboard. The sailor, a Scotchman, observes the area after reaching the shore. The sailor suspects that the captain left supplies behind for someone expected to return.

Annie recalls that her clothes were put in a box and that a pair of little blue shoes was among them. Annie suspects that Aunt Patsy stole the shoes. Lawrence expresses surprise at the accusation against Aunt Patsy, believing her to be honest. Annie describes Aunt Patsy as a trusted servant in their family. Lawrence has a sore ankle and receives condolences from Annie and Mrs. Keswick at breakfast. Lawrence expresses a desire to attend a negro church service to observe their religious practices. Miss Annie suggests taking a spring-wagon to the church instead of walking.

Mr Brandon has concerns about an obstacle to the union of Junius and Roberta due to the arrival of a suitor named Croft. Roberta enjoys city life, society, and travel, and may no longer consider a union with Junius. Mr Brandon believes that the estate of Midbranch should not be given to an outsider. Mr Brandon plans to visit widow Keswick to discuss the situation regarding Junius and Roberta. The distance to widow Keswick's house is about fifteen miles. Upon arriving at widow Keswick's house, Mr Brandon is received coldly. Widow Keswick expresses her need for a lawyer and her intention to seek assistance from Mr Brandon.

The captain claims an amount of forty million dollars. Mrs. Cliff expresses surprise at the captain's claim of forty million dollars. The captain states that forty million dollars is about one fifth of the value of the cargo he brought to France in the _Arato_. Mrs. Cliff protests against the proposed marriage at the American legation, advocating for a church ceremony. Edna insists on marrying at the American legation, where they can be married by an American minister. The marriage ceremony is arranged to take place privately at four o'clock that afternoon. The captain telegraphed Shirley and Burke to come to him in London after breakfasting at the Hotel Grenade.

Lawrence believes that settling the matter with Miss March would be in Junius's interest as a suitor. Junius suggests speaking to Miss March directly, but Lawrence disagrees, stating it would not resolve the situation. Lawrence claims that Miss March knows Junius is her lover but has not given a definite answer. Croft expresses doubt that Miss March would allow him to speak with her due to her refusal for an interview since his accident. Keswick interprets Miss March's refusal as a sign that she does not desire Croft's attentions. Lawrence feels that Miss March has taken offense without reason and seeks to clarify the misunderstanding. Lawrence considers Junius his last chance to communicate with Miss March, as other options have failed.

Lawrence expressed his intention to step aside if Miss March rejects him. Annie expressed skepticism about Lawrence's commitment to step aside. Lawrence stated that he would not pursue Miss March if she rejected him. Roberta entered the room and engaged in conversation without facilitating a discussion between Mr. Croft and Miss March. Lawrence felt nervous about overstaying his visit and had not yet been alone with Miss March. Miss March seemed to withdraw from observation after previously rejecting Lawrence. Mrs. Keswick informed Lawrence that the ladies had gone for a walk in the woods.

The character has been working on a trap that opens downward. The character believes that revealing certain information would disturb another person's peace of mind. The Miranda set sail for Rio Janeiro and then France after taking in water. Captain Horn felt tired but content as he smoked his pipe after completing his work. The treasure of the Incas was stored in the hold of the brig, acting as ballast. Burke suggested that the crew should acquire groceries and drinks, but the captain disagreed. The captain expressed concern about the dangers of entering any port on the west coast of South America with their current cargo.

The bathing-master swam out to a boat that was searching for bathers. A man jumped overboard from the boat to assist someone in the water. Three men carried a limp figure from the water to the shore. Miss Panney observed the situation but felt restrained from approaching immediately. Miss Panney decided to send a telegram to Ralph Haverley requesting his immediate presence. The telegram stated there was a dreadful disaster and urged Haverley to come immediately. Miss Panney learned from Mrs. Bannister that two individuals were believed to be beyond resuscitation.

Lawrence expresses a desire to accompany Miss Annie on a walk. Miss Annie is concerned that the walk may be too strenuous for Lawrence. Lawrence believes his ankle is strong enough for the walk to Aunt Patsy's and back. Aunt Patsy is pleased to see her visitors, especially Mr. Croft. Aunt Patsy plans to wear a dress to church the next day. Aunt Patsy mentions that Brudder Enick Hines will be preaching at the church. Miss Annie and Aunt Patsy reminisce about their past acquaintance.

The speaker does not know the Dranes personally but is willing to help them. Miss Panney wishes to keep La Fleur in the kitchen for the sake of a friend. La Fleur has fixed her own salary and does not intend to change it. Miss Panney plans to work on behalf of Miss Drane and requests La Fleur to consult her before taking any action. Mrs. Tolbridge inquires about a dessert called Blarney Fluff with sauce Irlandaise that La Fleur prepared. Dr. Tolbridge and Miss Panney discuss the lack of flourishing teachers in Thorbury due to children being sent away to school. Miss Panney expresses concern that if Miss Drane does not find work soon, it will negatively impact their quality of life.

Captain Horn reached a bay where the stream ran into the sea. The shores near the bay showed signs of having been washed by a flood. Captain Horn found debris from the Rackbirds' camp, including sticks, clothing, and cooking utensils. The bodies of desiccated Rackbirds were found partly buried in the sand. Captain Horn discovered a concealed sloop belonging to the Rackbirds, which was stripped of masts, sails, and the rudder. Cheditafa informed Captain Horn that the masts and sails had previously been carried to the camp. Cheditafa later indicated the presence of another boat, which was deemed unusable.

Lawrence expressed a desire to see Miss March. Keswick was unsure if Miss March still wished to see Lawrence. Croft wanted to find out Miss March's feelings by asking her directly. Keswick stated he would not assist Lawrence if it would offend Mr. Brandon. Mrs. Keswick welcomed Lawrence and insisted he stay for dinner. Lawrence was staying at a local hotel run by the storekeeper. Mrs. Keswick insisted that Lawrence stay with them instead of at the hotel.

The protagonist observed gun barrels and percussion caps before dodging and escaping on his horse. The protagonist shook his fist at Lawrence while still being covered by the gun's muzzles. The old lady confirmed to Lawrence that the gun was loaded with powder and Windfall's Teaberry Tonic Pills. The old lady expressed her displeasure about the annoyance caused to Lawrence in her house. Lawrence believed he was invited by Mrs. Keswick to marry Miss March to oppose her nephew's marriage plans. Lawrence wrote a letter to Junius Keswick detailing his search for him and warning him about an anti-detective. Lawrence chose not to disclose information about Keswick's cousin in his letter.

Miss Annie expressed contempt for Croft's opinion regarding the nature of their acquaintance. Croft sought to know Mr. Keswick's whereabouts but felt obliged to refuse Annie's request for his reasons. Annie believed Croft's interest in Mr. Keswick was related to his pursuit of Miss March. Croft denied Annie's accusation and expressed regret over her low opinion of him. Mrs. Keswick invited Mr. Croft and Miss March to her house to facilitate a marriage proposal. Mrs. Keswick insisted that Annie accompany her to search for a turkey-hen, despite Annie's reluctance. Croft felt uncomfortable about the situation with Miss March due to Mrs. Keswick's interference.

Mr. Herbert Bannister was expected to call upon the narrator. Dora asked her brother daily if he would visit Cobhurst. Herbert Bannister was busy with clients and could not visit Cobhurst. Dr. Tolbridge visited the Haverleys to discuss Mrs. Drane and her daughter. Miriam expressed interest in the daughter of Mrs. Drane after learning about her.

Miriam and Ralph are discussing their horse and wagon. Miriam expresses a desire to sell the horse and wagon. Ralph is concerned about their hunger and the lack of supper.
