There were no Egyptian soldiers or European traders in the streets. Food was scarce and expensive due to the fear of the Mahdi's followers. The sheik engaged in conversation with native shopkeepers about the prices of goods. The sheik's goods were sold at prices much higher than their original cost. Traders paid for the goods in cash drawn from buried hoards.

The girl has experienced improvement in her lip condition and sores. She mentioned that the pain from her injuries has decreased significantly in recent days. Isobel expressed readiness for breakfast and a walk after feeling better from a dip in water. Mr. Wilson's current status is uncertain, but there is hope that he is safe at Allahabad or with the troops. The Zemindar's son and one of his men safely reached shore and continued with Mr. Wilson. Mr. Bathurst described Mr. Wilson as kind-hearted, loyal, and brave, with potential to be a good officer. The troops approaching Cawnpore consist of about twelve hundred white troops and four to five hundred Sikhs.

G. A. Henty authored 'Condemned as a Nihilist: A Story of Escape from Siberia', which includes 8 illustrations by Walter Paget. G. A. Henty's 'Orange and Green: A Tale of the Boyne and Limerick' features 8 illustrations by Gordon Browne. George MacDonald wrote 'A Rough Shaking', illustrated by W. Parkinson, and it is described as one of his charming stories. 'At the Back of the North Wind' by George MacDonald includes 75 illustrations by Arthur Hughes. 'Ranald Bannerman's Boyhood' is another work by George MacDonald, featuring 36 illustrations by Arthur Hughes. The Princess and the Goblin and The Princess and Curdie are fairy tales by George MacDonald, both featuring illustrations. J. K. H. Denny's 'The Clever Miss Follett' includes 12 illustrations by Gertrude D. Hammond.

The division of the party is planned to start south. The party will break into six or eight parts and travel in different directions. The sheik intends to travel with his wife and child on camels while others will wait at the wady. The sheik expresses a desire for Yussuf to accompany them, and the matter is settled with the sheik. The Mahdi's officer inspects the divided camels and declares the division just. The sheik instructs his followers to abandon their plans and return to the wady. The sheik plans to journey north with his wife, Muley, and Yussuf to obtain a sum for the surrender of Muley.

Edgar recognized the advice given to him about his prospects for obtaining a commission in the military. He understood that the chances of obtaining a commission were exceedingly small, even for young men with influential fathers. Edgar had not joined the service with the intention of gaining a commission but had a longstanding interest in soldiering. He planned to save a portion of his pay to purchase his discharge if a better opportunity arose by the age of twenty-three or twenty-four. Edgar intended to learn a trade in the regimental workshops, such as saddlery or farriery, to earn a living abroad. He felt he had acted hastily in leaving Cheltenham but would make the same decision under similar circumstances. Edgar wrote monthly letters to Captain Clinton to inform him of his well-being.

Pinkerton is the captain of the house. Easton has never played in any matches at the house before. Edgar Clinton believes Easton is one of the best players on the football team. Glover stated that Easton's exam papers were the best but he only answered the difficult questions. Easton declined to go to India for the last Indian Civil exam. Skinner and others went for a walk that was described as vigorous. Wordsworth was bitten by a dog while crossing a field.

The cavalry were impressed with the formidable nature of their enemies. The Arab tactics involved throwing themselves down to stab horses and then attacking riders. The Royal Highlanders marched out six miles towards Tamai and formed an encampment defended with bushes and wire. The infantry joined the Royal Highlanders the following afternoon. The cavalry moved out the next morning, and the entire force started in the afternoon. The march was slow due to thick bushes and deep sand, making movement difficult. The zareba was completed to provide defense against potential enemy attacks.

The 65th regiment was ordered to hurry up due to a gap between them and the Highlanders. Lieutenant Graham, R.N., and the Naval Brigade attempted to fill the gap with three machine-guns. The enemy charged towards the 65th and the sailors, resulting in a hand-to-hand fight. The cavalry provided support by dismounting and firing into the enemy ranks. General Buller's square advanced and successfully repulsed the enemy attacks. Both brigades reformed and advanced towards a ravine filled with fleeing Arabs. The conflict resulted in the deaths of 120 British soldiers, with significant casualties among the 42d regiment.

Five days have passed since the narrator has been near the prison. The narrator decided to join their group that is fighting their way up. Bathurst observed that the Doctor was glad to meet them but also profoundly depressed. Bathurst learned that every woman and child had been killed that morning. Isobel suffered burns from acid, which she mentioned to the Doctor. The Doctor examined Isobel's injuries and noted that they would leave scars. Bathurst began to recount a story related to an earlier event involving the young Zemindar.

A wild-looking young native approached Edgar while he was on his camel. The native revealed himself to be Rupert, Edgar's brother, who had come to rescue him. Rupert was in disguise, wearing a wig made for him in Cairo. Edgar initially struggled to recognize Rupert due to his appearance. Rupert had obtained leave from Wolseley to search for Edgar after hearing he had been captured. El Bakhat and another Arab were surprised by the meeting between Edgar and Rupert. The group decided to move south-east to avoid pursuing horsemen.

The enemy fought sturdily but was defeated with significant losses, and the Nana's palace was destroyed. After Outram arrived with reinforcements, the volunteers did not accompany the column to Lucknow and were assigned to Cawnpore. The officer in command of the troop died of cholera shortly after Havelock's column departed, and Bathurst succeeded him. The troop faced frequent encounters with the enemy and was disappointed to be left behind when Sir Colin Campbell advanced. During an attack by the mutineers of the Gwallior contingent at Cawnpore, the troop was nearly annihilated but managed to save the 64th. Bathurst rescued Wilson, who had lost his left arm and sustained serious wounds, and Bathurst was later recommended for the Victoria Cross. Bathurst was offered a position as an extra aide de camp to Sir Colin Campbell due to his knowledge of the language.

Edgar struck a tramp with his riding-whip, causing the man to stagger back in pain. The fight between Edgar and the tramps lasted about a minute, ending with one tramp on the ground asking for mercy. Edgar instructed the ladies to go to town and send a man for assistance while he managed the tramps. Three infantry men arrived to assist Edgar after the ladies informed them of the situation. The tramps were subdued and taken to the police station in Aldershot by the soldiers. One of the ladies recognized Edgar as a trumpeter in D troop and expressed gratitude for his help. Major Horsley thanked Edgar for his actions, stating he would remember his gallant conduct.

Mrs. Clinton and Rupert discuss a mark on Rupert's shoulder. The mark is described as a tiny dark-brown mole, not larger than the head of a good-sized pin. Mrs. Clinton expresses doubt that the presence of the mark proves Rupert is their son. Edgar's letter mentions that a woman claimed one of the boys had a small mole on the shoulder. Mrs. Clinton suggests the woman may have been motivated by financial gain. The mark was almost invisible and was not noticed by others after the incident. Mrs. Clinton believes the woman could not produce evidence to support her claim.

Six female attendants carried Isobel downstairs, accompanied by Rabda and the mistress of the zenana. A large palanquin with bearers, four soldiers, and an officer was waiting outside the gate. Rabda was instructed to remain with Isobel and visit her friends in town later. The palanquin was taken to the Subada Ke Kothee, where it was carried across the courtyard to a prison for white women and children. Rabda ordered the bearers to return to Bithoor after setting Isobel down. Mrs. Hunter recognized Isobel and expressed concern for her condition. Rabda provided ointment and lotion to help Isobel, stating that she acted on the orders of Sahib Bathurst.

Bathurst expressed doubt that there would be an attack on officers or harm to women and children. Bathurst has not received any information from the natives regarding potential trouble. A juggler mentioned to Bathurst that he would repay a service with his life, which Bathurst now believes may have significance. The Doctor suggested that the juggler could be a valuable ally due to his connections and knowledge of local affairs. Bathurst planned to leave on horseback at six and then went to his bungalow. The Doctor reflected on Bathurst's serious demeanor and past rumors about him showing fear. The Doctor expressed concern for Bathurst's well-being if conflict were to arise.

The journey from Wady Halfa to Dongola was 235 miles. The day's march was generally about twenty miles, starting around five o'clock in the morning. The men initially walked leading their camels for two hours before riding due to the heat. The troops found the country bordering the Nile to be composed of low rocky hills and hard gravel. The men expressed regret for not bringing fishing equipment for entertainment and dietary variety. The camp site at Korti was appreciated by the men for its groves of palms and cultivated land. The troops crossed the Nile in boats after marching twenty miles up the river.

Bathurst entered a comfortably furnished apartment where a meal was laid out. Bathurst felt the effects of blood loss and anxiety and began to eat heartily. Rujub informed Bathurst that he and his group do not eat meat and live entirely on vegetables. A small native cart with a pony was waiting outside the apartment. Rujub discussed the reports of a force gathering at Allahabad and the British troops' chances against the Nana's forces. Bathurst and Rujub observed groups of people on the road as they traveled towards the palace. Rujub mentioned the strength of the British forces at Allahabad, which included one British regiment and a few other units.

Forster and Bathurst's animals were led out through a breach in the defenses at midnight. The horses' feet were muffled with blankets to avoid detection by enemy sentinels. Forster expressed hope to return in eight or nine days with a squadron of cavalry. After Forster left, there were sounds of gunfire and shouting from the enemy. The Major indicated that the signal had been given, confirming Forster was beyond enemy lines. Isobel and Mrs. Doolan discussed Forster's character and his departure. Isobel and Mrs. Doolan planned to go on duty in the sick ward at four o'clock.

The protagonist has been living in an oasis occupied by his tribe for many years. He is known to have killed a man, but vengeance against him has diminished over time. The protagonist has had conflicts with the Mahdi's people and is currently untraceable. A caravan started its journey to the oasis after a proposal was deemed promising. The caravan arrived at a deserted oasis ten days after leaving Khartoum. The sheik and Rupert discussed the likely route taken by the fugitives, favoring the southern route towards Emin's territory. The sheik planned to disguise Edgar for the next part of their journey.

The juggler may have the ability to read thoughts, although this is not well understood. Captain Doolan observed a scene involving the Doctor masquerading as a native and Bathurst with a native girl. The Doctor expressed uncertainty about the significance of the visions seen during the performance. The Doctor found the tricks performed by the juggler to be perplexing and difficult to understand. There is no known instance of jugglers answering questions about their art, which they treat as a religious mystery. The juggler and the girl disappeared immediately after the performance, leaving no trace behind. Dr. Wade noted that jugglers may perform supernatural feats without accepting payment, often to please a powerful Rajah.

Isobel prefers not to see Bathurst until tomorrow. Bathurst volunteered to join an expedition against a small party of Sepoy cavalry. The expedition started two hours before daybreak and attacked the Sepoys at seven o'clock. The infantry silenced the Sepoys' guns and the enemy fled, leaving their artillery behind. Four infantry members were killed and five volunteers were wounded during the fight. Bathurst sustained a pistol wound to his left arm, which was suspected to be broken. Dr. Wade ordered Bathurst to rest and monitor his wound for signs of fever.

Captain Doolan expresses skepticism about the longevity of youth and beauty in the current climate. The speaker prefers Wilson over Doolan, noting Wilson's potential and current infatuation with Miss Hannay. The speaker believes that having a crush can positively influence a young man's character. Captain Doolan criticizes men who overwork themselves without taking time for leisure. The Doctor suggests that Doolan is unlikely to be driven to extreme measures due to overwork. Doolan reflects on his past experiences under a demanding Captain and expresses contentment with his current workload. Bathurst indicates he is indifferent to horse racing and is ready to sleep.

The Doctor had killed many tigers and was optimistic about the upcoming hunt. Isobel consulted with Mrs. Hunter, the Doctor, and Rumzan regarding food and camping necessities. Two tents were prepared for the trip, one for the gentlemen and one for Isobel and Mary Hunter. Major Hannay expressed concern about Bathurst's absence from their recent gatherings. The group arrived at the camping site after dark, guided by a native with a torch. The dinner was cheerful, and the group was in high spirits despite being on a short camping trip. The tiger had killed a cow the previous day, and the hunt was planned for daylight.

Edgar has lost both his father and mother. Sergeant M'Bride considers himself as Edgar's guardian. Edgar wishes to enlist as a trumpeter. The adjutant is skeptical about Edgar's story. Edgar claims to have been learning the trumpet. The adjutant instructs the sergeant to take Edgar to the doctor for a medical examination. If Edgar passes the medical examination, he will be sworn in the following day.

The Rajah expressed a desire to see Isobel despite warnings about a possible contagious disease. The woman attending Isobel reported that she had been in a torpor and showed signs of a terrible change. The Rajah ordered that Isobel be wrapped in a closed palanquin and taken to the Subada Ke Kothee. Rabda, another woman, believed that Isobel's condition was not contagious and was caused by drugs. Rabda applied cooling ointment to Isobel's sores, which provided her relief. Isobel felt thankful that a plan to send her away was succeeding, likely to a place with other prisoners. Rabda agreed to accompany Isobel to ensure her safety from the Rajah's suspicions.

The craft of juggling is passed down from father to son. The narrator began working with his father as soon as he was able to walk. The narrator is bound by oaths that prevent him from revealing the secrets of their craft. Ralph Bathurst experiences fear at the sound of firearms. Bathurst received a message that Rujub's daughter was too ill to travel. Rujub's daughter recovered from fever after a week. Bathurst declined to see Rujub's juggling performance due to fatigue.

The sergeant died the day after he was found. Two letters were discovered on the sergeant, one addressed to Rupert and one to his father. The letters stated that the sergeant's wife's story was a lie and that he could not identify Rupert or Edgar. Edgar did not reveal himself to Rupert at Korti because he believed the woman's story to be true. Rupert expressed a desire to rescue Edgar after learning he had been taken as a slave. The sheik and Rupert discussed plans to travel to Massowah instead of Egypt or Berber. El Bakhat agreed to the terms of payment for delivering Rupert and Edgar to a port.

Rujub and Rabda entered the room after the evening meal. Rabda has seen and spoken to the lady Hannay, indicating a connection between them. Rabda reported that Hannay is lying quietly and appears to be happy despite having a bandaged face. Rujub instructed Rabda to communicate with Hannay and relay a message of encouragement. Rabda observed eight men sitting around a fire outside the prison, with one looking in at the prisoners. The door to the prison is locked, and the key is in the lock. Bathurst plans to monitor the sentry changes at the prison and gather information about the warders.

The Rajah expressed a desire to win after previous losses. General Wheeler commented on the Rajah's betting habits. The Rajah felt mistreated by the Government and planned to take action against its officers. The Rajah hosted a splendid entertainment for his guests. The Rajah summoned his officers Khoosheal and Imambux after the party. Imambux reported that several messengers had returned, and the Rajah chose to see them immediately. A native in rags reported to the Rajah about his activities in Meerut and the sentiments he spread among the Sepoys.

One of the soldiers had a leg broken above the ankle by an enemy bullet. The sheik instructed the application of splints and bandages to the injured soldier. Four sentries were posted at each corner of the fort during the night. The garrison experienced two false alarms during the night but remained vigilant. The sheik sent a young man to the wady to scout for enemy movement. The blockade lasted for four days with occasional exchanges of gunfire. Eighteen tribesmen arrived to assist the sheik and planned a coordinated attack on the dervishes.

The Heavy Camel Corps and the Naval Brigade formed a square with the Sussex taking the right rear corner. The Naval Brigade was positioned in the center of the rear line with a Gardner gun. Two guns of the Royal Artillery were located behind the fighting line, while camels carried water, ammunition, and cacolets in the center of the square. The square faced increased enemy fire as it moved out, with swarms of natives appearing on the hills. The march was slow to accommodate the guns and camels, and frequent halts were made to attend to the wounded. A number of green and white flags were observed at a distance, which were later revealed to be a mass of Arabs concealed in a gulley. The Arabs charged down upon the square, leading to a hand-to-hand fight after the rear face was driven in.

The group planned to avoid passing Cawnpore due to the perceived danger. The young Rajah agreed to help carry the sick. The plan involved landing at a spot with bushes and young trees to create stretchers. The boats were primarily kept on the left side of the river, but sometimes moved to the right bank due to shallows. The group encountered a hail from the shore while rowing near the right bank. Cannon and musket fire was directed at the boats, resulting in casualties among the rowers. Bathurst and several others jumped overboard and swam to the shore amid the chaos.

Jane Humphreys confused herself and others regarding the identity of her child. She initially believed she could distinguish between the children but became dazed and uncertain. Jane noticed a mole on one child's shoulder after undressing them, which she claimed would have helped her identify them earlier. The situation led to ridicule and conflict within the regiment, with discussions about potential financial gain from the mix-up. Jane admitted to intentionally dressing the children alike and expressed frustration over not recognizing the distinguishing mark. The narrator asserts that Jane did not know which child was hers and that she had not noticed the mark until after the change. Jane claimed that if she had been given more time to think, she would have been able to identify her child.

Captain Forster has a long tawny mustache, dark eyes, and very white teeth. Captain Forster was introduced to Isobel and expressed surprise at finding three unmarried ladies at Deennugghur. Isobel prefers the sociable atmosphere at Deennugghur over the formality of Cawnpore. The Major expressed concern that Captain Forster may not have enough to do in a small station like Deennugghur. Isobel described Captain Forster as very amusing after a pleasant dinner. Captain Forster visited the residents of Deennugghur and left his calling card. The Major confirmed that Bathurst was in the army during the fighting in the Punjaub.

Easton sought information about Trumpeter Smith from surviving officers of Edgar's troop. The officer described Trumpeter Smith as having an excellent character and being well-conducted. Trumpeter Smith came from the Hussars at Cairo and was popular among his regiment. He distinguished himself at El-Teb and was considered for the Victoria Cross. The officer believed Trumpeter Smith was likely captured by Arabs while trying to rejoin his regiment. Easton speculated that Trumpeter Smith might have waited for assistance instead of confronting the Arabs. The officer expressed concern that if Trumpeter Smith was taken prisoner, he might be sent to the Mahdi.

The native army is distributing chupaties and spreading rumors about the government's intentions regarding the cartridges. The man dressed like a trader has traveled through various districts and spoken with many former prisoners. Most of the former prisoners are old and unlikely to return to their previous activities, but they teach their descendants about the profession. The descendants of the Thugs are expected to assist in missions against the British, as they have learned to hate them. The Rajah is informed that the end of British rule is approaching, and the brotherhood will resume their activities. The Rajah believes that the people of India will rise against the British when the Sepoys signal a rebellion.

The Guards are likely to be involved in the upcoming military operation. The chief is expected to remain until Metemmeh is occupied and the boat column is on its way. Stewart will command the desert column during the operation. Easton believes that fighting will occur between Metemmeh and Khartoum. The Mahdi is expected to engage in battle to maintain his influence after previous conflicts. Easton has lost weight since arriving in the hot climate. There are seven or eight other individuals of similar standing present in the area.

The narrator heard about a tiger in the jungle near the village where they slept. The narrator is a juggler traveling through Cawnpore and Allahabad. Rujub's daughter, Rabda, was in danger when a tiger had its foot on her. Ralph Bathurst, a District Officer at Deennugghur, intervened to save Rabda from the tiger. Rujub and Rabda perform together as jugglers and have traveled together since Rabda's mother died five years ago. Bathurst requested Rujub not to speak about the tiger incident in Deennugghur. Rabda felt disoriented after the incident with the tiger.

The battles fought have typically involved two or three Sepoy regiments for every English soldier. The Sepoys believe they are capable of matching the English forces. The narrator expresses uncertainty about the reasons for a potential uprising. Isobel Hannay felt her first dinner party was a great success. The Major and Isobel's uncle returned home at half past twelve after a club event. The first race of the day was scheduled for two o'clock. Mrs. Hunter's carriage arrived at the race inclosure at half past one.

Edgar, also known as Trumpeter Smith, was called to Major Horsley's quarters. Major Horsley expressed gratitude for Edgar's previous service to his wife. Edgar expressed a desire to give up his trumpet to take a regular place in the ranks. Major Horsley advised Edgar against giving up his trumpet at that moment. Edgar wished for the opportunity to go up the Nile with the regiment. Major Horsley informed Edgar that he would be detailed to replace a trumpeter in the Heavy Camel Corps due to illness. The colonel initially thought Edgar was too young, but Major Horsley and the adjutant supported his selection.

Mrs. Clinton observes that Edgar has changed more than Rupert over the past three years. Rupert mentions that he has only had a year and a half of man's work compared to Edgar's three years. Captain Clinton notes that Rupert has widened out in the last year. Lord Wolseley spoke kindly of Edgar and Rupert upon his return to England. Edgar has been recommended for the Victoria Cross and for a commission after serving as a sergeant. Edgar is eligible for a Queen's Cadetship if he passes a qualifying examination in two months. Edgar successfully qualifies for a commission and is gazetted to a regiment stationed at Malta.

Isobel and the two Miss Hunters arrived at a scene filled with a throng of natives in bright colored garments and the scarlet uniforms of the Sepoys of the 103d and other regiments. The scene included native vehicles, elephants with painted faces, and howdahs shaded by pavilions glittering with gilt and silver. A long line of carriages was formed up, occupied by gayly dressed natives with rank that allowed them access to a privileged enclosure. Civilian and military officers in white or light attire filled the space between the carriages, with many others on horseback behind them. Dr. Wade expressed that the assembly was more picturesque than an English racecourse, but Mrs. Hunter noted that the natives might not be more trustworthy than those at home. Dr. Wade described the Oude men as notorious brawlers and fighters, suggesting they could be more dangerous than European roughs. Isobel observed a carriage with a magnificent pair of horses, which was identified by Dr. Wade as belonging to Nana Sahib, the Rajah.

The Major's niece is named Isobel Hannay. Isobel expresses that she does not believe she will fall in love easily. Isobel feels that being in India makes it seem like girls are only appreciated due to a lack of options. The Major's niece is well-received in the regiment, causing rivalry between two young men, Richards and Wilson. Travers, the Senior Captain, acknowledges Isobel as a nice and unaffected girl. Mrs. Doolan expresses relief that her husband is married before Isobel's arrival, fearing he would have fallen in love with her. Mrs. Doolan believes Isobel will have many suitors due to her attractiveness.

Bathurst expressed doubt about the motivations of those fighting, suggesting they are unaware of their true cause. Bathurst stated that the English would ultimately triumph despite the odds against them. Rujub acknowledged that the palace was doomed and initially thought its condition was due to an accident. Rujub explained that he could not prevent the attack on the boats due to prior knowledge of the surrender to the Nana. Rujub revealed that the Rajah ordered the killing of all men and the capture of women and children, except for Miss Hannay. Bathurst inquired about the timing of Rujub's daughter’s arrival, expressing concern about the wait.

The text lists several books by G. A. Henty, each accompanied by illustrations and published in crown 8vo format with cloth binding and olivine edges. The first book mentioned is 'Ronald', which features a hero similar to that of 'Quentin Durward' and includes a narrative of a journey across France. The second book is 'For the Temple: A Tale of the Fall of Jerusalem', which includes 10 illustrations by S. J. Solomon and a colored map. The third book is 'True to the Old Flag: A Tale of the American War of Independence', featuring 12 illustrations by Gordon Browne. The fourth book is 'The Lion of the North: A Tale of Gustavus Adolphus and the Wars of Religion', illustrated by J. Schönberg. The fifth book is 'The Young Carthaginian: A story of the Times of Hannibal', illustrated by C. J. Staniland. The sixth book is 'With Wolfe in Canada: Or, The Winning of a Continent', also illustrated by Gordon Browne.

The sheik decided to implement a plan to defend the zareba. The inhabitants of the douar were ordered to prepare for the defense. The zareba was constructed using bundles of grass and thorny bushes. The construction of the zareba was completed just as daylight broke. An Arab scout named Yussuf reported that the enemy would start their march that morning. The enemy was unable to remain in their current location due to limited food supplies for their camels. The sheik and Edgar selected a suitable location for the zareba on a patch of rock.

The leader of the party in the district and several Zemindars are expected to arrive with guns soon. The native troops at Cawnpore mutinied and were joined by Nana Sahib, who persuaded them to attack the whites. The Doctor expressed disgust at Nana Sahib's betrayal after years of friendship. Bathurst reported that the danger during his scout was slight and wished he had better news. The defenders gathered on the roof of the house, where lamps were placed and the garrison was grouped. Bathurst was warmly greeted by Major and Wilson upon his return. Bathurst successfully navigated past sentries to gather information without difficulty.

Easton asked Clinton if the substance on his skin would wash off. Clinton stated that the substance could be removed with some difficulty and mentioned he had another that needed renewing every week or ten days. Rupert cleaned his face and hands and put on his uniform. Rupert informed Easton about Major Kitchener's arrangements and the purchase of fast camels. Easton advised Clinton to take revolvers for protection during his escape. Clinton agreed to take a revolver and Easton offered him his spare one. Rupert confirmed that they were to retire to Wady Halfa, leading Easton to express strong disapproval of abandoning Dongola.

A staff officer informed Rupert and his aides-de-camp that Khartoum had fallen and Gordon was murdered. The Mahdi's flags were flying in Khartoum, and Wilson's steamers ran aground. Beresford was assigned to rescue the party if he could fight past the batteries. The news of the fall of Khartoum quickly spread among the officers, leading to feelings of grief and indignation. The expedition was criticized for its inefficiency and the wasted resources spent on it. There was a debate among the officers about whether to continue the expedition or withdraw. Rupert feared that the expedition would be abandoned, leaving his brother Edgar in danger.

Edgar received a helmet and other equipment to join the Heavy Camel Corps. The Heavy Camel Corps consists of men from the 1st and 2d Life Guards, Blues, Bays, 4th and 5th Dragoon Guards, Royals, Scots Greys, and 5th and 16th Lancers. Edgar felt smaller compared to the larger men of the heavy cavalry regiments. Edgar was assigned to share a tent with a soldier named Willcox. Edgar has been in the region for about a year and participated in the fighting at Suakim. Edgar was informed that they would be getting camels up the river at Assouan. Willcox is a member of the 5th Dragoon Guards and expressed relief at the opportunity for a change from home stations.

The fire was gradually suppressed by evening. The work of filling sandbags was completed, and doors and windows were barricaded. The dinner party was initially silent due to exhaustion but became more cheerful as the meal progressed. The native servants prepared the dinner table with care, and the cook made an excellent dinner. Isobel Hannay and Mrs. Rintoul contributed significantly to the defense by sewing sandbags. Captain Forster expressed concern about Bathurst's nervousness during the firing. Isobel Hannay defended Bathurst, stating it must be terrible to be so nervous.

The troops constructed a zareba after a short march in great heat and dust. Commander Rolfe of the Royal Navy observed the enemy and reported no immediate attack was planned. The troops were allowed to rest after Rolfe's report, while the cavalry signaled that all was quiet. At one o'clock in the morning, the enemy opened fire, but the majority of the bullets passed overhead. One man was killed and three others were wounded during the enemy's attack. After the enemy's fire diminished, the troops had breakfast and the cavalry arrived from another zareba. The infantry, commanded by General Davis and General Buller, advanced in two squares against the enemy.

Wilson's party experienced anxiety regarding the return of a steamer due to a strong battery below the spot where it had been lost. The steamer was delayed in returning, leading to heightened fears for its safety. Smoke was eventually seen ascending from the river, indicating the steamer's return, which was met with cheers from the men. The steamer had a narrow escape after engaging with artillery, sustaining damage to her boiler and having to anchor. Sir Charles Wilson's party was engaged with enemy forces while observing the steamer's situation and attempted to divert attention from it. General Buller and the 18th Royal Irish arrived on February 10th, but their purpose was to cover the retreat rather than continue the expedition. The entire force evacuated the forts and began their march down to Korti on foot due to a lack of camels.

The defenders observed an excited and violent discussion among the assailants. Fifteen assailants were killed, while two defenders, an old man and a boy, had fallen. The sheik asked Edgar to bandage his shoulder, which Edgar did using cotton cloth. The assailants began to scatter over the sand-hills and opened fire at the fort. The sheik believed the assailants would not make another daytime attack due to their numbers and injuries. The sheik speculated that the assailants would send camels back to the wells for water. The defenders planned to ration their water supply to last for nearly a fortnight.

The fuel used in the camp consisted almost entirely of dried camels' dung. Edgar collected fuel from the oasis using a rough basket. Amina expressed satisfaction with Edgar's work and rewarded him with a calabash of meal. Edgar assisted the negroes in watering a plantation of maize by drawing water from a well. A conflict arose when a negro insulted Edgar, leading to Edgar striking the negro. The sheik responded favorably to Edgar's explanation of the incident. Amina defended Edgar, stating he was a Hakim and had saved a child's life.

The tribe is encamped in a wady two days' journey to the north. Hamish is crucial for guiding the party to Wady El Bahr Nile. The encampment has been in place for six months due to the siege of Khartoum. Trade has been halted because of the siege, affecting the tribe's plans. There is uncertainty about the current control of Khartoum. The Mahdi's presence has disrupted trade and caused destruction in the region. The tribes are unable to unite against the Mahdi due to internal conflicts.

Edgar reflects on his decision to run away and expresses regret for not waiting to hear from Captain Clinton. Edgar believes that he cannot unsettle the relationship between Captain Clinton and his wife and Rupert. Edgar states that he does not consider himself the child of the woman who deceived him. Edgar acknowledges Captain Clinton and his wife as his parents until he ran away. Edgar has received a good education and has made friends in his regiment who support his advancement. Edgar was recommended for the Victoria Cross, which he believes will positively impact his future. The sergeant expresses confidence in Edgar's character, regardless of his parentage.

The regiment was disembarked at Assouan. Four companies went up in two steamers to Wady Halfa, which is one hundred and eighty miles higher up the river. The soldiers received their equipment and saddles at Wady Halfa. The camels used by the soldiers were collected from various locations in Egypt, Aden, and Arabia. The soldiers experienced difficulties in mounting and dismounting the camels, which had to kneel for these actions. Edgar expressed dissatisfaction with the camels after several days of training. The soldiers spent several days learning to ride the camels, resulting in many falls but no serious injuries.

The Major assisted in helping an injured individual up after a recent attack. Richards reported being hit in the right shoulder by a bullet during the attack. The Major confirmed that nobody else was seriously injured during the encounter. Mary Hunter informed the group that the enemy had retreated after the attack was repulsed. The Major ordered champagne to celebrate the successful defense against the enemy. Captain Forster sustained a bayonet wound while attempting to assist Bathurst during the fight. Bathurst was noted for his strong performance in battle, and it was believed he was not injured.

A woman met Edgar and claimed that he was her son, not the son of his current parents. The woman identified Edgar by a small mole on his shoulder, which he confirmed belonged to Rupert. The woman admitted to orchestrating a fraud to benefit Edgar and proposed that he should remain silent about it. Edgar expressed his distress over the situation and decided to leave his current family. He thanked his parents for their love and kindness, despite feeling that it was based on a deception. Rupert and Madge struggled to cope with Edgar's letter and their father's suggestion to discuss the matter calmly. Captain Clinton indicated the need to find Edgar, noting he had a twenty-four hour head start.

A Sowar delivered a letter from the Colonel to the Major regarding the 19th Native Infantry at Berhampore. The 19th Native Infantry refused to use the cartridges served to them. A Sepoy of the 34th at Barrackpore raised seditious cries and wounded the adjutant and sergeant major. The 19th Native Infantry is to be disbanded, and the 34th is likely to face the same fate. The Doctor and the Major discussed the potential for general disaffection among the troops. The Doctor expressed uncertainty about understanding the Hindoo mind and their true character. Bathurst had not seen Forster since he arrived and mentioned their past school relationship.

The gardens were illuminated by lanterns and lamps along the paths and around a large pond. The Palace or Castle was located behind the gardens and featured Oriental architecture. The crowd on the terrace consisted mainly of English men in uniform and evening dress, along with many ladies. A band from the 103d Bengal Infantry played music at one end of the terrace, followed by native musicians at the opposite end. The Rajah hosted a successful event that included a banquet, a native nautch, fireworks, and supper. The Rajah was known for his English tastes, socializing with officers, and hosting gatherings at his residence in Bithoor. The Rajah expressed a desire to win a horse race and was ready to wager on his newly acquired horse.

The party traveled with camels and stopped at a small pool after nightfall. Ben Ibyn indicated that they were on high land and would reach the mountains by the next night. The group needed to find the pass from Kassala to Massowah to ensure their safety. El Bakhat estimated that the gorge was three or four days' journey from Kassala with laden camels. The party decided not to proceed due to the risk of encountering horsemen from Kassala. They planned to travel north to reach Suakim instead of Massowah. The inhabitants of the villages they passed fled upon seeing the party.

The individual had a headache and preferred to be quiet and undisturbed. He did not wear his boots to the dormitory and placed them in the wood-closet rack. The boot-boy observed that the No. 6 rack was empty when he went to clean the boots. One of the servants reported that a window downstairs was open despite having closed it the previous night. The door to the yard had been unbolted and the lock appeared to have been forced. Rupert was advised to visit his father instead of sending a telegram regarding his brother. There were no letters for the brother in the afternoon mail.

The upper story of the fortified house was damaged by gunfire over the course of four days. The gate of the house was destroyed, and a gap in the wall was increasing in size due to enemy fire. Several casualties occurred, including the death of Herbert and serious injuries to Captain Rintoul. Mr. Hunter suffered from fever due to sun exposure, and several others were wounded by stone fragments. The defenders maintained steady fire despite heavy losses among the native gunners. Mrs. Rintoul displayed calmness and courage while assisting with the sick children, even after her husband was wounded. The Major instructed the Doctor and Farquharson to remain on the roof in preparation for a potential enemy attack.

The women of the regiment believed that Jane Humphreys had a clever plan regarding the change of children. Mrs. Humphreys remained mostly confined to her room after the incident. Captain Clinton and his wife received significant sympathy from the officers and their families. A discussion took place among the officers regarding maternal instinct and the ability to recognize one's own child. The doctor explained that human beings lack the strong sense of smell that animals possess for recognizing their offspring. The major expressed concern about Captain Clinton's uncertainty regarding the inheritance of his estate. The doctor suggested that Captain Clinton raise both children as his own until a resemblance develops.

Good looking men are perceived as less pleasant than others. A good looking man on board a ship was described as dull. The speaker does not mean all good looking men, but those who consciously pursue good looks. Wilson and Richards had a close race for third place, resulting in a dead heat. Major Hannay commented on the amusement of the race outcome. The race for Arabs featured the Rajah of Bithoor's horse as the favorite. Prothero's horse was also well supported due to the Adjutant's reputation as a rider.

The match involved two teams, the River-Smithites and the Greenites. The River-Smithites aimed to press the Greenites hard during the first half of the game. At halftime, neither team had scored a point. Edgar Clinton of the River-Smithites successfully carried the ball behind the Greenite goal. The umpire ruled in favor of the River-Smithites after a disputed play. The Greenites appealed the umpire's decision to the referee, who confirmed it. The game resumed after the Greenites initially attempted to leave the field.

The troops formed up for the night on rising ground near the wells after satisfying their thirst. Three hundred men volunteered to march back to the zareba to retrieve baggage before daylight. The men had no blankets and only their shirts and thin serge suits to protect them from the cold. A herd of lean cattle left by the Arabs was discovered, and some were shot for fresh meat. The baggage train arrived at seven o'clock, and the men prepared breakfast after a long period without food. The force set out for the river at four o'clock, with a distance of twenty-six miles to cover. The guides disagreed on the route, causing confusion and difficulties for the baggage animals.

The Major expressed irritation over Isobel's apparent enjoyment of Captain Forster's company. Bathurst had not been seen for over a fortnight before he arrived late one evening. Bathurst and Captain Forster were previously schoolmates but had not met since then. Isobel greeted Bathurst and commented on his busy schedule before engaging in conversation with Captain Forster. Captain Forster observed Isobel's reaction to Bathurst and speculated about a past flirtation between them. The Major approved the planned tiger hunt after a period of calm at the stations. Bathurst declined to join the tiger hunt party, which included several other individuals.

The men slept quietly despite the noise and firing from the enemy. Only two men were hit during the night due to the random firing of the Arabs. The number of enemy forces on the hilltops increased overnight. The men had breakfast consisting of tinned meat and biscuits. Major Dickson was shot through the knee, and Major Gough was knocked senseless by a bullet. Orders were issued for the men to prepare for action and to capture the wells. The Guards' Camel Corps and the Mounted Infantry formed the front of the square.

The Doctor and Bathurst discussed their experiences of jumping overboard during a crisis. Bathurst expressed regret for leaving Isobel Hannay, the woman he loved, behind when he jumped. Bathurst believed he acted out of fear and selfishness, abandoning Isobel to her fate. The Doctor reassured Bathurst that jumping overboard was a common instinct for survival. The Doctor argued that Bathurst's actions ultimately allowed for Isobel's rescue. Bathurst acknowledged Isobel's rescue but still felt guilt for his actions. The Doctor reacted with anger towards a villain who had taken Isobel to Bithoor.

The characters experience a sense of passion and a desire to kill during a fight. Miss Hannay stood up in excitement during the fight. The Doctor believes that a future scene they saw together will come true. Forster is leaving, and Wilson informed Bathurst about it. Bathurst expresses surprise at Forster's decision to volunteer. The Doctor has not asked Miss Hannay about her feelings for Forster. The Doctor advises Bathurst to focus on their current situation and remain vigilant.

Rupert expressed his readiness to travel to Khartoum to bring news to his lord. Major Kitchener declined to send anyone to Khartoum at that time. Major Kitchener initially did not recognize Rupert and was surprised to see him. A sheik and two natives were engaged in a heated discussion when Major Kitchener and Rupert approached. The sheik accused his followers of being unable to recognize a disguised white man. Major Kitchener explained that the sheik was trying to convince his men that whites could disguise themselves. Rupert revealed his closely-cropped hair after removing his wig, surprising the natives.

The rooms were occupied by ladies, their ayahs, and children, with one room designated as a nursery. Two rooms were allocated for the ladies and two for the men, while the courtroom served as a general meeting and dining room. Servants were monitored by their masters as they transported goods to a large underground room for sorting. Isobel Hannay and the two Miss Hunters were assigned to prepare a fire and boiling water for coffee. Captain Forster remained in his tent, prepared to charge the mutinous infantry if necessary. Most servants chose to stay with their masters, while only eight or ten opted to return to their villages. At daylight, the Major and his officers rode towards the parade ground, while others prepared muskets on the roof.

G. A. Henty is the author of several adventure novels for boys. The books include illustrations by various artists such as Alfred Pearse and Gordon Browne. Titles of Henty's works include 'Redskin and Cow-boy', 'The Dash for Khartoum', and 'By Right of Conquest'. Many of Henty's stories are set in historical contexts, such as the American Civil War and the rise of the Dutch Republic. Henty's books are noted for their engaging plots and vivid depictions of life during the periods they cover. The novels are published in crown 8vo format with cloth binding and olivine edges. Henty's works have received positive reviews from various publications, highlighting their appeal to young readers.

A Little English Gentleman is written by JANE DEAKIN. The Doctor's Lass is written by L. E. TIDDEMAN. Spark and I is a story told by a cat and is written by ANNIE ARMSTRONG. What Hilda Saw is written by PENELOPE LESLIE. Little Miss Masterful is written by L. E. TIDDEMAN. A Sprig of Honeysuckle: A Story of Epping Forest is written by GEORGINA M. SQUIRE. An Australian Childhood is written by ELLEN CAMPBELL.

Rupert has a letter from his father authorizing him to draw money for his plans. Rupert intends to rescue his brother Edgar from slavery among the Arabs. Lord Wolseley grants Rupert leave to carry out his rescue plan. Major Kitchener agrees to help Rupert procure camels and arrange for a sheik. Rupert plans to go to Dongola to lay in a stock of dye. Skinner is surprised to find a native sitting in his hut after returning from a ride.

The Doctor and the narrator discussed a Hindoo who stepped out of the wood, believing it to be the narrator. The narrator and the Doctor were uncertain if the Hindoo girl was the girl they were speaking about. The Doctor was recognized by Isobel Hannay when she saw him along the road. Bathurst introduced himself to the Doctor, who expressed gratitude for their survival. The Doctor explained that he jumped overboard when attacked and swam to safety. The Doctor waited until morning to leave his hiding place after hearing the attackers depart. The Doctor received help from a grateful peasant whom he had previously treated.

The group is concerned about passing Cawnpore safely. There is a belief that the lower they go on the river, the less likely they are to be disturbed by the natives. The Major's wound is causing concern among the group, with doubts about his recovery. Bathurst expresses a wish to change places with the Major due to his kindness. Wilson joins the conversation and mentions the heat and the work the ladies are doing. Wilson feels uneasy about the quietness after weeks of cannon fire and expresses doubt about being able to sleep. The group anticipates a cramped journey in the boats to Allahabad.

Madge and Rupert decided to go for a walk while waiting for a letter. Captain Clinton suggested that Madge's mother lie down until the letter arrived. Madge and Rupert expressed their feelings about Edgar, whom they considered their brother regardless of his parentage. Madge was confused about why Edgar ran away after learning he was adopted. Rupert speculated that Edgar might have thought he was adopted due to circumstances beyond his parents' control. Captain Clinton went to meet the groom who was bringing the letter. The letter revealed that there was a strong opinion that the confusion between the children was deliberate.

Three guns maintained a steady fire at the gate. The besieged engaged in a constant duel with the guns and occasionally targeted men in trees or on building roofs. Wilson was relieved from his duties in the gallery, with Bathurst taking over the task of removing earth. Wilson observed Bathurst holding up timber to prevent it from falling. Isobel noted that Wilson was the only lady who did not engage in conversation with Bathurst. Wilson expressed a strong dislike for Captain Forster and a fondness for Bathurst. Isobel clarified that Bathurst's reduced visits were due to reasons unrelated to Captain Forster.

A Bible was brought for the dying man to place his hand upon while he made a declaration. The dying man stated that he did not know whether Trumpeter Smith or Lieutenant Clinton was his son. The surgeon witnessed the dying man's declaration and signed his name as a witness. Rupert sought advice from Easton regarding steps to learn more about Edgar. Easton suggested that Rupert inform the commanding officer about the trumpeter being his brother and request a search for his body. The colonel promised to take steps to ascertain the fate of Rupert's brother and to recover him if alive. The next day, there was a significant outburst of firing in Metemmeh, believed to be related to a festival of the Mahdi.

The soldiers were engaged in a chaotic battle against the Arabs, with camels complicating the situation. The officers' commands were drowned out by the noise of musketry and the shouts of men. The Mounted Infantry and Marines opened fire on the Arabs while the Heavies fought hand-to-hand. The battle ended quickly, with the attackers suffering heavy casualties and retreating. The ground was covered with bodies of both the natives and soldiers from the 4th and 5th Dragoon Guards, Naval Brigade, 1st and 2d Life Guards, and the Sussex. Nine officers were killed and nine wounded, primarily from the Heavy Camel Regiment, along with eighty rank and file killed and over a hundred wounded. Colonel Burnaby and several other officers from the Heavies were among the dead, while many weapons were left scattered on the battlefield.

The Doctor examined a tiger that had been killed and noted it had three wounds. The tiger had one fatal wound in the chest and two others in the ribs. The Doctor mentioned that hitting a tiger at night is difficult due to visibility issues. Wilson commented that the tiger had been fine in its time, despite its damaged skin. The Doctor explained that man-eating tigers are often old and may suffer from poor health. Upon returning to the village, the Doctor and the subalterns were greeted with joy by the women. The Doctor had arranged for food to be prepared in anticipation of their return.

A battery was being erected some distance back, masked by trees. Isobel Hannay spoke to Mr. Wilson about his work as a miner. Mr. Wilson reported losing half a stone in weight due to his work. Mr. Wilson and Bathurst drove a hole five yards deep, referring to it as a gallery. Isobel Hannay expressed a desire to work on something after finishing with bags and bandages. The Major reported hearing sounds of axes and falling trees during the night. At daylight, a battery with embrasures for six guns was observed about four hundred yards from the house.

Robinson Crusoe is illustrated by Gordon Browne and published in a new edition. Gulliver's Travels is also illustrated by Gordon Browne and published in a new edition. Patience Wins: or, War in the Works is written by George Manville Fenn and includes 6 page illustrations. Mother Carey's Chicken: Her Voyage to the Unknown Isle is written by G. Manville Fenn and includes illustrations by A. Forestier. The Missing Merchantman is written by Harry Collingwood and includes illustrations by W. H. Overend. The Rover's Secret: A Tale of the Pirate Cays and Lagoons of Cuba is written by Harry Collingwood and includes illustrations by W. C. Symons. Girl Neighbours: or, The Old Fashion and the New is written by Sarah Tytler and includes illustrations by C. T. Garland.

Edgar is thirty-seven years old and Rupert is forty years old. Rupert mentions that neither he nor Edgar has reached their full width yet. Easton is described as a big fellow and a real friend to Rupert. Edgar has been in Cairo for nearly a year and has picked up the language quickly. Rupert studied maps thoroughly before starting his journey and plans to travel down by Kassala. Massowah is identified as the best place to reach for assistance. Rupert's conductor has brought enough merchandise to pay for food and shelter during their journey.

Dr. Wade warns Miss Hannay that Bathurst is a monomaniac. Dr. Wade believes Bathurst's earnestness harms his prospects and utility. Officials prefer subordinates who follow regulations without questioning. Dr. Wade thinks change in India must come gradually and from the natives themselves. Isobel feels disappointed by the lack of definite work upon her arrival in Cawnpore. Bathurst's remarks resonate with Isobel, opening her thoughts to deeper issues. Isobel notices that the native population is rarely mentioned in conversations.

Mr. Hunter described Bathurst as a fine young fellow, full of energy, and the best linguist in Oude. Bathurst does not engage in activities such as shooting or pig sticking and primarily focuses on work. Mr. Hunter has known Bathurst for six years and believes he has a fine character despite his unusual reserve. Bathurst has been in conflict with the Chief Commissioner on multiple occasions due to his strong opinions. Bathurst is perceived as impractical by some, with one individual referring to him as a knight errant. Men like Bathurst, who challenge unfair decisions, are often disliked by higher officials but can succeed in the long run. Upon arriving at Narkeet, Bathurst was informed by local head men about a tiger that had been heard roaring nearby.

Captain Forster was unaware of the Major's true feelings about Mr. Bathurst. The Major believes Mr. Bathurst is a rising young officer and is friends with Dr. Wade. Captain Forster had a negative impression of Mr. Bathurst from their time at school. Isobel expressed a high opinion of Dr. Wade, describing him as kind and helpful. Captain Forster made comments about Mr. Bathurst that upset both the Major and Isobel. Isobel did not like Captain Forster's remarks about Dr. Wade and Mr. Bathurst. Dr. Wade did not immediately confirm or deny the story about Mr. Bathurst leaving the army.

The Universe: Or The Infinitely Great and the Infinitely Little is authored by F. A. Pouchet, M.D. The Universe includes 272 engravings, with 55 being full-page size and a coloured frontispiece. The Wreck of 'The Golden Fleece' is written by Robert Leighton and features 8 illustrations by Frank Brangwyn. The Pilots of Pomona is another work by Robert Leighton, illustrated by John Leighton and includes a map. The Thirsty Sword: A Story of the Norse Invasion of Scotland is also authored by Robert Leighton and includes illustrations by Alfred Pearse. Quicksilver: Or, A Boy with no Skid to his Wheel is written by George Manville Fenn and features 10 illustrations by Frank Dadd. Dick O' the Fens: A Romance of the Great East Swamp is another book by George Manville Fenn, illustrated by Frank Dadd.

The text discusses various books and their reviews from different publications. Stories of the Sea is noted for its collection of maritime peril and suffering. An Unexpected Hero is highlighted as one of the best in Blackie's Two-Shilling Series. The Bushranger's Secret is praised for its plot and dramatic intensity. The Wreck of the 'Nancy Bell' is described as exciting and character-building. Bab: or, The Triumph of Unselfishness is recommended for children. Insect Ways on Summer Days is noted for being instructive and well-illustrated.

The Doctor and Richards discussed the possibility of taking action against a group they perceived as a threat. Bathurst had the task of informing others about an imminent danger, which was received with calmness. The group at Major Hannay's decided to stay and face the situation rather than attempt to escape. Major Hannay believed that staying put offered the best chances for survival until help arrived. Arrangements were made for the group to move to the courthouse for safety. Captain Forster disagreed with the plan to stay in the courthouse and suggested attempting to escape to Allahabad. The servants were given the option to stay with their masters or leave in the morning.

Isobel expressed indifference towards her standing in Cawnpore society. Isobel refused to attend an entertainment hosted by the Nana, citing a headache and discomfort with social gatherings. Major Hannay and Dr. Wade attended the Nana's entertainment without Isobel. Dr. Wade wanted to observe the Nana due to concerns about rumors of disaffection among the Sepoys. The Nana expressed regret over Isobel's absence and planned to inquire about her health the following day. The Nana appeared courteous but was noted to be irritable with his own people during the event. Isobel stated that she was not accustomed to much society in England and preferred to stay at home.

Rupert expresses concern about the whereabouts of Edgar. Clinton has not received any new information about Edgar, except for occasional letters stating he is well. Rupert believes Edgar is likely in the army and that a woman's statement about him was false. Skinner recalls Edgar's determination during a previous football match. Easton has given up wearing white shirts while in the Guards and has switched to flannels. Skinner joined the Marines due to a family connection and a preference for the sea. Rupert suggests that there may be a military move involving the Camel Corps soon.

The Dragoon troop suffered the heaviest loss. Easton and Rupert went to the new fort by the river to inquire about the troop. Easton asked a sergeant about the trumpeter of the Dragoon troop. The trumpeter was wounded at Abu Klea but was missing after the night march. Sergeant Bowen was found and brought in badly wounded. Easton informed Rupert that the trumpeter was missing and likely captured by Arabs. Easton suggested that the chances of the trumpeter being taken prisoner were as great as him being killed.

The young officer must be careful in his movements and speech to avoid detection as a spy. Major Kitchener and the sheik discuss the terms of the young officer's involvement. Rupert practices Arabic salutations and phrases to communicate with the sheik. The sheik approves of Rupert's ability to pass through a village without raising suspicion. Major Kitchener negotiates the terms regarding camels with the sheik. Rupert believes that the promise of camels will encourage the sheik to remain faithful. The young officer was highly recommended by Egyptian merchants in Cairo.

The Subada Ke Kothee is a large quadrangle with no windows on the outside. The main gate of the Subada Ke Kothee is guarded at night by two sentries outside. There is a strong guard within the Subada Ke Kothee. Rujub believes it would be too dangerous to attempt to bribe the guards. Rujub plans to go to Bithoor to speak with the Nana. The Subada Ke Kothee has a strong high wall forming one side of the square. Two sentries in red Sepoy uniform were observed at the gate of the Subada Ke Kothee.

The regiment left Aldershot and traveled by rail to Southampton. The regiment embarked on a transport ship that departed the following morning. The voyage to Alexandria took twelve days and was described as pleasant. Upon arrival in Alexandria, the regiment received news of General Baker's defeat near Tokar. The regiment proceeded to Cairo by train to take over barracks and horses. An expedition was planned to be sent to Suakim after the regiment's arrival in Cairo. The soldiers explored Cairo and noted the diverse population and local customs.

John Humphreys, now known as John Bowen, asserts that his wife's statement was a lie. John Humphreys claims his wife did not know which child was which and discovered a mark on the shoulder after the babies were mixed up. John Humphreys states that his wife intended to profit from the situation but could not identify her children. Rupert Clinton expresses relief that there has been no change in his relationship with Captain Clinton. Rupert Clinton learns from the doctor that Troop-sergeant Matthews is dying. Rupert Clinton seeks to speak with Troop-sergeant Matthews before he dies. Troop-sergeant Matthews confirms the existence of a letter and wishes to swear its contents are true.

The enemy's batteries intensified their attack the morning after the initial assault. The besieged faced worsening conditions over six days, with breaches in the wall and constant firing. The number of besiegers increased, including local country people and a regiment of Sepoys from Cawnpore. The defenders suffered casualties, with only six remaining able to carry arms, and several civilians and children also died. The defenders had constructed hand grenades to repel enemy assaults, which were effective in causing the enemy to retreat. The defenders were unable to consider flight due to their weakened condition and the ongoing siege. On the last day of the siege, Major Hannay was severely wounded, and discussions about surrender began among the defenders.

Mrs. Hannay expressed doubt about the happiness of having Isobel stay at home. Mrs. Hannay did not want her brother's money to go to a hospital for black women. Isobel's plan to become a governess was strongly opposed by Mrs. Hannay and Helena. Captain Hannay mentioned that his pay was sufficient for his needs but he had not saved much. Mrs. Hannay complained about the financial disparity between military and civilian pay. Dr. Wade was asked by Captain Hannay to take charge of Isobel during her voyage. Mrs. Hannay objected to Dr. Wade's comments about Helena's health.

The courthouse is rarely used and is suggested as a new headquarters. There are five cases of muskets and a considerable stock of ammunition in a small magazine. The plan is to move the muskets to the courthouse that night. The Commandant of the Hospital expresses contentment with his position and the potential of the house as a fortress. The Major believes that with the assistance of the Rajah of Bithoor, Cawnpore is safe from a general rising. A dispatch from the Colonel confirms rumors about Delhi, including the mutiny of regiments and the murder of Europeans. The native regiments in the Punjaub rose after news from Meerut and Delhi, but white troops responded effectively.

Captain Moffat's team scored seventy-four runs without a separation being made. Edgar had not bowled that season but had previously bowled fairly well. Edgar took the ball after Captain Moffat decided to try him at bowling. Edgar took seven wickets for twelve runs in the first innings. Edgar scored twenty-four runs before being caught out in the second innings. The Rifles scored seventy-six runs, falling short of the eighty-one runs needed to win. Edgar's bowling contributed to the Hussar team standing at the head of the Aldershot teams.

Bathurst proposed to begin mining immediately by driving a gallery from the cellar. The team aimed to extend the gallery fifty to a hundred yards beyond the wall towards a clump of bushes in Farquharson's compound. Bathurst suggested leaving a long fuse burning in the magazine to create an explosion after their departure. The operation would involve two people per shift, with three shifts working around the clock. Bathurst was appointed to take charge of the operation, assisted by Wilson, Richards, Saunderson, Austin, and Herbert. Twelve native servants volunteered for the work in exchange for half a rupee extra per day. The team began breaking through the wall and confirmed that the soil was earth, not rock.

The men found daytime journeys less fatiguing than nighttime ones. They aimed to reach the wells of Abu Klea by evening. The troops halted at eleven in a valley flanked by hills. The general ordered the men to fall in after receiving news of the enemy's presence. The enemy was discovered in large numbers on the hill, prepared to block the way to the wells. A halt for the night was ordered due to the unknown strength of the enemy and limited daylight. The enemy opened fire from a hill while the troops prepared to defend their position.

Nineteen out of twenty individuals will break down or become mere machines without a hobby. Every man ought to have some sort of hobby to take an interest in. Captain Doolan has plenty of enthusiasm but lacks stimulating activities. Life in a native regiment in India involves limited duties compared to civilian work. Captain Doolan expressed willingness to share civil work if pay was more equitable. The Doctor believes the pay disparity between military and civilian personnel is excessive. Captain Doolan's marriage has positively influenced his behavior and lifestyle.

The characters discuss their discomfort with wearing dress clothes in a hot climate. Bathurst expresses admiration for Miss Hannay, describing her as charming, pretty, bright, frank, and natural. Bathurst feels a strong conviction that he has met Miss Hannay before, despite the Doctor's assertion that it is impossible. The Doctor mentions a tradition regarding chupaties being sent among native troops and expresses concern about potential unrest. Bathurst observes no change in the natives' behavior and believes there is no widespread dissatisfaction among them. The Doctor warns that if there is discontent among the Sepoys, it could lead to a serious situation due to insufficient white troops in India. Bathurst argues that the Sepoys have everything to lose by rising against the British.

Edgar divided milk and dates with others in the encampment. Edgar, referred to as Muley, shares his provisions even with Hamish, who has not forgiven him for a previous altercation. Amina observes that another worker does more than the others and helps Edgar with language learning. Edgar made significant progress in the local language within two months, aided by prior knowledge from Suakim and Cairo. Hamish went missing one morning, and it was discovered that the best camel and two water-skins had been stolen. The sheik accused another negro of complicity in Hamish's flight and prepared to pursue him after suspecting he would report Edgar's status as a slave. The sheik ordered the loading of camels with valuables and crops to prepare for a potential escape from the encampment.

Isobel was summoned to Mrs. Hannay's room after returning to school. Mrs. Hannay received a negative report about Isobel from her mother. Isobel expressed that her family does not treat her brother Robert well due to his deformity. Isobel feels a strong emotional connection to Robert and is distressed by his treatment. Miss Virtue advised Isobel that it is not appropriate for her to judge her mother. Isobel expressed a desire to write to her Uncle Tom about Robert's education. Miss Virtue cautioned Isobel against writing in a disrespectful manner to her uncle.

Richards is eager to discuss the odds on some horses. The Major inquires if the Doctor will attend the racecourse. The Doctor expresses that one day at the racecourse is sufficient for him. Isobel expresses disappointment at Bathurst's sudden departure. The party attends an entertainment at Bithoor, where Isobel admires the gardens and palace. Isobel feels uncomfortable with the Rajah's attention during the evening. The Doctor mentions that the Rajah is a connoisseur of English beauty.

Rujub, the Juggler is an historical tale set during the Sepoy Mutiny in India from 1857 to 1859. The Sepoy Mutiny occurred under British rule, which was led by Lord Canning at the time. The first outbreak of the mutiny took place at Meerut, where native troops rebelled against the British. The Rajah at Bithoor secretly plotted against the English, leading to the surrender of General Wheeler at Cawnpore. The mutiny resulted in the deaths of thousands and threatened British rule in India. General Havelock and Sir Colin Campbell played key roles in relieving besieged Europeans in Lucknow. Rujub, the juggler, is a significant character in the story, known for his mysterious performances and friendship with the hero.

Bathurst is investigating a land dispute involving an irrigation ditch mentioned in the Talookdar's grant. He plans to review village records and question several of the oldest inhabitants. Bathurst listened to the statements of the villagers and cross-questioned them for accuracy. He spent two hours examining the land to determine which irrigation ditch was referenced in the records. The head man expressed confidence in their claim, but Bathurst noted conflicting evidence from both sides. Bathurst intends to meet with the Talookdar to discuss a potential compromise to resolve the dispute. A Rough Road: or, How the Boy Made a Man of Himself is written by Mrs. G. Linnæus Banks and illustrated by Alfred Pearse. Rupert plans to seek clues about Edgar's whereabouts from local people. Rupert believes that a white prisoner passing through would have generated talk.
