The narrator's mother hesitated to leave Boston for safety near the American army. General Gage refused to allow women or children to leave Boston. Hiram Griffin visited the narrator's home while they were having breakfast. Hiram and a comrade arrived at Cambridge after escaping Boston without danger. Silas remained with the army because there was no immediate need for him to return to Boston. Hiram was sent to summon the Minute Boys to help gather supplies for the army at Cambridge. The farms on the islands near Boston were to be ravaged to provide food for the American army.

Colonel Prescott encouraged the workers during cannonading to prevent retreat. The workers were motivated by the belief that their efforts were protecting the colony. The troops in Boston outnumbered the workers eight or ten to one. The workers completed the fortification except for the trench by noon. Drums, artillery, and church bells indicated troop movements in Boston. Major Brooks was sent away, leading to speculation about reinforcements. The workers were concerned about their ability to defend the fortification after their labor.

The matter of raising a company of Minute Boys was agreed to be left to Doctor Warren. Doctor Warren expressed surprise at the speed of the return of the boys. Doctor Warren praised the boys for their industry in support of the Cause. Archie suggested that a company of boys could be of service to the Cause. Doctor Warren approved the idea of raising a company of Minute Boys. The boys were eager to start enrolling the Minute Boys after meeting with Doctor Warren. Seth Jepson was the first lad the boys encountered after leaving Doctor Warren's house.

The speaker expresses hope that Hiram will help set Archie free. Hiram agrees to stay and watch over the speaker. The speaker admits to making a mistake by revealing too much information to the Committee of Safety. Hiram advises the speaker to find a way to keep Seth Jepson from being harmful or informed. The speaker decides to go home alone after discussing plans with Hiram. News arrives in Boston that twenty thousand men have gathered to oppose the king's troops. General Ward has taken command of the forces and a council of war has decided to besiege Boston.

A single militiaman was standing guard at the top of the cabin companion-way. Darius boarded the vessel and announced their intention to report to the commander. The soldier informed Darius that he could not see the commander at that moment. The commodore, Joshua Barney, emerged from the hatchway to inquire about the disturbance. Darius insisted on being accompanied by Jerry and another person during the report to the commodore. The commodore ordered preparations for a swift departure down the river with provisions. A guard-boat arrived with a canoe, which was identified as the swiftest craft on the river.

The characters discuss the challenges of gathering information for the Americans. Saul expresses confusion about the plans involving Uncle 'Rasmus. Pierre believes that a French boy can contribute to the efforts against Cornwallis's army. Uncle 'Rasmus prepares for a journey to York Town with blankets and a food package. Uncle 'Rasmus carries a heavy cane, which may serve as a weapon or a walking aid. The group intends to assist Uncle 'Rasmus on his journey to York Town. Saul questions the direction Uncle 'Rasmus plans to take.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The narrator was engaged in a physical struggle with an adversary who was attempting to strangle him. The narrator managed to weaken his adversary's hold after delivering two or three solid blows. The narrator was aware that reinforcements for the British forces were approaching during the fight. Darius intervened in the struggle, causing the adversary to release the narrator's throat. A lantern was brought by newcomers, illuminating the scene at the top of the stairs. Darius captured a British officer as he ascended the stairs, while the narrator seized the lantern. The narrator threatened a man believed to be the miller with his musket, prompting the miller to drop his weapon.

The narrator and others are hiding beneath shattered timbers with a view of the river. The area around them is under fire, resulting in casualties among their group. The narrator feels a sense of danger from both the enemy and their own side. The British forces are seen preparing for a retreat as the sun sets. Boats loaded with soldiers and baggage begin to leave for Gloucester Point. The narrator and little Frenchie discuss the need to prepare for a journey to the American lines. Concerns are raised about the well-being of Uncle 'Rasmus and the prisoners left in old Mary's cabin.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Jepson is skilled with a paddle and is expected to help advance their journey. Jerry inquired about how to find Jepson again. The group agreed to wait for a week unless they received important news. Jerry and Bill Jepson took their places in a canoe and prepared to set off. The pungy boat was turned towards the Delaware shore and quickly disappeared in the darkness. Jepson expressed confidence in the canoe's ability to handle the journey despite concerns about the weather. Bill Jepson offered to steer the canoe while Jerry and the narrator rested.

Seth became the first recruit of the group. Silas publicly spoke about their journey to Lexington. Archie expressed that the narrator was disgruntled about encountering Seth. The narrator suggested going home for something to eat before meeting comrades. Silas was eager to continue recruiting and did not want to idle at home. Archie reported that they had enrolled fourteen lads as Minute Boys. Amos Nelson, a Tory, claimed to know about their plans to aid the Cause.

Darius ran to light a lantern to assess the damage to the vessel. Captain Hanaford took control of the tiller to steer the pungy amidst darkness. The pungy was able to escape from the British gunners by rounding a bend. Darius reported that a solid shot had struck the pungy above the water-line but did not penetrate the timber. The crew celebrated their escape from a dangerous situation. The homeward voyage took approximately twenty-four hours without encountering any enemies. The government honored Commodore Barney's guarantee, allowing the narrator and Jerry to purchase a larger pungy.

The narrator expresses a desire to confront Horry Sims. The narrator is a member of a company of Minute Boys from Virginia. Saul is described as being angry and unresponsive to arguments or prayers. Pierre accompanies Saul and the narrator, showing loyalty and readiness for danger. The narrator is determined to find Silver Heels and rescue her. The narrator acknowledges feelings of fear in cold blood but experiences courage when angry. The group travels toward York Town in silence, with Pierre trying to maintain friendship.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The man provided a bag of corn meal and a large ham to Pierre and the narrator. The man requested that they not return with stories of hunger due to limited provisions. Pierre and the narrator went to old Mary's cabin after successfully foraging for food. Saul expressed impatience about being left in charge of the prisoners. Uncle 'Rasmus insisted on preparing the food instead of Pierre. The narrator and Saul discussed the possibility of the Jerseyman escaping. Uncle 'Rasmus believed the Jerseyman would successfully navigate the situation.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The book is titled 'Commodore Barney's Young Spies' and is authored by James Otis. The book was published by A. L. Burt Company in New York in 1907. The story is set during the year 1814, during the War of 1812. The main characters are Amos Grout and Jeremiah Sackett, who were both fifteen years old at the time. The narrative includes events related to the burning of the City of Washington. Vice-Admiral Cochrane wrote a letter to Secretary Monroe regarding the destruction of towns as retaliation. The letter from Cochrane was dated August 18, 1814, and was received by Monroe after the destruction of Washington.

Uncle 'Rasmus discussed the news of a visit to York Town with Saul. The cabin referred to as old Mary's was described as an ordinary hut built of logs. The cabin measured approximately twenty feet square and had a door made of puncheon planks. The cabin contained one room for living, eating, and sleeping, with a loft accessed by a ladder. The loft had crevices in the floor and small holes cut between the logs serving as windows. A chimney made of sticks and clay was located at the rear of the cabin, with a fireplace made of stones. A small well outside the front door was in a state of decay and questioned for its water quality.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Nearly every vessel is aground in the river. The British forces have landed more men than necessary to capture Charles and Calvert counties. The old man believes the British are aiming for Washington. There may be some plundering by British soldiers, but the townspeople are not expected to come to harm. Darius plans to pull up stakes and move away from the area. Elias Macomber is seen conversing with British officers and is suspected of being a traitor. Elias is preparing to embark in a canoe to spy on the river.

The narrator and Pierre walked through a village in York. They observed a guard-house with barred windows and a soldier standing in front. The narrator noted that a prisoner inside could not see the outside world. They attempted to find a way to warn the narrator's cousin but were unsuccessful. Pierre expressed that he could locate the guard-house in the future. They encountered Abel Hunt, a local youth with Tory leanings. The narrator was concerned that Abel Hunt might question their presence in the village.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Master Lord questioned Hiram about his comfort and presence. Hiram indicated that evidence against him could be found in the room above. Job Lord was bound and gagged and lying on a bed. Seth Jepson was brought into the cellar by Hiram. Hiram and Luke searched the house for evidence. A folded paper was found on the desk with the title 'Information for Job Lord to send to the rebels.' The paper contained a false account of the Britishers' activities.

The characters are attempting to find a way to help Archie, who is in prison. Hiram expresses a willingness to assist in the effort against the British forces. The group decides to take a risky water route to avoid British patrols. They land south of the Powder House and hide their boat among scrub oaks. The journey involves avoiding British patrols while traveling across Boston. They reach Silas Brownrigg's home after a roundabout route to ensure safety. Silas Brownrigg was informed about Archie's imprisonment earlier that day.

Doctor Warren advised against going among the lobster backs. Hiram Griffin informed the narrator about Colonel Prescott of the Pepperell Minute Men. The narrator is the captain of the Minute Boys of Boston. Colonel Prescott ordered the narrator to report for duty. The narrator's company has eleven members fit for duty, twelve if Hiram Griffin is included. The company is instructed to muster in front of General Ward's headquarters an hour before sunset. The company must provide themselves with blankets and one day's rations.

The characters are in a cabin while their friends are engaged in conflict outside. Pierre expresses a desire to prove their worth and gain credit in the struggle against the king. The narrator feels anger towards Pierre's optimism in a dangerous situation. The food supply in the cabin is nearly exhausted, with only enough for a light meal. Pierre insists on feeding the Tory prisoner before serving food to himself and others. Pierre demonstrates authority and care by prioritizing the prisoner's needs over his own. The narrator observes that Pierre gives larger portions to others than to himself.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The narrator expresses distrust towards Horry Sims, a Tory, and refuses to believe his words. Horry Sims reacts with anger after the narrator's outburst and threatens consequences from his allies. Pierre intervenes by stating that the British army is in a precarious position and cannot escape. The narrator and Pierre discuss the possibility of getting rid of Horry Sims to regain their freedom of movement. Little Frenchie suggests smuggling Horry Sims to General Lafayette's army for safekeeping. The narrator agrees to the plan of taking Horry Sims to Williamsburg to prevent him from joining his Tory friends. Uncle 'Rasmus warns that it may not be easy to leave the lines that night due to heightened vigilance among the soldiers.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The narrator approached a ship and called out for orders. A midshipman instructed the narrator to go about his business. Darius attempted to sell oysters to the crew of the Narcissus but was threatened. Darius chose not to leave the area immediately to avoid appearing anxious. The narrator mentioned that Joshua Barney needed to hear news. Darius expressed admiration for the commodore's ability to predict enemy movements. The narrator and Jerry planned to visit their homes but were instructed to remain aboard the Avenger.

The fate of a portion of the king's troops is being decided at sea. The French forces are holding their position in Chesapeake Bay against the British. Lord Cornwallis is expected to hold out for a long time due to fortifications around York. The French troops are believed to be capable of constructing strong entrenchments. Fitz Hamilton and Pierre Laurens are concerned about their cousin Saul Ogden's well-being. The distant sounds of battle distract Fitz Hamilton and Pierre from their worries about Saul. Fitz Hamilton and Pierre believe they will eventually learn the truth about Saul's fate.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Seth Jepson ate greedily when fed by Harvey. Master Lord refused to eat anything except water. The group took precautions to prevent their prisoners from crying out due to potential danger from Tory visitors. Archie proposed to gag the prisoners, but the narrator opposed this idea. Harvey paced and ascended and descended a ladder, causing distraction to the narrator. Job Lord claimed he would have set Silas free if he had been able to deliver the narrator and his companions to the British. The narrator suspected that they were being held as bait for a trap to capture other members of their group.

British soldiers were marching in the area, and officers were moving through the streets toward the entrenchments. Sounds of military activity, including pick and shovel work and the beating of drums, were present. The narrator was concerned about Uncle 'Rasmus's safety and feared he might have been arrested. Uncle 'Rasmus was found safe at the window of old Mary's cabin, which relieved the narrator. Uncle 'Rasmus expressed surprise at the narrator's affection and reassured him about his safety. Little Frenchie took precautions to avoid attracting attention while inside the cabin. The cabin was located on the outskirts of the village, reducing the likelihood of being seen.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Uncle 'Rasmus states that no British soldiers will cross the river that night due to the storm. The York River around Gloucester Point is described as dangerous and quickly changes to a boiling flood. The narrator sees Abel Hunt and Horry Sims leaving old Mary's cabin towards Governor Nelson's house. Uncle 'Rasmus advises the narrator to return to the cabin to avoid being captured by the British. The narrator expresses frustration at the idea of hiding in the cabin. Uncle 'Rasmus insists that the cabin is the only safe place in the village. Uncle 'Rasmus physically drags the narrator back to the cabin during the storm.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Seth Jepson played the traitor, which may result in the Minute Boys gaining a name. The Minute Boys were to be armed as soldiers, despite being young. The sloop was perceived as slow by the Minute Boys who were eager to obtain weapons. The Minute Boys anchored between Noddle and Hog islands before dawn. The weapons and ammunition were stored in the cuddy of the sloop. Hiram instructed three lads to act as sentinels on board the sloops. The Minute Boys visited John Weston's farm, where fifty or more sheep were penned.

Darius Thorpe reported for duty to Commodore Barney. Darius brought British prisoners and traitors with him. Commodore Barney recognized Darius and expressed pleasure at seeing him. Darius indicated that the craft was owned by Jerry and another individual. The prisoners included an officer and three sailors on parole, as well as two men aiding the enemy. Commodore Barney invited Darius and the others aboard to discuss the situation. The commodore suggested that Darius and the crew could serve a greater purpose than fishing.

The narrator believed the door to the cellar was covered to prevent visitors from seeing the entrance or to block sound. A quarrel or fight lasted for over half an hour, after which the participants seemed to have reconciled. The narrator fell asleep in the cellar and believed he had awakened to a new day. The cellar was completely underground, preventing any outside light from entering. Hiram attempted to open the trap-door but was unable to move it, causing alarm among the group. The lantern in the cellar eventually died, leaving the group in total darkness. Master Lord raised the trap-door, allowing light into the cellar, and later confirmed it was noon.

Silas proposed a surprising and satisfying plan related to their task. The group needed to gain the landing place quickly to reach Lexington. Doctor Warren's message was delivered before sunrise. The group rested in Master Hadley's barn after completing their task. Colonel Barrett prepared a written reply to Doctor Warren's message. Colonel Barrett indicated that the timing of the reply's delivery was not critical. The group planned to wait until nightfall to attempt getting into Boston.

Horry Sims lived on the old Livingston plantation, three miles above the narrator's home. Horry Sims was seen talking with a mounted officer in command of a dozen men. The narrator and Saul had not spent much time with Horry Sims in recent years. It was believed that Horry Sims' father remained loyal to the king and displayed disloyalty to neighbors. The narrator and Saul viewed Horry Sims as a rank Tory and avoided him to prevent conflict. The narrator and his companions hid themselves from view while observing Horry Sims and the officer. The narrator suspected that Horry Sims was providing information to the officer about their plantation.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The fleet was encountered late at night. The commodore was on board the Scorpion with the flotilla. Bill Jepson, a deserter from the British ship Severn, insisted on delivering a message to the commodore. The commodore recognized Jerry and the narrator upon their arrival. Bill Jepson provided valuable information about the vessels in the two fleets. The commodore expressed concern that the enemy would move soon. The narrator mentioned Elias Macomber, a prisoner who escaped and may have received aid from some men.

The speaker is in a conversation with a gentleman who trusts the speaker's father, Master Hancock. The speaker has a hidden boat at the old ship-yard for secret departures from town. The speaker and two companions have traveled to Roxbury multiple times without detection. The gentleman wishes to send a message to Colonel James Barrett, located near Lexington. The speaker and his companions are eager to deliver the message before sunrise. Doctor Warren agrees to let the three boys participate in the task and refers to them as Minute Boys. The boys are instructed to inform their parents about their mission before departing.

Captain Joshua Barney was ordered to fit up a fleet of small boats to protect the towns of the bay in April. The United States was at war with England at the time. The narrator and others were on their way to Annapolis with half a load of oysters. Darius, an old man on the boat, claimed to know Captain Joshua Barney well. Captain Joshua Barney was born around 1759 in Baltimore. Barney's early work included going to school until he was ten and then working in a store. Barney was apprenticed to Captain Tom Drisdale on a brig for a voyage to Ireland.

The Jerseyman advised waiting until Abel Hunt was conscious before gagging him. The narrator expressed concern about the challenges of caring for two prisoners. The narrator feared that Abel Hunt's presence would embolden Horry Sims. Master Morgan questioned how to manage two prisoners while they were also in a precarious situation. Pierre suggested putting both prisoners in the loft and keeping a guard by Horry Sims. Horry Sims pleaded not to be gagged, promising not to raise an alarm. Horry Sims was secured in the loft with strips of blanket and threatened with a gag if he moved.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Harvey Pearson has been seen more than once by the narrator. Seth is trying to learn about any plans to release Archie. The narrator believes it would be foolish to attempt a rescue for Archie. General Gage is allowing Archie to remain imprisoned. Seth visited Amos Nelson's home to gather information. A town meeting is scheduled for the following evening. The Tories oppose General Gage's arrangement for people to leave Boston.

The characters are concerned about the fate of Darius, who is missing after a battle. Bill Jepson was seen shortly before a retreat order was given, and he was sent back for ammunition. The group believes that if Darius is captured by the British, he will be treated as a deserter. The characters express a desire to search for Darius despite the dangers posed by the British. Jerry and Amos decide to leave the safety of their location to search for Darius. The group lacks a clear plan for the search and is uncertain about where to begin. The characters speculate that Darius may have gone to find food.

Captain Hanaford inquired about the situation from a man who exclaimed, 'The British!' The man informed Captain Hanaford that the British had evacuated the city during the storm. The man reported that people near the encampment were warned to stay indoors from sunset to sunrise. A planter reported that British soldiers were marching towards Nottingham. Troops that remained at Bladensburg after the battle were reported to be heading to Upper Marlboro. Captain Hanaford planned to hold a council of war after preparing breakfast to discuss their next steps. Darius confirmed the news of the British evacuation after visiting the encampment.

The shops were being robbed. The only way to leave the city by water would be on the Potomac River. The President's mansion was in ruins, with the walls still standing. A number of negroes were digging amid the ruins of the barracks. The old man identified his master as Massa Clayton. The American soldiers had set more than twenty prisoners free. The British were keeping American prisoners in a stone house near the arsenal.

Saul expressed skepticism about the effectiveness of a small group of Minute Boys. Pierre advocated for the enrollment of three lads as Minute Boys to support the Cause. Saul initially dismissed the idea of forming a company of Minute Boys. After a confrontation with Pierre, Saul changed his attitude and supported the formation of the Minute Boys. Saul and another Virginia lad joined Pierre, a French boy, to form a company of Minute Boys. The trio wrote a letter to Master Patrick Henry offering their services. Master Patrick Henry responded to the letter written by Saul.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The narrator fell asleep between Archie and Harvey and was awakened by Hiram. Hiram decided to take a route to Stony brook instead of the previously agreed path. The group arrived at the American outpost around nightfall. The captain at the outpost recognized the group and offered them food. Griffin revealed their plans to the captain, despite the group's intention to keep it secret. The captain expressed doubt about the group's chances of success in their venture. Hiram remained determined to proceed with their plan despite the captain's warnings.

Hiram and the narrator believe they are being held at the ship-yard due to the actions of others. The narrator considers the possibility that Seth Jepson may have caused their predicament but dismisses it. The narrator concludes that their situation is a result of chance rather than intention. Hiram and the narrator are unable to leave their hiding place due to the constant movement of their captors. They have no food or water, as they expected to reach Cambridge within a few hours. Hiram attempts to sleep while the narrator remains alert due to their vulnerable position. Several guard-boats are observed moving around the harbor, but no small boats are seen until after sunrise.

The narrator was made prisoner less than a mile from the American line. The narrator was taken to a village of canvas tents and shelters of brush-wood. The American flag was displayed in front of a marquee where the narrator was taken. The narrator's father welcomed him with affection upon his arrival. The narrator delivered a message from a Jerseyman named Morgan to General Lafayette. General Lafayette and other officers discussed the news after the narrator's report. The narrator's father expressed satisfaction rather than pride in his actions.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The little lad expressed concern about his cousin's absence, believing something serious had happened. The lad was frustrated that he was not woken to search for his cousin. Pierre believed it was necessary for the lad to regain strength before facing potential disaster. The lad feared his cousin Saul was either captured by soldiers or gravely injured. Pierre suggested they should not both go out to search for Saul due to the risk of being overheard. Horry Sims, a Tory, pleaded not to be gagged, fearing it would be torture. Pierre proposed to bind Horry securely in a corner of the room to prevent him from making noise.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The narrator seeks advice from his father, who is likely on vessels belonging to the flotilla. Darius expresses satisfaction with their recent actions and believes others could have performed better. The narrator acknowledges Darius's role in preventing the enemy from retaliating. Darius introduces a British officer who has been released from his restraints and given parole. The British officer discusses the differences between his previous ship and the narrator's vessel, the Avenger. The British officer acknowledges that there are two sides to every story regarding the war. The narrator mentions Jerry's brother being forcibly taken to serve on a British ship.

The characters discuss the possibility of rescuing a lad who has been taken prisoner. Hiram expresses doubt about the feasibility of rescuing the lad from his captors. Hiram emphasizes the importance of prioritizing the larger cause of freedom over the life of one individual. The characters prepare to leave in a skiff to avoid danger while crossing the water. Hiram suggests that taking the creek route may be safer than going by the river due to potential guard-boats. Hiram has been observing the situation around Cambridge and has formed a plan for crossing. The characters begin their journey by rowing the skiff away from the wharf.

The events took place in the town of York. General Lafayette was nearby with his army. My Lord Cornwallis was concerned about General Washington's troops. Horry Sims was threatened by little Frenchie during the incident. The group took Horry Sims to a shed filled with rubbish. Saul closed and partially secured the shed's door. Pierre planned to keep Horry Sims until night at old Mary's cabin.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: P. Van Ness was the commander of the militia of the District of Columbia. Van Ness sent a circular letter to the brigadiers of the Maryland militia requesting volunteers. General Smith issued a division order in response to the invasion and prepared General Stansbury's brigade for active service. General Stansbury left Baltimore for Washington with thirteen hundred men. Lieutenant-Colonel Joseph Sterett's force joined Stansbury on the evening of the 23rd. The British forces, commanded by Cockburn, moved up the Patuxent and reached Lower Marlborough on the 21st. The total force for the defense of Washington was about seven thousand strong, with nine hundred enlisted men.

The captain rebandaged the father's wound after arriving at the smoke-house. Jerry fetched fresh water from the well at the ruins of the tavern. The captain directed Jim, Dody, and Josiah to the location of the pungy with explicit directions. Jim and his friends left for the pungy without delay after receiving instructions. The captain planned to bring the rope to the jail shortly before ten o'clock. The narrator felt nervous about the potential outcome of their plan to free the sailors. The sun went down before the captain and the father made their start.

The characters are traveling to the town of York. Pierre warns Saul and another character about the dangers of approaching the British encampment. Saul expresses a desire to find their horses. Pierre suggests that they may not be allowed to wander freely in the town due to their association with the Hamilton plantation. Saul and the narrator realize that Horry Sims may be nearby and could identify them to the British. The characters have previously discussed their desire to join the American army. Pierre reacts with scorn when Saul dismisses his warnings.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The characters are instructed to stay under cover unless discovered by the British. Jerry leaves to fulfill a task while the narrator observes Macomber. Macomber attempts to communicate with a sentinel but is unsuccessful. Macomber appears to be focused on observing a prisoner named Darius. The narrator paces to avoid suspicion while keeping an eye on Macomber. Macomber eventually leaves to head towards the British encampment. The narrator plans to take Macomber's place at the window to attract Darius's attention.

The narrator observes Seth Jepson looking uneasily as if planning to escape. The narrator questions Seth Jepson about his freedom to walk the streets of Boston. Seth Jepson claims it is a duty to serve the king and denies any treachery. The narrator expresses a desire to physically harm Seth Jepson due to the danger he poses. Seth Jepson attempts to flee while shouting for help. The narrator restrains Seth Jepson by clutching his throat and pinning him down. The narrator threatens Seth Jepson with a knife to ensure his compliance.

The narrator experiences fear as they prepare for battle. The narrator reflects on the value of their mission, questioning the worth of fighting for cargo compared to human life. The narrator notes the presence of twenty armed British soldiers on the schooner's deck. The sloop is positioned to prevent British pursuit while preparing for combat. Hiram encourages the group to stand firm and prepare for the fight against the British. The group takes cover as British bullets begin to fly, but the aim of the British soldiers is poor.

The commander instructed to give the prisoner breakfast before marching. The fleet was expected to arrive at the rendezvous by early dawn. The Scorpion ran aground, causing delays for several smaller boats. Josiah Coburn was selected to feed the prisoner after drawing lots. The narrator's father arrived aboard the Avenger and complimented the crew. Commodore Barney used the Avenger as his flagship while waiting for the Scorpion. Commodore Barney ate breakfast with the crew while giving orders.

During the night of the fourteenth, redoubts were included in the second parallel. By five o'clock the next afternoon, howitzers placed in the redoubts were opened upon British works. Cornwallis faced a dangerous situation, being beleaguered by a superior force with crumbling defenses. Cornwallis sent a detachment under Lieutenant-Colonel Abercrombie to make a sortie against French-guarded batteries. The sortie was initially successful but the assailants were soon driven back by guards at the trenches. Cornwallis planned to abandon his position and attempt to flee to Gloucester with his troops. A storm prevented Cornwallis from successfully executing his plan to cross the river to Gloucester.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: A few individuals expressed anger about being sent to a location where an assault would be provoked. Hiram discouraged any negative comments about their leaders and labeled dissenters as cowards. Hiram claimed that heavy reinforcements were on the way from Cambridge, despite lacking knowledge on the matter. The British troops, commanded by General Howe, landed at Morton's point with military precision. The British troops took a long halt on Morton's hill to rectify a mistake involving cannon balls that were too large for their pieces. Colonel Stark's regiment and Reed's corps arrived to support the forces on Breed's hill. Hiram estimated that their numbers would reach about three thousand, while the total number of their forces was later recorded as not exceeding four thousand.

The narrator last saw Uncle 'Rasmus with a blanket over his knees, watching soldiers outside. Uncle 'Rasmus expressed that he does not need as much rest as younger individuals. Uncle 'Rasmus mentioned that soldiers had been working all night and seemed to anticipate a battle. The narrator felt anxious about the possibility of being caught in a battle between the two armies. Morgan entered the cabin after working all night in the trenches. Morgan was searching for Saul, who had gone missing after leaving the house the previous morning. Morgan expressed surprise at Saul's disappearance and questioned if Saul might have gone home.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The characters are discussing a situation involving a potential traitor named Job Lord. They believe they are currently safe but are wary of Job Lord's intentions. Hiram suggests they should act as if they are compliant with Job Lord's wishes. There is a concern that escaping could lead to greater danger from the British forces. Hiram begins to cut a crevice in the planks above them to listen to the conversation in the room above. The group is cautious about their situation and is considering their options carefully. They are currently in a hiding place and have limited food resources.

Saul Ogden is not in danger and is comfortable. The narrator and Pierre Laurens are in a cabin with a Tory prisoner. Pierre expresses a desire to inform Saul that they are ready to help him. The narrator is concerned about the potential danger to Morgan if they interfere. Pierre believes that Morgan has a reason for keeping them hidden. The plan is to let Saul know they are watching over him without acting immediately. The narrator agrees to follow Pierre's plan despite the risks involved.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Saul expressed concern about their decision to roam instead of assisting those in the entrenchments. Little Frenchie insisted on procuring provisions despite the dangers involved. The narrator admitted to being afraid to leave old Mary's cabin. The narrator felt cowardly after the struggle with Abel Hunt and the departure of the Jerseyman. Upon leaving the cabin, the narrator was initially fearful but became captivated by the scene outside. The narrator observed a large army preparing to capture Cornwallis and his men. Little Pierre noted that the red-coats appeared to be trapped in the village.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Job Lord's Tory friends were expected to arrive. Hiram Griffin lit a tallow dip before leaving the house. Archie and the narrator were prepared for a potential conflict. Hiram Griffin returned from the Bridewell. Hiram instructed the Tories to enter the house. The narrator and Archie attacked the first Tory who entered. Silas Brownrigg followed Hiram into the room.

The narrator and his friends were considered rebels and did not apply for permission to wander about. General Gage treated the narrator and his friends as prisoners. The narrator and Hiram Griffin attempted to escape after encountering a watch reinforced by soldiers. Hiram Griffin ran in a zig-zag course to avoid being shot by soldiers. The narrator leaped over a fence into Parson Reed's yard while fleeing. The narrator heard musket fire and was concerned for Hiram Griffin's safety. The narrator contemplated returning to help a comrade but decided it would be unwise.

Uncle 'Rasmus placed Horry Sims in a hidden space beneath the flooring to keep him out of sight from the king's soldiers. Horry Sims was found bound and lying in a narrow space between the puncheons. Horry Sims expressed discomfort from being tied up for an extended period. Pierre decided to release Horry Sims from his bonds despite concerns for safety. After being freed, Horry Sims was initially unable to move due to numbness. Horry Sims crouched in a corner after being released, appearing willing to remain a captive. The characters experienced fear from the ongoing cannonading outside the cabin.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The soldiers halted less than twenty yards from the cabin door to rest. Pierre observed that the soldiers were discouraged and had left the trenches without permission. The soldiers were armed and should have been at their posts. A shot from the American lines struck the group of soldiers, causing casualties. Pierre suggested that they take weapons and ammunition from the fallen soldiers. Pierre expressed concern that the soldiers' insubordination could lead to danger as the British forces retreated. Pierre emphasized the importance of being prepared to defend themselves and carry news to their people.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The group decided to return to Cambridge instead of risking their lives. They traveled westward towards the shore and reached a small gun-battery. The lieutenant in charge was initially skeptical of their loyalty to the Cause. Hiram managed to convince the lieutenant of their intentions after revealing a connection to Concord. The lieutenant agreed to provide a skiff for their attempt to enter Boston on a suitable night. They stayed with the soldiers for four days while waiting for the right opportunity. On a certain afternoon, they prepared their skiff for the journey to find Job Lord.

A man riding a mule approached the group from the direction of Bladensburg. The man was identified as the narrator's father, who was wounded in the right leg. The father had been injured during a battle and was searching for surgeons. He had bandaged his wound and attempted to escape on a mule after the final retreat was ordered. Darius claimed he could treat the father's wound with available resources. The group decided to proceed toward Washington despite the risks involved. The narrator expressed concern about the safety of their decision to move forward.

The Avenger was approaching a location where it was to be stopped. Jerry signaled that Elias Macomber was in sight. Darius instructed to head the boat towards Macomber's canoe. Darius disguised his voice to deceive Macomber into revealing the location of their people. Darius threatened Jerry with a musket to ensure compliance from Macomber. Darius knocked Macomber unconscious with the butt-end of a musket. Macomber regained consciousness after being stowed away in the hold.

General Gage issued orders that no person could leave Boston without a pass. Two hundred Tories were enrolled as a military company with Timothy Ruggles as their captain. The Minute Boys were perceived to be inactive during this period. Harvey Pearson attempted to communicate with Archie from outside the prison. Hiram Griffin suggested sending a messenger to Cambridge with news. The window of the room where Archie is held is approximately five or six feet from the street. Silas expressed excitement about the possibility of communicating with Archie.

The characters are attempting to pass by His Majesty's vessels without being discovered. Pierre expresses hope that they will be allowed to continue after explaining their purpose. The characters are concerned about the possibility of being sent to share Saul's imprisonment. They are hailed by a sentry from the _Charon_ who demands to see their pass. Pierre explains that they have no pass and are delivering a message. The sentry allows them to proceed without further orders. The characters successfully navigate past the vessels and continue their journey.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Darius warned that being captured while on their mission would result in execution. Jim expressed determination to continue with the mission despite the risks involved. The crew set sail on the pungy, with Darius taking the tiller. The narrator's father and other fleet members silently wished them well as they departed. Darius stated that their destination was for fishing, despite the crew's doubts about the mission. Jerry questioned the practicality of fishing when they were likely on a more dangerous mission. Darius insisted that they were still to act as oystermen as per the commodore's orders.

The combatants were engaged in a struggle to defend Master Morgan. Abel Hunt was attacked by a Jerseyman during the conflict. British cannon fire occurred simultaneously with the struggle. Master Morgan choked Abel Hunt into unconsciousness. The Jerseyman was injured and exhausted after the fight. Pierre Laurens took action to bind Abel Hunt to prevent his return to consciousness. Master Morgan expressed reluctance to kill Abel Hunt despite the circumstances.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Harvey expressed a desire to act as a messenger to the American encampment. Silas was chosen to go to the encampment with the gathered information. Seth Jepson was under constant watch by the group without any blame found in him. Silas planned to leave for the American camp secretly and without informing anyone. Hiram Griffin believed it would not be difficult to rescue a comrade from prison. The group was concerned about the possibility of being taken into custody for loitering.

The struggle against British misrule had begun. The Tories publicly celebrated what they claimed was a victory. The colonists were poorly armed and inexperienced in warfare. Archie's father was summoned to Cambridge on the evening of the battle. Archie's father advised the Minute Boys to remain undercover for several days. Archie visited the narrator's home to discuss plans for action. Hiram Griffin arrived with a message for Luke Wright.

The group is preparing to embark on a dangerous voyage in a canoe. Darius is the leader of the party during the voyage. The canoe is large enough to carry six people comfortably. The group intends to scout for British forces during their journey. A pungy from their village warns them that British ships are approaching. The warning indicates that there are more than a hundred British vessels less than a mile below Hog Point. Darius advises the group not to stop long at Benedict due to the approaching British forces.

Darius bound a man with strips of bags provided by Jim. The British sailors were found bound hand and foot upon regaining consciousness. A British officer refused to give his parole except to an officer of the American army or navy. Darius indicated that the prisoners would receive the same treatment as Elias Macomber. Jerry suggested taking a supply of meal to avoid shortages if they did not meet the fleet by noon. The prisoners were transported down the stairs, with some requiring assistance. Josiah arrived with the Avenger, and the prisoners and meal were stowed in the hold before starting up the river.

The characters are searching for Darius, who is believed to be confined in a building referred to as the 'stone house.' The area around the stone house has many loungers, some of whom may be British spies or sympathizers. The characters observe British soldiers and sentries near the stone house, indicating a military presence. Elias Macomber, a character who has previously escaped capture, is seen trying to look into the stone house. Jerry suspects that Elias Macomber informed the enemy about Darius's whereabouts, leading to Darius's arrest. The characters discuss the possibility of helping Darius and plan to inform others about their findings.

Frenchie asked about the provisions brought by Saul. Saul claimed to have enough provisions to last a week. Saul displayed cold boiled ham, corn-bread, fried hominy, and fried ham from his sack. The group planned to catch fish to supplement their food supply. The narrator's mother was frightened about their venture but did not oppose it. Saul wanted to leave immediately to speak with Uncle 'Rasmus, while Frenchie suggested waiting until later. The group approached the guard stationed along the entrenchments as they headed toward the town of York.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Two human beings are at risk of starvation. The enemy is retreating, but the night is half spent. The narrator expresses a desire to join the army in pursuit of the retreating enemy. The narrator recalls that they decided to call themselves Minute Boys. The narrator believes their people will cross over to the other shore to pursue the enemy. Uncle 'Rasmus is considered a potential burden due to his slow travel. Little Frenchie proposes a plan to release the prisoners and prepare for a quick departure.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The encampment contains seven thousand soldiers. The narrator and Pierre approach the village and find the troops manning the outermost entrenchments. The headquarters of my Lord Cornwallis appears deserted. The stable lines of the Rangers are empty of horses. The narrator expresses concern for a horse named Silver-Heels, which is likely at the front. Pierre suggests they take part in a battle to release a prisoner named Saul. The narrator and Pierre arm themselves with an axe and a pick for their plan.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Horry Sims was seen talking with men and pointing towards the Hamilton plantation. Horry Sims informed the men that a rebel owned the Hamilton plantation, which had valuable horses. The men were aware of the ownership of Silver Heels before taking her. The narrator realized that attempting to retrieve Silver Heels would be futile. Saul expressed anger about the theft of their horses and the need for action. Saul and the narrator planned to hold Horry Sims accountable for his actions. Saul intended to confront the British encampment despite his anger.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The narrator expresses a willingness to follow Pierre despite concerns about the potential failure of their plan. Pierre responds to the narrator's comments about a previous failure, indicating a desire to move forward. The narrator reflects on the possibility of aiding a boy named Saul Ogden but believes they will not succeed. The narrator feels remorse for leaving Uncle 'Rasmus behind and worries about the dangers they may face. Pierre leads the way to a skiff, which is described as small and conveniently equipped with oars. The narrator notes the presence of English ships at anchor, indicating the risk of being seen while they attempt to leave. The skiff is set on a course toward the Gloucester shore without being challenged by sentinels.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The President was on his way from the Potomac to review the troops. Commodore Barney opposed the review, as indicated by Darius's complaints. The troops remained in line for two hours before the review began. Scouts reported that the main body of the enemy was at Upper Marlboro. General Winder left the encampment to hold a conference with General Stansbury at Bladensburg. Two companies of Maryland militia, under Major Peter, arrived in camp showing signs of terror after skirmishing with the British. The troops arrived at the Eastern Branch bridge near midnight after marching over the same ground three times.

The narrator believed it was necessary to leave a woman to prevent her anxiety about Silas. The woman suggested the narrator go to Cambridge to speak with someone devoted to the Cause. Master William Mansfield lived in Mackrell lane and had remained in town due to a leg injury. The narrator spent no more than half an hour with his mother before leaving. On the way to Mackrell lane, the narrator was approached by Seth Jepson, who posed a threat. The narrator felt dazed and realized the danger posed by Jepson to himself and his comrades. The narrator considered the possibility of silencing Jepson to protect his group but was conflicted about killing him.

The characters are experiencing hunger and fatigue while surrounded by enemies. Darius has not returned, causing anxiety among the characters. Commodore Thomas Tingey was in command of the navy yard in Washington. Tingey received orders to set fire to public property if the British gained a victory. Property valued at about a million dollars was destroyed when Tingey applied the torch. The total estimated value of property destroyed in Washington by both British and Americans was about two million dollars. Elias Macomber is believed to have been released and is potentially boasting about his suffering at the hands of Americans.

Darius commanded the crew to paddle harder as they pursued Macomber's canoe. Macomber threw down his paddle in fear when Darius threatened him with a paddle. Darius restrained Macomber by the throat and ordered him to step into their canoe. Macomber expressed that Admiral Cochrane planned to destroy Barney's fleet on Friday. Darius stated that they had taken Macomber in charge and would keep an eye on him. Darius and the crew encountered the Byard boys' canoe while paddling. The Byard boys decided to follow Darius instead of returning to Benedict.

The group pressed closely around Job Lord to hide him from view and to maintain a rapid pace. They advanced to where the skiff was found without being challenged. A king's man assisted in their flight by holding the skiff afloat at the water's edge. Job Lord was thrust on board the skiff to keep him hidden from view. The group had a pass signed by General Gage that ensured their safe conduct. They successfully escaped from Boston without injury and took a spy to Cambridge. The escape was described as a close shave, with the possibility of being caught looming over them.

The characters are on a vessel navigating through a dark and rainy environment. Darius instructs the crew to remain silent and still to avoid detection. The narrator struggles to see the shore and is anxious about their situation. The crew hears voices from a nearby ship, indicating they are close to other vessels. The narrator fears a collision with other ships while trying to pass through safely. The crew experiences a sudden shock as they collide with another ship. A voice from the other ship calls out to investigate the presence of the narrator's vessel.

The narrator entered the town of York under false pretences. The narrator was weary from the journey and had not slept the previous night. The narrator was hopeful about seeing his mother and explaining their plans. The narrator felt burdened by the capture of Horry Sims. The narrator experienced fluctuating emotions of hope and fear during the journey. The narrator's mother was aware of the dangers associated with their plans. The narrator attempted to reassure his mother about their scheme despite her concerns.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The narrator reflects on a moment when they were chosen as captain of the Minute Boys. The narrator expresses regret for sharing sensitive information too freely. Seth Jepson informs the group about Archie Hemming's treatment in prison. The narrator suspects Seth Jepson of potentially being a traitor. Seth Jepson claims he learned about Archie from Amos Nelson. The narrator questions Seth Jepson's decision to converse with Amos Nelson, who is described as a Tory. The narrator feels self-reproach for revealing plans and information to the group.

The task involved seizing provisions from Noddle and Hog islands. Two small sloops were provided for the operation. Four trusted men from the army were selected to assist in the task. The Minute Boys were impressed into service for the operation. The plan involved gathering at the rope walk near Hudson's point before midnight. The area was under martial law with soldiers patrolling the streets. The narrator had difficulty gathering his comrades due to their scattered locations.

The American army has shown the ability to cope with trained soldiers. The narrator believes it is their duty to go on a mission despite their father's opposition. The narrator's comrades did not question their decision after the interview with their father. Hiram assumed leadership of the group and began to lay plans for the mission. Hiram proposed to travel down the Cambridge to Muddy River in a skiff to reach Dorchester. The narrator expressed concerns about the feasibility of Hiram's plan due to British fortifications. Hiram suggested that there are still people in Boston who support their cause.

The narrator encounters Abel Hunt, who questions him about his presence near the British encampment. Abel Hunt accuses the narrator of being a rebel while implying he is loyal to the British. The narrator explains that he is wearing the same coat he had when he received news from Boston. The narrator is concerned that if he does not engage with Hunt, it may lead to trouble. The narrator and Pierre entered York to see the soldiers but are now unable to leave. Hunt inquires about their activities since they could not pass the sentinels. Hunt asks the narrator about the last time he saw Horry Sims.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The narrator reflects on a previous decision not to speak against another boy due to his better behavior under difficult circumstances. The group leaves old Mary's cabin with two prisoners unguarded in the loft. Uncle 'Rasmus is described as unreliable in case the prisoners escape. The narrator believes that the danger has passed and that they will soon be with their friends. The narrator expresses hope of regaining possession of Silver Heels and Saul's mare. The group spends the day roaming the encampment without interference. Little Frenchie warns the narrator not to underestimate the danger that still exists.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The grass was stained with red, resembling a carpet of crimson. Muskets were discharged and reloaded while British forces returned fire with little effect. Cannon fire came from the king's ships and General Howe's guns. The battle created a chaotic environment filled with smoke and noise. The American forces cheered as they witnessed the British retreat. The American troops had forced back twice their number in approximately ten minutes. The narrator realized the cost of victory upon seeing wounded and dead comrades.

The narrator reflects on the potential need for water while using a cabin as a refuge. Uncle 'Rasmus stored provisions in a cupboard near the fireplace. Uncle 'Rasmus encouraged the boys to explore the town to learn about local military quarters. The narrator wanted to see Silver Heels, a horse belonging to Simcoe's Rangers. Saul expressed dissatisfaction with the group's pace and behavior. The narrator encountered Horry Sims while trying to catch up with Saul. Saul reacted angrily to the presence of Horry Sims, whom they considered an enemy.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Pierre Laurens provided encouragement and optimism to the narrator despite their limited food supply. Uncle 'Rasmus displayed a calm demeanor when discussing the potential for fighting in their town. The narrator expressed curiosity about Uncle 'Rasmus's feelings regarding the danger they faced. General Washington was mentioned as someone who would not neglect his duties in Virginia. The group speculated about the outcome of a possible naval battle between the French and the British. Horry Sims remained silent during the discussions, raising suspicions about his intentions. The group decided to skip dinner due to a lack of provisions, sharing their fast with the prisoner.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: In 1777, the individual shipped on the Andrew Doria for the defense of the Delaware River. After the scrimmage, he was drafted to the frigate Virginia and was captured by the British for nearly a year. He was exchanged for the lieutenant of the Mermaid and later served as a privateer with Captain Robinson. During a confrontation with the British privateer Rosebud, forty-seven enemy personnel were killed or wounded, while only one from the Yankee was wounded. He later married and was robbed while traveling from Philadelphia to Baltimore. He took service aboard the Saratoga, capturing multiple ships before being captured by the Intrepid. After escaping captivity, he was given command of the Hyder Ally and captured the British ship General Monk.

The group is hiding from British forces and is considering their options for escape. Darius insists that the party should stay together and not split up. The old man believes they are safe from bodily harm for the time being. Bill Jepson mentions that Captain Gordon of the Sea Horse is in command of the British forces. The group has provisions and begins to feel more cheerful about their situation. Darius suggests that they should not wait for the British to come down the river and proposes a plan to move. The older members of the party support Darius's idea, while one member expresses concern about taking risks.

Hiram expressed concern about their situation as prisoners and their access to food. Master Lord asserted that Hiram and his companions were not free to leave without his consent. Master Lord indicated that he was taking risks to aid Hiram and his companions. Hiram inquired about disturbances that occurred the previous night. Master Lord confirmed that he had been with three Tories the night before. Hiram learned that a boy named Silas Brownrigg was among the prisoners in the Bridewell. Master Lord stated that the Bridewell was guarded by forty men, with twenty on duty at all times.

Abel Hunt was roaming around the village seeking out the narrator and his companions. The narrator believed that Abel Hunt intended to harm them and might be trying to curry favor with British officers. The narrator and Saul had not done anything to provoke Abel Hunt's animosity. The cabin belonged to the Hamilton plantation, and the narrator suspected that Abel Hunt would watch it closely. The Jerseyman could not assist the narrator and his companions because he needed to remain hidden. Pierre Laurens was suggested as a potential problem-solver for procuring food without attracting Abel Hunt's attention. Abel Hunt burst into the cabin, causing fear among the narrator and his companions.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The narrator expresses doubt about the importance of catching a traitor compared to informing the commodore about the fleet's departure preparations. Darius insists on not leaving Jerry and the narrator at Hog Point due to their suspicion of involvement in Bill Jepson's desertion. Darius recounts that they attempted to find a boat on the Delaware shore but were unsuccessful. The Severn stopped their vessel, and a lieutenant with four marines conducted a thorough search. Darius describes an encounter with a midshipman who accused him of lying about the crew's whereabouts. The lieutenant accused Darius of helping a deserter and threatened to seize their vessel. Darius notes that they were saved from losing their vessel when signals were sent from the flagship.

Saul questions the logic of traveling to York Town at night instead of waiting until morning. Pierre explains that Uncle 'Rasmus is creating an excuse for Saul and Fitz to visit their horses. Saul expresses frustration about the need to carry food to Uncle 'Rasmus in old Mary's cabin. Pierre clarifies that Uncle 'Rasmus intends to sneak through the lines to avoid detection by the British. Uncle 'Rasmus plans to stay in York Town to facilitate the boys' movements without raising suspicion. The boys believe that caring for Uncle 'Rasmus will allow them to navigate York Town more freely. Horry Sims is mentioned as a character who might become suspicious of Uncle 'Rasmus's presence in York.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The crew planned to stream as soon as the tempest abated to avoid the British fleet. Captain Hanaford was shown a guarantee from Commodore Barney regarding the vessel's safety. The storm on the night of August twenty-fifth, 1814, was described as unprecedented. The pungy experienced severe rocking and required additional hawsers to prevent being swept away. The storm caused significant damage, including uprooted trees and destroyed houses. The crew decided to remain on the pungy until the storm subsided and the river was safer. There was concern that the British would search for escaped prisoners after the storm.

Darius questioned Jim about seeing a specific individual. Jim claimed to have seen the boats after a fight in St. Leonard's bay. The British frigate Loire had chased Commodore Barney's flotilla into St. Leonard's bay. Colonel Carberry's artillery drove the British away from St. Leonard's bay. Commodore Barney sailed to Benedict and then to Nottingham after learning of enemy vessels. Darius expressed concern about the danger of capture due to the presence of British forces. The narrator's father joined Commodore Barney's service, while many able-bodied men from Benedict did the same.

The tent was set up to provide shelter and store belongings safely. Darius Thorpe was responsible for the care of the group at Long Old Fields. The group had a supply of provisions gathered by Darius Thorpe. Darius Thorpe informed the group that a battle was expected within forty-eight hours. The main body of the British forces was located at Upper Marlboro. General Stansbury was at Bladensburg, and General Winder planned to go there for a conference. Darius Thorpe was tired from accompanying the commodore and following orders.

The purpose of holding women and children in Boston town is to use them as hostages. The speaker joined the company of Minute Boys to support the colony. The speaker advised a lad to continue his current path despite concerns about Tory connections. Only Silas, Harvey, and Hiram knew about the hope to release Archie. The speaker intended to keep the plan to release Archie a secret. Harvey Pearson confirmed he had not been near the prison since warning Archie. Hiram Griffin indicated that a stormy night would be necessary for a successful attempt to free Archie.

The captain of the other ship ordered the crew alongside to buy their cargo. The crew could have fifteen or twenty bushels ready by the next night if the wind holds. Darius expressed concern about the possibility of being searched and pressed into service. A midshipman and two marines boarded the vessel to conduct a search. The marines found three old muskets and questioned why the crew was armed. The midshipman and officers dismissed the crew's weapons and continued searching the hold. The search revealed only mud and oyster shells, indicating the vessel was likely an honest oysterman.

The narrator visited Benedict and reassured her about the British forces. Darius believed the British would halt at the village. Benedict suggested they wait instead of fleeing into the thicket with the children. The village was in a state of confusion, with many residents preparing to flee. The narrator was the last of his party to arrive at the shore. Darius hid the boat upstream for convenience in case of an emergency. The group found a vantage point across the river to observe the British forces.

The narrator expresses skepticism about associating with Seth Jepson, whom they suspect of Toryism. Silas and Archie defend Seth Jepson, claiming he is loyal to the Cause. The group decides to form a company of Minute Boys, including Seth Jepson among fourteen selected lads. They plan to seek advice from Doctor Warren before officially raising the company. The group travels at night to avoid detection by General Gage's men. The narrator's mother warmly welcomes him home after their journey. The narrator sleeps until eight o'clock, when Archie and Silas wake him to accompany them to Master Warren's house.

The British forces were observed preparing to take possession of a village. An armed brig was moored in the channel with a full broadside aimed at the settlement. Four hundred soldiers were present on the beach, ready for action. Numerous boats were landing soldiers, marines, and companies of negroes in British uniforms. It was reported that five thousand men were landed at Benedict. The area was heavily populated with armed men, but none crossed to the opposite side of the river. The arrival of the British fleet was limited to smaller vessels, with no larger ships appearing.

The characters are involved in a situation related to the Cause. Pierre and the narrator discuss the implications of a message delivered by Morgan. The narrator expresses concern about Saul's possible arrest. Uncle 'Rasmus is found in his invalid's chair with Horry Sims at his feet. The narrator and Pierre return without any news of Saul. Uncle 'Rasmus expresses sorrow over Saul potentially being captured by the British. The characters experience a mix of hope and despair regarding Saul's fate.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The narrator experiences extreme fatigue after a night of toil and a day of fighting. The narrator is in an encampment at Cambridge and feels physically collapsed. Hiram wakes the narrator after eight hours of sleep and informs him that much has happened. The narrator learns that many of the Minute Boys may have died, and Silas Brownrigg was taken prisoner. Hiram claims to have seen a grenadier seize Silas Brownrigg before they reached Charlestown Neck. Archie expresses a desire to help their comrade despite the dangers of entering Boston. The narrator warns that the British will be on high alert after the battle.

Barney was killed accidentally by the youngest boy of the family while fooling with a loaded pistol. Joshua shipped for Cadiz as an ordinary seaman and later signed as A1 on a brig bound for Italy. Joshua took command of the brig before turning sixteen years old after the captain fell ill. He sailed for Alicant and earned significant money for the owners before returning to Baltimore in 1776. Joshua served as master's mate on the sloop Hornet and enlisted a full crew from Baltimore. He participated in the capture of New Providence and later fought against British ships while on the schooner Wasp. Joshua received a lieutenant's commission and captured an English brig before being made prisoner and later exchanged.

The characters traveled back and forth for a distance of a quarter of a mile. They could see the riding lights of the ship clearly. Jerry expressed concern about a boat leaving the ship. The characters decided to keep a watch for a swimmer's head in the water. They heard whistling, indicating that Bill Jepson had escaped from the ship. Bill Jepson was found holding onto the gunwale of their canoe. Jepson mentioned he was from Baltimore and recognized Darius Thorpe as a friendly face.

The narrator expresses a desire to participate in the war against the British enemy. The journey to the fleet involves an eighteen-mile sail up the river. The wind is light, making it difficult to travel more than two miles an hour against the current. Darius advises the narrator to anchor the pungy before dark to avoid grounding. The pungy comes to anchor four miles above Benedict due to the wind dying completely. Darius warns against anchoring in the channel due to the potential threat from the enemy. The narrator acknowledges Darius's experience and agrees to follow his advice for safety.

The narrative takes place beyond Gloucester Point. Pierre expresses optimism about delivering a message to the American lines. The narrator has a strong affection for Fitzroy Hamilton, prioritizing his safety. Pierre and the narrator position themselves a quarter of a mile apart to await a messenger. The narrator observes a man dressed like a Virginia planter who appears to be waiting for someone. The man confirms he is waiting for a message and inquires about the narrator's interest. The narrator identifies himself as the son of Alexander Hamilton and mentions their mission.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The midshipman reported to an officer after showing British silver as proof of payment. Darius expressed his intention to fish around the islands. The crew of the Avenger felt relieved after avoiding service to the king. Darius mentioned the possibility of helping a sailor deserting from an enemy ship. The crew discussed the risks of assisting the sailor and the potential consequences. Jerry expressed concern for the sailor's safety if they left without helping him. Darius acknowledged the crew's ownership of the pungy and their right to make decisions.

The narrator refused to eat more than the portion allotted to him despite pressure from another individual. The old negro insisted that Pierre and the narrator should go through the town to gather information. Horry Sims expressed anger at being restrained in a corner of the room. The narrator observed a large number of soldiers and officers heading toward the water's edge near Lord Cornwallis's headquarters. The narrator heard cannon fire in the distance, indicating a naval battle was taking place. The British fleet was attempting to drive away vessels commanded by Count De Grasse. Pierre expressed concern that if the British fleet succeeded, General Lafayette's forces would be at risk.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The cannonading gradually ceased during the conversation among the boys. A Jerseyman entered the room in an exhausted state after running from the battlefield. The boys barricaded the door and darkened the windows to conceal the Jerseyman's presence. The Jerseyman's clothing was torn, indicating he had been involved in a struggle. He stated that he had been fighting in the trenches and had escaped from a wounded Britisher. The Jerseyman expressed concern that the Britisher might suspect him of being a spy but believed he could not relay information. He intended to remain hidden until midnight to attempt to finish his mission in York.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The narrator and companions visited a woman who needed to keep life in her body. The woman's son is named Hiram Griffin. The narrator promised the woman to seek out her son to inform him about her well-being. During their journey, the narrator and companions encountered about a dozen farmers who seemed knowledgeable about local political matters. The farmers questioned the narrator and companions about the Sons of Liberty and Minute Men. Silas discussed enrolling a company of Minute Boys during their journey. The narrator expressed reluctance to include Seth Jepson in their group due to his association with known Tories.

The battle of Bladensburg involved Commodore Barney, who was wounded and ordered a retreat. Commodore Barney was found by the enemy after falling from weakness during the retreat. General Ross and Admiral Cockburn offered assistance to Commodore Barney after he was found. Captain Dyson abandoned Fort Washington without firing a gun, leading to his dismissal from service. The British squadron anchored off Alexandria on August 28th and prepared to attack the town. Captain Gordon of the British squadron demanded harsh terms from the citizens of Alexandria to spare the town. The British squadron left Alexandria after burning one vessel and loading several others with goods.

The Jerseyman informed the group that the prisoners could not effect their release due to the noise of cannon and musketry. The Jerseyman decided to leave the group earlier than expected to attempt to slip through British lines. Pierre expressed doubt about the possibility of the Jerseyman's plan succeeding. The Jerseyman acknowledged the risks but felt it was necessary to attempt the venture for the Cause. Little Frenchie unbarred the door for the Jerseyman, who left without looking back at the group. The remaining group felt a sense of mourning after the Jerseyman's departure, fearing for his safety. Frenchie encouraged the group to focus on procuring food despite the somber situation.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Darius Thorpe expressed a willingness to fight against those who spoke ill of Joshua Barney. Darius was physically restrained by his comrades to prevent him from pursuing British loyalists. Darius promised to confront Elias Macomber after a battle involving the commodore. The group prepared to board the Avenger after a delay of nearly half an hour. The narrator experienced a change in perspective regarding the war after witnessing the fight. The narrator recognized the importance of defending their homeland and heritage. The narrator felt transformed from cowardice to a sense of duty towards their country.

The character was arrested in the town of York and suspected of being a spy. The narrator hoped the character was arrested for a lesser offense, such as disturbing the peace. Horry Sims, a Tory, attempted to negotiate a deal while in captivity. Pierre responded to Horry Sims' proposal with skepticism about his honor. Horry Sims claimed he could help find another character named Saul Ogden. Pierre expressed distrust in Horry Sims' ability to keep secrets if released. The conversation indicated a potential conflict between the characters regarding trust and loyalty.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Colonel James Barrett can be found at the home of Samuel Hadley near Lexington. A folded paper was given to the narrator by the doctor for delivery. The doctor advised that the message must be destroyed if captured by the king's mercenaries. Archie expressed confidence in their ability to escape Boston harbor. The doctor cautioned against over-confidence and advised caution until the message was delivered. The group decided to act as if they were simply going out for a sail to avoid drawing attention. They encountered few citizens on their way to the ship-yard due to the late hour.

Hiram began taking out larger stones and stowing them in two casks. The group worked quickly to fill the casks with stones and earth. The filled casks were placed in front of a rubbish hole, leaving a narrow passage behind them. Hiram believed they had created a tunnel nearly a foot from the surface. Hiram expressed concern about breaking through the earth without leaving evidence. The group discussed the possibility of using the tunnel to hide from Job Lord. Hiram suggested that one of them could be outside while the others remained hidden.

The narrator recalls an old shed used for stabling horses that is often filled with rubbish. Pierre expresses relief after the narrator explains the situation to him. Pierre warns Saul that his anger endangers them and advises him to control it. Horry Sims appears to understand he is in danger and acts like a trapped animal. The narrator intervenes to prevent Saul from confronting Horry Sims directly. Pierre asserts his right to protect himself and warns Saul about the consequences of his actions. The group decides to hide Horry Sims in the shed to avoid detection.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Seth displayed a willingness to obey Hiram's commands. Job Lord had previously meditated treachery against the Cause. Hiram prepared a meal using provisions found in the building. The meal was more enjoyable than previous meals during the venture. Job Lord promised not to raise his voice above a whisper until sunset. Hiram decided it was safe to allow Job Lord to speak. Hiram planned to transport the prisoners to Cambridge.

Archie believes there is a possibility of finding Silas despite the risks involved. The narrator expresses doubt about the feasibility of helping Silas due to the British guards. Harvey suggests that the Minute Boys should learn the fate of their missing comrades. The narrator feels a sense of duty to assist in finding the missing members of their company. The narrator's father strongly opposes the plan to enter Boston, citing the dangers involved. The situation is described as different from a previous rescue of Archie, as a battle has recently occurred.

Master Morgan provided a pistol and ammunition to the guards of the prisoner, Abel Hunt. The guards were instructed to kill Abel Hunt if he attempted to escape or raise an alarm. Abel Hunt was bound and unable to resist while being threatened by Master Morgan. The group used a rope made from a blanket to hoist Abel Hunt into the loft. The cannonading outside provided cover for the group to move without fear of being overheard. The narrator expressed concern about the future and the likelihood of being discovered by the British. Master Morgan called for the group to gather after they secured Abel Hunt.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town
