text: The conversation involves concerns about sailing up the river and potential danger from British forces. Darius Thorpe expresses his intention to prevent the speaker and Jerry from going ashore. Darius believes it is his duty to protect his shipmates from danger. The speaker realizes Darius is serious about the potential threat from the enemy. Darius explains the importance of reporting to Commodore Barney before attending to personal matters. Darius emphasizes that all Americans who agreed to aid in defense must be ready for duty. The crew approaches the fleet at night and identifies themselves as private service for the commodore.

The narrator expresses uncertainty about going to fight the Britishers during the War of 1812. The narrator feels uncomfortable as their mother prepares them for potential injuries. The narrator reflects on the challenges of navigating the Avenger without encountering British vessels. The narrator believes that the British fleet is positioned to attack Washington or Baltimore. The narrator meets their friend Jerry, who is eager to engage in the conflict. Jerry and other boys assume the Avenger will join Commodore Barney's fleet. The narrator is determined not to go up the river despite pressure from friends.

Hiram planned to go out around the town during the daytime. The narrator expressed concern about Hiram being taken into custody. Hiram believed his face was not known in the town and felt safe to go out. The narrator feared that Hiram could be caught with a document belonging to Job Lord. Hiram insisted he was not taking risks and was determined to leave. The other lads were disturbed by Hiram's decision to venture out. Job Lord warned that Hiram's actions could lead to their imprisonment.

The narrator discusses a plan to rescue a comrade from British forces. Hiram expresses the need for darkness to execute the rescue plan. The narrator shares a conversation with Silas, which pleases Hiram. Hiram mentions seeing Seth Jepson with British soldiers at the dock. The narrator intends to confront Seth Jepson to determine his loyalty. Hiram plans to speak with Silas Brownrigg before he leaves for Cambridge. Seth Jepson approaches the narrator at the dock and inquires about visiting Archie Hemming.

Commodore Barney's force was ordered to join the small army led by General Winder. General Winder had approximately twenty-five hundred armed and effective men in camp. The men in Winder's camp were described as undisciplined and untried. Civilians, including the President and his Cabinet ministers, were present and influenced Winder's decisions. The soldiers prepared for a march shortly after receiving the order. The soldiers did not express fear or grumbling despite understanding the danger they faced. Darius provided a tent and food for the soldiers while their baggage-train was still on the road.

The narrator was cutting up a leg of lamb and putting the slices into a frying pan. Master Lord observed the narrator with curiosity, suspecting awkwardness in his cooking. Master Lord expressed surprise when he noticed something unusual about the screen to the tunnel. Hiram Griffin attacked Master Lord after realizing the situation was critical. Job Lord demonstrated unexpected strength during the struggle with Hiram Griffin. The fight continued silently until the narrator and Archie intervened to subdue Job Lord. Job Lord yelled loudly when he found himself overpowered and helpless.

The narrator expresses pride in being recognized as a soldier by their elders. The narrator's father shows affection and pride in the narrator's accomplishments. General Ward ordered a military funeral for the fallen comrades of the Minute Boys. The Minute Boys were considered part of the army after the funeral. The Minute Boys discussed the possibility of returning to Boston to gather intelligence. The Minute Boys believed they were at risk of being recognized and arrested in Boston. Hiram, who was wounded, refrained from advising the others on whether to return to Boston.

Pierre expressed concern about the movement of baggage to the river and the gathering of horses. The conversation revealed that Cornwallis was preparing to retreat from the American forces. The narrator recalled that Cornwallis had previously boasted about defeating the rebels in Virginia. The British soldiers had begun to recognize the fighting capability of the American soldiers. The narrator felt pride in the American soldiers and disappointment in not being able to contribute to their efforts. The narrator ran to inform others that Cornwallis was getting ready to run away. Uncle 'Rasmus expressed joy at the news of the British retreat.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Hiram instructed to carry Seth Jepson up the ladder and leave him on the floor. Hiram asked if the ship-yard owned by Edes could be located. The group confirmed their familiarity with the location of the ship-yard. Hiram decided to leave Seth Jepson and two other men helpless and gagged. Hiram expressed a willingness to leave the men to starve rather than risk their mission. Archie was urged by Hiram to stop being soft-hearted and to focus on their task. The group left their location in haste, concerned about being pursued.

The group approached the shore without encountering any British sentinels. Hiram steered the skiff and instructed the group to remain motionless. Griffin propelled the skiff past the town to avoid detection. The group moved cautiously towards South street to find Job Lord's residence. Hiram led the group to knock on the second shutter of Job Lord's house. Master Lord instructed the group to go to the rear door for business. The group entered Master Lord's house after confirming their intentions.

Hiram believed he had found a valuable pass but would face trouble from the patrol. Seth Jepson appeared to regain some courage upon seeing Master Lord pleased. Archie expressed anger towards Seth Jepson for his cowardice. Job Lord did not support Seth Jepson's insolence and remained silent. The group was concerned about discussing plans in front of Job Lord due to the risk of him escaping. The situation was tense, and the group feared being discovered by the patrol. The narrator experienced heightened anxiety while trying to determine the time until sunset.

The characters are unable to purchase a rope despite shopkeepers being willing to assist. Jim Freeman suggests stealing the rope if no other options are available. Dody Wardwell proposes begging a shopkeeper for the rope. The narrator's father advises against stealing and suggests properly begging for the rope instead. Jerry and the narrator decide to search for oystermen to borrow a rope. The group decides to eat raw bacon and imitation bread before continuing their search. Jerry and the narrator set out to find an oyster pungy, encountering a vessel that is not accepting visitors.

The narrator was concerned about the fate of Benedict, who might already be a prisoner on an English vessel. The narrator observed a boat approaching and heard noises indicating that crew members were scrambling ashore. Elias Macomber was identified as a traitor who was providing information to a British officer. Macomber reported on the movements of a flotilla, mentioning thirteen barges and the schooner Scorpion with five hundred well-armed men. The British officer asked Macomber for a place on the river to hide during the day, and Macomber suggested a mill five miles upstream. Macomber agreed to accompany the British officer to ensure they were taken in by Essek Harland. The boat was then pulled upstream after the crew resumed their work.

A sufficient number of men must remain at their current position to prevent the enemy from dispersing their army. The British forces are currently confined to Boston. The narrator expresses frustration over the purpose of building intrenchments. The flag of New England was hoisted over the redoubt after work ceased. The last two casks of water were destroyed by enemy fire, leaving the men without water. General Putnam was in command of men constructing another breastwork at Bunker Hill. The narrator observed British troops being transported in barges with precision.

Commodore Barney suggested that the group should get under way immediately. Joshua Barney stated that oystermen do not carry modern arms. Commodore Barney had received requests for interviews from four gentlemen in Nottingham. Darius Thorpe saluted properly while waiting to ascend the stairs. Darius proposed to start their journey without knowing their destination. Darius informed Jim and his friends that they were to spy on the British fleets. Darius indicated that helping the government would be more significant than fighting aboard a vessel.

Pierre expressed doubt about the ability of the young Tory to guard himself. The only way for the Tory to escape from the loft is through the scuttle. Pierre indicated that if the Tory spoke above a whisper, he would be gagged. Fitz Hamilton felt it was reckless to leave the Tory alone in the loft. Pierre suspected the intentions of the stranger in the red coat were not hostile. Uncle 'Rasmus and Saul were present in the room with the red-coated man. The red-coated man appeared unconcerned and at ease in the presence of the rebels.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Cornwallis is surrounded by the French fleet, which includes the _Guadaloupe_ and the _Charon_. Only two of the ships in Cornwallis's fleet are armed for war, while the others are transports. Pierre believes Cornwallis will not attempt to escape past the French fleet. The British encampment is surrounded by American forces, with camp-fires and torches visible at night. There are sounds of gunfire and musketry indicating that both armies are on alert. The narrator and Pierre are tasked with foraging for provisions in the British camp. Pierre suggests they approach a nearby dwelling to seek help for food.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The redoubt built was eight rods square, with the eastern side bordering a large field. The northern side had an open passageway, and the breastworks on the easterly side extended about one hundred yards northward. A sally-port was located between the south end of the breastwork and the redoubt. Two strong fences made of stones and rails were built on either side of the entire works. His majesty's ship _Lively_ opened fire while the men were working on the fortification. Colonel Prescott encouraged the men to continue their work despite the ship's fire. The soldiers worked diligently, with some eating while others waited until the task was completed.

Elias Macomber was involved in a confrontation with Darius over comments made about Joshua Barney. Darius expressed anger towards those who spoke against Joshua Barney. Elias Macomber made derogatory remarks about Joshua Barney, prompting Darius to react. A physical altercation ensued involving Darius and several Tories after Elias's comments. Jerry joined the fight to support Darius while carrying a heavy bag of meal. Jim Freeman jumped into the water to assist Darius and Jerry during the fight. The outcome of the fight was claimed as a victory by Darius and his companions, despite both sides sustaining injuries.

The characters in the text include Harvey, Hiram, and the narrator. Hiram expresses concern that they may be followed after leaving Boston by water. Hiram believes that General Gage may take steps to prevent them from obtaining supplies. The Minute Boys of Boston are mentioned as being ready to resist the king's men. There are muskets and ammunition on board the other sloop. Hiram anticipates that British vessels will be sent out to pursue them. The urgency to take on cargo quickly is emphasized to prepare for a potential encounter.

The characters are prisoners in York Town. Pierre Laurens plans to attempt to secure horses and speak with General Lafayette. Uncle 'Rasmus appears to be ill and is sitting by a window. Uncle 'Rasmus is pretending to be sick to avoid suspicion from British soldiers. The characters have captured Horry Sims to protect themselves. They plan to keep Horry Sims hidden until they can bring him to Uncle 'Rasmus's location.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Master Lord expressed skepticism about the feasibility of a plan involving him and another individual being taken through the streets of Boston as prisoners. Master Lord indicated that he believed the king's officers were familiar with him and that another individual could not impersonate him. Seth appeared to gain some courage from Master Lord's conviction, showing a change in his demeanor. The narrator refrained from revealing their plans to Master Lord due to concerns about potential leaks. Laughter from Archie and Harvey, as Hiram recounted a story, seemed to disturb Master Lord and suggest that the plan was viable. Hiram planned to leave for his work around sunset and suggested that the others eat and share food with the prisoners. Master Lord predicted that Hiram would end up in prison regardless of the time he set out.

The characters discuss the presence of British soldiers surrounding their location. Saul Ogden expresses doubt about their ability to hold out against the British forces. Pierre believes that General Cornwallis will not divert troops to capture three boys and a negro. The characters consider the possibility of communicating with their forces despite the storm. Pierre argues that attempting to cross British lines during the storm would be dangerous. The characters work together to fortify their cabin against potential attacks. They use available materials to strengthen the door and windows of the cabin.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: A thousand or more armed men were sent out under cover of darkness for a significant reason. The group marched for nearly three hours before reaching Charlestown Neck. At Charlestown Neck, they found wagons filled with spades, pick-axes, and other tools. Colonel Gridley and Colonel Prescott consulted with other officers about their next actions. The group was ordered to a hill in Charlestown to construct breastworks. The work was done under the threat of British forces nearby, requiring caution and speed. The hill where they worked had steep sides and was near brick kilns, clay pits, and marshy land.

The characters are off St. Leonard's bay and have not seen their target, Elias Macomber. Darius expresses frustration about the situation and believes they will have an advantage once they are out of the river. Jerry suggests that continuing the chase may hinder their ability to collect oysters. The wind from the west is expected to help their vessel, the pungy, and there is a possibility of overtaking Macomber. Upon reaching the mouth of the river, they conclude that the chase has ended and Macomber is likely hiding on shore. They decide to dredge for oysters to provide an excuse for seeking out the enemy. By nightfall, they have collected fifteen bushels of oysters, which they believe will help them establish themselves in the business.

The men in the redoubt had insufficient bayonets and ammunition to resist a British attack. Many soldiers did not have a single charge for their muskets, prompting Colonel Prescott to order a division of available ammunition. Some soldiers attempted to gather rocks as missiles while others risked their lives to retrieve ammunition from the battlefield. The British forces were heavily firing on Charlestown Neck, making it dangerous for reinforcements to cross. General Ward at Cambridge lacked sufficient staff officers to effectively carry out orders during the battle. Colonel Gardner led three hundred men to Bunker Hill but was mortally wounded, causing confusion among his troops. General Howe was expected to launch a third assault with fresh troops, despite some soldiers hoping for a cessation of hostilities.

The action involved one hundred and thirty-six men, resulting in thirty killed and fifty-three wounded. Of the sixteen officers on board, fifteen were killed or wounded, and the captain received three wounds. The Hyder Ally had four killed and eleven wounded, and was armed with twelve six-pounders and four nine-pounders. During the action, thirteen broadsides were fired from the cannons and sixty to seventy rounds from muskets. Captain Barney took command of the General Monk after it was sold to the government. In 1789, Captain Barney embarked for Carthagena and later went to Havana before returning home. Barney was captured by an English privateer brig, but he and his men managed to retake their ship.

The men on the British ships were focused on their duties and did not pay attention to two lads rowing against the current. The cannon fire from the British ships and my Lord Cornwallis's encampment was loud and continuous. The fleet of small craft moved steadily toward its destination despite the cannon fire from the British. No British cannonballs appeared to hit the fleet, and no severe damage was observed among the vessels. The cannonading from the town continued, with varying intensity, but did not target the vessels near Gloucester. The water front of the village appeared deserted when the skiff grounded on the shore. The narrator and Pierre shared a sense of excitement and determination during their passage.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Uncle 'Rasmus plans to travel to York Town. Uncle 'Rasmus has not traveled far from home in the past three years. Uncle 'Rasmus intends to check on Marse Hamilton's property. The British are currently in York Town. Uncle 'Rasmus believes he can get through British lines with the help of children. Little Frenchie expresses enthusiasm about accompanying Uncle 'Rasmus. Uncle 'Rasmus plans to carry a blanket and food for the journey.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The jib and mainsail appeared damaged. The narrator instructed Hiram to steer the sloop. Harvey Pearson was the first to fire his musket. The enemy's forces were reduced after the initial volley. The narrator experienced excitement and confusion during the battle. Hiram was injured, with his left arm hanging useless. The Minute Boys of Boston successfully defended the sloop and repelled the enemy.

The characters Archie and Harvey experienced amazement after reading an order from Governor Gage. The narrator felt a sense of undefined fear despite the group's rejoicing over their situation. Hiram planned to present himself at the Bridewell at nightfall as part of their future plans. The group discussed the possibility that the officer at the Bridewell might recognize Master Lord and take action against them. Hiram instructed Luke Wright to take a pass and escape if he was held in custody. The group debated the morality of abandoning Hiram if he was captured. Hiram took on the role of cook while the group considered the suffering of Job Lord.

Captain Hanaford asked how the scuttle was accessed. Bill was one of the first put into the place and took advantage of the chance to snoop around. Bill found a key in the door that led to the attic, which was a store-room. The hatch was found bolted on the inside, making escape easier. Captain Hanaford expressed concern about being discovered due to a rope left dangling from the chimney. The British fleet was in the river, making it dangerous to sail upstream. A storm with strong winds and heavy rain prevented the pungy from leaving its mooring.

The narrator and Jerry are oystermen from Benedict seeking assistance. They owned a pungy named Avenger, which was burned at Pig Point. They encounter Robert Hanaford, an oysterman from St. Leonard's bay, who is also in trouble. Darius Thorpe is being held prisoner by the British and may be sent to the fleet. Bill Jepson from Baltimore is also a prisoner and is at risk of execution. Captain Hanaford offers to help the narrator and Jerry by providing rope and provisions. Hanaford expresses a willingness to assist in rescuing Bill Jepson and Darius Thorpe.

Hiram Griffin displayed a calm demeanor despite the imminent danger during the battle. The narrator expressed a desire for the enemy to attack sooner due to a lack of water. Archie warned the narrator that they might not have much time left to live. Hiram criticized Archie for making pessimistic predictions about their survival. The enemy began a third assault with artillery that caused significant casualties. All soldiers were ordered to retreat to the redoubt for better shelter from the enemy fire. The British soldiers adapted their tactics by shedding heavy gear and attacking at a weaker point.

Saul Ogden is the cousin of the narrator, Fitzroy Hamilton, and is three days younger than him. In August of 1781, Fitzroy Hamilton had just turned fifteen years old. Fitzroy and Saul were unaware of the ongoing conflict in America until the engagement at Spencer's Ordinary. Boys in Massachusetts and New York were enrolling as Minute Boys to support the cause of independence. Fitzroy and Saul met Pierre Laurens, a French boy from New Orleans, who informed them about the Minute Boys. Pierre Laurens inspired Fitzroy and Saul to consider forming a company of Minute Boys after the engagement at Spencer's Ordinary. The engagement at Spencer's Ordinary was a drawn battle, surprising Lieutenant-Colonel Simcoe.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Jim Freeman stated that the orders were to wait for the British forces to show themselves. Darius informed the group that the British were making camp less than two miles away. The group discussed the destruction of their fleet in anticipation of the British approach. Darius mentioned that they would inspect each craft to ensure flames could be started quickly. The narrator expressed doubt about the decision to burn the flotilla without defending it. The British were confirmed to be encamped for the night, with no immediate action expected until daylight. The group felt impatient about not starting the destruction of the fleet immediately.

Commodore Barney expressed frustration over delays while waiting for the fleet. Barney planned to leave Darius in command under Lieutenant Frazier. Barney intended to march to the Wood Yard with available men to support Winder's encampment. Darius was instructed to prepare the fleet for destruction if the enemy approached. Barney emphasized the importance of quick obedience to orders to avoid danger. The narrator was concerned about the fate of Elias Macomber during the planned destruction of the fleet. The narrator discussed the situation regarding Macomber with Jerry, seeking a solution.

Darius Thorpe was perceived by the narrator as a broken-down sailor, but Commodore Barney had a different view of him. Darius Thorpe expressed pride when he boarded the Avenger. Darius Thorpe insisted that the narrator and Jerry praise Commodore Barney. An officer from the schooner arrived to receive prisoners, necessitating the removal of traitors from the hold. The narrator suggested that Darius and Jim Freeman handle the duty of bringing the traitors from the hold. The narrator wanted to speak with his father before agreeing to serve under Commodore Barney. The narrator's father expressed approval of his decision to serve under Commodore Barney.

The boat is within five minutes' walk of the house. The sergeant is ready to help them leave town at any suitable time. Hiram believes they were in a delicate position and needed a scheme to escape safely. Hiram plans to go to the Bridewell with a soldier as an escort. Hiram thinks having a red-coated escort reduces the chances of being questioned. Hiram successfully returned, which pleased his comrades. Seth Jepson showed fear at the prospect of going to Cambridge.

The old sailor provided a meal and proposed to dress the father's wound before attending to his own needs. Darius washed and bandaged the father's wound and made him more comfortable. The group was hiding in a smoke-house to avoid detection by the British army. The retreat from Bladensburg began around four o'clock in the afternoon. Darius examined their refuge and opened a shutter to keep a lookout. Darius and the narrator observed the British army advancing near the Capitol building. General Ross and Admiral Cockburn were identified as high-ranking officers in the British army.

The Scorpion arrived at the stream attended by other vessels. The schooner was anchored alongside the pungy. Lieutenant Frazier ordered men to disembark after a private meeting with the commodore. Elias Macomber was handed over to a man from Nottingham with specific instructions regarding his treatment. Lieutenant Frazier invited Darius and the crew of the pungy to take up quarters on the schooner. Six men were sent down the river in canoes to monitor enemy movements. The remaining crew prepared for the potential destruction of the fleet.

The narrator is at the corner of Hull and Salem streets. The narrator believes that the British soldiers are not pursuing him. The narrator experiences fatigue after running and hides under the broken timbers of an old wharf. The narrator hears footsteps approaching and prepares to defend himself. The approaching figure is identified as Hiram Griffin. Hiram Griffin explains that he escaped by running quickly from the British soldiers. The narrator expresses regret for potentially causing Archie's capture.

The logs were used to take aim. A musket was discharged, missing the target and passing close to Abel Hunt's head. Abel Hunt and Horry ran away from the scene until they were beyond musket-shot. Abel Hunt and Horry returned with five soldiers after a brief absence. Pierre took command and instructed the group not to fire until they could hit the target. Pierre was the first to open fire during the confrontation. One British soldier was wounded and fell to the ground after being shot.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The American forces were engaged in close combat with British soldiers, referred to as 'lobster backs'. The Americans used the butts of their muskets as weapons due to a lack of ammunition. Colonel Prescott and Doctor Warren were among the last to leave the redoubt during the retreat. The American forces were attempting to reach Bunker Hill while being covered by fire from other American troops. Doctor Warren was reported killed during the retreat, which affected the morale of the American soldiers.

Abel Hunt is aware that Saul is the narrator's cousin. The horses on the Hamilton plantation have likely been seized. The narrator believes they can escape to the river while cannonading occurs. The skiff is still at the location where it was left. Pierre questions the narrator's eagerness to leave York. The narrator feels that leaving York could be perceived as cowardice. Pierre expresses concern about the narrator's potential future pain from their actions.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Darius went toward a chosen place of refuge, prompting others to follow him. Darius lifted the narrator's father from the animal's back and carried him into a rough building. The building was described as less inviting than the hold of the Avenger after a cargo of oysters was removed. Darius left to drive the mule toward a tavern, causing concern among the group. The narrator expressed regret for their earlier unkind words when Darius returned with hay for comfort. Darius traded the mule for supplies, including a ham, cotton cloth, and a jug of water. The group began eating the uncooked ham without waiting for Darius to join them.

The group was concerned about seeking refuge in a city that was about to be occupied by the British. The narrator and Darius assisted the wounded father on a mule as they approached the city. The group had limited funds consisting of two silver coins and two copper coins each, with Jim Freeman having two shillings. The group initially believed that the citizens of Washington would abandon the city after news of a defeat. Upon nearing the city, the group realized that the inhabitants remained in their homes. Darius opposed the idea of staying at a tavern due to the risk of being discovered by soldiers. The group debated the best hiding place, with Darius suggesting a smoke-house instead of a tavern.

Lord Cornwallis was in York Town and sought to learn about his adversaries. General Lafayette sent Morgan to enlist as a British soldier. The narrator set off from York Town toward Williamsburg with a message for General Lafayette. The narrator believed there was a low chance of safely completing the journey. The narrator encountered a voice demanding him to halt while approaching the American encampment. The narrator was relieved to find that the voice belonged to a friend in the uniform of Virginia riflemen. The corporal questioned the narrator's intentions and origin, suspecting him of dishonesty.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Lord Cornwallis refers to certain individuals as rebels and shows more favor toward Tories. The narrator and a character named Pierre arrive at the river front opposite Gloucester Point. Pierre expresses fatigue and suggests resting by the water's edge until sunrise. Abel Hunt follows closely behind the narrator and engages in a heated exchange regarding their social status. The narrator reflects on the differences among the people of Virginia and their potential reactions to the war. The narrator observes Pierre looking across the river, contemplating a plan that could be beneficial. Abel Hunt eventually lies down nearby, indicating he may stay for the night.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Bill Jepson sang and danced while insisting Darius join him as Jim Freeman provided music. The group felt jolly as they believed the enemy was no longer a threat while heading home. They discussed plans to buy a pungy for oystering after receiving payment for the Avenger. Captain Hanaford expressed surprise upon seeing the British fleet approaching Fort Washington. The British fleet included two frigates, two rocket ships, two bomb vessels, and one schooner. Fort Washington was considered a feeble fortress but capable of being strengthened. Despite recommendations for strengthening Fort Washington, no significant improvements were made before the British advance.

Hanaford maneuvered the pungy to avoid being stuck on the bank as an engagement was anticipated. Bill Jepson suggested returning up the river quickly. Darius agreed to move back but did not want to go far until assessing the situation. Captain Hanaford ordered the crew to assist in getting the pungy off the mud. The crew struggled to float the pungy due to the wind and its design. Captain Hanaford noted that the wind would calm down within an hour. The fort was destroyed by an explosion, causing debris to fall on the pungy.

The journey to the rope walk was not delayed due to familiarity with the route. Some lads at the rope walk were impatient after waiting six to eight hours. Seth Jepson left the group to attend to work his mother assigned him. Hiram expressed doubt about Seth Jepson's excuse for leaving. Thirteen lads were present at the rendezvous, along with Archie and Silas on board a sloop. Griffin, Harvey, and the narrator were concerned about Seth Jepson's potential betrayal. Hiram questioned how long it would take for a lad to go to the governor's house and return.

The characters are in a tense situation involving Master Lord and the potential arrival of outside visitors. Archie expresses concern about the conversation with Master Lord and warns Luke Wright to remain quiet. Three distinct knocks are heard on the outer door, indicating imminent danger. Harvey and Archie take measures to prevent the captives, Master Lord and Seth Jepson, from making noise. Luke Wright and Archie prepare to go to the room above to await Hiram's return. Archie and Luke Wright search for weapons to defend themselves in case of an attack. Luke Wright finds a three-legged stool and removes one of its legs to use as a weapon.

Master Lord is mentioned as a person of interest in the context of loyalty and secrecy. Hiram directed the narrator to take a position near the door of the building. The narrator observed the arrival of at least two men based on their footfalls. Hiram instructed Archie and Harvey to attend to the cooking of meat. Hiram and the narrator examined the walls of the cellar for a means of escape. They discovered a rubbish hole that appeared to be a previously closed entrance to the cellar. Hiram indicated that they should not converse and suggested the narrator return to listen for sounds from above.

Little Frenchie has a plan to capture a Tory villain and gain possession of a mare and Silver Heels. Little Frenchie did not reveal details of his plan while walking home. Little Frenchie demonstrated knowledge of military fortifications in York. The British line of fortifications extends from the river to the sloping grounds near the Pigeon Quarter. There are plans for seven redoubts and six batteries on the land side of York. My Lord Cornwallis has made his headquarters at Governor Nelson's house. Little Frenchie estimated that Lord Cornwallis's army consists of approximately seven thousand men.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The narrator hears several voices and looks out from the underbrush. Elias Macomber is talking with Jenkins outside a dwelling. Macomber expresses intent to inform the British fleet about American positions. Jenkins argues with Macomber about loyalty to the United States. The narrator and Jerry decide to wait to confront Macomber. They plan to consult with Bill Jepson after observing the conversation. Jepson acknowledges that Macomber is a spy and plans to prevent him from informing the British.

The characters include Fitz, Pierre, Saul, and Uncle 'Rasmus. My Lord Cornwallis traveled down the river to Portsmouth after leaving James Town. Cornwallis entered York Town on September 1, 1781, and began fortifying York and Gloucester. Uncle 'Rasmus expressed concern about Cornwallis's situation, suggesting he was in a difficult position. Saul questioned Uncle 'Rasmus's belief that the French general could harm the British. Uncle 'Rasmus mentioned the presence of French vessels near the Capes. Saul proposed that Cornwallis could retreat by land if he could not escape by water.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Master Lord has provided refuge for those in need since General Gage began making trouble. The British have not suspected Master Lord of aiding the Cause. Master Lord expressed concern that attempting to rescue a prisoner could harm the Cause. Hiram indicated that they were not relying on Master Lord for assistance in their mission. Master Lord acknowledged the difficulty of entering Boston since the battle. Master Lord advised the group to rest and remain quiet during the night. Hiram expressed distrust towards Master Lord after he left the room.

The skiff is nearby and can be boarded at leisure. Hiram plans to take a prisoner to the Bridewell with the help of a sergeant's man. Hiram believes he can select a prisoner based on General Gage's order. Hiram visited the guard-house to establish a reputation as a friend to the Cause. Hiram showed the sergeant General Gage's order for a Bridewell prisoner. The prisoner taken at Breed's Hill is intended to be used as bait for a trap. Hiram obtained information about the skiff used by Job Lord from the sergeant.

The narrator and Pierre are hiding on a river bank in York. Abel Hunt is the only person in York who seems to be watching them. After three hours, Abel Hunt becomes uneasy and checks to see if the narrator and Pierre are asleep. Abel Hunt decides to go to my Lord Cornwallis's headquarters after concluding that the narrator and Pierre are asleep. The narrator expresses concern that Abel Hunt might report them as the son of a well-known rebel loitering in the village. Pierre believes they should focus on their task rather than worry about potential dangers. The narrator and Pierre discuss the possibility of leaving York without alerting Abel Hunt.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Joseph Warren urged for the enlistment of men to form an army and send them to Headquarters at Cambridge. Warren emphasized the urgency of the situation, stating that delay could lead to death and devastation. The text references the year 1775 and the activities of the Minute Boys. The narrator received instructions and advice in Cambridge before attempting to return to town. Doctor Warren offered assistance to the narrator regarding transportation to the town. Hiram Griffin prepared a boat for the narrator to use on the river. The narrator and Hiram planned to travel together to Boston despite the risks involved.

Hiram and the narrator discussed plans for a rescue operation. They decided to prepare two or three skiffs and hide them in different locations. Potential hiding places were identified, including the rope walk at Barton's point and a burying place near the Bridewell. Hiram requested to be shown the hiding places to ensure he could find them in the dark. After discussing their plans, they went to the narrator's mother's house for supper. The narrator's mother expressed concern for her son's safety but supported his decision to participate in the rescue. Hiram brought a stout oaken stick from behind the kitchen door before they set out.

Hiram claimed the right to make the first venture because he believed he was the least known in Boston. Archie pointed out that Hiram's name had been listed with others who informed the British. Hiram argued that he would face less danger due to his anonymity in the town. The speaker asserted that he was chosen captain of the Minute Boys, giving him the right to lead. The speaker planned to visit his mother for information and advice on whom to contact regarding their cause. The group prepared to hide when they heard someone enter the room. Master Lord entered the room and was greeted by Hiram's inquiry about the time of day.

The narrator stood by a canoe while people in Benedict believed he was eager to fight for his country. Jim Freeman mentioned Elias Macomber, an Englishman who had been in the country for less than four years. Elias Macomber was making threats about what he would do when the British arrived. The narrator felt relieved for not expressing opposition to joining Commodore Barney's fleet. Darius arrived with a bundle wrapped in a blanket and mentioned the narrator's mother's emotional state. The village was informed that the narrator and Darius were going to Nottingham to join the commodore. Darius and the narrator were approached by women wanting to send messages or forgotten items to their relatives in the fleet.

Two boys lived in Benedict, Charles County, Maryland, near the mouth of Indian Creek. The boys were named Jerry and the narrator, who was seventeen years old. In 1810, Jerry's brother Tom was taken by British officers and forced to serve in the English navy for three years. The boys saved money to buy a sloop-rigged pungy named The Avenger for one hundred dollars. They purchased The Avenger in the spring of 1812 and intended to use it for the oyster business. During the second year of the war, their earnings from the oyster business decreased. In the spring of 1814, they made a trade with Darius Thorpe, who would sail with them for one-third of the profits.

The visitor is Hiram Griffin, a stout young man from Cambridge. Griffin traveled to his current location by walking, pulling a skiff, and swimming. Griffin's clothes were wet from his journey, and he made a puddle on the floor. Griffin delivered a message from Luke Wright, requesting that Luke and Archie Hemming come to Cambridge. Griffin indicated that it was unsafe to leave Boston during the day and that they should depart at once. The gathering in Cambridge is related to the rebellion against the king that began at Lexington. Griffin was aware of the location of Luke Wright's home due to clear directions given by Luke.

The characters are in a beleaguered village and discuss the local population's political affiliations. The speaker believes it is better to be held in a guard-house than to starve. The speaker expresses doubt that the local people could influence British officers. The speaker suggests that some Tories may be undecided about which side to support. The characters approach a dwelling and are greeted by an old man. The old man questions the characters' claim about needing food for an old negro. The old man leaves to retrieve something after a brief conversation with the characters.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The instructions from the War Department were to destroy the fortification rather than risk its capture by the enemy. The individual in command did not fire any guns before destroying the fortification. All members of the party in the pungy sustained bruises or scratches during the incident. Darius and Bill Jepson took a small boat to assist the pungy after the explosion. The group attempted to hide the pungy in a creek to avoid capture by the British fleet. The British fleet paused to assess the damage to the fortification, allowing the group time to escape. The group worked hard to move the pungy inland and hide it from view.

Uncle 'Rasmus was alarmed and distressed due to the absence of the narrator and Pierre. The narrator and Pierre needed to avoid performing a task set by the Jerseyman. The narrator believed they could not set off in a boat alone while being watched by Abel Hunt. The narrator thought Pierre could gain the attention of king's officers by offering information about spies. Uncle 'Rasmus was left in old Mary's cabin to guard a prisoner. The narrator estimated there was less than a quart of water left in the cabin. Abel Hunt suspected the narrator and Pierre were hiding something and questioned their lack of shelter.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Hiram pointed out five barges filled with marines approaching from Boston. General Howe has called for more reinforcements. The Minute Boys were seen searching the bodies of the dead for ammunition. The marines landed and advanced with greater fury than during the first assault. Cannon fire from the ships increased, causing fires in the town. A breeze cleared the smoke, revealing British troops marching up the hill. General Howe was reported to be marching in advance of his men.

The only other markets available were Annapolis and Baltimore. The ship was named Narcissus, which Darius recognized from a previous sighting. Darius expressed concern about being recognized by a man named Bill Jepson on the forecastle deck. Bill Jepson was a Baltimore man who may have been pressed into service. Darius was sympathetic to Bill's situation and considered helping him. The Avenger received orders to heave to after coming off the Severn.

The group prepared for an enemy approach by loading muskets and distributing cartridges. They made a meal from the last of their food after loading their weapons. The storm intensified, causing the cabin to rock violently and raising fears among the group. Uncle 'Rasmus suggested that the younger members of the group lie down to sleep, but they were unwilling due to the storm and impending danger. The sound of American cannon fire was heard, which Pierre interpreted as a sign of hope. The narrator decided to take watch in the attic with two loaded muskets. The hurricane subsided as the sun began to rise.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Jerry proposed a scheme to find the fleet. The plan involved visiting Benedict to gather information about the commodore. Jim Freeman warned that British forces were entering the bay. Jim expressed disbelief that the British would come into the Patuxent River. Jerry and Jim had been away for nearly ten days selling oysters. Admiral Cochrane had passed the capes with twenty-one vessels. Commodore Malcolm was reported to be below with a fleet of soldiers.

The little French lad insisted that the narrator display more humanity before stepping outside the cabin. The narrator preferred to assist in disposing of the prisoner rather than search for Saul alone. The prisoner was bound securely and treated as if he were a bale of merchandise. Uncle 'Rasmus was left in the cabin to act as a jailor while seated in a corner with a blanket over his knee. Pierre assured the narrator that Uncle 'Rasmus was capable of defending himself with his cane. The British army was actively working on their fortifications at night in York. The narrator and Pierre headed toward the quarters of the Rangers in search of Saul.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Hiram mentioned that Master Fish has a skiff hidden near his smokehouse. General Gage's orders have led to the confiscation of all craft in town. Hiram expressed urgency in getting the lad out of prison. Rain began to fall as Hiram prepared to act. Hiram used an oaken stick to pry open the window bars of the prison. Hiram successfully opened the window, allowing Archie to escape. Hiram pulled Archie out into the street while remaining alert for any danger.

The voyage was directed by the wind past Morton's point towards the Penny ferry. The sloop that was protected during the voyage was seen anchored in the distance. The cargo from the sloop was being taken to shore by boats, indicating that the operation had begun. The narrator expressed satisfaction and pride in their accomplishments during the mission. Upon reaching the Penny ferry, forty or fifty men were engaged in transporting sheep and grain. Archie and the narrator arranged for carts with horses to carry their dead and wounded. The reception at the encampment was warm, with praise from sailors and Doctor Warren for the actions of the Minute Boys.

Uncle 'Rasmus has lived on the plantation for nearly forty years. Uncle 'Rasmus is familiar with the paths through the plantation. The narrator expresses doubt about Uncle 'Rasmus's ability to navigate beyond the plantation. The group plans to travel to York and back to recover stolen horses. Frenchie questions the necessity of all three traveling the same distance twice. Saul suggests that one person should stay behind to bring food the next morning. The group decides that one member should return home to inform their mother of their plans.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The force is small, which the British learned at St. Leonard's bay. Bill, Jerry, and another individual planned to capture an enemy operative. Darius Thorpe was warned to prepare for an immediate move by the enemy. The group received provisions from the cook without waking Commodore Barney. They paddled down the river, avoiding stopping at their homes to prevent being seen. The group paddled continuously from the fleet until they reached Hog Point. They discussed the best approach to a house while considering the possibility of British activity.

The narrator felt secure from harm while waiting, believing the plan would be abandoned due to the shallow river above Nottingham. Darius was uneasy about remaining with the boats instead of acting as a spy, which indicated potential danger. A report indicated that the British forces were embarking on barges and small boats with artillery, suggesting they expected resistance. The narrator expressed a desire to inflict damage on the enemy, despite Darius's warning about the futility of such actions. Twenty men were posted as sentinels along the river, while the rest were prepared to ignite the fleet if necessary. Reports of the enemy's movement suggested a possible night attack, increasing the tension among the crew of the Avenger. The crew experienced significant suspense and anxiety while waiting for the enemy's arrival.

The narrator was aboard a ship and was tasked with opening oyster shells. A sailor on the ship whispered a message to the narrator to tell Darius Thorpe to be eastward of Tangiers that night. The narrator opened oysters quickly, impressing the officers who had difficulty doing so. The narrator proposed to sell the entire load of oysters at eight cents a bushel, which the officers accepted. Darius remained hidden in the hold of the ship while the oysters were being unloaded. An officer agreed to purchase oysters every other day while the ship remained at the station. The narrator attempted to gather information about when the ship might move but was unsuccessful.

The Boston Minute Boys have been involved in the war against the king. General Gage closed the port of Boston to all vessels except those of the king on June 1, 1774. General Gage brought soldiers from Halifax, Quebec, New York, and Ireland to maintain control over Boston. The closure of the port led to widespread poverty and starvation among the people of Boston. Support from other colonies and charitable contributions from London helped the poor in Boston during this time. The men of Boston began to organize for potential conflict against General Gage. Rumors circulated that the king's ships would fire on Boston due to the arming of its people.

The protagonist releases Horry Sims from his bonds. The protagonist warns Horry Sims against any future acts of aggression. The protagonist observes a sudden and violent tempest after releasing Horry Sims. The tempest includes strong winds, thunder, and heavy rain. Uncle 'Rasmus expresses concern about the storm and its implications. The protagonist informs Uncle 'Rasmus that the British are retreating to Gloucester Point. Uncle 'Rasmus insists that there will be no retreat that night.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The narrator's head was represented by a dummy made of blankets placed on the bed. Hiram instructed the narrator on how to escape through a tunnel. Hiram and others were stationed to monitor for any suspicious sounds during the escape. The narrator found the tunnel narrower than expected, causing concern about getting stuck. The narrator scraped away dirt until reaching the turf, allowing for an escape to the outside. The narrator emerged from the tunnel at the rear of the building, free to move away. The narrator carried a knife as the only weapon during the escape.

The narrator experienced anxiety after meeting Uncle 'Rasmus. Pierre initiated a conversation to distract from the surrounding danger. Uncle 'Rasmus expressed concern about the narrator and Pierre being captured by the enemy. Uncle 'Rasmus felt flustered and feared he would never see the narrator and Pierre again. Uncle 'Rasmus planned to leave Horry Sims behind if he had to escape. Uncle 'Rasmus described feeling hunger and thirst while waiting for the narrator and Pierre. Uncle 'Rasmus felt conflicted about his interactions with Horry Sims due to fear of being discovered.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The lad was not guarded and faced opposition from the king's forces in Boston. The Committee of Safety believed the Minute Boys could aid the Cause. Three skiffs had been secreted by those who supported the colonies. The father advised the lad to prioritize the good of the Cause above personal discomfort. There were less than five thousand men in Cambridge at the time. The Provincial Congress voted to raise an army of thirteen thousand six hundred men. Doctor Warren wrote an appeal for raising an army in response to violence against colonists.

The narrator was able to thrust their entire arm between the iron bars and the window-sash. Darius looked up and rose to his feet after the narrator began to tap gently. Darius communicated with Bill using gestures while leaning against the window sash. Darius mouthed the words 'On the roof--to-night--bring rope--ten o'clock' three times. The narrator estimated that approximately forty-three or four feet of rope would be needed for the escape plan. The jail, referred to as the 'stone house,' was three stories high with a pitched roof and four chimneys. The narrator encountered Jerry after backing across the street and discussed their observations.

Hiram began tearing his shirt into strips to create makeshift bindings for Seth's hands and feet. Seth did not resist while being bound and appeared terrified, believing he was brought there to die. Hiram warned Seth that their lives depended on his silence and threatened to kill him if he made an outcry. Seth promised to comply with Hiram's demands, expressing his fear through tears. Hiram carried Seth behind a screen of casks and laid him down in a tunnel. Hiram and the other boys discussed their dangerous situation, which was complicated by having a prisoner. They considered the possibility of Job Lord discovering Seth's presence and the consequences that would follow.

Jerry was astonished after hearing the story of the escape. The group had successfully located their missing comrade without trouble. Darius and Bill planned to gain access to the roof of the 'stone house' during the night. Jerry suggested returning to the smoke-house to discuss their plans and have breakfast. The group had less than three shillings, which was insufficient to buy the necessary rope. The narrator believed they had walked at least three miles to avoid detection. The comrades welcomed the narrator and Jerry upon their return to the smoke-house.

Darius suggested that escaping in a hurry might be easier by going into the woods. Darius expressed concern that if their plan failed, they would not need the canoe. Jerry paddled upstream quickly, eager to reach the rendezvous before the others who were walking. Darius led the group through the underbrush toward the highway while another member brought up the rear. The group moved cautiously as they approached their destination, aware of the nature of their mission. Darius and the group found the main door of the mill fastened from the inside. Darius led the group to an aperture in the mill's under-pinning to gain access.

Pierre proposed to embark in a skiff to deliver a message to the Gloucester shore. Fitz Hamilton expressed concern about abandoning Uncle 'Rasmus while he was holding Horry Sims a prisoner. Pierre argued that delivering the message was their duty, regardless of the risks involved. The journey to Gloucester would require passing near British warships, the _Charon_ and the _Guadaloupe_. Fitz Hamilton acknowledged the dangers of the venture but insisted he was not afraid. Pierre urged Fitz Hamilton to join him before daybreak to reach the Gloucester shore.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Silas proposed that they band together in the service of the colony. Archie supported the idea of raising a company of Minute Boys. The speaker expressed doubt about the wisdom of Silas's scheme. The speaker believed they could only trust a small number of recruits in Boston. Silas suggested they choose only trustworthy lads and consult their elders. The speaker preferred to keep their plans private to avoid alerting the enemy. The speaker concluded that they should focus on their current mission before discussing the Minute Boys.

One individual was shot in the leg and retreated to the redoubt. Pierre advised against shooting a man in the back and emphasized the importance of not shedding blood needlessly. Uncle 'Rasmus expressed skepticism about the British soldiers retreating for good. Pierre and the narrator reloaded their muskets and prepared for further danger. A squad of approximately twenty British soldiers emerged from the redoubt, accompanied by Abel Hunt and Horry Sims. The British soldiers divided into three squads to approach the cabin strategically. Pierre and the narrator argued about who should take a more dangerous position in the loft.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Elias Macomber is the individual the characters want to capture. Bill Jepson suggests that they should first go up the river and then return to capture Macomber. The canoe cannot carry four people, especially with a struggling prisoner. The characters decide to paddle close to shore to avoid being seen from Jenkins' house. The wind is favorable for their journey to Nottingham, allowing the canoe to sail quickly. Bill Jepson is steering the canoe and maintains a straight course. The characters pass by Benedict without stopping, indicating they are on urgent business.

At the close of the year 1774, there were eleven regiments of British soldiers in Boston. Five hundred marines were landed from the Asia Man-of-War. At the beginning of the year 1775, one hundred and fifty soldiers were on duty at the Neck night and day. Colonists smuggled weapons and ammunition past British guards in preparation for a potential conflict. Many firearms were captured by British soldiers after they discovered the smuggling activities. The narrator's father, Samuel Wright, had gone to Cambridge on business. The narrator and his friends encountered a Tory named Amos Nelson near the city dock.

The story 'Captain Brand, of the Schooner Centipede' is authored by Lieut. Henry A. Wise, U.S.N. The book 'Captain Brand' is recognized for its depiction of piratical life in the West Indies. The novel 'Nick of the Woods' by Robert Montgomery Bird was originally published in 1837. The story 'Nick of the Woods' presents a realistic portrayal of Indian and frontier life in early Kentucky. The romance 'Guy Fawkes' by Wm. Harrison Ainsworth centers around the Gunpowder Plot against the English government. The book 'The Spirit of the Border' by Zane Grey focuses on the Moravian missionaries in the Ohio Valley. The narrative of 'The Spirit of the Border' includes details about the establishment of the Moravian 'Village of Peace'.

The group of Minute Boys was in a state of fear while waiting for boats to arrive. Archie Hemming arrived on the first boat and embraced the narrator. The narrator suspected Seth Jepson of being a traitor for alerting the British to their location. The Minute Boys quickly boarded three boats and left the shore within four minutes of Archie's arrival. The group heard the sounds of British soldiers shortly after departing the shore. The Minute Boys were safe on board a sloop half a mile from the shore. Hiram Griffin urged the crew to navigate quickly toward Hog Island.

The narrator describes a journey to old Mary's cabin while feeling surrounded by enemies. The captor leads the group directly to the cabin without hesitation. The narrator contemplates fleeing for safety but ultimately decides to stay with his comrades. The group enters the cabin, which is the only shelter available in York. The British soldier in the cabin addresses the group, asking if they are from the Hamilton plantation. The soldier claims he is risking his life by interfering and asks for trust from the group. The narrator feels confused and bewildered during the encounter with the soldier.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The old man appeared as an invalid and showed signs of distress when confronted with the situation. Little Frenchie attempted to calm the old man by explaining their plan to keep Horry a prisoner. Uncle 'Rasmus expressed concern about the trouble they were in and the potential threat from the British. Pierre reassured Uncle 'Rasmus and emphasized the importance of holding their ground. The group discussed the need to keep Horry Sims quiet while also considering the possibility of obtaining horses. Pierre and the narrator walked around the village to observe the military encampment. Pierre noted the locations of seven redoubts and six batteries on the land side, among other military structures.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The old man left the tent after evading a question about his activities. Jerry and the narrator felt anxious about their upcoming encounter with the enemy. The narrator and Jerry decided to sleep to prepare for the challenges ahead. Darius Thorpe entered the tent near midnight after working with Commodore Barney. The narrator struggled to sleep due to thoughts of his family and the impending work. A call for all hands was sounded when the British forces appeared. Darius led the narrator and Jerry to join their comrades in formation to repel the attack.

The narrator provided an account of their activities after discovering a watch. The narrator and their companions were well-fed by a host and discussed plans to aid a comrade named Archie. It was decided to gather the Minute Boys at the ship-yard to discuss requests from their people at Cambridge. The narrator waited until daylight to return home to avoid being molested by British soldiers. The narrator's mother was anxious about their safety due to Archie's imprisonment. Hiram informed the narrator that the Minute Boys were assembling at the rendezvous. Silas kept the other Minute Boys hidden to avoid attracting British attention.

Hiram expressed confidence that he would come out best in the end. One member of the company suggested they might be taken into custody if their vessels failed to arrive. Hiram emphasized that being captured while performing a duty does not discredit a soldier. The group felt fear of Hiram's anger, especially those who had spoken of playing a trick on Seth. Hiram frequently went to the edge of the water, hoping to see the boats that were supposed to arrive. Hiram stated that there was no chance the boats would fail to come unless an accident occurred. After two hours of waiting, Hiram announced that the boats were coming just in time to save them.

Saul asked who would do the talking as they approached a battery with mounted guns. The narrator believed Pierre was the best choice to speak due to his quick wit and military knowledge. Pierre approached the sentinel and requested to speak with the officer of the day. The sentinel called the officer of the guard, who Pierre addressed courteously about an old slave needing help. The officer allowed them to pass the sentinel without time limits after Pierre's straightforward explanation. Saul took command of the group and led them toward old Mary's cabin. The area was busy with visitors, including those with Tory inclinations and local residents.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The characters are navigating a river in a canoe. Darius expresses concern about the presence of enemy vessels. They encounter four armed vessels and several barges while traveling downstream. Darius instructs the group to retreat upstream towards Benedict. The group arrives at the village of Benedict after a strenuous journey. Darius orders the group to stay put while he speaks with local residents. The arrival of Darius causes panic among the villagers.

The Committee of Safety held a secret session recently. There are suspicions of an important military move being planned. The Minute Boys have been ordered to be ready for special duty. General Ward, Colonel Prescott, and Parson Langdon were present at the assembly. A prayer was offered before the troops were ordered to march. Colonel Prescott led the march with two sergeants carrying lanterns. Hiram Griffin insisted on participating in the march despite his wound.

Saul questioned why his companions were still asleep instead of preparing to go into the village. Little Frenchie defended their decision to sleep in, stating that a good soldier should take advantage of rest. Saul expressed offense at Frenchie's comment about being a soldier. Pierre mentioned that he had enrolled as a Minute Boy and considered himself an apprentice learning from his elders. Saul claimed he had been awake for an hour before daybreak to complete his assigned work. Saul communicated that his mother was troubled by their plans to go into York but did not outright oppose it. The narrator expressed a strong emotional attachment to a horse named Silver Heels, indicating it was irreplaceable.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The characters are attempting to escape from Boston during a storm. Hiram leads the escape and urges the others to find a boat. The group runs swiftly towards Long wharf despite their fears. They encounter no one at Long wharf due to the darkness and storm. Hiram cuts the hawsers of a small boat to set it adrift. Archie and the narrator struggle to board the boat as it is swept away by waves. They initially fear leaving Harvey behind but discover he is also on the boat.

Hiram and the narrator did not read the entire document they found. Hiram found several documents indicating their host was in communication with the British. Hiram discovered a pass from General Gage allowing the bearer and friends to leave the city. The pass was considered valuable by Hiram and the narrator due to the political context. Hiram suggested they could leave without attempting to aid Silas Brownrigg. Hiram found another document that authorized Job Lord to take any prisoner from the Bridewell. The document was signed by the governor's aide-de-camp and bore the king's seal.

The narrator feels a sense of duty to accompany his companions despite the emotional pain of parting from his mother. The narrator's mother expresses her sorrow as he prepares to leave for York. The narrator experiences a mix of grief and relief as he walks away from his mother and their home. The narrator believes that remaining at home would prevent him from gathering the courage to venture into York. The narrator observes that soldiers and idlers are moving freely around the British encampment without being challenged. The narrator enters the village without encountering any obstacles or challenges. The narrator sees Uncle 'Rasmus at the window of old Mary's cabin as he approaches.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The location mentioned is the corner of Hanover street. The journey to the prison must be made in the open from Brattle street church. Harvey Pearson met the narrator and Hiram as they approached. Harvey indicated that Archie was expecting their arrival. Hiram planned to use an oaken stick to remove bars from a window. The weather was expected to produce a heavy thunder gust. Harvey mentioned that there were boats near Long wharf, but they were heavily guarded.

The narrator felt a strong desire to fight for liberty. The narrator believed the most dangerous part of the undertaking was passing Master Lord's building without being overheard. The narrator planned a route from Long lane to Dock square while avoiding patrols. The narrator successfully avoided detection by the patrol twice while moving through the town. The narrator had difficulty awakening their mother without attracting attention from neighbors. The narrator reassured their mother about their safety while staying at Master Lord's house.

A squad of soldiers was sent to assist an officer after a shot was fired. The soldiers were ordered to enter a building instead of firing a volley into it. Smoke was observed coming from the dwelling of Mr. Robert Sewall. Darius reported that soldiers were preventing people from saving belongings from the fire. Additional squads were sent to the rope-walk, tavern, and the National Intelligencer newspaper. Darius expressed concern that the entire city might be set on fire. Soldiers were seen plundering a shop and throwing goods into the street.

Captain Hanaford stated that it would take two hours to pull the pungy into the stream. Darius and Bill Jepson accompanied Captain Hanaford on deck to assist with the task. The creek was too narrow to turn the pungy, necessitating towing her out stern first. The pungy reached the mouth of the waterway half an hour before sunset. Captain Hanaford ordered Jim Freeman and Dody Wardwell to prepare supper while the men discussed the enemy's ships. The plan involved letting the pungy take its own course after rounding the point of the fort. The crew decided not to spread any sails for the venture due to visibility concerns in the darkness.

Hiram and his companions took a boat from the British during a storm. The British soldiers were seeking shelter from the storm and were not present. Hiram found oars to guide the boat while avoiding the land. Hiram expressed confidence in their successful escape and potential future actions against the British. Archie acknowledged the help he received from Hiram and his companions. Hiram indicated that their actions were motivated by duty rather than personal gain. Archie had been warned about the rescue attempt prior to it occurring.

The characters discuss the possibility of traveling to Nottingham. Jerry expresses a willingness to take the narrator to Nottingham if he agrees to join another ship. Darius finds food supplies, including two hams and a side of bacon, for their journey. The narrator hesitates about joining the group and feels conflicted about the situation. Jerry estimates they can leave in about an hour after gathering supplies. Darius believes the narrator is upset about leaving his family, while the narrator feels wronged by his friends.

The narrator enters a room and is embraced by Uncle 'Rasmus. Uncle 'Rasmus treats the narrator affectionately, which the narrator initially found annoying. The narrator inquires about his comrades and learns that Pierre is on guard duty and Saul has left to find his mare. Horry Sims is described as being comfortable in his imprisonment despite his situation. Pierre appears weary and is sitting near the scuttle, expressing a desire to swim when Saul returns. The narrator offers to take Pierre's place on guard duty after his journey. Pierre questions the narrator about his lack of sleep since leaving York.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The narrator felt that their stomach was never well filled from the time the Jerseyman left until they returned home. One of the three lads remained on guard duty while the other two watched the American army. The American army was preparing to attack the British forces in Virginia. The narrator observed the construction of a parallel, or embankment, near the British works. The American army opened fire on the British forces in the afternoon. The narrator experienced difficulty seeing the movements of the British due to smoke and other obstructions. The first parallel was commenced within six hundred yards of Cornwallis's works on a dark and stormy evening.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The young Tory's name is Horry Sims. Pierre shared details about their actions and intentions with a stranger. The stranger was dressed in red-coated attire, indicating he was an enemy. The group planned to keep Horry Sims as a prisoner in the loft. The stranger warned that others in York would want Horry Sims dead to protect their secrets. Pierre removed the gag from Horry Sims's mouth after bringing him to the loft. The group prioritized their own safety over Horry Sims's comfort.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Hiram proposes to create a dummy figure to deceive Master Lord into believing that Harvey is asleep in bed. The plan involves Harvey lying beside the dummy while Archie and another person remain at the table. Hiram acknowledges that if Master Lord discovers the trick, they will need to act quickly to prevent him from raising an alarm. Hiram believes they can subdue Master Lord if he approaches the dummy, allowing them to capture him. Once captured, Hiram plans to keep Master Lord bound until they are ready to leave town. Hiram expresses that they must take risks to achieve their goal of escaping without being captured by British forces. Archie raises a concern about the difficulty of concealing the tunnel after one person has exited.

A commotion occurred in the village when news was brought by a group. Darius returned with the four Byard brothers after a brief absence. Darius instructed that one person must go to the commodore with news. The Byard family prepared their canoe for a voyage downstream. Jim Freeman drew the short twig and was selected to go to the commodore. Darius ordered Jim to inform the commodore about the advance ships and to pay the Byards. Joshua Coburn was assigned to hide the boat further upstream while others were told to gather in half an hour.

The encampment was in a state of almost complete repose. The group approached the shed door and remained silent for a period of time. Saul expressed relief at the arrival of the others and mentioned concerns about being left alone. Horry Sims had not attempted to create a disturbance beyond making threats. Little Frenchie took command of the group and prepared a gag for Horry Sims. The group made noise while moving over the rubbish, which could have alerted nearby enemies. The group successfully exited the shed and felt they had overcome significant difficulties.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Amos Nelson threatened the narrator after being pummelled. Archie and Silas stood by during the confrontation with Amos Nelson. Amos Nelson claimed that the king's officers would punish the narrator and his friends. Doctor Warren intervened and criticized Archie for brawling instead of helping the Cause. Doctor Warren sought someone to carry a message into the country. The narrator expressed confidence in their ability to leave Boston unnoticed. Doctor Warren inquired about the narrator's relation to Samuel Wright.

Hiram rubbed a paste made from ashes over a freshly cut space to match the flooring. Hiram opened slight communication with the room above by creating tiny apertures. The purpose of the apertures was to potentially hear what Master Lord's visitors were saying. Job Lord entered the house cautiously and raised the trap-door to check on the group. Hiram greeted Job Lord in a friendly manner and invited him to join them for dinner. Master Lord claimed to have been successful in gathering information about prisoners at Breed's Hill. General Gage was reported to be planning to advance his outposts at Boston Neck.

The group spent time waiting for an opportunity to catch their game. They paddled to shore at night and concealed their canoe in the bushes. They fell asleep on the ground and awoke at sunrise. After breakfast, they concealed their boat further with foliage. Elias Macomber was seen pacing in front of the dwelling. The group planned to wait for Macomber to leave before approaching. One member returned to the shore to retrieve a musket and noticed the Avenger.

The American forces were positioned on Breed's Hill during the battle against the British. The American troops faced a shortage of ammunition as the battle progressed. The British artillery forced the American forces into a redoubt. The American forces inflicted significant casualties on the British, including the wounding of General Howe. The American troops resorted to throwing stones when they ran out of ammunition. Major Pitcairn, who had previously led troops at Lexington, was killed by a soldier in the American ranks. The American forces ultimately faced overwhelming odds as the British advanced.

The narrator and Seth Jepson moved quickly towards Beacon Hill. The narrator considered abandoning his comrades to find a skiff on the western shore. The narrator felt shame for considering his own safety at the expense of his comrades. The narrator decided to return to Master Lord's dwelling with Seth Jepson. The narrator and Seth Jepson traveled through various streets and alleys in Boston. The narrator noted the absence of life in the town during their journey. The narrator expressed concern about how to keep Seth Jepson quiet while executing their plan.

The speaker is identified as a deserter who cannot return without risking his life. Morgan suggests that only one person is needed to carry a message, while two should remain behind to guard a prisoner. Pierre expresses a desire to undertake the mission but is deemed unsuitable to leave his post guarding Horry Sims. The speaker volunteers to go on the mission, citing familiarity with the road to Williamsburg and the possibility of meeting his father. Uncle 'Rasmus supports the speaker's decision to go and insists that Pierre should stay behind. The speaker feels relieved by Uncle 'Rasmus's intervention, which prevents Pierre from protesting the decision.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The book features four illustrations by J. Watson Davis and is priced at $1.00. The story presents a vivid picture of Revolutionary scenes appealing to Americans. The Tower of London is a historical romance by Wm. Harrison Ainsworth set in the sixteenth century. In Defiance of the King is a romance of the American Revolution by Chauncey C. Hotchkiss. Garthowen is a story of a Welsh homestead by Allen Raine, featuring themes of humble life and enduring love. Mifanwy is a love story by Allen Raine about a Welsh singer, characterized by its simple and tender narrative. Darnley is a historical romance by G. P. R. James, following the times of Henry VIII and Cardinal Wolsey.

The alarm was a false one, and the commodore reassured his men about the situation. The soldiers were ordered to load all tents on the baggage-wagons as the army was to move within an hour. Darius Thorpe was the only member of the party who felt inclined to lie down during the night. The narrator and others talked quietly under the tent while Darius slept. The militia men appeared glum, which suggested they might not perform well in battle. The army was preparing to meet the British army, which had advanced to ensure their men were in good physical condition.

The crew took a guarantee from the commodore regarding payment in case of loss. Darius expressed concern about the decision made regarding Bill Jepson. The crew was in Pocomoke Bay and aimed to catch fifteen or twenty bushels of oysters. The crew had a good view of enemy fleets to the northward of New Point. The crew collected twenty bushels of oysters by dark, which was not profitable but served their purpose. Darius planned to wait at Tangiers until two or three o'clock in the morning for Bill Jepson. Jerry and another crew member decided to take a canoe to search for Bill Jepson.

The conversation included a question about the arrival of Barney's fleet. The group expected to reach Nottingham by noon if the wind remained favorable. Darius brought three sailors on deck who pledged not to attempt escape. Jerry prepared breakfast, which included fried ham and corn-dodgers. The British sailors were seated comfortably on the deck, despite being prisoners. Darius secured two individuals to a stanchion in the hold.
