The group spotted the flotilla anchored off Nottingham at half past twelve.

Doctor Warren entered the room after a ten-minute wait. Doctor Warren mentioned an opportunity to aid the Cause and expressed disappointment at not seeing two boys. The speaker informed Doctor Warren about a previous misadventure and inquired about helping a lad's release. Doctor Warren stated that the lad's father is a Son of Liberty, which would lead to increased guarding. The Committee of Safety believes the Minute Boys can help by bringing news from the town. Doctor Warren suggested hiding skiffs at various locations for sudden opportunities. The speaker found his father within a quarter-hour after asking Hiram Griffin for his location.

The group discussed their situation for a full hour while crouching in a corner. They planned to attack if any member showed signs of suspicion. The narrator felt a mix of hope and fear regarding Job Lord's arrival. When the trap-door opened, the narrator stood up in surprise. Job Lord commented on their hunger and the availability of food. Hiram expressed a desire to start their task immediately. Job Lord stated that their task would take time and they could afford to wait.

Pierre Laurens insisted that the narrator go to the floor below to rest. Uncle 'Rasmus prepared a bed of blankets for the narrator. The narrator fell asleep and was later awakened by Uncle 'Rasmus. Uncle 'Rasmus informed the narrator that Saul Ogden had not returned since leaving that morning. The narrator speculated that Saul may have been arrested or injured. The narrator quickly climbed the ladder to the loft to check on the situation. Pierre Laurens remained in the loft as a prisoner.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The narrator considers rowing up the coast of the island to Morton's point and the Penny ferry. The narrator decides against the venture due to the need to present himself at Cambridge and to preserve his liberty. The narrator believes he can aid a friend imprisoned on Queen street with the help of the Minute Boys. The narrator struggles to formulate a plan to help his friend but finds it difficult to make progress. The narrator falls asleep while trying to stay awake and guard their hiding place. Hiram informs the narrator that they have been in hiding for hours and have not seen any British soldiers. The narrator experiences hunger and thirst but cannot address these needs until they reach Cambridge.

Horry Sims may inquire about Uncle 'Rasmus's whereabouts. Uncle 'Rasmus was reportedly too ill to be moved before Lord Cornwallis's army entered the town. The narrator had a plan to assist Uncle 'Rasmus but he refused help and wanted to enter York alone. Uncle 'Rasmus only accepted assistance in carrying his blankets and provisions a portion of the distance. The narrator and others discussed the risks of suspicion from the British if Uncle 'Rasmus was found in a cabin with food. The group was focused on recovering stolen horses from the British army. There was a debate about whether to continue their work as Minute Boys while trying to reclaim the horses.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The group is trying to overcome difficulties related to their situation. Hiram explains how the tunnel could be useful, but they are not closer to their goal. They have entered the town but face greater challenges than before. Harvey questions whether it is day or night, as they have lost track of time. Hiram estimates that they have spent nearly two days in the cellar since their arrival. Hiram proposes to venture through the secret passage after their host visits again. Hiram acknowledges that the holes made for listening could also inform their host of their actions.

Fitzroy Hamilton expressed alarm when his cousin made a public statement about their secret plan. Saul accused Horry Sims of treachery regarding the horses. Horry Sims was confronted about his actions that led to the loss of the horses. Saul threatened Horry Sims with physical punishment for his betrayal. Horry Sims warned Saul that any actions taken against him would be repaid in kind. Saul and his companions were concerned about Horry's potential connections with British officers. The conversation escalated into a confrontation between Saul and Horry Sims.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Saul Ogden is confined in a guard-house where the Widow Marshall formerly lived. The guard-house is a small, one-storied log building located about two hundred paces behind the church. The charge against Saul Ogden is not determined but is believed to be minor. There is a single sentinel guarding the front of the building where Saul is held. Master Morgan advises against attempting to aid Saul's escape to avoid raising suspicion. The discussion about Saul's situation lasted for half an hour. The narrator ultimately agrees to abandon the plan to rescue Saul for the sake of Master Morgan's safety.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The characters are traveling on a boat during a storm. Hiram expresses confidence in his ability to navigate the boat. Harvey questions the decision to go to Cambridge after Archie's escape. The group is concerned about being suspected of involvement in Archie's escape. The storm is described as fierce but nearing its end when they reach shore. The characters plan to avoid Boston town for the next ten days.

The narrator reassures Uncle 'Rasmus about his welfare and expresses confidence in his ability to travel. Little Frenchie offers a pat on the shoulder but does not speak. Saul appears uneasy and does not say goodbye or make eye contact with the narrator. A red-coated spy takes the narrator by the arm and leads him out of the house. The spy informs the narrator about the presence of three sentinels and gives directions to avoid them. The narrator feels a sense of desolation and abandonment as he prepares for his mission as a spy. The narrator reflects on his doubts about his abilities compared to Pierre and feels compelled to move forward despite his fears.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The watch was changed on the ship before a crew member slipped over the side and swam away. The crew member swam half a mile from the Severn while avoiding detection. Jepson, the crew member, had been taken from an American merchantman five months before the declaration of war. Jepson described his life aboard British ships as a 'dog's life' and feared execution if caught. The conversation included plans for Jepson's escape to the mainland, with suggestions to put him ashore in Maryland. Darius, an acquaintance of Jepson, was involved in the operation and mentioned work for Commodore Joshua Barney. Jepson had gathered intelligence about British plans to strike Washington and Baltimore.

Hiram Griffin and Master Lord engaged in a conversation about their situation and the need for caution. Hiram expressed gratitude towards Master Lord for providing them with a hiding place. Master Lord indicated that he needed to gather information about General Gage's intentions. Hiram advised Master Lord to prioritize the Cause over their company. Master Lord left the building after locking the door behind him. Hiram suggested that they should carefully remove the casks blocking a passage. Hiram cautioned against hasty actions that could jeopardize their plans.

The narrator feels a sense of terror and helplessness in the face of danger. Pierre Laurens is observed by the narrator as he moves toward the door, seemingly attempting to escape. The Jerseyman engages Abel Hunt in conversation, attempting to negotiate their situation. Abel Hunt accuses the Jerseyman of being a traitor for associating with rebels. The Jerseyman responds calmly to Hunt's accusations, suggesting he may be trying to lead the rebels away from their errors. Hunt expresses his anger and asserts control over the situation, claiming he has the others under his thumb. The Jerseyman remains composed and challenges Hunt, indicating a willingness to confront him.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Pierre overtook the narrator and Saul during their flight. Pierre expressed triumph at their survival despite the danger. The narrator noted the presence of cannon fire nearby. Pierre believed the cannonading indicated a regular battle. The narrator and his companions reached their destination safely. Uncle 'Rasmus was initially frightened by the narrator's sudden entrance. Pierre searched for Horry Sims, concerned about the Tory's escape.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Darius indicated that they would not pursue the villain immediately to allow him time to escape. The group was hidden in a thicket while observing soldiers approaching their location. Darius was reluctant to leave the thicket despite the approaching soldiers. The group decided to wait until Elias had moved further up the river before embarking. They remained hidden for a couple of hours while keeping watch for any passing crafts. The group paddled leisurely at night, confident that their quarry could not escape by water. Darius took control of the canoe as they prepared to pursue their quarry when he was out of sight.

The narrator is given a command by Darius to observe the river closely. The narrator feels a sense of responsibility as the leader of the group. The group is instructed to remain silent and stationed at equal distances along the rail. The atmosphere is tense as the group listens for unusual noises in the darkness. The narrator hears the sound of oars, indicating the approach of a boat. The conversation overheard suggests that the approaching boat is manned by Britishers. The narrator suspects that some individuals may be betraying their group by providing information.

The text describes various historical romance novels and their themes. Richelieu is a tale set in France during the reign of King Louis XIII, written by G. P. R. James. Windsor Castle is a historical romance about Henry VIII, Catharine of Aragon, and Anne Boleyn, written by Wm. Harrison Ainsworth. Horseshoe Robinson depicts the efforts of colonists in South Carolina during the Tory Ascendency in 1780, written by John P. Kennedy. The Pearl of Orr's Island is a story set on the coast of Maine, written by Harriet Beecher Stowe. All mentioned books are available for purchase at A. L. BURT COMPANY.

The narrator expresses concern about the British forces, noting that their smallest force is three hundred. The men in the narrator's group are eager to obey the command to fall into line due to the serious danger they face. The group arrives at the Wood Yard, where General Winder had previously encamped and where Commodore Barney was expected to join. A messenger informs the lieutenant that American troops are hastening to Washington and that they must move quickly to avoid capture. The messenger reports that a portion of the British fleet under Captain Gordon is visible from High Point. The narrator describes the group's state of excitement and fear as they realize the enemy is close. The group has marched eleven miles with only one brief halt and is instructed to continue marching night and day for at least fourteen more miles.

Hiram suggested turning the boat in the opposite direction to avoid an approaching craft. The narrator observed a boat filled with men coming from the direction of the water mill. Hiram assisted in rowing the skiff, demonstrating significant strength. The narrator suspected that some men in the approaching boat were armed and had the bearing of soldiers. Hiram proposed landing near the shore of Noddle Island to avoid detection. The skiff was hidden in a clump of bushes after being carried out of the water. The men in the other boat were actively searching for the narrator and Hiram.

The characters discussed the usefulness of a walking stick in a specific situation. Hiram pointed out a mass of clouds in the southern sky, indicating a potential storm. The characters believed that the storm would provide cover from the Britishers. The narrator expressed regret for not preparing skiffs for a potential escape. Hiram confirmed that the approaching storm would create a dark and stormy night. The characters were focused on the rescue of Archie as their primary objective. The narrator feared that their efforts to rescue Archie might lead to their own capture.

The narrator and Pierre left the cabin after witnessing a scene of slaughter. Only one man from the squad was still alive, and he was in a state of unconsciousness. The squad had discarded their muskets in a pile near where they were resting. Uncle 'Rasmus suggested hiding the weapons under the floor. Pierre collected weapons and accouterments from the bodies that were not mangled. The narrator expressed frustration about the need to gather weapons, believing it to be unnecessary. Little Frenchie argued that having muskets could be beneficial in case of future danger.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The narrator describes a tense moment while waiting for battle. The narrator reflects on the potential shame of being perceived as a coward by their community. Darius instructs the men to remain steady despite their fear. The British forces are seen marching in formation, and rockets are fired at the narrator's group. A retreat occurs among the militiamen, while the flotillamen and marines do not waver. Commodore Barney commands the flotillamen to fire back at the British forces. The narrator becomes consumed by the battle, focusing solely on loading and firing their musket.

Pierre expressed determination to remain in the area. The red-coated spy inquired about the observations made regarding fortifications. Pierre provided military intelligence about the placement of redoubts and a battery. The spy acknowledged Pierre's keen understanding of military works. Pierre's father was a soldier, which contributed to his knowledge of fortifications. The spy instructed the messenger to inform General Lafayette about the fortifications and credit Pierre. The messenger was advised to leave immediately for Williamsburg due to potential dangers.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The speaker believes that their cousin would not leave without informing them if he had left for pleasure. There is concern that the cousin may have been suspected of being a spy, complicating their situation. Pierre learns that Lafayette's army is being reinforced by men from the North. General Cornwallis is taking precautions to keep his situation secret due to the potential for fighting. Morgan suggests that the village will be besieged before a battle occurs between the two armies. Morgan advises caution if Pierre and Fitz choose to explore the village. The speaker expresses frustration about their group's impact on the war effort and the potential consequences of their actions.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The conversation in the room ceased as the food was prepared. Hiram insisted that the three lads partake of the meal. Griffin believed the room above was empty after hearing the outer door close. Hiram expressed concern that Master Lord may not be trustworthy. Harvey questioned why Master Lord would not simply turn them over to the authorities. Hiram stated that they were safer as prisoners of war than in the power of Master Lord. Hiram's comments indicated he believed the situation to be desperate.

The narrator's mother initially opposed the venture, believing it was work for men. The narrator argued that they had promised Doctor Warren to undertake the task. The narrator's mother eventually agreed and prepared a small parcel of food. The narrator met Archie on Salem street, who also carried a parcel. Archie's mother expressed concern about the danger of the mission but ultimately accepted it. Silas arrived at the meeting place five minutes early, eager for the task. Doctor Warren arrived later and asked if the boys were ready for the journey.

Uncle 'Rasmus opposed the decision to release the prisoners. Uncle 'Rasmus believed that the focus should be on their own safety rather than the suffering of the Tories. The narrator felt compelled to release the prisoners as part of Pierre's plan. The narrator promised Pierre that the prisoners would be set free. The narrator cut the bonds of Horry Sims and instructed him to follow. The narrator decided not to remove the gag from Abel Hunt's mouth due to Uncle 'Rasmus's warning. Horry Sims was instructed to release Abel Hunt after the narrator explained the situation.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The man had previously caused injury to the speaker and was being threatened with a knife. The speaker expressed distrust towards the man, stating they would be vigilant for any visitors. Hiram advised the speaker to be prepared to use the knife if necessary. Master Lord, the man being threatened, claimed he would not attempt to call for help before sunset. Hiram believed they could take Master Lord to Cambridge, despite his objections. Seth Jepson, another character, pleaded for mercy after realizing his vulnerable position. Hiram expressed contempt for Seth Jepson's cowardice during the situation.

Red-coated soldiers are on alert to prevent information from reaching rebels. The group is hiding in a besieged town while holding a prisoner. The British army is closely gathered around the group, increasing the risk of discovery. The group must find a way to supply themselves with food without revealing their presence. The king's officers are quick to judge anyone suspected of being a spy. Morgan plans to attempt to communicate with their people despite the dangers involved. The group feels they have not accomplished anything beneficial by being in York.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Saul believed there was treachery involved in the situation regarding little Frenchie. The group debated whether to remain in their current location or return home. Saul wanted to pursue and punish the young Tory for his actions. The narrator argued against immediate retaliation, suggesting it would complicate their situation. While they were discussing their options, little Frenchie arrived, appearing exhausted. Little Frenchie explained that he had to accompany the young Tory to avoid suspicion. He claimed to have found a way to leave the Tory's company without raising alarm.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: All nature was at peace within half an hour, but man was still struggling to kill his brother. The guns within the lines were served rapidly, and cannonading continued for a long time, resulting in great destruction. Governor Nelson's mansion was taken possession of by Cornwallis and was used as a target by the Americans. During the attack, a dozen balls struck the mansion, damaging the walls and windows. Governor Nelson was leading the Virginia militia during the conflict. Abel Hunt and Horry Sims approached the cabin alone while carrying muskets. There was considerable confusion in the army due to part of it and much of the baggage being on the Gloucester side.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The enemy's ship was filled with sailors giving orders and cursing. A sailor reported that there was nothing of concern, but firearms were being handled nearby. A command to prepare and fire was issued, followed by a flash of flame illuminating the scene. The pungy was in danger of being attacked by the enemy's broadside. Darius and Bill Jepson took to a canoe to tow the pungy while Captain Hanaford ordered the crew to raise the sails. The enemy fleet was preparing to attack, with commands and movement heard from all directions. Three rockets were launched, allowing the British gunners to take aim at the pungy as it moved down the river.

Uncle 'Rasmus expressed urgency to leave and mentioned needing blankets and food. Fitz Hamilton and Pierre assisted Uncle 'Rasmus by rolling blankets and securing them on his shoulders. Uncle 'Rasmus planned to return before nightfall and asked Fitz to inform Missey of his departure. Fitz Hamilton felt it was reckless to involve Pierre in their plan to recover stolen horses. Pierre suggested that he might be the one dragging Fitz and Saul into danger. Fitz and Pierre fell asleep after Uncle 'Rasmus left, despite concerns about their situation. Fitz was awakened by Saul the next morning, feeling shame for having slept on the ground.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The narrator and Pierre Laurens approached a structure made of sticks and clay to begin a task. Pierre Laurens advised the narrator to work systematically to avoid making waste. The narrator recognized that Pierre should take the lead in their work together. Saul Ogden was heard from inside the structure, expressing concern about a sentinel outside. Little Frenchie reprimanded the narrator for raising his voice while they were in enemy territory. The narrator observed Pierre working diligently while they attempted to create an opening. Saul Ogden was eventually freed from imprisonment, followed by other prisoners attempting to escape.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Hiram failed to return as promised during the week that followed. Archie remained in camp due to the risk of venturing into Boston. Seth Jepson reported minor information from the enemy but nothing significant. General Gage allowed some people to leave Boston but restricted women and children from doing so. The population of Charlestown decreased from nearly three thousand to about two hundred due to panic. Rhode Island sent approximately fifteen hundred men under Brigadier Nathaniel Greene to aid the cause. General Gage declared martial law in Boston and offered a pardon to those who would serve the king, excluding John Hancock and Samuel Adams.

The lad spoke with boldness and a hint of anger. The narrator had suspicions about Seth Jepson and felt he was in his power. The narrator proposed that a group of lads should gather information about the British. Silas agreed to send someone trustworthy with Seth to monitor him. Silas expressed doubt about the effectiveness of their plan to keep an eye on Seth. Harvey Pearson claimed he knew where Amos Nelson was being held and could communicate with him. Silas suggested searching for a boat left near Fox Hill to aid their plans.

General Gage was preparing for an attack. The soldiers sang 'Yankee Doodle' as the British troops advanced. Officers instructed the soldiers to wait until the British were within seven or eight rods before firing. Doctor Warren encouraged the soldiers to maintain their spirit and aim accurately. Some soldiers disobeyed orders and fired their weapons before the command was given. Colonel Prescott threatened to shoot the first man who fired prematurely. Colonel Prescott eventually commanded the soldiers to fire, resulting in significant impact on the advancing British lines.

Job Lord was described as a man who had given evidence of his loyalty to the Cause. Master Lord led the group through a trap-door into a cellar that was more comfortably furnished than the room above. The cellar contained two couches made of saplings, a table, a fireplace, and two large lanterns. Master Lord inquired about the purpose of the group's visit to Boston and recognized Archie as the son of John Hemming, a known Son of Liberty. Hiram explained the group's reasons for leaving their encampment and their concerns about Silas Brownrigg's safety. Master Lord informed the group that some prisoners taken at Breed's Hill were in Queen-street prison and others in the Bridewell. The group suspected Seth Jepson of informing the British about their involvement at Hog island.

The soldiers experienced physical discomfort from the glare and fatigue during the battle. They were instructed not to fire until given the command, which they followed. Upon receiving the command, they successfully repelled the advancing red-coats multiple times. General Howe led the assault to encourage his troops during the battle. One Minute Boy was killed during the conflict, while others remained alive despite injuries. The soldiers felt a sense of victory after repelling the enemy, but were aware of their weakened state. The soldiers faced challenges due to a lack of ammunition as the battle progressed.

The _Lively_ is a ship of twenty guns carrying one hundred and thirty men. The _Falcon_ is also heavily manned, similar to the _Lively_. The _Somerset_ has sixty-eight guns and five hundred and twenty men on board. The total number of guns among the British ships is approximately one hundred and eighty-six. General Gage can transport between five to eight thousand men to Charlestown shore. The British battery of six guns on Copp's hill opened fire about an hour and a half after daybreak. The cannonading from the _Lively_ ceased after twenty minutes.

The Minute Boys entered the battle with fifteen members, including Hiram. Two members of the Minute Boys died, two were near death, and five sustained minor injuries. The injuries sustained by the Minute Boys were less severe compared to the damage inflicted on the British forces. At least five British soldiers were incapacitated, and only three or four escaped without injury. Hiram expressed dissatisfaction with not completing their task of collecting more cargo from Hog Island. The narrator insisted that the Minute Boys should prioritize caring for the wounded before attempting further actions. Only five men were observed on the deck of the schooner, indicating they had suffered significant losses.

The surrender of Lord Cornwallis occurred on October 19, 1781. General Lafayette acknowledged the contributions of the Minute Boys to the Cause. The British army under Cornwallis consisted of 7,247 soldiers and 840 cannon. The American forces opened the first parallel on October 6 and the second parallel on October 14. Cornwallis was allowed to send a ship to Sir Henry Clinton with news of the surrender. The American army played a British or German air during the surrender ceremony. Sir Henry Clinton sailed from New York with reinforcements on the same day Cornwallis surrendered.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The crew was sailing with minimal cargo aboard the pungy. The crew planned to approach other vessels to sell oysters. Darius and the narrator discussed the possibility of encountering enemy ships at night. The Severn and the Narcissus were identified as potential enemy ships. Darius believed it was equally risky to be overhauled by a frigate or a sloop. The crew was hailed by another ship while waiting until daylight. The crew attempted to sell oysters to the second ship after being instructed to heave to.

The British fleet is present in the area. Joshua Barney suggested selling oysters to the British fleet. The crew planned to dredge for a cargo before attempting to sell. The crew decided to go ashore for an hour at Benedict. Amos visited his mother, who expressed concern about his upcoming danger. Elias Macomber is believed to have joined the British, but there are rumors he returned. Jerry and Jim reported that Elias Macomber was seen returning to Benedict.

The character Bill Jepson expressed concern about the chances of a prisoner escaping. Bill Jepson stated that there are about seven thousand American troops, most of whom are inexperienced. The British forces are not larger in number than the Americans but are all trained soldiers. Bill Jepson mentioned that the American command structure is complicated with too many leaders. A despatch from Mr. Monroe indicated that the enemy was advancing towards Washington and that American troops were retiring. The despatch advised preparing to destroy bridges and removing records. The narrator's father shared a similar sense of despair regarding the situation of the American troops.

The narrator expresses concern for a colt named Silver Heels during a military retreat. Pierre reassures the narrator that other troops will act quickly to prevent the British army from escaping. The narrator fears that Lord Cornwallis will have a twelve-hour advantage in his retreat. Pierre insists that they will not wait idly and will watch for the British to leave their fortifications. The group plans to send word to the American forces once they confirm the British have retreated. Uncle 'Rasmus alerts the group to the approach of a crowd of British soldiers. The group observes nine weary British soldiers approaching their location.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The narrator and Pierre observe British soldiers riding away from the narrator's home. The soldiers are mounted on horses belonging to the narrator's father, including the narrator's favorite colt, Silver Heels. Pierre informs the narrator that the horses were taken from the Hamilton plantation for the officers of Lord Cornwallis's army. The narrator expresses anger and a desire to reclaim Silver Heels from the British soldiers. Pierre advises the narrator against confronting the soldiers, citing the danger of being captured. Colonel Simcoe of the Queen's Rangers is identified as the officer responsible for taking the horses. The narrator's father is mentioned as being among the rebels of Virginia.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: A fleet of barges came from Boston town carrying infantry, marines, and grenadiers. General Howe was perceived as cautious for waiting to engage until his army was reinforced. The British reinforcements arrived at Madlin's ship-yard, with some remaining on the shore and others marching to Morton's hill. Colonel Prescott and Doctor Warren were present with the Minute Boys as they took their positions within the redoubt. The Connecticut and New Hampshire men were positioned at the rail fence on the west side of the redoubt. The Minute Boys faced the British troops, who were better fed and armed, and outnumbered them two to one. Despite the overwhelming odds and lack of experience, the Minute Boys did not flinch and performed their duties.

Cornwallis occupied York Town with the main division of his army. Lieutenant-Colonel Dundas occupied Gloucester with about seven hundred men. The combined American forces, approximately twelve thousand strong, marched toward York Town. The French Legion and Virginia militiamen were sent to invest Gloucester. Colonel Alexander Scammel was surprised by Hessian horsemen and shot after surrendering. The allied armies' lines extended in a semi-circle nearly two miles from the British works. The American artillery was under General Knox, and various troops were commanded by Generals Steuben and Clinton.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Pierre believes he can give good advice to Saul and Fitz, who are angry and have lost sight of prudence. Horry Sims is in York Town and has done grievous wrong to Saul and Fitz. Pierre has met Horry Sims only once and believes he poses no threat to him. Saul points out that Horry Sims knows Pierre and his mother are guests at the Hamilton plantation. Pierre and his mother are French and recently arrived from New Orleans. The group decides it is better for Pierre to reconnoitre the area alone to learn the whereabouts of the stolen horses. Saul is eager to venture inside the British lines but ultimately agrees to let Pierre go alone for safety.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Colonel Peyton sent a slave named Joe to gather information about the British. Joe traveled from Williamsburg to inform General Lafayette about his findings. Pierre and the narrator initially believed they could spy on the British for their company of Minute Boys. They felt disappointed to learn that Joe was already performing the same task. Uncle 'Rasmus advised Pierre and the narrator to remain concealed until they could relieve Saul from his duties. They decided to sleep in the loft to avoid being discovered by soldiers. The boys fell asleep shortly after settling down on the hard floor.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Hiram expressed that he had not eaten for twenty-four hours. Hiram indicated he would not speak freely while Master Lord was present. Master Lord provided an ample supply of food, including corn meal, salt pork, and a leg of lamb. Master Lord brought a jar of whale oil and encouraged its use for lighting. Master Lord stated that they should remain content until he could signal for action. Master Lord bolted the trap door to prevent discovery of their hiding place. Hiram instructed to listen for any activity from the room above.

The narrator is advised to return home to inform his mother about his experiences. The narrator expresses hunger but declines food, choosing to set out on his return journey immediately. The narrator's father agrees to accompany him to the outposts to ensure his safe departure. The father expresses a preference for his son to serve in the ranks rather than as a spy. The father discusses the hopes of the Americans regarding Cornwallis and the situation of the colonies. The narrator reflects on his father's behavior, attributing it to a soldier's anxiety during a critical time. The narrator successfully travels from the American lines to the Hamilton plantation without encountering significant danger.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: The narrator was in the British camp hoping to see a mare. A man in the camp confronted the narrator and demanded to know their presence. The narrator threatened the man with punishment from their uncle's slaves. The man accused the narrator of being a rebel and called for the guard. Abel Hunt falsely claimed that the narrator attempted to kill him. The narrator was imprisoned in a guard-house and received inadequate food and water. The narrator believed their friends were attempting to rescue them during cannon fire.

source.author: James Otis
source.title: The Minute Boys of York Town

text: Hiram prepared a skiff for a voyage with two pairs of oars and three or four blankets. Hiram had completed much of the work to acquire the skiff before waking Luke Wright. Hiram was determined to go on the voyage regardless of whether others joined him. The group passed two breastworks without being hailed by those on shore. A sentinel at a three-gun battery demanded the group come ashore for questioning. Hiram satisfied the officer in command of the battery and returned quickly. The group arrived at the mouth of the river past midnight and concealed the skiff in bushes.

A small figure in a crumpled cap and apron is identified as a domestic servant. There is a public meeting planned to discuss the conditions of domestic servants, with six peeresses attending. The text describes a contrast between the lives of domestic servants and the wealthy, highlighting issues of overwork and underfeeding. The narrator expresses a desire to write books featuring women of the people, focusing on their struggles and realities. The narrator observes a thin-clad woman carrying loaves of bread, reflecting on the significance of daily bread for the poor. The narrator imagines a future where she hosts a salon for influential figures, including a character named Greyson. The narrator contemplates the societal struggles faced by the weak and aged in public spaces.

The protagonist enjoyed being the center of attention and made inquiries about others. The protagonist's wife interpreted a telephone message as coming from the dead. The wife found some comfort in the content of the message, which included references to a 'garden' and 'eternal sunshine.' The family experienced confusion and distress following the message, leading to a dinnerless night. The eldest son sent a wire the next morning confirming that their father was still in Colorado. The protagonist received criticism for the misunderstanding caused by his telephone call. A gathering at the St. Leonards' included county people and was perceived as dramatic by some guests.

The narrator experiences physical discomfort but feels uplifted while walking. A girl named Cissy walks alongside the narrator and expresses approval of him. Cissy's father owns a shop on Three Colt Street, and she is described as being of means. The narrator introduces himself as Paul and mentions that his father is a lawyer. Cissy and Paul part ways with an understanding that they may meet again. Paul's mother expresses concern about his appearance, while his father supports his behavior. The East India Dock Road is described as a busy thoroughfare in the present but was empty during the narrator's childhood.

The narrator expressed a desire not to go to a picnic and believed the others would be fine without her. The woman mentioned that it was difficult for her children to want to go to a picnic while leaving her at home. Robina confirmed that they had to reassure the woman that the picnic would not be enjoyable without her. A screech-owl was described as perching on a yew-tree and emitting a loud scream each evening. Ethelbertha believed the screech-owl was a sign of death, while Veronica liked the owl and attempted to mimic its sound. The narrator reflected on a woman who was considered the most beautiful girl in Tunbridge Wells twenty-seven years ago. Robina questioned the narrator about the accuracy of his recollections regarding the woman and her past.

The narrator put his name on a manuscript to conceal the identity of the actual author. The narrator's companion expressed surprise at being taken in by a man. The companion mentioned that she came to say 'yes' to a proposal made by the narrator the previous night. The narrator had a limited amount of money, which he considered using for travel or a revolver. The narrator moved to Deptford in London to avoid familiar faces and supported himself by giving singing lessons and tutoring. The narrator experienced a period of emotional numbness and illness while living in London. During his illness, the narrator received minimal care and relied on a pint of milk left for him each morning.

The narrator entered a room and observed a lock of hair that nearly reached the floor. The narrator pressed his lips against the hair until they bled. The narrator was informed that he had been gone for three-quarters of an hour. The narrator's companion expressed regret about a past relationship and mentioned divorce proceedings initiated by another man. The companion described himself as a gourmet rather than a gourmand regarding women. The companion was approximately fifty years old and was described as handsome and distinguished-looking. The companion's behavior towards his fiancée was characterized as affectionate and good taste.

The speaker expresses a desire for someone to perform tasks such as cleaning knives, fetching water, and chopping wood. Robina tends to dominate conversations and assumes others agree with her perspective. Dick indicates he will write to the speaker and suggests sending a hamper for a picnic. Veronica discusses her lack of experience with being 'blown up' as a measure of wrongdoing. Veronica argues that her intentions are pure and that she has not acted with malice. The speaker reflects on the consequences of actions and the concept of fate in relation to Veronica's survival. Veronica believes that her survival indicates approval from Providence regarding her conduct.

The Stranger represents Life, characterized by battle, strength, and learning from suffering. The characters awaken in a cafe in the Rue St. Louis as the waiter prepares to close. The Poet pays the bill with a handful of coins, but the waiter informs him that a stranger has already paid. The streets are empty and it is raining as the characters leave the cafe. The text reflects on the experiences of well-to-do children who are cared for and sheltered from hardship. The narrative describes the daily routines and comforts provided to privileged children. The children engage in various activities, including playing games, eating, and attending social events.

The narrator expresses a belief that unnecessary labor can be avoided in household tasks. The narrator lacks skill in needlework, while Dan has learned to use a thimble. The opera mentioned ran into the following year and was succeeded by another successful production featuring 'Goggles.' The narrator's current salary is thirty-five to forty shillings a week, which they consider princely. The O'Kelly advises the narrator against pursuing a career as an opera singer, citing concerns about their voice. The narrator dreams of becoming a successful actor and writer, envisioning a combination of both careers. The narrator's story was accepted for publication, but they have experienced previous disappointments with publications collapsing.

Paul is advised not to focus solely on money and fame when writing books. Paul's mother believes that authorship is a noble calling that brings happiness to others. The conversation includes a discussion about the difficulty of being good until one is grown up. Paul mentions having read 'The Last of the Barons' and some works by Charles Dickens. The gentleman expresses a preference for the humorous parts of Dickens' writing. Paul's mother finds some of Dickens' work to be vulgar but appreciates his beautiful and tender writing. The gentleman notes that Paul is an egotist, which he considers the beginning of all art.

Veronica often appears to be lost in thought, which can mislead strangers. Veronica expressed a desire to have a room of her own. Robin commented on the untidiness of Veronica's belongings. Dick and Robin discussed the organization of their living spaces. Veronica's gloves are frequently misplaced, leading to a search for them. The narrator confirmed the purchase of a house, which was not their preferred style.

The narrator crossed the road and went to the second floor of a building. There were two doors on the second floor, one marked 'Private.' The narrator knocked on the second door and received a response to enter. Inside the room, the narrator found a youth named Sylvanus Minikin at a small desk. Minikin informed the narrator that the room was one of the offices of Lott & Co. Minikin advised the narrator to leave, stating that Mr. Lott was a demanding employer. The narrator overheard a conversation from the private office after Minikin left.

The little girl's name is Sally. The narrator plans to write a play with Sally. The narrator will play a princess and Sally will play a wicked witch. Mr. Bute is going to paint scenery for the play. Robina is critical of men and has a gentleman who may be in love with her. Mr. Slee is preparing for an event with Irish stew and roly-poly pudding. The narrator and Robina went for a drive with Dick, who shouted swear words.

The drawing-room is reserved as a show-room for chance visitors. The narrator's father often left his office to play games such as cricket or ninepins. The narrator perceived his father's profession as playful rather than serious. The father's office contained big books, bundles of documents, and empty japanned tin boxes. The father was described as having small, bright, and piercing eyes. The narrator's father was considering home education for him instead of sending him to Eton or Harrow. Noel Hasluck, a fat man, expressed regret for not having had the opportunity for formal education.

Miss Janie suggested young Hopkins as a useful boy. St. Leonard expressed that his only fault with Hopkins is that he talks too much. The narrator prefers a country lad over Hopkins for a rural experience. Miss Janie promised to send a boy to the narrator. Miss Janie and St. Leonard discussed the donkey named Nathaniel. St. Leonard stated that Nathaniel has not brought any moral improvement to his family. Miss Janie mentioned that Nathaniel could be taught anything except to work.

Mr. Malooney is involved in a game with the Captain. Malooney finished his break for twenty-two points. The Captain expressed a dislike for noisy games. Malooney pocketed the Captain's ball and left himself in a difficult position. The Captain scored thirty-eight points while Malooney gave him twenty-four. The score was sixty-two plays one hundred and twenty-eight. Veronica caused a disturbance by tumbling over something in the room.
