A group of men in a densely-wooded area were planning an unprovoked assault on the settlers. Keona, who had a wounded arm, was inciting his fellow warriors to seek revenge against the whites.

Manton observed that the schooner was being drawn into a stream. Manton decided to risk navigating the narrow channel despite the danger. He ordered the crew to lie down on the deck and aimed the brass gun at the man-of-war. Montague commanded the _Talisman_ to fire its guns as the pirate schooner moved behind a rocky point. One cannonball from the _Talisman_ struck the pirate schooner's bowsprit, causing damage. The _Talisman_ experienced a delay in maneuvering due to the wreckage of its mizzen-mast fouling the rudder. When the _Talisman_ rounded the islet, the pirate schooner was no longer visible.

A young gentleman was ordered elsewhere instead of going as planned. Harry searched for the kettle while Charley prepared their bed. Charley used an axe to remove stumps and filled a hollow with collected materials. Charley brought a young spruce fir tree and used its branches to create a bed. Charley spread blankets and pillows under the canoe for sleeping. Harry and Charley ate supper together after a long day of fatigue. Harry prepared for bed by removing his wet moccasins and putting on a dry pair.

The natives were preparing for a potential war expedition. Keona observed the settlement from a mountain top and was chased by men from the Foam. Frederick Mason took precautionary steps the night before and consulted with Ole Thorwald. Ole Thorwald had posted scouts in the mountain passes and war-canoes were drawn up on the strand. Mason spent the night preparing to preach and was anxious about his daughter Alice's safety. In the morning, Mason was surprised by his maid Poopy, who expressed concern about his lack of sleep. Poopy informed Mason that Will Corrie had been at the house all night.

Bumpus received a large stone on his chest and several small ones on other parts of his body. Bumpus concluded that ghosts could not throw spears or fling stones, indicating that the man they were searching for was nearby. Bumpus feigned terror and fled, followed by Corrie, who screamed in real terror. Bumpus halted, dragged Corrie behind a rock, and secured his silence. A savage brushed past Bumpus and received a blow on his wounded arm, causing him to stagger and howl in pain. Bumpus and Corrie emerged from cover, and Bumpus fired a pistol, stunning three savages. Bumpus fought off multiple savages using his fists instead of drawing his sword.

The worthy man preferred stand-up fights on level ground. Gascoyne claimed to know every pass and cavern on the island. Gascoyne suggested dividing forces into three groups for an operation. One group was to be led by Mr. Thorwald through Goat's Pass. Another group was to be led by Henry Stuart to chase the savages. The third group, consisting of the vessel _Talisman_, was to bombard the native village. Montague expressed dissatisfaction with the assigned tasks.

The young man reported seeing thirty men with fire-tubes at the rapid water in Caniapuscaw. The young man traveled by kayak to bring news of the men to his community. The Esquimau community consisted of ten men, while the opposing group had thirty. The young man was not seen by the men he encountered while chasing deer. The young man offered an axe to his grandfather in exchange for permission to take his wife. The villagers prepared for flight upon learning of the impending danger. The oomiak is a large boat used by women to transport goods and families, while the kayak is used by men.

Charley found the animals to be numerous and the fish plentiful in the rivers and lakes. Charley expected the local nation to be brave hunters and to bring in large quantities of furs. Charley complimented the local nation on their bravery, activity, and perseverance. Charley advised the local nation to focus on hunting rather than engaging in war. Jacques Caradoc interpreted Charley's speech to the local nation. The meal served consisted of dried meat, reindeer tongues, and marrowbones.

The British navy is mentioned as a potential threat to a pirate's rescue. The character Ole expresses doubt about the interest of the British navy in a pirate. Ole has eleven men under his command for a planned attack. The men are described as natives, armed with heavy clubs, and instructed not to kill. Ole plans to attack the pirate and his party by surprise from the rear. There are four men in addition to the pirate that Ole intends to confront. Sambo is responsible for carrying ropes for binding the pirate.

La Roche reported that the Esquimaux were killing deer in the country. A herd of fifty or sixty deer was attempting to cross the river. The Esquimaux concealed themselves and their kayaks before chasing the deer. Stanley and Frank arrived at the scene during the slaughter of the deer. Chacooto, an Esquimau, demonstrated skill in driving a group of deer close to shore. Chacooto killed the deer with a single thrust of his lance. Bryan struggled to shoot a deer that had reached the land.

Annatock plunged his spear into the heart of a bear, causing it to fall dead on the ice. Peetoot celebrated the bear's death by dancing and shouting around its carcass. Peetoot's uncle ended his celebrations by hitting him with the butt-end of his spear. Peetoot ran to the village to inform others and fetch a sledge for the bear's carcass. A royal feast was held in the village, which lasted until the walruses, bear, and seals were consumed. As the weather became milder, the Esquimaux changed their footwear and prepared for summer activities. Peetoot caused damage to an igloo by running over it, leading to the end of the winter camp.

Frank Morton approached the camp carrying a heavy bundle. Frank stated that he had slain a noble buck and had loaded himself heavily to share the meat with the men. Frank parted ways with Bryan in the mountains and assumed Bryan had returned to camp. Stanley expressed confidence in Bryan's ability to navigate and survive in the wilderness. Francois and his companions arrived at the camp with several ducks and grouse. Stanley noted that the kettle was already full and supper was prepared. La Roche humorously commented on Bryan's reliability and the trouble he caused while preparing supper.

Stanley addressed his men after they finished supper in their new house. Stanley instructed his men to wake up early the next day. Stanley invited the ship's crew to dine with his men before their departure. Massan and Dick Prince left the fort at dawn with guns on their shoulders. Bryan left the house with a bag on his shoulder, heading towards the mountain. Massan and Prince returned with heavy loads of venison in the forenoon. Bryan returned to the fort with a bag of fish after fishing in the dark valley.

The igloos were constructed using soft snow and featured a key-stone principle in their design. Frank returned from an unsuccessful hunt to assist in the construction of the igloos. Two holes were left in the igloos to serve as doors, and slabs of clear ice were fitted into square holes above the entrances to serve as windows. The large igloo contained two doorways and an arched passage connecting it to the smaller igloo. Maximus brought a lamp made of soft stone from the Esquimau camp, which was used for warming the igloos and cooking food. Seal-fat was used as fuel for the lamp, which provided sufficient heat to warm the igloos without melting the snow walls. The floor of the igloo was made of snow, with one half raised for the bed, which was covered with deer-skin robes.

The ptarmigan has a brown coat in summer and retains some white feathers. Frank and Bryan encountered ptarmigans that were surprised by their presence. Bryan initially wanted to shoot the ptarmigans, but Frank advised against it. Frank pointed out a mountain spur in the distance, indicating a potential target. Bryan misidentified a deer as a crow while trying to see it from a distance. Frank instructed Bryan to wait in a ravine for the deer while he approached from another direction. Bryan reflected on his past experiences while humorously considering Frank's advice to not get lost.

Master Kennedy is referred to as the friend of a two-legged polar bear. The establishment of Stoney Creek is comprised within two acres of ground. Stoney Creek consists of eight or nine houses, with three visible from the lake. The 'great' house is a small edifice built of unsquared logs, partially whitewashed, with six small windows and a large door. There is a trading-shop and provision-store adjacent to the 'great' house, which has two doors and four windows. A twin building opposite the trading-shop contains furs and miscellaneous stores. Harry's opinion of Mr. Whyte changed, believing that his initial bad impression was due to Mr. Whyte's cool reception.

Arctic foxes can occasionally be seen in groups, playing among the ice. The accountant led his companions to a concealed entrance to his winter camp. The entrance was made through a dense mass of bushes. The center of the knoll had a clear space of about twenty feet in diameter surrounded by thick trees. The area was dark at night, with very little light penetrating from above. The accountant struck a light to start a fire in the dark space. The fire illuminated the area and changed the atmosphere from cold and gloomy to warm and inviting.

A storm struck the island with greater violence than expected. Henry was at the helm of the cutter as it was lifted over the reef and into deep water. The cutter became unmanageable after striking violently, dislocating its framework and tearing out the rudder fastenings. The vessel struck the rocks multiple times, ultimately leading to its total wreck. Henry clung to a piece of wood for hours while being tossed by the waves. When morning broke, Henry was still clinging to the broken lower-mast and found other pieces of the wreck nearby. Henry prayed for help and attempted to drag several spars towards him to get out of the water.

John Bumpus expresses indifference about preventing Gascoyne's escape. Bumpus warns Ole Thorwald that many people on the island support Gascoyne. Bumpus states that Henry Stuart believes Gascoyne does not deserve to be hanged. Henry Stuart has bribed the jailer to facilitate Gascoyne's escape at midnight. Bumpus informs Ole that Gascoyne will escape to a boat concealed off Long Point. There are two boats waiting for Gascoyne and his associates. Ole Thorwald agrees to take measures to prevent Gascoyne's escape.

The name of Christ is stated as the only means of salvation. The Indians are described as living without God and hope. Some individuals feel that the Christian religion is worthless for salvation without love for Jesus Christ. There is a discussion about the lack of missionary spirit among fur traders. Frank Morton is mentioned as someone who has made a profession of Christianity but has done little. Maximus harbors hatred towards the Indians, viewing them as responsible for his loss. The traders of Ungava focused on gathering provisions and establishing a fishery after the Indians left.

The group faced a snowstorm while trying to reach the woods. Hamilton went missing during the storm. Harry decided to search for Hamilton after realizing he was not with the group. Harry found Hamilton standing in despair and led him to safety in the forest. The route to the fort was sheltered, and they encountered no further issues. Letters from home caused a mix of emotions among the characters at the fort. Mr. Wilson, the doctor, and the skipper expressed surprise upon learning about the letters from home.

La Roche shouted for help while struggling in the water. Edith witnessed La Roche's distress and screamed for assistance. Dick Prince arrived at the scene and jumped into the water to rescue La Roche. Chimo, the dog, also jumped into the water during the rescue attempt. Frank, Stanley, and others gathered on the bank to help. Dick Prince managed to grab La Roche by the collar while swimming towards the shore. La Roche refused to let go of the fishing rod despite the danger.

A man fired a pistol at another, causing the bullet to graze the man's forehead. The shot alarmed the natives in the church and prompted an attack. The people of the settlement were able to seize their arms in response to the alarm. The attacking party had no plan and intended to rush the church at a signal from their chief. Gascoyne and Henry were among the first to leave the church to confront the attackers. The pastor rushed unarmed into the midst of the attackers to protect his child. Captain Montague and his officers arrived to assist the pastor during the fight.

Frank did not suffer any injuries from the wolf, but had a wound on his head and slight frostbite on his face. Edith attempted to revive Frank by rubbing his frostbitten face and encouraging him to speak. Chimo, Frank's dog, approached him and reminded Frank of recent events. Frank expressed a desire to return to the igloo and asked Edith to help him with his snowshoes. Edith supported Frank as he attempted to walk, but he struggled to maintain his balance. Frank fell multiple times and was unable to walk more than a short distance due to his condition. Despite her own weakness, Edith worked to keep Frank awake and moving until they reached the edge of the lake.

Redfeather and Jacques share a strong friendship that is further solidified after a conversation about a past event. Jacques offers Redfeather various valuable items, including his rifle, which Redfeather declines. Jacques expresses his intention to stay with Redfeather at the missionary settlement as a hunter and fisherman. Harry Somerville is experiencing disappointment due to being assigned to desk work at York Fort instead of pursuing outdoor activities. During the autumn of his second year at York Fort, Harry is tied to his desk due to the preparation of annual accounts. After the ship departs, Harry and the clerks are allowed to explore the swamps and woods, which improves Harry's spirits. As winter approaches, the residents of York Fort prepare for the harsh conditions by cutting firewood and making other necessary adjustments.

The story in 'Ungava' by R.M. Ballantyne illustrates the life of fur traders in North America around Hudson's Bay. Most major incidents in the story are based on factual events, with fiction used to create a readable narrative. The author acknowledges the Leader of the adventurous band for providing the groundwork for the story. The narrative begins with a young man shouting in a forest while leaning on a rifle. The young man encounters a squirrel and hears a gunshot, prompting him to move towards the sound. He finds another man named Stanley, who has shot a goose and is dressed as a hunter. The two men discuss their hunting experiences, with Stanley indicating he has had more success than the young man.

Stanley thanked Maximus for saving Chimo's life. Moses interpreted for Stanley and Maximus during their conversation. Maximus came to trade and brought two fox furs and three deer. Stanley expressed a desire for Maximus to stay at the fort as a hunter. Maximus recounted an attack on his people by Indians and the loss of his bride. Maximus became agitated upon seeing a piece of sealskin found at an Indian camp. Moses informed Stanley that Maximus believed the skin belonged to his wife and that the Indians had taken her.

The feet begin to lose sensation, starting with the toes and then the heels. The youth feels as if he is walking on his anklebones due to the loss of sensation. The prairies of Red River are covered in snow for five or six months each year. Prairie wolves can move easily on the snow's surface due to their light weight. In spring, the snow softens, making it difficult for wolves to move while horses can navigate better. Charley Kennedy is eager to participate in a hunt organized by the Hudson's Bay Service. The weather is warm with a temperature of 39 degrees in the shade, indicating the arrival of spring.

Charley placed his plate before a man after he finished his meal. The Indian began eating Charley's food and finished it in less than half an hour. One of the chiefs entertained the assembly with a chant while women outside provided an accompaniment. Jacques observed that Redfeather ate less than other Indians and had a comrade eat part of his share. Redfeather has lived among white men more than Indians in the last ten years. Redfeather announced his intention to leave his people, expressing sorrow over the decision. Redfeather resolved to go to the dwelling of a missionary after being troubled by strange thoughts.

Mr. Park is a chief factor traveling to Norway House. Gibault served hot tea, buffalo tongue, pemmican, hard biscuit, and butter for their evening meal. The primary food during the voyage consisted of robbiboo, a mixture of flour, pemmican, and water. Pemmican is made from buffalo flesh and is considered nutritious and palatable. The process of making pemmican involves killing a buffalo, drying the meat, and mixing it with fat in a hide bag. Pemmican is valued for its compactness and long shelf life, making it suitable for long journeys. The men ate their meals without plates, using wooden or pewter spoons to consume robbiboo.

Peter Mactavish mentioned that John Fowler, the miller, has purchased a new pony. The senior clerk requested Tom Whyte to ask John Fowler for the loan of the horse for Charley Kennedy. Tom Whyte had not run since being dismissed from the army twenty years ago for incurable drunkenness. The room where Tom Whyte sat was a typical dwelling for employees of the Hudson's Bay Company, made entirely of unpainted wood. The men's berths in the room were constructed like those on a ship, arranged in tiers around the room. The temperature in northern regions of America can drop to 50 degrees below zero at York Fort and lower than 60 degrees below zero at Great Bear Lake during winter. A youth walking in the cold may return with frostbite and hoar-frost on his hair and face due to the extreme temperatures.

Mr Kennedy is described as having a bent body, outstretched head and neck, and prominent eyes. Kate screams upon seeing her father and runs away into the woods. Mr Kennedy confronts Harry about insulting his daughter after inviting him as a guest. Harry expresses his love for Kate and states that he has asked her to be his wife. Mr Kennedy questions Harry about Kate's response to his proposal. Mr Kennedy insists that Harry should have asked for his permission before addressing his daughter. Mr Kennedy leads Harry to his house for further discussion on the matter.

Mr Addison took Charley by the hand and walked slowly through the wood while giving him advice. Mr Addison belonged to the Church of England but conducted services in a Presbyterian form. Mr Addison emphasized the importance of the love of God for happiness and hope in life. Charley embraced Kate passionately before leaving for the boats. Harry Somerville and others bid farewell to Charley as he hurried past them. Mr Kennedy expressed strong emotions while saying goodbye to Charley. The boats departed for the north with men springing into them and rowing vigorously.

Captain Montague suspects Captain Gascoyne of being the pirate Durward. The _Talisman_ and the _Foam_ will both benefit from the land-breeze. Captain Montague arrives at the _Foam_ and is received by Captain Gascoyne. Captain Gascoyne has twenty-two men on board the _Foam_. Captain Montague examines the papers and arrangements of the _Foam_ without finding any evidence of piracy. Captain Gascoyne explains the differences between his vessel and the pirate's vessel. The _Foam_ is described as having black sides and a smiling figurehead, while the pirate's vessel has a narrow streak of red and a scarlet griffin figurehead.

Corrie left to find help after a sailor encouraged him. The sound of a shell caused settlers to stop pursuing savages and rush to a burning house. The pastor's house was destroyed by the settlers working together. Alice was rescued from the house by Keona before it was destroyed. A small party of native settlers found one of Alice's shoes and tracked her footprints. Mr. Mason insisted on immediately following the tracks to find Alice. Gascoyne and Montague suggested having a council of war before proceeding with the rescue.

La Roche sat down to smoke his pipe but instead threw it into the river. La Roche drew a knife from his girdle and returned with a large branch. He stripped the leaves and twigs from the branch and retrieved a piece of stout cord with a cod-hook attached. La Roche dressed his hook using a duck feather and a tag from his scarlet worsted belt. On his third attempt to fish, La Roche hooked a salmon that weighed six pounds. La Roche fell into the water while trying to land the salmon. Bryan attempted to rescue La Roche but was restrained by Massan, who could not swim.

Gascoyne asked Corrie if he could swim and instructed him to swim to the schooner when he saw a white sheet waved. Gascoyne planned to swim to the schooner and send a boat for Thorwald if the crew was ashore. Gascoyne entered the sea quietly and swam towards the schooner without making noise. A watchman on the schooner noticed Gascoyne and threw a handspike at him, which missed. Gascoyne swam underwater to avoid detection and surfaced near the schooner's quarter. Gascoyne listened for sounds on the schooner and concluded that the crew was likely ashore. Gascoyne waited for the watchman to approach before attacking him.

The Esquimaux's chief wealth consisted of boots and deerskins, which the women prepared. Stanley encouraged the Esquimaux to hunt for furs instead of remaining idle on the coast. Several bands of Esquimaux arrived at Fort Chimo, forming a group of about three hundred people. The Esquimaux were generally found to be quiet, inoffensive, and honest. Stanley launched his boat with the help of the Esquimaux to take additional soundings. A child accidentally broke a window at the fort, leading the Esquimaux to bring a dog as compensation. Stanley agreed to accept the dog but ensured that the native who offered it would not suffer a loss.

The girl waited at the cave's mouth for the fugitives to reappear. She considered the possibility of an exit from the cavern at the other end. The girl ran into the cavern but fell after advancing about fifty yards. She lay still for some time, listening to the sound of her own heartbeat. After an hour, she returned to the mouth of the cave to rest and think. The girl expressed despair over her situation and began to cry. Master Corrie and his companion the Grampus heard unearthly sounds while tracing footprints.

The party received an account of the exploration that corroborated previous reports from Dick Prince and Massan. The evidence from various exploring parties was satisfactory and boosted the morale of the men. Timber was available near the proposed fort site, and there was an abundance of game and fish in the area. The fur-traders began constructing their winter dwelling as the hunting and fishing season was ending. The fort was designed in the shape of three sides of a square surrounded by a stockade, with specific areas designated for a dwelling-house, a store, and men's quarters. The first structure erected was a flag-staff for the Hudson's Bay Company flag, which was saluted with cheers. The construction method used for the houses involved a simple framework of timber that could be built with minimal tools.

The height of the space was increased to nearly six feet by the masses thrown out during the digging process. A large fire was kindled at one end of the space, which melted only a little of the surrounding snow due to the intense cold. At the other end of the space, a mass of flat pine branches was piled up to form a couch, with the upper end raised to create a bolster. Beside the bolster, there was a small wooden box, a round tin kettle, an iron tea-kettle, two tin mugs, a hatchet, and a large bundle tied in a green blanket. The area was described as having two apartments: an outer one with walls of tree-stems and darkness, and an inner one with walls of snow and a carpet of evergreen branches. Hamilton's friends removed his moccasins and rubbed his feet to restore circulation, after which they wrapped his feet in a thick blanket. Hamilton decided to wait for supper until his friends returned from checking the traps, despite feeling pain in his feet.

Corrie used his empty pistol to incapacitate a man attempting to assault his companion. Another assailant received a gash on the thigh from a broken sabre during the conflict. Eight savages were defeated in a short span of time. The remaining savages overwhelmed Bumpus and Corrie, burying them under their numbers. Poopy, bound and unable to intervene, witnessed the events with interest and expressed her fears with a subdued shriek. The captors debated the fate of their prisoners, considering options of death or keeping them as hostages. Bumpus struggled against his captors, leading to a violent reaction from one of the savages.

Stanley intends to send Oolibuck to the coast with four days' provisions to look for a ship. Oolibuck expresses confidence that two days' provisions are sufficient if he has enough ammunition. Stanley instructs Oolibuck to keep a lookout for the ship and to be cautious with his ammunition. Stanley directs Oostesimow and La Roche to build a small canoe from birch bark. The party in the camp finds their fishing nets rolled up instead of containing fish due to river currents. Stanley decides to set stake-nets immediately to improve their chances of catching fish. Frank Morton and Bryan explore the area behind the camp and discover a covey of ptarmigan.

The author expresses a strong desire to see and hear from Charley after many months. The author's parents are reported to be quite well. The father has increased his smoking habits since Charley's departure. The father has been engaged in mysterious work in the summer-house, which he never did before. The author describes an incident where the father reacted angrily upon being interrupted while writing. The mother was confined to the house for nearly three weeks due to an illness but is now able to go out for drives. The father took care of the mother during her illness, surprising the author with his nurturing behavior.

Henry told Corrie and Alice that he had something important to say to his mother. Corrie overheard Henry's words and felt curious about the mystery involving the pirate captain. Mrs. Stuart visited Gascoyne in jail, where she expressed concern about his situation. Gascoyne stated that he would not attempt to escape from jail despite Mrs. Stuart's pleas. Mrs. Stuart sought help from Montague, who informed her that he could not set Gascoyne free. Montague acknowledged Gascoyne's past services but stated he had a duty to convey him to England. Mrs. Stuart revealed to Montague that Gascoyne was her husband in hopes of influencing his fate.

The foremost animal took to the water and began swimming towards the opposite shore of the lake, followed by seven others. Three canoes pursued the deer after a sufficient time elapsed to ensure the animals could not return. Harry Somerville prepared to strike a deer with an Indian's spear while his companions targeted other members of the herd. Harry struck the spear deep into the deer's back, causing it to cease swimming and die. The party dispatched the entire herd using axes and knives and towed their catch to the shore. Mr. Whyte greeted Harry and Hamilton upon their arrival at Stoney Creek and requested to review their dispatches. Charley led his friends to their new residence while instructing Redfeather to ensure Jacques Caradoc's comfort.

Mrs. Stanley is transforming a soft yellow deerskin into a hunting coat for her husband. Frank Morton made a small rough table that is located close to the stove. La Roche brought candles made at the fort into the hall through a back door. Stanley entered the room and commented on the severe weather conditions outside. The thermometer outside is recorded at thirty below. The men in their habitation are enjoying their evening meal beside the stove. The storm outside is described as an awful night that has not been previously experienced at Fort Chimo.

Chimo responded to a cry by bounding in the direction it came from. Chimo's progress was halted when the sledge became jammed among the rocks. Edith was unable to hear Chimo's cries due to the gentle wind. Edith experienced anxiety and despair while searching for her sledge in the snow. Three days later, Maximus arrived at Fort Chimo with Frank Morton, who was found in an igloo. Maximus reported that little Edith Stanley was missing, prompting a search. The searchers found the sledge stuck among the rocks and Chimo nearly dead from cold and hunger.

Mr. Kennedy believes that his daughter Kate is too old to be focused on books and should help at home. Mr. Kennedy thinks that his son Charley should enter the service and believes he is clever enough to trade with the red-skins. Mr. Kennedy plans to bring his children home from school to place them in new roles. Kate is assigned the roles of housekeeper and tobacco-cutter. Charley is informed that he will work for the Hudson's Bay Company and is given a week to consider it. Charley expresses his discontent with the idea of working at a desk, stating he would rather be a buffalo. Charley and Kate share a close bond and support each other through their emotions.

Gascoyne was guided by Dick and another man from his cell to the outer door of the prison. The group exited the prison into the open air, where Gascoyne observed the men surrounding him in the dark. Gascoyne was led to a small bay where a boy approached Dick to confirm that everything was ready. Dick instructed Gascoyne to step into a large boat and sit beside an individual in a cloak. Gascoyne questioned Dick's authority, to which Dick asserted he had the power to enforce his commands. The boat was rowed by four strong men and was designed to withstand rough weather. After passing the barrier reef, the sails were hoisted and the boat moved swiftly out to sea.

Alice and Poopy were instructed by Montague to prepare supper. The supper consisted of hard biscuit and water. Montague and Corrie discussed their plans to escape from pirates. Montague acknowledged the desperate situation they were in. Corrie proposed daring strategies to confront the pirates. Alice and Poopy engaged in a game of 'tea party' with their supper. The pirate schooner _Avenger_ anchored at the Isle of Palms on the fifth day of its journey.

The captain of the schooner is described as having a large chin, iron jaw, and blue eyes. He wears a dark-coloured flannel shirt, trousers gathered by drab gaiters, and a scarlet belt with a long knife. The captain is approximately forty years old and is characterized as capable of both good and evil. The captain ordered a small boat to be lowered and took two men, including John Bumpus, to the shore. John Bumpus carries a small bundle tied in a red cotton handkerchief and expresses surprise at the captain's intentions. Bumpus believes in his own physical strength and feels he could defeat the captain in a fight. The captain informs Bumpus that he is free to leave his service but will not be taken back aboard the schooner.

Bumpus advises Thorwald to capture the pirate without informing Henry and his comrades. Bumpus states that he will be one of four men accompanying Gascoyne. Thorwald plans to arrive at Long Point before noon with a dozen men. Thorwald expresses contempt towards Bumpus's reluctance to assist in the fight. Thorwald leaves his house cautiously at night, resembling a burglar. Sambo, Thorwald's major-domo, meets him outside his gate. Thorwald expresses his dislike for ambushes and prefers open combat.

Louis lost his sweetheart due to his excessive use of a whip. Tim Roughead was known for causing mischief and nearly losing his life multiple times. Tim fell in love with a girl named Louise, who had previously jilted many suitors. Tim confronted Louise about her feelings and proposed to settle down with her. On the day of the wedding, Tim's horse misbehaved, causing him to fall and break his leg. After Tim's recovery, he discovered that Louise had married a young clerk and moved to Kentucky. Kate's horse ran away after a rabbit startled it, leading to a pursuit by her companions.

An Esquimau was taken on board to pilot the vessel to the fort. The captain expressed confidence in the Esquimau's abilities and noted his popularity among the crew. Stanley offered to help the captain by ensuring the crew worked diligently to unload the ship. The unloading process involved transporting various goods, including blankets, guns, and food supplies. Stanley invited the captain and his mates to dinner the following day. Stanley requested his wife to prepare two large plum puddings for the dinner.

A storm occurred among the mountains, followed by a clear day with bright sunlight. Stanley and Frank discovered that their dwelling was completely buried in snow. The only visible parts of the fort were the chimneys and the flagstaff. Stanley suggested they dig themselves out of the snow. La Roche entered the room and expressed concern about the situation. Frank used a shovel to remove snow from the doorway while others assisted. Edith helped pile the snow while her mother retired to her room.

The firm lost a vessel named the Brilliant, which sailed for the South Sea islands with a rich cargo and was never heard from again. The fat cashier calculated the loss of the Brilliant and was aware of the exact amount. The firm received a remittance from the Unknown, which included the value of the cargo and the estimated value of the vessel, repaid to the owners. Mr. Stuart informed his wife, Mary, that he had sent off the last remittance related to the Brilliant and had managed to repay the amount with interest. Mr. Stuart stated that he would continue to manage his mercantile business and donate all profits to charity for the rest of his life. Corrie went on a long voyage in the Avenger, where he met a woman named Susan, who later became a passenger on the ship. Corrie and Alice Mason were married on Green Isle, along with Bumpus and Susan, during a double wedding celebration.

Mr Kennedy, senior, had a power of persuasion that he did not frequently utilize. Mr Grant inquired about the availability of a horse for Charley. Tom Whyte informed Mr Grant that there was no horse available for Charley. The groom mentioned that he had borrowed the miller's pony for Charley. Charley and Harry decided to wait for the arrival of the expected horse. Charley expressed a desire to see the new horse that was only half broken. Charley saddled and bridled the new horse and rode out into the yard.

Frank became powerless and did not respond to his companion's efforts. Edith wrapped Frank in her cloak and went to the igloo to heat tea. Edith packed pemmican and biscuit while waiting for the tea to heat. Edith returned to Frank and Chimo with hot tea, but Frank did not initially respond. After rubbing Frank, he opened his eyes and was able to sip the tea. Frank was able to sit up and talk after drinking the tea, but soon fell into a deep sleep on the sled. Edith tended to Frank for two days, but he showed little improvement, leading her to decide to search for the Esquimau village.

John Bumpus was condemned to death by a group of influential and violent men who sought justice against him as a pirate. Bumpus expressed regret and mentioned a letter from a woman named Susan, which he wanted sent back to her. A young man resembling a sailor intervened and removed the noose from Bumpus's neck, causing mixed reactions from the crowd. The young man, referred to as Dan, stated that there was doubt about Bumpus being a pirate and called for a longer trial. Dan requested to read the letter from Bumpus to determine its significance for the case. The crowd maintained intense silence while Dan read the letter, indicating their anticipation of its contents.

The events described occurred over a brief period of a few hours. The _Talisman_ anchored in the bay after firing a broadside. Corrie and his companions, Alice and Poopy, were bound by savages. Alice was tied near the edge of a cliff and could not free herself. Poopy was positioned farther up the cliff and attempted various methods to sit up. Corrie was bound more tightly due to his resistance against the savages. Alice expressed hope for rescue, while Corrie tried to comfort her despite his own fears.

Frank had trouble keeping the fishing line tight as a fish descended rapidly. The fish stopped and lay at the bottom of the pool, refusing to move. Stanley was instructed by Frank to throw a stone at the fish to rouse it. The fish dashed across the river and attempted to escape down a rapid. Frank held onto the line despite the risk of breaking it to prevent the fish from escaping. Stanley successfully gaffed the fish after being cautioned by Frank. Frank caught three fish from the same pool before moving to try for a larger one.

The characters are engaged in clearing snow from Fort Chimo after a heavy snowfall. Stanley instructs Francois and others to open the dog-kennel and gather shovels. The snow drift around the fort is reported to be fifteen or sixteen feet deep. Maximus attempts to free himself from the snow by scraping it away from above his head. Maximus successfully breaks through the snow surface and steps into the sunlight. Maximus travels to the fort after obtaining medicines from Stanley for an old woman. Frank prepares to set out for fishing under the ice the following day.

The man-of-war entered the bay and anchored there. The _Foam_ remained anchored in the bay, raising suspicions about its status as a pirate schooner. A large boat from the _Talisman_ was in the water alongside, filled with armed men. Gascoyne was observed smoking on the quarterdeck, conversing with the British commander. The crew of the _Foam_ appeared uneasy about their fate under Manton's command. Manton displayed a calm demeanor while feeling anger over the actions of his crew. The young commander of the _Talisman_ felt confident about capturing the prize after witnessing events on shore.

Alice and Poopy were asked to leave before discussing a plan. Alice expressed her hope for success and ran down the mountain-side. Henry unfolded his plan to his companions after Alice left. Jo Bumpus was perplexed and conversed with himself about a puzzling situation. Jo Bumpus was smoking a pipe while reflecting on the situation. Jo Bumpus realized he should not discuss certain matters, even with himself. Jo Bumpus read a love-letter from Susan while sitting under a tree.

Ole Thorwald and Sambo went to the beach to secure a boat. The boat was fastened to an iron ring with a heavy iron chain and a padlock. Ole Thorwald placed the key of the padlock in his pocket after securing the boat. Thorwald planned to wait for Mister Gascoyne and mentioned the time as half-past eleven. Gascoyne was in a dark cell, resting with his face in his hands and occasionally sighing. Gascoyne expressed thoughts of pride and sin while muttering to himself in his cell. Gascoyne reflected on his past and questioned his belief in God.

The sleighs have been replaced by lumber-carts and gigs in Red River. The old Canadian has transitioned from using an ox-drawn water-barrel sleigh to a small wheeled cart. The trees have lost their white patches and the clump of willows has disappeared in the settlement. Spring has arrived in Red River, marking a significant change from winter. Red River is now flowing towards Lake Winnipeg, with boats and wooden canoes being used for travel. Birds and ground squirrels have become active, contributing to the lively atmosphere of spring. Frogs are vocal in the marshy areas, creating a continuous sound that newcomers may mistake for birds.

Alice asks Poopy if she has ever heard of friends who are actually enemies. Corrie expresses concern about Alice's father's thoughts on friends in the settlement. Alice recounts a conversation she had with her father regarding a wounded individual. Corrie mentions a man he refers to as the Grampus, whose real name is Jo Bumpus. Corrie informs Alice that there are reports of pirates on the island. Corrie explains that pirates are sea-robbers and that they have been attacking the local population. Corrie shares that Henry was nearly killed by one of the pirates but was saved by a mysterious individual and the Grampus.

The Esquimau ate raw deer meat due to his strong appetite and lack of food since morning. He displayed haste in his actions despite the peaceful surroundings. The Esquimau used a kayak, which is a long, thin, sharp canoe made of a light wood framework covered with sealskin parchment. The kayak is designed for one person and is propelled using a long paddle with a blade at each end. An Indian attempted to shoot the Esquimau but missed when his gun failed to fire. A chief scolded the Indian for his impatience and questioned the value of attacking the Esquimau. The Esquimau reached the coast and encountered a young girl, whom he kissed on both cheeks.

The chief performs a ceremony that includes raising a pipe and balancing it in various directions. The company observes the ceremony with interest, including women and children who appear serious. The chief delivers a speech that includes references to his own deeds and those of his forefathers, as well as criticism of other tribes. The speech concludes with the company expressing approval through a prolonged 'Ho!' The pipe-bearer presents the sacred stem to each member of the company for them to partake. Charley attempts to maintain a serious demeanor during the ceremony but struggles to suppress laughter. Charley delivers a speech in English, translated into the Indian language, informing the tribe about a new trading-fort established for their benefit.

The old woman saved the patriarch from drowning by pulling him onto the oomiak. The Indians scalped three dead bodies and discarded them into the sea. The Indians searched the huts for valuables but found very little. The most useful item found was an axe left behind by the old grandfather. The Indians set fire to the village after taking what they could carry. The chief ordered the death of the Esquimau girl, but her captor intervened. The chief allowed the young man to take the girl as his wife and they began their journey back to the Cree hunting grounds.

Harry lay down in the woods and pulled green blankets over himself. Harry prayed before lying down, which was a habit from his home life. Harry lived in a happy home in the West Highlands of Scotland before departing for the North-west. Harry's upbringing included a strong emphasis on Christian values and family love. Harry's early training helped him avoid many sins that affected other boys. Harry's memories of home and his mother's influence remained with him despite negative surroundings. Charley went to the margin of Lake Winnipeg while Harry rested.

Charley, Jacques, and Harry proceeded by the river while Redfeather and Hamilton launched their canoe on the lake. Jacques led his party to a point on the Duck River where they found two canoes. Jacques and a Canadian man entered one canoe, while Harry and Charley entered the other. Charley expressed concern that Misconna may have crossed the river already. Jacques assured Charley that Misconna would likely not reach the flat-rock fall before them. As they approached the fall, Charley decided to run it ahead of Jacques and Harry. An Indian shot an arrow that struck Harry in the shoulder, causing their canoe to capsize.

The expedition party consisted of fifteen members. The members of the party included MR. AND MRS. STANLEY, EDITH, FRANK MORTON, MASSAN, DICK PRINCE, LA ROCHE, BRYAN, FRANCOIS, OOLIBUCK, AUGUSTUS, MOSES, GASPARD, OOSTESIMOW, and MA-ISTEQUAN. The expedition was set to depart from Moose Fort. The party used three canoes made of birch bark. The largest canoe was sixteen feet long and five feet wide, carrying fifteen pieces of cargo and six crew members. The smallest canoe was designed to carry three men and was intended for hunting and scouting. Frank Morton was regarded as the best shot of the party.

Edith expresses her love for Prince and mentions that she hates one man. Edith identifies Gaspard as the man she hates because he struck her dog and is rude to others. Mrs. Stanley acknowledges Edith's feelings and encourages her to pray for Gaspard and speak kindly to him. Stanley informs Eda that he had arranged to follow to a far-off country next year and suggests bringing her along. Mrs. Stanley expresses her reluctance to let Stanley go without them and cannot wait until next year. George Barney, the Irish butler, announces that some men are waiting in the hall. Stanley addresses the men in the hall, asking them to voice any objections they may have.

Corrie was found asleep at the front door of the cottage, armed with a broken sabre and a cavalry pistol. Corrie was in love with Alice and intended to protect her from potential danger. He armed himself due to concerns about the unsettled condition of the times. Corrie fell asleep while trying to keep watch, despite his intentions to guard the threshold. Mr. Mason attempted to wake Corrie for five minutes before he responded. Corrie explained to Mr. Mason that he was watching for savages while others were asleep. The situation led to laughter among Corrie, Mr. Mason, Alice, and Poopy.

Harry misjudged the distance to a point he thought was near, which was actually two miles away. Hamilton expressed uncertainty about a blister on his left foot, which he found painful. Harry reassured Hamilton that blisters are a common experience in the area. The accountant had three traps set in the vicinity. Hamilton reported a strange sensation in his heels, which the accountant identified as frostbite. The accountant led Harry and Hamilton to a winter camp in the woods for treatment. The camping site was located on a knoll with fir trees, providing shelter and a view of the surrounding area.

A person on an elevated rock observed a canoe that was about to double a point of land. Massan expressed that the canoe was too far to hear their shouts. Stanley encouraged Massan to try shouting again, but Massan declined. Bryan attempted to shout to the canoe, but his effort was met with laughter from the group. The canoe disappeared after doubling the point. Bryan and La Roche decided to take a walk to the point ahead to wait for the canoes. Bryan shared his past experiences and reasons for leaving his native land during their walk.

Mike Brady prepared to let go of the sheet as a squall approached. The guide shouted commands to the crew as the squall hit the boat. An Indian cut the sheet and halyards to prevent the sail from filling with water. The boat took on water and was nearly filled to the gunwale. Mr Park instructed the crew to bail out the water using available containers. The crew successfully bailed out enough water to reset the sail and increase speed. The boat reached a sheltered bay where two other boats were found.

The elevation of the dome reached approximately twelve or thirteen feet. Frank proposed cutting a doorway into the dome to explore the spring. Edith expressed delight at Frank's idea and encouraged him to start the work. Bryan commented on the impracticality of spirits in the cold climate and mentioned finishing the ring-bolts for the sled. Frank and Bryan cut a block of solid ice from the dome, revealing a cavern with a light blue color. The cavern had luminous blue walls, icicles from the roof, and a bubbling spring in the center. Francois constructed a sledge for Edith modeled after those used by the Esquimaux.

Edith, Chimo, and two Esquimau girls ascended a steep path for a quarter of an hour. The group reached a ridge of rock that overlooked a small dark lake or pool. Chimo exhibited restlessness and growled in response to the wild environment. A deer, pursued by a wolf, ran past the girls as they stood by the cliff. The wolf caught the deer and killed it shortly after the chase ended. Chimo intervened by attacking the wolf while it was still with the dying deer. A fierce fight ensued between Chimo and the wolf.

Hamilton, Harry, and the accountant resumed their march as the snow ceased to fall and the moon illuminated their path. The scene was characterized by a calm arctic night, a snowy landscape, and a clear starry sky partially obscured by clouds. Harry expressed that the scene made him think of home, while Hamilton noted it reminded them they were in a foreign land. Both Harry and Hamilton had been raised in families that valued a relationship with the Almighty, leading them to reflect on spiritual matters during their journey. The travelers navigated a frozen swamp before reaching a belt of woodland near North River. North River appeared broad and frozen at this location, with the opposite shore barely distinguishable due to snow cover. Hamilton described the area as cold and desolate, while the accountant clarified that they were at the extreme mouth of North River.

Harry wore ankle-pieces and moccasins made of stout deer-skin. Harry's costume included deerskin mittens with separate bags for the thumb and fingers. The three friends prepared to leave their warm abode as the night became darker and the snow fell thicker. The accountant led the way along a wooden platform towards the gate of the fort. The three friends followed a track to where winter's firewood was cut, despite the thick falling snow. They needed to put on snow-shoes after leaving the beaten track to continue their journey through deep snow. Snow-shoes allow travelers to walk over deep snow with less effort compared to walking without them.

Frank did not return as the day drew to a close. Edith watched anxiously for Frank and eventually returned to the igloo feeling anxious and terrified. Chimo, the dog, entered the igloo and laid his head on Edith's lap. Edith expressed concern for Frank's whereabouts while embracing Chimo. Chimo exhibited strange behavior, including whining and running around without a clear purpose. Edith examined Chimo for signs of injury but found none, leading her to believe Frank was safe from wolves. Edith decided to follow Chimo, believing he would lead her to Frank.

La Roche inquired about dinner options from Mrs. Stanley. Mrs. Stanley requested to repeat yesterday's dinner, but La Roche informed her that fresh fish was unavailable. A vessel with a white triangular sail appeared against the dark rock near the river narrows. A schooner followed the first vessel, and artillery was fired as it approached the fort. Frank Morton greeted the fort's men with a cheer as he arrived on the vessel. A child named Edith was on the boat, and she called out to her mother upon arrival. Frank revealed that he found Edith and others trapped in a boat beset by ice near the river's mouth.

Mr. Kennedy, senior, stood in the doorway of his mansion with his hands in his vest pockets. The prairies were bright and beautiful that morning, with greener grass and sparkling dewdrops. The horses appeared to dance over the turf, which was springy and filled with wild-flowers. The plains were picturesque, featuring clumps of trees, wild shrubbery, and temporary lakes formed by melting snow. Kate led the group during their ride, with Jacques on her left and Harry on her right, while Charley brought up the rear. Kate's horse showed a desire to gallop, prompting Harry to help her check its speed. Jacques expressed admiration for Kate's spirited horse, which he believed would make a good buffalo-runner.

Harry arrived at the campsite by canoe. Mr Park is present at the campsite and is smoking a pipe. Harry has been sent by Mr Grant to take the place of another young gentleman. Harry expressed his excitement about hunting buffaloes and grizzly bears. Harry's canoe was turned bottom up by two Indians who were watching him. Harry and Charley decided to sleep under the canoe instead of using their own tents. The canoe provides limited shelter, only covering the body up to the waist.

Mr. Mason has captured the natives and believes he can easily defeat them in battle due to superior numbers and arms. Mr. Mason instructs the natives to lay down their weapons and march unarmed halfway to the settlement. Mr. Mason requires the entire tribe, including women and children, to assemble to hear his message. The natives agree to listen to Mr. Mason after he mentions the presence of women and children. The natives throw down their arms and a guard is placed over them to prevent recovery. Mr. Mason delivers a long sermon to the assembled natives, using specific biblical texts. After the sermon, the native warriors are marched off to the location where Mr. Mason promised to set them free.

Redfeather expressed a desire to leave his community, which surprised the party. The old chief complimented Redfeather on his bravery and warned him about the presence of evil spirits. Misconna, a muscular man with a villainous expression, objected to Redfeather's departure. Charley learned that Misconna was Redfeather's rival for Wabisca and had killed a trapper's wife. Despite Misconna's objections, Redfeather's decision to leave was accepted by the party. Redfeather agreed to travel with Charley and Jacques Caradoc for a few days, taking his wife in another canoe. Misconna secretly followed Redfeather and his companions, listening to their plans.

Mr. Rogan wishes to see the accountant. Harry Somerville and Hamilton were occupied in their apartments. The doctor walked up and down while smoking and made sarcastic remarks. The doctor refilled and relit his pipe at the stove. The skipper defended his use of a pillow for comfort. The accountant entered with a packet of letters. The inmates reacted with surprise and pathos while reading their letters.

Mr. Kennedy believes that tying down a horse is the best way to break it in. Mr. Grant suggests that breaking in horses in Mexico is done differently, using a lasso and allowing the horse to run free. Mr. Kennedy expresses skepticism about letting Charley run free and suggests he should be given equipment for the woods. Mr. Grant recommends giving Charley some freedom for a year to improve his willingness to listen. Mr. Kennedy describes his daughter Kate as gentle and obedient, contrasting her with Charley. Mr. Kennedy characterizes Charley as obstinate but good-tempered, noting he often gets into trouble. Mr. Grant questions whether Mr. Kennedy has explained the benefits of a job in his counting-room to Charley.

Charles Kennedy spent part of the previous year at Rocky Mountain House. Kennedy was selected as the clerk to accompany Mr Whyte to a new location. The party reached a spot by a large lake that was deemed suitable for establishing a settlement. Mr Whyte initiated the establishment of Stoney Creek by striking a larch tree. An Indian informed them of a large band of Knisteneux migrating nearby. Charley and interpreter Jacques Caradoc constructed a canoe to inform the natives of the white men's arrival. The native camp consisted of approximately eighteen or twenty tents and around one hundred individuals.

The accountant and Harry were checking traps for foxes. Harry set a steel trap for catching foxes, which is larger than a rat-trap and has two springs. Harry placed the trap carefully below the level of the snow and covered it with a thin sheet of paper and snow. Bait was scattered around the trap to increase the chances of catching a fox. The accountant suggested making a snow trap for white foxes before the moon set. Harry and the accountant observed a pack of white foxes while walking on the river. The accountant expressed contempt for the white foxes, noting their curiosity and tameness.

Bryan caught six or seven trout, varying from two to four pounds in weight. Bryan attempted to catch a larger fish but fell into the water while pursuing it. The fish Bryan was trying to catch was large and strong, causing him to struggle. Bryan managed to drag the fish into shallow water before the line broke. Bryan physically subdued the fish by seizing it and choking it under its gill. The fish Bryan captured weighed about twenty pounds. Lake trout in North America can weigh up to sixty pounds.

Frederick Mason returned to Sandy Cove and stood alone amid the ruins of his former home. The settlement's residents were deeply sympathetic to Mr. Mason's grief, resulting in a profound silence in the area. Mr. Mason experienced a moment of prayer while reflecting on his loss and the suffering of others in the village. A cry of anguish from a nearby hut reminded Mr. Mason of the death and mourning present in Sandy Cove. Mr. Mason spent much of the night comforting the bereaved and wounded in the village. The widow's cottage provided shelter for Mr. Mason after his night of comforting others. Mr. Mason expressed concern for Tom Armstrong's recovery and the tragic fate of Simon's family.

Horses moved in different directions over the white plains while sleigh-bells sounded faintly. The stars twinkled over the silent dwelling of the old fur-trader after half an hour. Harry Somerville was assigned to an important post in Red River colony. Mr Conway planned to preach to Indian tribes beyond Athabasca and decided to start his journey on snowshoes. Jacques agreed to accompany Mr Conway as a guide and hunter, with Redfeather as interpreter. Charley Kennedy and Harry Somerville felt sadness at parting with Mr Conway and Jacques. Jacques expressed a wish for guidance and blessings for his friends before they parted ways.

Mr Mason expressed concern about the whereabouts of a pirate schooner. Henry was asked to take command of a small cutter borrowed by Mr Mason. Mr Mason intended to consult Henry about their future actions regarding the pirate situation. Bumpus was mentioned as potentially being a pirate due to his association with the crew of the _Foam_ and the _Avenger_. Bumpus was found asleep in a small closet off the kitchen. Henry recounted an incident involving Jo's dangerous fall over the north cliff into the sea. Mrs Stuart expressed surprise at the mention of Jo's flight over the north cliff.

The narrator was confronted by a group who threatened him if he did not show them the direction to his camp. The narrator led the group close to his camp while trying to signal his companions without alerting the group. A prairie wolf's appearance prompted the narrator to make a loud noise to attract his companions' attention. The narrator escaped from the group after tripping one of them and diving into a clump of wood. The group pursued the narrator with arrows and bullets as he ran towards his camp. The narrator's companions shot one of the pursuers, causing the group to retreat. The narrator and his companions engaged in a confrontation that resulted in multiple injuries to the pursuing group.

Jacques and Charley were paddling upstream when they encountered a strong current. Jacques observed that a man, referred to as Injin, was acting strangely on the shore. Jacques and Charley decided they could not paddle upstream any longer and needed to run the rapid. They approached a heavy tree lying across the stream, which posed a danger to their canoe. Redfeather emerged from the woods and managed to throw the tree into the river, which helped the canoe pass safely. Redfeather was pulled into the river after stumbling as he threw the tree. Charley expressed gratitude to Redfeather for saving their lives after the incident.

The characters Bumpus, Corrie, and Poopy are involved in a situation in a mountain gorge. Poopy attempts to communicate with Bumpus and Corrie by shouting loudly. Bumpus and Corrie initially flee in fear upon encountering Poopy. Corrie recognizes Poopy after she calls out his name. Bumpus expresses skepticism about the existence of ghosts and claims it is a scientific delusion. Poopy is identified as Alice's black maid who looks after her. Poopy shares information about the fugitives, but her communication is unclear due to her anxiety.

The hunter regulated his pace to avoid interfering with the operation of shooting a bear. The bear was shot through the heart by the hunter as it rose to grapple with him. Young Hamilton fell into the water while trying to catch the bear after it was shot. Hamilton emerged from the water unhurt and dragged the dead bear to the shore. The group left the bear carcass behind for the wolves as it was valueless. They resumed their journey after drying their clothes and paddled energetically in silence. The next morning, they crossed the lake in about two hours and noticed smoke above the trees.

Stanley is trying to persuade his men to go on an expedition to Ungava. Stanley has not yet been successful in convincing his men to join the expedition. Dick Prince has been off hunting for a week and is not expected back for three weeks. Mrs. Stanley expresses indignation about the men's reluctance to go. Edith, the daughter of Stanley and Mrs. Stanley, draws a portrait of a dog named Chimo. Edith is described as having deep-blue eyes, soft golden hair, and a fair rosy complexion. Stanley asks Edith if she would like to go to a northern country with high mountains and deep valleys.

The text discusses the concept of _terra incognita_ and its implications for exploration. Frank is fishing on a river and has selected a salmon-fly from his book. The river features a large rock and a pool surrounded by an overhanging wall. Frank catches a trout weighing one pound while fishing. Stanley comments on Frank's fishing technique with humor. Frank quickly makes another cast after releasing the trout. A salmon jumps out of the water after being hooked by Frank.

The way was solid ice, preventing access until a change of wind occurred. Massan and Prince carried one canoe, while Francois and Gaspard carried another. La Roche took charge of the provision-basket and cooking utensils. Chimo supervised the proceedings while others searched for a suitable camping spot. Frank Morton found an elevated plot of gravel surrounded by willows for their encampment. Mr Stanley used flint and steel to strike a light for the campfire. The party used necessary articles for their meal, including a tea-pot, tin pannikins, and a large towel as a tablecloth.

Gascoyne is bound with ropes by the boatswain, Dick. Dick uses a hammer and chisel to remove Gascoyne's manacles. Dick intends to cover Gascoyne's mouth with a napkin to prevent him from alerting others. Gascoyne expresses anger at being bound before being informed of his situation. Dick offers to not gag Gascoyne if he promises to cooperate and not shout. Gascoyne reluctantly agrees to promise not to shout. Gascoyne resigns himself to his fate and tells Dick to proceed with his duty.

Henry expressed regret for his hasty actions regarding Gascoyne. Mr Mason suggested locking up Bumpus for safety while they are away. Gascoyne entered the room unexpectedly and locked the door behind him. Gascoyne confessed to being Durward the pirate during the meeting. Gascoyne admitted to deceiving Mary about his true identity. Mr Mason confronted Gascoyne about the severity of his actions as a pirate. Gascoyne denied being a murderer despite his confession.

A deer was shot and fell dead on the sand at the edge of the willows. Massan reloaded his gun after shooting the deer and spoke to his comrade Bryan. Bryan criticized Massan for shooting the deer before it had a chance to escape. Frank pointed out another deer that was out of reach, but Massan did not move. Dick Prince attempted to shoot the deer but missed, which surprised his comrades. Maximus returned from a journey to the Indian camp and assisted with skinning the deer. The deer meat was preserved for winter, with some dried and made into pemmican.

Grampus was described as being very imaginative and frightened of ghosts. John Bumpus believed in ghosts but would not admit it, experiencing an internal struggle between courage and fear. Corrie suggested taking a longer route over the hills to avoid danger. Jo denied the existence of ghosts, claiming they were scientific delusions. Poopy's cries contributed to the fear of Bumpus and Corrie as they encountered her in the dark. Bumpus and Corrie fled in terror when they saw Poopy, who appeared ghostly due to her dark body and white garments. Poopy attempted to chase after Bumpus and Corrie but struggled to keep up with their speed.

Mrs. Stanley expressed surprise that Frank was appointed to find their child. Frank stated that he did not find the child and credited Dick Prince and Gaspard for their efforts. Stanley inquired about the non-arrival of Maximus, who had been left at Moose Fort with his bride. Frank confirmed that Maximus and his wife started their return voyage to Ungava in a small canoe. Stanley expressed concern that something may have happened to Maximus. Massan asked Stanley about the placement of heavy goods. Frank and Stanley, along with Mrs. Stanley and Edith, gathered by the fireplace to discuss Frank's journey.

Toozle attempted to lick Alice's face, which she declined, leading him to lick her hand instead. Toozle, despite being a mature dog, continued to ignore Alice's objections to face licking. Toozle had previously believed that Alice was his mother during his infancy. Kekupoopi, a dark-skinned girl, arrived on the scene after being separated from her young mistress. Toozle expressed joy upon seeing Kekupoopi and attempted to lick her face, which she welcomed. Jo Bumpus wandered up the mountain-side to reflect on his concerns for his former captain. Will Corrie sought out Dick Price the boatswain to discuss his worries about Gascoyne.

Hugh Mathison is described as a rough and lazy servant. Baptiste and Hugh engage in a physical altercation after a confrontation. Mactavish intervenes to stop the fight and expels Hugh from the store. Baptiste vows to take revenge on Hugh after leaving the store. Baptiste prepares for a fight outside the fort after encountering Hugh. Different cultures have varying rules and customs regarding fighting. Baptiste and Hugh struggle together on the ground during their fight.

Gascoyne, the Sandal-Wood Trader is a story written by R.M. Ballantyne. The story is set in the Great Pacific. A little schooner is described as floating on the ocean. The schooner has a low black hull, taper masts, and white sails. The vessel is depicted as being in a state of inaction due to a dead calm. One of the crew members is described as a large, powerful man with red hair and a sun-burned face. The man is sleeping in a position that appears uncomfortable and may lead to choking.

Gascoyne was bound and freed by his son Henry, who cut the rope that restrained him. Mary Stuart expressed remorse to Gascoyne for her knowledge of the situation. Dick Price claimed he treated Gascoyne gently despite the circumstances. Jo Bumpus expressed relief at being able to breathe freely after Gascoyne's release. Gascoyne was uncertain about his duty now that he was free. Henry indicated that Gascoyne had no choice but to escape with them. Gascoyne and his companions discussed their future plans as they left Sandy Cove.

Mr. Stuart was a merchant who worked both as a businessman and a mechanic. He was known for his ability to manage his time effectively and work diligently. Mr. Stuart earned significant income from his business while also earning more than average wages as a working man. The ship _Avenger_ was erratic in her voyages and sailed to the principal islands of the South Seas. Henry, the captain of the _Avenger_, returned from a voyage with a wife and built a cottage for her. Mr. Corrie, the chief accountant in Mr. Stuart's counting-room, was known for his extensive letter writing. The merchant's business prospered significantly, leading to regular remittances of money sent to a firm in Liverpool from an unknown source.

An Indian sat apart from young men while smoking. A young man administered a long rebuke to the Indian. The Indian's expression changed from sullen to respectful as the young man continued to talk. The two friends experienced physical fatigue while traveling through snow and forest. They learned that blisters on their feet worsened during the healing process. Their conversation topics evolved from various subjects to nature observations as they became more accustomed to their journey. Harry Somerville and Hamilton arrived at Norway House and were to remain there indefinitely.

Travellers usually encamp for the night at sunset. The morning meal is preferred by the narrator over the evening meal. The narrator describes the morning as a time when spirits are freshest and highest. The two friends searched for game in the forest but were unsuccessful. Whisky-johns are small birds that appear larger due to their puffed feathers. Harry attempted to catch a whisky-john by hiding under a tarpaulin near a pemmican bag. Harry successfully captured a whisky-john but released it when it screamed loudly.

Surly Dick offered to show Lieutenant Mulroy how to steer for an island. Lieutenant Mulroy stated he would report Dick's assistance but would not plead for him. The ship _Talisman_ altered its course to 'north-half-east' based on Dick's directions. The lookout reported a boat on the lee bow while the _Talisman_ was tacking. Lieutenant Mulroy observed a raft with a flag and suspected a man was lying on it. Henry Stuart was on the raft, appearing dead after suffering from hunger for three days. Henry Stuart fell into a troubled slumber while praying on the raft.

Charley rode a horse that had a high head and tail, and a high-stepping gait. Harry suggested they head straight for the horizon after galloping half a mile. Charley's horse began to show signs of obstinacy by halting and backing instead of following Harry. Charley used a whip on his horse after it backed into a snow-drift. The horse sprang from the snow-drift with great speed, leaving Charley excited. The hunters were riding out on the snowy landscape in search of a wolf. The scene was characterized by a vast sheet of white snow and a blue sky, with patches of willows.

The calm that follows a storm is considered beautiful and agreeable to humans. The morning after the storm revealed a calm and beautiful scene, symbolizing tranquility. Edith expressed her joy upon seeing the calm sea after the storm. The island where the travelers were stranded was a small sand knoll with no vegetation. The sea around the island was smooth and clear, with waves rolling towards the sand-bank. A large iceberg had grounded near the northern end of the sand-bank, leaving pinnacles stranded on the beach. Mr. Stanley, Dick Prince, and Massan held a council to discuss their situation after the storm.

Francois and Massan discuss the absence of a third individual who is away on a hunt for three weeks. Mr. Stanley arrives at the wharf in a canoe and instructs two men to lift the canoe and take geese to the kitchen. Mr. Stanley expects the men to be ready with an answer regarding a pending expedition to Ungava in an hour. Some men express their reluctance to comply with Mr. Stanley's expectations regarding the expedition. Mr. Stanley enters his apartment and interacts with his wife, Jessie, who is working with her needle. Jessie was educated by her parents in the fur countries due to the lack of schools and books. Jessie becomes Mrs. Stanley and is the mother of a little girl, while her husband appears to be worried about something.

Gaspard received a rap on the leg from one of the poles. Bryan pushed Gaspard aside and went back to the canoe for another load. Stanley pitched a tent on the scrimp herbage and noted a spring of pure water nearby. Frank Morton and Stanley discussed the possibility of the location being suitable for temporary headquarters. Chimo brought a ptarmigan into camp, which was taken from him and cooked. The next day, the travelers left their cargoes behind and paddled away for investigation. Stanley planned to take a large canoe to examine the coast while Frank would take another canoe to explore the opposite side of the river.

Gascoyne and Montague left the ship and rowed away in a boat. Surly Dick remained on the ship, cheering and attempting to extinguish a fire. The ship was eventually lost to the flames and sank after a powder-magazine explosion. The Pacific Ocean is described as not always calm or stormy. The crew of the man-of-war was affected by the loss of their ship and displayed a somber demeanor. Gascoyne expressed a commitment to surrender to justice, while Henry suggested he should escape. Gascoyne believed he had forfeited his life and liberty to his country.

The crowd had largely forgotten the original purpose of their assembly and was engaged in a dispute. Dan stated that the post-mark of San Francisco on the back of a letter indicated it was not a forgery. Burke questioned the significance of post-marks, suggesting they could be forged. Dan argued that the specific ink used for post-marks is not commercially available, supporting his claim. Dan posed several questions to Burke regarding the timing and necessity of the alleged forgery. The crowd reacted positively to Dan's arguments, leading to cheers for John Bumpus. Jo Bumpus was eventually freed by Dan and later received a warm welcome from Mrs. Stuart.

Mr. Seaforth was treated for a severe medical condition after mistakenly taking medicine. The doctor cured Mr. Seaforth with difficulty, using an emetic and mustard blisters. Mr. Seaforth was transported in a cart over ploughed fields for treatment. The text references a significant flood that affected the settlement before the narrator and Charley were born. During the flood, Mr. Seaforth actively secured his property, starting with his boat and canoes. The flood caused many animals to be stranded around Mr. Seaforth's house, making movement difficult. Mr. Seaforth's valuables were loaded onto a boat just before the floodwaters rose rapidly.

Peetoot laughed and yelled until tears ran down his cheeks and rubbed noses with Chimo. Stanley held a levee that lasted most of the evening. A ball was organized in the men's house to honor the return of the giant with Aneetka. Aneetka wore the graceful costume of Indian women, while Maximus wore the capote and leggings of the voyageur. Bryan performed music and conversed in the Esquimau language during the festivities. Mirth and hope prevailed at Fort Chimo after the dangers of the first year had passed. Fort Chimo is no longer standing, with only a green patch of herbage remaining to mark its location.

Mr Kennedy, senior, discussed plans for the week with his son Charley during breakfast. Charley expressed a desire to spend the first day at home with his father and sister Kate. Mr Kennedy, senior, initially opposed Charley's suggestion and insisted on his own plans. Charley mentioned that Jacques intended to visit old friends in the settlement. Kate expressed enthusiasm about being introduced to Jacques, who is described as a bold hunter. Mr Kennedy, senior, decided not to join the ride due to his physical condition. Four horses were prepared for riding, three belonging to Mr Kennedy and one borrowed for Jacques.

The window-panes were coated with ice an inch thick. Old Robin drove his ox-cart to the river to fetch water. Winter continued to reign at York Fort for three months. A bright sun shone in the blue heavens but provided no heat. A group of men and four dogs were assembled on the frozen river. Mr Rogan advised the Indian driver to treat the dogs well. Harry Somerville and young Hamilton were wrapped up carefully.

Gascoyne and Henry leapt over fences and a rivulet while chasing each other. Gascoyne was faster than Henry during the chase up the mountain. Gascoyne shouted a farewell to Henry before disappearing over a ridge. Henry attempted to track Gascoyne but gave up after realizing it was futile. Henry returned to the cottage feeling disappointed after the chase. Henry expressed frustration at being outperformed by Gascoyne in running and wrestling. The widow Stuart observed Henry's disappointment and attempted to comfort him.

Mr. Kennedy was appointed to a remote location near the North Pole. Mr. Kennedy expressed strong dissatisfaction with the appointment in front of his family. Mr. Kennedy wrote a resignation letter to the Governor and Council of Rupert's Land. The council accepted Mr. Kennedy's resignation and appointed a successor. Mr. Kennedy moved his family to Red River Settlement in a bark canoe. Mr. Kennedy purchased a house with six acres of land and planted vegetables. Mr. Kennedy's children, Charles and Kate, attended a local academy and made rapid progress.

Montague heard a distant gun and expressed surprise to his companion. The commander of the _Talisman_ is expected to recognize the sound of his own guns. Gascoyne ordered his men to come aft for inspection. Montague selected surly Dick and John Bumpus to accompany him in the boat. Surly Dick initially showed triumph but then appeared dismayed when ordered into the boat. Surly Dick claimed that the schooner they left was a pirate. Bumpus defended Gascoyne and dismissed Dick's claim as an attempt to cause trouble.

Edith seated herself on a deerskin robe on a sledge with Annatock and Peetoot. The sledge was larger than the sled made for Edith at Fort Chimo and could hold eight or ten persons. The sledge's runners were shod with frozen mud and were constructed with lines of raw hide. Each dog was fastened by a separate line to the sledge, with the best dog in the center. Annatock used a whip with a handle of eighteen or twenty inches and a lash over six yards long. The team of dogs ran swiftly over the ice, pulling the sledge while Annatock drove them with his whip. They arrived at a location where several Esquimaux were searching for seal-holes.

Edith reported to her mother that the Esquimaux were dead on the sand and that the rest were gone. Frank and Stanley went to the camp and found eight dead people lying exposed on the rocks. Two additional deceased individuals had been buried under a heap of stones at the camp. Frank mentioned that the Esquimaux have a superstitious dread of the river, which they believe causes disease. The Esquimaux considered leaving the area for the winter to fish at the mouth of False River. Frank noted that Moravian missionaries had previously considered establishing a trading-fort at the river's mouth but abandoned the idea. Frank and Stanley discussed the role of missionaries in trading and their lack of religious outreach among the Indigenous people.

Jacques was not on the first trip of discovery along the shores of the Polar Sea but was sent in winter with provisions. Jacques found the explorers in poor condition, eating old parchment skins. Jacques and his comrade, Nipitabo, faced starvation on their return journey to the fort. Jacques and Nipitabo resorted to eating deerskin moccasins and later tough leather breeches to survive. Charley and Jacques encountered numerous fallen trees blocking the river during their journey. They spent three hours cutting through the trees and advanced only three miles.
