The Atlantic storm is causing a ground-swell that can be heard two miles inland. Amyas is in Smerwick bay, encouraging his crew despite the rough conditions. A thick gray cloud covers the area, obscuring the Kerry mountains and darkening the landscape. The Spanish fort, named Fort Del Oro, is occupied by eight hundred soldiers. Amyas and his crew have recently transported artillery to a battery near the fort.

Theon brought out old wine and proposed a toast to the Emperor of Africa. Hypatia sat in her chamber, feeling troubled and overwhelmed with thoughts. Hypatia believed that her political and active career was over. Hypatia felt a sense of despair about the state of the world and the gods. Hypatia questioned the existence and relevance of the gods in her life. Hypatia contemplated the nature of fate and the universe. Hypatia sought a truth and virtue that she believed were absolute and unchanging.

The incantation was completed as a woman looked into a mirror. Four men arrived, two on horses and two helping with a boat. Lucy Passmore confronted the men, accusing them of stealing a boat. One man shouted that a mermaid was in the boat. Lucy Passmore's husband expressed concern for her safety. Lucy refused to allow the men to take the boat without payment. The men eventually paid Lucy ten nobles to take the boat.

The old hermit invited Amyas, Cary, and Brimblecombe to his cavern for an evening. Brimblecombe expressed that the Indians were no worse than the Europeans. The old hermit had been starving himself to feed the children. The old hermit wished to share a painful tale with his guests. He claimed to be a former cavalier who participated in the conquest of Peru. The old hermit is eighty years old and was twenty when he sailed with Pizarro. The guests were surprised and interested in the hermit's story.

The characters are observing a situation referred to as the little Exodus. Miriam expresses regret about their ancestors' disobedience to the prophet Jeremiah. A girl is attacked by a man who is trying to steal her jewelry. A priest intervenes and is followed by a young monk who physically subdues the attacker. The monk destroys the stolen necklace and expresses disdain for material wealth. Raphael plans to leave for Alexandria and encourages Miriam to take her jewels. Miriam insists on her independence and rejects being called someone's daughter.

Indians carry it to save the women. The group must pass through Spanish settlements, including the town of Saint Martha. Cary reports that thirteen bodies are on the road and about ten more are above. A dozen volunteers step forward to retrieve the weapons and clothes of the fallen Spaniards. Ayacanora arrives with a blow-gun and bow, expressing joy upon seeing Amyas. After retrieving the weapons and armor, the group continues their journey toward the Magdalena. The slaves follow the English without gratitude, occasionally asking for coca.

The text references the private life of the fifth century and mentions Synesius and Isidore, the Abbot of Pelusium. The author acknowledges the possibility of anachronisms and errors in their work. The author expresses a desire to accurately depict the age, its manners, and its literature. The narrative begins in the year 413 of the Christian Era, with the young monk Philammon sitting on cliffs above Alexandria. Philammon is described as wearing a ragged sheep-skin and having long black hair, indicative of his youth and health. Philammon is searching for fuel for the monastery at Abbot Pambo's Laura in Scetis. Philammon discovers a temple carved in the sandstone cliff and is tempted to gather fuel despite the abbot's prohibition.

The conversation takes place between Amyas and Mr. Salterne. Mr. Salterne expresses a desire to feed a crew of fighters. Amyas suggests that one sword is sufficient if used quickly. Mr. Salterne offers a supper of a capon and partridges to Amyas. Mr. Salterne admits to having tried the crooked road in life. Mr. Salterne invites Amyas to see a room that has not been opened since a woman left. The room is described as neat, with items indicating it belonged to a woman.

The narrator was involved in a battle where he was stunned and fell to the ground. After regaining consciousness, he found that his lance was broken but still embedded in his opponent's brain. Upon crawling to his opponent, he discovered that the dead man was his brother. The narrator expressed a desire to escape the shame associated with being a Spaniard and a Christian. He has lived in solitude beneath a rock and tree for forty-four years, only leaving once to obtain seeds from Indians. John Brimblecombe, an English priest, offered counsel to the old man, emphasizing the importance of repentance. The old man struggled with self-forgiveness despite believing in God's mercy and forgiveness.

Tom Nash criticized another individual known as the maligner. Sir Piercie is described as belonging to a time after the reign of Elizabeth I. The character Amyas could not set sail due to strong winds. Amyas prepared the ship 'Mary Grenville' for departure when conditions improved. Will Cary led a procession of horsemen in Bideford, dressed in armor. Master Frank, who was wounded, chose to stay at the Ship Tavern instead of returning home. Amyas and Frank devised a plan to invite their old schoolmates to a supper at the Ship Tavern.

Bran instructs the slaves to steal what they can and escape through the back gate. A mob of monks, costermongers, dock-workers, fishwives, and beggars enters the building. Philammon, a young monk, is at the head of the mob. A speaker threatens the mob with a poisoned dagger and a dog that will not release its grip. The speaker exchanges his fine clothing for a ragged tunic and straw hat from a member of the mob. Philammon observes the mob destroying art and expresses regret over the destruction. The speaker comments on the mob's actions and their implications for Philammon's future.

Philammon spent a week in despair, neglecting food and remaining in a state of exhaustion. A gaoler informed Philammon that all prisoners were being granted freedom that day. Philammon expressed concern about his sister, Pelagia, and her performance. Philammon rushed out of prison and made his way to the theatre among other freed prisoners. Hypatia was present at the theatre, sitting near Orestes, and appeared haggard and constrained. The theatre performance depicted Libyan prisoners taken in arms against the Roman senate and people.

Raphael left Alexandria for Berenice with Eudaimon and his wife. Twenty years after Raphael's departure, Theodoret wrote about Cyril's death. Theodoret expressed that Cyril's death brought joy to some and grief to others. Cyril's legacy in history is noted as well-known, but his spiritual fate is not discussed. The Church of Alexandria became increasingly lawless and inhuman over the years. Hypatia's murder was a significant blow to philosophy in Alexandria. After Hypatia's death, philosophers were largely absent from historical records, except in Athens.

Amyas sings a Christmas carol about the birth of Christ. Raleigh comments on the simplicity of Amyas's song compared to more complex poetry. Spenser reflects on his own feelings of despair while listening to Amyas. Raleigh suggests that Amyas deserves a place in Spenser's 'Faerie Queene.' Amyas expresses a desire to write poetry about his experiences in the Spice Islands. Spenser argues that Fairyland exists wherever there is love and loyalty. Raleigh and Spenser engage in a discussion about ambition and self-perception.

The speaker describes a history of being reviled and persecuted. The speaker claims to have lived a life of wretchedness and unclean living. Sir Richard questions the speaker's tendency to compare himself to others. Yeo defends Mr. Oxenham, describing him as a noble and valiant gentleman. Yeo recounts a voyage to Nombre de Dios in 1572 with Mr. Drake and Mr. Oxenham. Yeo mentions a covenant made between Mr. Oxenham and Mr. Drake to sail the South Seas. Yeo expresses regret over the fate of the seventy men who sailed with Mr. Oxenham.

The scene begins with a foggy morning and a character singing a wild melody. The song describes an elk looking out from the pine forest, heavy with snow. Wulf expresses excitement and performs a dramatic act related to hunting. Philammon is shocked by Wulf's sudden outburst of passion and emotion. A group of revelers, including Orestes and Pelagia, emerges from the women's court. Philammon seeks to escape the revelers and receives a kind farewell from an old man. Later, Wulf and Smid discuss the sleeping revelers and share wine in the night air.

Cary joined a group discussing a woman named Ayacanora. Ayacanora described monkeys with human-like faces and tails. Yeo asked Ayacanora if she remembered any white people. Ayacanora expressed disgust at the mention of black monkeys. Ayacanora referred to a 'devil' that resembled a monkey with a gray beard. Yeo recognized Ayacanora and expressed joy at finding her. The crew reacted with confusion to Yeo's emotional response.

The speaker reflects on the distractions of life in Scetis and acknowledges that each person has a unique vocation. The speaker admits to being preoccupied with the actions and fates of others despite being in a secluded environment. The speaker questions whether an anchorite experiences fewer distractions than himself. The speaker describes the struggles of individuals who change their surroundings but not their inner turmoil. The speaker recounts the fate of a monk who, despite his ascetic practices, succumbed to pride and returned to a life of excess. The speaker expresses a growing obsession with the world he left behind, despite knowing it brings him no joy. The speaker feels a conflict between his desire to flee worldly temptations and the pull of his past life.

Seven swords adorned the Spanish stern, which was destroyed. The golden flag of Spain was trailing in the water. The ship's tiller was shot away and the helmsman was killed. The English ship moved two miles to windward before the armada could recover. The galleys had approximately forty oars each and were armed with cannons. The galleys contained slaves, with multiple individuals assigned to each oar. Amyas ordered the ship to wait for the galleys to approach before engaging.

Heraclian is preparing to rebel and has fitted out an armament for Ostia. Heraclian has stopped his own wheat-ships and intends to write to Orestes to stop his as well. Orestes is concerned about the possibility of being trapped by the information provided by the Jew. The Jew's source of information about Heraclian was a negotiation for a loan from the Rabbis at Carthage. Orestes is contemplating the wages that Count Stilicho desires for his services. Count Stilicho is said to have a force of forty thousand men, including Donatist supporters. Orestes considers that a hundred thousand men might be necessary to counter Count Stilicho.

Eustace is concerned about the fate of the Senora de Soto, who is currently with the notary. A man's voice is heard discussing witchcraft accusations against a woman. The woman expresses indignation and agony in response to the witchcraft charge. Eustace hears a wail from the woman, which deeply affects him. Eustace feels responsible for the woman's suffering and questions his own actions. Eustace acknowledges the merciful disposition of the Holy Office. Eustace decides to approach the principal of the Jesuits to continue his novitiate.

A fight occurred involving a group of ruffians and Yeo. Yeo wounded one of the ruffians, who was described as nearly as big as Amyas. Another ruffian was found dead in the straw. Yeo believed Eustace intended to steal horses and took refuge in the stable. Yeo engaged in a scuffle with two men who attempted to loose the horses. Mr. Evan Morgans, also known as Father Parsons, was found in a disheveled state. Eustace Leigh was present with Mr. Parsons when they were captured.

Orestes is frustrated with the situation regarding provisions in the empire. The secretary informs Orestes that many provisions have been unloaded due to recent largesses. The Jews have been buying and exporting provisions, which Orestes believes indicates they knew of Heraclian's failure. Orestes expresses anger towards Miriam, believing she betrayed him knowingly. The secretary warns Orestes that harming one Jew could provoke retaliation from the entire Jewish community. The secretary claims that the bonds are not in Miriam's possession and may be held by creditors in other cities. Orestes decides to concentrate the stationaries around his palace for protection and to potentially incite a riot.

Jeronimo Ortal found convents of the Sun fifty years prior to the events described. Amyas needed a crew of Indians for Cary's expedition. Ayacanora consulted the Piache and assembled the tribe to provide young men for the expedition. The Piache believed that the Good Spirit was lazy and the little bad spirit was more useful. The Piache planned to kill Jack with a poisoned arrow due to his preaching. The Piache possessed a holy trumpet that was essential for the fertility of palm-trees. The Piache announced his departure to a neighboring tribe, causing distress among the villagers.

Brimblecombe and Yeo announced that the quarter-deck was won. Amyas confronted the commander, who refused to yield. Amyas and the commander engaged in a fierce duel. Ayacanora intervened during the fight and killed the sea-captain. The Spaniards surrendered after their commanders fell. Amyas ordered the crew to retrieve the Santa Fe gold. Out of forty-four crew members, six were seriously wounded and none were killed.

The pious mourner expressed a desire to depend wholly on her majesty and requested two yeoman prickers and a couple of grooms of the deer. The Spaniard was relieved by Mary's death as it removed the fear of having to crown her instead of himself. Elizabeth began negotiations in response to the impending Armada. F. Drake wrote a letter to Captain Amyas Leigh discussing strategies for facing an enemy. Drake planned to attack the Spanish fleet and requested Leigh to bring a good ship to Plymouth. Amyas Leigh expressed his inability to join Drake due to his mother's restrictions but requested information about Don Guzman Maria Magdalena Sotomayor de Soto. Drake returned from a successful mission, having destroyed a hundred sail in Cadiz and taken three galleons.

The narrator was taken down the river with others after being captured. The old Don took a little maid with him in one boat, while Mr. Oxenham and Don Diego de Trees were in another boat. The narrator learned from Spaniards that they were to be taken to Lima for the Viceroy. The narrator escaped into the forest and reached an Indian town where he was treated well. The narrator married an Indian woman and had a child, forgetting his previous life. Armed men attacked the town, killing many, including the narrator's wife. The narrator was captured along with other townspeople and chained together.

Amyas and Will traveled in silence for many miles. Will decided to accompany Amyas to Ireland. Amyas expressed contentment that one of his rivals would be away from the Rose garden. They rode over Bursdon when Amyas thought he heard a horse's step. Bursdon and Welsford were described as a rolling range of dreary moors. Amyas speculated that Eustace's party might take a shortcut across Welsford. An unknown horseman was seen dismounting and leading his horse over a gap.

Hypatia is depicted as having forgotten what righteousness is like and is afraid of discovering it. The man in the text experiences a transformation that softens his features and changes his demeanor. Hypatia reflects on the changes in the man, who is identified as a former mocker and a powerful figure. Hypatia questions whether the man has found a God in the crucified figure he refers to. The text references Glaucon's definition of the perfectly righteous man and discusses the implications of being perceived as unrighteous. Hypatia expresses discomfort at the idea of a crucified God, while the man argues about the righteousness of individuals. The conversation between Hypatia and the man touches on philosophical concepts from Plato and the nature of righteousness.

The universe is described as mysterious and influenced by affinities and repulsions. Philosophers' mechanical explanations do not address the fundamental 'Why?' of natural phenomena. The text suggests that emotions and sensations may be present in all things, not just humans. It posits that if a universal spirit connects all entities, then magic is probable. The author questions the nature of the soul and its relationship with the body and matter. The text implies that methods and ceremonies of magic have been tested throughout history. Philammon experiences a revival of feelings towards Hypatia despite his internal struggles.

The text describes a man who was unable to play a winning game in a world he desired. He met Miss Foljambe, a young woman from Derbyshire, who was also disillusioned with the world. The couple received permission from Queen Elizabeth to leave Whitehall and settle in Burrough. Mrs. Leigh, a noble English churchwoman, had a melancholic past related to her Protestant upbringing. She recalled the execution of Joan Waste and Joyce Lewis, which haunted her dreams. Mrs. Leigh had to hide during the reign of Queen Mary due to her Protestant beliefs. After becoming a widow, she remained attractive and was known for her calm demeanor.

The characters use bamboos rigged with cross-pieces and hooks instead of ladders. The commandant expresses admiration for the ingenuity and valor of the English captain. Evans reports that the Don has been murdered and an Indian girl has fled. An elderly Englishwoman is brought into the cabin, dressed in the yellow 'San Benito' of the Inquisition. The woman shows scars on her arm and appears terrified and suspicious. The bishop reacts with horror upon seeing the woman and refers to her as 'Malefica.' The woman expresses fear of a monk present and believes she is in another trap.

Hypatia expresses reluctance to participate in a spectacle involving a dance of Venus Anadyomene. The speaker suggests that the spectacle would not corrupt morality, despite Hypatia's concerns. The speaker believes that Hypatia's presence would enhance the success of the event. The speaker sketches groupings for the performance, highlighting the beauty of the proposed scenes. Hypatia acknowledges the beauty of the sketches but remains concerned about the event's implications. The speaker plans to exhibit the performance in the Theatre, despite potential objections. Hypatia raises concerns about the appropriateness of using Dionusos's altar for the spectacle.

The narrator expresses a strong desire to find a young woman, feeling tormented by dreams of her. The narrator feels burdened by an oath related to the young woman and seeks assistance in keeping it. A character named Yeo is eager to accompany Amyas to Ireland and offers his skills as a gunner or pilot. Amyas receives dispatches and prepares for his journey home, instructing Yeo to take the short way over the moors. An old butler named Anthony warns Amyas about traveling alone with Yeo, suggesting he is not safe company. Anthony describes Yeo's strange behavior and warns of supernatural dangers associated with him. Despite Anthony's warnings, Amyas finds Yeo's conversation engaging and continues on their journey.

The Plebiscitum against the Jews was carried into effect under the auspices of a holy tribune of the people. Hypatia expressed concern for Aben-Ezra's safety and offered to help him find concealment. Aben-Ezra offered Hypatia an opal ring as a token of gratitude. Hypatia refused to accept the ring from Aben-Ezra. Aben-Ezra suggested selling the ring to escape to Synesius for shelter. Aben-Ezra attempted to throw the opal ring into the street to attract attention. Miriam intervened and snatched the ring from Aben-Ezra's hand.

The group has been idle for three days without accomplishing anything. Amyas suggests trying again to reach the mountains east of the Orinoco. The group previously failed to reach the mountains and lost five men in the process. Jack expresses fear of the Amazons, believing they are unnatural and dangerous. Yeo states that the group has lost half their company and spent their ammunition. Cortez and Pizarro achieved conquests through the use of firearms and horses. The group debates the effectiveness of their remaining men without ammunition.

The men of Devon followed their captain's lead and attacked the Spaniards. Five Spaniards were killed and a dozen more were wounded during the attack. The English had the advantage of the wall, which allowed them to defeat the Spaniards quickly. Only two Spaniards in full armor escaped without mortal wounds. Amyas and his men assisted Cary and his party during a sharp affray. The young girl mourned her father's death and ultimately jumped into the abyss with his body. Amyas emphasized the importance of not letting greed ruin their victory.

Philammon expresses that he does not hate the monastic tribe. Philammon is invited by a host to enjoy a meal after swimming in the sea. Philammon arrives at a lodging with a common staircase filled with children, cats, and chickens. A negress named Judith enters with dishes while the host demands breakfast. Philammon is surprised when Judith expresses her gratitude towards him for saving her from the Jews. The porter claims that Philammon is a good angel for helping Judith. The porter expresses a philosophical view on the connection between people.

A file of chained Indians is being driven forward by an officer using a manati-hide. An old gray-headed man and a slender girl are among the chained Indians. The officer encounters a tree blocking the path and orders the Indians to halt. The officer pricks the old man with his sword after he falls to the ground. The officer attempts to sever the chain binding the old man but instead cuts off his wrist. The girl leaps with the officer into the abyss below after he injures her companion. Amyas shoots the driver of the Indians with an arrow and rescues the girl.

Amyas expresses that he is not inclined to weeping or praying and prefers to focus on work. Salterne suggests that Amyas could kill a man and offers to finance a voyage to the Spanish Main for revenge. Amyas states that he currently possesses no worldly goods except for his clothes and sword. Salterne insists that he will spend his hoarded money for revenge on behalf of his child. Amyas refuses to act without his mother's permission, citing his obligation to obey her. Six weeks after a duel, Rose Salterne disappears, prompting a search involving local men and bloodhounds. The community speculates about Rose's disappearance, with differing opinions on whether she left willingly or met with misfortune.

Oxenham is recruiting men from Bideford and a few boys for a sailing expedition. Oxenham claims that sailing past Cape Finisterre is easy and offers a wager of twenty pounds. A man presents a white buffalo horn covered with etchings of land and sea to the group. The horn is said to have been obtained from a Portuguese man in the Azores. The horn displays various images including cities, harbors, and creatures, with notes indicating the presence of gold and silver. A school-boy expresses a desire to possess the horn and offers a tester in exchange. Oxenham refuses the boy's offer and suggests he fight for the horn instead.

Amyas and Salvation Yeo are involved in a military engagement. Salvation Yeo expresses frustration over missing his target multiple times. Yeo successfully shoots down the Spanish flag, causing a reaction from both sailors and soldiers. A tall officer from the opposing camp retrieves the fallen flag and raises it again. Amyas shows respect to the flag-holder by bowing, and the flag-holder returns the gesture. As night falls, the firing decreases and the soldiers prepare for rest. Two men enter the battery discussing English hexameters, reflecting on the state of poetry in 1580.

Amyas Leigh experiences a moment of frustration and sadness after losing an apple. Ayacanora comforts Amyas by retrieving the apple and expressing her desire to serve him. Ayacanora declares her commitment to Amyas, stating she will be his slave. Amyas reflects on his situation and expresses remorse for his feelings towards Ayacanora. Mrs. Leigh enters the scene, and a moment of connection occurs between her and Ayacanora. Amyas acknowledges the bond between him and Ayacanora, believing it to be divinely ordained. Ayacanora's singing ability returns, bringing joy to their home and symbolizing hope for the future.

The text discusses themes of beauty, faith, and personal circumstances in relation to a character's beliefs. The character reflects on the nature of a woman's Paganism and its impact on her morality. The character feels gratitude towards the woman for her kindness and support. There is an internal conflict regarding the character's ability to convert the woman to Christianity. The character contemplates the need for personal repentance before praying for others. The scene shifts to a meal where the character and others are joined by Miriam, who expresses dissatisfaction with their food. Miriam orders roast chicken and wine, attempting to uplift the mood of those present.

The text discusses interpretations of a book, likely the Song of Songs, and how various figures perceive its meaning. The bride's eyes are compared to the wisdom of the scribes, and her stature to a palm tree representing priests. The left hand under her head symbolizes the Tephilim worn by certain individuals, while the right hand represents the Mezuzah placed on doors. An academic Hebrew challenges the interpretations of the rabbis, suggesting they should focus on the plain words of the text. The narrative describes a vision where the academic argues that the book illustrates a transition from polygamy to monogamy. The rabbis react negatively to the academic's interpretations, perceiving them as blasphemous. The text concludes with a suggestion that the Catholic Church uses this book to support arguments for celibacy.

Cortez was compared to Captain Drake in terms of bravery and decision-making. Sir Humphrey Gilbert sailed on the small ship Squirrel to explore the southward coast. The Delight, the largest ship in the expedition, struck unknown shoals and lost most of its crew. The remaining crew, after suffering from hunger and cold, persuaded Sir Humphrey to return to England. During the return journey, the crew encountered a creature resembling a lion in the water. Sir Humphrey Gilbert was lost at sea when the Squirrel was swallowed by the ocean. Amyas Leigh recounted the events leading to Sir Humphrey's demise, which caused grief among his companions.

Earl Ordulf is mentioned in the text. Vindex Brimblecombe is described as an ancient schoolmaster. Brimblecombe is accompanied by five-and-forty boys. Young Will Cary is a character who interacts with Brimblecombe. Lady Bath is another character present in the scene. Brimblecombe recites a Latin epigram and a vernacular poem. A live shore-crab is found on Brimblecombe's neck during the event.

Evans informs Amyas that Frank was not present. Amyas orders the boat to return to shore, but the waves make it impossible. Simon Evans accuses Amyas of calling them cowards despite their efforts to save him. Tom Hart rescued Amyas from the water but was killed in the process. Amyas acknowledges the crew's duty and takes the oar from Evans. The crew is exhausted after reaching the ship and must lower another boat to assist them. Amyas expresses a desire for revenge against those responsible for Frank's fate.

Yeo remained with Amyas while Cary went elsewhere with Sir Warham St. Leger. Amyas's only companion was Don Guzman, who exhibited fits of deep melancholy and bursts of boastfulness. Don Guzman expressed feelings of misery and lamented the loss of his wealth and sword. He attributed his misfortune to a woman from Naples, claiming she took all his money. Don Guzman expressed a desire to find El Dorado and become Emperor of Manoa. He described a plan to confront a golden king with a crucifix and offer him baptism or death. Yeo expressed concern that Don Guzman was attempting to escape.

Wulf and Smid entered a crowd that reacted by yelling insults. Wulf and Smid used their swords against the crowd, resulting in casualties. Smid suggested taking a boat to confront the guards at the palace. Hypatia asked her father Theon about a letter he delivered to Philammon. Theon reported that Philammon tore the letter and left without responding. Hypatia expressed a willingness to return jewels rather than keep them as payment. Hypatia declared her intention to abandon politics and public speaking.

Cyril is described as a wise man who knows there is no use fighting those he cannot conquer. Cyril is able to obtain money from wealthy women for various charitable institutions. Philammon feels disillusioned by the reality of the Church compared to his idealistic beliefs. Philammon recalls warnings from Arsenius about the challenges he would face. Philammon believes that the Church cannot work freely while under the influence of worldly rulers. Hypatia is identified as a significant source of trouble for the Alexandrian Church. Philammon expresses a desire to emulate the martyrs and seeks an opportunity for self-sacrifice.

The characters received Holy Communion before preparing provisions and ammunition. Cary and Yeo informed Amyas that they had completed a task. The group set out on a journey upward and southward into an unfamiliar land. They encountered various natural features, including tree-ferns, bamboos, and club-moss. The men heard strange sounds, initially mistaking them for beasts but later identifying them as coming from an ape. A column of black smoke indicated a fire, which was later revealed to be from the ship Rose. Amyas decided to burn the ship, making retreat impossible and committing the group to their journey.

Will Parracombe was born several centuries before his time. Had Will Parracombe lived later, he might have published poetry or written plays. Will Parracombe was found drunk and threatening at the Mariners' Rest inn. An Egyptian rogue approached Will Parracombe and offered to tell his fortune. The Egyptian rogue gambled with Will Parracombe and asked about the voyage of the Rose. Amyas obtained a warrant against the landlady for harboring 'Egyptians'. The destination of the voyage was kept secret among the adventurers.

Cary expresses a desire to join Amyas in a venture to the Indies. Cary believes that if they do not find a specific person, they can still seek out the Plate-fleets. Cary's father is optimistic about having more heirs and is not concerned about Cary's risks. Cary has a negative opinion about his father's new wife, Mistress Abishag Jewell, and her claims to nobility. Amyas plans to go to London to discuss their plans with Frank and his mother. The other members of the Rose are currently occupied and cannot be involved in the new venture. Amyas departs for London the next morning, leaving Yeo with Cary.

The legends of gold in Manoa were similar to those seen in Peru and Mexico. The rocks of Guiana may contain precious metals like those in Peru and Mexico. The Carib tribes of the Orinoco reported tales of a gold-country similar to those that led Pizarro and Cortez to their discoveries. There was a belief that members of the Inca family and hidden Peruvian treasure still existed fifty years after the Spanish conquest. The existence of Amazons was supported by accounts from Spaniards and Indians who witnessed women fighting alongside men. A group of men swore an oath to search for the golden city of Manoa for two years, committing to mutual support and obedience. They planned to march south the following morning, trusting in God for guidance.

Jack read a letter and expressed disappointment about a gentleman's character. Cary insisted that Jack should not leave until Amyas returns. Jack agreed to stay for dinner at Cary's invitation. Jack planned to travel to London to speak to Mr. Frank after arranging for his church services. Cary provided Jack with a small loan for his journey. Jack returned to Clovelly Court after three weeks, feeling exhausted. Cary encountered Mr. Salterne and discussed the shipping trade.

Eustace Leigh greets his cousin Amyas with a mix of relief and anxiety. Eustace feels a sense of dread towards Amyas due to his physical strength. Eustace believes Amyas despises him and has always treated him as inferior. Eustace reflects on his own shortcomings and self-seeking behavior. Eustace attributes his struggles to his education by the Jesuits. Eustace expresses disappointment at missing Amyas's recent triumph. Eustace's family background is contrasted with that of his brothers, who are portrayed as true Englishmen.

The text discusses the actions and motivations of a character named Peter in the context of historical persecution. Peter experienced personal trauma, including witnessing his father become a cripple and his sister being killed. The character Cyril expresses his intention to excommunicate certain individuals from the Church for three years. Cyril believes that those he intends to excommunicate have already distanced themselves from the Church through their actions. The dialogue reflects a conflict between differing views on the nature of God's kingdom and the role of ecclesiastical authority. The text implies a critique of the Prefect's authority and questions his legitimacy as a minister of God. The conversation highlights tensions between secular and religious perspectives on justice and authority.

Pelagia felt terrified at the approach of a rugged figure. Wulf expressed admiration for Pelagia and wished her a worthy husband. The Goths unanimously considered Hypatia foolish for her actions. Pelagia was skilled in pantomime, dance, and music, catering to Alexandrian theatres. Pelagia developed a new affection for her Gothic lover, Wulf. An old monk cried upon seeing Pelagia and expressed sorrow for her fate. Pelagia questioned the monk about his tears and was confused by his comments.

The men were on a ship that was rolling in the sea with idle sails. Amyas expressed frustration about not having caught his prey after pursuing him for sixteen days. John Brimblecombe reacted with concern to Amyas's ominous words. Yeo suggested that he would be indifferent to the fate of their enemy, wishing for his safe return instead. The ship spotted another vessel after a cloud lifted, revealing a stream of sunshine on its masts. Cary questioned the tide and the ability to reach the other ship. Amyas displayed signs of distress and trembling when discussing the situation.

The English ships rescued those of London from the Spaniards. Cock, an Englishman, died honorably during the skirmish. The English ships were smaller but charged the Spanish fleet with agility. The battle was fierce, resulting in the capture of a Venetian ship and some smaller vessels. Lord Howard sent light craft to Portsmouth for ammunition. The fleets drifted helplessly with the tide due to calm winds. The fight became general with various English ships engaging the Spanish fleet.

Amyas Leigh and his brother Frank are pursued by a group of negroes. Amyas urges Frank to fight and they attempt to escape down a hill. The brothers face obstacles from prickly cactuses and stones thrown by their pursuers. They reach a pebble beach where they are attacked by the negroes. The governors' guard arrives and begins firing at the negroes to assist the brothers. Amyas is injured and falls into the water while trying to reach their boat. After the escape, Amyas discovers that Frank is missing and fears for his safety.

Pelagia and the Amal hired a splendid house in Alexandria. Pelagia has been living in the house for over three months. Pelagia is wealthy and has decorated the house to enhance its luxury. The Gothic guests of Pelagia freely allow her to dispose of their Roman spoils. The group in the house is unconcerned with the political turmoil outside. The inner court of the house features a fountain and tropical plants. The companions of the Amal include Goderic, Agilmund, and Smid.

Philammon expresses gladness to change the subject of conversation with Arsenius. Philammon mentions seeing Arsenius speak to Pelagia in the street. The little porter interrupts the conversation, stating that all Alexandria knows Pelagia. The porter claims that Miriam brought Pelagia from Athens to Alexandria. Arsenius questions Philammon about his relationship with Pelagia. The porter reveals that Pelagia has been a freedwoman for four years. Cyril has expelled all Jews from Alexandria four months ago.

Frank stood by, listening serious and silent while observing the surroundings. Frank felt a sense of awe and wonder as he watched the scenery around him. Yeo identified a cluster of tall peaks to the south as the mountains of Macanao. The group passed undiscovered the castle built by the Spaniards for pearl fishery protection. They encountered a caravel and three boats in a deep bight while sailing. Cary and Amyas led separate boats with a total of thirty-five men to explore the area. While navigating, they observed a school of sharks swimming below their boat.

Amyas and his crew have sailed four thousand miles to reach a low black cliff with a wall and a battery at either end. The area features narrow streets of white houses and is bordered by a mountain wall that casts deep shade. La Guayra is known for being one of the hottest places on Earth due to the radiation from heated rock. There is no harbor in La Guayra, only an open roadstead with five vessels at anchor. The crew observes two small merchant caravels and two long, low craft identified as galleys. A puff of white smoke from the eastern fort indicates that the fort is firing on the ship without warning. A large, low, white house on the mountain side is identified as the governor's house, indicated by the royal flag of Spain.

The speaker reflects on past glory and shame associated with violence. The speaker admits to participating in the murder of the Inca. Don Ferdinando de Soto is mentioned as having opposed the murder. The speaker confesses to enjoying acts of cruelty and violence. The speaker acknowledges a brother with whom he quarreled over a maiden. The speaker ultimately killed the maiden during the quarrel with his brother. The speaker expresses remorse for his actions and seeks to confess.

Lady Grenville is described as the beautiful St. Leger of Annery. Sir Richard and Amyas are engaged in a serious conversation about Amyas's future. Sir Richard expresses gratitude that Amyas has alleviated his concerns regarding his future. Sir Richard warns Amyas about the dangers of misusing love and the consequences it can have on a man's soul. Amyas is set to sail on the 'Mary' for Milford Haven with letters to Winter. Sir Richard advises Amyas that duty should take precedence over personal grievances. Sir Richard emphasizes the importance of hard work and the value of being faithful in one's responsibilities.

Miriam forced a ring onto Raphael Aben-Ezra's finger, claiming it would keep him safe. Miriam expressed a desire for Raphael to call her mother and mentioned her dislike for being called a witch or hag. Miriam indicated that she had given Raphael a dagger out of a violent impulse she felt towards him. Miriam claimed to have cast Raphael's nativity and warned him of a great danger and temptation he would face. Raphael felt bewildered by Miriam's affections and speculated about her intentions towards him. Philammon and the Goths entered the canal of Alexandria and observed the bustling activity of the seaport. The scene in Alexandria included a diverse crowd, various dialects, and large amounts of merchandise, particularly wheat.

Philammon encounters groups of negro slaves on the quay who are looking for purchasers. Philammon expresses a desire to escape from his companions, stating he is a monk. Wulf insists that Philammon should stay with him and offers to make him a warrior. Smid throws a hatchet at Philammon, which narrowly misses him. Wulf decides to let Philammon go after expressing disappointment in him. Philammon approaches Pelagia, who expresses interest in him and invites him to visit. Pelagia mentions living on a fashionable street, which Philammon does not recall.

Several sick men died, some from fever and others from being bled by the surgeon. Some of the sick men recovered with the help of herbs administered by Yeo. Provisions were plentiful due to daily trips to the ship and the capture of small animals. The crew collected fruit and vegetables, including mountain cabbage and fresh milk from the cow-tree. A careful watch was kept among the branches of a large ceiba-tree. The ceiba-tree had a trunk forty feet in girth and was over two hundred and fifty feet tall. Amyas spotted a large ship near the shore, which he believed was the same ship they had passed earlier.

Raphael expresses a negative opinion about lawyers, referring to them as rascals. The speaker expresses admiration for Hypatia, describing her as perfect and wise. Raphael has begun to doubt Hypatia's ability to make him a better man. The conversation includes a discussion about horses, specifically a colt bred from a Nisaean and a mare. The speaker mentions the need for a horse that can endure rough terrain and long distances. The speaker captures a jerboa for food, discussing the ethics of killing animals for sustenance. Raphael has developed a respect for dumb animals since his conversion by Bran, the dog.

Raphael's mother expresses pride in his qualities and lineage. Raphael confronts his mother about her possible involvement in a woman's death. Raphael's mother reveals that she stole a black agate talisman for him. Raphael believes that his mother has been misled about a figure referred to as The Man. Miriam, Raphael's mother, suffers a fatal injury and dies. The next morning, Raphael waits to speak with Cyril regarding murderers in sanctuary. A tribune informs Raphael that Orestes is demanding the surrender of the murderers.

The son of Troll is known for his exceptional cunning and various skills. He has knowledge of Latin and Greek, as well as reading and writing. Wulf the son of Ovida is mentioned as a competitor in the battle of mead-horns. Goderic and Wulf engaged in coursing and successfully hunted antelopes. The characters express disdain for the men they encounter in Alexandria. Agilmund recounts an encounter with a philosopher and a group of boys. Pelagia comments on the physical differences between herself and the men.

Philammon's companions discussed the triumph of the true faith and the overthrow of Paganism under patriarch Theophilus twenty years prior. Olympiodorus and his followers held the Serapeium against Christians, committing acts of violence against prisoners. Philammon expressed a desire to distinguish himself through a notable act of Christian bravery. Peter warned Philammon about the dangers of confronting Hypatia in her lecture-room. Cyril considered the need for martyrs and agreed to see Philammon after Peter reported his intentions. Cyril instructed Philammon to promise not to strike the first blow or engage in argument with Hypatia. Philammon was given money for his upcoming confrontation with Hypatia.

The protagonist experiences intense self-reproach despite knowing he is forgiven. He feels dread and despair upon realizing that God, whom he had defied, returned good for evil. The protagonist finds a sense of purpose and duty in his relationship with Victoria. He resolves to make amends for his sins through confession of the truth he has discovered. Miriam, the protagonist's mother, returns and expresses her joy at his arrival. Miriam reveals that the protagonist was adopted by Ezra, the merchant of Antioch, who craved for a child. Miriam offers the protagonist her keys and tells him that all her possessions are his.

Arsenius expresses concern about the dangers of solitude for a Christian man. Pambo argues that a man should not leave the community for solitude. Pambo prefers that wisdom be used for the good of the Church. Peter the Reader arrives with letters and messages from Cyril for Aufugus. Pambo acknowledges Peter's good reputation in the Church. Arsenius reads Cyril's epistle and reflects on current events. Arsenius expresses concern about the actions of Orestes and the influence of a heathen woman.

Hypatia and Orestes discuss the use of gladiators and wild beasts in entertainment. Orestes suggests that using prisoners for entertainment is a practical solution due to cost considerations. Hypatia expresses discomfort with the idea of using gladiators and prefers battles with wild beasts. Orestes mentions that there are fifty or sixty Libyan prisoners available for potential entertainment. Hypatia acknowledges that the lives of the Libyan prisoners are forfeit due to their status as rebels. Orestes recounts that his guards refused to fight the Libyan prisoners, asserting their dignity as men. Hypatia aspires to become the high-priestess of Athene and is bound to obey her tutor Julian's commands.

Amyas witnessed a violent confrontation involving a dagger and multiple blows. Amyas struck Eustace, who was revealed to be his cousin, with the hilt of his sword. Eustace was injured, with a broken jaw, and was compelled to surrender a packet of papers. Eustace swore that the papers he surrendered were all he possessed, but refused to name his accomplices. Amyas allowed Eustace to escape after he swore to the completeness of his papers. Frank fainted during the confrontation and was carried by Amyas to safety. The packet contained a letter informing of S. Josephus landing in Smerwick with Crusaders.

The porter expresses confidence in the immortal gods. Arsenius believes that an oath made to an idol is void only if the person considers it so. Arsenius requests the porter to convey a message to a woman in Alexandria. Arsenius identifies himself as the Father of the Emperors. Philammon does not remember his family from Athens. Arsenius mentions that Philammon had a sister who is three years older than him. Philammon expresses a strong desire to find his sister.

Hypatia contemplates whom to address in prayer and meditation, considering Athene as her chosen favorite. Hypatia feels conflicted about her submission to Orestes, whom she initially believed she could guide. Hypatia admires Orestes for his practical insight while simultaneously feeling disdain and mistrust towards him. Alexandrian politics continue with indifference towards the rulers of Rome and Byzantium, focusing instead on local issues. There are rumors of a general amnesty for prisoners, which satisfies various parties in Alexandria. Orestes's popularity grows as he provides largesses of corn, benefiting the local populace. The corpse of Ammonius, who was executed, goes missing, causing concern among Orestes's guards.

The eldest brother sent two young men to seek their master after three days of prayer and fasting. The two young men encountered a Moorish people who mentioned a priest had passed by them days before. The Moors described a woman who had arrived in the mountains twenty years prior, known for her beauty and rich garments. The woman embraced the eremitic life and became invisible to most, only appearing to a few women from the tribe. The two brethren found the body of Philammon the abbot and a beautiful woman in an open grave on the mountain. A bracelet of gold was found in the cave of the holy woman, which later proved to be a relic of sanctity. The bracelet was stolen by Vandalic barbarians but was later restored, leading to numerous miracles attributed to it.

The fleet must close around a galleon to prevent Drake and Hawkins from sinking it. The principal galleon of Seville, carrying Pedro de Valdez and other nobles, collides with another ship and loses its foremast. Despite the loss, the Spanish forces maintain faith in their patron saints. The English fleet suffers no casualties during the first day of battle. The battle diminishes the prestige of Spain in the eyes of the English. Amyas participates in the battle against a galleon named Sta. Catharina. The next morning, Amyas receives a letter from Drake regarding the encounter with Valdez' galleon.

The bishop rode with twenty armed retainers on horses that were underfed and trained for harsh conditions. They traveled through ruined villages and farms where inhabitants shared their misfortunes with the bishop. Inhabitants offered the bishop small remnants of food instead of asking for alms. The bishop, Synesius, expressed empathy for the suffering of the people but felt helpless to alleviate their misery. As they moved away from the war-torn areas, the bishop's mood improved and he engaged with his retainers about hunting. Raphael reflected on the history of the land and shared anecdotes about his experiences with the sea and food. They entered a breezy down area that was once fertile and suitable for farming, which Synesius identified as their hunting grounds.

Eustace Leigh is confronted by a horseman who is identified as Will Cary of Clovelly. Will Cary shouts for his companions to follow him in pursuit of a stag. Parsons expresses concern about the contents of his saddle-bags during the chase. Mr. Morgan Evans experiences despair and discomfort while riding. Richard Grenville, a knight, rides alongside Eustace Leigh and requests introductions to his guests. Eustace Leigh introduces Mr. Evan Morgans and Mr. Morgan Evans to Sir Richard Grenville. Sir Richard offers to have his groom assist Mr. Morgans and Mr. Evans with their saddle-bags.

Philammon observed a barge with a decorated awning and several pairs of black eyes looking at him. A hippopotamus attacked Philammon's canoe after he became distracted by the people on the barge. Philammon swam well and was not afraid of death, having contemplated it from childhood. Philammon freed himself from the harpoon line and attempted to stab the hippopotamus with a knife. The hippopotamus was ultimately killed by a harpoon from the barge after attacking Philammon. Philammon swam around his destroyed canoe, contemplating escape to the shore while considering dangers. Philammon was eventually rescued by the crew of the barge, who threw a noose over him.

Don Guzman was surrounded, disarmed, and carried into the village. Don Guzman expressed empathy for a prisoner who suffered captivity and loss of honor. The cacique ordered Don Sebastian to be bound to a tree and shot with arrows. Miranda pleaded for mercy for Don Sebastian before the cacique. The cacique agreed to spare Don Sebastian's life if Miranda consented to marry him. Miranda initially agreed to the marriage but later tried to retract her promise. Don Sebastian was stripped of his garments and forced to work under harsh conditions.

Jack was shot in the thigh during a confrontation with Spaniards, causing him to limp. Nearly forty armed men joined the fight against the Spaniards. The Spaniards retreated after encountering Jack and his group. Jack claimed to have killed nineteen enemies during the skirmish. Cary acknowledged Jack's bravery and apologized for previously mocking him. Jack attributed his courage to reading a passage from the Bible before the battle. Jack preached about his experience the following Sunday, and the congregation was pleased with his sermon.

The goodwife went down toward the boat with Rose behind her. The goodwife found the boat fastened and the oars aboard. Rose was instructed to dip her head three times in the sea and not to look to land or sea before saying the words. Rose stood between two walls of rock before entering the sea. The environment was described as silent with a faint bleat and wail from the cliffs. Rose performed a rite while holding a mirror and waded into the cold water. She pronounced an incantation while looking through her dripping locks at the magic mirror.

Cary and the Spaniard prepare for a duel with drawn rapiers and daggers. The duel begins with both combatants engaging in a series of attacks and defenses. Cary is injured when the Spaniard's rapier passes under his left arm. Sir Richard intervenes to stop the duel, stating that Don Guzman's honor is satisfied. Cary expresses a desire for revenge, but Sir Richard insists he must not provoke further conflict. Sir Richard attempts to speak to Don Guzman as a friend, warning him about the consequences of his actions. The conversation between Sir Richard and Don Guzman escalates, with both men asserting their positions.

The Prefect expresses a determination to fight alongside the Count for thirty years. Victorius and Victoria plead with the Prefect not to return to Carthage. Raphael suggests that the Prefect consult Augustine for advice. The Prefect considers the possibility of meeting Augustine before making a decision. The soldiers react positively to the announcement of a change in plans. The ship sets sail towards the western point of Sicily. Victoria expresses her desire for the Prefect to talk to Augustine.

Ayacanora experienced a significant emotional response while interacting with Amyas Leigh and Salvation Yeo. Amyas suggested that Ayacanora should attend to Lucy and continue their conversation the following day. Salvation Yeo expressed sadness over Ayacanora's connection to the young and his own emotional state. Ayacanora underwent a transformation, embracing her identity as an Englishwoman and displaying newfound self-restraint and softness. Amyas assigned Ayacanora a cabin and instructed the crew to treat her with respect as a lady and a Christian. Ayacanora attempted to imitate the formal behavior expected of her, despite feeling puzzled by Amyas's demeanor. The crew accepted Ayacanora's new status and adjusted their behavior, acknowledging her as a 'real born lady.'

Philammon approached the abbot while he was working on a palm-basket. The abbot questioned Philammon about the wood he found before the temple. Philammon did not enter the temple but looked at it. The abbot expressed concern about Philammon seeing women depicted in the temple. Philammon recalled a previous encounter with two beautiful creatures while launching a boat. Philammon expressed a desire to see the world and the great mother-church in Alexandria. Philammon argued that he could serve God better in the city than in the monastery.

The sailors drop back by twos and threes after a recall is sounded. The guns of Fort del Oro fire for half an hour without receiving a reply. The English maintain their victory after a sortie against the deputy's camp. Winter and the captains dry themselves around a peat-fire on the beach. Amyas Leigh brings a man in rich armor to the captains, who is later revealed to be alive. Admiral Winter reprimands Amyas for his lack of respect and failure to obey orders. Amyas defends his actions by stating he did not hear the recall and aimed to bring back useful information.

The number of floggings increased from about two a week to one per day. Amyas desired a sea-life and often drew ships and maps during school hours. On one occasion, Amyas drew a map featuring a castle, a dragon, and a ship. The other boys at Amyas's desk gathered to look at his drawing while Sir Vindex slept. Amyas ignored Sir Vindex's demand to show his work and continued drawing. Amyas struck Sir Vindex with a slate, causing him to fall to the floor. Amyas informed his mother about the incident, expressing uncertainty about his actions.

Mr. Oxenham went ashore with a lady and did not come forth for three days. The crew was dissatisfied with Mr. Oxenham due to a lack of pearls and the presence of Spaniards and negroes. Mr. Oxenham had made a bargain with the Cimaroons to give them all prisoners taken, except for gold. A Spanish prisoner pleaded with Mr. Oxenham not to be given to the Cimaroons, claiming they would roast him alive. Mr. Oxenham refused to hand over the prisoners to the Cimaroons, insisting they be returned to the ships. The Cimaroons left, vowing revenge after Mr. Oxenham's decision. Mr. Oxenham promised the crew 100 pezos of silver each to carry gold and silver over the mountains.

Peter expresses distrust towards someone due to indulgence towards the Donatists. Pambo suggests that indulgence to sinners is not the worst sin. Peter inquires about the response to be sent to the Holy Patriarch. The African bishops remain aloof despite attempts at unification. Philammon, their spiritual son, has abandoned his faith and fled with Hypatia. Pambo believes that Philammon must have been treated unjustly. Arsenius takes responsibility for sending Philammon into temptation.

Amyas plans to unload the Vengeance and prepare for sea as soon as he can fill his crew. Sir Richard summoned neighboring gentlemen to assist in the preparations for sea. Cary and Brimblecombe, along with thirty Clovelly men, joined the Vengeance without asking Amyas. Several families, including the Fortescues, Chichesters, and Stukelys, offered to furnish ships for the expedition. Merchantmen unloaded their Virginian goods to replace them with powder and shot. On June 21, the squadron sailed from Appledore pool under the command of Amyas. Ayacanora and Mrs. Leigh shared a moment of sorrow as the squadron departed.

Cary tells Amyas to face it full. Amyas expresses that he knows every detail of the surroundings despite being blind. Brimblecombe expresses concern that Amyas will take a fever if he sleeps in the sun. Amyas acknowledges his past wrongdoings and expresses a sense of relief. Amyas recounts a vision of the sea and various locations he has sailed by. Amyas describes seeing a galleon lying at the edge of the rocks. Cary and Jack observe that Amyas's eyes are clear and bright.

Peter became enraged and fell to the pavement while calling for help against Philammon. Philammon was accused of heresy and communion with heathens by Peter and the monks. Philammon claimed he was sent by the patriarch and demanded to leave safely. The crowd of monks attempted to attack Philammon, but some held back. Philammon expressed his intention to see Hypatia and convert her, believing he had the patriarch's permission. The archdeacon reported that they had been delayed by the tyrant and faced threats from lictors. Philammon was left alone in the street after the crowd returned to the patriarch.

Jack suggests that doing good is the best way to punish oneself for past wrongs. Amyas encourages the old man to help the Indians in New Granada as a way to find redemption. The old man expresses fear of facing the Indians due to his past actions. Jack believes the old man has the qualities of repentance, humility, and justice. The old man begins to interact with Indian children, indicating a change in his attitude. Amyas instructs the Indians to obey the hermit as their king to ensure their safety. The Indians respond to Amyas's instructions with melancholy acceptance.

The captain had sailed around the world and visited the country of headless men and flying dragons. Ayacanora admired the captain but received no acknowledgment from him as he was focused on his tasks. Mrs. Leigh and Ayacanora shared a moment of melancholy, with Ayacanora pretending to struggle with her reading. Mrs. Leigh attempted to teach Ayacanora the meaning of the word 'heroical'. Ayacanora expressed a desire to be an English girl, to which Mrs. Leigh confirmed her identity. Amyas entered the scene and discussed preparations for a journey, mentioning the need for hatchets. Ayacanora reacted emotionally to teasing from Amyas and destroyed a gift he offered her.

Brimblecombe accepted a sword from a Spanish officer but refused a gold chain, choosing to distribute it among his crew instead. Brimblecombe was described as a generous man who lived a life focused on duty and giving rather than receiving. He shared his wealth gained from wars with his sisters and the poor of his parish, living unmarried until his death. The narrative mentions a significant event at La Guayra, characterized by chaos and the firing of beacons to protect treasure. Amyas and his crew decided to leave the islands after an alarm was raised, heading southwest across a bay. Yeo and Drew were experienced mariners familiar with the coast, having previously traded there with Hawkins. The crew encountered rough seas and a strong eastward current while navigating near Cape Codera.

Ayacanora refused to wear Mexican feather-dresses, stating they were wild Indian things. The vicar took one of the mantles and converted it into an altar-cloth for communion at Northam. Ayacanora displayed a proud demeanor, which amused Amyas. Ayacanora snubbed the ladies of the neighborhood who came to visit, leading to few second visits. Ayacanora expressed a preference to remain with Mrs. Leigh rather than return to her previous life. Ayacanora showed familiarity with houses and livestock, indicating prior experience. Amyas bought Ayacanora a jennet, which she learned to ride quickly.

Philammon is guided through a city with a great Moon-gate into a main street. The city features a magnificent street crossed by another equally impressive street. At the end of the street, Philammon sees a vast semicircle of blue sea surrounded by palaces and towers. His guide points out various architectural wonders, questioning whether Christians built them. Philammon is astonished by the vastness and magnificence of the scene before him. The architecture includes styles from the Doric and Ionic to Roman and Egyptian influences. Philammon reflects on the greatness of the creators of the city's structures.

The narrator was held in barranco at Lima by the Holy Office. The narrator was warned that they could be taken next due to their conversations with a heretic. The narrator was left aboard the galley for a few months while fearing capture. A heretic who had been in contact with the narrator was burned along with five others before the narrator arrived in Lima. The narrator was sentenced to life in the galleys for suspected insincerity in their conversion. The narrator experienced a sense of assurance of salvation while facing their sentence. The narrator observed a well-armed caravel loading for sea from their barranco and considered escaping.

Amyas took charge of the poop, Cary of the forecastle, and Yeo, as gunner, of the main-deck. Drew, as master, settled himself in the waist of the ship. The English fleet faced and conquered Spanish armadas that were superior in size and number. Sir Richard Grenville's Revenge endured an attack from eight Spanish armadas for twelve hours before striking. Young Richard Hawkins's Dainty maintained a running fight with two larger Spanish ships for three days. Sir George Cary's ship, the Content, fought against four armadas and two galleys with limited crew and firepower. The English ships were shorter and more maneuverable than the Spanish ships, contributing to their naval success.

The Lady Hypatia gave a lecture on Helen's nepenthe. Philammon expressed interest in Hypatia's mention of him. Miriam confirmed that Hypatia spoke of a young Phoebus Apollo without naming him. The negress refused to drink due to a vow. Miriam suggested that wine could be both pleasurable and potentially harmful. The host was found sleeping with a smile, seemingly unaware of his surroundings. Miriam criticized the views of Christians and philosophers regarding manhood and the value of Jewish heritage.

The Jesuit went to the Holy Office and settled matters with the Inquisitors regarding Eustace's past services to the Church. Eustace Leigh left Cartagena for Nombre that night and sailed the following week. Eustace Leigh's fate after leaving is unknown; he may have become a General of his Order or returned to England. The narrative states that Eustace Leigh has become a tool of the Jesuit Society, losing his individuality and moral responsibility. Nearly three years passed since a group sought the Golden City, covering a vast area without success. The group searched along the Orinoco, Maypures, and the Amazon, and ventured into Peru without finding the city. The group consisted of four-and-forty men out of the eighty-four who initially left the tree of Guayra.

The speaker expresses a desire to stop a situation but feels bereaved of the power to do so. The speaker reflects on a time when they were a comfort to their friends and were regarded favorably by others. The speaker mentions two noble youths, Nicaeus and Philolaus, and urges that they return to possess their just rights. Hypatia expresses despair about her welfare, stating that it is gone and that she feels ruined. Raphael Aben-Ezra arrives and indicates that Hypatia's welfare is more important to him than his own. Raphael suggests that he may be born again into a different belief system, which Hypatia rejects. Hypatia questions Raphael about his change and expresses skepticism about his newfound perspective.

Pambo was elected as the abbot by the monks in the monastery. The monks showed loyalty and obedience to Abbot Pambo. Aufugus was respected by the monks and was known for his sanctity and humility. It was rumored that Aufugus had once been a great man from a significant city, possibly Rome. Abbot Pambo consulted Aufugus in private before informing the brotherhood about the sack of Rome by Alaric. Philammon knelt awaiting his sentence after a confrontation with Abbot Pambo. Philammon felt comfortable sharing his feelings with Aufugus after the abbot left them alone.

The text describes a scene involving the Plymouth fleet and the Spanish Armada. Lord Howard has searched for the Armada but returned to Plymouth due to shifting winds. Notable figures of the Plymouth fleet are gathered at the Pelican Inn on July 19. Walter Raleigh, Lord Sheffield, Lord Charles Howard of Effingham, and Sir Robert Southwell are mentioned as part of the gathering. Francis Drake is described as a determined and self-possessed man with a coarse appearance. The text contrasts the achievements of past thinkers and workers with the ignorance of those who benefit from their work.

Ayacanora threatened to kill a man who confessed to giving her wine out of fear for his life. Ayacanora developed a strong aversion to fermented liquors after experiencing a headache and cold treatment from Amyas. Amyas felt a sense of responsibility for Ayacanora's well-being and sought guidance from God regarding her care. Ayacanora refused to learn Christianity from Parson Jack and insisted on being taught only by Amyas. Ayacanora disliked John Brimblecombe and Will Cary, believing there should not be two caciques on board. Ayacanora displayed repugnance towards the negroes, initially hiding from them and later throwing objects at them. Ayacanora commanded the sailors and was treated like a princess, which provided amusement for both the crew and Amyas.

Philammon felt remorseful about his actions earlier in the day. He had previously viewed Christians, especially monks, as infallible and Jews and heathens as accursed. Philammon was haunted by the figure of Raphael, who appeared ragged and penniless yet self-assured. Philammon noted a similarity between Raphael and Arsenius in their ease, grace, and courtesy. A crowd of citizens was passing in and out of the patriarch's audience-room with various petitions. An old priest requested help from the archdeacon for a fever-stricken sailor's family. The archdeacon instructed Peter to find someone to assist the priest, suggesting Philammon for the task.

Sir Richard is the hereditary head of the Bridge Trust, which endowed the school and other Bideford charities. Vindex, the schoolmaster, has a son named Jack who is sixteen years old. Sir Richard threatens Vindex to keep their conversation confidential and not to speak of his godson near Mistress Salterne's. Sir Richard offers to help Jack attend Oxford or face imprisonment in Exeter gaol. Amyas Leigh rides joyfully towards Plymouth alongside Sir Richard after a three-year absence. The rector begins his sermon on the text regarding the Lord's dominion over the earth and discusses the iniquity of the Spaniards and the valor of Mr. Drake.

Eustace Leigh expresses admiration for Rose Salterne using various epithets. Rose Salterne feels uncomfortable with Eustace's advances and asks him to leave. Eustace believes Rose's protests are insincere and continues to hold her hands. Rose threatens to call for help if Eustace does not leave her alone. Eustace expresses frustration and jealousy, suspecting another suitor has been with Rose. After fleeing from Eustace, Rose decides to avoid the village to prevent gossip. Rose Salterne is characterized as a passionate and imaginative young woman influenced by local legends and tales.

Wulf is the son of Ovida. The giant is dressed in a mixture of Roman military and civil attire. Pelagia is a woman of about twenty-two years old, described as beautiful. Philammon refers to Asgard as the city of God. The giant instructs Pelagia to ask the monk about the river's origin. The river is said to rise in the Caucasus, but its exact location is unknown. The river is described as running through deserts inhabited by mythical creatures.

Pelagia declined an invitation but remembered the wild man. The Amal urged Pelagia to leave the wild man and not become a nun. Philammon was escorted away by attendants while carrying various items. Philammon asked a local man for directions to the patriarch's house. The local man, a Greek philosopher, expressed disdain for monks. The philosopher claimed to have learned from Hypatia and considered himself a fallen star. The philosopher asked Philammon to carry his basket of fruit while showing him the way.

Amyas met young Mr. Cary at the door ten days ago. Mr. Salterne opened the door for Amyas and expressed that he had been expecting him. Amyas informed Mr. Salterne that his general had died at sea. Mr. Salterne mentioned he had a venture in the ship that was lost. Mr. Salterne's apprentices expressed that they had been half-starved for three months. Mr. Salterne sent out for food and wine despite his usual frugality. Amyas questioned Mr. Salterne's behavior, wondering if he was flattering or mocking him.

The old Jewess hears a footstep and prepares for a visitor. She draws a dagger and steps boldly to the door. Philammon feels a sense of terror and danger while standing in the chamber. He hears whispering voices from behind a gauze curtain. Hypatia is revealed kneeling by the old woman, robed in white and adorned with diamonds and gold. Philammon instinctively saves Hypatia from a fire caused by the tripod. He flees the room and jumps out of a window towards the archbishop's house.

The armament was complete except for the crew, which was hastily assembled. The sailors on the bark Swallow were described as mutinous and piratical. The Church recognized its foe and ultimately conquered despite various challenges. Persecutors inflicted cruelties on the Church, which formed from fallen masses. The party prepared for a fresh voyage after finishing their canoes. They decided to travel by night to avoid discovery near Spanish settlements. Philammon notified his presence with a slight noise. Cyril, who sat on the throne of the Pharaohs, was described as having a stern and massive beauty. Philammon was about to jump when Cyril commanded him to stop. A deacon informed Cyril that the rabbis were below at his summons. Cyril decided to put Philammon under the supervision of Cleitophon.

The narrator returned with three ships after the initial party had been gone for two weeks. Upon return, the narrator found only the ruins of huts and wild deer, but no people. Amyas shared the story of the prize and other events with Salterne, who remained composed throughout.

Every citizen of the nation mentioned was compelled by law to practice the use of the bow from childhood. Smid attacked Philammon by seizing his throat and engaging him in a struggle. Philammon experienced a new sensation during the fight, which he found unexpectedly pleasant. The sexton was instructed to dig a grave for old Master Yeo. Mrs. Leigh remained at home during the burial service. Ayacanora sat beside Mrs. Leigh and was thinking of Amyas. Blancheflour, Sir Ysumbras, Sir Guy of Warwick, Palamon and Arcite, and the Romaunt of the Rose were among the text-books and canonical authorities referenced. Rose had a lingering fancy for Amyas Leigh, despite her feelings being influenced by other admirers. Rose hoped that Amyas had not forgotten her and was eager to hear about his adventures.

The boy recited his Creed and Lord's Prayer twice daily and attended church services every morning. He learned moral values from his parents, believing it was noble to do right and base to do wrong. The group faced hunger and suspicion that the negroes had betrayed them to the Spaniards. Mr. O. commanded the group to cut down trees and make canoes to reach the sea. The lady in the group endured hardships and provided comfort to others despite her own suffering.

The characters discuss sagas about gods, giants, and mythical creatures. Goderic mentions that his mother was an Alruna-woman. The speaker expresses a desire for a faith that is not based on arguments or reasoning. The speaker observes the actions of a family caring for wounded men without seeking fame or reward. Mr. Leigh believes that the declaration regarding the bull was unnecessary and that enforcement was rare. The conversation reflects tensions between Catholic beliefs and the authority of the English crown.

Amyas had a dozen men with him while the Indian men could muster nearly a hundred. Amyas forbade his men to draw their swords or retreat during the confrontation. The protagonist is uncertain about whether Rose is aware of his feelings for her. Rose is located in a farm-house beside the mill in the valley of Combe. Eustace and two Jesuits plan to attend church while secretly plotting against the established powers.

Ayacanora returned home to Burrough after attending a friar's sermon. Raleigh, an Indian, was baptized on March 26, 1587, as recorded in the Bideford baptisms. The poem concluded with a mention of the discovery of the golden tree and the Hesperids.

Amyas was afraid of being flogged for not completing his exercise. Sir Richard advised Amyas that those who cannot obey will never be fit to rule. Don Sebastian and the Lady Miranda communicated secretly despite obstacles. Miranda planned an escape with the help of the youngest wife of the cacique. Frank and Rose, along with a renegade Jew and a negro, were sentenced to death for being impenitent. The Jew and the negro were burnt at one stake, while Frank and Rose were burnt at another stake. Oxenham encouraged his men to join him in seeking fortune at sea.

Don Guzman settled in Bideford on his parole. Richard Grenville hosted a supper attended by Mayor Salterne. Don Guzman initially found the English customs puzzling but accepted the situation. Mayor Salterne attempted to engage Don Guzman in conversation about foreign lands. Don Guzman found amusement in the evening but remained cautious in revealing information.

The speaker allowed a woman a comfortable maintenance and claims to be free. Cyril has accused the Jews of plotting to murder all Christians. The sun will be turned into darkness and the moon into blood. The stars will fall from heaven and the skies will pass away like a scroll. Philammon is to take a week's provision of dried dates and millet for his journey. Pambo launches a canoe for Philammon as he prepares to leave. The scene shifts to a small room in a house on Museum Street in Alexandria.

The captain of the Spaniard urged his men to die like valiant mariners while some crew members called for mercy and surrender. The crew experienced cheerful moments while on the beach after spending four days in the tropic woods. Amyas and Don Guzman began to like each other despite initial taciturnity. Don Guzman shared details about his background, including his poor heritage and the uncertainty of his ransom. Amyas reads a manuscript that may lead to peril, while Don Guzman hints at its dangerous content. Salvation Yeo serves as Amyas's bodyguard and expresses a connection to Amyas's quest.

Hypatia experiences a strange meeting that leaves her bewildered. She feels a deep interest in Raphael, despite not having affection for him. Hypatia considers Raphael her only true pupil and possibly her only true master. She recognizes Raphael's practical cunning and moral earnestness as superior to those around her. Raphael has been practically useful to Hypatia, assisting with her mathematical problems and managing her students. He protects Hypatia from the criticisms of other philosophical schools. Raphael's wit and skills attract new students to Hypatia's lectures.

Old Salterne felt bound by courtesy and hospitality to share information about the Spanish monopoly. The Spaniards were not jealous of individual traders but of general attempts to deprive them of wealth. Old Salterne believed that Rose would not consider marrying a Popish Spaniard. Don Guzman frequented Old Salterne's house and developed a relationship with Rose Salterne. Rose Salterne found Don Guzman to be a man of high-bred grace and eloquence. The presence of Don Guzman was welcomed by many ladies in the area due to a lack of young gallants. Sir Richard advised Don Guzman to maintain good relations with local gentlemen and their daughters.

Orestes expressed that he was faint and disturbed by recent events. The Amal insisted that Orestes was his guest and that he would ensure Orestes would not leave sober. A monk was brought forward for Orestes to judge while dinner was being prepared. Smid mentioned that he had been bitten during a scuffle. The group discussed the fate of the monk, with some suggesting hanging and others proposing a more prolonged punishment. The monk identified himself as Ammonius and admitted to throwing a stone at Orestes. Philammon, a young philosopher, was also invited to join the gathering.

Augustine is expected to arrive the following day. The speaker plans to meet Augustine with armed men and hunt for food. The speaker expresses a desire to help another character, Raphael, with his issues regarding Judaism. Raphael has considered converting to Christianity but is conflicted about his motives. Synesius offers to assist Raphael in achieving his desires. Raphael feels a strong sense of conscience and honor, particularly in relation to a woman he loves. Raphael has experienced temptations and struggles with his desires and moral dilemmas.

The garden features various trees including planes, chestnuts, figs, and palm-trees. Ptolemy Philadelphus, Euclid, Theocritus, Callimachus, and Lycophron are historical figures associated with the location. The Museum includes picture galleries, halls of statuary, dining-halls, lecture-rooms, and a famous library. The library, founded by the father of Philadelphus, held four hundred thousand manuscripts during Seneca's time. The room is decorated in a pure Greek style with frescoes depicting scenes from old myths of Athene.
