source.title: The Rover Boys on Snowshoe Island

text: Tom is visiting the Sanderson homestead before leaving for New York City. Minnie Sanderson greets Tom with a warm smile. Mr. Sanderson expresses concern about a mortgage settlement. Henry Grisley and Belright Fogg arrive at the Sanderson homestead. Belright Fogg mentions having an account to settle with Tom's brother. Tom is no longer studying at Brill College. Tom expresses sympathy for the Sandersons regarding their loss.

source.author: Edward Stratemeyer
source.title: The Rover Boys on a Tour

text: The race continued as before. Mr. Sanderson's horse with the cutter was spotted at the railroad station. The horse appeared to be exhausted. Sam and the boys attempted to stop the departing train but were unsuccessful. The freight agent confirmed seeing a man with a heavy overcoat and fur cap board the train. Sam planned to send telegrams to Penton and Leadenfield to have the train searched. Dr. Havens and Dr. Wallington treated Songbird for a head injury at the Bray farmhouse.

source.author: Edward Stratemeyer
source.title: The Rover Boys on a Tour

text: Mr. Rover sent a telegram stating that the opposition of the Waltham interests in Wall Street had been withdrawn. Dick expressed concern for his father and decided to return to help him. Tom and Sam agreed to return as well, citing the poor weather during their tour. The group resumed their trip westward after fair weather and visited Colorado Springs and Manitou. They shipped their automobiles home by freight and returned to New York by train. Sam and Grace planned to marry early in the fall, with the ceremony expected to take place at the Cedarville Union Church. Wedding gifts began to arrive, including a bankbook from Mr. Rover and a gold wrist-watch from Sam to Grace.

source.author: Edward Stratemeyer
source.title: The Rover Boys on a Tour

text: The boys informed Jack's father, Dick Rover, about Carson Davenport and his associates. Dick Rover expressed his intention to investigate the situation regarding Carson Davenport. Carson Davenport claimed he could explain the situation to Dick Rover's satisfaction. Dick Rover mentioned that the title to Spell's land appeared to be clouded. Dick Rover planned to retrieve documents from a safe-deposit vault in Wichita Falls. Carson Davenport proposed a joint venture to drill for oil on the land. Dick Rover decided not to make any deals until he reviewed the documents in the safe-deposit box.

source.author: Edward Stratemeyer
source.title: The Rover Boys in the Land of Luck

text: The group traveled from Crumville along the highway leading north. They passed over a high bridge to cross the Hudson River into Poughkeepsie. The group stopped for lunch in Albany and decided to spend the night there. Mr. Dunston Porter was driving the car, allowing Dave to converse with passengers. The tourists aimed to reach Rayville that day, where Mr. Basswood had friends. They received directions from a man in a runabout at a crossroads. Dave lost sight of the Basswood car while navigating a dark, tree-lined road.

Josefina pretended to be surprised when questioned by the Spanish detachment about a tall fellow who had knocked over their guards. The leader of the Spanish detachment threatened Josefina with a sword while demanding to know the whereabouts of the man they were pursuing. Carlos Dunetta intervened to protect his sister, displaying himself at the top of the opening and confronting the Spanish soldiers. Carlos was shot in the arm and back during the confrontation, but his wounds were not life-threatening. Josefina tended to Carlos's wounds on the grass while the Spanish soldiers discussed his hiding place. Corporal Pedro Ruz insisted that Carlos be taken as a prisoner to Captain Coleo, regardless of his condition. Josefina was forcibly pushed back by one of the soldiers when she protested the treatment of her brother.

Half a dozen mice were hiding in the room. Stowell was alarmed by the presence of the mice and jumped onto a chair. Stowell intended to clear the mice out using a baseball bat. A mouse jumped into Stowell's shoe and then into his pajamas, causing him to yell. Stowell's struggle with the mouse resulted in a tear in his pajamas. Stowell opened the closet door and found a cadet with a handkerchief over his face. Stowell locked the closet door, believing he had caught the person playing a trick on him.

source.author: Edward Stratemeyer
source.title: The Rover Boys in the Land of Luck

text: The engines of the _Brooklyn_ began to work as the ship approached the harbor entrance. Commodore Schley decided to play a waiting game instead of rushing into battle against the Spanish squadron. The _Texas_ steamed past the _Brooklyn_ and close to the harbor, where a small Spanish land battery remained silent. The _Marblehead_ arrived with despatches for Commodore Schley and had a conference with him. Cuban spies reported that no Spanish warships were found outside of a small harbor vessel. The squadron received orders to sail for Santiago in the evening. Conditions on the ship were stifling, and crew members frequently sought fresh air.

Chester expressed relief that he was not drowned and praised the Rovers for their assistance. Blackie Crowden confessed to the Rovers that he attacked Songbird after being pressured by lawyer Belright Fogg. Crowden claimed he was coerced into robbing a young man due to a debt of three hundred dollars to Fogg. Crowden followed Powell to steal money from him after being threatened by Fogg. Crowden met Fogg at a road house in Leadenfield to pay the three hundred dollars. Crowden stated that he hid the remaining stolen money in a closet at the Ashton hotel. Crowden did not spend the stolen money and was afraid to return to the hotel to retrieve it.

source.author: Edward Stratemeyer
source.title: The Rover Boys on a Tour

text: The characters are traveling through crowded traffic towards Fifth Avenue. Jack's eyes appear inflamed, prompting his mother to inquire about it. Martha mentions that Ruth Stevenson suffered the worst in a recent incident. Mrs. Rover expresses concern about the boys making enemies. The Rover family hosts a grand reunion dinner for the young people. The gathering includes dancing and singing around the piano. Jack and Martha explain the incident on Bluebell Island to their mother.

source.author: Edward Stratemeyer
source.title: The Rover Boys in the Land of Luck

text: The American warships began to bombard Spanish strongholds. One of the Spanish batteries was completely silenced during the bombardment. The Spanish forces returned fire but had poor aim, resulting in few effective shots. A shell from the _Texas_ hit a powder magazine, causing a significant explosion. The bombardment lasted over an hour, silencing every land battery. The American forces decided not to advance further until the army arrived. The weather was extremely hot, leading to discomfort among the crew.

Colonel Colby and Professor Brice examined the site of a fire that occurred in the gymnasium. The fire was confined to three boxes filled with excelsior and two barrels containing straw and waste paper. Silas Crews, the gymnasium instructor, acknowledged that it was a mistake to store inflammable materials in the gymnasium. Colonel Colby instructed Silas Crews to ensure the heating system was started to prevent pipes from freezing. Colonel Colby questioned Randy and Fred about cigarette smoking by other cadets, Slugger, Nappy, and Codfish. Randy and Fred denied smoking and stated they had no need for a light while in the gymnasium. The news of the fire spread to the town and Clearwater Hall, with inquiries about any injuries.

source.author: Edward Stratemeyer
source.title: The Rover Boys on Snowshoe Island

text: Winfield Scott Schley is named after General Winfield Scott. Schley entered the Naval Academy in 1856 and graduated at the head of his class in 1861. After the Civil War, Schley was sent to the Pacific to suppress an outbreak among Chinese coolies in the Chin Chi Islands. Schley was made a lieutenant-commander and later took part in clearing the Congo River of pirates. Schley was awarded a medal by Congress for rescuing the Greely Expedition and was promoted to captain. Schley commanded the _Baltimore_ and received a medal from the King of Sweden. Schley resolved a diplomatic issue with Chile regarding American sailors in Valparaiso.

The main topic of conversation at Bear Camp was the news concerning Dave. Laura and Jessie expressed their feelings about Dave's situation, which brought Dave a moment of joy. Mrs. Wadsworth expressed concern for Dave and stated that they think highly of him. Roger and Phil discussed the possibility of the Porters adopting Dave if he is not proven to be their son. The boys at Bear Camp attempted to cheer Dave up and assured him of their support. Dave expressed his appreciation for his friends but indicated that the situation was a blow to him. Ben and Shadow discussed their feelings about Ward Porton and the resemblance between him and Dave.

The moving-picture company is filming outdoor scenes for fifteen or twenty dramas in the Adirondacks. Mr. Appleby is the manager of the moving-picture company. Dave Porter inquired about Ward Porton, who is a member of the company but not currently present. Dave Porter informed Mr. Appleby that Link Merwell is a fugitive from justice. Mr. Appleby expressed his desire not to have Link Merwell in his company. Della Ford invited Jessie Wadsworth and her party to visit their cottage near the lake. Jessie Wadsworth declined the invitation to participate in the moving picture.

Four wolves were fighting over a dead partridge in the snow. One wolf was carrying the dead partridge while the other three attempted to take it from him. The wolves stopped fighting and glared at the Rovers when they entered the opening. Jack shot one of the wolves in the foreleg, causing it to roll over in the snow. Fred shot the leading wolf in the throat, resulting in its death. The third wolf fled behind the rocks after witnessing the fate of its companions. Randy used his gun as a club to strike the wounded wolf, causing it to flee.

source.author: Edward Stratemeyer
source.title: The Rover Boys on Snowshoe Island

text: Dave and Phil went swimming as the weather was getting colder. Roger announced that it would soon be time for hunting. Dave expressed a desire to hunt a deer. Phil suggested hunting a bear that could weigh eight hundred or a thousand pounds. Shadow recounted a story about an encounter with three Modoc Indians and a bear. Laura stated that one scare from the wild man was enough for her. Phil proposed tracking the wild man from a cliff.

Laura expresses uncertainty about what to do regarding Jessie. Della Ford invites the boys to dinner and requests they bring a boy with a banjo. Phil agrees to visit Della Ford and mentions he thinks Dave has made a good impression on her. The boys discuss the possibility of Link Merwell coming to the camp. Laura informs Dave that Jessie has a headache and is resting. Mrs. Basswood states that Ben went to Carpen Falls with his father and Mr. Porter. Mrs. Wadsworth reassures Dave that Jessie's headache is slight and she will be fine by morning.

The command to give another broadside was issued, resulting in the port guns firing on the Spanish deck. The _Oregon_ assisted the flagship during the attack on the _Vizcaya_. The torpedo-boat destroyers _Pluton_ and _Furor_ were approaching the open sea at twenty knots per hour. The _Gloucester_, commanded by Lieutenant Wainwright, engaged the torpedo boats with gunfire. The _Oregon_ and the _Iowa_ provided support to the _Gloucester_ during the conflict. The _Pluton_ was hit by a shell and sank, leaving her crew in the water. The _Furor_ struck a reef and was forced to surrender after being heavily attacked.

Luke commented that the water looked good and took a drink. The boys agreed that the water was as good as any they had ever tasted. They found another trail veering to the westward and covered half a mile. The boys encountered rough rocks where the trail seemed to lose itself. Dave indicated that it was easier walking ahead and believed he saw the trail. The boys took a break to eat lunch and rest on some rocks and a fallen tree. Dave spotted smoke in a hollow, suggesting the presence of a human being.

Walter did not understand the Spanish soldier's words and was unaware of his danger until the soldier began to climb the tree. Corporal Ruz ordered a match to be lit and dropped into the hole where Walter was hiding. Walter extinguished the match that landed on his head, which alerted the soldiers to his presence. Corporal Ruz identified Walter as an American and questioned him about his origins, but Walter did not understand Spanish. The soldiers searched Walter's clothing and found nothing of value. The group consisted of eight soldiers armed with Mauser rifles, and included both older and younger members. Walter was taken to a small Spanish camp where he met Captain Coleo, who spoke English fluently.

Gif Garrison is recognized as the head of many athletic sports. Spouter Powell expressed that the gentle rains contribute to the greenery of the fields and hills. Dan Soppinger mentioned he has an essay to write on moisture. Fred expressed a desire for the rain to clear up so they could go to Haven Point. Mary telephoned Fred that she and Martha might go to see a moving picture. Randy and Andy engaged in gymnastic work, performing various evolutions on the turning-bars. Walt Baxter agreed to participate in a swinging contest against Randy and Andy.

source.author: Edward Stratemeyer
source.title: The Rover Boys in the Land of Luck

text: Colonel Colby was interrupted by a knock on the door. Asa Lemm expressed confusion upon seeing the cadets enter. The cadets, led by Gif and Randy, stated they had come to report and give themselves up. Professor Lemm accused the cadets of being rowdies and demanded severe punishment. Colonel Colby defended the cadets, stating they were only boys and did not warrant arrest. A confrontation occurred between Colonel Colby and Professor Lemm regarding the treatment of the cadets. After Professor Lemm left, Colonel Colby questioned the boys about their issues with him.

source.author: Edward Stratemeyer
source.title: The Rover Boys on Snowshoe Island

text: Walter was on the _Merrimac_ and spent time among the Cubans and Spaniards. Walter escaped from a Spanish prison and joined the marines at Guantanamo Bay. The officer expressed disbelief in Walter's story about his experiences. Walter's friends, Si, Caleb, and Paul, were surprised to see him and thought he was dead. Walter insisted that he did not commit suicide and was in good health. Walter was summoned to report to the captain's cabin on the _Brooklyn_. Walter was accustomed to elegant surroundings before living with Job Dowling.

The former teacher of Colby Hall expressed astonishment at the presence of Jack and his cousins. Jack and his cousins were on the island to hunt. Barney Stevenson was not present, having gone to Rockville on an errand. Slogwell Brown and Asa Lemm were part of a group that confronted Jack and his cousins. Asa Lemm indicated he had an account to settle with Jack. Slogwell Brown and his group planned to take possession of the island. Nappy stated that they intended to remove Barney Stevenson from the island.

source.author: Edward Stratemeyer
source.title: The Rover Boys on Snowshoe Island

text: Dave and Jessie had a disagreement while paddling a canoe. Jessie expressed her displeasure at being called silly by Dave. The coldness between Dave and Jessie increased over several days. Mr. Appleby arrived in a motor-boat with Tad Rason, Della Ford, and Aunt Bess. Dave and his friends were fishing at the dock when Mr. Appleby arrived. Mr. Appleby requested to borrow furniture for a scene in a drama. Tad Rason informed the boys that deer are scarce in their area but plentiful at the head of the lake.

The narrator's home is on Snowshoe Island in Lake Monona, about ten miles north of the current location. Barney Stevenson indicated that Bill Hobson's place is along the Rick Rack River. The group decided to make a litter of pine boughs to carry Barney Stevenson. Barney Stevenson was injured when a tree fell on him while he was aiming at a rabbit. The boys constructed a litter and carefully placed Barney Stevenson on it to transport him. The group encountered difficulties navigating the rocky terrain and heavy brushwood along the Rick Rack River. They eventually spotted smoke, which Barney Stevenson identified as coming from Bill Hobson's cabin.

source.author: Edward Stratemeyer
source.title: The Rover Boys on Snowshoe Island

text: The boys reached the hotel where the girls were eager to hear their news. Dunston Porter and Mr. Basswood suggested an early start the following morning. The two automobiles were overhauled and filled with oil, gasoline, and water. Ben mentioned a bad cut on one of the rear wheels and considered changing the shoe. The road from Rayville northwestward was in fine shape for the first thirty miles. The group had a substantial lunch packed by the hotel for their trip. A tire blew out on the Basswood car, causing alarm among the passengers.

Roxley scored one run in the second inning. Dare Phelps pitched out the next batter after a run was scored. A runner from first base was caught out while attempting to steal third base. Brill scored two runs in the third inning, making the score two to one in favor of Brill. Roxley tied the game at two to two after a fumble by the Brill second baseman. The score remained tied at two to two after the fourth inning. Roxley took the lead with a score of four to two after the fifth inning.

source.author: Edward Stratemeyer
source.title: The Rover Boys on a Tour

text: Caspar Potts expressed concern about the tenants disturbing a box. Dave retrieved a small blue wooden box containing thirty or forty dusty, aged books. Caspar Potts indicated that some of the books would add to their library. Dave and Caspar Potts encountered two visitors on the porch of the cottage. One visitor was Ward Porton, whom Dave had previously rescued from a fire at sea. The other visitor was Link Merwell, who appeared thin and careworn. Link Merwell expressed bitterness towards Dave and mentioned Job Haskers.

Walter Russell is considering enlisting in the navy during a war. Caleb Walton is a seaman who is currently recruiting for the _Brooklyn_. Phil Newell is a friend of Walter who introduces him to Caleb Walton. Caleb Walton has received orders to join the _Brooklyn_ and is short-handed by three men. Walter Russell provides his guardian's consent to enlist in the navy. The main business offices of the yard are busy with seamen, officers, and workmen. Captain Line expresses concern about Walter's age during the enlistment process.

Jack was attacked by Gabe Werner, who threw pepper in his and Ruth's eyes. Ruth experienced severe pain from the pepper and required assistance. Andy and Spouter helped Jack and Ruth by taking them to the water's edge to wash out their eyes. Jack's eyes were inflamed but he believed they would be fine after a while. Spouter suggested that Ruth should see a doctor for her eyes. The group was concerned about Ruth's condition and decided to return to town for medical help. Gabe Werner and Bill Glutts escaped in a motorboat before the group could pursue them.

source.author: Edward Stratemeyer
source.title: The Rover Boys in the Land of Luck

text: The speaker claims that his invisible ministers possess wisdom superior to that of learned individuals. The speaker expresses a strong personal interest in the welfare of Miss Lambert, who is to be his wife. Serviss expresses concern that the speaker's actions may harm Miss Lambert. The speaker dismisses criticism from the press and scientists, claiming they are engaged in important work. The speaker states that Miss Lambert's mother supports her involvement in their work. Clarke, a character in the text, is portrayed as both egotistical and deluded rather than malicious. The speaker criticizes scientists for their focus on trivial subjects instead of more significant matters.

The narrator kept count of the number of buckwheat pancakes a man could eat, which was either seven or eleven. The man once ate nine buckwheat pancakes the size of a dinner plate along with sausages. The man was capable of whirling a six-pound axe all day without pausing for breath. Den, the youngest of the Greens, was a boy about three years older than the narrator and later became a successful doctor in California. Ellis Usher, who lived in Sand Lake and often hunted with Den, is an editor in Milwaukee and a political leader in his state. The road from the farm to the village school crossed a sandy ridge that became hot in June, causing discomfort to the children. Matt Gallagher, a boy two years older than the narrator, often tormented him at school and threatened harm to the narrator's dog, Rover.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The narrator's family is traveling in a carriage on a frozen ground. Uncle David is leading the way in a similar vehicle, holding the reins of his horses. The narrator's mother is wrapped in shawls and is seated with the narrator and sister in the carriage. The family arrives at a cottage where Grandfather McClintock is sitting by an open fireplace. The cottage is a small building with four rooms and a kitchen, rented from a farm. Grandfather McClintock sold the original homestead on the LaCrosse River. The family plans to have oyster soup for supper, which is considered a treat.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The narrator and their sister studied the tracks made by birds and small animals on their farm. The narrator's brother was too small to accompany them on excursions. The village to the east was built by the 'Friends' who had a meeting house nearby. The narrator learned from their Norwegian neighbor's children that Norwegians ate from wooden plates and bowls. The narrator, their sister Harriet, and Lars Peterson attempted to train a yoke of yearling calves. The narrator's father hired two Norwegian immigrants to assist in clearing the land. The Norwegian immigrants communicated smallpox to the house-maid, leading to a serious health crisis in the family.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The narrator is from Wisconsin and has a desire to do something significant in the world. A person named Mr. Bashford invites the narrator to Boston to take a special course at the University and offers a letter of recommendation. The narrator feels excitement about the opportunity but also experiences dejection after Mr. Bashford leaves town. The narrator owns a small trunk, a couple of dozen books, a valise, and a few acres of barren land. The narrator contemplates selling their claim to go east, study, and eventually return to the west to teach. The narrator's father is puzzled and irritated by the narrator's desire to go east, believing it is an absurd plan. The narrator's mother supports the narrator's ambitions without objection, expressing faith in their abilities.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The narrator attended a modest school for four years and gained knowledge of literature and scientific discoveries. During the narrator's last winter at the Seminary, Adelbert Jones was their associate in housekeeping. Adelbert Jones, referred to as 'Del,' was the son of a well-to-do farmer living east of town. Del was known for his tall stature, large blond face, and concern about his freckles. The narrator once hired a horse and carriage to take Alice for a drive, which was their first and only attempt at such an outing. The town where the narrator lived was described as simple and democratic, lacking modern amenities like bathtubs. The town had some fine lawns and flower gardens, and the maples provided shade in summer and color in autumn.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: Clarke visits Julia and expresses concern about Viola's state of mind. Clarke reveals his love for Viola and asks Julia for permission to propose to her. Julia is surprised by Clarke's feelings for Viola so soon after his loss of Adele. Clarke believes Viola's musical education is crucial and fears for her if she goes to New York alone. Clarke insists that he needs authority over Viola as a husband to protect her. Julia is initially hesitant but ultimately consents to Clarke's request for marriage with Viola.

The narrator and Burton disliked the smell of manure and the clothing required for their farm tasks. They planned to leave the farm at the age of twenty-one and not return. As the season changed, their resentment faded, and they made no further complaints. The narrator took on responsibilities typical of an adult and felt strong and capable in his work. During harvest, the narrator operated a Marsh harvester on over one hundred acres of grain. Both the narrator and Burton were eager to return to the Seminary and participate in the Adelphian Debating Society. The narrator's father allowed his sons to enjoy leisure activities without enforcing religious observance.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: Weissmann proposes to found an institute for the study of the supra-normal. Serviss receives a telegram from Lambert stating the time of his arrival and requesting a meeting. Serviss feels relieved of responsibility but troubled by speculations about organic life. Serviss reflects on the nature of humanity and the concept of immortality. Lambert arrives and greets Serviss with a conventional demeanor but a distinctive appearance. Lambert expresses concern for the well-being of others and inquires about the situation. Serviss leads Lambert to a cab to discuss the facts regarding their mutual acquaintances.

The narrator's daughter is described as having a large head, wide dark eyes, and abundant hair. The narrator's wife, Zulime, experienced a sense of relief and beauty after giving birth. The narrator reflects on the significance of their daughter, Mary Isabel, in the context of family history. The narrator experienced feelings of despair and unworthiness after the publication of their work, _Hesper_. The narrator considered writing about Native American history, specifically the Sioux and Algonquin tribes. The narrator took on the role of caregiver during Zulime's convalescence, focusing on their daughter's well-being. The arrival of the child brought joy and a sense of purpose to the narrator.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The subject vowed to never use obscene or profane words and kept this vow for over thirty years. The subject did not raise his voice in anger or use inappropriate language around women. The subject was recognized as a fearless and indomitable mountaineer. Corn-planting was done by hand and involved neighbors helping each other. The period following corn-planting was characterized by less strenuous labor and building fence. The arrival of the circus was a significant event that brought excitement and imaginative experiences. Haying was described as a season of well-defined charm during the last days of June in Iowa.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: Osage was home to two judges, a state senator, and a congressman. A new opera house was built in Osage in 1879. Osage hosted events such as circuses, Fourth of July celebrations, and county fairs. The author encountered a book titled _The Undiscovered Country_ at the post office. The author decided not to pursue a career in law after a conversation with a law student named Lohr. The author experienced a sense of happiness during his youth, despite a feeling of impermanence.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The house is filled with men and women gathered around a table after a harvest feast. Mrs. Green performs fortune-telling using tea-grounds. She predicts that a soldier is coming to the narrator's mother. A soldier named Richard is seen approaching the house with a musket. Richard is initially unrecognized by the narrator, who perceives him as a stranger. The narrator's mother hesitates to embrace Richard due to his changed appearance. The narrator's younger brother, Frank, is frightened by Richard and does not approach him.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: Serviss expressed surprise at Britt's concession regarding faith in the future. Britt stated that every age is an age of transition and that people will always seek something to live for. Kate remarked on the change in Britt and Serviss due to the influence of a girl. Britt acknowledged that he and Serviss are human and have personal lives outside of their scientific work. Britt expressed a desire for health and mentioned his willingness to consider extreme measures against Clarke. Britt described Clarke as a 'male vampire' and expressed concern for Viola Lambert's well-being. Britt promised to keep in touch with Mrs. Rice and mentioned the possibility of manifesting to her.

Adele is mentioned as a significant figure in the narrative. The narrator believes that a medium has allowed them to communicate with Adele after her death. Viola, the medium, expresses a strong desire to reject her abilities and refuses to participate in further sessions. Mrs. Lambert invokes the aid of Donald McLeod, who is described as Viola's control. The narrator observes that Viola suffers during the session, leading to concerns about her well-being. The narrator expresses a desire to document and share the experiences gained through Viola's mediumship. The relationship between the narrator and Dr. Britt deteriorates due to differing beliefs about Viola's abilities.

The ballad discussed dates back to the conquest of the Allegheny mountains. The song served as a marching song for the author's grandfather's generation and influenced his father and uncles. The lyrics of the song evoke images of exploration, adventure, and the pioneer spirit. The author's father often sang to the family by the fire, despite not knowing many tunes. The author's mother had a gifted voice and sang various songs that the family enjoyed. Many of the ballads favored by the McClintocks were sad and focused on themes of loss. The song 'Freedom's Star' had a significant subconscious impact on the author's father.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The marsh across the lane was considered a dangerous place due to the presence of serpents. The narrator's father bought his farm just before the war and could not enlist until 1863. The father joined Grant's army at Vicksburg after making the last payment on his mortgage. The narrator's mother experienced significant emotional distress due to her husband's enlistment. The narrator has vague memories of their mother and the household activities during their father's absence. The father's military experience influenced his parenting style and discipline at home. The narrator recalls their father's return from the war as a vivid and significant memory.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The narrator spent the night in the quarters of an Inspector at the Crow Agency. The following day, the narrator attended a ceremonial social dance given by the Crows in honor of Chief Two Moon. Chief Two Moon is described as a handsome broad-shouldered man of fifty. The dance involved young men reënacting notable personal or tribal achievements in groups of eight. The narrator rode saddle horses across the Custer battle field toward Lame Deer the next morning. The narrator encountered cattlemen expressing hatred for the Cheyenne and their desire to take their land. The narrator arrived at the Lame Deer Agency and reported to Major George Stouch, a veteran officer of the regular army.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: Hale and Minot Savage were notable figures in theology. Dr. Bartol was a representative of the Concord School of Philosophy. The West Meeting House has remained largely unchanged since Revolutionary days. Edwin Booth had a significant influence on the appreciation of Shakespeare and English literature. The author frequently attended performances at the old Museum, paying thirty-five cents for a standing place. Booth's acting was described as a combination of painting, sculpture, and music. The author took detailed notes on Booth's gestures, accents, and cadences after performances.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The landscape features ripening barley, trees in heavy foliage, and a variety of insect life. Bobolinks and king-birds are present, with the former producing melodic sounds and the latter being aggressive. Purple-and-white clouds move across the sky, bringing rain and thunder. Grasshoppers and toads contribute to the soundscape, while kildees and snipe are seen in flight. The narrator observes that their mother is not well, struggling with the demands of housework. The mother manages to create garments and perform various household tasks despite her fatigue. The narrator is called to fetch a doctor for their sick father, indicating a sense of urgency.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The author and Harriet searched for books and stories in their neighborhood. The author read and enjoyed Jane Porter's _Scottish Chiefs_, _Tempest and Sunshine_, and _Ivanhoe_. The author borrowed publications such as _The New York Saturday Night_ and _The New York Ledger_. The author read _Godey's Ladies Book_ and _Peterson's Magazine_ as high-class periodicals. The author's father relied on _The Toledo Blade_ and _The New York Tribune_ for political advice. The author frequently read almanacs, which were small, poorly printed pamphlets related to patent medicines. The author spent significant time with various publications, which contributed to their education.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The author served as a hotel-keeper and a lecture agent for a club. The author arranged special luncheons for distinguished visitors to increase club attendance. The author's wife, Zulime, expressed contentment with their life despite financial limitations. Zulime managed household duties and maintained a positive attitude despite wearing threadbare clothing. The author experienced feelings of self-disparagement when comparing his home to those of successful writers and artists. The author traveled frequently between New York City and Chicago for his duties, limiting his writing time. The author felt a decline in his literary mission and questioned the value of his writing due to various personal and professional pressures.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The schoolroom experienced extreme temperatures, causing discomfort for the students. Dinner pails often froze solid, requiring thawing on the stove. The farm-yard was protected from prairie winds by long ricks of straw. Cattle in the barn endured a harsh winter, often burrowing in chaff for warmth. Some neighboring cows suffered from hunger and required assistance to stand. Pumping water for the herd was a demanding task, especially in cold weather. The order of cows drinking and entering the stable was strictly maintained.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The author experienced travel in comfort for the first time, including dining and sleeping on trains. The author traveled westward to Colorado, eager to explore the states and study the Rocky Mountains. The author participated in meetings of farmers in Kansas and Nebraska, observing discontent among them. In July, the author met his father in Omaha, where his father was a delegate from Brown County, Dakota. The author's father expressed pride in his son's success as a writer, despite initial doubts about his career. The author and his father attended sessions and discussed farming problems during their time together.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The text describes a party in London where a guest comments on Zulime's artistic career after her marriage to Zuhl. Zuhl expresses his belief in the equality of their partnership and supports Zulime's artistic freedom. Zulime prefers to focus on house-keeping rather than pursuing her art at the moment. Zuhl feels pressure from societal expectations regarding his role as a husband and Zulime's career. Zulime enjoys her new role as a housekeeper and takes pride in managing their home and garden. Lorado visits Zulime and questions the connection between her art training and her current activities. Lorado ultimately acknowledges that Zulime seems happy with her choices in life.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: Sullivan, who had been called to the West, wired from Chicago that _A Son of the Middle Border_ would make an admirable serial. The author sold _The Middle Border_ to _Collier's Weekly_ and received four thousand dollars in total from various publications. The author's father expressed amazement at the sale of the story and read the first installment with mixed emotions. Readers wrote letters to the editor expressing that the author's work resonated with their own life experiences. The publication of the book was delayed due to the Mexican war and the introduction of new articles in the magazine. Mark Sullivan advocated for the printing of six more installments of the author's story. The author felt unease about his father's loneliness while living alone in a big house.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: Mrs. Lambert reported that her daughter Viola began to experience strange occurrences after a series of nightly visits. Viola's left arm began to twitch uncontrollably, and she started writing in her father's handwriting. Viola was said to have written twenty different styles of writing by the age of twelve, all indicating she would be a great medium. Various disturbances occurred in the household, including stolen thimbles, falling vases, and rocking chairs. Viola entered deathly trances, during which her family feared she was dead due to her icy hands and feet. During a trance, Viola's demeanor changed, and she spoke in a voice that accused Kate of past grievances. Kate experienced a mix of fear and disbelief as she witnessed the events unfold, including the voice's accusations against her.

The author recalls experiences of husking corn by starlight on an Iowa farm. The author describes the restoration of a house, including clearing charred rubbish and installing a new metal roof. The author traveled to Chicago, promising to bring his children back for Thanksgiving. The author found the house in disarray upon returning, with dust and shavings on the floors. The author completed the woodwork and made the lower house livable in a couple of days. The children expressed excitement and fear about returning to the restored house. Neighbors helped prepare for Thanksgiving by curtaining windows and preparing food.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The narrative describes a setting where old men commune with their dead at night. The speaker suggests that heavenly visions are not expected in busy places like Broadway or business offices. The text discusses the concept that individuals see only what they are willing to see, referencing a known law of psychology. The speaker claims that invisible beings are present and eager to bless those in attendance. Serviss expresses disgust and anger at the situation involving Viola, whom he believes is being exploited. Clarke announces the presence of a spirit named Adele, which elicits excitement from the audience. Serviss is called upon by Clarke during the séance, leading to a moment of tension and anticipation.

The narrator reflects on the hard work and sacrifices of their mother and other wives in their community. The narrator intends to write an autobiographical manuscript about their family's daily life. The completion of a memorial to the narrator's mother alleviated feelings of self-accusation. The narrator's wife becomes the center of their world and a source of hope for happiness. The narrator's father expresses his memories of his deceased wife, Isabel McClintock, with affection. The father's memories of his wife are filled with joy and nostalgia, contrasting with the narrator's sense of loss. The narrator begins writing a novel titled _The Gray Horse Troop_ as a means of coping with personal grief.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The narrator's daughter is named Mary Isabel. The narrator reflects on the male-dominated nature of the world. The narrator expresses happiness in caring for his daughter. The narrator's father, referred to as the old soldier, frequently visits to see his granddaughter. The narrator is preparing for the publication of a new book titled _Hesper_. The narrator and his family move into a small apartment overlooking Morningside Park. The family hosts dinner parties for friends while managing their limited resources.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The narrator traveled to their claim accompanied by a young Englishman from London. The west wind was strong and cold during their journey, causing difficulties for the Englishman. The narrator arrived at their barn to find the doors heavily banked with snow. One of the narrator's horses became chilled and refused to eat upon arrival at the barn. A neighbor entered the narrator's shanty carrying a sack of coal to return what he had borrowed during a previous blizzard. The temperature dropped to forty degrees below zero the following morning, making it difficult to harness the horses. The narrator's experience during this harsh weather affected their enthusiasm for future endeavors.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The mother expresses concern about the grandfather's influence by Tony. The girl believes that the grandfather may not be aware of their troubles. Mrs. Lambert is apprehensive about meeting Mr. Pratt. Mr. Pratt is described as sullen, sour, and vindictive during breakfast. Mr. Pratt inquires about a recent séance and expresses distrust towards the girl. Clarke confirms that the atmosphere of the house negatively affects Viola. Mr. Pratt is frustrated about being excluded from the séance and questions the decisions made.

The professor claims to have a noble character. Viola is considered set aside to do God's work and ought not to marry. The professor does not believe it is Viola's duty to convert people to a belief in immortality. The professor expresses a strong belief in the importance of life on earth. The professor intends to take Viola away from her current life and stop her trances. The mother feels a sense of loss regarding Viola's potential separation from her. The mother is distressed by the prospect of losing communication with her deceased loved ones.

The author worked in the Congressional Library during the winter, focusing on the Reconstruction Period. The author began dictating the story of his life in the West, motivated by an upcoming trip to the North. The author planned to travel to the Yukon Valley by pack train over the British Columbian Mountains. In February, the author visited Ottawa to study maps and consult with Canadian officials about trails. The author had a friendship with Theodore Roosevelt, who was the Assistant Secretary of the Navy at the time. The author interacted with notable figures such as John Hay, Senator Lodge, Major Powell, and Edward Eggleston during the winter. Major Powell was recognized for his past as an engineer under Grant and for navigating the Grand Canyon.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The narrator's father was made beloved by the landlady and the cook at their lodgings on Elm Street. The narrator insisted that his father go to bed early to be in good condition for the parade the next day. The father expressed no desire to march in the parade and preferred to sit in the Grand Stand. The parade featured time-scarred veterans, many of whom limped and were white-haired. The father felt a poignant connection to the veterans and expressed a desire to be with his company. After the parade, the father appeared tired and reflective, but regained his energy after a night's sleep. The father enjoyed a sail across the Lake with other comrades, returning satisfied with his day.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: Mrs. Lambert called a doctor to study her daughter, who was speaking with the voice of her grandfather. The doctor diagnosed the girl with hysteria and advised taking her on a trip and keeping her nourished. The girl did not outgrow her condition, and she exhibited unusual phenomena such as moving objects and hearing electric snapping. The mother was alarmed by the disturbances and attempted to conceal the unusual occurrences in their household. The doctor noted that the girl experienced intrusive noises that caused her distress and fear of sleeping alone. The mother believed that the spirits of the deceased were trying to communicate with her through the girl. The girl underwent various phases of manifestations, including writing messages and speaking in different voices.

The narrator and their brother selected high-topped cavalry boots in different colors. The narrator's boots had red tops with a golden moon, while the brother's had blue tops with a golden flag. The family lived in an unpainted square cottage at the edge of Dry Run ravine. The cottage had a small lean-to, a sitting room, a bedroom, and a low unplastered chamber for the children. The family's furniture was described as cheap and worn, lacking beauty or distinction. The mother played the violin and had a repertoire of simple tunes. The family wore home-made clothing and the boys, including the narrator's eight-year-old brother, wore long trousers.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The narrator worked on a novel titled _Her Mountain Lover_ during his honeymoon. The narrator and Zulime occasionally went sleighing with Dolly and worked around the house. The narrator's mother wanted Zulime to stay close to her and welcomed the young wife's presence. The narrator expressed concern about asking Zulime to spend the winter in a small hamlet. The narrator planned a wedding trip to Washington and New York. The narrator's mother hoped they would stay all winter but felt sadness at their planned departure. Zulime expressed contentment with their life in the homestead but the narrator believed she preferred city life.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The speaker is attempting to systematize work to raise wheat at sixty cents a bushel with a goal of fifteen bushels per acre. The speaker expresses concern about the lack of money in the country and the state of poverty and drought. The speaker has not purchased a new suit in three years and mentions that his mother is also in a difficult situation. The speaker's father is on the County Committee and arranges for the speaker to speak in Aberdeen. The speaker plans to return in the fall to visit his mother after participating in a campaign. The speaker has decided to leave his position at the Boston School of Oratory to pursue writing. The speaker campaigned for the People's Party in Iowa for six weeks, experiencing the local agricultural conditions.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: B. O. Flower was the editor of the magazine _Arena_. The author had a positive meeting with B. O. Flower, who expressed interest in their fiction. The author became a regular contributor to _Arena_ and received payments that provided financial security. The _Century_ magazine accepted the author's short story _A Spring Romance_ and a three-part tale of Wisconsin. The author received nearly five hundred dollars for the stories accepted by _Century_. The author repaid a loan to their father and faced the new year clear of debt. The author and their brother moved into an apartment on Moreland street in Roxbury.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: Cows' flanks were tied to prevent them from kicking into pails during milking. Humboldt Bunn tied a heifer's tail to his boot straps and regretted it. Calves are described as greedy, noisy, ill-smelling, and stupid. Farmers kept from twenty-five to a hundred head of cattle and half as many colts. Cattle grazed on common grounds as soon as the grass began to grow in April. Colts were described as fuzzy and ungraceful at the beginning of the grazing season. The herds united into one drove, led by the swiftest and most tireless leader.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The narrator reflects on their past while working on their story of the Middle Border. Thanksgiving Day in West Salem is described as misty and dark, but the children are excited for the festival. The narrator's daughters are filled with youthful joy and look forward to Christmas. The narrator has been booked for a lecture at the University Club of Pittsburg in January. The narrator feels a sense of decline in health and creativity as they prepare to leave home. The lecture at the University Club is poorly received, leading to the narrator's feelings of disheartenment. The narrator misses the last train to the East and contemplates their next steps.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The author expresses a belief that American art is declining, particularly in Boston. The author notes that talent from New England is moving to New York, diminishing Boston's artistic prominence. The author attended a party hosted by Grace and Ernest Thompson-Seton in honor of Mr. and Mrs. Hamlin Garland. The author formed a friendship with Frank Norris, a California novelist, during a visit to Juliet Wilbur Tompkins. The author describes Edward MacDowell as the handsomest man in his circle and a delightful dinner companion. The author recalls a past experience of seeing Mrs. Grossman, Edwin Booth's daughter, at a performance of Macbeth. The author prefers life in New York over life in West Salem or Chicago.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: Zulime indicated that she wished to see the narrator and expressed her indecision about their relationship. Lorado, Zulime's brother, respected the narrator as a friend but was not favorable towards him as a suitor. The narrator traveled to the camp and was welcomed by Zulime. The narrator and Zulime spent nearly a week together in companionship during October. Zulime agreed to a wedding date of November 23rd after the narrator expressed urgency due to his age and family wishes. The narrator reflected on their time together as idyllic and expressed hope that Zulime would not regret her decision. The narrator received a letter from William Dean Howells, who was in Chicago and planned to travel to Kansas for a lecture.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The narrator is concerned about their mother's declining health and the need for construction to be completed quickly. The narrator is managing multiple crews, including carpenters, painters, and tinners, to expedite the construction process. The narrator experiences feelings of despair and inadequacy regarding their life circumstances and the prospect of involving Zuleema in their problems. The narrator writes daily updates to Zuleema, who responds positively and expresses that she misses him. Zuleema mentions a trip to Chicago with her sister but plans to return to camp at the end of the week. The narrator decides to meet Zuleema in Chicago to ask for her help in selecting furnishings for their mother's new room. Zuleema shows interest in helping with the furnishings, which makes the narrator feel more confident about their relationship.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The book is titled 'The Tyranny of the Dark' and is authored by Hamlin Garland. The book was published in May 1905 by Harper & Brothers. The story is set in the village of Colorow, which is surrounded by a colossal amphitheatre of stone. The village is located six thousand feet above the valley floor and features green and orange slopes leading to ice-fields. The railway enters the valley from the south, following a stream and navigating between cliffs. The town of Colorow is described as silent aside from the sounds of trains. The only other access to Colorow is via trails from Silver City, Toltec, and Vermilion.

Clarke is a clergyman who provides companionship to a woman feeling lonely. The woman admires certain aspects of Clarke's character but does not love him. Mr. Ward is introduced as the young driver of a mule-train from Boston. Mr. Ward is in the area for his health but admits he enjoys being there. Serviss observes the interaction between Viola and Mr. Ward with feelings of jealousy. Lambert is busy with new machinery and encourages Viola to show Serviss around. Viola feels embarrassed and self-conscious after Lambert jokes about her relationship with Serviss.

A series of throbbing raps came from the chair beneath her hand. Viola expressed fear of her grandfather's power and recounted a past experience of being thrown into a trance on a train. Morton expressed a desire to help Viola and suggested that a sitting may assist in understanding her. Viola indicated that inducing a trance was necessary to communicate with the voices. Clarke observed Viola's interaction with Morton with jealousy and disapproval. Morton's study was chosen for the test séance due to its secure exit and windows. Viola assisted in preparing for the séance, displaying eagerness and interest.

A young man rode behind two tired horses carrying a camp outfit. The young man was bareheaded and dressed like a plainsman. He smiled and bowed respectfully at a girl he saw while riding. The girl noticed the young man's strong and manly physique. The sunset scene evoked a joyful expression on the young man's face. The girl felt a desire to know more about the young man. Viola Lambert's mother expressed concern for her daughter's safety after dark.

The narrator describes a solitary task of plowing in the field. Franklin was assigned to herd cattle on harvested stubble and keep them out of the corn field. In October, the narrator became a corn-husker, and Franklin was promoted to plow. The narrator and Franklin had occasional respite during October and November due to cold rain. The narrator recalls buying a deck of playing cards from Metellus Kirby and the feelings associated with it. The narrator and his brother played cards in secret until their father discovered them and allowed them to play by the stove. The family eventually joined in playing cards, making rainy days less dreary.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The narrator's father and Professor Taft have fundamentally different lifestyles and interests. The narrator encourages Zulime to invite Professor Taft to West Salem despite the potential for disagreement. Don Carlos expresses pleasure at the invitation and promises to visit. The narrator and Zulime return to Wisconsin in April to find winter conditions with snow and frost. The father greets Zulime with tenderness and expresses his dislike for the house being empty. The father enjoys spending time in the garden and barn, finding comfort in the old place. Zulime appreciates the father's presence but wishes he would dress better when out in public.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The season's work included husking corn, which became more severe as the fields grew larger. In 1874, husking corn lasted well into November. The workers faced harsh weather conditions, including sleety rains and snow. Most boys did not own overcoats and wore the same suit for both summer and winter. Harriet and other women made their own dresses, with summer gowns typically made of white muslin. Addison Garland, the narrator's uncle, was a thoughtful and frail man who predicted future inventions and advised on farming. Garland introduced the family to graham flour, which replaced their usual bread, leading to mixed reactions.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: A smooth-handed faker sells prize boxes of soap and offers a dollar-back guarantee. The faker changes his wording to imply he can return dollars but does not guarantee it. A tall man lashes the faker across the face with a whip after realizing the deception. A little Scotchman beats the faker with a boot, causing him to fall from his carriage. The crowd disperses after the marshal arrives and takes the faker away. The narrator reflects on the contrast between their clean air and the tumult of the town. The narrator expresses a desire for a duster and faces resistance from their father regarding dress.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The narrator and a child named Mary Isabel enjoyed watching the sky and exploring nature. Mary Isabel was fascinated by snakes, bugs, worms, and spiders. The narrator built a 'House' in a maple tree for Mary Isabel to play in. The family experienced a sense of security and comfort in their home. The narrator made home improvements, including adding a bathroom and enlarging the dining room. The children slept together on a screened-in porch and asked the narrator questions about the universe. The narrator's father was becoming more reminiscent as time passed.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The narrator and their mother often reminisced about their life in Wisconsin. The narrator's father remained determined to improve their farming situation despite challenges. The narrator's mother began to help with household tasks despite her physical limitations. The narrator struggled with financial constraints and felt torn between staying on the farm and pursuing opportunities in Boston. A letter from the Secretary of the Cedar Valley Agriculture Society invited the narrator to speak at the County Fair, which pleased the family. The narrator planned to take their sister back to the seminary, with their mother's support despite the challenges. The sister, Jessie, was initially resistant to the idea of attending school in Osage.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The narrator felt confident and well-dressed after acquiring a new suit and accessories. The narrator switched from boots to shoes, reflecting a change in local fashion. The narrator and peers brought food from home, including doughnuts and bread, for their simple housekeeping. Burton expressed a desire to carry Ethel Beebe's books but never acted on it. Ethel Beebe was described as a slender, brown-eyed girl with a sense of humor. Burton frequently brought pies and cakes from Mrs. Babcock, leading to an unbalanced diet. The narrator kept a ledger documenting their low-cost self-boarding experiment.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The narrator visited Walt's room on the second story and felt resentment towards its unesthetic appearance. Walt was sitting in an armchair, wearing a broad Quaker hat, and was described as spotlessly clean. Walt had white hair, a light gray suit, and fine linen, which contributed to an impression of neatness. Walt spoke of his friends and enemies without rancor and exhibited a calm demeanor. The narrator felt that Walt was a significant literary personality after their meeting. The narrator's second visit to the West reinforced negative views about life on the plains. The narrator wrote a story titled _A Prairie Heroine_ and submitted it to the _Arena_, which accepted it and included a check for one hundred dollars.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The protagonist reflects on the nature of reality and the transitory aspects of life. He expresses a sense of futility regarding his concern for a girl he barely knows. The protagonist experiences a moment of exultation over his youth and the allure of love. Dr. Britt meets Kate for dinner and attempts to maintain a light atmosphere. Kate insists on discussing the situation involving Viola and her control, Clarke. Dr. Britt acknowledges his feelings of inadequacy regarding his inability to help Viola. Kate suggests a plan to rescue Viola, but Dr. Britt advises caution due to potential consequences.

Pratt is described as a selfish and brutal businessman. Viola feels trapped in her current living situation, which lacks wholesome conversation and privacy. Viola admires the housekeeping and decor of Kate's apartment. Clarke is perceived negatively by Viola, who sees him as a narrow-minded individual. Weissmann expresses interest in Miss Lambert and questions her role in Clarke's scientific pursuits. Clarke claims that Miss Lambert is the most marvelous psychic in the world. Weissmann criticizes Clarke for wanting to make Miss Lambert infamous instead of valuing her as a wife and mother.

The text describes a well-to-do Western mine-owner who is interested in a young girl named Viola. Viola's mother is a distinguished evangelist who subjected her daughter to convincing tests. Simeon Pratt sent a representative to investigate claims about Viola and her family. The detective reported that Viola and her family had a good reputation and were currently in Boston. Simeon Pratt attempted to persuade Viola to perform a sitting for him, but she initially refused. After sharing his personal sorrows, Viola agreed to a sitting, which Simeon reported as a remarkable experience. Simeon offered Viola and her mother hospitality in New York, ensuring her powers would remain private.

Simeon is known for entertaining women with unique talents. Viola's presence in Simeon's carriage sparked curiosity among his friends and the press. The news of Viola's association with Simeon spread quickly among the temple's followers. Clarke planned to use Viola's name for a public test of her abilities. Viola felt overwhelmed by her role in Pratt's household and resented her lack of personal time. Britt offered to help Viola escape from her situation but she declined his offer. Viola expressed her fears about the attention Clarke's plans would bring to her.

Burton's oratory skills were considered just by him. The New Opera House was filled with parents and friends for the first time during the 'Exercises'. The theme of the oration was 'Going West', inspired by the emigration fever. The oration was described as excited and florid, containing stirring ideas. The speaker experienced stage fright but managed to perform despite feeling emotional. Burton performed better than the speaker as he did not attempt oratorical flights. The principal showed reluctance to see the students leave, indicating his emotional attachment.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The first playground of its kind in Hamilton township was a tennis court. The narrator and others bought a lawn-mower, the second in the town. The narrator and others took down the old picket fence and planted trees and flowers. The narrator's book _Rose of Dutcher's Coolly_ received harsh criticism. The narrator spent July and August in Colorado and New Mexico, which influenced his writing. The narrator recorded impressions in a morocco-covered notebook during his travels. The narrator traveled to Santa Fé and Isleta with Charles Francis Browne and Hermon MacNeill.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The narrator's sister, Harriet, entered the Cedar Valley Seminary at Osage after a visit from a man who encouraged her desire for education. The narrator's father was reluctant to support Harriet's education, believing a district school education was sufficient for a farmer's needs. The Patrons of Husbandry, a social organization for farmers, was growing in the west during the years the narrator's family was on their new farm. The Grange Picnic, held annually on June 12, was a significant social event for the community, attracting many attendees. Families prepared for the Grange Picnic by cleaning and polishing their carriages or creating makeshift wagons for transportation. The County Fair, held in late September, became increasingly important as farming diversified and was considered a major event second only to the Fourth of July. The narrator's family enjoyed picnicking at the County Fair, bringing food prepared by their mother to eat while watching the races.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The narrator plans to return to Chicago after Thanksgiving to deliver lectures and continue writing. The narrator assures their mother that they can visit often and will come for Christmas. The narrator resides in a humble lodging on Elm Street, near Lake Michigan. The narrator has retained connections with periodicals such as Harper's and Century for income. The narrator believes Chicago will become the second great literary center of America. The narrator's first formal introduction to the literary and artistic circle occurs through a lecture on Impressionism in Art.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The uncle was stricken by a mysterious malady that also affected the narrator's mother. The uncle was lying motionless in his bed and had come down with a stroke without warning. Upon visiting, the narrator found the uncle sitting in a wheeled chair, helpless but cheerful. The uncle had been a man of dignity and abstemious habits, which were highlighted by his sudden helplessness. The narrator reflected on the uncle's past as a master of the threshing machine and a figure of admiration in his childhood. The narrator compared the uncle to Major Powell, noting their significance in the story of American pioneering. The narrator observed the decline of his mountain horse, Ladrone, who appeared weak and inactive.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The McClintocks signaled the start of the day's race with a musical sound that could be heard for miles. The threshing machine was either a 'J. I. Case' or a 'Buffalo Pitts' and was powered by five pairs of horses. The driver of the machine stood on a platform above the cog-wheels and had to maintain the correct speed of the horses. William and David were responsible for feeding the grain into the cylinder and maintaining the machine. The position of the feeder was highly regarded among boys, and Uncle David was admired for his skill in this role. The work environment included cold winds, flying dust, and the excitement of the threshing process. Ed Green was noted for his bravery while working near the tail of the stacker, despite the challenging conditions.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The narrator describes a summer spent in a mountainous area with clean air and beautiful scenery. Zulime, the narrator's wife, experienced a swift restoration to health during their stay. Louis Ehrich, a long-time friend of the narrator, contributed to their enjoyment during the visit. The Ehrichs invited the narrator and Zulime to a garden party at 'Glen Eyrie,' General Palmer's home. The journey to 'Glen Eyrie' involved driving through a beautiful garden and a narrow wooded canyon. The garden party featured a variety of guests and was hosted by General Palmer and his daughters. The setting of 'Glen Eyrie' combined elements of English architecture with native Colorado plants.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: Richard Garland has sold his farm in Green's Coulee to Mr. Speer. Mr. Speer intends to convert the farm into a model dairy farm. The narrator's mother is unhappy about leaving her home and family. Most of the narrator's mother's siblings live in the valley of the Neshonoc. The narrator's father is eager to move to Iowa, viewing it as a land of opportunity. The family debates emigration through a ballad sung by the mother. The father dismisses the mother's concerns about the dangers of moving.

The narrator feels relief after confronting their father about the need to return to their roots. Weissmann suggests using multiple senses and scientific methods to investigate spiritualistic claims. Throughout the journey, the narrator grapples with self-reproach for leaving their mother during a time of need. The narrator reflects on their past actions, feeling they have not given enough time and service to their mother.

text: Hamlin Garland began planning a trip to the Klondike in the spring of 1898 after finishing his book, LIFE OF ULYSSES S. GRANT. Garland dictated the story of his career, which became the basis of A SON OF THE MIDDLE BORDER. The manuscript was intended to chronicle the history of his family, the Garlands and the McClintocks, and the era of settlement from 1840 to 1914. A SON OF THE MIDDLE BORDER is a four-volume autobiography that took Garland fifteen years to write. Volume One of the autobiography is titled THE TRAIL MAKERS and is based on Garland's memories of pioneer life. The book was published by Grosset & Dunlap in August 1917 and has been reprinted multiple times since. The first chapter of the book describes Garland's childhood in a Wisconsin coulee during the year 1864.
