Miss Lambert reveals feelings of rebellion and hatred towards her current life and family dynamics. The speaker wishes to help Miss Lambert escape her suffering but acknowledges the control of her grandfather.

The protagonist experiences a profound emotional crisis after the death of his wife. He loses interest in material wealth and finds life to be futile without love. A delegation claiming to communicate with the dead brings him a message from his wife. He becomes a fervent spiritualist and decides to use his wealth to support spiritual causes. He builds a temple and hosts various spiritual practitioners at his home. He develops discernment in identifying fraudulent mediums and seeks to expose them. Viola Lambert is introduced to the protagonist through Clarke, who recognizes his generosity towards spiritual comforters.

Prospectors returned to the hotel from unclaimed territory, feeling jubilant after securing claims. The narrator expressed eagerness to stake a claim in the unclaimed land. The narrator traveled with a party of four, including Charles Babcock, to a pre-emption claim located by the narrator's father. The group camped in a rough shed built by the narrator's father after reaching the cabin. The narrator and Charles used a 'straddle-bug' as a monument to mark their claims. The presence of the straddle-bug protected the claims from being jumped by others for thirty days. The narrator felt a mix of joy and sadness about the settlement of the land, recognizing its impact on the natural environment.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The character is a traveler who comes from a long line of well-bred people. He is an analytical chemist and biologist who enjoys returning to nature after spending time in his laboratory. He has a preference for the deserts of Arizona and the mesas of New Mexico. He finds beauty in the mountains and the Continental Divide, which exceeds his expectations. He does not seek out strange women and is content with a brief encounter that leaves a lasting impression. Viola is a year-round resident who sometimes tires of her home during winter.

The narrator called for medical assistance for his child, particularly appealing to Doctor Evans. Doctor Evans diagnosed the child with diphtheria and stated that she needed antitoxin five days prior. The child's life was despaired of for forty-eight hours, during which a nurse provided constant care. The narrator experienced intense emotional turmoil and fear regarding his child's condition. The narrator's daughter, Mary Isabel, showed signs of recovery after a critical period of illness. The narrator felt a shift in his perspective on life and family after the ordeal with his daughter's illness. The narrator expressed a desire to return to the city for better medical care.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: Viola expresses frustration about a male character's behavior and threatens to leave the house if he does not improve his manners. Viola decides not to let the male character spoil her evening and focuses on enjoying her time with Clarke. Professor Serviss observes a significant change in Viola's demeanor, noting her transformation from a helpless state to one of confidence and radiance. Viola is dressed simply in pale blue and carries herself with a sense of authority that impresses Serviss. Kate expresses her admiration for Viola and wishes she had organized a larger gathering for her instead of a small dinner with scientists. Weissmann arrives at the dinner and shows marked interest in Viola, engaging her with compliments and attention. Kate attempts to facilitate conversation between Morton and Viola while managing the dynamics of the dinner party.

Tony expresses a strong refusal to allow a girl to go to another man. Tony appeals to Donald McLeod for intervention regarding the girl. Tony experiences a surge of emotions including fear, hate, and self-loathing. Mrs. Lambert tries to calm Tony and persuades him to return to his chamber. Pratt confronts Tony about his behavior and expresses anger over the disruption caused by Tony's speech. Pratt accuses Tony of being a hypocrite and threatens to expose him. Tony feels desolate after being threatened by Pratt and longs for the girl's companionship.

The narrator visited a hamlet that was six months old. Many men in the area were heading to the Jim River valley with hope for success. The narrator experienced a beautiful sunrise and felt connected to the new world. The narrator traveled by train to the James River valley, which appeared vast and flat. Aberdeen was the end of the train line and was near where the narrator's father was establishing a new home. The narrator walked across a treeless landscape and observed gulls gathering food. The narrator walked for two hours, watching Aberdeen fade into the horizon.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The pocket gopher created mounds of earth while mining the sod. Harriet and Frank returned to school, but the narrator remained to work on the farm. The narrator's father began fencing and breaking the sod of their homestead after planting on their rented land. Uncle David visited with a breaking plow and worked with the narrator's father to overturn the sod. The narrator's job included raking and burning brush while the men plowed the land. Various wildlife, including rattlesnakes and prairie wolves, were displaced as the land was cultivated. Neighbor Gammons and John Bowers were constructing a new home for the narrator's family.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The narrator experienced distress after witnessing a violent act against someone. The teacher noticed the narrator's distress and allowed them to leave school. The narrator ran home quickly, feeling pain and panic during the journey. Upon arriving home, the narrator was greeted by their dog, Rover. The narrator's mother reassured them that the situation was not as serious as they believed. The narrator's father became dissatisfied with their farming conditions over time. A merchant from LaCrosse initiated negotiations to purchase the family farm in 1868.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The narrator records significant events in his daughter's life in a diary each month. The daughter enjoys hearing about her past and asks her father if she was cute as a baby. She learns about Decoration Day, which she refers to as 'Flag Day,' and takes pride in her grand-sire's military service. The daughter participates in annual cemetery visits to honor veterans, unaware of the associated tragic concepts. The narrator expresses a sense of joy and rediscovery through his daughter's presence and innocence. The narrator's wife shows devotion to their daughter by designing clothes for her and caring for her during sickness. The daughter becomes seriously ill one September, leading to a moment of terror for the narrator.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The narrator describes their pink-mosquito-bar dress and vibrant demeanor. The second winter at the Seminary ended, leading to a return to farming activities. The narrator expresses difficulty in saying goodbye to companions Ella and Maud. The narrator and their peers became less interested in attending services at the school-house. A new pest, the chinch bug, threatened the wheat crop before harvest time. The narrator and Burton decided to hire a room and board to reduce expenses during the winter term. The narrator recalls the satisfaction of living independently with minimal furniture.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The narrator and Frank found a plank in a ditch that allowed them to slide down a track. They successfully coasted down the track with their valises, enjoying the experience. They passed workmen who expressed amazement and a superintendent who warned them to stop. After coasting down the track, they came to a halt above a station and left the plank behind. They tramped along the Amonoosuc River for two days, enjoying the scenery. They sought food and lodging at a farmhouse and a tavern before reaching the railway. They struggled to find jobs and faced hostility from local farmers as their money dwindled.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The narrator experienced indigestion and recalled memories associated with corn-husking days. The narrator's father insisted on husking corn on Thanksgiving Day to finish the harvest before a snowstorm. The narrator's mother prepared a turkey dinner that was fondly remembered. Zulime, the narrator's companion, spent time listening to comments from elderly women during family visits. Zulime received daily supper invitations and examined hand-made paintings with interest. The narrator was perceived unfavorably by some community members, who expressed doubts about his worthiness of Zulime. The narrator focused on writing and had little interest in the social activities of the younger generation in his village.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The author expresses concern about children crying for food in cities while fruits rot on the vines. The author traveled across the prairie with reformers, feeling that beneficial laws were about to be enacted. The author spoke at Populist picnics and traveled by freight train to various engagements. The author met an old neighbor, Cyrus, who expressed disillusionment about moving west. The author's parents attended a speech in Aberdeen, where they appeared preoccupied rather than attentive. The author's mother was slowly regaining the use of her limbs and expressed happiness for her son's success. Upon returning to Boston, the author felt a shift in their relationship with the city, perceiving it as less significant.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The narrator observes sightseers from an open window. A girl serves the narrator a poor breakfast. Lawyer Ricker is described as stately and bibulous with a red beard. Ricker is remembered for his lengthy courtroom speech about a horse-blanket theft. Ella McKee is recognized as a young woman resembling her sister Flora. David Babcock, an old farmer, expresses concern about the wheat crop. The narrator notes that many neighbors appear worn and sad.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The narrator reflects on the emotional impact of music, particularly the violin played by his Uncle's brother, David. The narrator's mother experiences a deep connection to northern melodies, while Aunt Susan and Maria prefer the human voice over mechanical instruments. The narrator decides to sing familiar songs for his family after putting away a machine that plays music. The narrator announces his departure, which causes his mother to react with silence and pain. The narrator has never worn a swallow-tail evening coat until his thirty-ninth year, which concerns his friends. The narrator associates the double-breasted black coat with dignity and professionalism, contrasting it with the swallow-tail suit. The social customs of the Columbian Exposition influence the narrator's perception of evening dress and conformity among artists.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The narrator could not live in any city and was unwilling to give up life in Chicago and New York for a permanent home in West Salem. The narrator received thirty-five hundred dollars from the serial use of _The Eagle's Heart_ and _Her Mountain Lover_, along with additional royalties. The narrator decided to invest in land in Oklahoma and purchased three hundred and twenty acres. Zulime was focused on the berry season and showed little interest in art or the Camp at Eagle's Nest. Zulime fell ill during a dry and hot July and was confined to bed for nearly three weeks. After Zulime recovered, they traveled to Colorado, experiencing extreme heat during the journey. Upon arrival in Colorado, they were welcomed by their friend Louis Ehrich and returned to the same room they had occupied on their wedding trip.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The old pioneer was found motionless on the floor of the barn. He had fallen while standing in the door waiting for the drayman. His heart had ceased to beat and he showed no signs of injury. The narrator and his uncle took the pioneer to the house and placed him on the couch. The narrator reflected on the pioneer’s life and influence over the past fifty years. The pioneer had lived for seventy years and moved westward from Maine. The narrator planned a soldier's funeral for the pioneer.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The young scientist expresses concern for Mrs. Lambert's emotional state. Mrs. Lambert believes that her daughter Viola is necessary to the spirit-world. The scientist believes that Viola's condition is desperate and could lead to insanity. Mrs. Lambert refuses to allow Viola to be treated by the scientist. The scientist claims to be open-minded about the spirit-world despite being a skeptic. The scientist offers to study Viola's psychic manifestations if they continue. Mrs. Lambert is alarmed by the scientist's intentions regarding her daughter.

The location described has transitioned from a center for miners and gamblers to a New England summer resort. The resort's economy is supported by a few large mines and the popularity of its mountains and medicinal springs. The mountains are known for their hot and cold waters, which are gaining recognition for their healing properties. Visitors to the area tend to keep their discoveries to themselves, leading to a slow spread of the location's fame. The community is beginning to appreciate its aesthetic surroundings, leading to the construction of log cabins. A young girl with gray eyes is depicted sitting beside a southern trail, feeling lonely and desolate while gazing at the sky. The girl is interrupted in her reverie by the arrival of two men and a small pack-train descending the mountain.

The narrator and his wife traveled to New York with thirty dollars. The narrator felt confident after a successful experience with a saw. The narrator and his companion were looking for Union Square and the Bowery. Broadway was described as being lined with low shops of red brick at that time. The narrator expressed concern about finding a place to sleep in New York. The narrator and his companion eventually found a small hotel on Fourth Avenue. They were given a room with half-windows at a discounted price.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The living room did not have a fireplace. The narrator expressed a desire for a fireplace, envying friends who had one. Zulime and the narrator had childhoods without fireplaces, using stoves and radiators instead. Zulime was hesitant about building a fireplace due to concerns about expense and the temporary nature of their stay. The carpenters and masons available lacked experience in building chimneys and traditional fireplaces. Mary Isabel, the narrator's daughter, had shown an interest in fireplaces from her experiences in other homes. The narrator decided to build a fireplace despite the challenges and limited space available.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: Viola Lambert has been experiencing trances since she was ten years old. Clarke is described as having a controlling influence over Viola and her mother. Viola's 'control' is identified as her grandfather, who instills fear in her. Viola is believed to be used as a medium for communication with spirits, including her father and first husband. There are concerns that a public challenge issued by Clarke could lead to Viola's exploitation by charlatans. Morton Serviss expresses a desire to protect Viola from potential harm due to her public exposure. Kate suggests inviting Viola and her family to dinner to observe her abilities in a private setting.

The narrator and his wife joined General Palmer's party for a trip to Cripple Creek. They traveled in General Palmer's private car, which delighted the narrator's wife. General Palmer invited them to join his camping party at Sierra Blanca for a week or two. Colorado Springs was hosting a Quarto-Centenary event with Vice-President Roosevelt as the chief guest. The Vice-President expressed a desire to meet the narrator's wife during his visit. The narrator accepted an invitation to breakfast with the Vice-President and other notable individuals.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The narrator and companions traveled from Portland to Bethel to visit a town described by their father. They planned to climb hills where their father had gathered berries and sit on the 'Overset' to view the landscape. In Locks Mills, they met old playmates of their father, Dennis and Abner Herrick, who were surprised by the narrator's tales of western life. The narrator and companions decided to shorten their stay in Locks Mills after feeling saddened by the locals' restricted lives. They sang and told stories in exchange for hospitality on their last night in Locks Mills. The group traveled to Gorham, eager to see the White Mountains, which they viewed as a test of their courage. While walking towards the peaks, they encountered a lonely old couple who provided them with food after a conversation.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: Bashford gave the narrator a card to Dr. Cross, a former parishioner in Jamaica Plain. The narrator decided to visit Dr. Cross despite dreading meeting another stranger. The ride to Jamaica Plain revealed the beauty of New England, with blooming apple orchards and lush lawns. Dr. Cross is described as a tall, thin man of about sixty years with dark eyes and a long gray beard. Dr. Cross had purchased a farm in Dakota through Mr. Bashford, which impressed the narrator. The narrator was invited to dinner by Dr. Cross's wife and left feeling more positive about the world. The narrator considered returning to work as a carpenter in Greenfield due to financial difficulties.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The article titled 'The Prairie in the Sky' was written for Harper's Weekly. The author reflects on a trip to high Colorado that inspired their literary career. The author collected a fragment of rock from the area to serve as a memory of the land. Lorado Taft introduced the author to his sister Zulime and artist Janet Scudder in Chicago. Zulime Taft was traveling to Paris to study sculpture for two years. The author expressed skepticism about the necessity of studying art in Paris. Miss Scudder defended the importance of Paris for an artist's education.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The dwelling described had rough plaster walls, a white pine floor, and scanty furniture. The family moved into their new house in September after completing it in July. Father was both carpenter and stone-mason during the construction of additional buildings. An old Englishman named Barker provided advice to Father while he was working on the well. The summer was marked by unprecedented dry conditions, leading to widespread fires in the region. Uncle David's stable burned down, and he narrowly escaped by burrowing through the side of the shed. The arrival of rain alleviated fears of fire, except for the memory of the Chicago fire.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The narrator recalls a childhood experience of following cows through tall grass and bushes at night. The narrator's father came to their rescue during a dangerous expedition, and the narrator does not remember being sent on a similar task afterward. The narrator's mother had less rigorous notions of training compared to the father. The narrator has vivid memories of winter, including snow drifts and the need for their father to dig trenches to reach the barn. The family engaged in various winter activities, such as shelling corn and quilting bees. The narrator found joy in a large apple thrown by Edwin Randal, which was a rare treat in their home. The narrator had a strong interest in reading, despite having few books, and was particularly moved by a poem in an agricultural report.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The narrator's right leg became lame, causing excruciating pain in the sciatic nerve. The narrator was determined to leave the Agency the next morning despite the pain. A trader offered to take the narrator to the railway, where he carried Navajo silver. The narrator reached Gallup at noon and spent the afternoon waiting for the train. The narrator caught the connecting train at Topeka and arrived at St. Joseph before the Burlington coaches from Chicago were due. The narrator surprised his wife at the station by taking charge of her valise as she stepped down from the Pullman car. The narrator gave his wife a silver bracelet from a Navajo silversmith, which she has worn for twenty-two years.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: Pratt expresses disapproval of Clarke's proposed challenge to the scientists. Clarke believes the press will not harm their reputation and will instead criticize the scientists. Pratt warns that the scientists will undermine him and disgrace Viola. Mrs. Lambert informs Pratt that Serviss is not married and has known Viola for nearly two years. Clarke realizes that Serviss is a young and attractive rival for Viola's affection. Clarke leaves the room in anger, feeling he has been foolish regarding Viola's feelings. Mrs. Lambert tells Viola they must leave the house immediately due to the ongoing conflict.

The narrator had no desire to go West and fight Indians or engage in criminal activities. Deacon Garland expressed strong disapproval of the narrator's reading choices. The narrator read a variety of materials, including _Paradise Lost_, which was challenging but enjoyable. The narrator observed significant changes on the farm, including fenced land and cultivated pastures. The narrator noted the decline of wildlife and natural beauty in the prairie due to settlement. The transition from farm to village life included continuing agricultural activities despite living in a town. Osage, a small town, was perceived by the narrator as both mysterious and dangerous due to the presence of a hostile group.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The narrator contemplates a decision between two social paths, one represented by non-conformists like Walt Whitman and the other by figures like Lowell and Howells. The narrator considers changing his appearance, including shortening his beard and adopting formal attire, to fit into social circles. The narrator feels excluded from social events and is influenced by friends who suggest that desirable women prefer men in evening dress. Zangwill advises the narrator to conform to social expectations, stating that formal attire makes authors indistinguishable from wealthy individuals. Howells suggests that the narrator buy an evening suit in England to justify his change in attire upon returning to Chicago. The narrator's decision to conform reflects broader social changes among young men in the West, indicating a shift away from traditional customs. The narrator experiences a sense of calm during his departure for England, which later transforms into exaltation as he observes the ocean.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The narrator's family arrived at a small house in Mitchell County. The father, mother, and two daughters left to stay with Uncle David, while the narrator and his brother stayed with a hired man. The narrator woke up to a new landscape that included a level plain and a low stone house a mile away. The hired man prepared cornmeal mush for breakfast, which the narrator ate. The family began setting up their new home upon the return of the parents and sisters. A herd of horses appeared on a hill, led by a sorrel pony, which delighted the narrator. The narrator and his brother spent their early days on the prairie getting to know the area and keeping cattle from straying.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: Marsh Harvester was not yet in general use. The McCormick required four horses to drag it and was effective. The narrator was promoted from 'bundle boy' to a binder at the age of fourteen. The narrator experienced physical strain while binding sheaves in the heat. Harriet brought the narrator a lunch consisting of milk, cheese, and fried-cakes. The narrator took a break to enjoy nature while resting during lunch. The noon meal consisted of boiled beef and potatoes, consumed quickly by the workers.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: Theodore Roosevelt was the Assistant Secretary of the Navy in January 1898. Henry B. Fuller visited Washington in January and provided detailed reports of his explorations. The author planned to start an expedition to the Yukon in April. John Hay was described as a compact and sturdy man with a clear complexion and a fine black beard streaked with white. General Longstreet was observed by the author in Washington, appearing as a deaf, hesitant old man. The author expressed a longing for the open air and wilderness as spring approached. The author collected cooking utensils, a sleeping bag, and pack saddles in preparation for a journey.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: Zulime decided to return to Chicago at the beginning of February. The last notable event attended by the narrator's wife was an open meeting of the National Institute of Arts and Letters. Howells presided over the program at the meeting and expressed regret about the narrator's wedding journey nearing its end. The narrator and Zulime traveled west the day after the meeting, feeling a need for retirement. The narrator faced challenges regarding his living situation, as he only had a bachelor apartment on Elm Street. The narrator's mother wrote to inform him that his aunt was very ill and needed him. Zulime insisted on accompanying the narrator to the Homestead despite the difficult circumstances.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The conversation involves characters named Julia, Clarke, Serviss, Tolman, Lambert, and Viola. Clarke is described as a crazy fool but not a cheater. Viola is committed to Clarke and feels that as a medium, nobody else would want her. Serviss expresses concern for Viola's mental state due to her spiritualistic faith. Lambert believes that Pratt may intercept visitor cards and control who sees his daughter. The servant informs Lambert and Serviss that the ladies are out and Mr. Pratt is engaged. Lambert insists on waiting for the ladies to return despite the servant's indication that they may be out late.

The narrator and his wife covered the coffin of a deceased individual with a flag instead of flowers. The deceased was remembered as a serene, white-haired veteran who taught his granddaughters to revere the flag. The narrator reflects on the lives of Isabel McClintock and Richard Garland, as well as other settlers from the period between the Civil War and World War I. The narrator expresses reluctance to publish his manuscript, acknowledging its imperfections and omissions. The narrator and his family moved from the La Crosse Valley to the East, leaving behind their childhood home. The narrator's daughters, Constance and Mary Isabel, are described as carrying forward the traditions of their ancestors. The family retains ownership of their old homestead, which holds significant memories for them.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: Clarke expresses suspicion regarding the nature of a woman's work. The conversation involves a discussion about the immortality of the soul. Serviss states that chemistry does not concern itself with the soul. Clarke believes that scientists ignore spiritism and remain ignorant of messages from the dead. Serviss argues that the question of immortality is insoluble and prefers to focus on practical scientific matters. Serviss expresses concern that Clarke's views are negatively affecting a young woman's happiness. Serviss plans to advise the girl's parents to send her away for musical studies.

The narrator reflects on memories associated with spring and gardens while contemplating a long journey. The narrator's mother experiences emotional distress over her son's impending departure. The mother spends her time observing daily activities around the homestead. The narrator feels a sense of obligation to continue with the journey despite his mother's feelings. Burton Babcock arrives at Ashcroft on the Canadian Pacific Railway to join the narrator for the trip. The narrator notices changes in both himself and Babcock since their childhood. Local citizens express concern about the difficulties of the journey the narrator and Babcock are about to undertake.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The narrator's mother was responsible for caring for two invalids and a fretful husband. The narrator's aunt was in a state of decline and was expected to pass away soon. The narrator's mother preferred to have her family close and enjoyed their company while she engaged in activities like sewing. Susan Garland, the narrator's aunt, passed away peacefully after a prolonged period of suffering. Susan Garland was the last of the narrator's father's immediate family and left him a small estate upon her death. The inheritance provided the narrator's father with a sense of security and independence that he had sought for over sixty years. The narrator's father experienced a significant change in character, becoming more relaxed and less worried about the weather and its effects on his life.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The narrator experiences satisfaction while driving a car up a hill, contrasting it with the past struggles of his team of cattle. The narrator receives an invitation to a 'Home Coming of Iowa Authors' and is encouraged by a companion to accept it. The narrator reflects on the inadequacy of his study, which has been in disrepair since a fire two years prior. The narrator expresses a desire to move his family to New York for better opportunities as a writer, contingent on his father's wishes. On October 20th, the narrator's father discusses his will and expresses concern about leaving his children behind. The family plays cards together, and the narrator's young daughter, Constance, wins against her grandfather, which pleases him. The narrator observes his father the next morning, noting his lack of alertness and later receives a call from his uncle Frank.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: Serviss was startled by the song 'The Banks of Loch Lomond' during a séance. Clarke was managing the séance and asked Serviss to sit beside the psychic, Viola. Serviss felt a strong desire to wake Viola during the séance. A tapping sound occurred during the séance, followed by a voice offering Serviss a chance to solve a mystery. Serviss touched Viola's wrist, causing her to convulse and cry out. Clarke admonished Serviss for mishandling the psychic, stating that her nervous system was under tension. The mother of Viola attempted to soothe her after the incident.

A calf lay beside its dam while an ancient bull stood apart. A large black bull, weighing two thousand pounds, moved restlessly among other bulls. The bulls exhibited aggressive behavior, growling and snarling at each other. There were fewer than two hundred bison remaining, representing a once vast population in America. The town of Missoula was abuzz with news of nearly three million dollars in gold-dust arriving from Alaska. The gold was reportedly mined from the Klondike region of the Yukon River. Merchants in coastal towns began advertising Klondike-related goods in anticipation of a gold rush.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The narrator corresponded with several classmates while concealing personal struggles. The narrator participated in singing at the County Jail with the Band of Hope. The narrator decided to become a carpenter, referencing an apprenticeship with their grandfather. The narrator worked as a laborer to earn money for tools, starting with grading work. The narrator experienced physical pain and exhaustion during the first days of labor. After a week of labor, the narrator bought tools and began working as a carpenter. The narrator gained strength and skill while working with a crew on construction projects.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The narrator awoke to a woman's scream and the sound of rushing feet. Zulime informed the narrator that Fan had set the house on fire. The narrator observed that half of the kitchen floor was already consumed by flames. The narrator attempted to use a garden hose to extinguish the fire but was unsuccessful. The narrator called for help from the porch but received no response. The narrator gathered important manuscripts and threw them out of a window for safety. A neighbor's wife assisted the narrator by bringing a valise to collect the manuscripts.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The narrator expresses a desire to take their uncle on a wilderness expedition. The uncle shows enthusiasm for the idea and offers to help with tasks during the trip. The narrator's mother expresses a sentiment of farewell, believing she may not return to the area. Aunt Lorette has passed away, and Uncle Frank is now living alone in the village. The narrator and Zulime plan a trip to Yellowstone and intend to camp independently. They travel from Bismark to Fort Yates across a dry prairie landscape. The couple crosses the Muddy Missouri River in a small rowboat and later dines at a boarding house.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: Zulime's two helpers were daughters of a neighboring farmer. Zulime was startled when one of the helpers took her seat at the table. My aunt, Susan Bailey, joined the table, adding to the scrutiny of the bride. My father declared Zulime as the captain of the household and offered her control over the kitchen. Zulime expressed a desire not to be the captain but was encouraged by my father to take charge. My father described the breakfast menu, which included steak, doughnuts, and buckwheat cakes. Zulime expressed her fondness for my mother and father after breakfast.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: Viola is considered innocent by the narrator. The narrator suspects his sister, Kate, may be involved in an imposture. The narrator expresses disbelief in the survival of the soul after death. The narrator distrusts Clarke and is concerned about his influence over Viola. The narrator fears that Viola's reputation may be damaged by a preacher. Clarke protests Viola's intention to leave Pratt's house. Viola expresses her dislike for Clarke and his associates.

The expedition lasted seventy-nine days in the wilderness. The travelers faced numerous challenges including flies, mosquitoes, rain, and difficult terrain. Burton demonstrated exceptional endurance and loyalty throughout the journey. On the seventy-ninth day, the travelers reached the Third Fork of the Stickeen River without finding gold. At Glenora, the travelers camped for two weeks to allow their horses to recover. The original plan was to continue to Teslin Lake, but the narrator decided to return home due to a letter from his mother.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The clergyman insists on being present at each sitting as the historian of the case. Clarke states that sittings must take place in Pratt's library with his presence. Morton advises against Clarke's terms to avoid branding Miss Lambert as an impostor. Viola expresses enjoyment of the evening despite being restrained during the tests. Clarke appears less admirable in appearance when leaving compared to when he was indoors. Weissmann reflects on the performance and suggests that next time Clarke and the mother must be eliminated. text: The narrator has a farm in Winnesheik, located on the edge of Looking Glass Prairie. The narrator's grandfather expresses a desire to spend his last days with his family in Neshonoc. David, the narrator's brother, expresses a desire to move west after their father and Frank are settled on a farm. The family celebrates their last Thanksgiving festival together, with oysters as the main dish. The narrator's mother sings a song that reflects her feelings of loss regarding the move. The narrator's father is portrayed as an explorer and pioneer, while the women express a more wistful sentiment.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The narrator expresses a desire to establish a ranch in Oklahoma. The narrator plans to keep saddle horses and cattle on the ranch. The narrator writes to his brother in Mexico to invite him to Oklahoma to manage the ranch. The family returns to Wisconsin during the summer when The Old Homestead is flourishing. The narrator's mother expresses a belief that she has a short time to live. The narrator's mother desires to see her grandchild. The family takes a drive to visit Frank McClintock, which is significant for the narrator's mother.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The narrator spent two hours each afternoon discussing the laws of dramatic art with Brown after school. The narrator read every listed book or article on expression and translated several French authorities for Brown. The narrator's weekly expenses exceeded five dollars due to theater and Boston Symphony concert attendance. The narrator felt a lack of financial support while gaining an education that he believed would be valuable. The narrator described New York, Chicago, Washington, and Philadelphia in terms of their cultural resources. The narrator experienced physical decline and longed for spring and sunshine during the winter months. The narrator visited his friend Bashford in Portland, which was his first sea voyage.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The narrator was left in charge of the farm and its tools while the owner drove away each morning. The owner communicated orders to the hired men through the narrator and supervised their actions. During the harvest, the owner took command in the field due to the rough nature of the harvest help. The harvest help consisted of nomads from the south who arrived in July and left in September. Some of the harvest hands had negative views of women, which shocked the narrator and his brother. The narrator and his brother were disturbed by the crude stories shared by the harvest hands. Saturday nights in town were associated with drunkenness and rowdy behavior among the harvest hands.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: Shane recalled his past breakfast experiences, specifically mentioning buckwheat cakes and sausages. The men discussed their past experiences as skilled laborers, including reaping and wood-chopping. Stevens noted that during their youth, they had good health and faith in the future despite lacking money. Lottridge claimed that there were no old people in their earlier days. The group played a game of 'Rummy' in the evening as a distraction from their current lives. The narrator contrasted the courage of the veterans with the attitudes of certain city men. St. Gaudens shared his experiences at the Club, including his dietary regrets and work with President Roosevelt.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: Viola expressed discomfort when speaking with a man whose eyes disturbed her. The man inquired if Viola had forgiven him for his actions the previous night. Viola mentioned that a painful contraction she experienced during a sitting was brief. The man claimed his entrance to the sitting was unplanned and he acted on impulse. Viola and the man reflected on their past interactions and shared memories. Viola revealed her feelings of being despised for being a medium. Mrs. Lambert attempted to counter Viola's negative perception of her social interactions.

Britt has studied old Randall's notes regarding a girl who is experiencing mental weakness. Britt believes that the girl's condition has worsened over the years and that she may benefit from joining Clarke. Serviss expresses frustration over the lack of authority to intervene in the girl's situation. Clarke is planning to publish something soon. Serviss reflects on the negative impact Clarke has on the girl's life. Weissmann discusses the complexities of spiritualism and its belief among many people. Weissmann shares an experience of witnessing an unaccountable phenomenon in his own chamber.

Charles Babcock and Albert Button arrived at the school-house with bob-sleds to take the entire school on an expedition. The Burr Oak School was larger than the narrator's school and was located near a forest and a deep ravine. The narrator first saw Bettie, Hattie, and Agnes during the visit to the Burr Oak School. Bettie and Hattie were fair-haired and blue-eyed, while Agnes had dark hair and black eyes. Expressions of affection were generally avoided in the narrator's community, with restraint being the norm. Social changes were occurring, with fewer community gatherings and more focus on work on new farms. Singing among young people was mostly limited to hymn-tunes, with the Moody and Sankey Song Book being popular.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The narrator began rebuilding and redecorating a house in October in preparation for their mother's arrival. The narrator purchased new furnishings and hired staff, including a cook and maid, for the home. The narrator met their mother at the station on November first and brought her to the newly outfitted home. The narrator's father arrived a couple of weeks later, prompting the mother to send out dinner invitations to family. The dinner included family members such as William, Frank, Lorette, Deborah, and Susan, but some were absent. The dinner featured various foods, and the family engaged in conversations about the past and present. The gathering included reflections on losses experienced over the years, as many family members had passed away.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The narrator and their family traveled to LaCrosse, a city located on the bank of a wide river. LaCrosse served as a port for steamboats during the summer months. The family crossed a narrow bridge over a dangerous current of open water while traveling. They spent the night in Hokah, a small town in a deep valley. The next day, they reached Caledonia, which consisted of a few frame houses and a grocery store. They arrived at a house belonging to a man named Barley, who was identified as a Quaker. The family settled in a log cabin two miles west of Hesper, which became a place of exploration for the children.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The narrator's mother prepared food, including potatoes and onions. The narrator's father worked with a team to draw off wheat, hogs, and hay. The narrator and their sister walked to school along paths made by farmers' bob-sleighs. The narrator owned a sled made of hickory, built by the village blacksmith. The family prepared for a migration, which surprised the narrator when it occurred. The narrator's mother expressed concern about leaving their home for an unknown destination. The family traveled in a sleigh, led by the father with the big bob-sled.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The character played the fiddle but found less joy in it due to stiffened fingers. Aunt Lorette, the character's wife, complained about being lame but prepared a chicken dinner. Aunt Lorette aimed to please Zulime and tried to live up to her expectations. Aunt Lorette's life had been characterized by hard work and a cheerful disposition despite challenges. The character and his family enjoyed a summer afternoon in the valley, appreciating its beauty. Uncle Frank expressed a desire to explore the wilderness, specifically grizzly bear country. The character's father expressed a desire to travel by steamboat and visit Yellowstone Park.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The mother of Viola made no objection to Serviss's interest in her daughter. Serviss and Viola rode up the mountain road side by side. Viola outlined her plans for a musical education during their conversation. Viola plays in the church of Reverend Mr. Clarke, who teaches her music. Reverend Mr. Clarke's wife passed away the previous year. Viola's father passed away when she was eleven years old. Viola's mother used to be a spiritualist and is now studying theosophy.

The narrator expresses a desire to recapture the Spirit of the Sunset found by their father in Central Minnesota in 1858. The narrator reflects on their responsibilities as the head of the house while planning a dangerous adventure into Alaska. The narrator's mother is living alone on a bleak farm in Dakota, while their father is also isolated and caring for horses. The narrator has not communicated with Miss Zulime Taft for over four years but learns she plans to return home during the summer. The narrator notifies Babcock to meet them in Ashcroft, British Columbia, on April 15th for an exploration trip. The narrator's mother expresses concern about the dangers of the planned exploration, which affects the narrator's enthusiasm. The narrator decides to return to writing fiction after completing their historical writing.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The cattle herding task required one boy from each farm to mount a horse at five o'clock every afternoon. The narrator and his brother took turns herding cattle and learned to ride well. The narrator observed the behavior and communication of cattle, gaining an understanding of their psychology. The herd would respond to a lone steer’s warning cry with alertness and urgency. The narrator became familiar with the flora and fauna of the open country while herding cattle. The meadows were described as beautiful and filled with various plants and wildlife. The narrator and Harriet would gather flowers in the meadows, experiencing a sense of joy and satisfaction.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: Morton assumed the opposite position when confronted by a true believer. Kate entered the room and reproached Morton for arguing. Kate informed Mr. Clarke that Viola wanted to sit for them. Morton was displeased that Clarke did not oppose Viola's request. Viola expressed a desire for an immediate test with her 'guides.' Viola described feeling a change in her state, from happiness to pallid languor. Serviss reassured Viola that he would be pleased to sit and talk with her.

The narrator expresses a sense of joy in traveling and experiencing the scenery. The narrator's goal was to obtain a teaching position, but efforts to apply were unsuccessful. The narrator traveled to Wabasha and then to a small town to visit relatives. The narrator arrived at the home of Mrs. Harris with only three cents. The narrator attempted to walk to a nearby village to seek a teaching position but was unsuccessful. The narrator experienced hunger and cold while reflecting on their situation. The narrator felt a sense of shame and mental suffering when seeking help from others.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: Zulime Taft and Hamlin Garland began their journey together in Springs. Hamlin Garland presented Zulime Taft with a view of Pike's Peak on a November morning. Zulime expressed genuine surprise and delight at the beauty of Pike's Peak. Gustave, the coachman for Louis Ehrich, met Hamlin Garland and Zulime at the Colorado Springs platform. Louis and Henriette Ehrich welcomed Zulime and Hamlin into their home for breakfast. The Ehrichs provided a hospitable environment for the newlyweds during their stay. Hamlin Garland planned to show Zulime the Crestones and Marshall Pass before returning to Wisconsin for Thanksgiving.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The narrator's wife maintained a positive outlook despite the decay of the previous generation. The narrator intended to base his next novel on the conflict at Cripple Creek between Free Miners, Union Miners, and Operators. The idea for the novel was inspired by a young boy's enthusiasm for miners, Indians, and cowboys during a visit to New York City. The narrator planned to create a story about a New York girl who is taken to Colorado and involved in miner conflicts. The novel was titled _Hesper, or the Cowboy Patrol_ and aimed to depict the role of cattlemen as allies of union miners during the Cripple Creek War. The narrator expressed that he had moved away from the themes of his earlier work, _Main Traveled Roads_, and felt it would be false to repeat that tone. In 1902, the narrator returned to the mountain West to depict a new conflict in his writing.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The threshing machine could not operate simultaneously for all farmers, requiring them to exchange labor with neighbors. During the autumn months, the sound of the threshing machine was prominent in the valleys. The narrator and his brother eagerly anticipated the arrival of the threshers when they were eight and six years old, respectively. The threshers arrived at night, and the narrator's father used a lantern to guide them through the gate. The narrator and his brother were instructed to go to sleep to prepare for an early morning. They awoke at dawn to the sounds of the men preparing the threshing machine and the smell of breakfast. The scene outside was characterized by frost, the sounds of horses, and the men preparing for work as dawn broke.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: Showers of rain alternated with sunshine in the described setting. The narrator's young wife is anticipating motherhood. The couple's homestead is perceived as growing in beauty and significance. Nature is depicted with active butterflies and busy bees. The narrator reflects on the aging population of the village. The narrator has lived a transient life before settling down. The village is characterized as a resting place for aging farmers and their wives.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: Serviss felt that sharing his experience with his sister increased the importance of his doubt regarding Viola. Kate questioned the impossibility of Viola having psychic powers and criticized the scientific community's certainty. Serviss expressed his discontent towards the unlovely aspects of Viola's life and his conflicted feelings about her. Morton found the journals related to Viola's faith to be poorly written and filled with inane content. Morton viewed the advertisements for psychics and mediums as distasteful and reflective of a morbid human condition. Viola was compared to an actress who shares in the struggles and envy of the dramatic profession.

Viola accepted an invitation to dinner from Kate without consulting her mother or Clarke. Mrs. Lambert expressed hope that Tony would feel like going to the dinner. Clarke received the invitation but did not want to attend due to curiosity about the hosts. Viola insisted on attending the dinner despite Clarke's objections. Pratt was unhappy about Viola's plans to attend the dinner because he had invited friends to see her that evening. Viola expressed frustration about being restricted and compared her situation to that of a convict. Mrs. Lambert supported Viola's desire to go out for dinner, stating they had not been out much since arriving.

Kate was involved in a struggle and was being strangled. Clarke instructed everyone to be quiet and take their hands off Kate. Mrs. Lambert expressed confidence that Kate was giving herself up. A series of raps on a cone indicated the presence of a spirit named Waltie. The table began to move as if pushed by Kate's feet. Morton felt resentment towards the situation and tightened his thread. A horn floated in the air and touched Kate, causing her to react.

The girl experienced violent manifestations until the age of sixteen, after which she went away to school. Joe Lambert married the girl's mother. The girl's mother was resigned and content with the return of her deceased family members. The girl received letters while at school detailing embarrassing returns of the 'spirits.' The girl faced torment during vacations due to the persistent presence of 'Waltie.' Clarke is preparing to renounce his pulpit to write a book on 'spiritism,' using the girl as a source for his work. Serviss attempted to take care of the girl but was not allowed by Mrs. Lambert and Clarke.

Weissmann and his assistant Morton had a restless night before their lunch meeting. Weissmann invited Tolman to join him and Morton for lunch to discuss their work. Tolman is described as a neat, blond man with fashionable clothing and beautiful hands. During lunch, Weissmann expressed his doubts about a recent test and its implications regarding a girl involved. Serviss, another participant, was concerned about the girl's potential as a trickster. Tolman provided insights on the influence of the preacher and the mother on the girl. The discussion included topics on hypnotism, suggestion, and the nature of phenomena related to spiritism.

The head of the Ethnological Bureau was a somber and silent figure. Edward Eggleston lived in a small brick house near the Congressional Library. Eggleston was known for his humor and was often surrounded by listeners. The author and Eggleston shared a common interest in the Western prairie. The author had a dinner with Theodore Roosevelt and Henry Adams where they discussed issues in Kansas, Nebraska, and Dakota. Roosevelt expressed enjoyment in having a knowledgeable guest at his table. The author had given up shooting, while Roosevelt enjoyed hunting.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The food being prepared was enough to feed all the Eagle's Nest campers. Only the McClintocks were expected for dinner, which included Uncle William, Aunt Maria, Frank, Lorette, and Deborah. Maria was not well enough to attend dinner due to the rain. Zulime was able to play old songs on the piano, which pleased the older relatives. The gathering was marked by a spirit of Thanksgiving despite its small size. Zulime expressed her enjoyment of being with the family and hoped they liked her. The morning after their arrival, breakfast was served at seven, which Zulime found challenging.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: Birds flying north provided joy to the narrator. The sand-hill crane was the last bird to migrate north and signaled the arrival of summer. The narrator experienced hunger while working in the field and looked forward to mid-day meals. The narrator's father was energetic and kept track of tasks without showing weariness. The afternoon brought a change in the environment, making the ground warmer and the sky more pleasant. The narrator found moments of respite while working, appreciating the beauty of nature. The prairie spring revealed various natural phenomena, including migrating geese and nesting ground sparrows.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: Maxwell, Richet, and Lombroso recognized the existence of a 'psychic force' in certain cases. The spiritist faith was deemed unacceptable as a working hypothesis by the individual discussed. Meyers proposed that raps, movements, and voices could be related to the subconscious mind. Maxwell concluded that mysterious phenomena are due to a natural force within the minds of sitters. Hypnotism has been used to study various cases of hallucinations and apparent abnormalities. The trance state is not necessary for hypnotism, and subjects do not follow improper suggestions. The mind's subliminal life is considered infinite and subtle, while consciousness limits its potentialities.

Mina cannot understand English but can understand any language and speak only in her native tongue. Clarke and Serviss conducted a test involving simultaneous speaking and voice communication. Mrs. Lambert allowed Kate to cover her mouth during the test to facilitate the experiment. R.M. Waldron, Viola's father, expressed concern about his daughter's reluctance in her mediumship work. Waldron hoped that after a public test, they would demand less from Viola. Clarke proposed organizing a committee to test Viola's powers in exchange for canceling a public demonstration. Viola experienced a paroxysm during the session, indicating a significant event was about to occur.

Clarke questions the mechanism by which drugs affect cells. The composition of the germ of tetanus is described as a minute bar with a spore at the end. The elemental composition of plasm remains a mystery despite scientific advancements. The preacher expresses a belief in a new form of spiritism as a coming religion. Serviss argues that matter is not inert but is permeated with life and force. Serviss has not investigated spirit manifestations but is informed about morbid psychology. The preacher accuses scientists of being dogmatic and bigoted like theologians.

The speaker lectured at the Young Men's Union on 'The Philosophy of Expression.' The speaker expressed surprise and delight at the lecturer's positive tone and epigrammatic phrases. The lecturer invited the speaker to visit him at his office the following morning. The speaker visited the lecturer's office located at No. 7 Beacon Street. The lecturer offered the speaker a place in his school without requiring tuition. The school attended by the speaker had around seventy or eighty pupils, mostly girls from New England and Canada. The speaker was asked by Professor Brown to assist in reading the proof-sheets of his new book.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: Dr. Serviss believes that the young woman can become as normal as any other girl due to her good physical health. Dr. Serviss is confident in his ability to free the young woman from her trances if she breaks all ties to her 'controls.' Dr. Serviss emphasizes the importance of the young woman's sovereignty over her soul and mind. The young woman expresses concern about the potential consequences of cutting ties with her mother. Dr. Serviss insists that the young woman must sever all associations from her past, including her relationship with her mother, to live a full life. The young woman feels comforted by Dr. Serviss's presence and expresses trust in him. Dr. Serviss is motivated by the challenge of the young woman's case and is willing to invest his resources in her investigation.

The narrator expresses envy and discontent regarding the clothing of peers, particularly John Cutler and Arthur Peters. John Cutler owned three neckties and wore broad cuffs with engraved gold buttons. The narrator describes a gradual loss of fear regarding entering chapel, preferring to stay behind a taller classmate. The narrator enjoyed school and participated in various activities, including a debating society and games. During winter, the narrator appreciated the comfort of their home and the absence of difficult outdoor tasks. Wendell Phillips lectured in town, but the narrator found the experience disappointing compared to expectations. The narrator preferred a temperance lecturer named Beale for his passionate oratory style.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The soldier laid off his heavy army shoes in the little front room. The mother brought a pillow for the soldier to rest his head on the floor. The soldier requested hot biscuits, honey, and plenty of coffee to eat. The family went out to the barn to watch the mother milk the cow. The narrator recalls feeling a deep connection to the soldier, who is revealed to be his father. The earliest memory of the narrator includes sitting on the doorstep with his sister Harriet during mid-summer. The narrator's house was a small frame cabin on the eastern slope of a ridge facing a wide valley.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: Miss Taft demonstrated versatility in painting, modeling, cooking, and sewing. As Stewardess, Miss Taft managed marketing and organized the kitchen during chaotic times. Discussions about art occurred at the table and on the bluff, with Miss Taft participating without losing her temper. The narrator reflects on a peaceful time before World War I, characterized by a lack of fear and social unrest. The narrator shared moments with Zulime, including a walk in the woods and a horseback excursion. The narrator read pages of a manuscript to Zulime, expecting and receiving favorable comments. The narrator planned to make improvements to the homestead, including adding a new dining room and an extra story.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: Pratt is immobilized and Serviss feels joy as he perceives Clarke's determination. Clarke claims his actions have been for the good of the world. Lambert tells Clarke that he has been a curse to Julia and that she looks older since leaving the valley. Clarke expresses his love for Viola and claims that spirit forces have promised her to him. Viola descends the stairs, eager to flee, and Clarke laments her departure. Serviss intervenes to prevent Clarke from following Viola as she leaves. Viola expresses terror and entreaty, stating that they are calling her and will not let her go.

The narrator inquires if Mr. Howells is available and is informed that he is at dinner. The narrator presents a letter of introduction and is shown to a reception room by a colored porter. Mr. Howells enters the room and greets the narrator with a cordial tone. Mr. Howells listens intently as the narrator discusses their theory of literature and the importance of the local novel. The narrator expresses the belief that American literature must be national and reflect local conditions. Mr. Howells compliments the narrator's work and encourages them to finish and publish their essays. The narrator feels satisfaction from Mr. Howells' praise, recognizing his status as a leader in the naturalistic school of fiction.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The narrator expresses admiration for Wolf Voice, who rode back to Fort Custer with them. Wolf Voice, Two Moon, American Horse, and Porcupine were influential in the narrator's writing of _The Captain of the Gray Horse Troop_. The narrator and their companion traveled to the Flat Head Reservation to see a herd of buffalo. The herd of buffalo is owned by Michel Pablo and consists of about two hundred animals. The buffalo are not confined and roam freely, feeding as they need food or water. The narrator describes the landscape as primeval and unmarked by human cultivation. The narrator and their brother successfully locate the buffalo in the valley.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The girl expresses her frustration about staying in the house and doubts her father's intentions. Mrs. Lambert is horrified by her daughter's change in attitude and believes she is possessed by an earth-bound spirit. Clarke approaches Julia to deliver a message to Viola, appearing pale and distressed. Clarke expresses his deep emotional pain over Viola's actions and fears losing her. Mrs. Lambert tries to comfort Clarke, suggesting that Viola's behavior is just a temporary mood. Clarke becomes increasingly agitated about Viola's interactions with another man, Pratt. Viola refuses to allow her mother to come to her and reflects on her feelings about Clarke and Pratt throughout the night.

Primeau stopped his team near the bank of a creek to point out an old man sitting on a mound. The old man was described as wrinkled with age, wearing ragged clothing, and had a sad expression. He was mourning the death of his grandson and had been wailing for a long time. Slohan, the old man, was a former leader of Sitting Bull's bodyguard. Later in the afternoon, Slohan approached on a pony and appeared less despairing. Slohan spoke about his chief's role in the wars against the white man, using both speech and sign language. The narrator expressed a desire to share Slohan's story of Sitting Bull.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The trees that were planted grew into a grove and a garden provided small fruits and vegetables. Farm machinery improved, but the housework burden on the mother increased. The mother performed most of the housework, including cooking, sewing, washing, churning, and nursing. Neighbors frequently called for Isabelle Garland in times of trouble. David owned a long-barreled rifle that remained unused in the kitchen. The ideals of the countryside changed, and hunting became less significant. Threshing time became more of a job with hired hands, and David participated with his machine.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The preacher expressed a strong opinion against spiritualism and psychic phenomena. The preacher and Serviss discussed the nature of X-rays and light. Serviss suggested that the discussion was detracting from their vacation. Viola was asked to play music to lighten the atmosphere. Clarke interrupted Viola's playing, suggesting she was affected by the previous discussion. Clarke sang 'The Banks o' Ben Lomond' with notable beauty. Serviss complimented Clarke's voice and encouraged him to sing more, while Clarke stated his voice was meant for religious service.

The event involved students standing on a platform in front of an audience of three hundred peers. Students were self-conscious about their clothing, with boys wearing poorly fitting coats and trousers, and girls wearing self-made gowns. Hamlin Garland was called to perform and experienced a mix of nervousness and a sense of calm as he faced the audience. Garland's recitation was likely a classic piece of literature, which he delivered with confidence despite its bombastic nature. The principal praised and criticized Garland's performance after he finished, which he accepted and resented respectively. Another speaker, a younger girl, was recognized for her dramatic reading ability and emotional depth in her recitations. Most students were children of farmers, while a few came from village homes in western Iowa and southern Minnesota.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The narrator is a teacher seeking shelter while traveling back to Byron. The first household the narrator approached was unwelcoming and the husband was only moderately cordial. The narrator felt guilty for not being able to pay for the hospitality offered by the first household. The narrator left the first household abruptly when the woman stepped out of the room. The narrator walked in darkness and rain, feeling despair due to lack of money and shelter. The narrator considered that local farmers might know the Harris family and could help him. The narrator found a second household where the farmer was welcoming and invited him inside.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The subject experienced an irreparable loss due to not seeing his granddaughters. He expressed discomfort about his declining physical abilities in letters. He invited family to help him with gardening tasks as he struggled with physical labor. He accepted his decline as a natural part of life and showed contentment with his situation. He reflected on the loss of his comrades and acknowledged the nearing end of his generation. He faced death with a sense of faith and readiness, having lived a long and generally happy life. He engaged in singing songs from his past, which evoked deep emotions and reflections on aging.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The text discusses the potential benefits of freeing a woman from her trances to improve her mental health. The author believes that changing mental stimuli can restore perfect mental health. The hypnotic state is characterized by the working of the subliminal consciousness in unusual directions. The author plans to separate the woman from her mother to help her recover. The author acknowledges the emotional pain this separation may cause for both the woman and her mother. Kate informs Morton that women have been locked in their rooms due to fear of Clarke and Pratt. Morton suggests that Mrs. Lambert go West with her husband to allow the woman to recover.

A pretty girl visited the home of one of Burton's aunts, which excited Burton and his brother Charles. The girl came from Dubuque and had a cosmopolitan air of tolerance. Burton had the opportunity to visit his aunt frequently, while the narrator could only see the girl at church. Burton attempted to give the girl, Nettie, some Siberian crab-apples but left when he saw another man in the parlor. The narrator and Burton often boarded themselves and struggled with food, sometimes leading to cooking mishaps. They attended the Lyceum at the Burr Oak school-house during winter months and participated in debates. The narrator was influenced by Joaquin Miller's poem, _Kit Carson's Ride_, and admired its epic quality.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The neighbors often helped with extra work. Blue racers and rattlesnakes were common during mid-summer months. Harriet rescued little Frank from a diamond-back rattler after their cart overturned. A man lifted a rattlesnake with a fork while pitching grain to a wagon. Another large yellow-back snake was killed in the barnyard. Garter-snakes and black snakes were present but not feared as much as bears and wildcats. Various myths about snakes were believed by local children.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: The narrator's father left his Iowa farm to claim unclaimed land. The narrator felt a strong desire for adventure and exploration. The landscape in the new location was different from Iowa and Minnesota. The village was described as a summer camp with citizens discussing development. The narrator worked on his father's claim and earned two dollars per day. The narrator traveled to Hastings and then decided to take a steamboat to Redwing. The narrator stayed at a boarding house in Redwing and wrote letters to friends.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Son of the Middle Border

text: Zulime did not share the narrator's melancholy and concealed it under a smiling stoicism. Zulime adapted from a life of luxury to cooking her own meals and scouring pots. The narrator's brother, referred to as Franklin, decided to quit acting after twelve years. Franklin sought financial assistance from the narrator to buy out his share in the Homestead for a new opportunity in rubber plantation management. The narrator was working on two writing projects, one titled _The Steadfast Widow Delaney_ and the other _On Special Duty_. The narrator enjoyed riding his horse, Klondike, and was a familiar figure in the area. The narrator experienced his first long ride in an automobile during a visit to the Eastons in LaCrosse.

source.author: Hamlin Garland
source.title: A Daughter of the Middle Border

text: The narrator's mother was a compassionate figure who assisted women in childbirth and families in distress within a five-mile radius. The narrator experienced a painful farewell with his mother and sister before leaving for Osage. The narrator had previously negotiated with his father to continue his education in exchange for not asking for further support. The father offered the narrator thirty dollars for travel expenses, which the narrator accepted. The narrator felt a sense of doubt and nostalgia as he left his family home and the familiar landscape behind.
