There are multiple personas of Thomas Sandys, including a good-natured cynic and a haughty boy who is done with the girl. The grave author persona of Sandys is focused on writing his life story without mentioning the other personas. Thomas Sandys has been invited to the Spittal, the seat of the Rintoul family, where he expects to meet charming girls. He finds a lost glove of Grizel's and keeps it in his pocket, knowing she is unaware of its existence. Thomas imagines walks with Grizel, where he envisions her looking up at him adoringly.

Babbie is staying with Nanny overnight and came to Thrums to amuse herself. Gavin expresses disappointment in Babbie's actions and insists she must leave immediately. Babbie challenges Gavin's authority and expresses her defiance. Gavin indicates that he has taken command of Babbie since their kiss. Babbie desires to hear Gavin express his feelings for her but he refuses to do so that night. Gavin decides they must set out immediately, insisting on accompanying Babbie. Babbie struggles against Gavin's insistence to take her arm as they prepare to leave.

Grizel is a character who has a complex relationship with Tommy. Tommy expresses a commitment to continue being kind to Grizel despite her actions. Tommy wrote a letter of condolence to Dr. McQueen but never sent it. The narrator intends to expose Tommy's flaws while acknowledging his virtues. Grizel has a protective and loving attitude towards Tommy, despite his shortcomings. Grizel's childhood experiences with Tommy included playing games together. Tommy's acceptance of Grizel into his group was significant due to her background.

Grizel reflects on her relationship with Tommy and her feelings of being unlovable. Grizel believes her strength comes from her promise to help Tommy. Grizel examines herself to determine if she is too ugly to be loved. Grizel considers that men may love women for their helplessness. Grizel recalls that she has always been in a position of managing others. Grizel thinks that her dynamic with Tommy has reversed their roles in the relationship. Grizel concludes that Tommy might love a more traditionally feminine woman.

Elspeth experienced frequent attacks of bronchitis. Tommy had a complicated relationship with Shovel regarding their feelings for Elspeth. Tommy attempted to measure Elspeth's growth using his mother's old boots. Elspeth's growth was irregular, with fluctuations in her height. Tommy devised a method to keep Elspeth upright using sticks from firewood. Tommy taught Elspeth to walk and speak. Elspeth's first spoken word was 'Tommy'.

Babbie confessed to watching Gavin from behind a tree instead of returning to Nanny's. Babbie expressed a desire for a man who is brave and a leader, not idle like the men she knows. Gavin affirmed that he does not spend his days in idleness. Babbie stated that the man she could love must take the side of the weak against the strong. Gavin claimed that it is always his tendency to take the side of the weak. Babbie indicated that the man she desires must compel her to do his bidding. Rob Dow learned of the meeting in the wood, which affected him negatively.

Bell Birse never had a chance to refuse someone. John believed Andrew's letter was cunning and revealed Bell's feelings for Davit Allardyce. Mr. Cathro questioned who wrote Andrew's letter. The Dominie had written to Meggy Duff's daughter in Ireland asking for ten shillings. Meggy confirmed she had sent ten shillings this time, more than previous amounts. Tommy wrote a letter to Katherine using Meggy's own words to appeal for help. Mr. Cathro was aware of Tommy's involvement in writing letters but did not confront him.

Grizel decided to travel to London by train to see Tommy, who she believed was ill. Corp expressed concern about Grizel's decision and the potential gossip it might cause. Grizel had withdrawn money from the bank a week prior to be prepared for her journey. Grizel wore a brown jacket and fur cap during her train journey because Tommy liked them. During the train ride, Grizel frequently asked if the train was going to London. Upon arriving at Tommy's lodgings, Grizel learned that he had left for the Continent a week ago. Grizel stated that she was engaged to be married to Tommy, despite his absence.

Thomas was the elder of two children. The children went to Scotland to live with an uncle after the death of their parents. Thomas was noted for his modesty during his boyhood. Mr. David Cathro, M.A., was Thomas's old schoolmaster and praised his industry and amiability. Thomas inherited a strong will and purpose from his mother. Thomas was not proud of his strong will but liked to hear it discussed. Thomas had limited interaction with women and preferred to avoid sentimental conversations.

Grizel left her home, and David followed her shortly after. Maggy Ann answered David's summons but did not accompany him upstairs. David found Grizel in the parlour, where she was crying over a letter. David had never seen Grizel cry before, and he believed the time had come for something significant. Grizel opened the door for David during his next visit and expressed joy at finding him. David noticed that Grizel was trying to hide her earlier distress and was acting vivaciously. Grizel asked David what was troubling him, recognizing his concerned expression.

Pym asked Tommy if he had a dog, to which Tommy replied that it was not a dog. Tommy opened the door to reveal a girl of twelve sitting on a tiny roped box. The girl was dressed in dull-coloured wincey and appeared cold, patient, and lonely. Tommy identified the girl as his sister Elspeth and stated that they were orphans. Pym expressed surprise and excitement at the idea of Tommy being married, which Tommy denied. Six years later, Tommy became a famous man, surprising Pym with his knowledge about women. Tommy took care of Elspeth by insuring his life for her benefit and providing her with books and a piano.

Cathro expressed frustration about Tommy Sandys, stating he has taken away his sense of humor. Mr. McLean noted that Tommy Sandys seems to have a considerable sense of humor himself. Cathro described Tommy Sandys as someone who constantly changes his character and can exhibit extreme traits. Cathro mentioned that Tommy Sandys has been wearing a black jacket with crape on the cuffs and appeared forlorn at his desk. Cathro confirmed that Tommy Sandys does not have a deceased relative, as his only relative is a healthy sister. Cathro indicated that he was hesitant to ask Tommy Sandys about his appearance due to the boy's mysterious nature. Cathro's wife discovered the reason behind Tommy Sandys' mourning attire.

Grizel expresses happiness and insists that she cannot explain her feelings. David is confused about Grizel's feelings and the identity of another woman he believes she is fond of. Grizel confirms that David loves another woman, Elspeth. David admits to loving Elspeth after Grizel encourages him to be honest. Grizel believes that David has treated Elspeth poorly by expressing his feelings while not being free. Grizel hints at a deeper connection between Elspeth and another person, which she cannot disclose. Grizel reflects on her happiness and the positive days she has experienced.

Gavin returned to McQueen's house shortly after leaving it. Some speculated that Gavin returned to retrieve his cravat. Gavin returned to confess that he had lied to McQueen about helping Babbie escape. McQueen was sitting in his chair, looking at an open locket when Gavin entered. Gavin informed McQueen that his mind was made up regarding a matter they discussed. Margaret spread a shawl over her son, believing he was asleep. Gavin expressed that he carries both the joys and sorrows of the people.

Gavin and Babbie engage in a conversation where Babbie accuses Gavin of being nasty. Babbie offers Gavin a bunch of holly berries in exchange for not discussing duty. Gavin refuses the holly berries and insists on discussing his duty. Babbie expresses concern that Gavin is angry with her for a previous statement. Babbie mentions she must leave in five minutes due to a requirement at home. Gavin expresses trust in Babbie despite her teasing about his role as a minister. Babbie and Gavin briefly discuss their thoughts about each other, with Babbie wondering about their heights.

Gavin observed a singer approaching him while she danced up Windyghoul. The singer was fifty yards away from Gavin and appeared to be unaware of his presence. Gavin's mother, Margaret, expressed concern for the townspeople during a crisis. Jean, a character in the text, was distressed about her parents' safety. Men were seen running past Gavin, trying to escape from Thrums. A gypsy woman led a group of armed men towards the square, prompting excitement among the townspeople. Gavin heard a horn sound three times, which signaled him to hurry to the square.

Jean wishes to consult Tammas Haggart about something he has done. Jean had been considering where to hang her washing before seeing Rob Dow. Rob Dow confronts Jean and accuses her of being one of the women he despises. Rob Dow claims to be drunk and expresses frustration about his situation. Rob Dow questions Jean about the minister carrying flowers in his pouch. Rob Dow destroys the holly that Jean had, claiming it was the end of the minister's flowers. Rob Dow reveals he is searching for an Egyptian woman and mentions his encounter at the Kaims.

Tommy is described as being engrossed in his exercises for an extended period. Pym believes that Tommy lacks sentiment and interest in women. Tommy struggles with shyness and has difficulty expressing interest in women. Tommy has a preference for stylish clothing but often denies himself to buy gifts for Elspeth. Despite his efforts to engage socially, Tommy is perceived as aloof by his dance partners. Pym's friends ridicule Tommy for his appearance and lack of social skills. Tommy is determined to improve his social interactions, despite feeling discouraged.

The narrator encounters Mr. Dishart and a strange woman on a hill. Mr. Dishart identifies himself and expresses composure despite the narrator's dread. The narrator feels shame for being false to Margaret upon calling out 'Gavin.' The strange woman attempts to lie in Mr. Dishart's interest but stops out of reverence for Gavin. Gavin addresses the narrator with suspicion and states that he will explain nothing. The strange woman asks the narrator for directions to old Nanny Webster's house. The narrator reflects on his feelings of faith in Gavin while feeling timid and conflicted.

Grizel expresses a desire to love someone. Tommy feels sympathetic towards Grizel and becomes emotional. Grizel claims to love herself, pointing to her reflection in a mirror. Grizel's affection for herself is viewed as barely respectable by Tommy. Grizel's unresponsiveness leads to her losing potential friends. Grizel fears her father's arrival, which she dreads despite the town's desire for it. Grizel is troubled by remarks about her and her mother, particularly those made by the doctor.

The narrator felt ashamed and pitied herself after an event involving Aaron. The narrator pretended to admire her husband and boasted about his position despite her true feelings. Aaron Latta attended the narrator's wedding wearing mourning attire and expressed his disapproval. The crowd outside the wedding commented that the event felt more like a burial than a marriage. The narrator concealed her sorrow during the wedding supper while secretly resenting her husband. Instead of a carriage, the crowd sent a hearse to take the narrator and her husband away. The narrator secretly paid for the wedding supper and carriage using her savings to maintain appearances.

The narrator denies having anything of the kind during a conversation. McKenzie and Rintoul are present during the conversation with the narrator. The narrator mentions encountering a gypsy girl earlier in the evening. The narrator left the gypsy girl near Caddam Wood. McKenzie warns the narrator to forget about the gypsy girl. The earl and McKenzie are traveling away from the hill after their visit. The gypsies deny seeing the minister and express disbelief in the existence of the mysterious Egyptian.

Blinder advised a girl to avoid ill men, referencing her father as an example. The girl expressed sorrow and ran away quickly after the conversation with Blinder. Tommy went to Double Dykes, worried about the girl's safety. Grizel was at home, feeling threatened by her father and expressed a desire to run away. Tommy suggested that Grizel should use her money to escape before her father arrives. Grizel felt that running away alone would not be respectable. Tommy and Grizel had a disagreement about leaving together, leading to a tense parting.

An hour after a conversation, a character reflects on his distance from his books and observes a funeral. The character feels a sense of pride when he learns he has carried the highest bursary. Aaron and Mr. Cathro meet in the square, where Mr. Cathro expresses concern about Tommy's despondency. Aaron notes that Tommy has been working harder than ever and seems eager about his writing. Mr. Cathro has a history of writing letters for people who cannot write, which he enjoys. Andrew Dickie approaches Mr. Cathro to request a letter for Bell Birse, expressing his desire to marry her. Mr. Cathro refuses to write the letter as requested by Andrew, leading to Andrew's departure.

Grizel expresses a willingness to let go of her feelings if she is not loved in return. Tommy acknowledges that Grizel loves him but wishes she did not. Grizel is uncertain about her feelings and reflects on the nature of wishes. Tommy believes that if Grizel no longer wants to love him, she will stop loving him soon. Grizel is distressed by the implication that she could love Tommy less. Tommy suggests that Grizel may still care for him in a lesser way. Grizel reacts with anguish when Tommy states that she loves him less.

Grizel and the male character discuss their feelings for each other. Grizel expresses delight that the male character is sure of her feelings. The male character reveals he put Grizel's glove under his pillow. Grizel shares that she used to hear the glove's heart beating when it was under her pillow. The male character describes a night filled with contradictory emotions and thoughts about Grizel. Grizel states she loves the male character's book because it is part of him. The male character expresses a desire to be loved for his appearance rather than his work.

Ogilvy is deceased. Gavin was married to a woman referred to as the Egyptian. Gavin instructs that his wife should go to his mother and remain with her. Gavin acknowledges the emotional response of the people around him. Gavin expresses his belief in God's goodness. Gavin reads a passage from the Bible, specifically from the fourteenth chapter of Matthew. Gavin advises his congregation to focus on spiritual treasures rather than earthly ones.

Gavin and Babbie discuss the wrongs they believe they have done. Babbie insists that she has not pretended to love Lord Rintoul. Gavin believes Babbie must inform Lord Rintoul that she does not love him. Babbie plans to return to the Spittal without anyone knowing of her absence. Gavin expresses concern that if Babbie marries Lord Rintoul, he will regret it. Babbie believes that her marriage will be viewed negatively by others in Thrums. Gavin states he will never marry, despite Babbie's insistence that he must.

A woman lay in a fever at the doctor's house for many days. A man with a drawn face watched over her during her illness. The woman experienced confusion about her surroundings and had wild demands. The man was able to interpret her thoughts and soothe her during her episodes. Elspeth spoke to the woman about Tommy's love for Grizel and her refusal of him. It was believed that the woman's mental state was affected by her father's behavior. Tommy confessed to the doctor about his actions and expressed a willingness to reveal everything.

Nanny took Gavin's hand timidly and would have kissed it if he were not a minister. The doctor warned Gavin against making an appointment with the gypsy due to potential gossip in Thrums. Gavin accepted the doctor's warning but felt offended by the implication made in Nanny's presence. The Egyptian insisted that Gavin must come alone and that they all promise not to reveal Nanny's friend. The doctor agreed to keep silent about the matter unless he suspected dishonesty. Nanny expressed hope that her stocking-foot would be full of gold. McQueen questioned the gypsy's identity, noting her ability to switch to the Scotch tongue easily.

Thomas Sandys was a young man of letters who gained recognition before his untimely death. He cleared £11 10s from his endeavors. Sandys had a modest opinion of his own work and disliked being praised. He lost his parents at a young age; his father was a retired military officer and his mother was a devout Scotchwoman. His contemporaries discussed his individuality and noted that he was greater than his books. Sandys's life and death were characterized by a sense of tragedy and unfulfilled potential.

The sheriff is angry with Wearyworld for ignoring his duty. Wearyworld claims he was in bed when he heard a disturbance. Wearyworld saw an Egyptian girl around twelve o'clock before the disturbance. The Egyptian girl asked Wearyworld if he was police and mentioned a horn she found. Wearyworld blew the horn and the girl ran away without taking it back. The sheriff orders Halliwell to capture the Egyptian woman. The sheriff intends to search for the woman himself before daybreak.

The Dominie expresses frustration over Tommy's letter-writing and its effect on his reputation. Grizel suggests that it would be a triumph if Tommy beats Mr. Ogilvy's student. The competition takes place at the Thrums school with several ministers and Mr. Ogilvy present. The subject of the essay for the competition is 'A Day in Church'. Tommy appears confident while Lauchlan McLauchlan struggles to start his essay. Mr. Ogilvy and Mr. Cathro switch roles during the competition, with Ogilvy pacing anxiously. Mr. Ogilvy reflects on the importance of writing throughout his life.

Tommy remained by Grizel's side for eighteen months without losing hope. David suggested to humor Grizel, but Tommy refused and continued to teach her. Tommy believed he was preventing Grizel from slipping back into her previous state. Grizel struggled to remember her past and often expressed pain when trying to think. Tommy repeatedly reminded Grizel of the old doctor, who had cared for her. Grizel sometimes showed a vague understanding of her condition and expressed sorrow. Tommy's efforts to teach Grizel included asking her questions about her identity.

Hendry Munn is questioned about rumors regarding Mr. Dishart's murder. Hendry mentions that a woman was seen with the dominie. The precentor demands to know the identity of the woman. Hendry claims the woman is the Egyptian. Tammas Whamond reacts violently to Hendry's statement. The congregation outside the church becomes animated with excitement. The precentor decides to lock the church doors and take the keys.

The narrator describes a man who has a powerful influence over them. The man is contrasted with Aaron, who is depicted as less masterful. The narrator admires the man's commanding presence despite recognizing his brutish nature. The narrator and Aaron were called for the first time on the Sabbath after the man arrived. The narrator feels that the man understands their innermost thoughts and emotions. The narrator recounts a significant event at the Cuttle Well involving Aaron and the man. Aaron is pressured by the man to change a name written in the dirt, leading to a loss of respect from the narrator.

Tommy found a bundle of treasures belonging to Elspeth at the door. The cottage was originally a farmhouse and was no larger than Aaron's. Only one of the two front windows of the cottage showed a light. Tommy and Elspeth approached a window while holding hands. The kitchen they peered into had furniture and fixtures typical of poor dwellings. The Painted Lady used a large velvet glove to handle coals. The room had various oddities, including a spinet and a rocking chair.

Grizel was left a house to live in, which she was told should be her home. Grizel expressed a desire to go home after returning to the house. Corp's baby brought Grizel joy and made her feel at home. Grizel showed a willingness to mend the child's pinafore, indicating a sense of belonging. Tommy and Gavinia discussed Grizel's need for care and her desire to stay in her old rooms. Grizel was reinstalled in her old rooms after a week. Tommy searched for a missing parcel containing papers that Grizel may have hidden.

The male character expresses a desire to be married but admits to not loving the female character in the conventional sense. The female character, Grizel, seeks clarification about the male character's feelings. The male character acknowledges that he does not want to marry anyone, despite feeling he could die for Grizel. Grizel tells the male character that he is free and encourages him not to feel tragic. Grizel offers the male character a ring, expecting him to put it on her finger. The male character expresses a desire to maintain their previous relationship, but Grizel refuses. The male character impulsively declares his love for Grizel and proposes, but Grizel reveals she has already refused him.

Tommy mentions that Lochiel has two hundred spearsmen. Tommy is waiting to meet Lord Airlie at the Loups o' Kenny when the moon rises. Tommy states that auld Bradwardine is as spirited as ever. Tommy indicates that there are fifty wild Highlandmen in the cave of Clova. Tommy is currently at St. Germains and has a price on his head. Tommy reveals that Black Cathro mistakenly believes he is a boy named Tommy who lives at a nearby house. Charles Edward landed in Scotland on the following Saturday evening.

Grizel often experienced joy when visiting Elspeth's baby girl and young Shiach. Tommy observed that Grizel's happiness was often followed by depression after her visitors left. Grizel sometimes engaged in self-talk and prayer during her moments of depression. Tommy decided that Grizel should not see the children again due to the harm they caused her. Tommy was writing magazine papers and felt that the public had forgotten him. Tommy referred to his lost manuscript as his great work and expressed difficulty in rewriting it. Tommy remained devoted to Grizel throughout the year, tending to her needs despite the challenges.

Margaret returned to the parlor after hearing the heater being adjusted in the kitchen. Tammas Whamond, the precentor, demanded to be let in to deliver news to the minister's mother. Whamond claimed that the minister was no longer a minister because he had married a gypsy woman and run away with her. Jean Proctor refused to open the door for Whamond, insisting that the minister's mother should hear the news from him directly. The rain forced Whamond to leave after he threatened to break down the door. Margaret expressed concern for her son, and Jean lied to reassure her that nothing was wrong. Babbie was the first person to arrive at the door after Jean had barred it.

Tommy expresses dismay about being fifteen miles away from Elspeth at the Dubb of Prosen. Aaron believes that it is better for Elspeth to learn to do without Tommy. Tommy is anxious about how Elspeth will react to the news of their separation. Elspeth mistakenly thinks she will be going with Tommy to the Dubb of Prosen. When Tommy finally tells Elspeth the truth, she becomes hysterical and requires medical attention. Aaron attempts to comfort Elspeth after Tommy's departure, but she does not respond positively. Mr. McLean has sent Tommy a pound, indicating he is no longer involved with him.

The narrator had a brief conversation with Gavin about his mother. The river had risen several feet since the narrator last spoke to Waster Lunny. The mist was descending the hills, indicating worsening conditions. The narrator planned to reach Thrums by going around the Kelpie brig to cross the river. The narrator expressed concern about potential danger during his journey. The narrator requested that his old desk, containing items from Margaret, be destroyed unopened if anything happened to him. The narrator revealed to Gavin that he was married to Margaret and that Gavin is his son.

The woman danced in muddy water and beckoned to Gavin. Gavin pursued the woman up Windyghoul but lost her at the mouth of the avenue. Gavin searched for the woman but could not find her. Gavin realized his boots were muddy and returned home in anger. Gavin encountered Charles Yuill, who was weak and fearful of soldiers. Yuill asked Gavin to swear he was not involved in the weavers' riot. Gavin attempted to stop Rob Dow from joining the gathering in the square.

Gavin was with families whose bread-winners were in the lock-up. The sheriff and Halliwell were in the round-room of the town-house. The sheriff expressed dissatisfaction with the operation, stating it was a fiasco. Halliwell claimed to have brought the policemen into the area. John Dunwoodie was brought into the round-room by a policeman. Dunwoodie admitted to being in Tilliedrum just before the operation. The sheriff suspected Dunwoodie of having alerted the town about the preparations.

Gavin pulled down the blind after seeing a flash of light outside the window. The light was from a lantern held by Babbie. Gavin was surprised by Babbie's visit at a late hour. Jean was reading a chapter from the Bible before going to bed. Gavin felt apprehensive as he descended the dark stair. Babbie expressed a desire to leave and return to Nanny's. Gavin urged Babbie to tell him what had happened to her.

The gypsy expresses distress about being seen by Riach. Halliwell believes the gypsy's fear of Riach is the reason for her distress. The gypsy claims to have met the sheriff in Glen Quharity. The sheriff was riding a horse and was on his way back from Lord Rintoul's place. The gypsy tells Halliwell that she drew information from the sheriff without him realizing it. Halliwell expresses admiration for the gypsy's ability to deceive the sheriff. The gypsy shows emotional vulnerability, crying and expressing regret about her feelings.

The Little Minister is a work by J. M. Barrie. The book contains multiple chapters, including 'The Love-Light' and 'The Night-Watchers'. The story features a minister from Thrums named Gavin Dishart. Gavin Dishart arrives in Thrums with his mother when he is twenty-one years old. The narrative includes a past encounter between a minister and a woman who was to be his wife. The setting includes the town of Thrums and its surroundings. The book explores themes of love and relationships.

Grizel walked away from a group of children without flinching and lay down on the ground when she reached the Den. Grizel had tears in her eyes but her cheeks were dry. Grizel asked Tommy about red spots on cheeks and coughing up blood. Tommy hesitated to answer Grizel's questions about her mother's health. Elspeth carried a Testament given to her by the Rev. Mr. Dishart. Grizel expressed skepticism about the ease of salvation as described by Elspeth. Grizel insisted on obtaining Elspeth's Testament despite Elspeth's reluctance to sell it.

Lady Pippinworth went upstairs to get her goloshes while Tommy watched her fondly. Tommy brought a cloak with a Mother Goose hood to Lady Pippinworth after she returned. Lady Pippinworth asked if it was cold, and Tommy insisted she wear the hood. Tommy and Lady Pippinworth walked in the garden where other visitors were present. Tommy attempted to engage Lady Pippinworth in conversation but received little encouragement. Lady Pippinworth expressed fear of speaking due to potential listeners. Lady Pippinworth decided to go inside after expressing tiredness.

Elspeth is described as a timid creature who shows best among other timid individuals. Tommy hired a piano for Elspeth, which she played for shy visitors. Some men attempted to gain Elspeth's favor by disparaging other women, which Tommy disapproved of. Elspeth expressed admiration for Tommy, considering him the one perfect gentleman in the world. A young man proposed to Elspeth, but she declined, leading to her brother's indignation with him. Tommy believed that Elspeth would not accept any suitor, as he felt she was incapable of loving anyone but him. Tommy's devotion to Elspeth was partly due to his belief that they shared a similar inability to love.

Grizel did not care for study and preferred sewing or dusting. She learned French and the pianoforte to please the doctor. Grizel became very focused on making garments for babies when she heard of new births. She often disagreed with authors in books, which irritated her. Grizel expressed her dislike for Sundays due to the requirement of sitting still. The doctor often watched Grizel and thought about her, especially when she was troubled. Grizel's nurse followed the doctor's instructions closely and enforced strict routines for patient care.

Mrs. Jerry expressed a desire for proof of Tommy's feelings. Tommy acknowledged that Mrs. Jerry is different from other women. Mrs. Jerry felt strange and terrified that Tommy recognized her uniqueness. Tommy experienced emotions he had not felt with other suitors. Mrs. Jerry ultimately decided that she could not accept Tommy's feelings. Tommy contemplated the possibility of Mrs. Jerry revealing their conversation to Elspeth. Tommy and Elspeth discussed returning to Thrums and mentioned several acquaintances.

Aaron attempted to rise but was pushed back into his chair. Tommy expressed that love cannot die and is always young. Tommy decided to leave the house to avoid conflict with Aaron. Tommy made a cushion for Aaron's chair to leave a positive impression. Elspeth noted a newfound serenity in Tommy. Tommy felt grateful for Elspeth and wanted to protect her from distress. Grizel believed that Elspeth could be won over despite Tommy's doubts.

Gavin expressed his commitment to his people. The doctor advised to drive a gypsy woman out of town before soldiers arrived. The gypsy woman, referred to as 'the Egyptian,' was unknown to the townspeople. Several people reported seeing soldiers advancing from Tilliedrum. Andrew Struthers commanded a group of armed weavers in the town square. Gavin confronted Struthers and ordered him to leave him alone. Gavin called forward several men from the crowd, asking them to lay down their weapons.

The narrator arrived at the school-house around a quarter-past nine on a misty night. The narrator was weary and sat down without removing their bonnet. The sound of wheels alerted the narrator to the approach of a trap in the glen. The trap stopped, and a conversation between McKenzie and Rintoul was overheard. McKenzie and Rintoul were searching for the school-house in the mist. Lord Rintoul was described as a tall, thin man with an unsteady head and restless hands. McKenzie and Rintoul requested a lamp from the narrator after being caught in the mist.

Ivie McLean often walks along the cliffs to a fishing village. Miss Kitty was asked by Ivie to sing 'The Land o' the Leal' during tea at the cottage. Ivie McLean is nearly forty years old and has been a bachelor for some time. Fifteen years prior, Ivie was in love, but the girl did not wait for him. Miss Kitty is turning thirty-seven in August and expressed a desire to stop wearing curls. Miss Kitty is the better businesswoman between her and Miss Ailie, managing their accounts. Ivie McLean has known the sisters for months before realizing Miss Kitty was his favorite.

The characters in the text express feelings of aging and a future without each other. Tommy expresses surprise at Grizel's return and questions her motivations. Grizel reassures Tommy that she is not angry with him. Tommy admits to having been cruel and expresses a desire for Grizel to remain with him. Grizel's grip on Tommy signifies her joy and willingness to forgive. Tommy acknowledges that he admires Grizel's character more than before. Grizel reveals her internal struggle with feelings of pride and self-respect.

Elspeth expresses concern that Tommy is angry with her. Tommy acknowledges his feelings of being taken aback by Elspeth's happiness. Elspeth believes she has been a barrier to Tommy's happiness with other women. Tommy feels that having Elspeth is enough for him. Elspeth hopes that Tommy will find love with someone else. Elspeth mentions that she has told David about her situation with Tommy. Tommy remains silent when Elspeth suggests that Grizel might be the woman for him.

Elspeth described someone as daft. Grizel stated that the person is generally timid. The Painted Lady's child made three calls the next morning. One gentleman initially did not remember the child during the visit. Grizel expressed concern about her mother's health during the visits. The names of the gentlemen visited by Grizel are not known. Grizel's friends noticed that someone was visiting their lair and using their firewood.

Grizel hesitates to open a letter, feeling a mix of elation and fear. Grizel recalls her mother's past comments about letters and their emotional impact. David Gemmell visits Grizel to discuss cases but notices her distracted demeanor. Grizel conceals the letter from David, which is unusual for her straightforward nature. Grizel plans to meet Tommy on the croquet lawn to gauge the letter's significance. Grizel reflects on her doubts about Tommy, feeling disloyal for questioning him. Grizel ultimately realizes Tommy still loves her before their meeting.

The narrator saw a child on the waste ground between the school and home. The child was accompanied by their mother, who was laughing and gesturing. The narrator encountered Adam Dishart's black dog while at their desk. The narrator found dog paw marks on the ground after leaving the school. The child's mother was no longer at the door when the narrator returned. The narrator expressed urgency to leave with the child and their mother. The couple sat in silence, waiting for the child's father, Adam.

Babbie loved the little minister, Gavin, for the best qualities she had seen in a man. Babbie experienced her first Sabbath day alone in a mudhouse in Windyghoul while Gavin preached in the Auld Licht kirk. Babbie's love for Gavin felt as old as herself and brought her both joy and sorrow. Babbie realized that her love for Gavin was not meant for her, which caused her emotional pain. The narrator expresses a desire to write great books but struggles with self-doubt and the limitations of his experiences. Babbie understood that she and Gavin were separated by an obstacle he was unaware of. Babbie believed that if the obstacle were removed, she would humbly give herself to Gavin.

Corp is nicknamed because he takes fits, during which he lies still like a dead person. Corp's aunt is wrathful and has physically punished him for his fits until he grew too large for her to do so. Mr. Ogilvy, the school-master of Glen Quharity, arranged for the Lady of the Spittal to visit Corp. Corp felt uneasy about the visit because his aunt would be away and he would have to answer questions. Tommy, a friend of Corp, expressed a desire to have Corp's fits and offered him advice on how to respond to questions about them. During the visit, the Lady and Mr. Ogilvy found Corp to be a success, with one giving him a shilling and the other taking notes. Tommy had arranged to impersonate Corp during the visit, while the real Corp listened from beneath the bed.

Dite is to be married to the Painted Lady if she cannot find a better option. The Painted Lady is described as a small, brightly dressed woman with a white-and-pink face. Dite attempts to read a letter addressed to someone at Double Dykes. The smith is surprised to find that the letter is addressed to Double Dykes. Blinder, the blind tailor, explains that Double Dykes is the name of a farm and refers to the current occupants. The Painted Lady has never received a letter since moving to Double Dykes. The Painted Lady is easily startled and has shown interest in the letters at the smithy's window.

Gavin took cover behind a tree at the approach of an enemy. The gypsy had two empty pans in her hands and entered the wood after looking towards the minister. Gavin discovered he had been hiding behind the tree and came into the open. The well that Babbie and Gavin visited was dry and filled with broom, stones, and broken rusty pans. Rob Angus was the strong man who transported the stone to Caddam. Gavin helped Babbie move a stone that she struggled with, despite his own physical discomfort. Babbie expressed admiration for Gavin's strength, which he found surprising.

Cathro expressed disappointment about the students he is preparing for college. Cathro mentioned that a talented student, Gavin Dishart, is being sent to Mr. Ogilvy instead of him. Cathro described Tommy Sandys as a backward student with uncertain potential. McLean questioned the decision to send Tommy to the examinations given his perceived deficiencies. Cathro believes Tommy may have an inner resistance to traditional learning methods. Cathro noted that Miss Ailie believes Tommy has a gift for the ministry. Cathro indicated that he would take credit for Tommy's success or blame Miss Ailie for his failure.

Rob Dow was found lying a prisoner beneath a tree. Fifty hands released Rob Dow, while two men were tasked with bringing him along slowly. The island where the two men stood was small and unstable, measuring little bigger than common round tables. Attempts to rescue the men using ropes were unsuccessful due to the force of the river. A trunk of a tree was dragged to form a bridge, but it ultimately splashed into the water and was lost. The people on the bank began to improvise a rope from cravats and remaining rope tags, but felt helpless. Gavin and the earl displayed contrasting reactions to the situation, with Gavin remaining firm and the earl appearing distressed.

Corp informed several neighbors that Gavinia is to have him. Corp visited an old lady and a small boy to share the news about Gavinia. Gavinia felt flustered by Corp's public announcement of their relationship. Grizel reassured Gavinia that Corp's declaration was sweet and a sign of love. Corp announced the arrival of a boy to Grizel, following Gavinia's instructions. Grizel expressed excitement about the baby and inquired about the name. Corp decided to name the baby Thomas Sandys Shiach, considering family connections.

A blue suit previously owned by Sam changed owners to Tommy. Tommy experienced shyness when he first wore the suit. Tommy intended to walk past Reddy's house to show her his new trousers. Reddy had been dead for a long time when Tommy returned to look for her. Tommy's mother saw him waiting for Reddy and cried for the first time since Reddy's death. Tommy cried because he wanted Reddy to see his new trousers, which had pockets. Elspeth fell ill with an ailment called croop, prompting Tommy to take an interest in her.

Thomas Sandys was a man of character. He was known as the Perfect Lover and lived his life devoted to his wife. His affection for his wife began in his boyhood and remained constant until his death. Sandys experienced unreciprocated love for a long time before marrying. A committee was formed to create a memorial for Sandys, but it was poorly attended and disbanded. The biography of Sandys was published twenty-five years later with a changed title. Grizel, Sandys' wife, sought the truth about his life and continued to love him after his death.

The character's name is Gavin Dishart. Gavin's mother instructed him to discard a knife given to him by his father. The narrator left Harvie that night in a carrier's cart. The narrator expressed a desire to bury himself from Margaret. Gavin and the narrator discussed Gavin's mother and her actions after Adam Dishart's death. Gavin admitted to forgetting his mother during a critical moment with Babbie. Gavin planned to set out to the Spittal before the narrator reached Thrums.

The text discusses the views of Mr. Dishart regarding the beauty of the soul versus the beauty of the face. The narrator expresses discomfort with Mr. Dishart's behavior, comparing it to a change of government. Snowfall prevents the narrator from traveling to town for news, isolating the school from Thrums. Birse shares gossip about Mr. Dishart's change of texts, suggesting there are multiple explanations for it. Tammas Haggart claims to have seen Mr. Dishart tear a page from the Bible and throw it into the fire. The congregation decides to view the incident as a positive event for their kirk, partly to undermine the Established minister. Gavin's popularity increases despite the controversy surrounding his change of texts.

The Bible that lay on the summer-seat was a great pulpit Bible taken home by Gavin to secure loose pages. Gavin studied from the large Bible the day before the riot but used a small Bible for the rest of the week. A message was found scrawled across chapter eight of the large Bible, signed by Babbie the Egyptian. At the beginning of the year, no snow was visible in Thrums, although clods of snow lay in Waster Lunny's fields. The doctor's dog-cart was observed at the Auld Licht manse, leading to various incorrect surmises among the Tenements. McQueen, the doctor, was known for his brusque manner and unusual methods, including letting in fresh air by breaking windows. Jean expressed apprehension when answering the door to the doctor, aware of his ability to alter health conditions quickly.

Dunwoodie expressed that his son was resistant to becoming a gentleman and preferred to return home. Dave Langlands claimed that John Dunwoodie was innocent and that the Egyptian woman raised the alarm. Langlands stated he was in a windmill with another man when they heard someone running outside. An Egyptian woman warned them that soldiers were coming and urged them to flee. Langlands admitted he did not blow the alarm horn and claimed he respected the law. He described the Egyptian woman as having rowan berries in her hair and wearing a green wrapper and a red shawl. Wearywarld, a local policeman, entered the scene after a search for him.

Grizel opened the door of Corp's house and found Corp and Gavinia at home with their baby. Gavinia expressed pride in Corp's actions and welcomed him with smiles. Corp initially downplayed his role in a heroic event involving a glove. Gavinia revealed that Mr. Sandys had confessed all details about the glove. Corp speculated that the glove was a love-token from a London woman. Gavinia was curious about the identity of the woman associated with the glove.

Grizel expresses her deep love for Tommy, stating that nothing can separate them except death. Tommy feels a strong emotional connection to Grizel and is deeply affected by her words. Grizel admits to loving Tommy more than God and acknowledges the intensity of her feelings. She prays regularly, thanking God for Tommy, but reveals that her faith is conditional on his well-being. Grizel states that if Tommy were to die, she would stop praying and question the existence of God. Tommy feels uncomfortable with Grizel's challenge to God's nature and existence. Grizel expresses a protective instinct towards Tommy, indicating a desire to shield him from harm.

Grizel experiences physical pain when trying to hide her feelings. The doctor admires Grizel's impulsiveness but finds it sometimes unsettling. The doctor dies during the scarlet-fever year. Grizel and the doctor acknowledge their feelings for each other before his death. Grizel expresses that she believes she contributed to her own growth. The doctor reassures Grizel that she will not fear love when it comes. Grizel feels happy and unafraid due to her relationship with the doctor.

The doctor questioned the minister about a gypsy girl and a financial transaction involving Nanny. Gavin, the minister, defended the gypsy girl, stating she has some justification for being considered a lady. The doctor expressed skepticism about the gypsy girl's character and questioned her background. Gavin admitted to helping the gypsy girl escape from soldiers and was not ashamed of it. The doctor warned Gavin that he was being watched for meeting the gypsy girl in public. Gavin declared his love for the gypsy girl and his intention to marry her. The doctor warned Gavin that revealing his relationship would lead to a vacancy in the Auld Licht kirk of Thrums.

Babbie returned to Gavin while he was at the well. Babbie was carrying empty pans and looking at the ground. Gavin expressed guilt upon seeing Babbie. Babbie claimed she returned to fill the pans with water. Gavin apologized for his previous comments to Babbie. Babbie indicated that she would not listen to any negative remarks about herself. Babbie was upset and crying during the conversation with Gavin.

Grizel is not engaged to be married. David expresses a desire to marry Grizel. Dr. McQueen wished for David and Grizel to marry. Grizel believes that Dr. McQueen never expressed his wishes directly to her. David mentions that Dr. McQueen was concerned about Grizel's happiness. David refers to a boy from Grizel's past who he believes is not good for her. David admires Grizel and considers her the noblest and bravest woman he has ever known.

The biographer reflects on the nature of love and idealism. The text discusses the impact of a woman's purity on a man's love. Babbie is described as a captivating figure in Gavin's life. The narrator expresses a personal connection to Gavin's story. The narrator had hoped for a resolution to past troubles with the arrival of a new minister. Margaret is mentioned as having kept a significant secret from Gavin. The narrator experiences renewed emotional pain related to past events.

Tommy acknowledges to Aaron that he has known something all along. Aaron expresses anger towards Tommy, accusing him of manipulation. Aaron believes that Tommy is aware of his influence over Elspeth. Aaron observed a moment when another man was about to propose to Elspeth. Tommy expresses that Elspeth's marriage would bring him more joy than it would to Aaron. Aaron feels a sense of despair and does not look up when the doctor and Elspeth enter the room. Aaron runs out of the house, eager to share news with Tommy.

Gavin met Sanders Webster, the mole-catcher, who persuaded him to take a path home through Caddam Wood. Sanders informed Gavin that the Wild Lindsays, a gypsy family, were in Caddam Wood. The Wild Lindsays were known to threaten farmers by day and dance at night. Sanders mentioned Lord Rintoul's house at the top of Glen Quharity, known as the Spittal. Sanders described a young lady who was to marry Lord Rintoul, noting a significant age difference between them. Sanders recounted an experience at a ball where he saw the young lady and fell off a flower-pot. Sanders claimed that the young lady responded positively to his compliment about her beauty.

Mr. Sandys sprained his ankle and required the doctor immediately. Dr. Gemmell examined Mr. Sandys's ankle and later left the house. Grizel felt a mix of emotions regarding Dr. Gemmell's visit and her past interactions. Dr. Gemmell often consulted Grizel about his patients and his work. Grizel recognized Dr. Gemmell's respectful treatment of her as stemming from his knowledge of her history. Dr. Gemmell informed Grizel that Mr. Sandys's injury was a dislocation, not a sprain. Grizel questioned Dr. Gemmell's understanding of Mr. Sandys's condition.

Tommy expresses frustration towards Grizel for her comments about him. Grizel attempts to help Tommy but he feels diminished by her treatment. Tommy acknowledges that he could not hurt Grizel if he were not flawed. Grizel questions the monstrousness of Tommy's kindness towards Elspeth. Tommy reflects on how Grizel has shared her ideas with Elspeth. Grizel is knowledgeable about old furniture and its value. Tommy notes that Grizel is giving items to Elspeth that were once hers.

Tommy Sandys has written two books, one of which is not yet published. Mrs. Jerry expresses excitement about Tommy's upcoming book. Tommy's new book is dedicated to Pym and is described as a unique literary work. The book is composed of essays without named characters or dialogue, focusing on universal human experiences. Critics have mixed opinions about the book, with some preferring Tommy's previous work, 'Unrequited Love.' Society initially overlooked Tommy's new book, but it gained appreciation from thoughtful readers. Grizel criticizes the book, questioning Tommy's understanding of unrequited love.

Grizel developed a theory about the dynamics of strength and weakness in relationships. Grizel believed that the strong like to be leaned upon and the weak like to lean, regardless of sex. Tommy expressed discomfort with Grizel's implication that she cared for him because he was weak. Grizel aimed to help Tommy become a stronger man without expecting his love in return. Tommy reflected on the potential consequences of a girl like Grizel loving a man like his father. Grizel hoped that her efforts to help Tommy would lead to a positive outcome for both of them. Elspeth's wedding day was mentioned as a significant event, but it was not the focus of Tommy and Grizel's story.

Grizel turned away from the doctor during their conversation. The doctor complimented Tommy for bearing the pain of a dislocated ankle. Grizel reflected on the strong bond between Tommy and his sister Elspeth. Grizel sent a message inviting Mr. and Miss Sandys for tea, without mentioning Tommy's injury. Elspeth declined the invitation, stating that Tommy's injury was more serious than Grizel believed. Maggy Ann reported that Elspeth found Grizel's invitation heartless. Tommy expressed a willingness to forgive Grizel for her perceived insensitivity.

Grizel believed she was meeting her father. McQueen assured Grizel that he would not let her go back unless she wanted to. Grizel agreed to go with McQueen after he promised to support her if her father came. Tommy expressed concern about being left out of the situation. McQueen questioned Tommy about his intentions regarding Grizel. McQueen sent Tommy home and advised him to keep the incident a secret. McQueen engaged Grizel in various activities while they were in his parlor.

Aaron Latta was known for his laughter. Elspeth was to be Grizel's husband. Grizel expressed joy and gratitude for her situation. Grizel had a strong, round figure that took various poses when standing or walking. Grizel thanked God for her ability to help others. Grizel had never worn a ring that she desired. Grizel believed that God was testing her through her struggles.

Tommy observed that the mourners were present at the funeral. The minister hesitated before signaling John to proceed with filling in the grave. Mr. Dishart declared that the grave is locked until the day of judgment. Grizel remained at Double Dykes, waiting for her father to arrive. Neighbors speculated about Grizel's father's potential response to the Painted Lady's death. Grizel had several gold pieces and nearly twenty pounds in the bank after paying the funeral expenses. Grizel expressed to Tommy that she did not wish to stay with the neighbors, feeling they only offered charity.

Grizel climbed in without giving the password to retrieve the shawl. Tommy mentioned that Grizel and the Painted Lady sometimes come at night to kindle the fire. The Painted Lady is said to wander the Den when she has a daft fit. Grizel is believed to follow the Painted Lady to ensure she returns home. Gavinia, a maid from the besieged city, was pursued by a masked man while eating a bridie. Gavinia was captured and taken to the Lair by her pursuers. Gavinia expressed a preference for being carried by a specific fellow while being taken to the Den.

Tommy and Corp discovered that the light had gone out in the house. They heard the sound of a door closing and found it locked when they approached. Tommy advised Corp not to mention their experience to Elspeth to avoid frightening her. When they returned to the _Ailie_, they found Miss Ailie with Mr. McLean. Mr. McLean sought pardon from Tommy for his past actions against the Throne. He offered to settle down as a law-abiding citizen and requested Tommy's intercession with the Queen. Mr. McLean proposed marriage to Miss Ailie, who expressed joy at the offer.

Tommy expressed his fondness for old friends and kissed Gavinia on the cheek. Corp commented on Tommy's unchanged nature after his visit. Gavinia remarked on Tommy's behavior towards women. Tommy experienced silence and discomfort in the presence of Grizel. Tommy and Elspeth were curious about each other's opinions of Grizel. Tommy felt joy upon seeing Grizel, who had grown up since their last meeting. Grizel wore a dress with brown and yellow colors and observed Tommy during their interaction.

The narrator recounts a conversation with a young girl about her parents' marriage. The girl demonstrates a strong memory and storytelling ability at a young age. Margaret, the girl's mother, was unaware of the challenges her husband Gavin faced as a minister. Gavin's congregation initially turned against him during a difficult period but later reconciled. Gavin's mother, Margaret, eventually accepted his wife Babbie after some time. Mr. Carfrae was asked to return to Thrums to address the vacant Auld Licht kirk. Dr. McQueen, who was Gavin's best man, died from scarlet fever after attending many cases.

Lowe's admission to the cabinet was made impossible by his declaration against lowering the borough franchise. Mr. Goschen was included in the cabinet despite only having been in parliament for three years. Mr. Gladstone expressed caution regarding Mr. Bright's potential impact on the government and the bill. Palmerston invited Cobden to join his cabinet in 1859, and they discussed Bright's avoidance of personal attacks. Mr. Gladstone's early weeks as leader of the House were marked by mildness and conciliatory behavior. The Queen expressed her gratification to Mr. Gladstone regarding his leadership in the House of Commons. Mr. Gladstone commemorated Lord Palmerston's contributions to freedom in Europe and his interest in the African race.

text: Mr. Gladstone voted in the minority against the condemnation of Ward's book and the proposal to strip its writer of his university degree during the proceedings at Oxford on February 13, 1845. Mr. Gladstone believed that the censure combined condemnation of opinions with a declaration of personal dishonesty, which he thought was not suitable for human adjudication. The series of proceedings against various individuals, including Newman, Pusey, and Maurice, is significant in the history of English toleration. Mr. Gladstone protested against the condemnation of Pusey in June 1843, which was passed without hearing him or stating reasons. In October 1845, Newman was received into the Roman communion, a step Mr. Gladstone considered to have calamitous importance. Mr. Gladstone sought an explanation from Manning regarding the common bond among converts to Roman Catholicism, which Manning attributed to their 'want of truth.' Most ordinary churchmen remained in their positions during this period, including Pusey, Keble, and Gladstone.

text: On July 10, Lord Granville suggested to Mr. Gladstone that they ask the Queen to persuade Hohenzollern to refuse the candidature. Mr. Gladstone agreed that it would not be wrong to ask the Queen for assistance in obtaining a refusal from Hohenzollern. Mr. Gladstone also suggested sounding the Italian government regarding the Duke of Aosta. On July 12, it became known that Prince Leopold had renounced the candidature, either spontaneously or through his father. The French government was in an embarrassing position and feared that the ministry might be overthrown if they did not obtain further satisfaction from Prussia. Mr. Gladstone sent a note to Paris emphasizing the responsibility that would rest on France if they did not accept the withdrawal of Prince Leopold's candidature. The note from Mr. Gladstone was sent to Paris on July 13 and reached Lord Lyons after the council of ministers had already begun.

The author proposed using the custom of the country as the basis for compensation on eviction. Lowe expressed feelings of heavy responsibility and apprehension regarding the situation. The cabinet agreed on compensation for improvements and the right of new tenants at will to compensation on eviction. Mr. Gladstone wrote a letter to Lord Granville to be shown to Lowe, which was effective in addressing concerns. Lord Bessborough faced criticism for encouraging communication with Sir John Gray regarding Irish tenants' opinions. Mr. Gladstone emphasized the importance of addressing the Irish question in his correspondence with the Queen.

text: The text discusses the implications of certain delusions related to government capabilities and the moral responsibilities of the state. It mentions the impact of tariff legislation on labor conditions and its role in countering socialism. Mr. Gladstone was focused on religious affairs at Oxford during Sir Robert Peel's government from 1841 to 1845. Gladstone perceived a societal prejudice against clergy and laymen associated with Oxford, affecting their advancement in state affairs. The Oxford movement, which began in 1833, transitioned into a second phase by the next decade, revealing significant changes. The publication of Froude's _Remains_ in 1838 marked a divergence from traditional high church views. Tract Ninety, published in 1841, aimed to clarify the Articles of Religion and was met with skepticism by Gladstone.

text: The arbitration process was complicated by disagreements between the American and British representatives. Mr. Gladstone informed the Queen on June 13 that the cabinet had not reached a decision regarding the arbitration. On June 15, Mr. Gladstone and Granville visited Mr. Hammond and received a protocol from Geneva. The British agent requested an eight-month adjournment at Geneva due to disagreements on the arbitration's scope. Mr. Adams proposed that the arbitrators make a spontaneous declaration to exclude indirect claims from consideration. The arbitration proceeded after the indirect claims were ruled out by the arbitrators. In September 1872, the five arbitrators unanimously found Great Britain liable for the acts of the Alabama.

text: The author is preparing bills for improvements and finds this work healthy and delightful. On January 24, the author expects Argyll to share dinner and anticipates a comfortable conversation. The author notes that Herbert appears to be in better health but is concerned about worsening revenue prospects. On January 25, the author is engaged in discussions about estimates, focusing more on the navy than the army. The author has managed to reduce navy estimates through a threat of resignation and is now addressing army estimates. Public opinion in Worcestershire reflects dissatisfaction with Gladstone's competence and his handling of the income tax. The author expresses a desire to escape London politics and appreciates the fresh air and nature at Hawarden.

text: Lowe expressed little hope for a successful outcome to his efforts before the session. Lowe believed that the men he placed in power would betray him during political negotiations. The liberal cave from the previous year was dissolved, with Lowe and some members voting with Mr. Gladstone. A new group of dissidents, called the party of the Tea-Room, emerged in place of the liberal cave. Many politicians were reluctant to support the return of Lord Russell and Mr. Gladstone. Lord Halifax noted the chaotic state of politics during this period. Mr. Gladstone was perceived as earnest and strict, contrasting with the indifference of the House.

text: Mr. Gladstone's total expenditure on the Hawarden estate was £267,000. Mr. Gladstone aimed to keep the Hawarden estate in the family and relieve it from debt since 1847. In 1867, a settlement was made involving Sir Stephen Glynne, Mr. Gladstone, and their spouses regarding the Hawarden estate. Mr. Gladstone required the terms of the settlement to be approved by Lord Devon and Sir Robert Phillimore. Mr. Gladstone became the owner of the Hawarden estate in 1874 after the deaths of Sir Stephen Glynne and his brother. In April 1875, Mr. Gladstone took steps to make his eldest son the owner in fee of the estate. Mrs. Gladstone retained possession and control of the castle and its contents for life.

text: The total taxation burden will be larger during wartime than in peacetime. Payment by war-taxes is considered more beneficial for the public than peacetime taxes. In the autumn, a dispute occurred between the chancellor of the exchequer and the Bank of England. The Bank of England claimed that a change in issuing deficiency bills was illegal. The chancellor of the exchequer received legal backing for his position from the law officers. Mr. Gladstone expressed anger over the Bank's refusal to accept the legal opinion it had requested. Mr. Gladstone believed that effective reforms require a finance minister with a strong position.

source.author: John Morley
source.title: The Life of William Ewart Gladstone (Vol 1 of 3)

text: Disraeli was suggested to lead the Commons due to his previous leadership experience and greater number of followers. A correspondent reported that the conservative party believed electing Mr. Gladstone as their leader was the only way to save the party. The difficulty with Disraeli was linked to his relationship with Lord Derby, which might be hard for Derby to disown. Disraeli invited General Peel to an official dinner in 1857 to consolidate party support. Mr. Gladstone advised against attending Disraeli's dinner, citing public jealousy over political position changes without prior cooperation. Mr. Gladstone expressed willingness to communicate with Lord Derby on public affairs, despite not being in party relations. Mr. Gladstone's friends advised against approaching Lord Derby, citing concerns over political alignment and the need for more tangible reasons.

text: The author expresses a desire to minimize time spent in the House of Commons. The author believes that the welfare of mankind is primarily influenced by the world of thought rather than politics. Sir Stephen Glynne died in June, and Mr. Gladstone described him as a man of refinement and modesty. Mr. Gladstone acknowledged the support of the Duke of Argyll and the duchess during a difficult time for his wife. The author finds ecclesiastical turmoil painful and criticizes certain bills as unwise. Mr. Gladstone expressed concerns that continued contentious parliamentary sessions could lead to the disestablishment of the church.

source.author: John Morley

text: Mr. Gladstone expressed concern about the influence of the papal system and hoped for a real minority to speak out. The Italian government considered running bishops against nominations from Rome to combat the pope's influence. Mr. Gladstone noted that ultramontanism had assumed an anti-social character, particularly in the Syllabus. The French government issued mild protests regarding the council but did not withdraw their garrison. Mr. Gladstone communicated to Archbishop Manning the impediments to Irish legislation due to the Syllabus and papal actions. In a parliamentary division, 451 members supported the majority, while 88 resisted and 62 called for further examination. On July 18, the definition of infallibility was accepted in St. Peter's by a vote of 533 to 2.

source.author: John Morley
source.title: The Life of William Ewart Gladstone (Vol 2 of 3)

text: Mr. Gladstone vacated his seat by accepting the office of lord high commissioner of the Ionian Islands. Mr. Gladstone was re-elected without opposition on February 12, 1861. A cabinet resolution to surrender the Ionian protectorate was made on December 8, 1862, with only Lord Westbury opposing. Mr. Gladstone sent home and revised three reports on the mischiefs of Ionian government, which were printed for cabinet use. The reports on Ionian government did not appear to receive much attention from the cabinet or were laid before parliament. Mr. Gladstone returned to England in March 1859 and found the conservatives struggling with parliamentary reform. Mr. Gladstone held the Oxford seat without opposition during a period of political confusion.

source.author: John Morley
source.title: The Life of William Ewart Gladstone (Vol 1 of 3)

text: Mr. Gladstone's doctrine suggests that an opposition should not attempt to overthrow a government it cannot replace. The conservative opposition of 1873 rejected the Irish bill due to concerns about its impact on Irish education. A significant portion of the liberal party also objected to the Irish bill on similar grounds as the conservatives. Mr. Disraeli argued that Mr. Gladstone's claims about parliamentary authority were not supported by legislative practice. Mr. Disraeli consulted his friends and concluded that a conservative ministry would be detrimental to public interests. Mr. Gladstone received a message from the Queen on March 16, 1873, regarding the possibility of resuming office. Mr. Gladstone agreed with the Queen's assessment that no further efforts from the opposition could be expected.

text: Gladstone was in high spirits and full of talk during the visit. The party traveled to Sayada by barge and cutters from the gunboat. Upon landing in Sayada, the group was met by the governor of the province. The journey from Sayada to Filates involved a rugged and mountainous path of about 12 miles. The group was received at Filates by the local population, including the Valideh's grandson. The Valideh welcomed the group at the castle, which is a large ruinous enclosure. Dinner consisted of thirty-two separate dishes served in a large room with candle-holding Albanians.

text: The government is under strain due to the administration in the House of Commons, with many offices represented by heads in the House of Lords. The speaker has public engagements in Edinburgh on the 2nd and 3rd and in Glasgow on the 1st. Lord Russell has agreed to postpone cabinet meetings for a fortnight after Saturday. Lord Palmerston is scheduled to be buried in the Abbey on Friday. Sir R. Peel is likely to be offered a peerage. There are concerns about the structure of the government between the two Houses. The speaker's first public appearance as leader of the House of Commons was made at Glasgow.

source.title: The Life of William Ewart Gladstone (Vol 2 of 3)

text: Mr. Gladstone delivered a speech at a feast in Newark in June that lasted from four o'clock to eleven. His speech lasted nearly an hour and included various minor speeches. Mr. Gladstone criticized the government for relying on the support of O'Connell and denounced systematic agitation to undo the Irish alliance. He emphasized the importance of the church question in determining the fate of the government. Mr. Gladstone defended the Protestant faith as beneficial for both England and the population of Ireland. His views on Irish debates were influenced by a statement from Lord John Russell regarding the identity of the Irish population.

source.author: John Morley
source.title: The Life of William Ewart Gladstone (Vol 1 of 3)

text: Napoleon III. was the sovereign leading a people who harbored animosity towards Britain. Mr. Gladstone expressed regret over the agitation encouraged by his speeches to force the government to change its decisions. Mr. Gladstone and Lord Palmerston engaged in a spirited correspondence regarding government expenditure and taxation. Mr. Gladstone distanced himself from the opinions of Mr. Bright and Mr. Cobden, particularly regarding taxation changes. In January 1862, Mr. Gladstone faced challenges due to increased military estimates announced by Sir George Lewis. Mr. Gladstone proposed reductions in military spending and aimed to lower the income tax. Public sentiment shifted by midsummer 1862, indicating a change in perception of Lord Palmerston's leadership.

text: The text provides a set of suggestions on the art of speaking, including the use of plain language, short sentences, and distinct articulation. It emphasizes the importance of testing one's own arguments and being familiar with the subject matter. The text references the teachings of Quintilian and Cicero regarding the qualities necessary for effective oratory. Mr. Gladstone's speaking style is described as a combination of eloquence and a style suitable for debate. Sir Robert Peel advised Mr. Gladstone to be long and diffuse in his speeches to appeal to diverse audiences. The text asserts that Mr. Gladstone's success in the House of Commons was due to his deep understanding of subjects and his ability to convey belief in his arguments. It notes that many leading ministers in the House of Commons have not been orators, contrasting them with Mr. Gladstone's capabilities.

text: Mr. Gladstone corresponds with a French statesman about the prohibition of pork in various cultures. The prohibition of pork is noted as a contradiction between the practices of the Phœnicians and Jews. A young member of parliament discusses the eating of horseflesh with Mr. Gladstone. Mr. Gladstone suggests that the Greeks did not eat horseflesh in the heroic period due to its relation to human feelings. Gustave d’Eichthal draws Mr. Gladstone's attention to the practical use of Greek as a potential national language. Guizot expresses a desire for more independence in the Anglican Church and plans to send meditations on Christianity. Henry Taylor encloses a letter from Southey to Charlotte Brontë regarding her literary aspirations.

text: Mr. Gladstone's parents took him to Edinburgh in 1814. He spent a spring in Edinburgh in 1828 before going to Oxford. Mr. Gladstone had a friendship with Chalmers, which included walks together. Chalmers was described as having no small talk and being focused on great subjects. Mr. Gladstone appreciated Chalmers and expressed this in various ways. In January 1834, Mr. Gladstone stayed with relatives at Seaforth before returning to Oxford. During his time at Oxford, Mr. Gladstone engaged in various conversations and wrote several papers.

text: Bright's letter is characterized as able and manly, and the author respects the spirit behind it. The author believes Bright should distinguish between selfish interferences and operations supporting public law in Europe. Mr. Gladstone, in a 1887 vindication of the Crimean War policy, denies that the cabinet drifted or was in conflict during negotiations. Gladstone states that he experienced sharper divisions in other cabinets compared to the Aberdeen cabinet. Gladstone acknowledges that there was conflict among the four ministers concerned with foreign affairs. The cabinet's course during the Crimean War led it away from the desired outcome, despite Gladstone's assertion of its harmony. Twenty years after the Crimean War, Gladstone observed that public sentiment had not significantly changed.

The church in Rome has a new clergyman, Mr. Crowther, who delivered an admirable sermon. The departure of the French garrison from Rome is confirmed, which is expected to uplift the local population. The author experienced discomforts during the trip, including two apartment fires and a severe case of influenza. Mr. Gladstone showed little interest in archaeological wonders but enjoyed listening to Italian sermons. Mr. Gladstone had audiences with Pope Pius IX and ten cardinals, and he met with the king of Florence.

The commission was deemed unconstitutional and illegal by eminent counsel. The inquiry conducted by the commissioners was completed in April 1852. Mr. Gladstone regarded the report as one of the ablest productions submitted.

text: Discussions of the time focused on the unqualified construction of Pitt's policy of loan. The political and moral reasons for meeting war demands by tax rather than loan influenced the economic view presented. The condemnation of loans was emphatic, stating that raising funds for wars by loan deceives the people. The author wrote to Northcote in 1862, complimenting his book on finance and discussing the effects of taxes versus loans. The author argued that war loans create a temporary stimulus to labor but lead to increased competition for jobs when the stimulus is withdrawn. The author acknowledged the necessity of loans while advocating for a larger share of war expenditure to be funded by taxes. The author noted that during war, wages tend to rise, but after the war, many are dismissed from public employment, leading to reduced wages.

text: The parliament of the clergy of the Church of England was allowed to resume active functions in 1852 after being suspended since 1717. Mr. Gladstone aimed to revive the corporate organization of the Church of England, particularly after the Gorham judgment. Bishop Wilberforce was a key figure in efforts to restore order within the Church of England. Mr. Gladstone expressed his views on the need for effective organization of the clergy in a letter to Bishop Wilberforce dated January 1, 1854. He argued that a more organized church would strengthen its pastoral work and improve its public perception. In 1860, a volume titled 'Essays and Reviews' was published, featuring contributions from six clergymen of the Church of England. The essays in the volume were generally mildly rationalistic and lacked uniformity in tone and depth.

text: Mr. Gladstone sat on the ministerial side of the House from 1853 to 1866 without breach of continuity. During the first Derby government, Mr. Gladstone sat below the gangway on the opposition side. During the Palmerston administration of 1855, Mr. Gladstone sat below the gangway on the government side. Mr. Gladstone remained below the gangway after the second Derby accession to office in 1858. Mr. Gladstone wrote to his father on August 4, 1830, regarding his choice of profession. Mr. Gladstone expressed a growing inclination towards the ministerial office over a considerable period. Mr. Gladstone acknowledged that his desire for other pursuits was unstable and temporary.

Princess Alice has a black boy who has attracted attention in Deeside. The Queen finds it difficult to see people who did not know the Prince before his death. The Queen has expressed mistrust in Lord Russell's judgment in foreign affairs.

text: The episcopal order promoted absolutist centralization within the church. The principle that the pope's judgments were subject to the assembled representatives of the Christian world was overthrown. The constitutional party in the church appeared to be on the verge of triumph at the council of Constance, during the conflict between the French episcopate and Innocent XI., and when Clement XIV. addressed the Jesuits. From July 1870, the constitutional party's influence diminished significantly. The Syllabus of 1864 condemned various freedoms, including free speech and liberty of conscience. The text discusses the potential for the restoration of papal power through force and the support of an organized party. The mental attitude of Roman Catholic individuals in England and Ireland regarding political power and neutrality is questioned.

The Octagon contains materials relevant to the study of parliamentary crises. Bishop Phillpotts expressed reverence for Mr. Gladstone's principles in a letter dated Christmas Day 1863. General Booth noted that the officers and soldiers of the Salvation Army prayed for Mr. Gladstone's well-being. Mr. Spurgeon acknowledged Mr. Gladstone's impact on the nation and expressed admiration for his integrity. Various religious figures sought Mr. Gladstone's guidance on domestic issues and moral dilemmas.

The Queen required positive information regarding Mr. Gladstone's willingness to act in a government. Lord Hartington returned to Windsor after refusing a task he believed would result in failure. Lord Granville and Lord Hartington arrived at the author's house to convey the Queen's command. The author expressed gratitude for the high honour and patriotism shown by Lord Granville and Lord Hartington. Granville agreed to take the foreign office, while Hartington considered the India office.

The speaker indicated dissatisfaction with Stanley's management of the New Zealand question. The speaker acknowledged the extraordinary demands of their position and the physical strength required to fulfill them. text: Mr. Gladstone expressed concerns about the neutrality of England's position regarding potential conflict involving Belgium. On July 25, the _Times_ published a document revealing a proposed agreement between France and Prussia regarding Belgium. The public reacted with shock to the publication of the proposed agreement, suspecting it might be a forgery. Mr. Gladstone received confidential information from the Prussian ambassador about the existence of the draft agreement. On July 30, the British cabinet decided to propose a treaty to Prussia and France concerning the defense of Belgium's neutrality. The treaty proposed by England stated that if either France or Prussia violated Belgium's neutrality, England would cooperate with the other for its defense. The treaty was signed on August 9 after initial hesitation from France.

text: Mr. Gladstone made a controversial statement about the American Civil War at a banquet in Newcastle on October 7. His comments suggested that the Northern states would eventually have to accept the reality of the Southern states' independence. The immediate reaction to his statement was significant, leading to speculation about the British government's potential recognition of the South. This speculation caused uncertainty among cotton traders, resulting in countermanded orders and a threatened supply of cotton. Mr. Gladstone's language drew criticism from various correspondents, prompting him to issue a formal response disavowing responsibility for the interpretations of his words. Lord Russell, in a reply dated October 20, expressed concern that Gladstone's statement implied recognition of the South, which the cabinet was not prepared to grant. A week later, Lewis clarified the situation in a speech at Hereford, stating that the Southern states had not established their independence and were not entitled to recognition.

Lavington and visited his home and Mrs. Cobden. Mr. Gladstone noted the death of the Duke of Newcastle on October 19, 1864, as the loss of his last political friend. Dr. Kingsley informed Mr. Gladstone of the Duke's death via telegram shortly before it was reported in the papers. Mr. Gladstone reflected on the character of life as a dispensation of pain in relation to the Duke's death. On July 6, 1865, Parliament was dissolved. Mr. Gladstone considered abandoning his seat for the university but ultimately decided to continue representing Oxford.
