His speech highlighted issues in Naples, the Romagna under papal rule, and the lawlessness of the Duke of Modena. Mr. Gladstone's speeches in 1864 and 1865 strengthened his influence among liberal supporters in Britain. Garibaldi received a grand reception in London in April 1864, attracting large crowds. The public was drawn to Garibaldi for his reputation as a fighter and symbol of human freedom. Mr. Gladstone later reflected on Garibaldi's noble demeanor and integrity.

Mr. Gladstone withdrew a motion after the government declined to accept it, surprising the Tories. Mr. Gladstone became colonial secretary at the end of 1845 and was seen as a strong addition to the progressive section of the cabinet.

Mr. Gladstone noted the regularity and subordination within the duke's family. He expressed admiration for the duke's lack of personal pride and his resolute adherence to his conscience. Mr. Gladstone spent time with Milnes Gaskell at Thornes and later visited his sick mother in Leamington. He wrote articles for the Liverpool Standard and celebrated five Eton first classes at Oxford. Mr. Gladstone opposed the practice of opening public houses during the election campaign, viewing it as a moral issue.

Aberdeen noted that most treaties concluded after great wars were viewed as humiliating. Mr. Gladstone wrote letters to Lord Aberdeen and Sir Walter James while in Penmaenmawr. Mr. Gladstone reflected on the challenges of public life and its impact on personal well-being.

text: Mr. Gladstone was offered the office of president of the board of trade by Robert Peel on May 13, 1843. Robert Peel proposed Mr. Gladstone's appointment to the cabinet to the Queen, which was readily accepted. Mr. Gladstone expressed gratitude for Peel's offer and acknowledged his past errors. Mr. Gladstone initially approached the board of trade without enthusiasm but found the work fulfilling. Peel discussed various topics with Mr. Gladstone, including the opium question and the preservation of bishoprics in North Wales. Mr. Gladstone considered retiring from public service but ultimately decided to accept the cabinet position after consulting with colleagues.

Baring highlighted the discord among cabinet members, including Palmerston, Gladstone, and Lord John Russell. The Peelites, numbering forty, were seen as a weak support base for the government due to their divided loyalties. Baring mentioned that the church views of the cabinet were weak, causing distrust among Protestants and evangelicals. Gladstone later remarked that the cabinet did not show signs of its dual origin despite some individual differences. Mr. Gladstone expressed a belief in the importance of the well-being of the church of Rome.

Mr. Gladstone received a letter from Lord John informing him of a loan guarantee for Morocco, which he intended to resist. Carelessness in language can lead to significant misunderstandings and mischief. Mr. Gladstone defended the consistency of his speeches over time, particularly between 1833 and 1850. He believed that change of opinion in public figures should be monitored but is less harmful than persisting in wrong actions. Mr. Gladstone's use of qualifying words often led to misunderstandings with his audience.

Mr. Gladstone noted that he did not advise on dissolution but suggested resignation as the appropriate course of action. text: Between 1830 and 1873, there were twelve parliamentary crises involving a change of government. In nine of the twelve cases, the opposition was ready to take office and did so. In three cases, the opposition attempted to form a government but ultimately failed. The three failed attempts occurred in 1832, 1851, and 1855. In each failed attempt, the opposition did not relinquish their efforts until they believed all means of action were exhausted. On May 7, 1832, the opposition's motion in the House of Lords was deemed fatal to the Reform bill, leading to the resignation of Lord Grey's government. On February 20, 1851, Lord Russell's government was defeated by a majority of its own supporters in the House of Commons.

The transfer of land to W. H. Gladstone is subject to the payment of specified annuities. Mr. Gladstone advised W. H. Gladstone never to mortgage any of his land, citing negative consequences experienced in Hawarden. Mr. Gladstone expressed confidence in W. H. Gladstone's prudence and intelligence regarding the management of the estates. In a letter dated October 3, 1885, Mr. Gladstone discussed W. H. Gladstone's potential retirement from the general election. Mr. Gladstone highlighted the responsibilities of landowners to serve in parliament while considering the unique challenges of their estate. Mr. Gladstone acknowledged the impact of recent depressions in corn and coal on the estate's financial stability.

Cavour's dealings with the French Emperor were characterized by a complex political dynamic. The overthrow of the Derby government coincided with the struggle between Austria and the Franco-Sardinian allies. The preliminaries of Villafranca were signed on July 11, 1859, ending an inconclusive war. Cavour resigned from office in anger over the outcome of the Villafranca agreement.

Mr. Gladstone is not afraid of the suffrage and is willing to risk the treasury. He is seen as capable of reforming the ecclesiastical system and conciliating Ireland. Public sentiment towards Mr. Gladstone includes admiration and hope for national improvement.

Lord Aberdeen was considered an impossible choice for leadership, and the public was calling for Lord Palmerston. The Peelites had previously refused offers from Lord Derby and Lord John, and were now faced with the decision to refuse Lord Palmerston. Lord Aberdeen emphasized the importance of public necessity and the support of their former Whig colleagues. There was a belief that any government with notable figures in the cabinet, excluding Lord John, would gain public support. On February 4, it was reported that Palmerston had received the commission to form a government. The Peelites initially refused to join Palmerston's ministry on February 5 but changed their decision and joined on February 6.

Mr. Gladstone engaged in various activities including correspondence, estate matters, and reading during his political preoccupations. Poerio indicated that exposure would benefit their country despite potential backlash from the Neapolitan government. Palmer's legal perspective was seen as a source of anxiety among Tories, Whigs, and some Radicals. The debate in the Commons lasted over three and a half months, longer than the Church bill. Mr. Gladstone was chosen as the first lord rector of the University of Edinburgh later in the year. His rival for the position was Lord Neaves, who was recognized as a lawyer, humorist, and scholar. In April of the following year, Mr. Gladstone delivered a rectorial address that emphasized the importance of time management and the pursuit of knowledge. Mr. Gladstone's address was influenced by his own career and aimed to inspire young people.

Lord Winchilsea opposed any national endowment of Romanism. Mr. Disraeli suggested that Mr. Gladstone's resignation over Maynooth marked the end of his political career. Mr. Gladstone voted for the second reading of the Maynooth bill on April 11, despite opposing public opinion and his own constituents. Mr. Gladstone's legislative achievements included significant reforms in tariff legislation, removing duties on numerous articles. Mr. Gladstone maintained good relations with his former colleagues after his resignation.

text: The introduction of the ballot was considered dangerous and contradictory by the country and parliament. Daniel Webster advised against the introduction of the ballot, stating it could not coexist with monarchical institutions. Mr. Gladstone indicated that the people's bill had been passed by the House of Commons and would be presented to the House of Lords. The cabinet, under Mr. Gladstone, decided to withdraw the bill if the House of Lords maintained its stance on optional secrecy. The House of Lords eventually conceded to the ballot measure after public agitation. The ballot had a significant impact in Ireland by dislodging the political power of the Irish landlord. The efficacy of secret voting is seen as negative but it prevents obvious mischiefs.

text: In the autumn of 1856, ecclesiastical questions were a significant interest for Mr. Gladstone. Mr. Gladstone expressed indignation over the condemnation of Archdeacon Denison for heresy. Mr. Gladstone had long interviews with Archdeacon Denison and drafted responses for him. Mr. Gladstone believed that Denison should have been allowed to demonstrate that his doctrine aligned with scripture. In 1856, Mr. Gladstone reflected on his increasing involvement in politics, church struggles, literature, and family responsibilities. In February 1857, Mr. Gladstone met with Lord Derby to discuss his disapproval of Lord Palmerston's government. Mr. Gladstone was willing to support measures to displace Lord Palmerston's government without concern for who would succeed.

text: The principles of colonial administration have been reversed, viewing colonies as petty states rather than municipalities with internal freedom. The original idea was that colonies should be municipal bodies under imperial powers, with positive restraints imposed by the mother country. The speaker claims that adhering to the original principles would have saved millions for the exchequer and fostered better societies. Mr. Gladstone made observations regarding the Irish Financial Relations Commission report of 1894. In 1853, a duty of 8d. per gallon was imposed on Irish spirits, while Scotland had a duty of 1s. per gallon. The Income-Tax was extended to Ireland in 1853, with the expectation that it would be temporary and cease by 1860. The principle of a temporary income-tax was not forgotten, and in 1874, Gladstone proposed to repeal it.

The weather conditions prevented the landing of building artificers or their removal from the beacon on the evening of 17th June. James Glen worked to reassure his companions on the beacon during a night of rough weather. On Sunday, 18th June, the weather improved, and artificers found their companions on the rock in good health. Stevenson wrote a series of letters to the Times in 1891 and 1892 to address the issues in Samoa. Stevenson believed that reconciling Laupepa and Mataafa and replacing the Chief Justice and President were necessary for resolving Samoan troubles. War broke out in Samoa in 1893 between the supporters of Laupepa and Mataafa, resulting in Mataafa's defeat and exile. In 1899, England withdrew its claims in Samoa, while America retained Tutuila and Germany acquired Upolu and Savaii. German officials governed the larger islands peacefully and recognized Mataafa's position among native chiefs until his death. Stevenson's legacy was initially unpopular with German officials, but he is now honored and his policies are followed.

Flora remains silent and uncomplaining while being cared for by her family, despite her deep grief. Dr. Spencer engaged with the family by being busy in the dining-room or taking walks with the children. Margaret enjoyed Dr. Spencer's sketches and he began teaching Blanche to draw. Margaret discussed with her father the need for a nurse to help with the children while she is unwell. Flora expressed concern that bringing Aubrey into the school-room made other children idle. Mr. Rivers created prints and an engraving of a fine head of Alexander. Margaret and Norman were focused on framing the engraving. Ethel found the interest in framing frivolous and felt neglected. Three significant events occurred in January, including the opening of a school at Cocksmoor. Margaret contributed books and plum-buns for the school's opening. Ethel felt a sense of responsibility and shyness when interacting with the children at the school. Mr. Wilmot addressed the mothers and children at the school opening, emphasizing the importance of teaching.

The Daisy Chain, or Aspirations is a book by Charlotte Yonge. The book is described as a mixture of a tale for the young and a novel for their elders. It began as a series of conversational sketches and evolved beyond its original intention. The story is presented as a Family Chronicle, documenting home events during early life. The author suggests that the moral of the tale is for the young to reflect on their aspirations. The narrative includes characters such as Ethel, Flora, and Miss Winter. The setting includes a room in an old country town house with specific furnishings and decorations.

Mrs. Green spread malicious reports about Cherry Elwood. Mrs. Elwood reacted strongly to the reports about her daughter. Cherry Elwood maintained a quiet dignity and tried to calm her mother. Cherry's presence improved the order and cleanliness of the school. Cherry became popular with mothers and won the hearts of children. Ethel was often frustrated with Cherry's teaching methods and dialect. Cherry had previously suffered a severe injury that left her a cripple for life.

Dr. May was unable to get the necessary information from the distressed individual and had to refer to Flora. Ethel discovered that Meta would be upset to part with her until after the funeral. Flora encouraged Ethel to stay, believing her presence would be comforting. Meta often sought strength in solitude, while Flora found relief in discussing ordinary topics with Ethel. The speaker acknowledges their role in inciting others to pull down fences. Dr. May expresses concern about the fairness of awarding a scholarship to Harvey Anderson. Harry wrote 'Norman is Dux!' on pieces of paper and placed them around the house. Ethel felt disappointed by Norman's behavior after he became Dux. Flora acknowledges that a certain individual likes to think of himself as important. Ethel expresses concern about Flora's decision to put the individual into Parliament for her own satisfaction. The prince sought to emulate historical figures like Julius Caesar and Alexander to win the affection of a lady. The game involved agreeing on a word to be guessed through storytelling. Meta volunteered to guess the word while Harry expressed doubt to Mary. Flora told a story about a young girl named Marie who climbed Mont Blanc. Harry shared a story about an old sailor on the Alcestis and a monkey he encountered. The ladies to be propitiated include the Nine Muses, Ethel, and Mrs. Rivers. Ethel was assigned to visit Miss Anderson, Miss Boulder, and Mrs. Ledwich. The Ladies' Committee accepted their representatives with full consent.

Norman was devising a beginning by the way of George. Dr. May expressed the need to address a situation without putting Ethel in the forefront. Dr. Spencer, who was polite, indicated that the group was ready. A procession began with the minster choristers and Dr. Spencer as architect. Little Gertrude was led forward by Harry and Hector during the ceremony.

Tom felt a sense of shame and degradation after an incident at a public-house. Tom believed he would be unworthy to read with his sisters due to his actions. Norman expressed hope for Tom's future despite Tom's feelings of despair. Tom was concerned about a debt of eight shillings and tenpence halfpenny. Norman advised Tom to confess to their father to regain his esteem. Tom was fearful of his father's reaction and the potential knowledge of his sisters. Norman successfully brought Tom to their father to discuss the situation.

Ethel's aunt expresses concern about Ethel's father, who appears aged and thin. Ethel mentions that her sister Margaret is generally bright and happy but is experiencing health issues. Margaret's health problems include faintness and a condition related to her heart and spine. Ethel's father copes with the situation through his loving nature. Ethel describes Meta Rivers as capable and energetic, suitable for her brother Norman. Ethel has not seen her sister Flora for a year due to George Rivers' aversion to the Grange. Mrs. Arnott plans to visit Margaret after breakfast for an update on her condition.

Margaret expressed relief that Richard was spared the refusal of a vicar position. Ethel inquired about the appointment of Mr. Wilmot as vicar. The doctor stated that Richard was not old enough for the vicar position and recommended Edward Wilmot instead. Mr. Wilmot accepted the offer to become the vicar. Ethel mentioned the excitement about the opening of Cocksmoor school. Flora believed Richard would have faced financial burdens if he had taken the vicar position. Mr. Wilmot was welcomed back and engaged in conversation about the parish and local schools.

Meta proposed to let her maid, Bellairs, stay for a night or two to test her father's sincerity. Mrs. Larpent was reluctant to grant more than one night for Bellairs to stay. Meta assured Bellairs that she could stay as long as necessary to make her mother comfortable. Lady Leonora intended for her niece, Miss Rivers, to be fashionable and admired under her protection. Mr. Rivers was hesitant to move to London due to his dislike of the city and the trouble of relocating. Lady Leonora expressed concern about the lack of suitable society for Meta at the Grange. Flora successfully visited the Grange and conversed with Lady Leonora.

Hector will be returned to his guardianship under Captain Gordon and Ethel. Ethel expresses mixed feelings about the news regarding Hector. Margaret is pleased with the news and expresses gratitude for the outcome. Richard has been informed about the situation and shows concern for Margaret. Ethel acknowledges that Richard played a significant role in the positive outcome. Margaret reflects on the blessings that have arisen from past pain and grief.

Harry killed a partridge while out shooting with two friends. Harry felt guilty about the incident and was reluctant to confess to his father, Dr. May. Margaret encouraged Harry to tell their father about the incident for his own peace of mind. Harry was concerned that Dr. May would be angry upon hearing the confession. Dr. May was surprised by Harry's confession but listened attentively. Harry spoke firmly when confessing to Dr. May, indicating a desire for honesty. Dr. May's reaction was one of affection and inquiry, suggesting he was ready to forgive.

Blanche was climbing on her father's knee, asking for one of his Sunday stories. Etheldred felt disappointed but was glad to see her father engaging with Blanche. The story told by the father was about David, presented in a scriptural and poetical manner. Tom and Blanche discussed how they could be like David, the shepherd boy. Harry was waiting for a letter from Alan Ernescliffe regarding his future. Margaret informed Harry that the letter was in her room and encouraged him to consider it carefully. Alan Ernescliffe mentioned that the profession Harry was considering offered a fair chance of happiness.

Dr. May and Norman are at the bottom of a valley where a stream is rushing along. The stream is described as turbid creamy yellow and creates whirlpools as it crosses the road. Norman appears pale and is hesitant to cross a foot-bridge guarded by a handrail. Dr. May prevents Norman from attempting to return to the bridge after he expresses a desire to conquer his fear. Norman feels anxious about not being able to cross the bridge and compares himself to others. Dr. May reassures Norman that he will allow him to cross the bridge again when he is ready. Norman expresses frustration about his situation and the pressure to maintain his academic standing.

Richard brought his sister Ethel to visit an old woman instead of the doctor. The old woman expressed gratitude for the doctor's help and welcomed Ethel. Ethel inquired about the old woman's grandchildren, who were playing outside. The old woman called for her granddaughters, Polly and Jenny, to come inside. Ethel brought garments for the grandchildren and discussed their use for school and church. Richard and Ethel visited John Taylor, who had just come out of the hospital. Mrs. Taylor expressed concern about finding sponsors for the children's christening.

Ethel was preoccupied with thoughts about her sisters rather than Glenbracken. Mr. and Mrs. Rivers visited before the consecration, stopping to see Margaret and leave Mary. Flora appeared ill and was shocked by Margaret's condition during the visit. Flora decided to spend the day with Margaret instead of attending the consecration. Mary returned home looking well-dressed and youthful, displaying her improved manners. Mary expressed joy at being home and shared her experiences and gifts from Flora and George. Complaints arose about Mary and Blanche talking late into the night after Mary's return.

Ethel has a strong desire to undertake a project that has been her wish for a long time. Margaret expresses concern about whether it is appropriate for Ethel to take on such a significant responsibility at her age. Mr. Wilmot believes that Ethel's energy should be directed towards practical work, such as school-keeping. Margaret acknowledges that Ethel's hope for the project has motivated her to improve her home duties. Mr. Wilmot warns against interfering with young people's aspirations, as it can lead to negative outcomes. Margaret feels overwhelmed by her responsibilities and struggles to manage the needs of her family. Mr. Wilmot encourages Margaret to trust that her efforts will be compensated despite her challenges.

Margaret tried to calm and encourage Ethel as she prepared to leave. Adams was to drive Ethel in the gig. Dr. Spencer wrapped Ethel in cloaks and shawls before she left. Ethel observed the stars and felt a sense of calmness during her journey. Ethel was surprised by the servants' reaction upon her arrival. Meta greeted Ethel and expressed concern for their father. Dr. May informed the girls that their father's struggle was over.

Flora had a busy day with various activities including shopping and making canvassing calls about the orphan asylum. Meta expressed that she is glad to have some time at home and does not attend large parties or balls this year due to her mourning. Flora was admired at parties and referred to as the beauty of the season by others, including an old French marquis. Meta and Harry discussed New Zealand, including the Maori pah and the challenges faced by the younger generation in education. Harry's stories occupied Meta and Norman until long past midnight. Flora entered the room dressed in a rich black watered silk gown and silver ornaments, appearing graceful and distinguished. Flora recognized Harry as her brother upon his arrival, expressing joy at his return.

Tom is hiding behind a desk when Mr. Harrison enters the room. Anderson shuts a book and tries to distract Mr. Harrison while Tom is anxious about being discovered. Larkins makes a comment about Mr. Harrison not knowing what he has. Mr. Harrison inquires about a piece of blotting-paper found in the school. Tom fears that Mr. Harrison will recognize the blotting-paper and its connection to him. Mr. Harrison questions several students about the condition of a book left in school. All questioned students, including Tom, deny knowledge of how the book was damaged.

Ethel and Norman went up to bed arm-in-arm. Ethel asked if she could wish her father good-night. Richard allowed Ethel to enter the room to see her father. Ethel observed a mournful look on her father's face during their conversation. Flora was found sobbing on her bed, calling for her mother. Richard entered the room to comfort Flora and Mary. Ethel read to her sisters until they fell asleep.

Ethel kissed the little governess's forehead and wished her goodnight before leaving. Ethel felt that being rough and merry was beneficial for Miss Bracy, despite appearing careless. Ethel reflected on her day and her thoughts about her niece, Leonora, while sitting by the fire. Ethel read the Service for Baptism from her Prayer-book and thought about her sister's orphaned christening. Ethel envisioned a future for Leonora that included a fashionable life and a focus on marriage. A family gathering took place on New Year's Day, where Flora organized a second dinner in honor of Miss Leonora Rivers. Lady Leonora formed a friendship with Mrs. Rivers, who was well-regarded by others.

Margaret expressed unease about Ethel's ability to assist her. Ethel was careful and frightened while trying to help Margaret. Dr. May noticed Margaret's discomfort and sought to address it. Ethel felt distressed by Dr. May's anger and criticism. Flora helped Margaret find a more comfortable position. Margaret experienced a headache in addition to her back pain. Margaret and Ethel reconciled at bedtime, with Margaret expressing gratitude.

Ethel asked about Harry's appearance and was informed he looked much the same as when he left. An old naval friend of Harry's father has hopes of a ship and promised to take Harry with him. Ethel inquired about Harry's return, but her father could not provide a specific answer. Norman gave the key to Richard and invited Ethel to his room while he unpacked. Ethel received a present from Norman, which was a book titled 'Lyra Innocentium'. Norman's father gave him a book titled 'Bishop Ken's Manual' for Confirmation. Norman expressed his belief that Ernescliffe is in love with Margaret, and Ethel promised to keep it a secret.

Norman believes that a character will be cured of his fears when he outgrows them. Norman plans to go up for a scholarship in a month. Norman expresses a desire for Margaret not to know about the scholarship until further notice. Ethel feels that she is not as important to her father as she once was. Margaret has noticed a shift in her father's attention towards Ethel. Ethel shares a secret with her father that strengthens their bond. Ethel and her father share a likeness of mind that develops their relationship.

Alan took all the waiting on Margaret exclusively to himself. Alan spent his mornings in the drawing-room alone with Margaret for ten days. Alan took on the role of an affectionate elder brother to the rest of the family. Margaret and Ethel enjoyed Alan's presence during evening conversations. Dr. May struggled to make a decision regarding Alan and Margaret's engagement. Flora provided support to Margaret and helped create a conducive environment for the lovers. Margaret sought her eldest brother's judgment but found it difficult to obtain.

Harry is characterized as kind, generous, and mischievous. Mary is described as rough, merry, and devoted to Tom. Harry and Mary are noted to be very similar except for Harry's curly hair. Norman and Ethel resemble their father in cleverness and strong feelings. Ethel has personal challenges including a quick temper and heedlessness. Norman is successful in school and has not shown tendencies toward conceit. The narrator expresses hope for Ethel's independence from the need for praise.

Meta's weather was described as fresh and joyous when the August sun rose. Dr. May carried off Harry and Mary to visit patients on the same road. Mrs. Charles Wilmot and her little girl joined the party. Meta wore pink summer robes and was described as joyful and light-hearted. The group traveled through lanes and fields, encountering harvest workers and enjoying songs and laughter. Norman tumbled Mr. May down a grassy slope while the others played joyfully. The young antiquaries discussed historical topics related to the old lines of encampment they were exploring.

Meta believes that having power to do good brings happiness. Norman argues that a profession can become an unreality. Meta expresses confusion over Norman's views on self-deception. Norman compares the feeling of self-deception to a wanderer fearing a mirage. Meta suggests that belief can serve as a spell to overcome delusions. Norman feels trapped in a confusing mental state, likening it to a horrible dream. Meta remains optimistic and believes that nature will help Norman forget his worries.

Ethel expresses her awareness of her ill-humour and her sister Flora's patience. Flora suggests sending Ethel with Norman to dine at Abbotstoke Grange on Wednesday. Ethel doubts that she and Mr. George Rivers would get along. Flora and Fanny Anderson exchange civilities and discuss previous events. The committee consists of nine ladies, with Mrs. Ledwich as chair and Miss Rich as secretary. The proceeds of the fancy fair amount to one hundred and forty-nine pounds fifteen shillings and tenpence. Flora suggests discussing steps for acquiring land during the committee meeting.

Meta expressed a desire to stay at home while saying goodbye to her friends at Stoneborough. Flora promised to send educational materials to Cocksmoor school and invited Miss Bracy's sisters to visit. Flora maintained correspondence with Margaret, keeping her informed about daily activities and political news. Dr. Spencer inquired about Flora's news updates, suggesting she should be a special correspondent. Flora visited Miss Walkinghame in Richmond and was welcomed by Lady Walkinghame. Sir Henry Walkinghame, who had recently returned from the continent, joined Flora and Meta for dinner and music. The Easter recess was spent at Lady Leonora's house in Surrey instead of the Grange.

Flora expressed concern about leaving Margaret without support in case she becomes overwhelmed. Flora believes that a certain individual is not helpful in difficult situations. Ethel felt horrified by Flora's assertion of independence from the individual's orders. Richard discussed the situation with his father, Dr. May, who was uncertain about promoting an engagement due to Margaret's health. Ethel was preoccupied with thoughts of Margaret's recovery while teaching her lessons. Mary was excited about two new scholars who had superior attainments and were taught by 'Sister Cherry.' The house had been improved from its previous state and was now more comfortable, despite some remaining issues.

Mrs. Arnott finds her niece Margaret in a very different state than before, appearing wasted and broken. Dr. May informs Mrs. Arnott that Margaret has behaved well and slept soundly. Aubrey announces the arrival of the gig and shares his latest design for a cathedral. Margaret expresses excitement about the consecration and shows a model of the church made by Richard. Ethel is teaching Aubrey arithmetic in a unique way that only Norman seems to understand.

Ethel often expresses solid thoughts that impress Margaret. Margaret reflects on the nature of ambition and the desire to be first. Mrs. May suggests that seeking to be first in affection may lead to self-seeking. Margaret acknowledges that her affection for Richard makes her feel like she is first. Mrs. May advises against measuring affection and emphasizes giving it freely. Mr. Ernescliffe inquires about the walking party as Norman, Flora, and Miss Winter gather. Norman goes to hurry Ethel, who is delayed by her studies.

Ethel expresses concern about Daisy's sensitivity and her reactions to criticism. Dr. May questions Ethel about her comments regarding Daisy's temperament. Ethel admits to feeling overwhelmed by frequent arguments with Daisy. Dr. May advises Ethel to be more forbearing with Daisy's feelings. Ethel believes that Daisy's touchiness stems from pride rather than humility. Dr. May intends to apologize to Daisy for any distress caused. Ethel feels misunderstood and believes her honesty has been misinterpreted.

Harry expresses a desire to do his duty despite the dangers involved. Harry's father acknowledges his son's maturity and agrees to consider his wishes. Etheldred observes that the Taylors attended school on Sunday, but the Halls did not. Ethel condemns Granny Hall for not attending school and expresses frustration over wasted resources. Mary and Tom welcomed Hector to play in the garden. Mary and Blanche constructed pottery under Hector and Tom's supervision. Miss Winter disapproved of the children's play in the dirt.

Flora is introduced as the enchanted princess. Blanche is searching for her watch-guard and is in despair. Mr. George Rivers attempts to assist Blanche but causes her indignation. Aubrey was taught by Ethel, who sacrificed her studies to fulfill home requirements. Aubrey developed a strong interest in books and classical tastes under Ethel's guidance. Edward Anderson and Axworthy broke school rules with the understanding that the second boy would support them. Richard expressed surprise at Tom's misunderstanding of the word 'oppositus'. Ethel corrected Tom's interpretation of 'oppositus' as a participle. Harry distracted Tom while he attempted to determine the derivation of 'oppositus'. Tom incorrectly suggested that 'oppositus' derived from 'op-possum'. Richard requested Harry to stop distracting Tom during their lesson. Ethel noted that Tom provided the correct answer to an arithmetic problem without understanding the process. Ethel felt dismay at Tom's behavior and Richard's indifference during the lesson.

Ethel is eager for classical learning and questions whether her ambition is appropriate. Ethel prioritizes her father and Cocksmoor over her desire for knowledge. Margaret informs her father about Ethel's prolonged engagement with Norman. Dr. May agrees with Miss Winter's view that Ethel should not undertake too much learning. Margaret observes that Ethel treats her with respect and authority despite their age difference. Flora and Mary do not require Margaret's interference, unlike Ethel. The setting sun illuminates the school at Stoneborough where young boys are clearing away books.

Ethel did not tell Miss Bracy that she was ill-tempered. Mary claimed that Miss Bracy said Ethel called her ill-tempered. Miss Bracy was upset and cried before Dr. May arrived. Dr. May encouraged Miss Bracy to not brood over vexations. Miss Bracy acknowledged her feelings were over-sensitive.

Ethel expressed her grievances about Miss Winter and M. Ballompre. Norman, who attends school half a mile away, regularly comes home to inquire about his sister. Flora called everyone to dinner and Norman took it upon himself to serve Margaret. Nurse informed Margaret about a girl named Taylor from Cocksmoor who is interested in a position. Margaret approved of Lucy Taylor, who is set to start on Saturday.

Ethel preferred to remain still and not go outside until evening. Dr. Spencer waited at the door for confirmation of a report about a sailor. Will Adams announced that Master Harry had come home at Cocksmoor school. Norman returned home quickly, while Richard expressed concern for Margaret. Richard suggested that Mary should lie down in her room if she could not behave properly.

The great day for Norman was the 20th of December. Ethel was concerned about Norman's performance and wanted him to surpass Harvey Anderson. Flora and Ethel bring a baby named Gertrude Margaret to their father. The father expresses tenderness towards the baby, referring to her as 'Daisy blossom' and 'little Maggie.' Richard and Flora are concerned about Dr. May's emotional state and his desire to see his deceased wife's face. Dr. May requests his wife's ring, which Richard brings to him. The grave of Margaret is located in the cloister attached to the minster.

Flora expressed concern about George's feelings after he was asked to leave her. Dr. May insisted that George leave Flora because he believed George's affection was harming her. Flora felt guilty for George's distress and wanted to go to him immediately. George was initially confused upon waking and did not speak until Dr. May reassured him. Flora was physically weak and emotionally affected after the previous night. Flora only seemed to respond to George, while she struggled to engage with others. Flora dressed and sat with George to comfort him, despite her own fatigue.

The speaker believes that complete freedom from work is the only remedy for Norman. The speaker advises against Norman fretting about being surpassed in his studies. The speaker expresses a preference for Norman to be healthy and useful rather than a nervous scholar. Norman expresses relief that he can read as long as it does not harm him. Dr. May observes the landscape and recalls bringing his wife to the same location. Dr. May leaves Norman to attend to a girl recovering from a fever. Dr. May discusses Norman's character and concerns about his health with Margaret.

The protagonist observed something moving towards home from an alley. Tom was found under the bedclothes, believing he was being pursued by a policeman. Dr. May was called to a house near the river on Friday and left around eight o'clock. Norman appeared distressed when he encountered Dr. May and struggled to speak. Norman revealed to Dr. May that he had been expelled from school. Norman blamed Anderson for his expulsion, claiming he incited trouble among the town-fellows. Dr. Hoxton suspected Norman of inciting the trouble despite Norman's insistence of his innocence.

Harry reported that Norman performed well in a recent academic competition. Anderson ranked fourth in the competition, below Forder, Cheviot, and Ashe. June experienced a giddy spell during dinner but was fine afterward.

Ethel believes that their father should know everything about the family. Ethel is upset after a discussion regarding Tom's behavior. Flora expresses concern about how Ethel would inform their father about Tom. Margaret thinks that while Ethel's principle is correct, it may not be practical. Richard and Flora agree with Margaret's view on the matter. Margaret feels a strong responsibility to spare her father from worry. Ethel is dissatisfied with Margaret's approach and desires more straightforwardness.

Blanche was found sobbing in distress by Ethel. Blanche's distress was caused by George's facetious jokes in the presence of Hector. Ethel attempted to comfort Blanche, who was reluctant to leave the cupboard. Ethel asked Flora to suggest to George that he change his style of wit. Flora promised to provide all the sights in London to the children and masters to Mary and Blanche. Ethel expressed a sense of sadness despite the overall triumph of the group. Miss Bracy attempted to kiss Ethel's hand after complimenting her understanding.

Flora cut a great snow-white cake for the luncheon. George proposed to run away with Daisy, who kicked and screamed. Flora and George departed for the Continent after the wedding. Ethel expressed a desire for quiet time to think about her new life. Ethel arranged her properties in her new room and reflected on her duties.

Ethel expresses feelings of unworthiness and sadness to her father, Dr. May. Dr. May reassures Ethel that her actions have awakened grace in others. Ethel acknowledges her selfish behavior towards Dr. May, Miss Bracy, and Flora. Dr. May advises Ethel that harsh truths can sometimes be beneficial. Ethel plans to write to Richard and send a message from Dr. May. Flora revises a letter to the principal, which is approved by the Ladies' Committee. The clergyman noted that Una frequently mentioned 'Mr. Richard May' and 'Miss Athel' when asked about her education. Una's mother expressed gratitude towards Dr. May and his family for their kindness to Una. Una contracted typhus fever and was in a half-delirious state, often repeating hymns and psalms. Una expressed regret for not being able to say goodbye to Miss May before her family moved.

Flora insisted on yielding the post of honour in the Ladies' Committee. Dr. Spencer believed the ladies were grateful for his good advice. Charity Elwood was sent for six months' finish at the Diocesan Training School. The Alcestis had taken fire on April 12 of the previous year. Captain Gordon's official report listed three missing officers and their seamen. The second cutter, under command of Mr. Ernescliffe, had disappeared after a night of storms. Margaret expressed relief that she did not write a letter that would have parted her from Richard.

The funeral for Mr. Rivers was scheduled for Monday at the church where he was buried. Ethel expressed her inability to attend the funeral due to her commitment to Margaret. Flora, despite her illness, managed household duties but remained emotionally detached. Meta and George displayed visible grief during the funeral, while Flora maintained a composed demeanor. Flora locked away her child's possessions after the funeral. Preston, a housekeeper, was deeply affected by the tragedy and expressed her sorrow to Flora. Flora reassured Preston about their meeting, showing kindness despite her own grief.

Dr. May expressed confidence in Meta's happiness. Mr. Rivers relied on Flora for support regarding Meta. Dr. May felt uneasy about Mr. Rivers' unusual heaviness and depression. A message was received indicating that Miss Rivers needed Dr. May's immediate presence. Ethel received a note from her father stating he was very ill and requested her to come to Meta. Ethel experienced a moment of shock upon reading her father's note but quickly became eager to help Meta. Dr. Spencer offered to assist by preparing Ethel's father's belongings.

Ethel felt timid in her affection and only dared to kiss and whisper to the children. Dr. Hoxton's carriage arrived to take the bride, prompting Ethel to follow instructions without much will of her own. During the ceremony, George appeared nervous and sheepish, relying on his best man, Norman. Dr. Hoxton performed the wedding ceremony with Richard assisting, and his voice was considered impressive. Ethel struggled to sign her name as a witness due to trembling hands, and Mary helped her with the signature. Margaret welcomed the guests in a soft blue dress, looking calm and bright despite Ethel's concerns about her appearance. Flora was nervous and hurried while giving Ethel parting directions about household comforts before the wedding.

Ethel asked where to find Flora and was informed that she was with Margaret. Flora was in a hurry to get handkerchiefs and indicated that Margaret was not in her own room. Harry reported that their father, Mr. Ward, was with him and had a severely injured arm. Margaret was described as insensible, and there were concerns about her head. Norman learned that their father's arm was broken in two places and he was in an unconscious state. Mary informed Harry that the baby had been fed and was now quiet. Norman encountered a council in the drawing-room consisting of Alan Ernescliffe, the surgeon, and Mr. Wilmot.

Meta has a fanciful father and a brother who is described as stupid and idealess. Norman believes that some sensible men enjoy shooting and mentions Ogilvie as an example. Dr. May expresses pity for a character who seems to find existence hard work. Margaret suggests that fondling names should be kept private and not used in front of strangers. Dr. May agrees that baby-names should not be used outside the home and can harm a girl's self-respect. Flora states that friends should help maintain a girl's dignity by not using nicknames publicly. Ethel jokes about the pressure of having a do-nothing brother and the implications for Meta.

Ethel expresses concern that sick people regard Dr. May as more important than their clergyman. Flora states that Dr. May is highly respected in the town, which benefits their committee. Ethel and Flora discuss their advantages of better birth, education, and property in the town. The children are outside playing with soap-suds and tobacco pipes after Hector and Tom's departure. Aubrey and Mary engage in blowing bubbles, with varying degrees of success. Daisy expresses disappointment after trying to catch a bubble and finding it gone. Norman recalls a past incident involving a bubble and a housemaid's reaction.

Margaret feels ashamed of her speech. Ethel acknowledges that Margaret misses their father. Margaret has repressed her emotions, leading to a breakdown. Richard is perceived as the reasonable member of the family. Dr. Spencer observes that Ethel is better able to handle Margaret's condition. Margaret intends to meet Flora without witnesses. Flora's visit is disappointing as she avoids discussing her grief.

Very few people go to church regularly in the community. Elwood, Taylor, Sam Hall, and many women attend church in the evening. All children who are big enough attend Sunday school. Willie Brown is trying to become Dr. Spencer's groom. Ben Wheeler worked in the quarries and did not learn bad words. Mr. Wilmot is considering having a curate specifically for Cocksmoor. Richard accepted Mr. Wilmot's proposal to become the Cocksmoor curate.

Margaret is in need of assistance at home. Cocksmoor is described as a destitute place. Mr. Wilmot is interested in improving conditions at Cocksmoor. Richard and Ethel have a plan to address issues in Cocksmoor. Mr. Wilmot intends to speak to Mr. Ramsden about their plans. Ethel remains silent during the discussion but is pleased with Mr. Wilmot's approval. Dr. May expresses satisfaction with Richard's project and shares this with Margaret.

Ethel performed an exercise that had no detectable faults except for poor writing. Miss Winter considered Ethel's writing too atrocious to show to M. Ballompre. Ethel produced a second writing specimen that had defects due to carelessness. Miss Winter believed Ethel's poor performance was a result of ill temper. Margaret felt grateful to Miss Winter for not bringing Ethel into disgrace. Margaret was conflicted between her admiration for Ethel and the concerns raised by Miss Winter. Ethel expressed that she was busy with Thucydides and could not stay to talk with Margaret.

Mr. Rivers went to sleep after dinner. Meta expressed no intention of returning with her uncle on Monday morning. Margaret noted that Meta's current position reflects her substantial usefulness. Meta has transitioned from a life of mere accomplishments to one focused on duty and responsibility. Meta diligently manages her time for reading and studying. Meta is learning needlework to assist the poor people in her community. Meta took on the role of house manager after the old housekeeper left two years ago.

Norman and Margaret are siblings who discuss family matters. Margaret reports that Flora is doing well but is thought to be overexerting herself. Flora plans to show her baby to Margaret in a week, though it may not be allowed. George Rivers is preparing to stand for election as Mr. Esdaile intends to resign. Dr. Spencer informed Flora about Mr. Esdaile's retirement, which excited her. Ethel is to be the godmother of Flora's baby, and Flora intends to ask Mr. Ogilvie to come. Meta has been helpful and has brought her housekeeping books to Flora.

Ethel expressed concern about her brother Norman's situation and shared what she had heard in the afternoon. Dr. May was initially indignant about Norman's involvement with certain books, which he believed were harmful. Dr. May asked Ethel if Norman was safe and held the faith, to which Ethel confirmed. After a conversation with Norman, Dr. May expressed concern that Norman was serious about his intentions. Norman planned to write to his uncle, Mr. Arnott, in New Zealand to inquire about a mission. Norman was to return to Oxford and add a course of medical lectures to his studies. Mary was engaged in dusting and arranging Harry's books and birthday gifts on his eighteenth birthday.

Captain Gordon regarded the subject as an example of what a sailor should be. Margaret expressed her emotions through journaling for Alan while maintaining her role in the household. Margaret became personally invested in Ethel's Cocksmoor pursuits and took a leading role in planning and utilizing Mr. Ernescliffe's benefaction. The Elwood family gained a favorable reputation among the Mays. Cherry was well-educated by a clergyman and his wife, differing from the usual acquaintances of the girls. Mr. Hazlewood confirmed the positive assessment of the Elwoods and supported Cherry's appointment as a teacher. Margaret actively engaged with Cherry and the children, learning about their history and character.

Bill Blake has brothers who want anything that is available. Tom and Blanche might take something to Bill Blake's brothers. Old Bishop Whichcote's rules allow only daily mutton for meals. Harry and Hector discuss the merits of cakes and pies. The doctor reminisces about tarts that used to grow on Cocksmoor. Ethel asks her father for a pair of spectacles for a walk. Harry protests against Ethel wearing spectacles during the walk.

Meta expresses uncertainty about her obligations and independence. Dr. May suggests that Meta is still very young. Meta believes that good men do not like heiresses. Dr. May reassures Meta that her presence is valuable to Flora. Etheldred expresses a dislike for having to be civil to her neighbor. Ethel feels guilty for not being more accommodating to Dr. Spencer's efforts. Ethel wishes to avoid the social obligations of being the lady of the house.

Harry returned home yesterday. Flora expressed happiness at Harry's arrival. George welcomed Harry home and attempted to order food for him. Flora has a baby whom she described as a model baby. Flora plans to take her baby home to acquire color. Flora and her family plan to spend six weeks with the Walkinghames at Ryde. Norman felt excluded from the family's enjoyment during the conversation.

The text discusses the character and temperament of a woman described as porcelain-like and brave. The speaker believes that actual work in a good cause is preferable to idleness. The speaker expresses confidence that the woman would willingly face hardships. Norman has a positive relationship with the woman and recalls their first meeting fondly. Lord Cosham, as a philanthropist, supports missions and discusses them with Norman in a calm manner. A compromise is reached that allows Norman a year to complete his studies before making decisions about engagement and missions. Meta expresses concerns about the potential complications of decisions made without careful consideration.

Tom was present at an assembly where a sailor was welcomed home. Harry interacted with distinguished guests and displayed ease in conversation. Flora expressed doubt about Harry's dancing ability. Harry danced with the daughter of his new acquaintance and was well-received. Norman was hesitant to dance and preferred to stay against a wall. Flora mentioned the presence of Sir Henry Walkinghame, who admired Norman's prize poem. Harry believed Norman was more impressive than himself due to his accomplishments.

Flora is concerned about her baby's health and seeks advice from Dr. May. Flora describes her baby as sleepy, fretful, and unamused. Dr. May expresses surprise that Flora has not brought the baby home. Margaret believes it would have been better for Flora to bring the baby home. George informs Dr. May that Flora has not left the baby and has not sought advice until Dr. May's arrival. Dr. May plans to visit Flora and the baby the following day by train.

Ethel is sitting near a window with a book, a dictionary, and a pencil. Margaret expresses concern for Ethel's feelings regarding a situation at Cocksmoor. Ethel is frustrated with Flora and Mrs. Hoxton for their involvement in Cocksmoor. The Ladies' Committee is inspecting Cocksmoor School and finds it lacking in several areas. Mrs. Hoxton plans a bazaar to raise funds for Cocksmoor School. Ethel believes the bazaar will lead to the founding of Cocksmoor School based on vanity and frivolity. Margaret acknowledges the need for the school but is unsure about the bazaar's implications.

Young Ernescliffe was taken to Dr. May's house for recovery after being unable to sit up. Dr. May's family had recently welcomed their eleventh child two days prior to Ernescliffe's arrival. Mrs. May was sympathetic towards Ernescliffe but had concerns about having a stranger in her home. Ernescliffe became well-liked by the May family, with everyone expressing admiration for him. Ernescliffe participated in discussions about the name of the new baby, contributing his favorite name, Margaret. The family decided to choose the baby's name through a drawing, which resulted in the names Gertrude and Margaret being selected. Dr. May and Mrs. May had contrasting appearances and dispositions, with Mrs. May being described as small and serene, while Dr. May was tall and lanky.

Three children were entirely ignorant of the Lord's Prayer. Jane and Fanny Taylor, Rebekah Watts, and Mrs. Green's little boy reported using morning and evening prayers. Some children repeated the old rhyme about 'Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.' Mr. Wilmot promised a Prayer-book and a Bible to children who could repeat the Catechism and read a chapter, respectively. Lessons were assigned to be ready by the following Tuesday, including verses from Psalms and the Catechism. Margaret was first carried downstairs, which caused excitement among the family. Margaret felt a sense of confusion and effort to maintain a cheerful demeanor during the commotion.

Margaret was made to collect something for someone. Tom had a bottle of ointment for his hair. Harry suggested comparing Tom's hair color to a carrot. Norman and others were in high spirits and shared witticisms. Norman expressed disgust at the state of society. Flora greeted Norman with cold fingers and a mournful expression. Flora's appearance contrasted with her attempt to show gladness.

Bellairs promised to call Ethel to be with her young lady, reporting that she was sound asleep. Ethel was up and had been with Dr. May before she was summoned to Meta. Meta was found half dressed and hastening to avoid making Dr. May late for breakfast. Ethel reassured Meta that Dr. Spencer would take care of the patients. After breakfast, Meta expressed confusion and gratitude to Dr. May. Dr. May informed Meta about her father's last hours, which led to her shedding quiet tears. Meta returned to her tasks, writing letters and seeing Mr. Charles Wilmot, while managing her grief.

Ethel expressed concern about having vexed her father. Margaret informed their father about Ethel's troubles. Ethel's father acknowledged his harshness towards her. Ethel felt disheartened by her inability to do good due to her awkwardness. Norman's sixteenth birthday was noted, but their father seemed to have forgotten it. Ethel planned to read to Margaret before joining Norman for Latin and Greek. Norman was found asleep with his head on an open book during the day.

Ethel was unable to find a nurse and her supplies, which caused her frustration and affected her ability to write. Ethel had a dispute with Margaret regarding her progress and commitments. Margaret expressed concern that Ethel was taking on too much work, which was affecting her performance. Ethel mentioned that she was struggling with difficult Latin and Greek assignments. Margaret pointed out that Ethel was trying to keep up with Norman, who was more advanced and had additional responsibilities. Ethel felt overwhelmed and bothered by her workload, leading to feelings of being rushed and vexed. Margaret suggested that Ethel consider reducing her commitments to improve her situation.

Mrs. Arnott observed improvements in Cocksmoor during her visit with her nieces. The cottages in Cocksmoor appeared more unified and less desolate than in the past. Richard promoted cottage gardening, leading to better maintenance of the cottages. Mrs. Taylor still spoke with a piteous voice about her daughters, despite their well-doing. Margaret was less capable of engaging in activities she once enjoyed, but remained cheerful. Dr. Spencer and Dr. May discussed old Edinburgh stories in the evening, maintaining a lively atmosphere. Mrs. Arnott enjoyed spending time in Margaret's room, where they could converse without interruption.

Richard is studying hard at home with increased hopefulness and vigor. Ethel suggested to Richard that he could be the Curate of Cocksmoor in the future. Richard found the prospect of being a curate to give him motivation for his studies. Norman has been assisting Richard with his studies since returning from London. Tom was surprised to find Mr. Harrison's book in their home. Mary identified Harry's blotting-paper in Mr. Harrison's book. Harry had drawn sailors' buttons on his blotting-paper during a previous holiday.

Dr. May and Dr. Spencer are former fellow students who have reunited. Dr. Spencer defends the nine muses and has a youthful perspective despite being considered old-fashioned. Harvey Anderson attempts to engage Dr. Spencer in patronage and argument but finds him unyielding. Ethel observes the differing perspectives on argument between Dr. Spencer and Harvey Anderson. Dr. May visits Mr. Rivers, who is disappointed that George and Flora will not return from Scotland for another month. Mr. Rivers expresses concern for his daughter and wishes to see her in good hands. Dr. May reassures Mr. Rivers about his daughter's future and independence.

Dr. May, Richard, and Ethel traveled to the Grange and found Hector reading 'Wild Sports of the West'. Norman and Meta were sitting by the fire talking when Ethel and Meta spent time together before the gentlemen arrived. Ethel learned from Meta that she had confided the existence of Decius Mus, which Ethel had previously considered a secret. Ethel encouraged Norman to complete the poem Decius, which he worked on enthusiastically when referred to as a devotion. Ethel stitched the completed poem with a narrow red and white ribbon and persuaded Norman to send it in. Norman's success in winning a prize was met with a sense of routine acceptance by Ethel and others. Flora and George planned to visit Oxford for the Commemoration and wanted Meta and Ethel to attend.

Norman entered the room and collapsed into a chair, appearing pale and trembling. Ethel expressed concern for Norman's condition and attempted to support him. Norman gasped that Margaret was alive but could not provide further details. Norman indicated that their father was injured, specifically mentioning a broken arm. Ethel learned from Harry that their father was being attended to by Mr. Ward and Alan Ernescliffe. Ethel found the younger siblings huddled together in the nursery, with Mary watching over the infant. Harry informed Ethel that their father was in his dressing-room and that his arm was being set.

Ethel was walking home with Dr. Spencer after he was driven off at speed. Ethel informed Dr. Spencer that her mother was killed in an accident when her father's arm was hurt. Ethel mentioned that her sister Margaret cannot walk due to harm done to her spine. Edward Anderson, articled to Mr. Bramshaw, inquired about Harry and mentioned a paper that his mother wanted to send. Ethel expressed concern for news of her brother's ship, Alcestis, in the Pacific. Dr. Spencer was shocked by the news of Ethel's mother and expressed concern for May's happiness. The children were playing in the garden when Ethel and Dr. Spencer arrived.

Edward Anderson is facing expulsion as determined by Dr. Hoxton. Sam Axworthy is the son of a low, uneducated man and has a surly, obstinate temper. Dr. May interceded for Edward Anderson's pardon, but Dr. Hoxton insisted on strict justice. Flora expressed contemptuous pity for Mrs. Anderson's pride in her children. Norman believes that the absence of Axworthy will allow for better order at the school. Edward Anderson expressed sorrow and regret for his actions and wished to redeem his character. Norman's father has already spoken on Edward's behalf to Dr. Hoxton.

Ethel expresses joy about a situation involving her sister Margaret. Margaret feels a mix of gratitude and sorrow regarding the situation. Ethel believes their father, referred to as papa, will be relieved by the news. Margaret acknowledges her initial uncertainty about seeing someone. Ethel informs Margaret that their father will be coming at tea-time. Flora feels alienated and mortified due to her lack of confidence and sympathy from others. Alan Ernescliffe is present during the tea gathering, engaging in conversation with Margaret and the children.

Norman expresses a desire to become a missionary in New Zealand. Ethel is surprised by Norman's wish to part from their father. Ethel believes their father would consent to Norman's mission. Norman feels weary of his current life of competition and controversy. Ethel expresses a wish to accompany Norman on his mission. Norman acknowledges that he has felt bewildered and questioned the truth. Ethel reassures Norman that the difficult time he experienced is in the past.

Norman was grateful for the friendship shown to him by little boys who were younger than him. Captain Gordon had acquired a ship and hoped to take Harry with him. Norman's brother, Tom, appeared to be avoiding him and looked harassed and miserable. Norman sought to have a conversation with Tom, who was distressed and crying. Tom expressed that he felt responsible for the situation and mentioned being bullied. Tom reported that other boys were glad about his troubles and had threatened him. Anderson senior intervened to stop the bullying that Tom was experiencing.

Norman and Meta discuss a woman who struggles with her looks when alone. Meta expresses gratitude for the woman's gentle and considerate nature. Norman and Meta reflect on the intertwined nature of joy and grief. They discuss the enduring nature of love despite distance and hardship. Meta mentions that Uncle Cosham is pleased with Norman's speech. Norman is uncertain about whether Dr. May has informed Uncle Cosham of his intentions. Meta expresses her belief that Norman's purpose in life is important to him.

Mrs. Ledwich is mentioned in the context of children being neglected. Dr. May expresses dissatisfaction with the Ladies' Committee's decisions. Richard and Ethel propose to teach the Cocksmoor children. They plan to hire a cottage for teaching at a low cost. Ethel has been thinking about this teaching initiative for two months. Dr. May agrees to their plan and suggests inviting Mr. Wilmot to discuss it. Ethel and Richard express gratitude for Dr. May's support.

Margaret believed that forfeits should not begin until the date of the agreement. The walking party returned late after star-gazing and engaged in a dispute about constellations. Dr. May corrected the globe for the southern latitudes and discussed stars with the children. Ethel lifted the globe to avoid it being forgotten, while Norman praised her tidiness. Harry expressed excitement about the idea of voluntary forfeits for leaving items around. Dr. May dedicated an hour each day to reading with Norman, Ethel, and Harry to supplement Mr. Ramsden's teaching. Ethel and Flora visited Miss Walkingham, but Ethel expressed her disinterest in meeting her.

Flora expressed her emotions uncontrollably and sought comfort from Margaret. Ethel observed a procession enter the aisle during a service and felt a sense of disbelief. Ethel experienced a deep thanksgiving during the service, which she had imagined many times before. Ethel's thoughts were focused on Margaret throughout the prayers and praises during the service. Ethel felt a moment of grief when considering Margaret's potential inclusion in the thanksgiving for the departed. Ethel experienced a profound sense of joy and praise during the service, feeling uplifted beyond herself. After the service, Ethel engaged in conversation about Miss May and her impact on the children of Cocksmoor.

Harry expresses remorse and seeks his father's forgiveness. Dr. May comforts Harry and acknowledges his straightforward confession. Harry feels intense love for his father and sister during a moment of reflection. Harry contemplates the idea of becoming a sailor and the adventures it entails. Dr. May is surprised by Harry's persistent desire to be a sailor. Harry insists that his wish to be a sailor is serious and not a passing fancy. Dr. May acknowledges Harry's determination and the challenges of being a sailor.

Margaret Rivers felt admiration and sympathy for a connection she had with someone. Etheldred was unable to sleep and reflected on her feelings towards her father. Etheldred experienced shame for her impatience regarding her father's attention. Norman Ogilvie had shown interest in Etheldred during the week. Etheldred struggled with the decision to prioritize her father's needs over her own happiness. Etheldred believed that her father would miss her if she left. Etheldred resolved to return home to support her father despite her feelings for Norman Ogilvie.

In the morning, Norman's pain had lessened and he appeared less feverish. Harry reported that Norman had been talking in his sleep and groaning until Harry woke him. The children were kept in the drawing-room, and only Richard and Mr. Ernescliffe knew the reason for the strange steps in the house. Witnesses of the overturn agreed that the new black horse was not fit to drive. Harry visited his father, who invited any of them to come in and see him. Norman struggled to visit his father, feeling pale and breathless, and needed support from Ethel. Richard later invited Norman and Ethel into the study, where they faced the reality of their father's condition.

Mary and Flora were preparing for a gathering with Blanche and Aubrey, who were arriving in a gig driven by Norman. Tom and Hector Ernescliffe were invited to the party. The young people were happy as they arrived at the common and were greeted by their pupils. Mrs. Green's house became crowded as everyone entered, and Mr. Wilmot began to examine the children. Una M'Carthy demonstrated significant progress in her learning and was recognized by Mr. Wilmot for her achievements. Flora and Blanche arrived at the gathering, and the room became too hot, prompting a discussion about opening a window. Ethel and the others eventually decided to move outside for the party due to the heat.

Norman had a significant visit with old Mr. Wilmot, a distinguished Balliol man. Mr. Wilmot maintained a strong interest in Oxford throughout his life. Norman felt honored to assist Mr. Wilmot in showcasing his book collection. Ethel expressed gratitude to Norman for his help with their scholars. Norman reflected on the value of teaching and the humility it brings. Ethel found joy in Norman's assistance during a challenging summer. The upcoming bazaar created excitement and distraction in Ethel's community.

Margaret expresses contentment with quiet time for reflection. Ethel dislikes quiet time and feels unhappy during it. Margaret reflects on her situation and the absence of her mother. Ethel and Margaret discuss their plans to teach children at Cocksmoor. They plan to start teaching every Friday and hope to inspire the children to learn. Margaret recalls her mother's regrets about not being able to help the poor more. Richard is perceived as slow to act, and there is concern about timing and obtaining necessary permissions.

Mary realized that Harry gave his paper-case to Tom, which led to its presence at school. Tom's father, Dr. May, expressed anger and concern when he discovered Tom's involvement. Tom exhibited signs of distress and attempted to avoid answering questions about the blotting-paper. Dr. May took Tom into the study for further questioning after a scene of distress occurred. Mary felt alarmed and believed she was the cause of the situation, leading her to seek comfort from Margaret. Dr. May planned to take Tom to Harrison the following morning due to the seriousness of the situation. Dr. May discovered inconsistencies in Tom's account, particularly regarding Ned Anderson's involvement.

Blanche and Aubrey expressed to Margaret that they would enjoy church more if Richard preached every Sunday. Dr. May reported that Richard's sermon had made a positive impression, with many people thanking him. Flora appeared pale and serious on her last home Sunday, focusing on Margaret and little Gertrude. Norman believed in George's perfections and influenced others to view him positively despite his shyness. Flora broke down in tears beside Margaret's sofa, expressing her reluctance to leave. Flora composed herself quickly when Mary entered the room, preparing her bridesmaids for the wedding. Meta Rivers arrived looking pretty, which was noted by those present.

The little bird felt grief and restlessness, believing it was useless in the world. A voice spoke to the little bird, explaining its purpose was to delight its master. The voice encouraged the bird to value its own happiness as a sign of its master's care. Meta expressed her understanding of the story told by Dr. May, comparing herself to humming-birds. Jem Jemmings was investigated by the doctor, who found him truthful and ready to help. A letter was to be written to Jem's father regarding his travel plans on Friday. Norman felt a sense of disgrace as he prepared to return to school after a joyful day.

Ethel and Margaret discuss plans to help Cocksmoor. Margaret suggests making clothes for Cocksmoor's grandchildren. Ethel expresses concern about whether her vow to help Cocksmoor is silly. Margaret believes they should start with small, certain actions. Mary assists Ethel with her dressing after she comes home cold and wet. Dr. May visits Margaret for a report on his activities. Margaret reflects on her responsibilities regarding Ethel's ambitions.

Dr. May offers to give Meta a lift. Norman expresses his feelings towards Meta and refers to her as 'my pretty one.' Dr. May reveals that Meta's father approved of Norman as a suitable match for her. Meta expresses gratitude to Dr. May and reaches out to Norman. Sir Henry Walkinghame and his servant overtake Dr. May, Meta, and Norman. Meta suggests that her uncle should be informed about her relationship with Norman. Dr. May and Norman agree that it is important to disclose their feelings to Meta's uncle.

Norman expressed that if something is illegal, someone will take legal action. Norman decided to take a walk along the riverbank after the boys divided into smaller groups. Norman was interested in botany and enjoyed studying it with Margaret. There was a report of rare yellow bog-bean growing in a meadow about a mile and a half up the river. While walking home, Norman heard a loud shout and saw black specks in a forbidden field. Upon returning home, Norman discovered that his brother Tom was missing. Norman found a group of boys around a bonfire in the field, and a policeman instructed them to leave.

The day was bright, clear, and warm, suitable for an outdoor event. Ethel intended to fulfill her promise to Margaret by enjoying herself. The garden featured a marquee and a pyramid of flowers for sale to benefit a bazaar. Meta Rivers greeted Ethel and her companions upon their arrival. Blanche was anxious to find Flora and her watch-guard. Flora was noted for her impressive work on the bazaar, having arrived early to make finishing touches. Flora was dressed in a white muslin and broad chip hat, which made her look elegant.

Ethel expresses concern about telling Margaret that her father is not coming back. Mary shows excitement upon seeing Harry and asks him to speak to her. Ethel and Harry ascend the stairs to see Margaret after she requests Harry's presence. Margaret eagerly reaches out to Harry when he enters the room. Harry informs Margaret that her father died in the Loyalty Isles from fever while working for them. Margaret asks to be left alone after receiving the news about her father. Dr. May embraces Harry upon seeing him but quickly leaves to check on Margaret.

Flora declared she would be at Stoneborough for the nomination. Flora arrived with her daughter three days before the nomination, surprising Margaret. Ethel expressed surprise that Flora brought her baby before the christening. Aubrey and Gertrude wore blue and orange rosettes and shouted 'Rivers for ever!' Flora appeared anxious and excited during the nomination day. Dr. May received cheers during the event, and George Rivers made a speech. The opposite candidate did not come forward at the nomination.

Richard and Ethel discuss the importance of children knowing good things before they understand their meaning. Ethel believes that memory and affection develop before comprehension. Margaret expresses concern that the Ladies' Committee may not understand Ethel's ideas. Ethel mentions that Flora has the ability to influence people. Ethel informs Richard that Mr. Wilmot has not been well and has gone to take care of his duty. Ethel is upset about the M'Carthys leaving for Wales without her knowledge. Ethel expresses her fondness for Una and her disappointment over her departure.

Margaret expresses a sense of security as long as Richard is in the house. The doctor discusses his positive experience at Abbotstoke Grange and mentions Norman's good manners. Norman reports that their father is asleep and describes the Grange in an animated manner. Margaret expresses a desire to see the beautiful conservatory at the Grange. Ethel struggles to choose books for Cocksmoor due to feeling overwhelmed by the options. Richard is occupied writing notes for their father and is not to be disturbed. Norman is engaged in a leather-work project involving ivy leaves.

Hector stood still and upright, with his eyes fixed far away. Gertrude spread mortar with satisfaction as she prepared for the placement of the corner-stone. Harry took Gertrude's hand, but she ran to her father when she saw Dr. May. Margaret pressed a pearl hoop into Ethel's hand, asking her to give it to Dr. Spencer. Ethel recognized the pearl hoop as Alan Ernescliffe's betrothal ring. George Rivers preferred that ladies not delay the departure of the carriage. Four young gentlemen planned to walk to Abbotstoke and dine at the Grange.

Richard is concerned about Mr. Southern's health and is sorry for his daughter. Dr. May arrived too late to see Mr. Southern alive and stayed with his daughter until another family member arrived. Dr. May expressed a sense of loss regarding Mr. Southern, who was a familiar presence in the community. Margaret invited Dr. May to drink tea with her in her quiet room. Ethel was searching for books on schools and displayed confusion while organizing them. Flora criticized Ethel's method of stacking books and offered to help. Ethel completed her task of organizing the chiffonier and found her long-lost book 'Undine'.

Ethel expresses her feelings about a brooch and does not want it to be considered a present from Mr. Ogllvie. Flora and Ethel have a conversation where Ethel asks Flora not to call her 'my dear.' Meta expresses a desire to visit a burned girl while Mr. Wilmot is away, and Flora agrees. Ethel and Meta walk to the cottage, where they are greeted with gratitude by the sick girl. Meta reflects on the sadness of seeing others and the peacefulness of quietness. Ethel and Meta discuss their feelings about their situation, finding a strange sort of happiness in their affliction. Ethel and Meta acknowledge the goodness of God in their lives despite their troubles.

The children stood in a long line on the common for an event organized by Flora and Ethel. Mary and Blanche distributed presents to the children during the event. Norman took a kettle from Mary, which upset her dignity. Granny Hall expressed excitement over Blanche and Aubrey, leading to a humorous exchange with Aubrey. Mr. Wilmot selected three children to recommend to the Sunday-school and penny club at Stoneborough. Richard preferred to walk home independently, while Norman expressed discomfort about a headache. Mr. Rivers invited the children to his daughter's school-feast.

Ethel expressed her feelings of neglect and frustration regarding her children and their education. Flora and Ethel discussed a parcel of books sent by Mr. Wilmot for teaching purposes. Richard took over Tom's lessons from Miss Winter, which made Ethel listen with interest. Richard had a dislike for spectators during Latin lessons due to a past experience. Tom performed well in his Latin and Greek lessons, impressing Ethel. Ethel encouraged Richard to let Tom skip some parsing, but Richard insisted on continuing. Tom answered a parsing question correctly, demonstrating his knowledge.

Ethel was missed by the household, particularly by Dr. Spencer, during her absence. Flora brought Ethel back, resulting in joy among Aubrey and Daisy and a revival of spirits in the household. Mrs. Arnott's visit was comforting to Dr. May despite the sorrow surrounding it. Norman and his wife accompanied Mrs. Arnott, expressing their emotions about the parting. Ethel reflected on her life choices and the nature of love and affection after Norman's marriage. Ethel recognized her role as a mother figure to the younger ones while accepting the possibility of becoming solitary in the future. Dr. Spencer was drawn to hear Richard minister at St. Andrew's Church.

Richard expresses a sense of usefulness to his father. Harry wants to speak to his father about going to sea. Harry will turn thirteen on May 4th. Margaret reflects on Harry's desire to become a sailor. Harry dismisses other career options such as being a doctor, clergyman, or lawyer. Harry feels conflicted about discussing his recent outing with his father.

Flora expresses concern about her father's well-being and her relationship with him. Ethel mentions that their aunt is satisfied with Meta's situation. Flora observes that Meta appears to be in low spirits and inquires about Norman. Flora insists that Norman and Meta must marry and go with their aunt. Ethel doubts that Norman and Meta would agree to the marriage proposal. Flora believes that the marriage would alleviate Norman's misery and benefit Meta. Tom feels comfortable with his deceit despite knowing it is wrong. Norman May, as head boy, attempts to uphold authority and check abuses at Stoneborough. Harvey Anderson opposes Norman May and gathers support from idle and mischievous students. Tom is taught by the younger Anderson to deceive and avoid learning lessons. Strict rules confine students to their bounds, with exceptions during holidays and certain hours.

Hector expressed frustration with Captain Gordon and Maplewood, indicating he might leave them. Ethel communicated with Hector about Cocksmoor, but Captain Gordon claimed no financial obligation. Margaret attempted to console Hector but found his letters burdensome. Tom felt isolated without Hector or George Rivers and was preoccupied with the Cocksmoor project. Richard was released before Easter and resumed his responsibilities at home and Cocksmoor. Mr. Wilmot assigned Richard to oversee the hamlet, which had a challenging population. Ethel's teaching had a positive impact on her immediate students.

Dr. May experienced anxiety and an unsatisfactory feeling regarding Flora. Flora was a valuable person who managed household affairs and cared for Margaret. Dr. May felt a lack of confidence from Flora and perceived her as older and wiser. Norman and Flora were described with positive attributes, including Norman's noble looks and Flora's gracefulness. Flora informed Dr. May about Mr. George Rivers, which surprised both of them. Dr. May expressed concern about Flora's interest in Mr. Rivers, questioning his intellectual capacity. Flora reacted with disappointment to Dr. May's concerns about Mr. Rivers.

The narrator hired a house on ---- Street near Charing Cross. Two maids and a footman were hired and dressed in good livery. The narrator arrived in London in good health and passed as a French lady.
