The narrator secured a mortgage for £14,000 with the assistance of Sir Robert Clayton. The narrator gave birth to a boy about four miles from London. The narrator sent a letter to the child's father in Paris, expressing regret for his departure. The father did not respond to the narrator's invitation to visit again.

The space between the poles of two groups is designated for free conversation, traffic, and commerce. Weapons are not allowed in this space, and if violence occurs, the truce is broken. A larger number of natives visited one evening, bringing provisions in exchange for toys. The narrator chose to sleep on the boat while others slept on shore, where they later heard a call for help. Five muskets were fired by the narrator's men during the incident on shore. The narrator and their men faced an attack from three to four hundred natives while trying to assist their comrades. The narrator's group managed to rescue seven men, three of whom were severely wounded.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The Portuguese captain was made the universal heir in the will of the narrator. The Portuguese captain could not act as executor without proof of the narrator's death. The Portuguese captain registered the narrator's will and put in a claim. The narrator's partner and trustees offered to account for six or eight years of profit believing the narrator was lost. The income from the plantation increased each year, but initial disbursements were large. The Portuguese captain owed the narrator four hundred and seventy moidores of gold, sixty chests of sugar, and fifteen double rolls of tobacco. The Portuguese captain provided the narrator with two hundred Portugal moidores in gold as a supply.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The three men returned to the Spaniards after an encounter, displaying aggressive behavior. One of the three men mocked a Spaniard by twirling his hat and threatening him. The Spaniard retaliated by knocking down the man who mocked him with a single punch. Another man from the three fired a pistol at the Spaniard but missed, causing a minor injury. The Spaniards emerged from a cave and disarmed the two remaining men after the initial confrontation. The Spaniards refused to return the arms to the three men due to their previous threats and actions. The two men returned in anger after discovering their plantation had been destroyed.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator constructed a cave or vault using long poles and flags for thatch. On December 10, a large quantity of earth fell from the cave's ceiling, prompting the narrator to reinforce it. By December 11, the narrator had propped up the ceiling with two posts and boards. From December 17 to December 20, the narrator organized the interior of the cave by placing shelves and nails on the posts. On December 27, the narrator killed a young goat and nursed another back to health, considering breeding tame creatures for food. From January 1 to January 3, the narrator experienced hot weather, attempted to hunt goats with a dog, and began constructing a thick wall for protection. The wall construction took from January 3 to April 14 and measured about twenty-four yards in length.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator provided milk in an earthen pot and bread to a man referred to as Friday. Friday expressed pleasure at the food and complied with the narrator's actions. The narrator indicated to Friday that he would give him clothes, which made Friday glad. Friday pointed out the location where he had buried two men and suggested they dig them up to eat. The narrator expressed anger and disgust at the suggestion of cannibalism and led Friday away. The narrator and Friday discovered a site covered with human bones and signs of a feast after a battle. The narrator burned the remains of the bodies and gave Friday clothing from a wrecked ship.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The young clergyman was surprised and distressed that he could not communicate with the woman due to language barriers. The clergyman believed that the woman should be baptized. Will Atkins, the woman's husband, had encouraged her to embrace a religious life and had introduced her to concepts of God. Will Atkins expressed concern that his own sinful life might negatively influence the woman's perception of religion. The clergyman successfully communicated the knowledge of Christ and redemption to the woman, leading her to request baptism. The clergyman performed the baptism discreetly to avoid revealing his Roman Catholic affiliation. During the baptism, the clergyman used Latin and French, ensuring that his religious identity remained unknown to others present.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: Amy was between forty and fifty years old at the time of the events described. The narrator felt a lack of comfort and counsel during a difficult period lasting nearly two years. The narrator had two sons, one in Messina and the other in the Indies, and two daughters. The narrator chose not to see either daughter to avoid revealing his identity. Amy provided a good education for both daughters and managed their affairs. An accidental discovery occurred when both daughters visited Amy at the same time. One daughter believed Amy was her mother, leading to an emotional reaction when Amy clarified her role.

The text discusses 'The Fortunate Mistress' by Daniel Defoe, published in March 1724. The narrative features the life of Mademoiselle de Beleau, known as the Lady Roxana, during the time of King Charles II. Defoe died in April 1731, and no second edition of the work appeared until after his death. Various editions of 'The Fortunate Mistress' were published after Defoe's death, some of which continued the story of Roxana. The continuation attributed to Defoe in the 1745 edition is likely not written by him, as it includes discrepancies in Roxana's age and death date. Roxana was born in 1673 and was ten years old when her parents fled to England around 1683. The text notes differences in style between Defoe's original narrative and the later continuation.

The narrator retrieved pieces of cable and some iron from the ship after laborious efforts. The narrator spent thirteen days on shore and made eleven trips to the ship. During the twelfth trip to the ship, the narrator discovered a locker containing razors, scissors, knives, forks, and money. The money found included European coins, Brasil coins, pieces of eight, gold, and silver, which the narrator deemed of little use. The narrator attempted to prepare a raft but decided against it due to rising winds and the need to return to shore. The narrator swam back to shore with difficulty due to the weight of the items and rough water conditions. The narrator shifted focus from the ship to securing themselves against potential threats on the island.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator feels that a valuable secret depends on a specific occasion. The narrator fears being recognized by a girl, which would lead to his undoing. The narrator considers pretending to faint to create a distraction. The ship is located close to the shore, allowing easy access to land. The narrator experiences conflicting emotions when kissing the girl, who is his child. The narrator struggles to conceal his disorder while interacting with others. The narrator is in a state of extreme anxiety about being discovered.

The narrator expresses a desire to assist a woman who has been kind to them. The narrator's spouse has given the woman some support, which the narrator encourages her to accept. The narrator informs the woman that they have resolved to provide for her in a way that is separate from her husband's resources. The narrator suggests that the woman should save the income from their support to increase her financial security over time. The narrator emphasizes that the annual payment of forty pounds must return to their family after the woman's lifetime. The narrator reflects on their own past hardships and expresses empathy for the woman's situation as a mother with children. The narrator believes that their own experiences with loss and hardship motivate their desire to help the woman.

The narrator lists several airing places in England, including Tunbridge, Epsom, North Hall, Barnet, Newmarket, Bury, and Bath. The narrator's agent, a Quaker, decides not to inform the narrator's husband about a certain story. The Quaker believes that the narrator should decide whether to share the story herself. The Quaker writes to the narrator, suggesting that she send Amy to her due to a potential need. The letter from the Quaker is mistakenly sent to Amy instead of the intended recipient. The Quaker expresses concern for the narrator's safety and sends a messenger to inquire about Amy. The Quaker uses caution in her conversation with a young woman to avoid revealing the narrator's whereabouts.

Friday believed that the savages in the canoe would not survive the storm and would either drown or be driven south. Friday thought the savages would be too frightened to return and would tell their people they were killed by thunder and lightning. The savages in that part never attempted to go over to the island afterwards due to fear of being destroyed by fire from the gods. The narrator was initially apprehensive about the return of the savages but became less fearful when no more canoes appeared. The Spaniard informed the narrator that there were sixteen more of his countrymen and Portuguese living peacefully with the savages but struggling for necessities. The Spanish ship was bound from the Rio de la Plata to the Havanna and was carrying hides and silver. The survivors of the shipwreck had arms that were useless due to spoiled powder and had no means to escape their situation.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator killed three birds and hung them in chains as a deterrent. The presence of the scarecrows caused birds to avoid that part of the island. The narrator harvested corn at the end of December, which was their second harvest of the year. The narrator made a scythe from a broad-sword to cut down the corn. From half a peck of seed, the narrator obtained nearly two bushels of rice and over two and a half bushels of barley. The narrator decided to preserve the entire crop for seed for the next season instead of consuming it. The narrator faced challenges in processing the corn into meal and baking bread due to a lack of tools.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The women wore short aprons and long antique gowns with sleeves and a train. Their heads and breasts were adorned with flowers, and they were veiled. The slaves accompanying them had long black hair braided and tied with ribbons. The women danced in a style that was unfamiliar to the audience, accompanied by a guitar and a low-sounding trumpet. The narrator was dressed in a Turkish robe of crimson and green with a higher head-dress adorned with jewels. The audience called out 'Roxana' during the performance, indicating the narrator's prominence. After the dance, the narrator received compliments from a gentleman who was later identified as the Duke.

The narrator has been a common servant for eighteen years. The narrator's daughter, Susanna, recounts her family's history. Susanna's third child, a daughter, lived with a family that moved to Boulogne, France. The daughter married a man with the consent of her host family and her husband became a shipmaster. Susanna's youngest sister died of smallpox after living with relatives. Susanna's youngest brother was apprenticed to a carpenter and later educated for a merchant career. The narrator's husband, referred to as my lord, plans to provide for Susanna and Thomas without consulting the narrator.

An eddy ran back to the north-west with a sharp stream. The narrator put their boat into the stream of the eddy and spread their sail. The eddy carried the narrator about a league towards the island but two leagues northward. The narrator found themselves open to the northern shore of the island. The current or eddy spent after more than a league of travel. The narrator found smooth water and reached the shore after about an hour. The narrator resolved to make their way westward along the shore to find a safe harbor for their boat.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator's husband hired a stage-coach to travel to the city of Menin. They intended to travel by water down the river Lys to Ghent and then take a coach to Isabella fort. From Isabella fort, they planned to cross the river to Anvers and then travel by land to Breda. They stayed in Breda for two days to rest before continuing their journey to Rotterdam. The narrator and her husband lived in ready-furnished lodgings on the Great Quay in Rotterdam for a month. The narrator's husband went to the Hague first to prepare a house for their reception. The narrator received a letter from her husband informing her of his arrival to take her home.

The narrator had a coach and horses, along with servants, by permission of a lord. The narrator visited Paris and the Tuileries garden with the prince. The prince used a coach belonging to the Count de ---- to maintain anonymity during their outing. The prince took the narrator to the palace of Meudon, where they stayed for three or four days. The king visited the palace of Meudon while the narrator and the prince were there. The narrator encountered her first husband, Mr. ----, while in the guard-chamber at the palace. The narrator confirmed her husband's identity by recognizing him and hearing him speak.

The speaker is an old man and a young doctor who is not well qualified to answer difficult questions. Friday questions why God does not kill the devil if He is much stronger than him. The speaker explains that God will punish the devil at the judgment and cast him into the bottomless pit. Friday expresses confusion about the concept of being preserved to repent and be pardoned. The speaker believes that divine revelation is necessary for understanding Jesus Christ and salvation. The speaker prays for guidance to instruct Friday in the knowledge of God and salvation. The speaker discusses the redemption of man and explains why Jesus did not take on the nature of angels.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The crew expressed their unwillingness to use violence against the narrator. The crew threatened to leave the ship if the narrator did not disembark. The captain communicated with the crew about their demands and the narrator's ownership of the ship. The crew insisted they would not work with the narrator on board. The captain preferred to lose the ship rather than disoblige the narrator. The narrator agreed to stay on shore and requested his belongings and money. The captain returned to the ship to inform the crew of the narrator's decision.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: Four individuals were involved in cultivating land and planting seeds. They sowed twenty-two bushels of barley and sixteen jars of rice. The group had to ration their barley for their own food for six months. They marked trees for cutting down to create planks for building. They produced about a dozen large oak planks for construction. The group increased their flock of tame goats by obtaining about twenty young kids. During harvest, they collected over two hundred and twenty bushels of barley.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: Friday mentioned that he kills bears in his country using long arrows. The group was in a wild place with their guide injured and uncertain about what to do. The howling of wolves caused fear among the group, reminiscent of a previous experience in Africa. The ground was covered with snow, and wolves had descended into the forest and plains due to hunger. The guide warned that a dangerous area lay ahead where more wolves might be found. The group encountered five wolves crossing the road while traveling through the first wood. Upon entering the plain, the group found a dead horse that wolves had been feeding on.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator expressed a settled resolution to leave England. The narrator informed the Quaker of their decision to leave, which made the Quaker feel sorry. The narrator's husband confirmed his support for the decision to leave and planned to depart in ten days. The couple planned to travel to Dover, cross the Channel to Calais, and then proceed to Paris. The couple decided to consign their goods, money, and plate to several merchants for safety during their journey. The couple planned to travel with two footmen and one maid, while hiring a coach for their journey. The Quaker requested to accompany the couple to Dover, which they agreed to.

The speaker had despaired of being found for two years and had ceased all inquiries. The speaker explained their retreat and lifestyle as reasons for not being found. The speaker claimed to have abandoned all conversation, taken up another name, and lived remote from London. The speaker stated they had not received any letters from the other person and felt punished for their previous weakness. The other person had letters directed to the speaker that were not delivered due to a lack of knowledge about the speaker's identity. The other person expressed disappointment and mentioned having done penance for the perceived slight against the speaker. The other person reflected on their regret regarding their past actions and the treatment of the speaker.

The narrator expresses concern about being discovered by a lady. The Quaker offers to inform the lady to avoid the narrator if she is unwilling to see her. The lady reacts angrily and threatens the Quaker with curses. The narrator decides not to go to London after initially planning to follow the Quaker. The Quaker sends a letter to the narrator requesting a private meeting. The narrator delays her trip to London due to concerns about being watched. The Quaker mentions that her agent, Amy, has not seen the troublesome lady recently.

The narrator first set foot on the island on the 30th of September 1659. The narrator observed that they were in the latitude of 9 degrees 22 minutes north. To keep track of time, the narrator carved notches on a post, marking days and months. The narrator salvaged various items from the ship, including pens, ink, paper, compasses, and books. The narrator found three Bibles and several other books among the salvaged items. The narrator brought two cats and a dog from the ship, with the dog swimming ashore the day after the narrator landed. The narrator expressed a need for tools such as a spade, pickaxe, and shovel for their work on the island.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The speaker inquired about the distance from their island to the shore and the safety of canoes. Friday informed the speaker that there was no danger of canoes being lost and described the current and wind patterns. The speaker understood that the current was caused by the river Oroonoque, near which their island was located. Friday identified his people as the Caribs, which are associated with the region from the mouth of the Oroonoque to Guinea and St. Martha. Friday mentioned that beyond the west, there were white-bearded men who had killed many people, referring to the Spaniards. The speaker expressed hope of escaping the island with Friday's assistance and sought to teach him about religious knowledge. Friday described a deity named Benamuckee, who he believed created all things and to whom the deceased went.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator attempted to remove a boat that was stuck on an island. The narrator spent three to four weeks trying to move the boat using levers and rollers. After finding it impossible to move the boat, the narrator began digging away the sand to undermine it. The narrator considered making a canoe or periagua from a tree trunk, believing it to be easy. The narrator did not account for the difficulty of launching the boat into the water after constructing it. The narrator felled a cedar tree with a diameter of five feet ten inches at the stump and twenty-two feet long.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator received twenty ducats for a leopard's skin and forty ducats for a lion's skin. The narrator sold various items from his ship, including guns and bees-wax, totaling about two hundred and twenty pieces of eight. The narrator settled in the Brasils and lived with a plantation owner who had a sugarhouse. The narrator obtained a letter of naturalization and purchased uncultivated land for his plantation. The narrator had a neighbor named Wells, a Portuguese of Lisbon born to English parents, with whom he shared a plantation. The narrator and Wells initially planted for food and later began planting tobacco and preparing land for sugarcane. The narrator expressed regret about his situation and reflected on his previous life in England.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator expressed kindness and respect towards the man despite resisting his advances. The man attempted various methods to persuade the narrator to marry him but was unsuccessful. The man believed he could take advantage of a situation to persuade the narrator to marry him. The narrator and the man shared a close relationship that maintained modesty and decency. One night, after spending time together, the man insisted on going to bed with the narrator. The narrator initially resisted but ultimately allowed the man to stay with her. The man proposed marriage to the narrator after spending three nights together.

Amy dismissed a girl who was trying to find her. Amy traveled to London by hackney-coach while the girl took a boat. Amy stayed in a village called Woodford for about six weeks. The Quaker informed Amy that the girl had been searching for her in Tunbridge. The Quaker advised the girl to stop pursuing Amy and assured her that Amy did not wish to see her. Amy felt uneasy after losing her assistant and confidant, the Quaker. The Quaker reported that the girl had been frequently visiting her for news about Amy.

The narrator considers joining a Christian ship for potential rescue. The narrator experiences a disturbed mind and impatience due to prolonged troubles. The narrator feels a strong desire to escape to the mainland. The narrator dreams of encountering savages and helping one escape, who then becomes his servant. The narrator wakes up feeling joy from the dream but is disappointed to realize it was not real. The narrator concludes that capturing a savage prisoner could be a means of escape. The narrator grapples with the moral implications of attacking savages to achieve his escape.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator made no pies and had limited ingredients, primarily the flesh of fowls or goats. The narrator spent most of the third year managing harvest and husbandry. The narrator reaped corn in its season and stored it in large baskets until it could be threshed. The narrator had a stock of about twenty bushels of barley and rice and wanted to build bigger barns. The narrator resolved to sow the same quantity of barley and rice each year to ensure sufficient bread supply. The narrator contemplated the prospect of land seen from the island and wished to escape to the main land. The narrator considered the dangers of encountering cannibals and the risks of being killed if captured.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The group had no arrows, materials to make arrows, or edged tools and weapons. The situation was dire for both the group and the Englishmen, who faced destroyed provisions and spoiled harvests. The Englishmen had a stock of cattle and some corn as their only resources. One of the three Englishmen, William Atkins, was killed by an arrow. The Englishmen planned to drive the savages to the southeast part of the island to avoid encounters. The Spaniard governor proposed capturing a savage to act as an interpreter and negotiate terms for coexistence. One savage was eventually captured and, after being treated kindly, became more cooperative.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator reduced their food intake to one biscuit-cake a day. On May 1, the narrator discovered a small barrel and pieces of a shipwreck on the shore. The barrel found was filled with gunpowder that had taken on water and hardened. The shipwreck was found to be higher out of the water than before due to an earthquake. The narrator attempted to search the ship for usable items but found it filled with sand. On May 3, the narrator cut through a beam of the shipwreck but had to stop due to the tide. The narrator caught a young dolphin while fishing on May 4 and dried the fish to eat.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator and his companions prepared to escape from a camp at night to avoid the Kalmuck Tartars. They traveled for two hours and covered nearly forty miles before resting in the Russian village of Kirmazinskoy. After resting, they continued their journey and passed the Kirtza river, arriving at the populous town of Ozomya. In Ozomya, they learned that they were out of danger from the Kalmucks and stayed for five days to rest and acquire fresh horses. They reached Veussima on the river Witzogda and prepared for a seven-day passage to Archangel. The narrator and his companions sailed from Archangel on August 20 and arrived in the Elbe on September 13. After selling their goods in the Elbe, the young lord left to seek protection in Vienna, and the narrator returned to London on January 10, 1705.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The text discusses the roles and responsibilities of women in relation to their husbands. It suggests that women are often perceived as being in subjection but actually have significant control over their lives. The author argues that a single woman has full command over her estate and decisions. The text critiques the notion that affection between a husband and wife eliminates the idea of bondage for women. It highlights the potential for women to experience sudden financial ruin due to their dependence on their husbands. The author expresses the belief that women should not give up their autonomy for the sake of a relationship with a man. The text concludes with a warning about the precariousness of a woman's situation when reliant on her husband's fortunes.

The speaker is concerned about the potential loss of their jewels if they fall into the hands of the court of justice. The speaker fears being forced to confess to a crime they did not commit if apprehended. The merchant advises the speaker to leave quickly to avoid capture. The merchant offers to arrange safe passage for the speaker to Rotterdam. The merchant plans to deceive the Jew regarding the speaker's intentions with the jewels. The speaker has prepared for departure and only needs to gather a few belongings. The merchant intends to show a letter from the speaker to delay the Jew while the speaker escapes.

A gentleman arrived at the door after ferrying over the Maas from Willemstadt. The narrator recognized the gentleman as their merchant from Paris, who had previously helped them. The merchant expressed relief at seeing the narrator safe and mentioned that staying longer in Paris would have been dangerous. The narrator expressed gratitude to the merchant for saving their life and mentioned being in debt to him. The merchant decided to lodge in the same house as the narrator, which was recommended by a mutual friend. The two began discussing their recent experiences after a few days of settling in. The narrator recounted their voyage, including a storm that forced them into Harwich and the fear of their companion.

Amy found the captain after he gave her directions. The captain did not change his name, believing no inquiries would be made after him. Amy approached the captain in his quarters, and he was surprised to see her. The captain initially expressed fear and confusion about Amy's identity. Amy informed the captain about the poor condition of his former mistress. The captain explained that he left because he could not bear to see the poverty affecting them. Amy recounted the distress of her mistress and mentioned that she could no longer stay with her due to financial constraints.

The Portuguese pilot had a pistol in his pocket that was unknown to the Tartars. The pilot shot one Tartar in the head, killing him instantly. The pilot attempted to strike another Tartar with a scimitar but missed and injured the Tartar's horse instead. The injured horse threw its rider down and attacked the Tartar. A Chinese man, who had lost a camel, seized a weapon from the fallen Tartar and killed him. The third Tartar fled when he saw the pilot's pistol being reloaded. The narrator sustained a head injury but recovered in a few days.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator was called the Countess de ---- and experienced a period of glory and prosperity. The narrator's spouse declared that they had been married for eleven years before arriving in Holland. The couple acknowledged their son, who was in England, as legitimate and arranged for him to be brought to Holland. The couple's two sons and a daughter were raised in Nimeguen and were brought to visit them in the Hague. The narrator's spouse managed their public image and relationships to protect their son's legitimacy. The narrator expressed a lack of affection for their child compared to the affection shown by their spouse. The narrator had shown general neglect of their child during their years of revelry in London.

Amy expressed disbelief about a situation that was described as dire. The narrator recounted a conversation between her husband and the captain. Amy reacted with anger and blamed the narrator for not allowing her to harm another character. The narrator changed her gown and returned to her husband after a period of distress. The husband did not continue the story about the captain and believed it to be inconsequential. The narrator felt relieved by her husband's ignorance regarding the situation. The narrator planned to take her husband out of town to avoid a potential meeting with the captain.

The bullet wound was located in the man's breast, and he bled inwardly, resulting in his death. The man buried two bodies in the sand to prevent them from being seen by others. The narrator took the man to a cave on the island instead of his castle. The narrator provided the man with bread, raisins, and water to alleviate his distress. The man was described as handsome, well-made, and approximately twenty-six years old. The man's skin color was described as a bright dun olive color, and he had long black hair and a good countenance. The narrator taught the man, named Friday, basic words and concepts, including his name and the terms Master, Yes, and No.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The journey lasted three days and nights, requiring the travelers to carry water in leather bottles. The area traversed was referred to as No Man's Land, part of the Great Karakathy, and was considered to belong to China. The region was known for being dangerous due to the presence of thieves and was described as the worst desert encountered during the march. The travelers encountered small groups of Tartars, who did not appear to have hostile intentions initially. A group of Tartars shot five arrows at the travelers, injuring a horse, which was left behind the next day. The travelers continued their journey for nearly a month, passing through villages, some of which were fortified against Tartar incursions. While attempting to buy a camel, the traveler was attacked by five Tartars, resulting in a blow to the head.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The prince described the narrator as the most beautiful creature on earth. The prince expressed surprise that he had never seen such beauty in France before. The prince and the narrator shared a meal that included champagne, water, sweetmeats, roasted partridges, and a quail. The prince insisted that the narrator sit and eat with him instead of serving him. The prince requested to speak with the narrator as equals, despite their difference in rank. The prince poured sweetmeats into the narrator's lap after their meal. The prince's gentleman efficiently managed the service during the meal.

Will Atkins expresses concern about discussing religion with his wife. Atkins believes his wife will reject the idea of a just God due to his past behavior. The clergyman suggests that repentance would make Atkins a better minister to his wife. The clergyman explains that God is merciful and allows time for sinners to repent. Atkins acknowledges he knows the truth about God and repentance but feels it is too late for him. Atkins feels unworthy to discuss repentance with his wife due to his past actions. Atkins expresses emotional distress about his situation, indicating he feels hopeless.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The speaker discusses the concept of being in the way of God's blessing and mentions visible assistances and deliverances. A character expresses modesty and readiness in response to the speaker's inquiry about God's blessing. The character references the story of Achan from the Bible to illustrate that one person's actions can affect the entire group. The speaker expresses regret for interrupting the character and invites him to continue the discussion while walking to the Englishmen's plantation. The character proposes to lay down a few foundational propositions for their discussion, acknowledging their differences in doctrinal articles of religion. The character emphasizes the importance of not offending God by neglecting His commands or committing sins. The character identifies three specific issues that may hinder God's blessing on the speaker's endeavors.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The conversation involves ships and trading affairs. The speaker has not seen a certain man for about eleven years. The speaker expresses surprise at seeing the man, believing he was in another part of the world. The speaker's companion suggests that the man may have come to seek the speaker. The companion's servant is instructed to follow the man and inquire about him. The servant discovers that the man rode through an inn and does not gain any information. After several weeks, the servant identifies the man as a Dutchman and a French merchant from Rouen.

Amy promised to keep the man's existence a secret from her old mistress if she returned to England. The man expressed that he was in the highest position he could achieve in France due to a lack of money and connections. He mentioned a missed opportunity to become a lieutenant due to the inability to pay eight thousand livres. Amy expressed concern for her old mistress's situation and believed the man would help her if he were in a better position. The man indicated he would send relief to his old mistress if it would not harm her future. Amy discovered that the man did not have a genuine offer for a lieutenant's commission and that his statements were inconsistent. Amy was tasked with investigating the man's character further to verify his claims.

Four Englishmen have taken women from among the savages as their wives and have had many children with them. These Englishmen are not legally married to the women according to the laws of God and man. The Spaniard governor required the Englishmen to choose the women by consent and keep separately to them. The essence of matrimony includes mutual consent and a formal legal obligation between the parties. The Englishmen may abandon the women and their children at any time without legal repercussions. The speaker argues that allowing this situation to continue dishonors God and undermines the speaker's efforts in the area. The speaker believes that a formal contract made before witnesses would constitute a lawful marriage in the sight of God.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The character experienced a misfortune involving a loss of over £8000 sterling. Amy expressed joy regarding the character's situation and questioned the value of a story about a prince. The character reflected on their desire to be a wife to a prince rather than a mistress to a king. The character acknowledged the influence of pride and ambition on their thoughts and desires. The merchant noticed the character's unusual disorder and suggested going into the air for relief. The character initially reacted negatively to the merchant's suggestion, fearing it implied they were crazed. During a later conversation, the merchant referred to the character as his princess, which affected the character emotionally.

The captain was under a charter-party to pursue a voyage by the way of Brasil. The passengers expressed concern about being carried to the East Indies. The captain agreed to take the passengers to Newfoundland to find a ship back to Canada. The captain considered it reasonable to change course due to the passengers' distress. The crew encountered several ships bound to Europe but could not take on passengers due to provisions concerns. The captain put all the French passengers on board a bark at Newfoundland to take them to France. A young priest and four seamen joined the captain's ship for the voyage to the West Indies.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The text discusses the fair dealings of a group with a Portuguese pilot. The author expresses a belief that Christianity has a civilizing effect on people. The group sails north along the coast of China to avoid European ports. The author expresses a strong fear of being captured by Chinese authorities. The group encounters a Portuguese pilot who offers to assist them. The pilot suggests that Macao would have been a better port for trading opium. The pilot provides information about navigating to the city of Pekin via the canal system.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator reflects on the obligations and fidelity shown to them by a merchant in Paris. The narrator considers the wealth they possess, which amounts to between three and four thousand pounds a year. The narrator resolves to end their relationship with the merchant due to the allure of a higher social status as a princess. The narrator experiences a feverish state of mind influenced by their pride and thoughts of greatness. The narrator learns from a letter that the prince they admired has been injured while hunting a wild boar. The prince's gentleman has gone to check on his health and promised to return with news. The narrator feels uncertainty and concern for the prince's well-being and reflects on the loss of potential glory associated with him.

The creek's water level prevented passage, prompting a call for a boat. Three men were taken from the boat, leaving two behind, while the boat was secured to a tree stump. The narrator and his group surprised the two men, one on shore and one in the boat. The man on shore was knocked down by the captain, who then threatened the man in the boat. One of the two men yielded and later joined the narrator's group. Friday and the captain's mate successfully distracted the remaining crew, tiring them out. The remaining crew expressed confusion and despair upon finding their boat aground and their comrades missing.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator resolved to go to Lisbon to gather information about their plantation in the Brasils and their partner. The narrator arrived in Lisbon in April, accompanied by their servant, Friday. In Lisbon, the narrator found the captain of the ship who had previously rescued them at sea. The captain informed the narrator that he had not been to the Brasils in nine years but confirmed that the narrator's partner was alive when he left. The narrator's trustees had both died, and the plantation's produce was appropriated by the procurator fiscal for charitable uses. The captain mentioned that the narrator's partner was becoming wealthy from the plantation and that the king's third of the narrator's part was worth over two hundred moidores a year. The captain assured the narrator that they would be restored to possession of their inheritance, with the support of the surviving trustees.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The captain and the husband engaged in a conversation where the husband offered money as satisfaction for a disappointment. The husband gave the captain three or four guineas despite the captain's initial refusal. The narrator experienced increasing anxiety after hearing what the captain had said. The husband believed that the captain had miscommunicated his message. The narrator successfully concealed her distress from her husband. The narrator expressed her fears to Amy, indicating that they were in a dire situation. Amy was concerned about the narrator's emotional state and urged her to calm down.

A man was found hanging from a tree with his throat cut. The narrator attempted to restrain his men from further violence after witnessing the hanging. Eight of the narrator's men, along with the boatswain and his crew, left to continue the violent actions. The narrator returned to the boats with only the supercargo and two men after failing to control his crew. Around forty armed men were present at a nearby location when the narrator reached the sea-side. The narrator's crew attacked the forty armed men, killing sixteen or seventeen and setting their houses on fire. The narrator expressed anger towards his nephew, the captain, for his actions during the incident.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The text discusses the importance of early education and its lasting impact on individuals. A man reflects on the teachings of his father regarding the value of the Bible during a challenging situation. The young woman and a youth on board a ship possess Bibles among their goods. The young woman recounts the extreme hunger experienced by her and others on the ship. She describes the physical sensations and psychological effects of starvation over several days. The young woman dreams of being at a market in Barbadoes, which highlights her desperation for food. The text illustrates the consequences of famine on both physical health and mental state.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator expressed reluctance to promise to go beyond his own island. The narrator's companion explained that returning with a loaded ship would not be possible due to merchant restrictions. The narrator and his companion devised a plan to carry a framed sloop on board the ship for assembly on the island. The narrator's wife had died, leaving him without close family to influence his decision about the voyage. The widow of the narrator's friend supported his decision to go on the voyage and helped make arrangements for his family. The narrator made a will and arranged for the education and maintenance of his children during his absence. The narrator and his companion set sail on January 8, 1695, with a cargo of necessary supplies and several skilled workers.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator kept two or three tame animals and household kids that he taught to feed from his hand. The narrator had several parrots that could call out the name Robin Crusoe. The narrator caught tame sea-fowls on the shore and cut their wings. The narrator's castle wall was surrounded by a grove of trees that provided a habitat for the sea-fowls. In December of his twenty-third year, the narrator saw a fire on the shore, which caused him great concern about the presence of savages. The narrator prepared for defense by loading his muskets and pistols and praying for divine protection. After two hours of waiting, the narrator decided to investigate the situation by climbing to the top of a hill.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator took Friday to work again and offered him a boat to return to his own nation. The narrator had a frigate on the other side of the island that he cleared of water. Friday was skilled at managing the boat and expressed doubt about its size for a long journey. The narrator mentioned a larger boat that had been left unused for many years and was in poor condition. Friday expressed a desire to go home but did not want to go without the narrator. Friday believed the narrator could do good by teaching others about God and living a new life. The narrator decided not to send Friday away and recognized Friday's strong affection for him.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator and Friday are preparing to confront a group of savages. Friday expresses fear that the savages have come to capture and eat him. The narrator comforts Friday and assures him that he is also in danger. The narrator prepares weapons, including fowling-pieces, muskets, and pistols. The narrator observes twenty-one savages, three prisoners, and three canoes using a perspective-glass. The savages are planning a banquet involving the three prisoners. The narrator and Friday march out to confront the savages with their weapons.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator was a shipwright who worked hard to create a boat despite many failed attempts. The narrator taught his companion, Friday, about navigation, including the use of a sail and rudder. Friday was initially amazed by the boat's operation but became an expert sailor over time. The narrator noted that the clear weather reduced the need for a compass, as stars and the shore were visible. The narrator had been in captivity for twenty-seven years, with the last three years being different due to Friday's presence. The narrator expressed gratitude for his situation and felt hopeful about imminent deliverance. During the rainy season, the narrator secured the boat in a creek and prepared for a planned voyage.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator was left on shore to tend to the garden and perform household tasks while his patron went to sea. The narrator contemplated escape for two years but found no feasible way to do so. The patron frequently took the ship's pinnace out fishing, accompanied by the narrator and a young Maresco. During one fishing trip, a thick fog caused the narrator and his companions to lose sight of the shore and drift out to sea. The patron decided to take more precautions for future fishing trips after the incident at sea. The patron ordered the carpenter to build a cabin in the long-boat for more comfort and safety during fishing trips. The narrator was skilled at catching fish, which pleased the patron during their fishing excursions.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The Spaniard proposed to the natives to either plant for themselves or serve in families without being made absolute slaves. The natives accepted the proposal and were allotted land and plantations, with some choosing to be employed as servants. The Spaniards occupied the original habitation and extended their plantation eastward along a brook. The English settled in the north-east part of the island and moved southward and south-west towards the Spaniards. The west end of the island was left uninhabited to allow for the presence of savages without disturbing the planters. The clergyman and the narrator planned to convert the savages by dividing the responsibility between the Spaniards and the English. The narrator realized he had not left a Bible for the new converts, contrasting with the widow who sent him three Bibles and a Prayer-book.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The speaker expresses regret for not understanding the importance of loving the Christian church and the souls of others. A conversation occurs between the speaker and another individual about the potential to help others understand Christianity. The individual suggests that it is not too late for the speaker to change their perspective and assist others. The individual expresses a desire to talk to a group referred to as 'poor men' about Christianity. The individual emphasizes that Christian knowledge should be spread by all possible means. The speaker reflects on their previous view of certain individuals as slaves rather than potential converts to Christianity. The speaker feels confounded and self-critical after the discussion about the opportunity to help others.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: Women were obliged to enter into compacts to maintain order and justice. Without these compacts, men would abandon their wives and children. The dialogue includes a discussion about marriage and inheritance. W.A. claims that marriage is appointed by God. W.A.'s wife expresses disbelief in the concept of God making the earth. W.A. admits to living without God and acknowledges his faults. W.A.'s wife questions why God allows people to live wickedly.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: Sir Robert Clayton provided advice and assistance regarding a mortgage. The speaker received an annual income of £700 from Sir Robert Clayton. Sir Robert suggested that the speaker could increase her fortune by saving money and managing her expenses. Sir Robert estimated that the speaker had an income of £2000 a year based on her lifestyle. The speaker was advised to save £1000 annually to double her savings in ten years. Sir Robert presented a plan showing that saving £1000 a year could lead to £21,058 in twelve years. The speaker expressed a preference for immediate wealth over future wealth.

Amy promised not to discuss the narrator with the gentleman unless he initiated the conversation. The narrator allowed Amy to go to France under strict conditions regarding her behavior. Amy had four inquiries to make on behalf of the narrator and one for herself during her trip. Amy successfully traveled to France and sent a letter from Calais three days after leaving London. In Paris, Amy learned that the Dutch merchant had returned to Paris, lived there for three years, and then moved to Rouen. While heading to Rouen, Amy encountered the gentleman associated with the Prince de ----. The gentleman informed Amy that the prince had gone to Germany.

Lady Roxana's was one of the places the narrator lived at. Thomas was a valet at my Lord D----'s next door to Lady Roxana's. The narrator's daughter became acquainted with Mrs. Amy, who was previously known as Roxana's woman. The narrator sought to find her mother and had two encounters with her, one on a ship and another at a Quaker's house in the Minories, London. The narrator was imprisoned in Whitechapel jail for a false debt and later in Marshalsea prison. A young woman confined for debt helped the narrator by informing the Quaker landlady of her situation, leading to her release. The narrator confirmed that Thomas is the second child of her mother, making him the brother of her daughter.

The narrator left the island on December 19, 1686, after being there for 28 years, 2 months, and 19 days. Two of the five men swam to the ship and requested to be taken on board due to fears of being murdered by the other three men. The captain initially pretended to have no power to take the men on board without the narrator's consent. The narrator took relics from the island, including a goat-skin cap, an umbrella, and a parrot, as well as tarnished money and money found in a wrecked Spanish ship. The narrator arrived in England on June 11, 1687, after being absent for 35 years. The narrator's benefactor was alive but had experienced misfortunes and was a widow, and the narrator assured her of no trouble regarding debts owed. The master of the ship, whom the narrator saved, presented him with a compliment and a gift of almost two hundred pounds sterling.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator's men have mutinied against him. The narrator has been set ashore in a desolate place with two men: one is his mate and the other a passenger. The narrator believes the place to be uninhabited and fears for their safety. The mutineers have two firearms, one of which was left in the boat. The narrator proposes to either kill the mutineers or take them prisoner. The narrator makes two conditions for the men: they must not claim authority on the island and must provide free passage to England if the ship is recovered. The men agree to the narrator's conditions and express gratitude.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The old man, Friday's father, informed that five men had chosen women for their wives. The men built new huts or tents for their lodging with the help of the Spaniards. The two honest men had their huts closer together, while the three wicked men were farther away. The two honest men had worse wives compared to the three wicked men, who had clever and industrious wives. The two honest men significantly outperformed the three wicked men in terms of cultivation and management of their land. The two honest men restored their plantation after it was destroyed twice and had flourishing crops. The three wicked men, despite being less quarrelsome, remained idle and their crops were poorly managed.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator experienced a storm at sea that caused feelings of fear and sea-sickness. The weather improved the following day, with calm seas and clear skies. The narrator's companion downplayed the storm, referring to it as a minor squall. The narrator consumed punch with his companion, leading to drunkenness and a loss of resolve. The narrator attempted to suppress feelings of guilt and reflection through drinking and socializing. The ship anchored in Yarmouth Roads due to contrary winds, remaining there for seven or eight days. Many ships from Newcastle also anchored in Yarmouth Roads while waiting for favorable winds.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator observed the sea for boats approaching the island for two to three months without any discoveries. The narrator expressed a desire to kill twenty or thirty naked savages due to their customs, which he found horrifying. The narrator began to question his justification for acting as judge and executioner against the savages. The narrator reflected on the nature of the savages' actions, noting they did not view their behavior as a crime. The narrator compared the savages' actions to those of Christians who kill prisoners in battle, suggesting a moral equivalence. The narrator concluded that the savages had not harmed him and that it would be unjust to attack them. The narrator criticized the conduct of the Spaniards in America for their treatment of indigenous people.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator found two pots of good succades and two more that were spoiled by salt water. The narrator discovered shirts, white linen handkerchiefs, and colored neckcloths. The narrator found three bags containing about eleven hundred pieces of eight and six doubloons of gold. One chest contained clothes of little value and two pounds of glazed powder. The narrator obtained two pairs of shoes from drowned men and two more from a chest, but they were not like English shoes. The narrator found about fifty pieces of eight in royals in a seaman's chest. The narrator lived on the island for nearly two more years while contemplating escape.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator's house was comparable to that of the nobility. The narrator experienced a moment of happiness despite having committed serious crimes. The narrator's misfortunes began when her daughter unexpectedly entered the parlour. Amy fainted upon seeing the narrator's daughter, who had been released from jail by a Quaker. A confrontation occurred between Amy and the narrator's daughter, leading to chaos in the house. The narrator's husband was out hunting during the incident. The narrator and Amy planned to find the daughter and offer her money to keep quiet.

The text discusses the hardships faced by women who have lost their fortunes and the potential for their children to suffer as a result. The narrator expresses personal experiences of near starvation and emotional distress. A male character suggests that they could live happily together without engaging in business, as their fortunes would be equal. The narrator expresses concerns about the power dynamics in marriage, emphasizing that the laws of matrimony grant authority to the husband. The male character argues that marriage is a divine institution meant for happiness and legal inheritance. The narrator acknowledges the advantages of marriage but states a personal inability to reconcile with the institution. The narrator mentions two potential ways to restore honor without resorting to marriage.

The narrator realized that what he thought was a continent was actually a long ridge of islands. The savages who visited the narrator's island were not Caribbees but other islanders closer to his location. The narrator visited several islands, some of which were inhabited and some were not. On one island, the narrator encountered Spaniards who were there to make salt and catch pearl-muscles. The Spaniards belonged to the Isle de Trinidad, located farther north at 10 and 11 degrees latitude. Upon returning to his island, the narrator recognized the area and anchored his ship near his old habitation. Friday expressed sadness about not being able to see his father, who he believed had died long ago.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: William Atkins and his men engaged in a battle against a group of savages. Atkins discovered that the savages were initially terrified by the sound of gunfire, believing they were being killed by gods. During the conflict, Atkins was wounded, and two of his men were killed by arrows. A slave who fought alongside Atkins killed five savages using an armed staff and a hatchet. The savages suffered significant casualties, with over fifty killed and many more wounded. After the battle, the savages did not pursue Atkins and his men but celebrated their victory. Atkins and the Spaniards decided to wait until morning to engage the savages again.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The group formed a triangle with a tree as a breastwork to protect their horses. Wolves charged at the group, driven by the sight of the horses. The group fired multiple volleys, killing seventeen or eighteen wolves and wounding many more. A horn of powder was used to create a fire trap, which injured several wolves. The group killed approximately three score wolves during the encounter. Upon reaching the town, they found the inhabitants in a state of alarm due to previous wolf and bear attacks. The next morning, the group's guide was unable to continue due to severe injuries.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator reflects on their distress and compares their current condition to their initial expectations. The narrator attributes their survival to the providence of God, which allowed them to access a ship near the shore. The narrator expresses gratitude for the tools and resources obtained from the ship, which were essential for their survival. The narrator contemplates how their situation could have been worse if they had not salvaged anything from the ship. The narrator acknowledges their past life, which lacked a sense of religious duty and awareness of God. The narrator describes how their seafaring life led to a loss of religious sentiment and a hardened attitude towards danger and death. The narrator reflects on their past wickedness and the providences that have occurred since arriving at their current location.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator expresses regret over their relationship with a man named Amy, whom they view as a source of temptation. The narrator acknowledges that their relationship with Amy is considered adultery by both divine and human laws. The narrator reflects on the kindness shown to them by the gentleman and their failure to respond with gratitude and obedience. The narrator admits to feeling trapped by poverty and the lack of support from friends or family. The narrator describes their youth and vanity, which contributed to their susceptibility to the gentleman's affections. Amy encourages the narrator to consider alternative arrangements to satisfy the gentleman's desires. The narrator feels that refusing the gentleman could lead to a return to their previous state of misery.

The narrator instructs Friday to follow his actions precisely. The narrator and Friday fire their weapons at a group of savages. Friday kills two savages and wounds three, while the narrator kills one and wounds two. The remaining savages are in a state of confusion and fear after the gunfire. The narrator and Friday rush towards a victim lying on the beach. Friday shoots at the fleeing savages, killing two and wounding a third. The victim, who identifies as a Christian and is from Spain, is rescued by the narrator.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator expresses a strong desire for companionship after witnessing a shipwreck. The narrator reflects on the absence of fellow-creatures during their solitary life. The narrator repeatedly wishes that at least one person had survived the shipwreck. The narrator describes physical reactions to their intense longing for companionship. The narrator mentions seeing the corpse of a drowned boy after the shipwreck. The narrator considers venturing out to the wreck in search of survivors or useful items. The narrator feels compelled to act on the strong impression to explore the wreck.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator observed a distant object at sea, which they suspected was a ship. The narrator concluded that the object was a ship at anchor after observing it throughout the day. The narrator discovered the wreck of a ship on concealed rocks after reaching the south-east side of the island. The wreck occurred due to the ship being driven onto the rocks by strong winds from the east. The narrator speculated on the fate of the ship's crew, considering various scenarios of their potential survival. The narrator expressed gratitude for their own survival while reflecting on the misfortune of the shipwrecked crew. The narrator noted that even in dire circumstances, there can be reasons to be thankful.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The coachman drove quickly, and the group entered the west gate of the city at dusk. They stayed at an inn on High Street near St. Mary Bredman's church. The narrator experienced anxiety and fatigue, leading to physical discomfort. The landlady advised the narrator to eat a poached egg, drink sack, and go to bed. The Quaker expressed concern for the narrator's well-being. The Quaker suggested sending a servant named Tom to Dover to inquire about a young woman. After a good night's sleep, the narrator felt better and had a hearty meal at dinner.

The narrator describes a period of retreat during which they accumulated a significant amount of money. Upon returning to society, the narrator feels tarnished and discolored but maintains a youthful temperament. The narrator is not as popular as before but still has company from high-quality individuals who visit them. The narrator is perceived as wealthy, which affects how others approach them. A person of honor with a great estate attempts to court the narrator, initially discussing wealth before shifting to love. The narrator accepts valuable gifts from the suitor but is cautious about commitments and expenses. The narrator expresses a preference for independence over settled allowances, likening them to a form of bondage.

The scene described involves a man and his wife who are observed expressing deep emotion and seriousness during a conversation. The narrator expresses a belief that the couple's sincerity may lead to a positive outcome in their spiritual journey. The clergyman believes that if the couple embraces Christianity, they will influence others to do the same. The narrator questions the clergyman about the implications of the couple being outside the Catholic Church. The clergyman identifies himself as a Catholic priest and expresses a charitable view towards those outside the Catholic faith. He emphasizes the importance of distinguishing between Protestants and Pagans in terms of their knowledge of God. The clergyman hopes for the eventual restoration of all to the Catholic Church, regardless of their current beliefs.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: Will Atkins and his wife were not present when the other couples were married. The clergyman expressed curiosity about Will Atkins' whereabouts. The narrator and the clergyman found Will Atkins and his wife engaged in serious conversation. Will Atkins was observed pointing to various elements of nature while speaking to his wife. Will Atkins knelt down, lifted his hands, and appeared to pray, though his words were not audible. The clergyman was emotionally affected by the scene, shedding tears. Will Atkins and his wife eventually knelt together for a period of time.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: Will Atkins did not kill his father with his own hands. Will Atkins expressed remorse for his actions towards his father. R.C. acknowledged his own feelings of guilt regarding his father. R.C. believed that Will Atkins' repentance was more sincere than his own. A young clergyman was affected by the conversation between R.C. and Will Atkins. Will Atkins was discussing God and religion with his wife. Will Atkins resolved to amend and reform his life after his conversation with his wife.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator had several meetings with a gentleman who expressed concern for a child. The narrator experienced mixed feelings of affection and doubt regarding the gentleman. The narrator was apprehensive about revealing her past life to the gentleman. The narrator and the gentleman avoided discussing their main subject during their meetings. The narrator received a letter from Amy regarding the gentleman's circumstances. Amy informed the narrator that the gentleman had faced losses and was living in London. Amy also mentioned that a prince had gone to Germany and was living retired.

The rainy season varied in length depending on wind conditions. The author took precautions to avoid being outdoors during the rain. The author attempted to make a basket using local twigs but found them too brittle. The author had prior experience observing basket-making techniques. The author discovered that certain local twigs were suitable for basket-making. The author made several baskets for various purposes, including storing corn. The author lacked proper vessels for liquids and had only a kettle from the ship.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The group built two huts on an island, situated under a hill and surrounded by trees. They requested dry goat-skins for beds and were provided with tools, seeds, and other supplies by the Spaniards. The group lived separately for about six months and managed to harvest a small quantity of crops. They struggled with making boards and pots and faced difficulties during the rainy season, risking their grain spoiling. The Spaniards assisted them by creating a storage hole in the hill to protect their supplies from rain. After approximately three quarters of a year, the group planned to capture natives from the continent to do their labor. The group committed acts of violence, including wounding a slave and plotting to murder the Spaniards.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator sold their cargo and converted their effects into bills of exchange. The narrator experienced a strong aversion to traveling to England by sea. Two ships the narrator considered for travel to England were lost, one captured by Algerines and the other wrecked near Torbay. The narrator's old pilot advised against traveling by sea and suggested alternative land routes. The narrator decided to travel by land to England, accompanied by a group of five others and several servants. The group set out from Lisbon well-mounted and armed, with the narrator designated as the captain. Upon reaching Madrid, the group decided to stay briefly before continuing their journey in October.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator took a dose of tobacco before lying down. The narrator read the Bible but found it difficult to concentrate due to the effects of tobacco. The narrator reflected on the biblical promise of deliverance during a time of trouble. The narrator prayed to God for deliverance before going to bed. The narrator consumed rum steeped with tobacco before sleeping. The narrator slept for an extended period, waking up around three o'clock in the afternoon the next day. The narrator felt refreshed and stronger upon waking but did not feel as well the following day.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: Old Friday instructed a group of about thirty-seven individuals to agree to a proposal for food or face destruction. Twelve Spaniards, two Englishmen, and three Indian slaves delivered food and provisions to the group. The group was confined to a neck of land surrounded by high rocks and had access to fertile land. The Spaniards and Englishmen taught the group to plant corn, breed goats, and make wooden tools. The group was prohibited from interacting with other Indians to prevent their settlement from being betrayed. The group became skilled in wicker-work, creating various items such as baskets and furniture. The arrival of additional supplies and tools improved the living conditions of the group, allowing them to build better huts.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator and Xury waded ashore carrying arms and two jars for water. Xury found a creature resembling a hare, which they killed and consumed. They discovered fresh water in the creek when the tide was out. The narrator had previously traveled to the coast and was aware of the nearby Canary Islands and Cape Verde Islands. The area they were in was uninhabited, except for wild beasts, due to the abandonment by the Negroes and the Moors. The narrator attempted to reach the Pico of Teneriffe but was forced back by contrary winds. Xury advised the narrator to move farther from the shore due to the presence of a 'dreadful monster.'

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator constructed a complete enclosure with a wall around their cave. The day after finishing the wall, the narrator experienced a severe earthquake. During the earthquake, the ground shook three times at eight-minute intervals. A large rock fell near the sea, creating a loud noise that startled the narrator. The earthquake caused the sea to move violently, with stronger shocks likely occurring underwater. After the earthquake, a hurricane developed, lasting about three hours before calming down. The narrator felt terrified and dejected during these events but eventually decided to return to their cave.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator and their partner were privately married with only Amy and a Quaker friend present. The narrator's partner expressed relief at their marriage and mentioned past financial losses. The partner stated intentions to avoid business and leave management responsibilities to the narrator. The couple enjoyed a quiet wedding day without any guests other than their close friends. The Quaker provided a dinner for the couple during their wedding week, which the narrator wished to pay for. The couple had previously been together for eleven years before their marriage. Amy, a friend of the couple, was unaware of their prior relationship.

The narrator experienced physical pain that caused them to wake from sleep and fear for the loss of two fingers. The narrator feared cruel treatment from captors, recalling the story of Amboyna and the potential for torture by the Dutch. The narrator believed that captors might force confessions of piracy through torture and execute them under a guise of justice. The narrator and their partner were tormented by these fears, despite knowing that ship captains had no authority to act cruelly towards them. The narrator reflected on their life of difficulties and felt it was unjust to face new sorrows in old age for a crime they did not commit. The narrator considered their situation as a possible punishment from Providence and contemplated their past actions. The narrator resolved to resist being mistreated and preferred to face savages rather than captors who might inflict prolonged suffering.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator's father advised him not to pursue a life that could lead to miseries, emphasizing that he was not required to seek his own livelihood. The father expressed his willingness to support the narrator and help him settle into a stable life. The father referenced the fate of the narrator's elder brother, who was killed in the Low Country wars after ignoring similar advice. The father became emotional during the conversation, particularly when discussing the loss of his elder son and the potential consequences of the narrator's choices. The narrator initially resolved to stay at home but later decided to run away to explore the world. The narrator informed his mother of his desire to see the world and requested her assistance in gaining his father's consent for a voyage. The mother reacted negatively to the narrator's request, believing that the father would not agree to it due to concerns for the narrator's well-being.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The child became an officer of the Garde du Corps of France and later a colonel of a regiment of dragoons in Italy. The narrator describes her life as one of high value and affection from a person of quality, despite being a mistress. The narrator did not ask for favors from her partner and maintained her independence. The only favor the narrator requested was for her partner's gentleman, who had offended him, to be pardoned. The narrator's maid, Amy, became intimate with the gentleman after he was pardoned. The narrator was concerned that Amy might become pregnant but this did not occur. The narrator planned to return to Paris as winter approached after ensuring her child had a good nurse.

The Portuguese and the Spaniards were described as struggling with misfortunes and often resorting to despair. The narrator had supplies from a shipwreck that aided in their survival, despite being alone. The Spaniards believed they would not have been able to retrieve as many supplies from the ship as the narrator did. The Spaniards landed on an island without provisions, despite being informed of another island with food. The island they landed on was inhabited by savages who lived indolently and provided limited sustenance. The Spaniards attempted to civilize the local savages but were unsuccessful and faced extreme hunger. The Spaniards noted that their hardships led them to rely on the narrator for relief.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator's first voyage was successful due to the captain's integrity and honesty. The narrator gained knowledge of mathematics and navigation during this voyage. The narrator brought home five pounds nine ounces of gold-dust, which yielded almost 300_l_ in London. The narrator experienced sickness during the first voyage due to the climate.
