After the captain's death, the narrator embarked on a second voyage with the captain's former mate. The second voyage was marked by misfortunes, including an encounter with a Turkish rover of Sallee. The narrator was captured and made a slave after the ship was disabled in the battle.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator left the Quaker to receive information about her daughter from Tom, the footman. Tom returned from Dover two hours before the narrator arrived at the inn. Tom reported that a young woman was searching for a Dutch merchant and her mother in Dover. The young woman had visited every public inn in Dover and planned to go to Deal and then to the Hague. The Quaker expressed relief that the young woman had already passed the road before them. The narrator gave Tom half a guinea for his efforts and joined her husband and the Quaker in the parlour. The narrator and her husband discussed the options for traveling on board a vessel.

The narrator's companion expressed a desire to settle in a place chosen by the narrator. The narrator preferred to live abroad to avoid being recognized in England. The narrator enjoyed the idea of being a countess despite not being a princess. The narrator discussed her living options with Amy, who suggested she could be both a baronet's lady in England and a countess in Holland. The narrator pretended to prefer living in England but did not want to live in London. The narrator's companion planned to have his naturalization bill passed before their marriage. The narrator received a patent for baronet and a diamond-set picture from her companion before their marriage.

The narrator discovered a secure cave with no visible creatures or dampness. The narrator planned to move their magazine of powder and spare arms to the cave. The narrator found that about sixty pounds of good powder remained dry in a barrel that had been wet. The narrator buried a goat that died near the cave to avoid unpleasant odors. The narrator had been living on the island for twenty-three years and felt naturalized to the environment. The narrator taught a parrot named Pol to speak, and it lived with them for twenty-six years. The narrator's dog was a companion for sixteen years before dying of old age.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The Spaniards disarmed the three vagrants and did not allow the two Englishmen to pursue them with firearms. The governor of the Spaniards promised the Englishmen to seek justice for them without violence. The two Englishmen reluctantly agreed to wait for the Spaniards to resolve the situation. The three vagrants returned to the Spaniards after several days of wandering and requested to be accepted back into the group. The Spaniards consulted with the Englishmen before deciding on the fate of the three vagrants. The Spaniards required the three vagrants to rebuild the huts and restore the land to its previous state. The Spaniards eventually allowed the three vagrants to have arms again after a period of living together.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The good woman's charity was intended for the comfort and instruction of others. William Atkins expressed joy about a religious discussion between his wife and a young woman. The young woman was described as a new instructor sent to help with religious matters. The narrator provided a Bible to William Atkins and his wife during their discussion. William Atkins believed that God had answered his prayer by providing the Bible. The young woman clarified that God's providence can fulfill petitions without miraculous intervention. William Atkins displayed profound gratitude for receiving the Bible.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: Amy informs a man that his chamber is ready for the night. The man expresses affection and kindness towards the narrator. The man states that he cannot marry the narrator due to his existing marital situation. The man assures the narrator that he will not ask anything that would compromise her virtue. The narrator feels a sense of obligation and gratitude towards the man for his kindness. The man declares his love for the narrator while emphasizing that his intentions are honorable. The narrator agrees to the man's requests within the boundaries of honor and virtue.

The speaker was informed that a lord had taken pains to find her and believed she had gone to England. The lord had intended to marry the speaker and take her to Germany if he had found her. The speaker's maid, Amy, was aware of the situation and had not yet informed the lord that she knew the speaker's whereabouts. Amy learned that a Jew had fled after being involved in a robbery attempt in Paris and had not been heard from in over six years. The speaker's husband, a brewer, was wounded in the battle of Mons and died in the Hospital of the Invalids. The speaker was considering a relationship with a merchant while receiving news about the prince's affections. The speaker expressed a desire for a quiet country life, but her merchant partner preferred to stay near London for business.

The narrator paid £60 a year for handsome and richly furnished apartments. The narrator employed a coachman, a footman, a companion named Amy, and three maids. The narrator dressed in fashionable clothing and did not desire jewels. Amy spread information about the narrator being a wealthy widow from France with £40,000. The narrator received proposals from fortune-hunters seeking to marry for financial gain. The narrator refused offers from gentlemen of good families who were financially needy. The narrator expressed contentment with being single and financially independent.

The men on the ship were extremely hungry and consumed food with great greediness. Two men were in danger of their lives due to their excessive eating. The narrator recalled their own experience of starvation upon arriving on the island. The mate reported that three passengers in the great cabin had not been fed for two or three days. The narrator ordered a boat to deliver food to the starving crew on board the ship. The surgeon instructed the men to boil the meat and distribute it carefully to prevent overeating. The narrator personally went on board the ship to assess the condition of the passengers.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The author spent a significant amount of time cutting and preparing heavy posts in the woods. It took the author two days to bring home one post and a third day to drive it into the ground. The author used a heavy piece of wood and later an iron crow to drive the posts, which was laborious work. The author considered their condition and wrote down their thoughts to alleviate mental distress. The author compared their miseries and comforts in a written account to find reasons for gratitude. The author acknowledged that despite their desolate situation, they had survived when others had not. The author described their habitation as a tent surrounded by a strong palisade of posts and cables.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The speaker discusses the concept of Jesus Christ as a redeemer with a person named Friday. Friday compares the ability of God to hear prayers to that of their god Benamuckee, who requires people to travel to the mountains to communicate with him. Friday mentions that only old men, referred to as Oowookakee, go to speak to Benamuckee and return with messages. The speaker observes that priestcraft exists among various religions, including those of ignorant pagans. The speaker attempts to explain the concept of the devil to Friday, discussing his rebellion against God and his influence on mankind. Friday questions the speaker about the strength of God compared to the devil, leading to a discussion about God's superiority. The speaker emphasizes God's omnipotence and aversion to sin while explaining the role of the devil in opposing God's plans.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator observed nine naked savages sitting around a small fire. The savages appeared to be preparing human flesh over the fire. The savages had two canoes that they had pulled up on the shore. The narrator noted that the savages would leave with the returning tide. The narrator felt a sense of confusion and fear upon seeing the savages. After the savages left, the narrator discovered evidence of their previous activities, including blood and bones. The narrator experienced constant apprehension about the return of the savages for over fifteen months.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: Amy expressed her long-standing love for a boy and resolved to do something extraordinary for him. Amy paid the boy one hundred and twenty pounds to ensure he would not lose out by returning home. The boy's uncle and his wife, a kind woman, were involved in discussions about the boy's welfare. The uncle's wife mentioned that the boy has two sisters who are not being cared for and are in a difficult situation. Amy indicated that she would assist the boy but prioritized his well-being over that of his sisters. Amy had several meetings with the boy to arrange for his schooling and clothing without revealing the full truth to him. A maid-servant of Amy's returned from the city distressed after learning that her brother had been taken home by a lady.

The speaker believes that the future depends entirely on the listener's actions. The speaker suggests that the listener should legally marry two individuals rather than separate them. The speaker proposes a written contract signed by both parties and witnesses as a valid form of marriage. The speaker expresses surprise at the listener's misunderstanding of his intentions regarding marriage. The speaker notes that the English subjects have lived with the women for almost seven years without teaching them about Christianity. The speaker criticizes the neglect of the English subjects in teaching the women about God and worship. The speaker expresses a desire for the women to learn the general principles of the Christian religion.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The old pilot served as both captain and engineer. The crew was instructed not to fire until the enemy was within pistol shot. The crew killed fourteen enemies and wounded several others during the first volley. The enemy retreated approximately one hundred rods after the initial attack. The enemy regrouped and increased their numbers to about three hundred, setting up eleven or twelve huts and tents. The crew spent the night strengthening their position and keeping watch. A Siberian servant offered to guide the crew to a safer route to avoid the enemy.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The Spaniard governor ordered that the two Englishmen be sent to a cave in the valley and guarded by two Spaniards. The two Englishmen, encouraged by the arrival of the Spaniards, decided to seek out the savages. The Englishmen found evidence that the savages had attempted to carry away their dead comrades. The Englishmen observed the savages embarking in canoes and felt relieved to be rid of them. The Englishmen received assistance from their countrymen to rebuild their destroyed improvements. Three of the savages' canoes washed ashore with two drowned men, suggesting they encountered a storm at sea. Five or six months later, the Englishmen were invaded by a fleet of twenty-eight canoes full of armed savages.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator reflects on the age of her mistress, who is nearly fifty and unlikely to have children. The Quaker landlady visits the narrator and Amy in the morning, offering them cakes and chocolate in bed. The Quaker treats the narrator and Amy generously throughout the week, providing a variety of food. The narrator has two maids, a coachman, and a boy assisting her, while the Quaker has one maid and borrows two more for the occasion. The narrator provides fine plate to the Quaker for use during the week, instructing her to treat it as her own. The narrator enjoys being addressed as 'her ladyship' and finds pleasure in the novelty of the title. The week is characterized by innocent mirth and pleasant interactions, with no music or dancing.

The narrator acknowledges the kindness of a lord and expresses a desire to serve him. The lord declines an offer he believes is not from Heaven and expresses satisfaction in parting as an honest man. The narrator sends a small present to the lord, which includes tea, damask, and Japan gold. The lord accepts part of the present but declines the rest and requests the narrator not to pursue the previous matter. The lord asks the narrator to extend kindness to his son, who is over two hundred miles away. The narrator agrees to help the lord's son and indicates that it is out of respect for the lord. The lord's son arrives with horses loaded with valuable furs, and they discuss travel arrangements.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The ship had lost its main-topmast, fore-mast, and bowsprit. The ship fired a gun as a signal of distress. The ship was from Bristol and was bound home from Barbadoes. The crew had been at sea for nine weeks and had encountered multiple storms. The crew was almost out of provisions, having not eaten for eleven days. There were three passengers on board who were in a deplorable condition. The second mate reported that the passengers had not been heard from for two days.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator sent away Friday's father and the Spaniard in a large canoe to fetch the Spaniard's companions. The narrator had no hope for his own deliverance at the time he sent them away. The return of Friday's father and the Spaniard was a surprise due to the narrator's absence and the presence of three strangers. Friday's father reported calm weather and a smooth sea during his voyage back to his countrymen. The countrymen were overjoyed and surprised to see Friday's father, who had been presumed dead. The countrymen prepared to leave with Friday's father after he showed them arms and provisions. The countrymen borrowed two large canoes from friendly savages under the pretense of going fishing.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The speaker expresses concern about a man and his relationship with Amy. Amy suggests that the speaker should go to bed with the man. The speaker acknowledges feelings of love for the man. Amy argues that the speaker is free to marry since her previous husband is no longer in the picture. Amy believes the man has improved the speaker's situation significantly. The speaker is uncertain about the man's intentions regarding a romantic relationship. Amy asserts that it is customary in some places for a man to take another woman if his first wife is unfaithful.

The Englishmen reached the land in two days but did not go ashore due to the local people's alarm and preparation for conflict. They sailed north for six or seven hours and discovered that the land they saw was an island, not the mainland. Upon entering an opening in the sea, they observed another island to the north and several more to the west. The Englishmen landed on one of the western islands and found the local people to be courteous and friendly, offering them food. The locals informed the Englishmen about fierce neighboring tribes that practiced cannibalism, but claimed they only ate prisoners taken in war. The Englishmen were offered five women and eleven men as prisoners, which they reluctantly accepted after some debate. In return for the prisoners, the Englishmen gave the locals a hatchet, an old key, a knife, and several bullets.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The character gave his father raisins before running away quickly. He returned after a quarter of an hour with an earthen jug and two loaves of bread. He gave one loaf of bread to the narrator and carried the water to his father. The water revived his father more than any spirits the narrator had provided. The Spaniard was weak and unable to stand due to swollen ankles. Friday helped the Spaniard by rubbing his ankles and bathing them with rum. Friday carried the Spaniard to the boat and paddled them both safely to the creek.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator was fined three shillings by the caravan leader for being two hours behind schedule. The great China wall was built as a fortification against the Tartars and spans nearly a thousand English miles. The wall is approximately four fathoms high and thick in some places. The narrator observed the wall for about an hour while the caravan passed through the gate. The narrator questioned the wall's effectiveness against a well-equipped army. The area beyond the wall was found to be thinly inhabited, with people living in fortified towns due to threats from the Tartars. The narrator noted the Tartars appeared disorganized and lacked military discipline.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator managed servants and cultivated land, leading what he considered an agreeable life. He farmed on his own land without paying rent or being limited by articles. The narrator experienced a significant change in his life following the loss of his wife. His wife was central to his affairs and helped guide him away from ruinous projects. After her death, the narrator felt isolated and confused, likening his feelings to when he first arrived in the Brasils. He observed the struggles of people around him, noting their labor for bread and indulgence in excesses. The narrator reflected on his previous life in the island, where he had no need for excess and recognized the importance of seeking fulfillment beyond material possessions.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: Roxana was born in Poitiers, France, and brought to England by her parents around 1683 due to religious persecution. Her parents were of better social standing than most refugees and had secured their possessions before fleeing France. Roxana's father was financially stable upon arriving in England, having sold valuable goods and not needing assistance from other refugees. Roxana enjoyed living in London, a city she found appealing due to its crowds and social life. The narrative emphasizes Roxana's self-criticism and repentance rather than promoting her actions. The writer aims to expose vice and discourage immoral behavior through the story, despite acknowledging that some may misinterpret it. The publication is intended to provide moral lessons and improvement for virtuous readers.

The husband informed Amy that he would dine alone and instructed her to tell his wife to dine when and where she pleased. Amy expressed her distress after speaking with the husband, stating that he was in a deep study and did not wish to speak with her. The wife confronted her husband in his study, asking why he was in an unforgiving mood and what she had done to deserve it. The husband accused the wife of deceit, claiming she had not mentioned her children during their initial interactions. The husband noted that the wife neglected to discuss her children when they were considering marriage, despite mentioning his own. The husband criticized the wife for refusing to settle her own fortune and for not acknowledging her daughter. The husband challenged the wife to reconcile her actions with her sense of humanity.

The narrator wrote a letter detailing an assault involving long-boats and expressed a desire for justice if the assailants returned to England. The old pilot read the letter multiple times and confirmed the narrator's commitment to the message. The pilot did not carry the letter back as he never returned to England. The narrator and his partner sailed to Nanquin and learned that two Dutch ships had already reached the area. The pilot suggested a port called Quinchang, where European ships did not typically go, as a safer option. Quinchang was known for occasional fairs with Japanese merchants buying Chinese goods. The narrator and his crew agreed to sail to Quinchang and successfully reached the port after five days.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The merchant discussed the financial advantages of trade and the wealth of successful merchants compared to noblemen in England. He suggested that tradesmen in London could provide better fortunes for their children than the gentry of England with incomes below £1000 a year. The merchant recommended that the narrator invest her fortune with a successful merchant who could secure her financial independence. The narrator expressed a desire for independence and rejected the idea of marriage as a state of inferiority or bondage. Sir Robert acknowledged the narrator's views but noted that few women shared her mindset or had the resolve to act on it. The narrator indicated that her previous marriage did not encourage her to pursue a second one and that she preferred her current state of freedom. Despite her wealth, the narrator felt harassed by suitors and was focused on a higher ambition than mere romantic pursuits.

The narrator loaded a boat with various supplies including bread, water, rum, raisins, rice, an umbrella, goat's milk, and cheese. The narrator prayed for guidance before setting out on a voyage along the shore of the island. The narrator expressed fear about the dangerous currents surrounding the island and the possibility of being lost at sea. The narrator observed the tide and currents from a high point to determine a safe return route. The narrator noted that the ebb current set out close to the south point of the island and the flood current came in close to the north shore. The narrator planned to set out the next morning with the first of the tide. The narrator successfully reached the wreck of a Spanish ship within two hours of setting out.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator and their spouse arrived at an inn in Sittingbourne. The inn's larder was empty, prompting the landlord to offer to kill a pig and some pigeons for dinner. The narrator and their spouse dined with the landlord, his wife, and two daughters, spending two pounds ten shillings. One of the landlord's daughters mentioned a young woman who resembled the narrator and had stayed at the inn previously. The narrator suspected that the young woman was their daughter, who was searching for them. The narrator learned that their daughter had traveled on foot and inquired about them at various inns. Upon arriving in Canterbury, the narrator discovered that their daughter had left the city a week prior.

The man believes he is a heretic and fears the Inquisition. He has been left with only a little household stuff and two slaves after the Inquisition seized his estate. He requested to escape to an island with his wife and two daughters, offering a small stock to begin with. The narrator concealed the man and his family on board a ship until they could leave. The cargo sent to the island included livestock and materials for planting sugar-canes. The narrator engaged three Portugal women to go to the island for the Spaniards. The arrival of the cargo was welcomed by the inhabitants of the island, who numbered between sixty and seventy people.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator's friend informed her that her husband, who was part of the gens d'armes, was dead. The narrator's friend congratulated her on being a free woman after her husband's death. The narrator expressed a lack of desire to remarry due to negative experiences with her first husband. The narrator compared the roles of a wife and a mistress, highlighting the perceived advantages of being a mistress. The narrator noted that a wife has rights to her husband's possessions and status, while a mistress does not. The narrator described the potential consequences for a mistress if her partner falls into misfortune or seeks repentance. The narrator received several letters from a merchant friend in Paris while she was in Holland.

The narrator and their partner experienced anxiety while at sea. Upon reaching shore, they felt a sense of relief and satisfaction. The old Portuguese pilot helped them find lodging and a warehouse for their goods. Their lodging was a small house built with canes and surrounded by a palisade. They were provided with a guard to protect their goods, who was compensated with rice and money. The Portuguese pilot introduced them to three missionary priests in the town. One of the priests was a Frenchman named Father Simon, who was more sociable than the others.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator is the third son of a family and was not trained for any specific trade. The narrator's father provided him with a basic education and intended for him to pursue a career in law. The narrator had a strong desire to go to sea, which conflicted with his father's wishes and the advice of his family. The father expressed concerns about the dangers and hardships associated with pursuing adventures at sea. The father argued that the middle state of life is the most suitable for human happiness, avoiding the extremes of wealth and poverty. The father noted that the middle state is less exposed to the calamities and hardships faced by both the upper and lower classes. The father emphasized that a middle fortune allows for virtues, enjoyments, and a peaceful life.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator expresses gratitude for the presence of Friday, a 'poor wild wretch'. The narrator feels a sense of joy and purpose in their solitary life, believing they are an instrument of Providence. The narrator and Friday lived together for three years, during which they experienced happiness. Friday is described as a good Christian, and the narrator believes they were both penitent. The narrator engaged in reading the Scripture and teaching Friday about its meaning. The narrator observes that the knowledge of God and salvation is easily understood from the Word of God. The narrator dismisses religious disputes as useless to their situation, relying instead on the Word of God for guidance.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The captain and his two comrades took weapons to confront the mutineers. The two men fired at the mutineers, resulting in one being killed and another wounded. The captain knocked down the wounded mutineer with the stock of his musket. The remaining mutineers begged for mercy and promised to be faithful to the captain. The captain agreed to spare their lives but kept them bound. Three additional men returned and submitted to being bound after hearing the gunfire. The captain and the narrator shared their histories, leading to an emotional response from the captain.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The husband believes that a man he intends to hire has been honest in his dealings. The husband plans to hire the man when he arrives as ordered. The narrator proposes a walk on the pier with the Quaker and Isabel to avoid the hiring situation. The husband informs the narrator that he has hired the man, whose name is Thomas. Thomas has mentioned living with notable families, including my Lord's and the Lady Roxana's in Pall Mall. The narrator is concerned about being recognized by her son, Thomas. The next morning, Thomas begins his new job and assists with the transportation of their luggage.

The narrator experienced anxiety and distress regarding their financial situation and past hardships. The narrator had five children and recalled a time of desolation when they were left to care for them. The narrator sold their jewels, retaining only a diamond ring, a diamond necklace, and a pair of earrings worth about 600 pistoles. The narrator sold their jewels at the Hague for 7600 pistoles and had a total of over twenty-one thousand pistoles in ready money and bank accounts. The narrator applied to several merchants to obtain bills of exchange payable in London to remit their money safely. After spending nine months in Holland, the narrator took a packet-boat from the Brill and arrived safely at Harwich. The narrator was pregnant and expressed a desire to be rid of the burden but acknowledged the necessity of enduring it.

A porter and two large boxes were brought by a man, along with another heavy box carried by his servant. The man unpacked the boxes, which contained primarily books, papers, and parchments. He revealed to the narrator goldsmiths' bills and stock in the English East India Company amounting to about sixteen thousand pounds sterling. The man also presented nine assignments upon the Bank of Lyons in France and two upon the rents of a town-house in Paris, totaling 5800 crowns per annum. Additionally, he had 30,000 rixdollars in the Bank of Amsterdam and jewels valued at approximately £1500 or £1600. The man showed various business ventures, including an eighth share in an East India ship and a large cargo of goods in Lisbon, totaling about £27,000 sterling and £1320 a year. He mentioned a right of reversion to a paternal estate and a mortgage of 14,000 rixdollars, which added about £3000 more to his wealth.

Amy persuaded another woman to accompany her to Greenwich by offering to pay for a boat to bring her back. Amy expressed her feelings of ingratitude towards the woman for treating her rudely despite her kindness. The woman acknowledged that Amy's actions were done at her mother's request and not out of personal obligation. Amy became enraged when the woman recognized her true identity and her connection to her mother. Amy threatened to throw the woman into the river during their boat ride. The narrator felt disturbed by Amy's violent suggestion and became angry with Amy. The narrator revealed that she had kept Amy for almost thirty years and considered her faithful despite her wickedness.

The governor, a Spaniard, experienced unease and could not sleep one night. The governor's thoughts were tumultuous, focused on men fighting and killing each other. Another Spaniard woke up and expressed concern about potential mischief nearby. The Spaniards had kept possession of the main apartment, while the three Englishmen were quartered separately. The Spaniards decided to go out and investigate after discussing their uneasy feelings. They saw a light and heard voices of many men while approaching the top of a hill. The narrator had previously taken precautions to prevent the discovery of any inhabitants on the island.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The group landed about a mile from their huts after an hour. They believed they were betrayed and bound the remaining slaves. Two faithful men were tasked with leading their wives and belongings to a safe location in the woods. The group released their milch-goats to mislead the savages into thinking they were wild. The men sent a slave to the Spaniards to alert them and request help. They observed the savages approaching their habitation and saw their huts burning. The men retreated further into the woods to avoid detection by the savages.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator experienced anxiety and fear of being attacked by savages. The narrator avoided firing his gun near the area where savages were known to come. The narrator spent a year and three months without seeing any savages. In May, during the narrator's twenty-fourth year, he had an encounter with the savages. On the sixteenth of May, a storm occurred, followed by the sound of gunfire at sea. The narrator believed the gunfire was from a ship in distress signaling for help. The narrator prepared a signal fire on the hill to attract the attention of the ship.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The weather was not calm, which affected the decision to go to sea. Will Atkins, despite his wound, was the best counselor in the situation. Atkins advised to prevent the Indians from returning by destroying their boats. Some individuals were concerned that the Indians would flee into the woods if attacked. The group decided to destroy the Indians' canoes to protect their colony. The Indians reacted with cries and gestures, pleading for their boats to be spared. The Spaniards failed to guard their plantations while dealing with the Indians.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator is anxious about the whereabouts of Amy, who has been missing for over a fortnight. Amy had taken all her clothes and money before leaving, and did not leave any information about her destination. The narrator reflects on Amy's long-term loyalty and friendship, feeling regret for having dismissed her. The narrator and their spouse had planned to support Amy financially, but did not communicate this to her. The narrator decides to leave for Holland, believing it will provide them with peace. The narrator feels lost and helpless without Amy, who managed their finances and business affairs. A Quaker friend of the narrator reports being haunted by the narrator's daughter, indicating ongoing distress.

The narrator felt restrained in expressing their passion and had no one to confide in. The narrator was compelled to listen to a story about Roxana, which was also about themselves. The speaker described the living conditions and social activities of her lady's household. The speaker mentioned that she received two guineas and a half from a division of twenty guineas among the servants. Mrs. Amy was identified as the favorite servant who received a significant amount of money. The speaker indicated that Mrs. Amy had laid up over £500 and was rumored to have connections with a young lord. The speaker later saw Mrs. Amy, who arrived in a coach, suggesting she had improved her circumstances.

The narrator experienced intense emotional distress after believing that Amy had harmed her child. The narrator's husband was out hunting during her emotional breakdown. The narrator expressed anger towards Amy, blaming her for the situation. The narrator's husband noticed her distress and encouraged her to share her feelings. The narrator sought comfort from a Quaker, who reassured her about Amy's well-being. The narrator was unable to shake off her fears and continued to think about Amy obsessively. The narrator imagined various violent scenarios involving the girl she believed Amy had harmed.

The speaker reflects on the disparity between the gifts received from the prince and their own feelings of unworthiness. The speaker criticizes the tendency of wealthy individuals to lavish gifts on those they consider inferior, which they believe leads to their own ruin. The speaker recounts a past filled with hardship, including poverty, despair, and the loss of their children to the parish. The speaker acknowledges their past as a sex worker, driven by the need for survival and devoid of virtue. The speaker expresses astonishment at the blindness of people who value physical beauty over moral integrity. The speaker aims to illustrate the destructive nature of vice and its impact on human reason and conscience. The speaker contemplates the potential regret of the prince once he grows tired of the relationship.

The horses observed were described as poor, lean, and starved. The group went hunting for sheep, which were noted to be wild and swift. The group encountered about forty Tartars during their hunting expedition. One of the Tartars blew a loud horn, which was believed to summon more Tartars. A Scots merchant from Moscow led the group to charge the Tartars after hearing the horn. The Tartars initially missed their arrows when firing at the group. The encounter resulted in the death of about five Tartars, while the group suffered no casualties.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The court was predominantly male, with the queen not frequently appearing in public. The king had several mistresses, and the courtiers were described as wicked. The narrator received visits from notable individuals introduced by two female acquaintances. A gaming party was organized by the narrator's female companions, who aimed to introduce more people. The narrator hosted a ball in her apartments, preparing multiple rooms for the event. My Lord ---- sent music from the playhouse for the ball, and the attendees danced. Masquerading gentlemen arrived at the ball, and the narrator was informed that the king might be among them.

The captain of the ship was murdered by the Malaccans at Sumatra. Three crew members were also killed during the incident. Some crew members ran away with the ship and became pirates. The speaker was advised to leave the area quickly to avoid being captured. Two men on board had outstanding pay due to them from a previous ship. The speaker agreed to pay the two men in exchange for their assistance. The ship was chased by five sloops or boats full of men.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: Sir Robert made a proposal regarding frugality near the end of the year. The narrator decided to save seven hundred pounds a year and sought Sir Robert's assistance in investing it. Sir Robert informed the narrator that she had lost half a year's interest of £350 due to not collecting her interest at the half-year mark. Sir Robert offered to pay interest on the £700 until the next year when he would help invest £1400. The narrator received a mortgage for £2200 at 6 percent interest, adding £132 to her annual income. Sir Robert and the narrator shared similar views on the value of merchants compared to nobility. Sir Robert presented a marriage proposal from a merchant, which he believed was a superior offer.

The narrator received a letter from a friend in Paris who expressed regret over their past actions together. The friend asked for forgiveness for being the aggressor and forgave the narrator for past grievances, except for the refusal of a proposal. The friend warned the narrator of potential future misfortunes, including being ruined by a bad husband. The narrator felt stunned and frightened by the friend's predictions and expressed a desire for the friend's support in times of distress. Despite the emotional impact of the letter, the narrator did not wish to marry the friend and instead entertained thoughts of seeking fortune in London. The narrator reflected on their own vanity and the missed opportunity to secure their future by rejecting the friend's proposal. The narrator acknowledged their past influence on men of high rank and their aspirations for a prominent position in London.

The narrator attempted to persuade a lord to leave her for the princess, citing the laws of matrimony. The narrator expressed that she could not bear the thought of losing the lord, even if it meant he would be honest. The princess fell seriously ill and wished to speak with her lord before her death. During their final conversation, the princess expressed her affection for the lord and urged him to be just to any future princess. The princess died the day after their last conversation, leaving a significant emotional impact on the lord. Following the princess's death, the lord changed his behavior, becoming more reserved and committed to a virtuous life. About ten days after the princess's funeral, the lord sent a message to the narrator indicating a desire to end their relationship.

A long-boat was sent ashore with twelve men and the mate to seek out some rogues. The rogues fled into the woods upon seeing the boat and could not be found. The mate considered destroying the rogues' plantations but ultimately left everything intact. Two new-comers were initially rejected by three other English men who were described as wicked. The two new-comers built huts on the north shore of the island to avoid danger from savages. The Spaniards provided the two men with corn for seed, which they planted successfully. The three English men later attempted to bully the two new-comers and set fire to their hut.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The man expressed confusion and left the room after a conversation with the woman. The man had previously saved the woman's life and traveled from Paris to Rotterdam to seek her. He proposed marriage to the woman despite her being pregnant with his child. The man offered to relinquish his claims to the woman's estate and manage it himself. The woman had the opportunity to leave a life of crime and live in comfort and honor. Despite the man's pleas, the woman remained obstinate against marriage and they parted ways. The man left a letter for the woman requesting that she secure a sum of money for their child's education.

The narrator is the widow of a man who was murdered while going to Versailles. The murdered man left his jewels with the narrator to avoid being robbed. The Dutch merchant believed the narrator's account of her situation. The Jew expressed malice towards the narrator and intended to accuse her of murder. The Jew planned to claim the jewels for himself and suggested the narrator should be apprehended. The Dutch merchant was informed of the Jew's intentions and took the matter seriously. The narrator feared that if her marital status was questioned, it would lead to complications regarding the jewels.

The narrator killed a leopard and the Negroes expressed admiration for it. The Negroes intended to eat the leopard's flesh and were thankful when the narrator allowed them to take it. The Negroes skinned the leopard using a sharpened piece of wood. The narrator declined to eat the leopard's flesh but requested the skin, which the Negroes gave freely. The narrator received roots, corn, and water from the Negroes before leaving them. After eleven days of travel, the narrator identified land as the Cape de Verd and the Cape de Verd Islands. The narrator spotted a Portuguese ship but concluded it was not bound for the shore.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator reflects on the nature of the earth, sea, and existence. The narrator concludes that God has created and governs all things. The narrator questions why God has allowed them to experience suffering. The narrator feels a sense of guilt and reflects on their past actions. The narrator finds a piece of tobacco in a chest, which they believe may help with their condition. The narrator also retrieves a Bible from the chest. The narrator experiments with the tobacco to see if it can alleviate their distress.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The child mentioned in the text lived for not more than two months. The narrator expressed relief that the child did not survive due to the difficulties of traveling. The narrator and my lord planned to return to France after the prince's negotiations ended. The narrator had considerable treasure in France and received frequent letters from maid Amy confirming its safety. The journey back to Paris included stops in Venice, Turin, and Milan, and took approximately two years. Upon returning to Paris, the narrator found their family unchanged and was joyfully reunited with Amy. The narrator secured a wealth of ten thousand pounds and later had a third son after returning from Italy.

The Spaniards were described as modest, temperate, virtuous, good-humored, and courteous. The Spaniards did not exhibit cruelty, inhumanity, or barbarity. The Spaniards decided to awaken and capture three sleeping savages to prevent them from discovering the island's inhabitants. The captured savages were initially frightened and feared they would be harmed. One of the captured savages escaped and was believed to have returned to his community. Two months later, six canoes of savages arrived on the island, indicating that the escaped savage had informed them of the Spaniards' presence. The Spaniard governor noted that the odds were unfavorable for the two Englishmen against the larger number of savages.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The ship's company initially had very little food for themselves. Passengers in the cabin experienced severe neglect and had no food for six or seven days. A mother, who was reported to be of good sense and breeding, died after sacrificing her food for her son. The son was found with a piece of an old glove in his mouth and began to revive after receiving some broth. A maid was discovered in a state of distress, having been starved and emotionally affected by her mistress's condition. The ship's surgeon managed to revive the maid, but she remained in a state of distraction for some time. The crew's primary responsibility was to relieve the distressed ship's crew without delaying their journey.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator plans to initiate a legal process against another party. The narrator communicates with a third party about a missed appointment. The narrator prepares for travel by sending belongings and money to a merchant. The narrator entrusts seven thousand eight hundred pistoles and an assignment on a townhouse to a third party. The third party provides the narrator with a bill of exchange and other financial instruments. The narrator departs France with assistance from the third party and a servant. The narrator reflects on the dangers avoided and expresses gratitude for the assistance received.

The narrator's acquaintance, Amy, was tasked with inquiring about a merchant in Rouen. Amy discovered that the merchant had lived in Rouen for two years before returning to Holland. The merchant later returned to Rouen and lived there for another year before moving to London. Amy learned the merchant's London address from an old Dutch skipper who had previously served him. The narrator received multiple accounts from Amy regarding the merchant's whereabouts over several months. While traveling back to London, the narrator encountered two gentlemen speaking Dutch, one of whom was identified as the merchant. The narrator experienced confusion upon recognizing the merchant during the encounter.

The narrator received a toilet and a sideboard made of massy silver from a prince. The prince provided the narrator with three suits of clothes made of brocaded silk, one figured with gold, one with silver, and one in crimson. The narrator had five morning dresses in addition to the three suits of clothes. The prince also sent fine linen and lace to the narrator, leaving no room for additional requests. The narrator expressed concern about being too costly for the prince as a mistress. The prince assured the narrator that he would continue to provide for her without her needing to ask. The narrator dressed in a suit that she believed the prince would like, which included a lace headpiece valued at two hundred pounds sterling.

A great ship was on fire in the middle of the sea. The narrator ordered five guns to be fired to signal help to the burning ship's crew. The burning ship blew up and sank during the night. The narrator caused lights to be hung out and continued firing guns throughout the night. In the morning, two boats from the burning ship were discovered, carrying sixty-four people. The burning ship was identified as a French merchant-ship of three hundred tons, homeward-bound from Quebec. The fire on the ship began in the steerage due to the negligence of the steersman.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator experienced extreme perplexity, melancholy, and discouragement for nearly a year. The narrator's husband had two married sisters and other near relations who were unhelpful in providing information about him. The narrator's brother faced financial disaster and imprisonment six months before the husband's elopement. The narrator had children to care for and faced severe financial distress without any means of support. The narrator began to sell valuable items, including plate and jewels, as their financial situation worsened. The narrator had no hope of seeing their husband again, who lacked the ability or inclination to provide assistance. The husband was described as disinterested in work and unable to manage basic tasks such as writing or understanding English.

The narrator planned to leave the island with his men and had arranged passage to England. The captain could only take the prisoners to England in irons to be tried for mutiny, which could lead to execution. The prisoners preferred to stay on the island rather than risk being taken to England and hanged. The narrator decided to set the prisoners at liberty and provided them with firearms, ammunition, and survival instructions. The narrator informed the prisoners about the fate of their captain, who was hanged at the yard-arm of the ship. The narrator shared his experiences and survival techniques on the island with the prisoners. The narrator promised to persuade the captain to leave additional supplies for the prisoners.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator found a large old he-goat and three kids, consisting of one male and two females. The old he-goat was fierce, and the narrator chose to let him go instead of trying to capture him. The three kids were tied together and brought home with some difficulty. The kids began to tame after being fed sweet corn. The narrator planned to breed the kids for goat's flesh and realized the need to keep tame goats separate from wild ones. The narrator sought a suitable piece of ground for enclosure that had herbage, water, and cover. The initial plan for the enclosure was too large, leading the narrator to reduce it to about one hundred and fifty yards in length and one hundred yards in breadth.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator expresses a desire to wait in Nanquin for an opportunity to load goods and find passage to another place in India. The narrator undertakes several journeys into the country, including a ten-day journey to the city of Nanquin. Nanquin is described as a well-built city with straight streets and a population that is claimed to be around a million, though the narrator doubts this figure. The narrator compares the living conditions, government, and wealth of the people in the region unfavorably to those in Europe. The narrator believes that the military and naval capabilities of European nations far exceed those of China. The narrator asserts that Chinese armies would be ineffective against disciplined European forces and fortified towns. The narrator critiques the quality of Chinese firearms and military discipline, stating they are inferior to European standards.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: A small bed was ordered to be carried into the speaker's chamber. The speaker confronted his lordship about the sudden separation of beds. His lordship suggested that the speaker could contact a former lover for companionship. The speaker expressed feelings of malice, grief, shame, and revenge. The speaker and Amy discussed the servants' potential reactions to the family disturbance. The speaker lived in isolation with Amy and Isabel for a month. The speaker's daughter visited his lordship and appeared satisfied afterward.

The narrator was brought to London at around ten years old. The narrator's father lived in good circumstances and died after eleven years. The narrator learned English perfectly and adopted English customs. At about fourteen years of age, the narrator described themselves as tall, well-made, and quick in discourse. The narrator received a dowry of 25,000 livres and was married to an eminent brewer at fifteen. The narrator lived with her husband for eight years and kept a coach for outings. The narrator described her husband as handsome, tall, and a good dancer.

The narrator experienced cold, shivering, and a violent headache on June 24. On June 25, the narrator suffered from a violent ague that lasted seven hours. On June 26, the narrator killed a she-goat and managed to eat some of it despite feeling weak. On June 27, the ague returned violently, causing the narrator to remain in bed all day without food or water. The narrator prayed to God during this time but felt weak and light-headed. The narrator had a terrifying dream involving a man descending from a black cloud with a weapon. The narrator reflected on a lack of divine knowledge and a history of wickedness during the past eight years.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator expresses a willingness to embrace a proposal for trade. The narrator and his crew faced challenges in finding a suitable ship and English sailors. The crew included an English mate, a boatswain, a gunner, a Dutch carpenter, and three Portuguese foremast-men. The voyage included stops at Achin in Sumatra and Siam, where they exchanged wares for opium and arrack. The narrator notes the high value of opium among the Chinese during that time. The narrator reflects on the wealth accumulated by English officers and merchants in India due to free commerce. Despite the financial success of the voyage, the narrator feels a restless desire to travel and return home.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The mate shot the new captain through the head, resulting in his immediate death. The ship was taken without any additional lives being lost after the captain's death. The captain fired seven guns as a signal of success to the narrator. The narrator was waiting on the shore for the signal until nearly two o'clock in the morning. The captain embraced the narrator and informed him that the ship was now his. The ship was anchored about half a mile from the shore after the crew took control. The captain provided the narrator with a drink to help him recover from his surprise.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The gentleman expressed love and promised to demonstrate it to the satisfaction of the narrator. The narrator acknowledged the gentleman's control over the house and her, within previously discussed limits. The gentleman could not stay the night due to business in London but promised to return the next day. The narrator felt grateful and began to love the gentleman for his assistance in her life. The gentleman planned to send food from London for a supper and referred to it as a wedding supper. The narrator was surprised by the mention of a wedding and questioned its implications. The gentleman indicated that they would discuss their situation after supper.

The speaker poses two significant questions regarding the financial circumstances of the listener's marriage. The first question concerns the listener's ability to support his wife and maintain her lifestyle when they go abroad. The second question inquires about the wife's fortune and estate, questioning whether the listener is keeping her at a standard above her means. The listener responds that he is confident in his ability to maintain his wife regardless of her financial background. The speaker clarifies that the questions were intended to lead into a serious discussion about the wife's financial situation. The listener requests to postpone the discussion until the next day to assess their financial situation together. The speaker agrees to the postponement, and the conversation concludes for the time being.

The girl is nineteen or twenty years old and initially struggles to speak. The girl insists that Amy is her mother and expresses distress when Amy denies it. Amy tries to comfort the girl by stating she will continue to be kind to her. The girl claims she can keep a secret and pleads with Amy not to disown her. Amy feels confused and alarmed by the girl's insistence and emotional state. The girl becomes more violent in her demands for recognition from Amy during subsequent visits. Amy attempts various methods to pacify the girl, but her efforts lead to further distress.

The governor advised to make haste forward while keeping the pursuers occupied. The caravan traveled for two days and nights before stopping at a village called Plothus. The caravan then proceeded towards Jarawena, a colony of the czar of Muscovy. During the journey, the caravan entered a vast nameless desert and passed by a lake called Schanks Osier. The caravan noticed they were being pursued by a large body of horsemen while traveling west. The caravan camped in a narrow strait between two woods, preparing for a possible attack. The pursuers demanded the return of men who had allegedly harmed their priests and burned their god Cham-Chi-Thaungu.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The two Englishmen and the Spaniard believed that one of the three should be hanged for attempting murder. The governor Spaniard opposed the execution of an Englishman, citing that he had saved their lives. The governor insisted that even if he had been killed by an Englishman, he would still advocate for pardon. It was agreed that the three individuals should be disarmed and expelled from the society. The expelled individuals were forbidden from interacting with the rest of the society and were to be shot if they caused any disorder. The governor decided to provide the expelled individuals with provisions for eight months and tools for farming. The expelled individuals left the society but returned after a few days to report their chosen location for settlement.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: Rain occurred, accompanied by thunder and lightning, causing fear of damage to powder. On November 14, 15, and 16, boxes were made to store powder in small parcels. A large bird was killed for food during this period, but its species was unknown. On November 17, digging began behind the tent into the rock for convenience. Tools needed for digging included a pickaxe, shovel, and a wheel-barrow or basket. An iron tree was found and used to make a shovel after considerable effort. Eighteen days were spent widening and deepening the cave for storage and living purposes.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: Father Simon, a French priest, was appointed to go to Pekin by the chief of the mission. Father Simon invited the narrator and his partner to accompany him on the journey to Pekin. Father Simon expressed a desire to convert heathens and possibly the narrator and his partner, whom he referred to as heretics. The narrator compared Father Simon to a priest he had known in the Brasils, noting differences in zeal and piety. The narrator and his partner were uncertain about their business and considered sailing to the river of Kilam and the city of Nanquin. The narrator felt that Providence was guiding their affairs and believed they would eventually return to their home country. A Portuguese pilot introduced a Japan merchant to the narrator and his partner to inquire about their goods.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The tools and supplies left behind included harrows, ploughs, pickaxes, crowbars, broadaxes, saws, nails, staples, hinges, hammers, chisels, knives, scissors, and two tons of unwrought iron. The magazine of powder and arms provided was sufficient for the inhabitants to march with muskets and defend against potential threats. A young man and a maid, the latter described as sober, well-educated, and religious, were brought ashore after the ship's journey. Both the young man and the maid requested to remain on the island and were allowed to join the established community. The maid and young man were allotted a plot of land where they set up three tents or houses, surrounded by a palisade. The island was divided into three colonies: the Spaniards with old Friday, the new settlers including the maid and young man, and Will Atkins's colony with four families. The capital city of the island was concealed within thick trees, making it difficult to discover without prior knowledge of its location.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The ship experienced a severe storm for twelve days, during which the crew could do nothing but drift. One crew member died from calenture, and another man and a boy were washed overboard during the storm. After twelve days, the ship's master determined their location to be approximately 11 degrees north latitude and 22 degrees west longitude from Cape St. Augustino. The master consulted with the narrator about their course, as the ship was leaky and disabled. They decided to head towards Barbadoes instead of returning to the coast of Brasil, hoping to reach it in about fifteen days. A second storm struck while they were at 12 degrees 18 minutes latitude, pushing them further off course. The ship struck a sandbank, causing the crew to fear for their lives as the sea broke over the vessel.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator experienced extreme hunger and physical weakness, leading to a lack of sleep and severe discomfort. The narrator's young master announced the death of his mother, but she was later found to be alive with very little signs of life. The narrator suffered from severe stomach convulsions due to lack of food and was unable to leave the bed. The ship's crew did not have any food to eat and believed the narrator and his companions were dead. The narrator describes the dire situation they were in, suggesting that without intervention, they would have died from starvation. The narrator chose not to inform the people about the sloop he had constructed due to concerns about potential division and conflict among them. The narrator also decided not to leave behind weapons on the island to prevent the possibility of piracy.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The husband left five thousand livres to his wife at his death. The husband's elder brother mismanaged the money and lost it. The husband's father died two years after the wife's father, leaving him the brewhouse trade. The husband lacked business acumen and neglected his accounts. The wife's attempts to persuade her husband to manage his business were unsuccessful. The husband eventually decided to lay down his trade due to financial difficulties. After selling the brewhouse, the husband had between two and three thousand pounds in his pocket.

The narrator passed for a Quaker among people who did not know them. The narrator had been accustomed to using a coach and expressed a desire to have one again. A coachmaker was hired to provide a plain coach for the narrator, which was lined with light grey cloth. The narrator dressed in Quaker attire and went out with a friend, aiming to be concealed and not recognized. The narrator experienced feelings of regret and melancholy regarding past actions, particularly related to a friend, the merchant of Paris. The narrator frequently thought about the merchant and discussed these thoughts with their friend Amy. Amy suggested visiting the merchant to see how he was, but the narrator strongly opposed the idea.

The narrator left a remote city in the beginning of June. The caravan consisted of thirty-two horses and camels, with the narrator's guest owning eleven of them. The journey included passing through a large and difficult desert. The narrator's party avoided major towns to evade strict Muscovite garrisons. The first city encountered after crossing the river Kama was Soloy Kamaskoy. The people in the region were mostly Pagans, with some identifying as Christians of the Greek church. The narrator's party faced potential danger from thieves during their journey.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator is alone in a remote part of the world, nearly three thousand leagues from England. The narrator considers various routes to return to England, including traveling through the Great Mogul's country and taking caravans to Aleppo and Scanderoon. The narrator has the option to wait for English ships coming to Bengal from Achin, but lacks connections with the English East India Company. The narrator has two companions: a clerk to the purser and his nephew's servant. The narrator stays in a lodging house with several merchants, including English, French, and Italian individuals, for over nine months. The narrator possesses valuable English goods and a considerable sum of money, including a thousand pieces of eight from his nephew. An English merchant proposes a trading voyage to China, suggesting they pool their resources to hire a ship.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The Englishman claimed that the island belonged to the natives and that no one had the right to make them servants. The Spaniard suggested that by the same reasoning, they should also be servants to the Englishman. The Englishman threatened to burn the natives' new huts and prevent them from building on their land. A group of Englishmen, including Will Atkins, planned to attack the Spaniards and destroy their castle. The Englishmen wandered the country at night and overslept, missing an opportunity to attack the natives. When the Englishmen arrived at the natives' huts, they found them abandoned and assumed the Spaniards had warned them. The Englishmen destroyed the natives' houses and belongings, leaving little evidence of their existence.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator made Mr. Thompson, an English mate, the captain of the ship. The river mentioned is located on the north side of a bay that leads to Siam. An Englishman, a gunner's mate from an East India ship, approached the narrator with a warning. The Englishman informed the narrator that the town of Cambodia is about fifteen leagues up the river. The Englishman warned the narrator of potential danger from five long-boats full of men. The narrator expressed confusion about the threat posed by the Company's ships and Dutch ships. The Englishman suggested that the narrator should leave immediately to avoid being attacked.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The author created a portable shelter that could spread and let down, covered with skins to protect from rain and sun. The author lived comfortably by resigning to the will of God and engaging in self-reflection. For five years, the author maintained a routine of planting barley and rice, curing raisins, and hunting. The author constructed a canoe by digging a canal to bring it into the creek, which was nearly half a mile away. The first canoe was too large to launch, leading the author to learn from the experience for future attempts. The author spent nearly two years building a smaller boat, which was not suitable for crossing to Terra Firma. With the completed boat, the author planned to explore the island by sailing around its coast.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The text mentions a widow and children of an Englishman who was killed. A young man and a maid are referenced, with the maid being married before departure. Two carpenters, a tailor, and a smith were brought along, with the smith serving as a gunsmith. A man referred to as Jack of all Trades was also brought, and he was married to the maid who arrived with the young man. A French ecclesiastic, described as a Roman Catholic priest, was taken from the ship's crew. The ecclesiastic is characterized as grave, sober, pious, and charitable despite his religious background. The narrator and the ecclesiastic engaged in a conversation about religion, agreeing to avoid disputes on differing beliefs.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator did not consider his circumstances as a punishment from God for his sins or rebellious behavior. During a dangerous expedition in Africa, the narrator did not think about God or seek divine guidance. After being rescued by a Portugal captain, the narrator felt no gratitude for his survival. Following a shipwreck on an island, the narrator expressed no remorse or reflection on his situation as a judgment. The narrator initially felt joy at surviving a shipwreck but did not reflect on the significance of his preservation. The narrator's thoughts rarely included the idea of his afflictions being a judgment from God. The narrator's sense of God and his judgments diminished even after experiencing natural disasters like an earthquake.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator's nephew expressed regret over the murder of a seaman named Thomas Jeffrys. The crew reportedly killed or destroyed about one hundred and fifty people, including men, women, and children. Thomas Jeffrys was left dead where he was found, having been hanged and severely injured. The boatswain defended the crew's actions by stating that they were provoked by the natives who had attacked them first. The voyage was bound for the Gulf of Persia and the coast of Coromandel, with plans to touch at Surat. Five crew members were killed or captured by Arabs while on shore in the Gulf of Persia. The narrator believed the crew's violent actions would lead to divine retribution.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The speaker expresses a belief that trust is essential to avoid deception. The speaker's companion expresses disappointment in the speaker's reasoning and indicates he would not have acted as he did had he known the speaker's intentions. The companion plans to return to Paris to avoid further reproach from the speaker. The speaker is conflicted about the companion's departure and does not want to let him go. The speaker discovers she is pregnant with the companion's child but has not informed him. The companion expresses reluctance to leave without the speaker and mentions a tempting invitation to the East Indies. The speaker insists that the companion should go anywhere but Paris, where she cannot accompany him.

The speaker agreed to a financial arrangement with her husband, preferring to manage their assets collectively. The speaker expressed a desire to give her estate to her husband's children as a gift in case of her mortality. The husband proposed to settle a thousand pounds upon a friend, the Quaker, for her life, amounting to sixty pounds a year. The speaker suggested giving the Quaker a purse with a hundred guineas as a present and a yearly amount of £40 secured as a compliment. The husband acknowledged the Quaker's kindness and presented her with gold as a token of gratitude. The Quaker expressed her goodwill without expectation of reward and mentioned previous valuable gifts she received from the speaker. The Quaker felt that the speaker and her husband left her in a position of greater debt than before due to their generosity.

The narrator and her husband, along with three gentlemen, were taken to the turret of a house. The turret provided a view of London from over thirty feet above the previous room. The narrator expressed skepticism about the location being London despite the gentleman's assurances. The gentleman used a pocket-glass to help the narrator observe landmarks in London. The narrator recognized St. Paul's Cathedral, the Monument, and other buildings during her observations. The narrator identified Aldgate Church and the Tower while looking through the glass. The narrator ultimately acknowledged that the view was indeed of London.

The narrator refers to herself as a widow. Dinner was prepared, and only the narrator and a man were present. The man encouraged the narrator to be cheerful and offered her comfort. The narrator had not eaten well in a long time and enjoyed the meal. The man expressed his desire to help the narrator recover from her difficult circumstances. Amy, the narrator's maid, was very happy and dressed up after dinner. The man gave the narrator a guinea for her immediate needs and also gave Amy half-a-crown.

The narrator had an established plantation and stock before considering a voyage. The narrator agreed to go on a voyage if his plantation was looked after in his absence. A formal will was made by the narrator, designating the captain of the ship as his universal heir. The ship was fitted out with a cargo primarily consisting of trade items for the Negroes. The ship set sail on September 1, 1650, heading towards the African coast. The ship encountered good weather until reaching Cape St. Augustino. A violent tornado or hurricane affected the ship during the voyage.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator was advised by the captain of the ship to send a letter and procuration to retrieve his money in London. The captain suggested that the narrator only order one hundred pounds sterling to minimize risk. The captain successfully sent a full account of the narrator's story to a merchant in London, who then delivered the money. The merchant invested the one hundred pounds in English goods and sent them to the captain in Lisbon. The cargo included tools and utensils necessary for the narrator's plantation. The narrator experienced significant financial success from selling the goods received from the captain. The narrator purchased a Negro slave and an additional European servant for his plantation.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The character is preparing to get a foreign bill accepted from Amsterdam. He decides not to carry his jewel-case because he may not return until night. He gives his gold watch and a diamond ring to another character for safekeeping. He expresses that he does not anticipate any danger but agrees to return by daylight. The other character feels uneasy about his departure and fears for his safety. He reassures the other character by stating that all his possessions will belong to them if anything happens. The other character experiences a moment of fear and emotional distress regarding his departure.

Mrs. Amy visited the narrator after a few days at home. Mrs. Amy claimed she had procured false evidence to imprison the narrator's pretended daughter. The narrator sent a friend to pay the debt and release the prisoner. Mrs. Amy expressed her intention to visit the narrator's mother as soon as possible. The narrator's letter was taken by the pretended daughter during a brief absence. The pretended daughter claimed to be the eldest daughter and provided details about her siblings. The pretended daughter recounted her arrest and imprisonment in Whitechapel jail.

Amy devised a plan to find lodging in a remote part of town to remain unknown. Amy went out for five hours to secure the lodging. Amy found a house in a court in the Minories that was run by a female family. The woman of the house had four children, two maids, and was looking for boarders. Amy agreed to pay £35 for half a year, with an option for £50 if a maid was included. The woman of the house was described as courteous, well-bred, and pleasant. The narrator decided to take up lodging with Amy and lived in a secluded retreat.

The narrator's daughter was seen alone in a hackney-coach outside the narrator's lodging. The narrator's husband had taken the coach to London that morning. The narrator felt confused and unsure of what to do upon seeing her daughter. The daughter suggested that the narrator visit a neighbor to avoid detection. The narrator fabricated a story to explain her visit to the neighbor. The daughter sought out the Quaker, who was aware of her but claimed not to know her business. The Quaker advised the daughter to leave and not to follow her.

One of the men on the ship reported that they had sprung a leak and that there was four feet of water in the hold. The crew was called to the pump to address the water in the hold. The ship's master ordered a gun to be fired as a signal of distress when he saw light colliers nearby. The narrator fainted due to surprise when the gun was fired and was initially ignored by the crew. The water in the hold continued to increase, indicating that the ship would founder. A light ship sent a boat to assist the crew, which was difficult to approach due to the conditions. The crew managed to get into the boat and began rowing towards the shore, witnessing their ship sink shortly after.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator called Amy and encouraged her regarding her relationship with a gentleman. Amy had a daughter, which was nursed, and later returned to live with the narrator. The gentleman expressed no desire to resume a previous relationship with Amy. The narrator experienced moments of dark reflection and emotional turmoil despite outward appearances of happiness. After living with the gentleman for over two years, the narrator became pregnant and gave birth to a daughter who died at six weeks old.
