The narrator later gave birth to a son, which pleased the gentleman. The gentleman planned to travel to France for two months and sought the narrator's consent before making his will.

The old man expressed sorrow about being left alone after a journey of twenty-five days. He informed that a caravan of Muscovy and Polish merchants was preparing to leave for Muscovy in four or five weeks. The old man learned about the caravan from an acquaintance who had recently come from Astracan. The narrator felt a secret joy upon hearing the news about the caravan. The narrator and his partner decided to travel to England with the caravan if the pilot agreed to accompany them. They agreed to compensate the pilot with a quantity of coined gold and cover his travel expenses. The narrator communicated their decision to the pilot, indicating he would not return alone.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator observes a group of men from a distance while remaining hidden. The narrator prepares for a potential confrontation by arming himself and his companion, Friday. The narrator decides to approach three distressed men who are resting under a tree. The narrator calls out to the men in Spanish and then in English to identify himself. One of the men expresses confusion and fear upon seeing the narrator's appearance. The narrator reassures the men that he is a human and offers assistance. One of the men indicates that their situation is dire and requires immediate help.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator reflects on the impact of certain events on their way of living. The narrator expresses concern for their children and their upbringing. The narrator's only son was rescued from being an apprentice to a mechanic. The son was delayed nearly three years in his development due to his previous circumstances. The son was placed with a flourishing Italian merchant and sent to Messina, Sicily. The narrator paid £4000 to support their son, which was more than the merchant proposed. The narrator struggles with concealing their identity from their son while providing for him.

The narrator was rescued by a ship after signaling for help. The narrator identified himself as an Englishman who escaped from slavery at Sallee. The captain of the ship refused any payment for the rescue and promised to return the narrator's belongings in the Brasils. The captain took possession of the narrator's belongings and provided an inventory of them. The captain offered to buy the narrator's boat for eighty pieces of eight to be paid in the Brasils. The captain also offered to buy the narrator's boy, Xury, for sixty pieces of eight but agreed to set him free in ten years if he converted to Christianity. The ship arrived in the Bay de Todos los Santos in about twenty-two days.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The speaker was not willing to endure hardships for a pension. The speaker's counterpart expressed intentions to make their life easy and valued them above £500 a year. The speaker initially felt that the £500 offer was excessive but eventually agreed to it. The counterpart provided a goldsmith's bill for £300 as a pledge to ensure the speaker would not be a loser by not making a formal bargain. The speaker began to treat the counterpart with more kindness after the private engagement. The speaker considered becoming less public to avoid unwanted visits from others. The speaker found the visits from certain individuals to be tedious and impertinent.

The men were already in the water when the pinnace was manned to rescue them. The pinnace successfully picked up three men, one of whom was nearly drowning. After rescuing the men, the crew sailed farther out to sea as other boats approached. The Dutchman revealed that the ship's seller was a thief who had run away with it. The captain of the ship was murdered by natives on the coast of Malacca. The Dutchman escaped to a Dutch ship after wandering in the woods. The ship was sold to pirates in Bengal, who had already captured other ships.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator describes a pressure or hint that influences their decisions. The narrator advises others not to ignore secret intimations of Providence. The narrator expresses concern for their safety over their food supply. The narrator avoids making noise or fire to prevent detection. The narrator discovers a natural cave while cutting down branches for charcoal. The cave is located at the bottom of a great rock and is described as a safe retreat. The narrator uses charcoal to cook food without creating smoke.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The clergyman gave a benediction in Latin after the marriage ceremony. Will Atkins either did not recognize the language of the benediction or did not pay attention to it. The clergyman encouraged Will Atkins to reform his life and not dishonor the grace of God. The clergyman expressed a desire to convert thirty-seven savages but was convinced that it was impractical. A young man from a famished ship's company requested to marry a Christian woman on the island. The young man was persuaded not to rush into marriage due to his age and circumstances. The young man expressed a desire to settle on the island and requested some property and necessities.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The ship was in a wrecked condition. The crew attempted to save the ship and their lives using boats. The Cochinchinese attacked the crew while they were in a vulnerable position. An English seaman captured a Cochinchinese man and killed him. A Dutchman defended the long-boat by knocking down five attackers with a musket. The carpenter used boiling pitch and other materials to scald the enemy, causing them to jump into the sea. The enemy's cries were described as howling, which varied by nationality.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The trustees lived in the Brasils and were believed to be wealthy. The trustees accepted an offer for a property and remitted 33,000 pieces of eight to a correspondent in Lisbon. The author signed the instrument of sale and received bills of exchange for 32,800 pieces of eight. The author reserved a payment of 100 moidores a year during the life of an old man and 50 moidores afterwards to his son. The author was dissuaded from traveling for almost seven years by a widow and took care of his two nephews during this time. The author married and had three children, but his wife died, prompting him to consider further adventures. In 1694, the author went on a voyage to the East Indies, where he visited his former colony and learned about the Spaniards and their interactions with others.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator reflects on their condition, feeling forsaken by God and man. The narrator concludes that it is possible to be happier in their solitary condition than in any other state. The narrator expresses gratitude to God for opening their eyes to their former life and for their wickedness and repentance. The narrator has a Bible that was packed by a friend in England and saved from a shipwreck. The narrator divides their time among duties to God, hunting for food, and preparing meals. The narrator notes that the heat limits their working hours to about four in the evening. The narrator describes the laborious process of making a board for a shelf, which took them forty-two days.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The Spaniards and other Christian nations of Europe view the extermination of certain indigenous people with abhorrence and detestation. The actions of the Spaniards are described as butchery and cruelty, unjustifiable to God or man. The name of a Spaniard is considered frightful and terrible to people of humanity and Christian compassion. The narrator reflects on the morality of attacking indigenous people and concludes it is not their business to engage unless first attacked. The narrator believes that killing indigenous people could lead to their own destruction due to potential retaliation. The narrator resolves to conceal themselves from the indigenous people and not to leave any signs of human presence. The narrator expresses gratitude for being prevented from committing acts they now view as sinful.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The husband spent all his money foolishly over a period of three years. He associated with huntsmen and horse-coursers rather than valuable company. The narrator's husband expressed a desire to seek his fortune due to their miserable condition. The husband left home one morning to go hunting and did not return. The narrator did not see or hear from her husband or his two servants after he left. The narrator was initially not surprised by her husband's absence but became frightened over time. The narrator was left with five children and about seventy pounds in money for their subsistence.

The author spent twenty days cutting down a tree. It took the author fourteen additional days to remove the branches and limbs of the tree. The author spent a month shaping the tree into a boat-like form. The author took nearly three more months to hollow out the tree and create a boat. The finished boat was large enough to carry twenty-six men. The author faced difficulties in getting the boat into the water due to its location one hundred yards away and uphill. The author reflected on the challenges faced and the lessons learned during the process.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator describes her husband as a handsome man and a good sportsman. The narrator expresses regret for marrying her husband, whom she considers a weak and empty-headed individual. The narrator advises young women to avoid marrying a fool, stating that it leads to misery. The narrator highlights the difficulties of being married to a conceited and obstinate man. The narrator mentions that her husband would become angry if she did not engage in conversation with him. The narrator's father died four years after her marriage, and he disapproved of her match.

Three gentlemen, who were servants, arrived on Saturday with wines and sweetmeats. The narrator purchased twelve dozen fine damask napkins and tablecloths for the event. The gentlemen brought their own china dishes and plates, preventing the use of the narrator's purchased plate. On Tuesday, a large number of gentlemen and ladies attended the event, overwhelming the narrator's apartments. The street was filled with coaches and fine glass chairs, making it impossible to accommodate all guests. A strong party of guards was present to manage the crowd and maintain order. A noble person arranged for two ladies dressed in traditional attire to be conveyed into the narrator's apartment.

The narrator did not know if a woman would recognize her if told who she was. The narrator planned to reveal herself to the woman during a visit to Amy but was prevented by Amy. The narrator considered her life and resolved to change it to avoid being scandalous to her family. The narrator had another daughter who could not be located for several years. The narrator felt she was in a position to reform her life after moving from her old station. The narrator was frequently visited by old acquaintances, which she found unwelcome. The narrator expressed uneasiness about not being able to converse with her three grown children.

The narrator and a Quaker were sitting in her chamber at around four o'clock. A gentleman arrived at the door, accompanied by a footman, and requested to speak with the narrator. The gentleman spoke broken English and used a name for the narrator that was not the name he had known her by. The Quaker brought the gentleman into a parlour and went to check if the narrator was present. The narrator felt frightened and conflicted about meeting the gentleman. The narrator had previously sent someone to France to inquire about the gentleman. The Quaker attempted to offer the narrator a cordial to help with her distress.

The girl was directed to improve her appearance, take lodgings, and learn skills to present herself as a gentlewoman. She was advised not to marry until she secured a fortune that would allow her to maintain her future status. The girl visited Mrs. Amy to share her good fortune, and they began an intimate acquaintance. The girl had previously been a servant in the narrator's family, which created a dilemma for the narrator regarding her identity. After several visits, the girl expressed concern about never having seen her mistress, except for one occasion when the mistress was disguised. Mrs. Amy was aware of the girl's past and reported her comments to the narrator, who felt relieved that she was not recognized. The narrator experienced mixed emotions about the situation, feeling both restrained and hopeful about revealing her identity to the girl.

The narrator considers a friend to be disinterested and honest in dealings. The friend has a proposal that could balance accounts between him and the narrator. The narrator expresses willingness to help the friend, except for one unspecified matter. The narrator suspects the friend may have faced a disaster in business. The friend has discussed his treatment by a Jew and the expenses incurred. The narrator offers to send five hundred crowns as a present to acknowledge the friend's justice. The friend refuses to accept any money from the narrator.

The governor decided to take five men as assistants and keep two others as prisoners. Three prisoners were sent to the castle as hostages for the fidelity of the five assistants. If the five assistants proved unfaithful, they would be hanged in chains alive on the shore. The total number of men involved in the expedition was twelve, excluding the five hostages kept in the cave. The captain and his mate prepared two boats for the expedition. The captain and his mate successfully took control of the ship by overpowering the second mate and carpenter. During the takeover, the mate was wounded by a musket-ball fired by the new rebel captain.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: A justice of the peace ruled that the Chinese man accompanying the narrator was the servant of the stranger who requested him to buy a camel. The narrator paid for the camel after the justice's ruling. The city of Naum is a fortified frontier of the Chinese empire. Messengers were sent to halt all travelers and caravans due to the appearance of ten thousand Tartars about thirty miles beyond Naum. Two hundred soldiers were sent from a garrison to assist the caravan, along with three hundred soldiers from the city of Naum. The caravan was organized with soldiers from Naum in the front, soldiers from the garrison in the rear, and the caravan in the center. The narrator and his companions prepared for battle when the Tartars appeared, but the Chinese soldiers began to show signs of fear.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator reflects on her life of vice over a period of six-and-twenty years without remorse or repentance. The narrator has been in England for eight years and has accumulated a yearly income of two thousand eight hundred pounds. The narrator received financial support from her lord, which often exceeded seven to eight hundred pounds a year. The narrator left five children when she departed from England fifteen years prior, with the eldest being under six years old at that time. The narrator sent a person named Amy to inquire about her children, but both the children's caretakers had died. Amy's second inquiry about the family that took care of the children yielded no satisfactory information.

The narrator's maid, Amy, brought a small breast of mutton and two bunches of turnips for dinner. The narrator experienced overwhelming emotions upon seeing two friends and fell into a fit of crying. Amy informed the friends about the narrator's circumstances, which deeply affected them. The friends decided that the children should be taken to a relative's house by Amy, while the narrator would leave for a few days. The children were born in a parish where the landlord allowed the narrator to live rent-free for a year due to compassion. The narrator initially felt distressed about parting with her children but eventually agreed to the plan to ensure their survival. Amy took the children to one of their aunts and instructed the eldest to enter the house first.

The narrator experienced severe cold after arriving from Old Castile, where the weather was hot. Friday, a character in the text, was frightened by the sight of snow-covered mountains and cold weather. After arriving in Pampeluna, heavy snowfall made the roads impassable. The narrator and companions stayed in Pampeluna for twenty days due to the severe winter conditions. Four French gentlemen found a guide who led them over the mountains with less snow obstruction. The guide agreed to lead the narrator and others through the mountains if they were armed for protection against wild beasts. The group set out from Pampeluna on November 15, following the guide through a winding route to avoid heavy snow.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The chaplain informed the narrator about the situation regarding a codicil. Physicians advised my lord to settle his worldly affairs as he was near death. The narrator believed the physicians might exaggerate the severity of my lord's condition. My lord's son was kept from the university and stayed close to his father during his final days. My lord ordered the sealing of all doors in his dwelling house at The Hague before his death. My lord gave the physicians a bill of £100 for their care before dismissing them. My lord passed away calmly at the age of fifty-seven, with the chaplain present.

The narrator and Xury anchored in the mouth of an unknown river seeking fresh water. They planned to swim ashore at night but were deterred by frightening noises from wild creatures. Xury expressed fear and suggested they wait until daylight to go ashore. The narrator and Xury observed large creatures approaching the shore and heard their loud howls. The narrator fired a gun at a creature swimming towards their boat, causing it to retreat. They realized the danger of going ashore at night due to both wild animals and potential encounters with savages. Xury offered to go ashore to find water, expressing concern for his safety, leading the narrator to decide they would both go.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The gentleman expressed a desire to help the narrator and her maid, Amy. He acknowledged Amy's loyalty and honesty towards the narrator. The gentleman offered drinks to both the narrator and Amy. After the gentleman left, Amy expressed confusion about his intentions. The narrator reassured Amy that the gentleman meant to do them good. Amy suggested that the gentleman might have ulterior motives due to their poverty. The narrator and Amy discussed the possibility of the gentleman making a proposal.

The narrator expresses a strong aversion to boarding a particular vessel again. The narrator describes constant fear as a significant source of misery for mankind. The narrator believes that fear suppresses the mind and diminishes natural vigor. The narrator discusses the potential to convince others of their innocence regarding piracy based on various circumstances. The narrator reflects on the perception of danger from English and Dutch captains towards them. The narrator and their partner experienced sleepless nights filled with nightmares related to their fears. The narrator recounts an incident where they injured their hand while dreaming of a confrontation with Dutch seamen.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The speaker expresses feelings of unhappiness and describes humans as unguided creatures. The speaker acknowledges the kindness and sincerity of a friend's offer. The speaker questions whether the friend believes in their sincerity regarding their contempt for the world. The speaker reflects on the potential dangers of returning to a former life of greatness. The speaker prefers to remain in confinement rather than risk losing their current happiness and liberty. The speaker experiences a physical reaction to their emotional struggle, resulting in a violent sweat. The friend later enters the room and indicates they have recovered from the emotional turmoil.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The author created wicker-baskets to hold two dry and hard pots to prevent them from breaking. The author filled the space between the pots and the baskets with rice and barley-straw. The author successfully made smaller earthenware items such as pots, dishes, pitchers, and pipkins. The author discovered a broken piece of earthenware in the fire that had become hard and red. The author experimented with fire to create whole pots, stacking them and surrounding them with firewood and embers. After several hours of heating, the author produced three pipkins and two pots that were well-burnt and one was glazed. The author expressed a desire to create a stone mortar for processing corn.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator and others followed a man who climbed an oak tree. The man laid his gun down on the ground about five or six yards from the bottom of the tree. A bear approached the tree, smelled the gun, but did not take it. The bear climbed the tree while the man, referred to as Friday, jumped and shook a bough to make the bear unsteady. Friday attempted to coax the bear to come closer by speaking to it. Friday eventually slid down the bough to retrieve his gun and prepared to shoot the bear. Friday shot the bear just before it could set its hind feet on the ground.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator experiences intense fear and anxiety upon arriving at his castle. He cannot remember how he entered the castle, whether by a ladder or a hole in the rock. The narrator's fear leads to sleeplessness and dismal imaginations about potential dangers. He considers the possibility that a devil or some dangerous creature may have visited his island. The narrator reflects on the improbability of a devil leaving a footprint in the sand. He concludes that the danger may come from savages from the mainland who could have reached the island. The narrator fears that if the savages find his boat, they may return in greater numbers and destroy his provisions.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator attempts to assist Amy, who is in a state of unconsciousness on the ship. Amy eventually regains consciousness but does not initially remember what happened to her. Amy expresses fear of being damned due to her past actions and a belief that she will be lost forever if she drowns. The narrator reflects on their own guilt and connection to Amy's past actions. The narrator acknowledges their role in leading Amy into a life of vice. Amy vocalizes her fears and regrets, while the narrator internally mourns their shared fate. The narrator tries to calm Amy and prevent others on the ship from understanding her distress.

The fears of death diminished after the danger passed. Amy expressed gratitude for her deliverance from the sea upon reaching shore. Amy was more penitent and aware of her deliverance than the narrator. The narrator experienced a silent grief and horror during the storm. The narrator felt a terror for their past wicked life but lacked true repentance. Both the narrator and Amy's feelings of repentance faded over time. The narrator decided to go to Holland for business reasons despite Amy's objections.

The narrator observed that a group of people did not come from the shore but from the southernmost end of the island. The narrator called Friday to be cautious as they were uncertain if the newcomers were friends or enemies. The narrator used a perspective glass to observe a ship lying at anchor approximately two and a half leagues away from their location. The ship appeared to be an English ship, and the boat was identified as an English long-boat. The narrator experienced confusion and joy upon seeing the ship, but also had doubts about the intentions of the ship's crew. The boat approached the shore but did not land at the narrator's location, which was about half a mile away. Upon landing, the group consisted of eleven men, three of whom were unarmed and appeared to be prisoners.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator traveled through a forest at the foot of the mountains during a severe winter season. The narrator and their group were warned about the dangers of wolves attracted to their horses. The group managed to fend off the wolves using fire and a stratagem involving powder. The narrator traveled from Tholouse to Paris and then to Calais, landing safely at Dover on January 14. The narrator's principal guide was an ancient widow who helped manage their affairs in gratitude for financial support. The narrator considered leaving their effects with the widow to travel to Lisbon and the Brasils. The narrator faced a dilemma regarding the Roman Catholic religion before deciding to stay at home.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The character in question is described as having a scoundrel character and being untrustworthy. He has used a false claim about a lieutenant's commission to borrow money from others. He falsely reported having a wife and five children in England whom he claimed to support with his pay. He has incurred debts and faced threats of being expelled from the _gens d'armes_. Amy decided it was unsafe to help him further due to his character and the potential risks involved. During a conversation with Amy, he repeatedly lowered the amount of money he requested until he borrowed a small sum. Amy and the narrator planned to avoid encountering him again to prevent any dangerous situations.

The author built a chimney in an apartment that heated six rooms equally without visible fire or smoke. The apartment was located in a town near the Frozen Ocean and Nova Zembla. The city was populated by noblemen, princes, gentlemen, and state criminals from Muscovy. Notable individuals mentioned include Prince Galilfken, General Robostisky, and other persons of note. The author made acquaintances with several gentlemen during winter nights spent in the city. A conversation with a prince led the author to discuss his own governance and power compared to the czar of Muscovy. The prince expressed that he found more happiness in his banished state than in the highest authority he held.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator enclosed all provisions and goods to protect them from the wet. The narrator created a cave behind the tent, which served as a cellar. A storm caused the narrator to worry about the potential destruction of their powder. The narrator divided their powder into about one hundred parcels for safety. The narrator discovered goats on the island, which were difficult to hunt. The narrator observed the goats' behavior to improve their chances of hunting them.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The speaker asserts ownership of a will. The speaker expresses a willingness to endure hardship rather than compromise their character. The speaker's partner threatens to change the will if certain matters are disclosed. The couple's son returns home with bank-notes totaling £12,000. The partner claims to have provided £5,000 each to his children from a previous marriage. The partner states that the family's financial situation has worsened since moving to Holland. The partner insists that he has not intentionally wasted any of the speaker's resources.

The night was cloudy, but the moon provided enough light to see the idol. The people appeared to be resting, except for three priests in a hut who were talking. The group considered setting fire to the idol but found it too bulky to carry away. One member suggested making the priests prisoners instead of killing them. The group used twine to tie up the priests after seizing them. They encountered additional priests and bound them in the same manner. The group eventually found four more individuals in the hut and bound them as well.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator experiences fear upon entering a cave and seeing a reflection that resembles a creature. The narrator attempts to overcome fear by reasoning that nothing in the cave is more frightening than himself. Inside the cave, the narrator hears a loud sigh and broken noises, which causes a strong surprise and fear. The narrator discovers an old he-goat lying on the ground, gasping for life due to old age. The cave is described as small, approximately twelve feet in diameter, and shaped by natural processes. The narrator finds a low passage in the cave that requires crawling on hands and knees to enter. Upon returning to the cave with candles, the narrator discovers a larger vaulted area with reflective walls that may contain precious stones.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator built a bower on one side of the island and decided to travel to the sea shore on the opposite side. The narrator took a gun, hatchet, dog, powder, shot, two biscuit-cakes, and a bunch of raisins for the journey. Upon reaching the sea, the narrator observed land in the distance, which he estimated to be fifteen or twenty leagues away. The narrator speculated that the distant land was part of America and possibly near Spanish dominions inhabited by savages. The narrator found the side of the island he was on to be more pleasant than his own, with open fields, flowers, and fine woods. The narrator caught a young parrot during his journey and eventually taught it to call him by name. The narrator had an adequate supply of food, including goats, pigeons, and turtle, and did not need to venture for food during his travels.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The chaplain advised the speaker to make friends with her lord and to ensure he makes another will. The speaker expressed concern about her financial security if her lord were to die. The speaker confronted her lord about his will and the lack of communication regarding the settlement of his estate. The lord stated that he believed all possessions of a wife become his after marriage unless a prior settlement is made. The lord mentioned he had married the speaker's children and provided them with noble fortunes. The lord revealed that he had left all his possessions to their son, with £500 allocated for the speaker. The speaker rejected the £500 and demanded to be left in full possession of half of her lord's fortune.

The narrator found chequered shirts in the chests of other seamen and preserved them. The narrator had almost three dozen shirts among the men's clothes of the ship. The narrator could not bear the heat of the sun when completely naked. The narrator attempted to make jackets from the thick watch-coats left behind by the seamen. The narrator saved the skins of four-footed creatures and made a cap and a suit of clothes from them. The narrator spent time making an umbrella to protect against rain and heat.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: Two years after the marriage, the man made his will, leaving the woman a thousand pounds and all her household items. The man paid Amy all the wages owed to her and gave her five guineas for her loyalty and kindness. The woman felt a conviction that she was a whore, not a wife, and could not refer to the man as her husband. The couple lived an agreeable life together without any interruptions to their mutual kindness until the man's death. Amy expressed concern about the woman not being pregnant after a year and a half of marriage. The woman offered to arrange for Amy to sleep with the man, but Amy declined the offer. The woman attempted to undress Amy and lead her to the bed with the man, but Amy resisted.

The individuals mentioned were not adequately equipped for battle, lacking powder and shot. In battle, they were at a disadvantage compared to the savages, as they had no bows or arrows. They used halberts and sharpened sticks to defend themselves and sometimes drove back enemy forces. They created large wooden targets covered with animal skins to protect themselves from arrows. Five of them were knocked down by the savages, and one was taken prisoner, causing great grief among the group. They were relieved to see their friend return alive after initially believing he was dead. They expressed immense joy at receiving supplies, including bread, which they had not seen in a long time.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The speaker is bound to the East Indies on a ship freighted by merchants. The speaker has already been in the current location for thirteen days. The speaker agreed to a maximum stay of twelve days and faces a demurrage fee of 32 sterling per day after that. The ecclesiastic expresses a desire to save seven-and-thirty souls and offers to undertake the mission himself. The ecclesiastic believes that converting the seven-and-thirty men is worth the risk of his life. The speaker is surprised by the ecclesiastic's sincerity and zeal for the mission. The ecclesiastic is willing to give thanks if he can be an instrument in saving the souls of the men.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The travelers did not approach the Tartars and vice versa. The region after the desert was inhabited with towns and castles established by the czar of Muscovy. The czar of Muscovy has issued strict orders to protect caravans from Tartars. The governor of Adinskoy offered a guard of fifty men for safety to the next station. The Tonguses were described as pagan and barbaric, living in houses made of animal skins. The river Janezay is said to separate Europe from Asia and is part of the ancient Siberia. The Muscovite governors acknowledged that pagan subjects were not closer to Christianity under Muscovite rule.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator resolved to travel by land along the shore. The narrator describes their unusual attire, including a goat's skin cap and jacket. The narrator wore open-kneed breeches made from the skin of an old he-goat. The narrator carried a broad goat's skin belt with a saw and hatchet attached. The narrator had two pouches made of goat's skin for carrying powder and shot. The narrator traveled for five or six days along the sea shore. The narrator aimed to reach a point of rock that they had previously anchored their boat near.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator reflects on their past decisions and dissatisfaction with their current situation. The narrator believes that their original sin was opposing their father's advice. The narrator was once a planter in the Brasils and could have been successful if they had remained there. The narrator left a stable plantation to become a supercargo in Guinea to fetch Negroes. The narrator regrets their decision to leave the Brasils, believing patience would have led to greater wealth. The narrator describes their state of mind during a sleepless night in March, reflecting on their life. The narrator compares their initial happiness on the island to their later feelings of anxiety and care.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator receives a cordial and a spicy preserve from a woman. The preserve masks the smell of the cordial and leaves no trace on the breath. The narrator hesitates before going down to meet a man in a dining room. The woman leaves the narrator to consider the situation and returns to usher the man in. The narrator feels confused about how to greet the man and initially adopts a stiff demeanor. The man greets the narrator with formality, believing the woman is still present. The man expresses surprise at not having found the narrator in four years despite his efforts.

The narrator observes a shore spread with human bones, including skulls, hands, and feet. The narrator notes a place where a fire was made and a circle dug in the earth, suggesting it was used for inhumane feasting on human bodies. The narrator experiences nausea and vomits after witnessing the horrific scene. The narrator expresses gratitude for being in a part of the world away from such brutal creatures. The narrator reflects on their eighteen years on the island without encountering other humans. The narrator feels an aversion to the cannibals and remains pensive and sad for almost two years. The narrator avoids searching for their boat and considers making a new one due to fear of encountering the cannibals at sea.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: An honest man was attacked with a pole but avoided the blow and ran into a hut. The comrade of the honest man followed him into the hut and they both emerged with muskets. The honest man struck down the attacker with the stock of his musket before others could assist. The attackers had firearms but were deterred by the resolute stance of one of the honest men. The attackers agreed to take their wounded comrade and leave after a parley. The honest men planned to confront the three attackers and the Spaniards for a fair battle. A Spaniard reproached the three Englishmen for their treatment of the honest men and their ruined plantation.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The captain took another boat with thirteen men to shore. The captain was surprised to see only two men in the boat with the narrator and the supercargo. The captain expressed impatience to know what was happening due to the noise and increasing flames. The captain decided to help his men despite the risks to the ship and voyage. The captain ordered two men to row back for twelve more men, leaving sixteen men on the ship. The group moved towards the source of the fire without following a path. They encountered the ruins of a house and several dead bodies, which caused them horror.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The mandarin's steward collected provisions from the travelers. The travelers were part of a retinue that included about thirty other people. The country provided provisions at no cost, while the mandarin took money from the travelers for them. The journey to Pekin lasted twenty-five days through a populous but poorly cultivated country. The local population exhibited pride despite their poverty and poor living conditions. The travelers found the roads well paved and convenient, but were struck by the locals' arrogance amidst their simplicity. A country gentleman was described as riding in a state that combined elements of pomp and poverty.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator expressed remorse for past sins and prayed for mercy. The narrator resolved to lead a virtuous life if spared from death. The storm lasted all night, causing fear and uncertainty about their fate. The ship eventually made landfall on the coast of Suffolk, England. The ship was severely damaged and at risk of sinking if not laid on shore. Amy initially doubted the sight of land and feared for their safety. The ship reached the open harbor of Harwich, providing relief to the narrator and Amy.

The ship was on a trading voyage and had a supercargo on board to direct its motions after arriving at the Cape of Good Hope. The ship made a brief stop at the Cape of Good Hope to take on fresh water before continuing to the coast of Coromandel. The narrator expressed apprehensions about encountering a French man of war and two large merchant ships while at sea. The ship first touched at the island of Madagascar, where the local people were described as fierce and treacherous but treated the crew civilly. The crew traded with the people of Madagascar and received eleven bullocks in exchange for small items like knives and scissors. The narrator was curious and frequently went on shore during their stay at Madagascar, where they established a truce with the local people using boughs.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The ship was in a dreadful condition and unable to get off the sand. One boat was lost after dashing against the ship's rudder and either sunk or driven off to sea. The crew consisted of eleven members who committed themselves to the sea after launching another boat. The sea was described as being very high and dangerous, making survival seem unlikely. The crew rowed towards the shore, uncertain of the land's nature. A large wave overturned the boat, separating the crew and causing them to be swallowed by the water. The narrator managed to reach the shore after being carried by the wave but struggled to avoid being taken by the sea again.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The tent constructed was one hundred and twenty paces round on the outside and seven feet high. The inner tent was twenty-two paces round and built stronger with eight corners supported by strong posts. The structure utilized wooden pins and iron spikes made from old iron left behind. A forge was created with wooden bellows, and charcoal was made for metalworking. The inner tent was divided into six apartments, each with a door leading to the entry and the outer walk. The outer circle contained ten rooms, including six accessed through the inner tent and four warehouses. Will Atkins and his companions, along with a widow and her three children, lived in the tent.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator expresses contempt for a man, suggesting he serves as a warning against marrying foolish individuals. The narrator indicates that a man of sense can recover from failure, while a fool remains permanently undone. The narrator has returned to Paris at the request of a prince. The prince visits the narrator to congratulate her on her return and acknowledges that she has given him a son. The prince gives the narrator a purse containing three hundred pistoles as a gift. The narrator and the prince engage in playful banter regarding the nature of gifts and favors. The prince is not a subject of France but resides in Paris and is involved with the court.

The Prince de ---- had a relationship with the jeweller's widow. The narrator expressed willingness to follow the Prince's directions to avoid public scrutiny. The Prince suggested that the narrator take a country house away from the city for privacy. The narrator decided against the country house to remain closer to the Prince. The narrator's companion, Amy, informed neighbors that the narrator had gone to England. The Prince frequently visited the narrator, sometimes staying for two or three nights. The narrator felt a sense of fulfillment in her relationship with the Prince.

The narrator filled a glass of wine and brought it to a prince on a fine salver. The prince expressed a desire for more company and intended to keep the salver for his use. The narrator mentioned having a homely lodging for the prince. The prince sent his servant to fetch personal items for an overnight stay. The prince appointed the narrator as his chamberlain and dresser. The narrator changed into a new dress, which surprised the prince. The encounter between the narrator and the prince resulted in a night spent together.

The men requested to take a canoe, arms, and ammunition from the Spaniards to seek their fortune on the main land. The Spaniards warned the men of the dangers they would face, including starvation and murder. The men insisted on leaving, stating they would be starved if they stayed and had no families to mourn them if they were killed. The Spaniards provided the men with two muskets, a pistol, a cutlass, and hatchets for their defense. The men received provisions including bread, goat's flesh, dried grapes, fresh water, and a live kid before departing in a canoe. After twenty-two days, one of the remaining Englishmen spotted three men approaching, two of whom were armed. The Spaniards initially thought the newcomers were savages but later recognized them as the returning Englishmen.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator attempted to escape from an island where there were seventeen bearded men. The narrator and Friday worked together to find a suitable tree to fell for making a canoe. Friday selected a tree that resembled tustick or Nicaragua wood for the canoe construction. The canoe was completed after about a month's labor and was capable of carrying twenty men. The narrator planned to add a mast, sail, anchor, and cable to the canoe. The narrator found two usable pieces of old sails and made a three-cornered sail for the canoe. The rigging and fitting of the mast and sails took nearly two months to complete.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator experienced violent rain that forced them into a cave for safety. The narrator cut a hole in their fortification to allow water to drain out. The narrator considered building a hut in an open place for safety from earthquakes. The narrator spent the 19th and 20th of April planning to move their tent to a safer location. The narrator resolved to build a wall with piles and cables before moving their tent. The narrator had three large axes and several hatchets, but they became dull from use. The narrator created a foot-operated wheel to grind their tools while keeping their hands free.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator heard wolves howl in the forest on the frontiers of Languedoc. The narrator experienced a victory without bloodshed, except for one man killed by a fellow. The narrator expressed concern about killing, even in self-defense, and believed it was a sad life to kill fellow creatures for survival. The narrator and their partner managed to repair the ship and prepare for departure. The enemy was deterred from attacking again after their initial encounter with the ship. The narrator and their crew resolved to leave their current location due to the fear of being surrounded by enemies. The crew set sail towards the isle of Formosa to obtain water and fresh provisions.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator expresses a strong aversion to idolatry. A conversation occurs about the treatment of a Russian who offended idol worshippers. The Russian was captured, tortured, and sacrificed to the idol. The narrator recounts a story about violence against a village in Madagascar in retaliation for the murder of a man. The narrator and his companion discuss punishing the idol responsible for the violence. The narrator is joined by Captain Richardson and another comrade to carry out their plan. They prepare for their expedition by disguising themselves and mixing combustible materials.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator discovered a region with abundant fruits, including melons and grapes. The grapes were found to be ripe and rich, but the narrator was cautious about eating them due to past experiences in Barbary. The narrator decided to dry the grapes in the sun to preserve them as raisins. The narrator spent the night in a tree and traveled four miles the next morning, keeping due north. The narrator found a fresh water spring and described the surrounding area as green and flourishing. The narrator gathered grapes, limes, and lemons to prepare for the approaching wet season. Upon returning home, the narrator discovered that the grapes had spoiled due to being crushed.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The relationship lasted eight years during which the man did not engage with other women. The woman acknowledges that she was a costly mistress but attributes his devotion to his affection for her. The man had previously maintained two or three mistresses but ceased to do so during the relationship. An older woman, who guided their travels, confirmed the man's previous gallantry and his sudden devotion to the woman. The man had a significant fortune and held various employments both in and out of France. He was married to a princess known for her beauty, wit, and virtue, and they lived in harmony despite his infidelities. The princess was aware of her husband's affairs but remained a generous and kind wife, causing him to feel guilty at times.

The Dutch East India Company is mentioned in relation to a marriage taking place on the coast of Malabar. The wedding ceremony was performed on a Wednesday evening in the presence of my lord, a sister of the bridegroom, and Thomas, the bride's brother. The fortune paid for the marriage was £2000. My lord denied my request to be present at the wedding ceremony. My lord stated that reconciliation between us would not occur until one of us is near death. I expressed a desire to see my daughter before she sailed to the Indies. I attempted to present a gold repeating watch to my daughter before her departure.

The author carried a sufficient quantity of linen and English clothing materials for the Spaniards, estimated to last seven years. The total weight of clothing materials, including gloves, hats, shoes, stockings, beds, bedding, and kitchen utensils, exceeded two hundred pounds. The author also transported nearly a hundred pounds of iron-work, nails, tools, and other necessary items. The author carried a hundred spare arms, muskets, fuzees, pistols, shot, three or four tons of lead, and two pieces of brass cannon. An additional hundred barrels of powder, swords, cutlasses, and parts of pikes and halberts were included in the cargo. The voyage began on February 5th from Ireland and faced delays due to contrary winds, resulting in a stop in Galway for thirty-two days. During the stop in Galway, the author acquired several hogs and two cows with calves, which were intended for the island.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator proposed to his lordship to take new lodgings for privacy. The narrator believed he could live handsomely without spending much money. His lordship agreed to the proposal and found a suitable lodging for the narrator. The lodging allowed his lordship convenient access through a door that opened into the park. One night, the narrator was in bed with Amy when his lordship unexpectedly arrived. His lordship expressed curiosity about whether Amy was a man or a woman. After confirming Amy's identity, his lordship went to bed in another chamber.

The group of Englishmen observed two savages approaching and decided to let them pass unless they were spotted. Three additional savages followed the first two, moving directly towards the tree where the Englishmen were hiding. The Englishmen recognized one of the three savages as a runaway who had previously escaped from them. The first shot fired by the Englishmen killed one savage outright and wounded another, while a third was slightly injured. The remaining five savages, frightened by the noise, initially stood still before approaching the wounded man. The five savages were unaware of the danger they were in and did not understand the cause of their companions' injuries. The Englishmen felt regret for having to kill the savages, who had no understanding of the threat posed to them.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator was about two months away from giving birth when a prince was present in the house. The prince entered the room to offer encouragement during the birth and later returned to visit the narrator and the child. The narrator gave birth to a boy, and the prince rewarded the nurse, Amy, with ten pistoles for the news. The narrator reflects on the implications of the child being a reminder of the prince's early crime and the mother's wickedness. The text discusses the burdens faced by mothers of illegitimate children and the financial support provided by wealthy men for their offspring. The prince arranged for a settled allowance for the children through an assignment on the Bank of Lyons after their relationship ended. The children were raised privately and did not know their mother beyond the narrator's account.

The author was unqualified to be a stone-cutter and lacked the necessary tools. The author searched for a suitable stone to make a mortar but found none that could be used. The rocks on the island were sandy and crumbling, unsuitable for making a mortar. The author decided to use a large block of hard wood to create a hollow for grinding corn. The author made a pestle from iron-wood to pound corn for bread. The author faced difficulties in making a sieve to separate meal from bran and husk. The author created earthen vessels for baking bread using a method involving fire and embers.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The group marched with the last two hundred men assigned to guard the camels and assist if needed. The Tartars approached in a large number, estimated to be at least ten thousand. The leader ordered the two wings of the group to fire a salvo at the Tartars when they were within gun-shot. The Tartars halted and decided to abandon their approach after receiving the salvo. The group arrived at the city of Naum, where they thanked the governor and collected about one hundred crowns for the soldiers guarding them. The city of Naum had nine hundred soldiers stationed there due to the historical proximity of the Muscovite frontiers. On April 13th, the group reached the frontiers of the Muscovite dominions, with the first city identified as Argun.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The speaker discusses the possibility of moving to their friend's country where his family is well known. The friend expresses a willingness to embrace the offer but does not want to take the speaker away from England. The speaker mentions their view of marriage as a form of captivity and their intention to act as a servant in the relationship. The speaker contemplates living in the country or leaving England if they were to accompany the friend. The arrival of a letter from Amy influences the speaker's thoughts about becoming a princess and living in a court. The speaker experiences a period of distraction and confusion regarding their feelings for the friend. The speaker feigns illness to avoid further interaction with the friend while contemplating their future.

The narrator traveled to London by land and faced internal struggles about his future. The narrator felt shame about the idea of returning home, fearing judgment from neighbors and family. The narrator experienced a reluctance to return home and eventually decided to seek a voyage instead. The narrator boarded a vessel bound for the coast of Africa, referred to as a voyage to Guinea. The narrator did not ship as a sailor and did not learn the duties required for a position on the ship. The narrator met a ship captain in London who invited him to join a voyage without expense. The narrator carried a small adventure with him, which he increased significantly through the captain's guidance.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator obtained about eleven or twelve shillings in money through a collection among acquaintances. The narrator had a maid named Amy who continued to work without wages and helped financially when possible. The narrator intended to send for a poor woman who had been a dependent on their family for assistance. The narrator was in distress, having five children under ten years old and no money to buy food. Amy was sent out to sell a silver spoon to buy something from the butcher. The narrator was found sitting on the ground surrounded by old rags and crying when the old aunt and the poor woman arrived. The narrator's home was stripped of most goods due to financial distress, leaving it in a state of ruin.

Daylight began to appear, and the characters did not perceive anyone else on the island. Two armies engaged in a fierce battle, which lasted for two hours. Friday's father advised the group to remain hidden for their safety. The Englishmen's curiosity led them to observe the battle from a concealed location. Three fugitives from the defeated army fled into the grove near the Spaniards' dwelling. The Spaniard governor ordered the capture of the three fugitives instead of killing them. After the battle, the Spaniards found about thirty-two dead men and several weapons on the battlefield.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: Daniel Defoe wrote about the virtues of well-bred and well-taught women. Defoe's work _The Fortunate Mistress_ is more structured than his other novels except for _Robinson Crusoe_ and _Journal of the Plague Year_. The narrative of _The Fortunate Mistress_ lacks a strongly defined plot but maintains some continuity with its characters. The story of _The Fortunate Mistress_ ends abruptly, leaving the fates of Roxana and Amy unclear. The author claims that the story is based on true events and differs from other modern narratives. The author conceals names and details to protect the identities of individuals involved in the story. The writer asserts familiarity with the lady's first husband and believes this lends credibility to the narrative.

The narrator hoped to stay at a friend's house. The narrator's husband needed to be informed about the situation. A young girl expressed that the narrator resembled a lady she knew. The girl believed the lady she mentioned was dead. The narrator wore a loose robe that was suitable for a chamber. The girl's comments about the narrator's dress led to further conversation. The mention of the name Roxana caused the narrator significant distress.

Eleven men and five women were taken as prisoners from the island. Approximately twenty young children were found on the island. Supplies including arms, powder, shot, clothes, tools, and two workmen were left on the island. Five cows, three of which were pregnant, along with some sheep and hogs were sent from the Brasils to the island. Three hundred Caribbees invaded the island, leading to conflicts with the inhabitants. The inhabitants of the island eventually regained control after a storm destroyed the Caribbees' canoes. The narrator expresses a persistent desire to venture abroad despite having sufficient resources.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: A ship bringing shares into the Texel foundered while chained to a privateer. Two or three crew members reached The Hague after the ship sank. The privateer and a trader engaged in battle in the Mediterranean, resulting in both ships being lost. Only two crew members from the trader and three from the privateer survived the engagement. The narrator faced financial difficulties and proposed moving to Amsterdam with Isabel. The narrator was arrested for a debt of £75 shortly after settling in Amsterdam. Isabel Johnson reported that the narrator became devoted to religion while in jail and died on July 2, 1742.

On October 20, the narrator overset their raft and recovered many goods when the tide was out. On October 25, heavy rain and wind caused a ship to break apart, leaving only wreckage visible at low water. On October 26, the narrator searched for a location to establish a habitation and marked out a semicircle for an encampment. From October 26 to October 30, the narrator worked hard to move goods to the new habitation despite heavy rain. On October 31, the narrator killed a she goat and later killed her kid for food. On November 1, the narrator set up a tent under a rock for the first night. On November 5, the narrator killed a wild cat and preserved its skin.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The Quaker expressed that the proposed method of travel was the safest, quickest, and cheapest. The husband hired a master of the packet-boats and reserved the great cabin for the next day's journey. Dinner was served in a parlour that was suitable to their rank, featuring a large service of plate. The couple discussed hiring servants for their journey from Dover to Paris, a common practice among travelers. The footmen departed for London, while the Quaker and coach were scheduled to leave the next day. The new chambermaid, Isabel, was hired to assist the narrator during the journey. The husband considered hiring a young man seeking employment as a servant after assessing his qualifications.

The narrator's partner decided to buy a ship that was for sale. They paid for the ship and took possession of it. The crew of the ship was missing because they had not received their wages. The crew had traveled to Agra and planned to go to Surat and then by sea to the Gulf of Persia. The narrator learned that the previous captain had been killed and the crew had stolen the ship. The narrator and his partner acquired the ship without thoroughly investigating its history. They planned a second voyage to the south-east for trading purposes.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator employed a spy to monitor a man who was deemed a potential threat. The spy provided a detailed journal of the man's daily activities. The monitoring was expensive, costing approximately one hundred and fifty livres a month. The man being watched led a seemingly insignificant and idle life. The man spent much of his time sleeping or drinking at a tavern. The narrator felt it was necessary to keep the man under constant surveillance for personal safety. The journal of the man's life was described as lacking significance.

The girl was advised to go to Spitalfields after leaving her place. She received £20 to buy clothes and was told not to go into service anymore. Madam Amy congratulated the girl on her new clothes and offered her advice on humility. The narrator was setting up a new figure in town while masks and balls were being organized. Sir Robert Clayton assisted in procuring a master for the narrator's son, who was later sent to Italy. The narrator's relationship with her lordship was deteriorating, leading to mutual dissatisfaction. After a two-month absence, the narrator decided to take control of the situation regarding her relationship.

The journey crossed a wild uncultivated country from a river to the great river Oby. The inhabitants of the area are primarily pagans, with some being sent from Russia. Muscovite criminals who are not executed are banished to the region around the river Oby. The capital of Siberia is Tobolski, where the narrator spent some time. The narrator considered winter travel options to England and the challenges associated with them. Traveling by sledges and rein-deer is common in winter for Russians. The narrator decided to winter in Tobolski due to the availability of provisions, warmth, and company.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator expresses gratitude towards a Dutch merchant who helped him. The narrator is uncertain about the outcome of his situation and feels uneasy. The narrator has concerns about potentially being cheated regarding bills. The narrator experiences joy upon seeing England from the ship. The ship's master informs the narrator that he cannot land in England. The weather changes and a storm begins to develop while at sea. The narrator has some prior experience with the sea from childhood.

The narrator received a black box tied with a scarlet ribbon and sealed with a noble coat-of-arms from a gentleman of the prince. The box contained a grant or assignment from the prince, providing the narrator with two thousand livres a year during her stay in Paris. The grant mentioned the murder of the narrator's late husband, Monsieur ----, as the reason for the financial support. The gentleman declined a monetary offer from the narrator, stating that the prince would disapprove of him accepting it. The gentleman assured the narrator that she was in the good graces of the prince and would hear more from him. The prince intended to visit the narrator without ceremony and sent his gentleman ahead to inform her. During the visit, the narrator expressed her gratitude to the prince for his kindness and refused to rise until he allowed her to kiss his hand.

The author expresses skepticism about the positive views of the Chinese people held by others. The author describes the Chinese as ignorant and poorly governed. The author compares the Chinese to the Muscovite empire, suggesting both are similarly ill-governed. The author notes that the czar of Muscovy could easily conquer China if he chose to do so. The author critiques the Chinese knowledge in sciences and mathematics, stating they are significantly lacking. The author mentions being in the heart of China, near thirty degrees north latitude, after returning from Nanquin. The author and companions decided to travel to Pekin with the retinue of a mandarin.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator felt unease and dissatisfaction after returning to London. The narrator had previously enjoyed an active life but found idleness intolerable. In 1693, the narrator's nephew returned from a voyage to Bilboa. The nephew proposed a voyage to the East Indies and China as private traders. The narrator had been contemplating a trip to Lisbon to consult an old sea-captain. The nephew's proposal aligned with the narrator's desire to revisit his old habitation. The narrator agreed to accompany his nephew if he secured an agreement with the merchants.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator's husband preferred that she stay until the afternoon to speak to the captain the next morning. The narrator resolved to prevent her husband from seeing the captain. The narrator pretended to change her mind about going to North Hall. The husband expressed that he had no business that was more important than accompanying the narrator. The husband planned to write a note to have someone else handle his business with the captain. The narrator reflected on her hypocrisy while her husband showed tenderness and sincerity. The couple decided to set out early in the morning, with the narrator suggesting Tunbridge as their destination.

The narrator faced financial difficulties after the death of their lord and had not yet received their £500 inheritance. The narrator considered various investment options and ultimately decided on merchandise as a profitable venture. The narrator consulted a merchant who offered shares in two ships: one for trading to Africa and another for privateering. The narrator was initially hesitant about investing in the privateer due to concerns about its operators but eventually agreed to invest in both ships. The narrator received their £500 inheritance and sold personal belongings to raise an additional £1100 for the investment. The ships were well manned and armed, and the partners refused to insure them before they set sail from different ports. The narrator received a letter from their son, who planned to attend the university in Paris and later travel in Europe, but this was the last correspondence between them.

The author experienced a cold fit on July 2 and renewed their medicine. On July 3, the author missed the fit but did not fully recover their strength for several weeks. The author reflected on their past deliverance from sickness and felt they had not properly acknowledged it. On July 4, the author began reading the Bible seriously every morning and night. The author felt a deep sense of repentance for their past life and prayed for repentance with a new understanding. The author recognized that deliverance from sin is a greater blessing than deliverance from affliction.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The garrisons and governors in certain towns and stations in Britain were Russians who practiced paganism. The author describes the Russians as barbarous, except for not practicing cannibalism. The journey included a twenty-day travel through a desert or forest between Arguna and Nertzinskay. In a village near Nertzinskay, the author observed a wooden idol that was described as frightful and grotesque. The idol was approximately eight feet high and dressed in sheep-skins, with no legs or proper proportions. The author witnessed a group of people prostrating themselves before the idol, which was associated with animal sacrifices. The author expressed a strong reaction to the worship practices observed, viewing them as a sign of ignorance and superstition.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator considers altering her plans to travel to Holland due to concerns about sea sickness and potential storms. The narrator's husband requests that she postpone the voyage until after a certain event, suggesting she prepare to stay where she is. The narrator has reasons for wanting to delay the voyage, particularly regarding her current condition and the presence of another individual. The husband reassures the narrator that he can manage any financial implications of canceling the trip and will handle communication with the ship's captain. The narrator expresses concern about the expectations of the captain's wife and sister regarding the trip. The husband believes that delaying the trip will not cause significant issues and offers to explain the situation to the captain's family. The captain mistakenly believes the narrator is expecting a child, which complicates the situation further.

The group consisted of canoes with varying numbers of men, ranging from six to seventeen. The individuals in the canoes expressed wonder upon approaching the long-boat. An engagement occurred when some canoes came too close, resulting in arrows being shot at the long-boat. One man in the long-boat was wounded by an arrow during the initial engagement. Friday, a companion of the narrator, was killed by arrows shot from the canoes. The narrator ordered the crew to fire back at the canoes after Friday was killed. The narrator's initial intention was to frighten the canoes with gunfire, but the situation escalated due to the attack.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The captain brought various supplies to the narrator, including bottles of cordial waters, Madeira wine, tobacco, ship's beef, pork, peas, biscuit, sugar, flour, lemons, lime-juice, shirts, neckcloths, gloves, shoes, a hat, stockings, and a suit of clothes. The narrator felt uncomfortable wearing the new clothes provided by the captain. The captain expressed concern about the prisoners, particularly two who were deemed incorrigible and refractory. The captain indicated that if he took the two troublesome prisoners, they would need to be in irons and delivered to justice at the nearest English colony. The narrator offered to persuade the two prisoners to request to be left on the island. The narrator summoned the five prisoners to the bower to discuss their behavior and the consequences of their actions. The narrator informed the prisoners that their captain had been executed and questioned them about their actions as pirates.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator asks a Quaker woman to sell her old clothes as a disguise. Amy comments that the disguise makes the narrator look younger. The Quaker woman initially declines to sell her clothes but later agrees to give them in exchange for a better suit. The narrator pays the Quaker woman three guineas more than the cost of the clothes. The Quaker woman has a good house and some jointure that supports her and her children. The narrator gives a piece of fine holland as a present to the Quaker woman, who is surprised and initially refuses it. The narrator learns to dress and speak like a Quaker through their interactions.

The Brasil ships brought both letters and goods to the narrator. The narrator experienced a sudden illness due to the surprise of joy upon receiving wealth. A physician was called to treat the narrator's illness, which was alleviated by bloodletting. The narrator acquired over 5000_l_ sterling in money and an estate in the Brasils worth over a thousand pounds a year. The narrator rewarded the old captain who had helped him by returning the money he owed and providing a yearly grant to him and his son. The narrator faced challenges in managing his newfound wealth and securing it safely. The narrator considered returning to England to manage his affairs and take his effects with him.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator gathered a large quantity of grapes and hung them on tree branches to dry in the sun. The narrator carried back limes and lemons from a journey. The narrator contemplated the fruitfulness and pleasantness of a valley but considered it the worst part of the country. The narrator decided not to remove from their current location by the sea-side due to the possibility of future advantages. The narrator built a bower surrounded by a strong double hedge for security. The narrator finished the bower at the beginning of August and began to enjoy their labor. From August 14th until mid-October, it rained more or less every day, sometimes preventing the narrator from leaving their cave.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator left a lady due to financial constraints. The landlord seized the lady's goods, leading to her eviction. The narrator observed the house shut up a month after leaving. Neighbors reported that the lady was in poor circumstances and received some assistance. The lady was seen in the city looking shabby and was thought to be working for her livelihood. The narrator's husband left her £25 and did not inform her of his survival to allow her the chance to remarry. Amy expressed doubt that her mistress would remarry without confirmation of the husband's death.

The narrator made a jerkin of goat's skin and a cap of hare-skin for Friday. Friday initially found it awkward to wear the new clothing, particularly the drawers and waistcoat. The narrator constructed a tent for Friday between two fortifications for lodging. A formal door was made for the tent, which could be barred at night for security. The narrator felt that Friday was a faithful and sincere servant, showing affection similar to that of a child to a parent. The narrator reflected on the capabilities and affections shared by all creatures, despite their circumstances. The narrator expressed melancholy about the underutilization of human faculties and the lack of life-saving knowledge.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The _gens d'armes_ are a small detachment that attended the king but are not his ordinary guard. Some _gens d'armes_ were ordered to march towards the Rhine and are expected to return to Orleans. The _gens d'armes_ were expected to be in Paris the following week. The narrator arranged to observe the _gens d'armes_ march in Paris with the help of a gentleman. The _gens d'armes_ entered Paris in new clothing and arms, and their standards were to be blessed by the Archbishop of Paris. A notable member of the _gens d'armes_ was referred to as the giant of Gascony. Amy inquired about a particular Englishman she believed to be dead, who was seen among the _gens d'armes_.

The narrator constructed lockers and boxes on their boat for storing provisions and ammunition. An umbrella was fixed at the stern of the boat to provide shade from the sun. On November 6th, in the sixth year of their captivity, the narrator set out on a voyage. The island was small, but the narrator encountered a ledge of rocks and a shoal of sand while exploring. The narrator made an anchor from a piece of broken grappling found on the ship. The narrator observed a strong current near the point of the island that posed a danger to their return. The narrator waited two days due to unfavorable wind conditions before attempting to navigate the waters.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator's father was a brewer who lost a fortune due to extravagance. The narrator's mother was left nearly penniless with five small children after the father's downfall. The narrator was sent to live with a relative after the mother could not care for the children. The narrator ran away from the relative's home at the age of nine due to cruel treatment.
