The narrator expressed a desire to serve and claimed to be honest despite lacking a good character reference. The narrator experienced a sudden illness and emotional distress after encountering a young man. The narrator's husband considered hiring the young man for their service.

A boat was found stripped of its contents and had a large hole in its bottom. The crew of the boat attempted to communicate with their companions by shouting and firing small arms, but were unsuccessful. The crew decided to return to their ship to inform others that their men were murdered and the long-boat was damaged. The captain was initially confused and feared losing the ship, but then became frightened by the crew's new plan. The crew left three men in the boat while the rest went ashore to search for their missing companions. The seven men who came ashore stayed close together and did not venture far from the shore. The captain suggested that the crew fire another volley to attract their companions' attention, allowing for a potential surprise attack.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator decided to provide more land for planting corn to feed both himself and Friday. Friday worked willingly and hard on the larger piece of land for the corn. The narrator communicated to Friday that the corn was for making more bread for both of them. Friday expressed understanding and a willingness to work harder for the narrator. Friday began to talk well and understand many things the narrator asked him about. The narrator felt a growing affection for Friday, who also seemed to love the narrator. Friday shared that his nation had previously engaged in battles and sometimes captured men.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The Quaker entered the conversation smiling and expressed relief that the speaker was finally free from visitors. The speaker felt tired of a young girl's lengthy storytelling. The Quaker noted that the young girl was careful to mention she was a cook-maid. The speaker expressed concern that the young girl's background might negatively affect her reputation. The Quaker suspected that the young girl had ulterior motives in her discourse. The speaker was alarmed by the Quaker's observations but did not want to share any secrets. The young girl mentioned that Mrs. Amy had become wealthy and kept a coach, which helped alleviate the speaker's concerns about being identified.

The Spaniard was given a pistol and sword to fight against his attackers. The Spaniard successfully killed two of his attackers before being thrown down. The Spaniard shot and killed a savage who was attempting to take his sword. Friday pursued the fleeing attackers with a hatchet and killed three of them. The Spaniard was given a fowling-piece and wounded two savages, but they escaped into the woods. One savage escaped into the sea and swam to a canoe with three others, one of whom was wounded. A total of 21 attackers were accounted for, with various numbers killed or escaped.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The colony included five Englishmen and their wives, who were described as well-governed and laborious. The wives of the Englishmen had taught their children to speak English, although initially in a broken manner. The children of the colony were all under six years old when the narrator arrived. The Spaniards in the colony expressed feelings of despair and misery during their time among the savages. One Spaniard believed that it was unwise to succumb to misery and emphasized the importance of seeking help and improvement. The Spaniards noted that they had not demonstrated application or ingenuity while living among the savages. The narrator made improvements in his solitude that were considered more successful than the circumstances of the Spaniards.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The Quaker asked about Roxana, prompting a discussion about her. The captain's wife described Roxana as a charming woman who was seldom seen. Roxana was rumored to be sent for to court. The captain's wife confirmed that Roxana was indeed a beautiful woman. The captain's wife claimed that Roxana did not use makeup. The captain's wife recounted a ball hosted by Roxana where many nobles attended. The Quaker noted that the king might have attended the ball in disguise.

The narrator was uncertain about a situation involving a merchant and received a letter from Amy. The narrator initially intended to treat the merchant rudely but changed their mind. Amy arrived unexpectedly in a coach with several bundles after a fourteen-day wait. Amy informed the narrator that the prince was alive but in poor condition due to an injury from a wild boar. The prince had recovered from a severe illness but was now penitent and unable to pursue the narrator. The prince sent fifty pistoles to Amy for her trouble, acknowledging her efforts. Amy attempted to comfort the narrator, suggesting that the prince would return to his old ways after his recovery.

The narrator carried items to a cove on the east end of the island, where he believed it was safe from savages. He removed a mast, sail, and a makeshift anchor from the cove to avoid detection. The narrator kept to himself and only left his cell to tend to his she-goats and flock in a safer part of the island. He expressed concern that savages might have visited the island without his knowledge. The narrator reflected on the dangers he faced and felt gratitude for being kept safe from unseen threats. He contemplated the idea that unseen forces may guide decisions that ultimately lead to safety.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator's daughter and her new husband, along with the husband's sister and the narrator's son Thomas, went to dine at the house of a rich uncle of the bridegroom before boarding a ship. The narrator's lord went to the same location in a sedan about an hour after the family left. After dinner, the family boarded the Indiaman, where the narrator's lord and son Thomas stayed until the ship's crew prepared to sail. The narrator's lord expressed his wishes for the prosperity of the narrator's daughter, whom he had provided for by sending her to the Indies with a man of merit and fortune. The narrator's lord planned to provide for the narrator's son Thomas in a handsome manner before concerning himself with his son by the narrator. The narrator's lord purchased a large plantation in Virginia for Thomas and provided him with shares in four large trading vessels. A gentleman selling the plantation had brought pictures of his family, including a daughter whom the narrator's lord found beautiful and inquired about her marital status.

The anonymous author of the continuation of Defoe's work has successfully replicated Defoe's detailed style. The character of Roxana's daughter is portrayed with less fidelity to Defoe's original conception. The Dutch merchant's character has developed a vindictiveness not present in earlier depictions. Defoe's characters, particularly Roxana and Amy, are more vividly portrayed than most of his other characters. Roxana is characterized as practical, cold-blooded, and selfish, often viewing her children as encumbrances. Roxana displays moments of noble emotion, indicating complexity in her character despite her selfishness. Defoe's portrayal of female characters, particularly Roxana, suggests he understood women's emotions better than those of men.

The narrator expresses a strong dislike for Rome, describing it as the most unpleasant place to live. The narrator notes the presence of numerous ecclesiastics and servants in Rome, suggesting a social hierarchy. A violent altercation involving footmen from two great families resulted in multiple injuries and fatalities. The prince is described as kind and obliging during the journey, maintaining a respectful demeanor. The prince acknowledges that the narrator helped him remain virtuous during their travels in Italy. The narrator mentions being pregnant again during the journey and giving birth to a son in Venice. The narrator reflects on the prince's changed attitude towards women compared to previous behavior.

The narrator traveled with a gentleman through the Alps, where they used a horse-litter carried by mules due to the terrain. The coaches used for the journey were sent back to Lyons while the narrator and the gentleman continued to Rome and then Venice. The gentleman engaged in conversation with the narrator and showed her various sights, sharing historical information about them. The narrator reflects on the gentleman's character, noting his otherwise excellent qualities despite his involvement in whoring. The narrator spent nearly two years on the grand tour, primarily residing in Rome and Venice, with brief visits to Florence and Naples. The narrator learned the Turkish language and culture from a female Turkish slave purchased by the gentleman during their travels. The narrator also learned Italian and developed a strong affection for Italy, particularly Naples and Venice.

The narrator received letters from a young man in England to deliver to his friends in London. The young man promised that upon his redemption, the plantation and improvements would belong entirely to the narrator. The young man revealed that he was not the one getting married; the match was between Jack of all Trades and his maid Susan. Susan was described as honest, modest, sober, religious, and a capable manager. The narrator married Jack and Susan on the same day and provided them with a portion of land for their plantation. Will Atkins was responsible for dividing the land among the settlers to prevent disputes over their locations. The narrator advised the settlers to live in love and good neighborhood and noted the presence of thirty-seven Indians living independently on the island.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator experiences fear during a storm at sea. The narrator observes the Dutch sailors' panic and does not understand their language. Amy, who is sea-sick, expresses concern for the narrator's pale appearance. Amy looks out at the storm and returns in a state of panic, believing they will drown. The narrator attempts to comfort Amy, despite feeling frightened themselves. Amy is thrown down by a violent wave and appears unconscious after hitting her head. The narrator calls for help but is unable to attract the attention of the sailors.

The narrator made an exception to avoid public passage boats due to concerns about crowds and convenience. The narrator's spouse hired an English merchant ship bound for Rotterdam, securing the entire great cabin for their passage. The captain of the ship invited the narrator and their spouse to dine on board the next day. The captain mentioned that he had considered taking his wife and her kinswoman on the voyage if the narrator went with him. The narrator's friend, the Quaker, accompanied them on the ship instead of Amy, who was engaged in searching for a missing girl. The missing girl had gone to stay with a friend who was married to a shipmaster at Redriff. Upon boarding the ship, the narrator discovered that the captain's wife was their former cook-maid, who was revealed to be their daughter.

The children of a poor lady were taken away by churchwardens due to her distress and inability to care for them. The youngest child was placed with a good nurse, while the other four were sent to live with their father's substantial relatives. The poor lady fainted when her children were taken from her and was later put into a madhouse by the parish. A gentlewoman's husband expressed concern for the children's situation, despite his wife's objections. The wife argued against taking in the children, stating that they should not take resources away from their own children. The husband emphasized the importance of charity and helping those in need, regardless of family ties. The wife insisted that charity should begin at home and refused to take in her relatives.

The narrator claims to have all they are capable of enjoying and feels like a ruler over their possessions. They have an abundance of resources, including corn, tortoises, timber, and grapes, but only utilize what is necessary. Excess resources, such as cut trees and surplus food, go to waste or are left unused. The narrator possesses about thirty-six pounds sterling in money, which they find useless and would trade for practical items. They express gratitude for their current state of life, finding comfort in what they have rather than focusing on what they lack. The narrator reflects that discontent arises from a lack of thankfulness for one's current possessions.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator employed a maid named Amy to gain access to a Dutch merchant. The narrator possessed money and jewels of significant value and considered leaving them with the merchant. The narrator had no contacts in London to send bills for the money and jewels. The Dutch merchant initially suspected Amy of attempting to deceive him. Upon meeting the narrator, the Dutch merchant advised her to take bills upon Amsterdam for security. The Dutch merchant offered to help sell the jewels in Paris and convert them into money. The narrator experienced fear when a Jew showed interest in the jewels, leading her to consider fleeing.

The captain advised to keep the enemy off with great shot and then use small arms to prevent boarding. The crew prepared for battle while remaining out to sea, observing five large long-boats pursuing them. Two of the pursuing boats were identified as English and were significantly ahead of the others. A gun was fired without a shot to signal the pursuing boats to halt, and a flag of truce was displayed, which went unanswered. The ship fired upon the pursuing boats after taking down the white flag and raising the red flag. One of the shots disabled the hindermost boat, causing it to take on water and stop. The ship's gunner successfully fired upon the foremost boat, causing significant damage and disorder.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator felt trapped and unable to disguise their identity during a meeting. The narrator's husband and the captain engaged in discussions about the ship and unrelated business. The captain left the narrator alone with a girl in the great cabin. The narrator observed that the girl did not seem to recognize them. The girl mentioned she had seen the narrator before but could not recall where. The narrator confirmed they had lived in Rotterdam and joked in Dutch with a Dutch boy. The captain's wife invited the narrator and others to visit her house after their meeting.

The individual was unable to send an agreeable answer for some time due to resentments. After six or seven months, the individual's resentments wore off, leading to a return of affection. The individual sent several letters, specifically seven or eight, but received no response. The individual traveled to England while on business in Holland but found that his letters had not been called for. The individual took up residence in England, believing he would eventually meet or hear from the other person. The individual had lived in England for over four years without thoughts of leaving, except to return home to die. The other person informed the individual that his son was alive and expressed regret for not informing him sooner.

The narrator expresses a reluctance to part with Friday, who has been a faithful companion. The narrator is concerned that Friday may be confused about religious beliefs if he is left with another person. The narrator believes that forcing Friday to leave would be unjust, as they have made mutual promises to each other. The narrator suggests that Friday's father, who understands Spanish, could serve as an interpreter. The narrator gathers a group of Englishmen to discuss their scandalous lifestyle and marital status. The Englishmen explain that they consider themselves married because they have agreed to live with the women as wives. The narrator acknowledges that the Englishmen may be considered married in the sight of God.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: Amy is the mother of the girl mentioned in the text. The girl served under Amy in the narrator's family. Amy initially communicated with the girl through another person. The girl expressed a desire to find her mother, Lady Roxana. Amy was upset when she learned that the girl knew about the narrator's marriage. Amy threatened to harm the girl out of frustration. The narrator advised Amy against harming the girl.

The codicil stated that if the narrator received more than £500 after the death of the deceased, the remaining funds were to be given to poor families in The Hague based on merit and necessity. The narrator's son was restricted from providing any financial relief to the narrator, with severe consequences for his estate if he did. The executors were unaware of the codicil's contents until it was publicly read, except for the chaplain who had advised against adding it. The narrator had the title of a countess and £500, but lacked additional means of support aside from a valuable wardrobe. The narrator moved from her lodgings to a private gentleman's house about a mile from The Hague after the death of the deceased. The narrator sought out Amy, who had previously lived in a now-empty house, and learned from neighbors that Amy's situation had deteriorated. Amy was reported to have kept a house of ill-fame and was later taken to a hospital due to health issues after being sent to a poorhouse.

The girl believes that the Lady Roxana is her mother. The girl has been lost to her mother since childhood and has never been recognized by her. The girl served as a housemaid to the Lady Roxana but did not know her at that time. The Quaker does not know the names of all the Lady Roxana's servants. The girl inquires if the Lady Roxana's favorite maid is named Amy. The Quaker expresses that she does not know the maid's name but mentions that they call her Cherry. The Quaker is moved by the girl's plea for assistance in contacting the Lady Roxana.

The girl expresses distress and wishes to speak to her mother. The Quaker informs the girl that her mother is not in the house. The girl insists she can prove her relation to her mother. The Quaker offers to help the girl find lodging for one night. The girl decides to return home but plans to search for her mother in the future. The Quaker warns the girl that her search will cause unnecessary trouble. The girl believes she may still gain information about her mother.

The narrator initially struggled to undress a character referred to as 'a little' but eventually succeeded. The narrator describes an encounter where a character named Amy is put to bed with a man against her will. Amy expresses regret and distress the following morning, feeling ruined and undone. The narrator claims not to consider herself married and believes she has no authority to prevent the man from marrying Amy. The man involved in the encounter develops a strong aversion to Amy after the incident, while he feels affection for the narrator. The narrator attempts to reconcile the man and Amy after the incident, leading to further encounters between them. Amy ultimately becomes pregnant as a result of her encounters with the man.

The narrator's mother refused to support his desire to leave home and reported the conversation to his father. The narrator's father expressed concern that the narrator would be miserable if he left home. The narrator ignored his parents' advice and left home without informing them. The narrator boarded a ship bound for London on September 1, 1651. The ship encountered a severe storm shortly after leaving the Humber, causing the narrator to feel sick and terrified. The narrator reflected on his decision to leave home and felt remorse for disregarding his parents' counsel. The narrator made vows to return home and never go to sea again if he survived the voyage.

text: The ship's forecastle was stuck in the rocks and her main-mast and fore-mast were broken off. A dog was found on the ship, which jumped into the sea and was rescued but was nearly dead from hunger and thirst. Two drowned men were discovered in the cook-room of the ship, with their arms around each other. The ship contained spoiled goods and some casks of liquor that were too large to handle. Two chests believed to belong to seamen were retrieved from the ship. A cask of liquor, approximately twenty gallons, was also taken into the boat. The cargo included a fire-shovel, tongs, two brass kettles, a copper pot, and a gridiron.

text: A gentlewoman named Mrs. Amy visited the narrator after a period of absence. The narrator had a private conversation with Mrs. Amy about significant events that occurred during her absence. Mrs. Amy suggested that the narrator's adversary would lead to her ruin and mentioned a previous proposal to murder her. The narrator expressed anger towards Mrs. Amy for mentioning murder and accused her of being responsible for the adversary's imprisonment. Mrs. Amy revealed a plan to have the adversary arrested for theft after her release from prison. The narrator's husband discussed acquiring the title of Count or Earl. The husband successfully obtained the title and presented the patent to the narrator.

The Quaker kept a woman in suspense until Amy arrived. Amy was confused by the Quaker's account and informed another person about it. Amy decided not to go to Tunbridge first but to Newmarket or Bury. Amy was distressed by the woman's pursuit and felt unsafe. Amy resolved to confront the woman at the captain's house in Redriff. Amy encountered the woman at Tower Wharf after she crossed the water from Redriff. Amy concealed her resentment towards the woman while planning her own actions.

The narrator and their friends lived cheerfully in March as the days grew longer and the weather improved. Other travelers began to prepare sledges to travel over the snow. The narrator planned to go to Archangel, knowing that ships from the south would not depart for that region until May or June. Many travelers left for Moscow to trade furs and buy necessities, while others headed to Archangel. The narrator considered why the banished people did not attempt to leave Siberia despite their freedom of movement. A conversation revealed that the travelers were effectively imprisoned due to geographical and governmental barriers. The narrator contemplated helping a person escape to Archangel, where they could secure passage on a ship.

text: Amy expresses that she would consider lying with a man for bread due to starvation. The narrator refuses to lie with a man even for an estate to live on. Amy states she would do anything, including being a whore, to help the narrator out of her sad condition. The narrator emphasizes that she would rather die than consent to prostitution for assistance. The garden is in disorder and overrun with weeds due to the narrator's inability to hire a gardener. A man is brought in by the narrator's acquaintance to help restore order to the garden. The narrator dresses as well as she can and feels pleased that her acquaintance notices her improved appearance.

The narrator and the Moor were fishing when the narrator decided to toss the Moor overboard. The Moor was a strong swimmer and called out for help after being thrown into the sea. The narrator threatened the Moor with a fowling-piece and instructed him to swim to shore. The narrator then turned to a boy named Xury and asked him to swear loyalty in exchange for future rewards. The narrator sailed away from the Moor and changed course to head south and by east. After five days of sailing, the narrator did not stop or go ashore due to fear of the Moors.

text: The boatswain was the principal ringleader of the mutiny and appeared dejected. The captain and Friday shot the boatswain, killing him instantly. Another crew member was shot and fell but did not die until an hour later. The captain's group, consisting of eight men, advanced towards the mutineers in the dark. Robinson called out to Tom Smith to negotiate a parley with the mutineers. The captain offered quarter to the mutineers if they laid down their arms, except for Will Atkins. The mutineers surrendered and begged for their lives, appearing penitent.

text: The narrator confided in Amy about their situation and expressed concern over being ruined. Amy felt responsible for the narrator's predicament and was distressed by it. The narrator was worried about a girl who had discovered their identity and location. The Quaker visited the narrator and informed them of an impending visit from the captain's wife and daughter. The Quaker's timely arrival prevented an unexpected encounter between the narrator and the captain's family. The narrator considered denying their presence but decided against it due to the Quaker's honesty. During the visit, the narrator hinted at their ill health and the possibility of delaying a trip to Holland.

Amy asked a girl to leave her house after a disagreement. The girl packed her belongings and left, indicating she might not return. During a boat trip to Greenwich, the girl expressed her knowledge of Amy's past and current life. They walked in Greenwich Park for over two hours while arguing. The girl refused to enter a wooded area in the park, citing safety concerns. Amy maintained her composure despite the girl's accusations and jealousy. Amy eventually took the girl to a house in Greenwich where she was known.

The narrator rewarded an old captain who had been his benefactor. The narrator sent one hundred pounds to the widow of his first benefactor through a merchant in Lisbon. The narrator also sent one hundred pounds each to his two sisters, who were not in very good circumstances. The narrator considered going to the Brasils but was unsure about leaving his stock with someone trustworthy. The narrator decided to go to England to find reliable acquaintances or relations. The narrator wrote letters of thanks to the prior of St. Augustine, his two trustees, and his partner. The narrator sent gifts of Italian silks and English broad-cloth to his partner's family.

text: The men expressed a desire to keep their wives and not abandon them. Will Atkins stated he would not leave his wife even for a position in the navy. The men were willing to marry their wives formally if a clergyman was present. The speaker had a French clergyman who could not speak English. The men did not inquire about the clergyman's religious affiliation. The men agreed to meet the next morning for the marriage ceremony. The women were informed about the marriage law and were satisfied with the arrangement.

text: The narrator traveled from Calais to Paris with her husband, self, chambermaid, and two hired horsemen over five days. Upon arriving in Paris, the narrator expressed regret about the trip but decided to remain retired due to the short duration of their stay. The narrator and her party stayed at a merchant's house in the Rue de la Bourle, near the Carmelites, in the Faubourg de St. Jacques. During their eight days in Paris, the narrator visited several locations including the gardens of Luxembourg, Notre Dame, Hôtel Royale des Invalides, gardens of the Tuileries, suburbs of St. Lawrence, gardens of the Louvre, and a playhouse. The narrator inquired about her son Thomas's family background, revealing that he had no memory of his parents but mentioned having one brother and three sisters. Thomas stated that he had heard his mother had died in a workhouse after being brought to distress. Thomas described the Lady Roxana as a beautiful woman who kept great company but had a questionable private life.

The narrator used chests to keep themselves in place while on a raft. The water rose, allowing the raft to float again, which the narrator then pushed into the channel. The narrator sought a place to reach the shore to avoid being carried too far up the river. The narrator found a cove on the right shore of the creek and guided the raft towards it. The narrator moored the raft by sticking two broken oars into the ground after the tide was high enough. The narrator climbed a steep hill to assess their surroundings and discovered they were on an island. The island appeared barren and uninhabited, with the narrator observing various birds but being unsure of their edibility.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: The narrator spent a week on the island to rest after a long journey. The narrator made a cage for a creature named Pol, which had become familiar with him. The narrator retrieved a kid that he had previously confined and fed it. The kid became tame and affectionate towards the narrator, becoming one of his domestics. The narrator observed the anniversary of his landing on the island on September 30th, marking two years of solitude. The narrator reflected on his solitary condition and expressed gratitude for the mercies he experienced. The narrator began to find happiness in his current life, contrasting it with his past experiences.

text: The narrator created a living space using skins of animals he had killed, soft materials, and a blanket. He constructed enclosures for his goats, which he worked hard to maintain to prevent them from escaping. The narrator used small stakes to reinforce the hedge around the goat enclosure, making it stronger than a wall. He believed that keeping a breed of tame creatures would provide him with a sustainable source of food. The narrator grew grapes for winter storage of raisins, which he considered a valuable part of his diet. While visiting his boat, the narrator discovered a naked human footprint on the shore, which surprised him. The sight of the footprint caused the narrator to feel terrified and confused, leading him to look around anxiously.

text: The victim was robbed and killed by three masked men on horseback during the day. One of the robbers stabbed the victim with a sword, resulting in immediate death. The robbers knocked down the victim's footman and searched the victim's belongings after his death. The robbers were believed to have killed the victim due to their disappointment in not obtaining a case of diamonds. The victim was found to have only a ring, six pistoles, and seven livres in small money after the robbery. The coachman was the only witness who could provide limited information about the robbers. The victim was buried in a manner that falsely represented him as a Catholic, facilitated by a deceitful individual.

Amy expressed her desire to show kindness to a child she had previously known. The man provided an account of how he had cared for the child, including maintaining, feeding, clothing, and educating him. Amy requested that the child be taken away from his hard-working trade, stating she would provide for him. The man indicated that taking the child away would result in a loss of £20 he had invested in the child. Amy offered to reimburse the man the £20 and proposed to provide an additional £100 for the child's schooling and board. Amy planned to have the child learn Latin, merchants' accounts, and writing to prepare him for a career as a Turkey merchant. Amy stated her intention to make the child her heir and promised to provide any necessary funds for his future.

The narrator reflects on their past life and feels oppressed by guilt and fear of dying. The narrator recalls their father's advice and prediction regarding their life choices. The narrator expresses feelings of distress and calls out for help after realizing the consequences of their actions. On June 28, the narrator wakes up feeling somewhat refreshed after a fit of illness. The narrator prepares for the return of their illness by mixing water and rum and cooking goat's flesh. The narrator eats turtle's eggs and recalls that it is the first time they have asked for God's blessing on food. The narrator feels weak and struggles to walk, reflecting on their miserable condition.

text: The speaker expresses satisfaction with a proposal to become a lady or countess in England. The speaker discusses the value of titles and their impact on respect and principles. The speaker's companion mentions the possibility of obtaining a title through naturalization and purchase. The companion has a nephew who holds the title of count and is willing to sell it for a thousand pistoles. The speaker prefers the option of purchasing the count title but insists on paying for it. The companion refuses to let the speaker pay for the title, citing a previous refusal of money. The conversation reflects on their past experiences and the uncertainty of their future residence.

The girl claims her mother is a woman who ran away with a jeweller to Paris. The girl's father abandoned her mother, leaving behind two sons and two daughters. Mrs. Amy, the mother's servant, allegedly caused the girl to be imprisoned for debts. The girl asserts that she is the person she claims to be and has knowledge of her mother. The lord recalls his acquaintance with the mother during the sale of jewels when she was in distress. The mother acknowledges being the wife of a brewer and having five children with him. The mother states that she married the jeweller after her husband's death.

The text describes a series of extreme emotional and physical reactions observed in individuals on a ship. A man exhibited a range of behaviors, including being dumb, dancing, tearing his hair, and crying, within a short period. The surgeon on the ship had to let blood from over thirty individuals due to their severe conditions. An old priest appeared to drop dead upon boarding the ship but was revived by the surgeon after blood was drawn. The old priest later experienced a state of madness due to overwhelming joy about his circumstances. A younger priest displayed calmness and gratitude, prostrating himself in thankfulness for his deliverance. The younger priest later expressed his gratitude to the narrator for saving him and others.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: Thomas Jeffrys was found hanged and mutilated. Sixteen or seventeen principal Indians were found in a nearby house, some of whom were wounded. The sight of Jeffrys' body incited the men to seek revenge against the Indians. The men created wildfire to set the town on fire in multiple locations. As the fire spread, many Indians attempted to escape but were killed or injured. The house where the Indians were located collapsed, killing those inside. The men did not fire their guns initially to avoid alerting more Indians.

source.author: Daniel Defoe

text: The shore on the worst side of the island was covered with numerous turtles. There were many kinds of fowls on this side of the island, including penguins. The author found it more difficult to approach goats on this side of the island due to the flat terrain. The author traveled about twelve miles along the shore towards the east. The author became lost in a large valley surrounded by hills and could not see the direction of his dwelling. The weather was hazy for three or four days while the author was in the valley. The author captured a young kid and intended to raise a breed of tame goats.

source.author: Daniel Defoe

text: The group began to descend and move northward, relying on their guide. Three wolves and a bear emerged from a hollow near a thick wood. Two wolves attacked the guide, one biting his horse and the other attacking him. Friday rode up to the guide and shot the wolf attacking him. The guide was injured by the wolf, suffering bites on his arm and knee. After Friday killed one wolf, the other fled, having caused minimal harm to the horse. A subsequent encounter occurred between Friday and the bear, which was surprising to the group.

source.author: Daniel Defoe

text: The journey described involves traveling through a region inhabited largely by pagans. The distance to the sea eastward is at least twelve hundred miles. The distance to the bottom of the Baltic Sea westward is at least two thousand miles. The distance to the Indian or Persian Sea southward is five thousand miles. All rivers in the region run to the east and flow into the great river Yamour. Several rivers to the north of the Yamour run due north and join the great river Tartarus. The czar of Muscovy has established cities and towns in various locations for military garrisons.

text: De Foe wrote a work addressing the discontent in England during peacetime compared to wartime. He was rewarded by King William with a pension and appointed pamphlet-writer general to the court. De Foe retired to Newington with his family after receiving royal patronage. Following the death of King William, De Foe faced difficulties and engaged in religious controversy. He published a tract titled 'The shortest Way with the Dissenters,' which was misunderstood by some as a serious recommendation of persecution. De Foe was prosecuted for his pamphlet, surrendered to authorities, and was sentenced to imprisonment, standing in the pillory, and fined. He wrote a hymn to the pillory, expressing defiance towards his accusers.

source.author: Daniel Defoe
source.title: The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1808)

text: There were thirty individuals gathered around a fire, cooking meat and dancing in various gestures. Two individuals were dragged from boats for slaughter, with one being knocked down and cut open by others. One victim managed to escape and ran towards the coast where the narrator's habitation was located. The narrator was frightened when the escaping victim ran in his direction, fearing he would be pursued. The escaping victim swam across a creek to evade his pursuers, who were delayed by the swim. Two of the pursuers could swim, while one could not and chose to return instead of crossing. The narrator decided to intervene and attempted to save the escaping victim by positioning himself between the pursuers and the victim.

source.author: Daniel Defoe

text: The narrator and Friday rescued two guests who were unable to walk. The narrator and Friday constructed a tent using old sails and tree boughs. The narrator provided beds made of rice-straw and blankets for the guests. The narrator considered himself a king with dominion over the island and three subjects of different religions. Friday was a Protestant, his father was a Pagan and cannibal, and the Spaniard was a Papist. The narrator ordered Friday to kill a yearling goat to prepare a meal for the guests. Friday was tasked with retrieving muskets and burying the dead bodies of the savages.

text: The speaker discusses the implications of a woman engaging in a relationship with a man before marriage. The speaker argues that yielding to a man before wedlock leads to lifelong shame and reproach. The speaker believes that if a woman marries a man after being his mistress, she will always carry the stigma of that relationship. The speaker asserts that if a woman and man part ways, the memory of their relationship fades over time. The man acknowledges the speaker's main points but suggests that women should choose capable and honest partners for managing estates. The speaker warns that relying on others to manage finances can lead to loss of money. The speaker emphasizes that women should not fear the trouble of managing their own affairs.

The merchant bought all the opium and paid in gold and small coins. The merchant proposed to hire the ship to go to Japan and send the crew to the Philippine islands. The narrator considered going on the voyage to the Philippine islands but was persuaded against it by his partner. The narrator's nephew expressed interest in undertaking the voyage as a merchant. The narrator was reluctant to part with his nephew but considered the potential advantages of the voyage. The narrator's partner offered to leave his share of the ship to the steward if he undertook the voyage.

text: Daniel De Foe was born in London around the year 1663. His father, James Foe, was a butcher and a protestant dissenter in the parish of St. Giles's, Cripplegate. De Foe began his career as an author by writing a pamphlet against the Turks during the siege of Vienna. He participated in the insurrection under the Duke of Monmouth and returned to London after its failure. De Foe engaged in trade as a hosier and later as a maker of bricks and pantiles, but faced financial difficulties. He paid off most of his creditors after being freed from his debts by composition. In 1700, De Foe published the satire 'True-born Englishman' to address criticisms of King William and his supporters.

source.author: Daniel Defoe

The woman pointed out the significant difference in their financial situations, stating that he was rich and she was poor. The man presented a written contract in which he committed to cohabit with the woman and provide for her as a wife. The contract included a penalty of £7000 for abandoning her and a bond for £500 to be paid after his death. The man expressed his affection and asked the woman to consider his proposal without delay. He argued that their private arrangement did not require the usual courtship rituals and emphasized his genuine affection through actions. The man assured the woman that he would treat her as his wife for the rest of his life.

The merchant and the Jew agreed to consult an advocate for advice on selling jewels. The merchant planned to keep the jewels to show to another person for a better price. The Jew expressed confidence that the woman would never regain possession of the jewels. The Dutchman informed the woman of the Jew's malicious intentions regarding the jewels. The woman expressed concern about proving her marriage due to its private nature in England. The merchant warned that the Jew might falsely accuse the woman of wrongdoing. The woman felt that her innocence could be compromised by the Jew's willingness to lie.

The narrator's ship arrived at the bay of All Saints in the Brasils after twenty-two days. During the voyage, the crew encountered a large number of canoes, initially estimated at a thousand. Upon closer observation, the actual number of canoes was determined to be about 126.

The captured individual was eventually taught some English and became more cooperative. The captured individual mentioned that five nations were preparing to fight against two nations. The captured individual spoke in a guttural manner that was difficult for the narrator and his group to understand.

text: The narrator expresses a desire to avoid seeing the court and the crowd. The narrator suggests postponing a trip to Holland and proposes a route through Harwich, Newmarket, and Bury to Ipswich. The narrator considers leaving Amy behind as an assistant but ultimately decides against it due to concerns for her safety. The narrator describes their friend the Quaker as kind and honest, willing to help but not engage in dishonorable actions. The narrator leaves instructions for the Quaker regarding how to handle visits from the troublesome girl.

The narrator had a supply of food that could sustain them until the next harvest. The narrator and the sixteen Spaniards worked to create wicker baskets for storing corn. The Spaniard was skilled in making wicker-work and suggested the need for defensive measures. The narrator instructed the Spaniard to return to the main land with specific conditions regarding the safety of the island's inhabitants. The Spaniard and the old savage took a canoe to the main land, equipped with muskets and provisions. The narrator waited for eight days for the return of the Spaniard and the old savage. The narrator was alerted by Friday about the arrival of the boat from the sea.

text: The narrator reflects on the loss of comrades who drowned, noting that only their hats, a cap, and two mismatched shoes were found. The narrator is stranded on shore after a shipwreck, feeling uncertain about how to survive. The narrator has no clothes, food, or drink, and fears perishing from hunger or being attacked by wild beasts. The narrator possesses only a knife, a tobacco pipe, and a small amount of tobacco. The narrator finds fresh water to drink and climbs a thorny tree to spend the night for safety. The next morning, the weather is clear, and the ship has been moved by the tide closer to the shore. The narrator discovers a boat washed ashore but cannot reach it due to a wide inlet of water.

text: The principal of the estate accessible after the death included a thousand livres, plate, and household items. A foreign bill intended for acceptance in Versailles was lost, but a second bill brought by the manager saved the money. The thieves who robbed and murdered the individual were afraid to send anyone to get the bill accepted. Amy, the maid, managed to secure everything and sent the key to the head manager of the business. The narrator received legal advice in Paris to make a process in dower upon the estate. The manager returned to England satisfied with the unaccepted bill of exchange and other items totaling seventeen thousand livres. The narrator became known as 'La belle veufeu de Poictou' and gained popularity among ladies of quality after her husband's death.

The narrator reproached himself for not planting enough corn to last until the next season. He resolved to have two or three years' worth of corn stored to avoid starvation. The narrator experienced a change in feelings about human companionship while isolated on an island. He reflected on the sovereignty of God and his own duty to submit to divine will. The narrator spent considerable time in contemplation about his situation and divine providence. He found comfort in scripture during a moment of fear regarding potential danger from savages. After praying, the narrator felt encouraged and uplifted by the words he read in the Bible.

Billy climbed on top of a fence and watched an old man plow a field. Saxon encouraged Billy to ask the old man if he could try plowing. Billy took the plow from the old man and began to plow the field. The old man provided instructions to Billy while he plowed. Saxon observed that the old man resembled the description of the lineman's father. The farm was described as old-fashioned and poorly maintained. Saxon's inquiries revealed that the old man's children lived in cities and occasionally helped him.

The land was described as rich and abundant with wild game. Mr. Roberts drove cattle from the San Josquin to the Columbia River with the help of forty men. The hills around Santa Rosa were populated with deer and elk. The narrator's father hunted grizzlies in Cache Slough north of Sacramento. Saxon had never slept outdoors before and found it uncomfortable. Saxon and Billy discussed the possibility of encountering rattlesnakes while camping. Both Saxon and Billy had never camped out before and were adjusting to the experience.

The protagonist ordered root beer or ginger ale and endured the chaffing of others. He observed the effects of alcohol on those around him and felt grateful for his own sobriety. The protagonist experienced a new form of intoxication through love, literature, and personal cleanliness. He attended a theatre performance in hopes of seeing Ruth and spotted her from the second balcony. The protagonist noticed two young girls smiling at him, which elicited a mix of emotions including warmth and pity. He felt a sense of shame regarding the attention from the girls, recognizing the class differences between them and Ruth. As he left the theatre, he encountered the two girls again, who approached him and initiated a greeting.

A man ran naked except for narrow trunks across the sandhills. The man had a cherubic face, curly yellow hair, and a muscular body. Saxon and Billy observed the man as he approached the surf. The man dived into the waves and swam against the current. Saxon expressed anxiety while watching the swimmer's struggle. After half an hour, the swimmer was able to swim strong beyond the surf. Billy expressed admiration for the swimmer and his own desire to learn ocean swimming.

Saxon expressed fear and nervousness in a conversation with Mercedes. Saxon had a clear understanding of love and relationships from her experiences. Saxon was aware of the importance of maintaining her husband's love. Saxon recognized Billy's positive qualities and appreciated him as a partner. Mercedes Higgins provided Saxon with new ideas and insights about love. Saxon dedicated herself to improving her household and personal appearance. Saxon studied physiology and hygiene to enhance her health and beauty.

Ruth is interested in pursuing a career as a teacher. Martin is considering common labor or an instructor position at Hanley's cramming joint. Martin believes that love is independent of reason. Olney argues that Latin is not necessary for Martin's goals. Ruth defends the value of Latin as mental training. Olney claims that only certain professions require knowledge of Latin. Martin credits Ruth as his teacher for what he has learned.

Martin Eden had La Grippe, which he described as less severe than break-bone fever. Martin Eden contracted break-bone fever while living in a secret colony of lepers on one of the Hawaiian Islands. He initially landed on the beach after deserting a schooner and lived off wild fruits for three days. Martin found a trail leading to a mountain valley where a settlement of lepers existed. The leader of the leper settlement was a kind old man who had guns and trained inhabitants. A half-Chinese, quarter-white, and quarter-Hawaiian girl helped Martin escape from the settlement. The girl showed early signs of leprosy and was well-educated, with a wealthy mother in Honolulu.
