Marmaduke consumes two ices while watching Lalage eat.

The text is from 'AN UNSOCIAL SOCIALIST' by George Bernard Shaw. A woman of forty exits an oaken door onto a landing in an old English country house. The woman observes the landscape through a tall, narrow window as the sun sets. Three girls descend the stairs, creating noise and excitement. Miss Wilson, the lady above, calls the girls to come up to the classroom. The girls display different reactions to Miss Wilson's call and their appearance. Miss Wilson is aware of the difficulty in confronting the third girl due to her demeanor.

Marmaduke expresses that he is in trouble and seeks Marian's support. Marmaduke offered to marry Susanna Conolly, but she refused. Marmaduke does not intend to marry Constance and is indifferent to her feelings. Marian promises not to inform Constance about Marmaduke's intentions. Marmaduke feels pressured by his family to pursue the match with Constance. Marmaduke criticizes Constance's intelligence compared to Susanna Conolly. Marmaduke plans to return to London, hoping the situation will resolve itself.

Lilith claims to have set Adam free. Eve expresses dissatisfaction with the repetitive nature of human life. Eve notes that all men, except Adam, are her sons or descendants. Eve reflects on the lack of novelty in the experiences shared by her descendants. Eve expresses hope for the future and the potential for new creations. Eve describes some of her descendants as weak and vain, yet capable of dreaming. Eve mentions Tubal, who created a wheel.

Marian felt a strong impulse to flee while in the second room. Marian encountered Conolly unexpectedly in the doorway. Conolly raised his hat and prepared to pass by Marian. Marian and Conolly discussed pictures in the gallery. Marian was saluted by many acquaintances during her visit. Marian expressed a desire to sit in another room to avoid Mr. Douglas. Conolly inquired about Marian's name preference during their conversation.

The small capitalists are left stranded as larger capitalists relocate to areas with cheaper production costs. Workers will emigrate in pursuit of factories, but their population will grow faster than they can leave. British factories will be replaced by villas, and manufacturing districts will become fashionable resorts. Imports will be used to pay for rents and dividends, which will not be offset by exports. The demand for Protection will increase, but it will not be implemented due to its failure to benefit workers. A large unemployed proletariat will emerge, demanding access to land and machinery, but will be denied. The capitalist community will eventually face a collapse due to a halt in imports and a failure to restore production.

The envoy reflects on a previous oracle consultation that his predecessor, Sir Fuller Eastwind, had fifteen years ago. The envoy's daughter recalls the oracle's answer to Eastwind, which inspired their party and contributed to their election victory. The envoy expresses doubt about the integrity of Eastwind's consultation with the oracle. The elderly gentleman insists on telling the truth about the oracle's message, despite the potential political consequences. The envoy decides to report the oracle's message as it was given to him, stating he will not lie. The elderly gentleman feels perplexed and wretched about the situation and seeks guidance from the oracle. The oracle appears to the elderly gentleman, revealing her true form and addressing his fears.

Marian was informed by the doctor that she might expect to become a mother next fall. Marian felt overwhelmed by the realization that reconciliation with her husband was no longer possible. Marian initially refused to see the body of Susanna but later overcame her repugnance to avoid appearing unkind to Conolly. The body of Susanna was decently laid out with a bandage on her forehead and religious items placed on her breast. Mrs. Myers expressed concern and resumed conversation after the police left. Marian left the house to visit her friend Mrs. Crawford to narrate the events of the day. Mrs. Crawford suggested that Marian's husband might visit her following the incident.

The text discusses the concept of a Church and its relation to religion. Mahomet is mentioned as a wise man who founded a religion without a Church. The speaker claims that bishops and priests obstructed reform for two hundred years. The Prime Minister expresses willingness to assist with the reception of a colonizing party. The colonizers are considering starting in North America due to the different skin color of the people. The Elderly Gentleman raises concerns about the popularity of the colonizers in North America. The text concludes with a sense of despair from the Elderly Gentleman.

Leonardo da Vinci remarked that the earth is a moon of the sun. Newton developed the theory of gravitation. Sir Humphry Davy invented the safety-lamp. Darwin was recognized as an Evolutionist, leading to the emergence of Neo-Darwinians. The Neo-Darwinians became influential in current Science by 1906. A European catastrophe occurred due to Neo-Darwinism in politics. The author expressed doubt about the human animal's ability to solve social problems.

The text discusses the exploitation of individuals by able administrators who dominate them. It describes a situation in Europe where one half is attempting to harm the other half. The author questions the effectiveness of religion in providing practical solutions for societal issues. Sidney and Beatrice Webb are mentioned as dedicated students of political science in England. The text argues against teaching political science and citizenship in schools. It criticizes the current educational system for promoting outdated moral values. The author concludes that mankind cannot be saved by external authorities, including educators.

Agatha was skating when she was approached by Mr. Trefusis. Mr. Trefusis revealed to Agatha that he is married to Hetty. Agatha became distressed upon learning about Mr. Trefusis's marriage. Jane assisted Agatha to a chair after she expressed her fatigue. Mr. Trefusis left the skating area after Agatha asked Jane for help. Mr. Smilash received a telegram from Jansenius, London, regarding Henrietta's illness. Mr. Smilash instructed the messenger to return to Lyvern and arrange for transportation to the railway station.

Mesopotamia was previously cast off by the Roman Empire. The first man to live three hundred years was an Englishman. The English race had lost intellectual credit and referred to one another as fatheads. Ireland was described as an emerald gem set in a silver sea by early bards. The Irish emigrated to various countries after the British Empire left them to themselves. The Irish claimed to be the lost tribes of Israel and sought to regain their prestige. Upon returning to Ireland, the older generation embraced the soil while the younger generation expressed disappointment.

The characters in the text discuss the relationship between Marmaduke and Constance. Elinor and Marian express differing opinions about Marmaduke's feelings towards Constance. Lady Constance writes a letter to Marmaduke in her brother's study. Constance's brother questions her about the letter she is writing to Marmaduke. Marian is described as having a positive view of people, including Marmaduke. Nelly is suggested to be jealous of Constance due to her feelings for Marmaduke. The conversation reveals tensions and differing perspectives on character and conduct among the characters.

Elinor has not heard Marmaduke sing since a concert at Wandsworth over three years ago. Marian sang several songs, including 'Rose, softly blooming,' 'The Oak and the Ash,' and 'Auld Robin Gray.' Marmaduke's singing was not as fresh or spontaneous as it had been at Wandsworth. Conolly entered the room and initially looked for his wife after hearing singing. Conolly reported that he visited a woman who is a confirmed dipsomaniac and did not want to see him. Conolly advised the woman to abstain from alcohol, but she responded sarcastically. Marian became silent and less commanding after Conolly's arrival.

Susanna refuses to accept money from Bob, stating she would rather starve. Bob expresses frustration about living with Susanna and mentions he has endured her behavior for nearly a year. Susanna decides to leave and tells Bob he can have the child. Douglas walks along Uxbridge Road to Holland Park on a Sunday afternoon. Douglas meets Mrs. Conolly, Miss McQuinch, and Marmaduke in the park. Marian informs Douglas that Ned Conolly is absent due to family affairs. Marian suggests they reminisce about their past to create a pleasant atmosphere.

Marian heard unsteady footsteps on the stairs and saw a strange woman descending toward her. The woman had black hair, was dressed in a crimson satin dressing-gown, and appeared to be in pain. The woman identified herself as Susanna Conolly, Marian's sister-in-law. Susanna Conolly mentioned that she had gone off in her appearance and advised Marian against drinking champagne. Marian informed Susanna that her brother, Ned, was in England and that she was alone. Susanna was unaware of recent events and asked Marian what had happened. Marian revealed that she had left Ned and was uncertain about her marital status.

Marian and another character discuss their friendship and past misunderstandings. Marian's father is out of town until Monday and has been talking about Douglas. Marian suggests that Douglas visit her father at the club if he wants to see him in the morning. Mrs. Leith Fairfax arrives and reminds Marian that it is past six o'clock. Elinor is seated in the vestibule with Conolly when Marian and Mrs. Fairfax find her. Marmaduke Lind enters the building and greets Douglas enthusiastically. Marmaduke invites Douglas and others to a housewarming party on week-nights.

Cain expresses disdain for the way men fight for women's admiration and the superficiality of their relationships. Eve criticizes Cain for his view of women and his actions, suggesting he is a slave to superficial desires. Cain believes that his fighting makes him admirable and desirable to women. Eve argues that Cain's actions do not reflect true strength or love. Cain claims that Lua, a woman, is better to live with than Eve. Eve points out that Cain's relationship with Lua is based on manipulation and pain. Adam intervenes in the conversation, suggesting that enough has been said.

The text discusses the evolution of religion and its intellectual roots in philosophy and science. LUBIN expresses a belief in his potential leadership for the next three hundred years. CONRAD mentions that some authorities believe the human race may be superseded by a new form of life. FRANKLYN states that the force behind evolution is determined to solve the problem of civilization. CONRAD asserts that the power referred to as God operates by the method of Trial and Error. LUBIN questions whether citizens will also live for three hundred years like statesmen. BURGE emphasizes the need to draft a Bill to put their ideas into practical parliamentary shape.

Jesse Trefusis, M.P., died a millionaire in Kensington. The narrator expresses disdain for social arrangements that allow certain careers to be viewed positively. The narrator feels discomfort at the wealth and idleness of those who imitate Trefusis. Henrietta reassures Sidney that she does not blame him for the situation. Sidney reflects on his family's wealth and descent from a county family. The narrator describes how his grandfather cleared peasants from their homes to increase profits from livestock. The narrator contrasts the actions of his grandfather and father regarding land use and labor.

Sholto Douglas is in communication with Mr. Lind regarding Marian. Mr. Lind expresses approval of Sholto's intentions for Marian. Mr. Lind mentions that Marian's marriage will entail a lonely life for him. Sholto Douglas is seeking Mr. Lind's sanction before obtaining Marian's final consent. Mr. Lind has financial concerns due to the extravagance of his sons. Sholto Douglas offers to take full responsibility for Marian's welfare. Mr. Lind and Sholto Douglas visit the Conolly Electro-Motor Company of London.

Gertrude and Agatha watched a storm from a window outside Miss Wilson's study. Agatha felt courageous during the storm, while Gertrude expressed fear and unease. Gertrude suggested returning to bed due to safety concerns. They heard a bell ringing from the gate of the college grounds. Miss Wilson was alerted by loud knocking at the house door. A voice outside claimed there was a dying woman and three children needing to be let in. Miss Wilson struggled to maintain her composure while trying to communicate with the person outside.

The characters in the text include Erskine, Trefusis, Gertrude, and Lady Brandon. Erskine feels that Trefusis does not love Gertrude and considers him inferior. Gertrude's manner towards Erskine softens, leading him to believe she is tempting him to propose. Sir Charles expresses sympathy for Erskine but is pleased that Trefusis's attentions to Agatha are not serious. Erskine writes three sonnets about hollow friendship and shares them with Sir Charles. Trefusis questions why Erskine has taken to writing bitter poetry and inquires about his intentions towards Miss Lindsay. Sir Charles confirms that Erskine does not intend to propose to Miss Lindsay.

Gertrude is traveling to town by train with her maid. Trefusis offers to take charge of Gertrude during the journey. Sir Charles expresses concern about Trefusis traveling with Gertrude. Gertrude initially intends to deny Trefusis but ultimately agrees to his company. Sir Charles decides to leave Gertrude in Trefusis's care. Erskine reacts with anger upon learning that Trefusis is on the same train as Gertrude. Erskine plans to follow the train on his bicycle to confront Trefusis.

The Rev. George is intrigued by a woman's bold moral attitude and self-respect despite her sin. He believes there is potential for redemption in her character. The Rev. George imagines how her life might improve with his guidance instead of that of Marmaduke. He experiences a spiritual awakening and prays earnestly for forgiveness. The Rev. George delivers a sermon questioning how Satan can cast out Satan. He warns against justifying the Bible with scientific explanations. The sermon addresses the moral decline in London and criticizes societal behaviors.

Mr. Lind offered Douglas ten thousand pounds to marry his daughter, which Douglas declined. Mr. Lind expressed anger towards Douglas and threatened to expose him in clubs. Douglas instructed his servant to remove Mr. Lind from the premises. Douglas felt upset after the confrontation with Mr. Lind and sought solitude in the streets. Douglas encountered Lord Carbury, who noted that public opinion about Douglas had not yet faded. Douglas revealed to Lord Carbury that Mr. Lind's daughter is a woman of poor character. Douglas stated that Conolly, who had mistreated Mr. Lind's daughter, is reluctant to confront him.

The Newly Born is three years old. Acis points out Strephon, who is sorrowful and has chosen a girl two years old as his sweetheart. The Newly Born expresses a desire to love Acis forever without growing up. The She-Ancient examines the Newly Born and determines she may live. The She-Ancient explains that children with anything wrong do not live in their community. The She-Ancient informs the Newly Born that she has four years of childhood ahead of her. The She-Ancient warns the Newly Born that she will eventually face an accident that will end her life.

Elinor expresses resentment regarding a compliment about Marian. Conolly feels undeserving of the compliment and questions if he will be forgiven for supplanting Marian's ideal partner. Elinor believes that Marian would not be attracted to unworthy individuals. Mrs. Leith Fairfax recognizes Douglas despite his changed appearance and attempts to engage him in conversation. Douglas is unaware of the impact of his literary work and lives in seclusion. Mrs. Leith Fairfax mentions a critic's praise of Douglas's unfinished drama and sonnets. Douglas expresses indifference towards literary distinction and prefers to discuss other topics.

Trefusis left his father-in-law's house in anger after a confrontation about his feelings for Hetty. Henrietta Trefusis was buried in Highgate Cemetery the day before Christmas Eve. Three noblemen attended the funeral in carriages, along with many friends and clients of Mr. Jansenius. The funeral included elaborate arrangements, such as long-tailed black horses and hired mourners. Mr. Jansenius expressed his grief during the burial, while a boy named Arthur felt conflicted about his emotions. Trefusis did not attend the funeral, leading to negative comments from family members and friends. Trefusis objected to an epitaph written for Henrietta, claiming it was untrue, and ordered a cheaper tombstone.

The Archbishop plans to organize long-lived people and bring them together. Burge-Lubin expresses concern about the Archbishop's plans. Confucius believes that nothing can stop the change that is occurring. The Negress communicates with Burge-Lubin from Fishguard Bay. The Negress invites Burge-Lubin to join her for the afternoon. Burge-Lubin learns that he may live longer than he expected. Confucius warns Burge-Lubin about the risks of traveling by parachute.

Marian expresses a strong reluctance to meet a man she refers to, stating she would prefer not to see him at all. Marian believes it is better for the man to be free and feels he was disappointed in her. Marian reflects on her growing independence and strength during her isolation. Marian acknowledges that taking care of another woman has helped her rely on herself more. Mrs. Crawford encourages Marian to stay for the evening, mentioning that the General wants to see her. Three visitors arrive during the evening, including a gentleman and his wife, who admire Marian's dress. Marian compares the visiting gentleman's politeness to that of English gentlemen and finds him overly respectful.

Marian expresses concern about her cousin Marmaduke's well-being. Conolly advises Marian not to meddle in Marmaduke's affairs. Marian believes that Marmaduke needs to be rescued from a bad influence in London. Conolly is aware that Marian's family wants Marmaduke to marry Lady Constance. Marian asserts that Marmaduke is honorable and not trifling with Lady Constance. Marian describes a woman in London as clever, handsome, and abominable, who has a negative influence on Marmaduke. Conolly intends to find out Marmaduke's address through the woman mentioned by Marian.

Shakespear's Hamlet is distinguished from his other plays by its moral complexity. Ibsen's work is considered superior to Shakespear's due to its original morality. Ibsen understands that ordinary people often cannot apply moral principles and rely on arbitrary rules of conduct. Writers of the first order challenge readymade morality, while those of the second order accept it as the basis for moral judgment. The author claims that their work, referred to as the Irrational Knot, features a non-readymade morality. The characters in the author's work exhibit their own moralities rather than conforming to societal norms. The author asserts that the themes in their work reflect a broader revolt against readymade morality in the nineteenth century.

Marian expresses silent distress when discussing a misfortune. Mr. Conolly does not consider his sister's profession a misfortune. Mr. Conolly questions Marian about her willingness to associate with his sister. Marian indicates she would not have the opportunity to associate with Mr. Conolly's sister. Mr. Conolly argues that marrying would not improve his sister's social standing. Mr. Conolly believes that societal opinions do not affect actresses. Mr. Conolly expresses ambition to become a noted man and possibly win the affections of a duchess.

Lady Carbury and Constance were in a carriage coming out of the Park. Constance recognized Marmaduke and Sholto Douglas while they were talking. The Countess asked the driver, Josephs, to slow down to speak to Marmaduke. Marmaduke expressed reluctance to engage with the Countess and Constance. The Countess invited Marmaduke to dinner, mentioning that the Bishop would be present. Marmaduke declined the invitation, citing his dislike for the Bishop. The Countess indicated that Marmaduke's reputation had improved and that he would be welcomed.

The Baal altar is not erected for the honor of God. A woman claimed to possess garments worth two hundred pounds. The speaker criticizes the value of the woman's attire as representing sin. The speaker questions the effectiveness of relying on appearances and wealth to combat sin. The speaker highlights the issue of sin in London, attributing it to the influence of Beelzebub. The speaker condemns hypocrisy and the false justification of sin in society. The speaker warns that individuals will ultimately be accountable for their own souls.

Miss Lind can sing an A note sometimes, but only when she is alone. Conolly perceives Miss Lind as a commonplace amateur compared to his sister. Miss McQuinch feels jealousy towards Miss Lind's singing skills. Douglas expresses a lack of interest in music and describes his disposition as not maudlin. Miss Lind receives respectful but not enthusiastic applause after her performance. Marmaduke makes light-hearted comments about the audience's reception of music. Marian and Douglas have a conversation about his presence and her comfort at the event.

Gertrude fainted and expressed regret for it. Mr. Trefusis offered to accompany Gertrude to the Beeches for safety. Gertrude insisted she did not need assistance and preferred to walk alone. Mr. Trefusis noted that Gertrude was not well and encouraged her to accept his help. Gertrude responded sharply to Mr. Trefusis, stating he was rude and officious. Mr. Trefusis criticized Gertrude's reaction and emphasized the responsibilities of being a lady. Gertrude expressed her disinterest in Mr. Trefusis's views during their conversation.

Marian often occupied the position of a guest, which trained her to impose constraints on herself. The speaker expresses anxiety over Marian's actions without his knowledge. The speaker visited Mr. Conolly to discuss his conduct toward Marian. The speaker believes Mr. Conolly is unsuitable for Marian due to his social and religious views. Marian asserts that she does not want to hear about Sholto Douglas. Marian feels angry about being told to leave the room during an incident with Sholto Douglas. Marian states that she has promised to marry Mr. Conolly and feels bound by that promise.

Elinor expresses doubt about Mr. Lind's authority over Marian. Mr. Lind requests Elinor to influence Marian to return. Elinor agrees to influence Marian only if Mr. Lind withdraws his opposition to her marriage. Mr. Lind states that Marian must choose between him and Mr. Conolly. Mr. Lind expresses frustration over Marian's potential marriage to Mr. Conolly. Mr. Lind suggests that the clergyman should negotiate with a woman associated with Marmaduke. The Rev. George Lind receives a letter with a blue satin bag inside.

The narrator is a married woman who desires her husband to return to her. Mrs. Miller is a professor at Alton College who disapproves of Miss Wilson's teaching methods. Mrs. Miller has a cat named Gracchus, also referred to as Bacchus. While correcting papers, Mrs. Miller hears a distressing cat cry and rushes to investigate. Agatha is a student who interacts with Mrs. Miller and is not affected by her disdain. Miss Ward enters the room and expresses dislike for Gracchus without noticing Mrs. Miller. A housemaid named Susan informs Mrs. Miller that Gracchus is asleep in her room.

The text discusses the potential for an election to be influenced by the death rate and scientific facts. Savvy and Haslam express amusement about old Lubin and Burge. Lubin and Savvy's father survived the war, but their sons were killed in it. Savvy mentions that Jim's death affected her mother significantly. Haslam reflects on the political incompetence of those who lost their sons in the war. Conrad and Franklyn discuss the reception of the gospel of the brothers Barnabas. The scene shifts to a summer afternoon in the year 2170 A.D. in the official parlor of the President of the British Islands.

Agatha expresses regret about her engagement to Trefusis. Sir Charles is concerned about Trefusis publicly associating his name with a cause he does not support. Jane believes Agatha wants to marry Trefusis as much as he wants to marry her. Trefusis informs Erskine that he is going to marry Agatha Wylie. Erskine initially suspects Trefusis of misleading him regarding his engagement. Trefusis advises Erskine not to let Gertrude marry for money. Agatha expresses a desire to leave and run away by the next train.

Zozim comes from the temple wearing a robe and a wreath of mistletoe. Zozim carries a staff with a curiously carved top. The oracle is delayed due to a member of the envoy's party. The envoy expresses a desire for a friendly chat about colonization. The envoy mentions the Turanian Empire and its emperor. Zozim states that the old uns prefer Mahometans. The elderly gentleman discusses the advantages of the Mahometan Reformation.

Buffon was considered a better Evolutionist than others mentioned. Empedocles proposed that all forms of life are transformations of four elements: Fire, Air, Earth, and Water. The Empedocleans and Evolutionists opposed the belief in the separate creation of all life as described in Genesis. Linnaeus, a famous botanist, initially believed in the separate creation of species but later questioned the possibility of species transmutation. Goethe suggested that all species share a common stock and that the environment influences their development. Erasmus Darwin, the grandfather of Charles Darwin, supported the idea of evolution and adaptation to the environment. Erasmus Darwin published his declaration of faith in 1794, defining the concept of evolution as a gradual process.

Agatha is sarcastic towards a gentleman who claims to be hiding from a romantic lady. The gentleman states that he proposed to the romantic lady and she accepted. Agatha feels a craving for a solitary hiding place before an impending interview with her guardian. Agatha is engaged in a tennis event where Smilash is preparing the courts and serving refreshments. A message is sent requesting Agatha's attendance, causing a distraction among the young ladies. Agatha finds her mother and two other women in a drawing-room, where her mother appears tearful. Mrs. Jansenius informs Agatha that her uncle is in the next room with Miss Wilson.

Mrs. Jansenius expresses hope that Agatha will not throw away her education. Mrs. Wylie informs Agatha that her Uncle John is angry and will not speak to her if she quarrels with Miss Wilson. Henrietta believes Uncle John is anxious for Agatha to succeed rather than angry. Mrs. Wylie urges Agatha to apologize to Miss Wilson for her previous comments. Agatha expresses indifference towards the pressure to apologize and leaves the room leisurely. Mr. Jansenius feels disconcerted by familiarity and irreverence from others. Agatha has a history of ridiculing Uncle John and feels contempt for his authority.

Marmaduke expresses his disdain for a woman he refers to as Constance. Marmaduke states that he has moved out of his father's home due to uncomfortable circumstances. Marmaduke lives at a place in Hammersmith with Lalage Virtue, whose real name is Susanna Conolly. Lalage Virtue is the sister of Marian's husband and Marian's sister-in-law. Marmaduke describes Lalage as a highly skilled and versatile woman. Marmaduke reveals that Lalage has developed a serious drinking problem. Marmaduke expresses concern about the impact of Lalage's behavior on their child.

The Elderly Gentleman is the President of the Baghdad Historical Society. The Elderly Gentleman believes that communities that sought immortality were the most wretched in history. The Elderly Gentleman criticizes the pursuit of long life, stating it has caused unnecessary pain and labor in his life. The Elderly Gentleman accepts a lifespan of seventy years and values usefulness, justice, mercy, and goodwill over longevity. Zozim expresses skepticism about the Elderly Gentleman's views on living three centuries. The Elderly Gentleman feels that the difference in lifespans is insignificant in the context of eternity.

Mr. Lind expresses astonishment at the actions of a fellow he believes has had opportunities to associate with Marian. Mr. Lind reflects on his past experiences with Marian's mother, who left him for a charlatan. Douglas indicates he is unable to discuss recent events and leaves the room after expressing feelings of betrayal. Mr. Lind is left alone, feeling discomfited and pacing the room before going to bed. Marian is in her room, trying to manage her hysteria while Elinor expresses her disdain for Mr. Lind. Elinor criticizes both Mr. Lind and Douglas, expressing satisfaction with her own responses during the recent conflict. Marian feels conflicted about her father's actions and acknowledges her own deception regarding her engagement.

Church-going is practiced because it is respectable and is a habit of the upper caste. Marian is involved in business matters that she does not want others to interfere with. The clergyman visiting Conolly intended to borrow a portmanteau. Conolly wrote a letter to Marian discussing visits from Mrs. Fairfax and George. Mrs. Fairfax expressed concern for Marian's well-being and suggested she should not be left alone. The clergyman's portmanteau burst while traveling from Edinburgh. Conolly converted a spare room into a laboratory and is considering fitting it up like a studio.

Marian expresses a desire to go home but feels sorry to leave her current location. Marian plans to inform someone about her train schedule but states they do not need to meet her. Marian feels disgusted with everything and everyone at the moment. Marian and Elinor are drinking tea in the drawing-room at Holland Park on a Saturday afternoon in December. Elinor no longer resides with the Conollys and is visiting Marian. Marian acknowledges that she loved Ned when she married him and still loves him. Elinor comments on Marian's change in attitude towards reading her last book.

The elderly gentleman expresses a desire to drown himself. A man with the number one on his cap intercepts the elderly gentleman at the pier. The woman uses a tuning fork and mentions Burrin Pier before leaving. The elderly gentleman feels that the woman has been of no help and accuses her of taking his shilling. The man explains the classification of people into primaries, secondaries, and tertiaries based on their ages. The elderly gentleman identifies himself as Joseph Popham Bolge Bluebin Barlow, O.M. The man suggests calling the elderly gentleman 'Daddy' instead of using his full name.

The protagonist feels that her companion intends to abandon her. She expresses her anger and frustration when pressed for a response. They arrive at a wharf and walk through a lane to the main street of Lyvern. The protagonist realizes her opportunity to appeal to her companion has passed. She is hesitant to create a scene in public due to fear and her emotional state. The companion returns alone to the chalet and is met by two policemen. Agatha frequently breaks Rule No. 17 at Alton College, which prohibits disturbing the kitchen staff.

Marian expresses a fear that Ned may harm her as they go downstairs. Ned asks Marian if she will return to their life at Holland Park. Marian declines to return, stating she would disgrace him. Ned argues that Marian's perceived disgrace does not affect him. Ned believes that freedom is an illusion and that true choice comes with consequences. Marian acknowledges the value of freedom but feels she should not return. Ned accepts that Marian may refuse his offer and indicates he will adapt to either outcome.

Mrs. Leith Fairfax, Conolly, and Douglas left the gathering after saying goodbye to Marmaduke and Elinor. Elinor planned to walk to St. James's Street to take a carriage home through the park. Douglas offered to accompany Elinor and her party to the club. Conolly returned to his sister's carriage after Elinor and the others left. Susanna informed Conolly that she had become an aunt to a girl named Lucy. Conolly and Susanna discussed their current lives and past experiences in the theatre. Douglas received a lunch invitation from Mr. Lind at his club on Monday morning.

ZOO appears in a purple robe at the temple doorway. The Envoy, the Elderly Gentleman, the Wife, and the Daughter enter the temple, following ZOO. Zozim remains alone in the portico after removing his disguise. Inside the temple, a gallery overlooks an abyss, and a violet light shoots upward. The characters express awe and prepare for the appearance of the pythoness. ZOO dismisses the significance of the temple's atmosphere and advises the others to keep their wits about them. The pythoness rises from the abyss, terrifying the onlookers.

Marian entered the room and asked about a duet. Douglas mentioned that he left his father asleep in the dining-room. Elinor expressed annoyance at the admiration for a particular photograph. Douglas and Elinor discussed past memories and photographs. Elinor recalled that she had a childhood impression of Douglas as a demigod. Douglas and Marian planned to sit outside under a tent. Marian requested a woolen item from the sofa to use as a shawl.

The troops want to go home and enjoy the glory they have earned. The risk of death for each soldier increases with prolonged fighting. Napoleon believes that his life holds greater value than that of his soldiers. Napoleon feels trapped between the desire for victory and the consequences of war. The Oracle advises Napoleon to die before his glory diminishes. Napoleon accuses the Oracle of lacking respect for human life after she shoots him. Zoo arrives with a party that includes the British Envoy and his family.

The characters in the text are engaged in a conversation about a letter and feelings of love and jealousy. Henrietta expresses anger and indignation towards Sidney regarding his affections for Agatha. Sidney finds humor in the situation and reflects on the nature of love and relationships. Henrietta accuses Sidney of being selfish and not considering her feelings. Sidney acknowledges his selfishness and questions Henrietta's right to be upset about his interactions with Agatha. Henrietta insists that Sidney has no right to express affection towards anyone but her. The conversation escalates to the point where Henrietta threatens to leave despite the lack of transportation.

The Male Figure and the Female Figure engage in a conversation about their nature. Arjillax expresses a desire to destroy the automata. The Newly Born and others express loathing towards the automata. The He-Ancient describes the automata as mere reflexive beings without self-control. The Male Figure offers to sacrifice himself to spare the Female Figure. The Female Figure expresses a willingness to die alongside the Male Figure. The bodies of the automata and Pygmalion are ordered to be taken away and disposed of.

Marian had a twenty pound note and a few loose dollars in her purse. Marian decided to move into cheap lodging and live economically due to her limited funds. Marian expressed uncertainty about her financial situation and whether she had forfeited her property by eloping. Mrs. Crawford is fifty years old and described as stout but leaner in the face than typical Englishwomen of her age. Marian revealed to Mrs. Crawford that she had left her husband and had about one hundred dollars. Mrs. Crawford advised Marian to return to her husband, suggesting that all men are a bit selfish. Marian clarified to Mrs. Crawford that Mr. Forster is not her husband.

Sir Charles expressed a desire to never enter a certain house again. Trefusis wrote a letter to Donovan Brown discussing two individuals he encountered. One individual mentioned in Trefusis's letter is a baronet and amateur artist who signed a petition after being introduced to Donovan Brown's name. The second individual is Chichester Erskine, a young poet who signed the petition reluctantly. Trefusis mentioned a young lady who could serve as a model for Hypatia and expressed a desire to marry her to Erskine. Agatha was reading on the doorstep of the conservatory when Trefusis approached her. Trefusis observed the movements of several individuals using a field-glass from the roof of his house.

Sholto Douglas appeared at Kew Gardens on a Sunday afternoon. Marian approached Sholto Douglas while he was gazing at the waterfowl. Sholto Douglas experienced a moment of revulsion upon seeing Marian, recognizing a dangerous passion. Marian and Sholto Douglas exchanged pleasantries about their health and appearances. Marian mentioned that her husband, Mr. Conolly, was studying Eucalyptus species nearby. Sholto Douglas acknowledged that he had not seen Marian since he got married. Marian expressed a preference for flowers over trees while at the gardens.

Savvy expresses skepticism about the fixed nature of wages and distribution in political economy. Lubin acknowledges Savvy's perspective but is surprised by her dismissal of Karl Marx's economics. Savvy rejects both Karl Marx's economics and Darwin's theories, calling them outdated. Franklyn comments on Savvy's lack of manners due to her youth. Lubin admits to being open to new ideas despite his busy professional life. Lubin offers to present the case to the House or the country if provided with necessary documents. Lubin states he has no objection to labeling the current state of affairs as Socialism.

Darwinism has prompted a reaction aimed at achieving a new Reformation and establishing a credible religion. Samuel Butler was a pioneer in the reaction against Darwinism. Physiologists are divided into Mechanists, who view life as physical and chemical action, and Vitalists, who believe in a Vital Force that distinguishes living from dead bodies. The Old Vitalists were criticized by the New Vitalists for their mechanical conception of life. The New Vitalist perspective has evolved from the Old Mechanist view and incorporates metaphysical elements. The discovery of Evolution has contributed to the development of metaphysical Vitalism as a more concrete belief system. Protestantism emphasizes the importance of individual perception of an inner light over reliance on religious authorities.

Marian expresses her intention to withdraw. Miss McQuinch states that she played poorly on the piano. Conolly asks who will accompany him for his song. Miss McQuinch declines to accompany Conolly due to her performance. Marian offers to accompany Conolly despite her self-identified lack of skill. Conolly and Marian perform together, and she is surprised by his singing ability. Mrs. Leith Fairfax expresses interest in Conolly's performance.

The Elderly Gentleman is a retired chairman and currently serves as president of the British Historical and Archaeological Society. The Elderly Gentleman was born in Baghdad and claims he does not need a mental health resort. The Woman indicates that the Elderly Gentleman is on the west coast of Ireland, where natives of the Eastern Island seek mental flexibility. The Elderly Gentleman offers a shilling as compensation for potential trespassing. The Elderly Gentleman states that the Prime Minister, Mr. Badger Bluebin, is his son-in-law and is visiting with family. General Aufsteig, who is part of the Elderly Gentleman's party, is identified as the Emperor of Turania traveling incognito. The Woman expresses confusion over the Elderly Gentleman's presence and questions the necessity of his visit.

Agatha is referred to as a 'golden idol' by a male character. Agatha expresses confusion about being called a 'golden idol'. Agatha believes she is a commonplace person. The male character suggests that Agatha does not see herself as others see her. Agatha feels a sense of alarm about her situation and expresses a desire to leave. Mrs. Trefusis finds her parents unsympathetic regarding her marriage. Mrs. Trefusis discusses her husband's flight with a friend who finds his behavior scandalous.

The characters express disdain for tradespeople and country squires. One character respects their father for working hard, despite his unethical actions. The text critiques the artistic class for their perceived superiority and entitlement. It argues that artists seek financial advantages over laborers despite similar work demands. The text suggests that artists are often celebrated for their work while being compared unfavorably to laborers. One character mentions a specific example of a girl who supported her family through drawing. The character feels trapped in their position as a landlord and capitalist.

Art is described as an illusion. The statue is said to come to life always. The characters discuss the nature of existence and the body. The He-Ancient expresses a desire to be a vortex. The She-Ancient states that the body is intolerable and imprisons them. The Ancients find it difficult to communicate with the younger generation. Acis acknowledges the challenge of living for thousands of years.

The conversation involves two characters discussing love and personal feelings. One character expresses a sense of hopelessness in love and a desire to live without memories or future concerns. The other character comments on the first character's comfort and perceived laziness. There is a mention of a third character named Ned, who is envied by one of the speakers. The dialogue explores the nature of love, with one character claiming to have never experienced true love. The conversation includes reflections on life, purpose, and the perception of love as a significant or insignificant factor. The characters engage in a playful exchange about their perceptions of beauty and compliments.

The speaker argues that gentility alone does not guarantee suitability as a husband. Marian is satisfied with the speaker's manners and character. The speaker claims to be the first in his trade and asserts the superiority of his rank. The clergyman reveals that he knows a secret about Mr. Marmaduke Lind. The clergyman warns that Marian is about to marry someone living in sin with their cousin. The speaker states that he has already informed Marian about the situation before proposing. The clergyman expresses his inability to understand Marian's feelings and plans to speak to her.

Mrs. Hickling was imprisoned for seven days for taking an old wooden gate from Sir Charles Brandon's land. Mrs. Hickling expressed defiance towards Sir Charles Brandon during their conversation. Sir Charles Brandon accused Mrs. Hickling of taking the first half of his garden gate the previous Saturday. Gertrude has changed since she poisoned herself and has been in a vile temper for two days afterward. Agatha noted that Gertrude falls into long reveries and does not hear what is going on around her. Erskine has become more attentive to Gertrude, who previously snubbed him. Sir Charles Brandon suggested that Jane should write her own letters instead of asking Miss Wylie for help.

Gertrude is advised by Trefusis to marry Erskine. Trefusis believes that love alone cannot sustain a relationship. Trefusis expresses concern about Gertrude's potential marriage for wealth and position. Erskine is described as a poor man who is honorable and loves Gertrude. Gertrude's family is expected to disapprove of her marrying Erskine. Trefusis argues that marriage is a function that requires fulfillment. Gertrude expresses uncertainty about marrying at all.

Mdlle. Lalage Virtue has received severe criticism in a paper for her performance. Sholto Douglas entered a hold in New York and went to a room on the first floor. Marian was sitting in the room with a letter in her lap. Sholto Douglas mentioned that someone has filed a petition for divorce. Marian acknowledged that she was aware of the divorce petition. Sholto Douglas expressed dissatisfaction with their current situation in New York. Marian stated that her husband's suit cannot be defended.

The speaker identifies as a gentleman and asserts a commitment to honesty in belief. The speaker emphasizes the importance of scientific assumptions for forming human society. The elderly gentleman acknowledges the significance of scientific discoveries but argues that anyone can make discoveries. The speaker claims that scientific discoveries have discredited traditional religious beliefs. The elderly gentleman notes that as astronomy advanced, belief in a deity residing in the sky diminished. The speaker argues that discoveries have not increased wisdom but have only increased knowledge. The conversation includes a discussion on the difference between consciousness of a fact and true knowledge.

Smilash was serving guests while wearing a white apron and gloves. Miss Wilson and her visitors arrived as Smilash was returning to the table with an empty tray. Smilash accidentally collided with Mrs. Jansenius and did not apologize. Smilash threw his tray into the air, which landed on Josephs. Agatha and Henrietta encountered Smilash in the shrubbery, where Agatha played a practical joke. Henrietta fainted, and Smilash caught her in his arms. The news of Henrietta's fainting spread, prompting a search party to form.

Strephon enters the temple, expressing that his heart is broken. Ecrasia looks for another partner but finds that everyone has left. A vague radiance near the temple shapes into the ghost of Adam. The ghost of Eve appears in response to Adam's call. The ghost of Cain, the first child and murderer, appears between Adam and Eve. The serpent, who taught Adam and Eve, becomes visible coiled in the trees. Lilith, who claims to have suffered to create man and woman, appears between Cain and Adam.

The race learns in a manner similar to the individual. A child relapses to a point indistinguishable from the beginning of learning. Certain habits are transmitted without noticeable relapse. Breathing and blood circulation are automatic habits that begin at birth. Complex habits require conscious effort to acquire, unlike automatic habits. The Lamarckian evolutionary process suggests development can occur without Circumstantial Selection. Individuals may lose control over habits they have acquired unconsciously.

Eve expresses concern about dying before Adam. Adam acknowledges the possibility of new Eves but believes they would not be the same. Eve suggests that new Adams and Eves would create a garden of strangers. The Serpent implies that the new Adams and Eves might kill them. Adam believes that a voice in the garden will prevent new beings from killing. Eve states that she does not want Adam to die before her. Adam expresses feelings of uncertainty and fear about the future.

Gertrude took a pair of gardening gloves from her hand-basket and began working with hemlock leaves. Trefusis was standing a few yards away, watching Gertrude while Max, the dog, was trying to get Trefusis's hand into his mouth. Gertrude experienced a sensation of something happening above her and found herself lying on the ground with her parasol over her eyes. Trefusis helped Gertrude sit up and reassured her that she did not need to go home. Gertrude insisted that she must go home, stating it was a matter of life or death. Trefusis explained that Gertrude had fainted after inhaling the scent of water-hemlock while gathering it. Gertrude expressed surprise at the danger of hemlock and felt tired after regaining consciousness.

The house described is dilapidated and has broken flooring and patched windows. Three families occupied the best room in the house at the time of the photograph. The landlord of the house holds it from a peer and lets it out in tenements. Seven inhabitants of the house had previously worked in the speaker's father's mill. The speaker's father replaced many workers with a machine he purchased for fifty pounds. The speaker's father was a successful tradesman and a member of a secret society. The speaker claims to possess very little wealth, most of which was spent long ago.

The Maiden expresses that she no longer feels attraction towards Strephon. Strephon comments on the rapid aging of The Maiden. The Maiden acknowledges her transition from childhood to maturity. Strephon reminds The Maiden of their vow made in the temple of love. The Maiden believes the vow has broken itself due to her change. Acis informs Strephon that the hour of birth is overdue. An Ancient Woman approaches the altar and addresses Strephon.

The physician felt uneasy in conversation with Trefusis. Henrietta's pain did not serve any good purpose according to the physician. The physician believed that the general practitioner had treated Henrietta unskilfully. Trefusis asked if Henrietta knew she was dying. The physician decided not to inform Henrietta of her danger. The general practitioner entered after the physician left. Mrs. Jansenius requested the doctor to excuse Mr. Jansenius due to his grief.

Douglas visited his mother twice in one week. Marian visited Douglas's mother without prior notice. Douglas expressed a lack of interest in visiting Marian's house frequently. Douglas's mother expressed concern about potential unpleasantness with Marian's partner, Conolly. Douglas described Conolly as sensible and not savage. Douglas left his mother's house to avoid spending the afternoon with her. Marmaduke Lind approached Douglas to invite him to lunch at the South Kensington Museum.

The poet was inspired to write a drama entitled 'Hypatia' after falling in love with Gertrude Lindsay. Gertrude Lindsay had Grecian features and knowledge of calculus acquired at Alton. Sir Charles and Erskine were in the picture gallery when the ladies came downstairs. Lady Brandon ordered that luncheon not be served until the arrival of another gentleman. Mr. Trefusis entered the scene in a snuff-colored coat and was indifferent to the social dynamics. Trefusis expressed skepticism about the meaning of an etching presented to him. Trefusis stated that photography is a more perfect process than etching and portrait painting.

The speaker claims to have never deceived the listener or told falsehoods. The speaker expresses frustration over the listener's inability to communicate truthfully. Marian acknowledges that she has deserved unkind words from the speaker. The speaker criticizes societal influences that led to the downfall of a woman named Eliza. Eliza is described as clever and good-natured but ultimately succumbed to a preventable disease. Marian expresses concern about the speaker's potential actions regarding Eliza's altar. The speaker and Marian discuss the implications of beliefs held by an Irish Catholic servant.

The Archbishop expects to live for three hundred years. Barnabas expresses doubt about the Archbishop's longevity. Burge-Lubin speculates that he may share the same fate as the Archbishop. The Archbishop mentions that Burge-Lubin's ancestor believed he would live for three hundred years. Burge-Lubin's ancestor was shot due to his belief in his longevity. The Domestic Minister is required to report to the President once a quarter. The Domestic Minister enters the room and is described as a handsome woman.

The conversation involves two individuals discussing their thoughts and feelings while walking. One individual reflects on the topic of housemaids' knee and the maintenance of steps. The individual expresses a desire to replace the current steps with materials that are easier to clean. The other individual defends the current state of the house and questions the disparagement of the housemaid, Armande. Miss McQuinch arrives and is noted to look older with a drier complexion but has improved her appearance. Marian is complimented on her beauty, which is a change from previous observations. Miss McQuinch has been waiting for about fifteen minutes and admires the organ in the house.

Jane expresses that the house would be dull without her presence. Agatha criticizes Jane's behavior and suggests she should wash her face. Jane pleads with Agatha not to pursue her husband, Sir Charles. Agatha finds amusement in Jane's distress and plans to look for Sir Charles. Sir Charles is found in the library, avoiding domestic troubles. Erskine and Gertrude engage in a game of billiards, but their conversation remains trivial. Erskine struggles to express his feelings for Gertrude during their game.

Trefusis expresses a desire to part from Henrietta due to their relationship hindering their usefulness. Trefusis suggests that they can communicate or meet after their separation. A barge is mentioned, which Trefusis intends to take to Lyvern. A man with a whip is described as trudging beside a horse that tows the barge. Trefusis discusses the concept of labor and the treatment of workers with the man beside the horse. Trefusis carries Henrietta over a plank to the barge. Henrietta expresses frustration about discussing the troubles of other women.

The conversation takes place between Douglas and Marian regarding their feelings for each other. Douglas expresses confusion about Marian's regard for him before the London season. Marian indicates that she does not wish to engage in jealousy or misunderstandings. Douglas believes he has received unequivocal signs of Marian's affection. Marian denies any romantic feelings towards Douglas and wishes to remain friends. Douglas decides not to pursue Marian further, feeling she does not appreciate his passion. Marian critiques Douglas's demeanor, suggesting he is emotionally cold.

The note was written on scented paper and decorated with a miniature representation of a pierrot. The note was addressed to Mr. George from Lalage Virtue and mentioned plans involving a girl named Lucy. The Rev. George put the note in a rack over the mantelpiece before transferring it to his pocket. After breakfast, the Rev. George traveled by rail from Sloane Square to West Kensington and walked to Laurel Grove. An elderly maid opened the gate for the Rev. George and led him through the shrubbery to the house. Susanna was dressed in a luxurious costume and asked the clergyman for his opinion on its correctness as Eastern dress. The clergyman expressed that he was not an Orientalist and his studies were different from Susanna's.

The conversation takes place in a drawing-room. Marian sent a note indicating she would be out and that the other person was away. Marian was at home the previous day except for two hours when she was out with Sholto. Marian packed her trunks and left, instructing the cabman to drive to Euston. The other person has a note on their dressing-table that may contain an explanation. The other person does not wish to open the note and expresses indifference. The conversation ends with a suggestion to follow Marian and bring her back.

Trefusis expressed that a man with a conscience has no choice in matters of conviction. Trefusis initially hesitated to sign a petition due to distrust of the rulers. Donovan Brown encouraged Trefusis to sign the petition to support laborers. Sir Charles agreed to sign the petition after Trefusis's encouragement. Erskine was uncertain about signing the petition but ultimately decided to do so. After signing, Erskine expressed regret about visiting Trefusis and signing the petition. Sir Charles dismissed Erskine's concerns about Trefusis and the petition.

The conversation involves a request for assistance in finding lodging. Mrs. Crawford expresses confusion and concern about the situation. The speaker, identified as Marian, insists on facing the world alone. Marian reveals that Mr. Forster's real name is Douglas. Mrs. Crawford is surprised by Marian's revelation about Douglas. Marian states that she has no right to her former name and requests to be called by her assumed name. Mrs. Crawford suggests a place for Marian to stay that she previously lived in.

Marian is concerned about living in a new area and expresses this to her companion. Mrs. Myers is the landlady of the boarding house where Marian is considering staying. Marian is informed that there is a woman living on the same floor who is often drunk. Marian decides to accept the room despite the presence of the other tenant. Marian sends a telegram to her friend Elinor regarding her new address. Douglas has paid all expenses related to Marian's stay at the hotel before leaving. Mrs. Crawford offers to assist Marian with her luggage and suggests she have lunch before returning.

The snake has invented poison for protection. Cain expresses a desire not to kill women or his mother. Cain wants his mother to create more men and women. Cain imagines leading two great hosts of men in battle. Eve feels reduced to a mere convenience for creating men. Cain rejects living a life like his father's, preferring to hunt and fight. Eve expresses anger towards Cain's boasting about Lua.

The doctor was offended by a statement regarding death. Mrs. Jansenius observed Trefusis's behavior and confirmed her negative opinion of him. Trefusis left the room after feeling out of sympathy with the others. Trefusis hesitated before entering a room where a woman indicated someone was present. Trefusis experienced a painful sensation and turned pale upon seeing his wife's lifeless body. Trefusis reflected on his feelings of grief and relief regarding his wife's death. Trefusis addressed the dead figure of his wife, expressing complex emotions about their relationship.

Trefusis plans to order a hansom after his journey. The doctor expresses concern about Trefusis's prompt decisions. Trefusis believes Jansenius may react poorly to personal loss. The doctor suggests Trefusis go upstairs to see something related to Henrietta. Trefusis refuses to spare feelings for the living and expresses frustration. Mrs. Jansenius listens to Trefusis and the doctor discussing the situation. Trefusis states he has no complaints regarding the care Henrietta received.

Cain expresses a desire to reject the earth and its labor, preferring a higher existence. Adam emphasizes the importance of the earth and its ability to sustain life. Eve criticizes Cain's thoughts about rejecting human existence and the implications of his desires. Cain claims he does not want to be a bear or eat children, but seeks something nobler. Adam and Cain engage in a confrontation, with Adam threatening Cain with his spade. Eve intervenes to calm Adam and Cain, expressing dissatisfaction with both their approaches to life.

Researchers conducted experiments on dogs to understand the function of glands by removing them or altering their nerves. Lorenz Oken contributed to the understanding of uninjured creatures by exploring the concept of the Holy Ghost. Schopenhauer published his treatise on The World as Will in 1819, linking the driving force behind Evolution to a will-to-live. The pre-Darwin period was characterized by ongoing discussions about Evolution, contrary to the belief that it was a pre-evolutionary time. Goethe highlighted the significance of the debate between Cuvier and St Hilaire regarding the number of species in the French Academy. From 1830 to 1859, there was a decline in the popularity of Evolutionism, coinciding with Darwin's early life and education. Darwin's work, Origin of Species, published in 1859, reintroduced the topic of Evolution after a period of stagnation.

The boy took the money and ran off quickly. Trefusis left the chalet and locked the door behind him. Trefusis was picked up by a trap and taken to the railway station. Trefusis traveled on a London train for nearly three hours. Upon arriving in London, Trefusis was driven to his father-in-law's house in Belsize Avenue. Trefusis was informed by a maid that the doctor would see him immediately. The physician informed Trefusis that he had arrived too late and that all was over.

Mr. Conolly expresses doubt about the effectiveness of the clergyman's influence over Marian. The clergyman believes that a priest may have better success in appealing to duty than a father to affection. It is raining when the clergyman leaves Mr. Conolly's house. Marian has run away to Mrs. Toplis's at St. Mary's Terrace. Elinor is accused of corrupting Marian, which she denies. Mr. Lind orders Elinor to occupy her rooms until she returns to her parents. Mr. Lind offers to cover Elinor's expenses until she goes to Wiltshire.

The speaker agrees with the proposal and states there will be no coalition this time. Every candidate must pledge to Free Trade, Disestablishment, Reform of the House of Lords, revised Taxation of Land Values, and measures regarding Ireland. FRANKLYN expresses disinterest in the proposal and criticizes the political views of the speaker's friends. FRANKLYN argues that the supporters of the Church are united, while the speaker's group is divided. BURGE claims to stand for liberty of conscience. FRANKLYN accuses BURGE's party of being a mix of conflicting ideologies that would lead to failure. BURGE denies responsibility for past political actions and attributes them to a former Prime Minister.

Conolly expresses a desire to invest money and discusses the potential for repayment through inventions. Miss Lind indicates she has experience with money through managing household affairs. Lord Carbury interrupts a conversation between Conolly and Miss Lind. A letter from Marmaduke arrives, addressed to Lady Constance. Elinor reads the letter from Marmaduke, which mentions his enjoyable time in Paris and a silk gift for Constance. Marian accuses Elinor of hurting Constance by revealing that Marmaduke did not propose. Elinor and Marian speculate about the identity of a companion mentioned in Marmaduke's letter.

Mr. Conolly learned to dance and bow before he was twelve years old from an experienced master in Europe. Mr. Conolly mixed with counts, dukes, and queens in his father's opera company. Marian expressed concern that Miss McQuinch would be wondering about her whereabouts. Mr. Conolly stated he must return to town by the last train that night. Mr. Reginald Harrington Lind visited Mrs. Douglas in Manchester Square. Mrs. Douglas is a widow lady older than Mr. Lind and has a rather glassy eye and shaky hand. Sholto was away for two years, traveling in Paris, Venice, and Florence.

MRS LUTESTRING questions the Archbishop about his age. BURGE-LUBIN jokingly claims the Archbishop is two hundred and eighty-three years old. BURGE-LUBIN expresses frustration with the ongoing discussion. BARNABAS insists on uncovering the truth behind a supposed swindle. MRS LUTESTRING claims to have met the Archbishop before. MRS LUTESTRING states her age as two hundred and seventy-four. BURGE-LUBIN acknowledges MRS LUTESTRING's age after initially denying it.

Marian wrote a letter stating that her marriage was a mistake and that she is leaving with Douglas. Mr. Conolly is advised to pursue Marian and Douglas and to show that he cares. Elinor expresses grief and blames Mr. Conolly for the situation with Marian. Mr. Conolly acknowledges that it is too late to change the situation. Elinor criticizes Mr. Conolly for not valuing Marian's happiness. Armande informs Mr. Conolly that dinner is ready and that the mistress was particular about it. Mr. Conolly reflects on his loss of Marian and her role in managing the household.

Miss McQuinch expressed her disdain for Marmaduke. Miss McQuinch listed several grievances against various individuals, including Sholto and George. Mrs. Fairfax became talkative after consuming sherry but soon began to yawn. The audience showed little interest in the performances, including Miss McQuinch's and the concertinists'. Conolly and Marian sang 'Tom Bowling,' which was well received by the audience. Marmaduke declined Marian's offer to share a carriage after the concert. Marmaduke and Conolly decided to take a hansom to see Lalage Virtue in the burlesque.

The She-Ancient addresses Arjillax and Ecrasia regarding their artistic pursuits. Arjillax expresses dissatisfaction with modeling children. Ecrasia believes that art is essential to make reality bearable. Acis prefers real human connections over dolls and statues. The He-Ancient asserts that individuals can create only themselves. Ecrasia argues that the ancients would understand the importance of beauty in art. The He-Ancient acknowledges that even ancients have their troubles.

The child is impatient to be born and is shouting and kicking. The She-Ancient instructs to bring the child out into the sun. A procession emerges from the temple carrying a huge egg covered with a pall. The egg is opened by the She-Ancient, revealing a Newly Born girl. The Newly Born girl is described as pretty and fresh, with albumen clinging to her. The Newly Born is named Amaryllis by Acis. Amaryllis expresses love for Acis and desires to be held.

The text discusses the labor conditions of children working in a lace school. The lace school is described as a filthy room, twelve feet square, where children worked for fifteen hours a day. The children in the lace school were not allowed to wear boots to prevent muddy lace. The text mentions the United States of America as a place where black chattel slaves were turned into wage-slaves. The author contrasts the physical characteristics of his mother with those of a Lancashire lass, suggesting they might be sisters. The text includes a comparison between a bargee on the Lyvern Canal and a senior nobleman of the British Peerage. The author refers to a group of individuals labeled as enemies of society, including Nihilists, Anarchists, and Communards.

Marian ran to a terrace of the Cottage to access a glass-roofed apartment. A man sat at a large table in the room, working with a small round block and pegs. The man was wearing a large straw hat and was focused on an instrument resembling a small clock. Marian mistakenly thought the man was Lord Carbury and apologized for disturbing him. The man introduced himself as Mr. Conolly and stated he was only a workman. Conolly explained some aspects of electricity to Marian, who was impressed by his knowledge. Conolly commented on Lord Carbury's scientific capabilities and resources.

In photography, thought and judgment are considered more important than drawing. In etching and daubing, execution is valued more than thought due to the manual skill required. Literature is produced by printers and papermakers, making the author's physical ability less critical to their work. The speaker suggests that photography will replace much of painting and historical pictures in the future. The speaker predicts that musical instruments will become more manageable, reducing the need for extensive technical skill. The speaker believes that works of fiction will be replaced by engaging conversation and that the concept of art will change. Trefusis argues that starvation for artists is largely a result of societal structures, not a lack of demand for art.

Mrs. Fairfax expresses doubt about Mr. Conolly's feelings regarding a conversation they had. Mr. Conolly acknowledges that he has observed circumstances affecting Marian's welfare. Mrs. Fairfax advises Mr. Conolly not to mention her in any correspondence with Marian. Mrs. Fairfax reveals her concern for Marian's well-being and expresses her lack of personal interest in her. Mr. Conolly shows gratitude towards Mrs. Fairfax for her honesty and concern. Mrs. Fairfax leaves Mr. Conolly's presence after expressing her worries about Marian. The Rev. George arrives shortly after Mrs. Fairfax departs to visit Mr. Conolly.

Legends are a common heritage of the human race, but should not be believed literally. Don Quixote's enjoyment of stories made him a gentleman, while believing them literally led to his madness. In England, good books of Eastern religious legends are read by Protestants and Atheists, while Indians and Roman Catholics tend to avoid them. Freethinkers are currently the primary readers of the Bible, aside from some reluctant parsons. The belief in legends as literal truths transforms them from parables into falsehoods. There is a suggestion to pool legends from various cultures to create a shared religious folklore. The text argues that the sweetness of religion is conveyed through storytelling and that the perception of fictions as literal truths hinders understanding.

Jane was reluctant to leave because she was jealous of Gertrude potentially gaining Agatha's affection. Agatha complimented the house and Sir Charles after Jane's departure. Agatha remarked that Jane had married in her first season and considered Sir Charles a man of great culture. Gertrude expressed disapproval of Agatha's language and was serious about it. Agatha suggested that Jane wanted to help her and Gertrude find husbands. Gertrude resolved to discourage the attentions of Chichester Erskine, suspecting he was recommended by Jane. Chichester Erskine was a young man of gentle birth who had published a tragedy and was interested in fine art.

Conolly expresses interest in the operations being discussed. The conversation includes a mention of Sark and a suggestion for one party to visit. Mrs. Fairfax is mentioned as having come for a book she lent. The clergyman indicates that Marian is alone and Conolly suggests that Douglas is involved with her. Conolly asserts that Douglas is in love with Marian and that she is aware of it. The clergyman is surprised by Conolly's views on Marian's education and feelings. Conolly criticizes the education Marian received, claiming it is based on misrepresentations.

Agatha expresses amusement at being called ill-bred. Miss Lindsay does not understand Agatha's perspective on moral science. Agatha retrieves a book titled MY FAULTS from a shelf. Sarah Gerram confesses to slapping Miss Chambers and knocking out her tooth. Helen Plantagenet confesses to taking first place in algebra unfairly with Miss Lindsay's prompting. Agatha tickles Gertrude, who reacts with distress. The characters discuss who should record their faults first.

Mr. Conolly demonstrated an electric engine that minimizes waste compared to steam engines. Electricity is a stronger force than steam but has historically been less utilized due to cost factors. Conolly's electric motor can produce six-horsepower while weighing less than thirty pounds. Conolly claimed that flying machines capable of transporting passengers could be developed within a few years. Douglas expressed skepticism about the feasibility of flying machines. Conolly showcased various models, including a locomotive and a sewing machine, emphasizing their low operational costs. Douglas felt uncomfortable during the exhibition, perceiving a knowledge gap between himself and Conolly.

The conversation takes place at the South Pole. The Elderly Gentleman expresses a refusal to know a man he sees almost every day. The Elderly Gentleman has attended the Summer Sports at the South Pole twice. The Elderly Gentleman disapproves of microscopes and believes they can lead to dangerous perceptions. The text mentions a general massacre of men of science in the twenty-first century of the pseudo-Christian era. The extension of life to three hundred years is noted as having provided capable leaders. ZOO and The Elderly Gentleman discuss the implications of scientific knowledge and its impact on imagination.

The process of discarding an organ or habit is slow and often interrupted by relapses. Relapses in habit acquisition occur both at the individual level and across generations. Raphael, despite his lineage of painters, had to learn to paint as if no one before him had done so. Embryonic development involves a return to a basic state, starting as a speck of protoplasm. The process of human development condenses millions of years of evolution into a nine-month period. The concept of recapitulation suggests that individuals must undergo a condensed version of human history during development. Some individuals can perform complex tasks, such as chess, with ease, contrasting with the struggles of others.

Mr. Haslam is introduced as the Rector. Savvy has not written any books. Savvy's name is short for Savage. Lubin's favorite poet is Horace, specifically Quintus Horatius Flaccus. Burge believes the Church can be progressive if certain elements are removed. Savvy expresses interest in the Labor movement, Theosophy, and post-war reconstruction. Lubin prefers to engage in conversation with Savvy rather than discuss politics.

Marmaduke overtook Lalage while she was walking. Lalage did not respond to Marmaduke's attempts to communicate. Marmaduke threatened Lalage and physically restrained her by putting his hand on her arm. Lalage struck Marmaduke across the face, knocking off his hat. A crowd gathered after the altercation, and a cabman approached the scene. Lalage expressed her anger and frustration over a broken bracelet and an injury to her wrist. Lalage and Marmaduke ended up in a cab together, with Lalage demanding to go to Bijou Theatre.

Trefusis faced accusations of parsimony and opposition to the Janseniuses' wishes. He was condemned to six months' imprisonment for seditious libel, but his sentence was quashed due to a flaw in the indictment. Agatha believed Trefusis to be heartless and selfish, but not as coarse and ignorant as others portrayed him. Agatha found her first season in society to be extremely dull and questioned her future happiness. She experienced a contrast between her previous college life and the superficiality of social gatherings. Agatha alarmed her mother with her ambitions to become a hospital nurse, public singer, or actress. Mrs. Jansenius supported Agatha's desire for knowledge, believing it would lead to wiser actions.

Mr. Jansenius is a wealthy citizen and a public benefactor. Mrs. Jansenius is the mother of Henrietta. Agatha Wylie has been requested to withdraw from Alton College. Maria Wilson is the author of the letter requesting Agatha Wylie's withdrawal. Mr. Jansenius is upset about the situation involving his daughter Henrietta. Henrietta expresses her frustration and insists on her right to speak and act as she pleases. Mr. Jansenius is determined to confront Sidney regarding his responsibilities.

Elinor and Douglas discuss attending the theatre together. Marian expresses her annoyance towards Elinor and her current life situation. Douglas offers support to Marian, indicating he wishes to see her happy. Marian tells Douglas he should not visit her anymore and suggests he pursue a career. Marian becomes emotional and cries, expressing her feelings of misery. Douglas suggests that Marian leave England with him for a better life. Douglas professes his love for Marian and offers her a choice for their future together.

The narrator is reading _Reynold's Newspaper_ while having breakfast. The narrator expresses a lack of social prejudices and acknowledges that some gentlemen deserve respect. The clergyman believes that a suitable brother-in-law should belong to the same social rank as his sister. The narrator argues that suitability is not solely determined by social rank. The narrator presents an example of a hardworking man who is honest but does not fit the traditional definition of a gentleman. The clergyman and the narrator discuss the meaning of the term 'gentleman' and its implications for social class. The conversation highlights the complexity of defining social suitability in relationships.

Sidney Trefusis expresses a desire for obscurity and mentions that his solicitor will contact Henrietta's father regarding business matters. Mrs. Trefusis observes her mother reading a letter and questions Sidney Trefusis's sanity. Henrietta expresses feelings of abandonment and believes Sidney Trefusis must return to her. Mrs. Jansenius suggests that they cannot act until they hear from the solicitor and offers Henrietta a place to stay. Henrietta feels a sense of desolation upon realizing her father's house is no longer her home. Mr. Jansenius is described as a dignified man of imposing presence, nearing fifty years old. Mr. Jansenius is a banker who aims to maintain and grow his inherited capital while educating his children as Christians.

Mrs. Scott sang 'Caller Herrin' with Ned at the piano, receiving great applause. Ned complimented Mrs. Scott on her ability to sing a ballad. Mrs. Scott expressed that she had never sung in public before this occasion. The narrator has not sung for Ned since Mrs. Scott's performance, except occasionally when asked. The narrator feels nervous singing in front of Ned and notes that he no longer accompanies her. Miss McQuinch and the narrator discussed the changes in the narrator's relationship with Ned after marriage. The narrator observed that Ned has become more considerate but has also stopped discussing his work with her.

The conversation involves a serious discussion between a doctor and Susanna. The doctor informs Susanna that her brother, Ned, is about to be married. Susanna reacts with disbelief and expresses her surprise at the news. The doctor reveals that Ned is engaged to his sister, Marian Lind. Susanna comments on the implications of the marriage for her relationship with Marmaduke. The doctor advises Susanna to end her connection with Marmaduke due to the impending marriage. Susanna questions why Marian should have everything go her way despite her advantages.

The Newly Born expresses a desire for power. The She-Ancient warns The Newly Born about the consequences of having power. The She-Ancient states that children were once given the world to play with but did not improve it. Acis comments on the longevity of the She-Ancient and the changes in others over time. The Newly Born inquires about Festival Day and what a sculptor is. Acis advises The Newly Born to observe and not ask questions initially. The scene includes protests from voices in the temple regarding the actions of the characters.

Mr. Jansenius expressed his desire to have no further communication with Mr. Smilash. Mr. Jansenius stated that all of England is open to Mr. Smilash except for his house. Miss Wilson received a telegram indicating that Mrs. Trefusis has returned to London without explanation. Smilash suggested that Mrs. Trefusis may have been harmed or that the telegram could be a falsehood. Miss Wilson instructed the inspector to ensure that Smilash leaves the college promptly. Smilash requested payment for his services, claiming he was owed ninepence. Miss Wilson ultimately gave Smilash a shilling and told him to leave.

The conversation involves two individuals discussing changes in their perceptions of each other. One individual expresses a desire to visit the mother of the other individual. The mother has not acknowledged the individual since their marriage. The mother is said to have more spirit and has not forgiven the individual for past actions. A man in a brown suit is observed walking towards the individuals. The man is recognized by one of the individuals, causing a change in demeanor. The man expresses a desire to spend time with the individuals at Holland Park.
