Miss Wilson returned money to a man named Smilash, stating it did not belong to her. Smilash expressed gratitude and inquired about employment opportunities. Miss Wilson declined to employ Smilash, stating she had no need for his services. Miss Wilson gave Smilash a shilling for his previous assistance in getting cabs. Smilash claimed to have a good character and mentioned the rector of his native village, Auburn. Miss Wilson noted that Smilash had previously stated a different name to Mr. Fairholme. Smilash admitted to having been in prison six times due to drinking but claimed to have been sober for eighteen months.

Darwinism is closely related to Capitalism, leading Marx to view it as an economic product. Darwin's main postulate regarding population pressure was derived from Malthus's treatise on Population. Darwin also obtained the idea of unlimited time for population pressure from geologist Lyell. The Ricardo-Malthusian economists promoted the fatalistic Wages Fund doctrine before Darwin published his work. There was a significant political and clerical propaganda promoting the idea that progress depended on unrestrained competition and the elimination of the weak. The proletariat viewed Capitalist liberty as wage slavery without the protections of chattel slavery. Bastiat argued that unrestrained plutocracy would resolve social questions more effectively than other forms of governance.

The woman wants the speaker to return to save her child from her. The woman claims that the speaker was the last restraint on her behavior. The speaker believes the woman's message is influenced by alcohol consumption. The speaker and the woman shared their income and responsibilities as if they were married. The speaker desires to take the child away from the woman but feels unable to do so. The woman has a strong desire for independence and refuses to marry. The speaker expresses a wish for the woman to stop drinking to improve their relationship.

Haslam is the rector and feels he should call on people. Franklyn Barnabas is a former clergyman and has a brother named Conrad Barnabas, who is a Professor of Biology at Jarrowfields University. Haslam expresses that he is not intellectual enough to pursue other options and finds the Church acceptable for his time. Franklyn Barnabas reflects on his experience in the Church and his realization of his own ignorance. Conrad Barnabas comments on the potential for personal growth if he had a significantly longer lifespan. Haslam mentions a bird in his garden that sings a phrase related to his feelings about the Church. The parlor maid is asked about letters for the post and reveals she is planning to leave.

The shepherd requested an increase in wages due to the loss of his hut. Sir John informed the shepherd that his position could be filled by less expensive labor. The shepherd was unaware that Sir John's explanation about political economy was untrue. The narrator suggested the shepherd move to a place with a higher market price for labor. The shepherd was willing to move but lacked the financial means to do so. The narrator lent the shepherd money for his journey to Australia. Miss Wilson questioned Mr. Trefusis about his self-perception and the name he chose for himself.

Eight young ladies were watching a man who fell while skating. The man expressed regret for trying to skate like gentlemen instead of sticking to simpler activities. Miss Ward allowed the man to assist her in putting on her skates. Agatha Wylie was shy and constrained during her interaction with the man. The man admitted to lying about being sent by Miss Wilson to assist with the skates. The girls enjoyed skating and became animated as they grew accustomed to the activity. The man felt gloomy while observing the girls skating and laughing.

Lalage pulled a cherry out of the narrator's mouth during a performance. The narrator felt embarrassed and childish after the incident. The narrator returned to Cambridge and began reading after the incident. The narrator visited the theater again and interacted with Lalage. Conolly and Lind attended a performance and recognized Lalage. Lalage expressed anger towards Conolly for not informing her about Lind's visit. Conolly clarified that Lalage is his sister, not his wife.

The character is kept in a pocket, which is described as a bad place for men. Miss Wilson went indoors without further comment after observing Mr. Smilash. Agatha approached Mr. Smilash while he was resting and expressed doubt about his laborer status. Mr. Smilash confirmed he is not a laborer and displayed a fine hand. Agatha and Mr. Smilash exchanged names, with Mr. Smilash suggesting they use their last names. Agatha mentioned that visitors from London are coming to take her away. Mr. Smilash expressed disappointment about Agatha being taken away.

Gertrude expresses doubt about being loved by men. The male character insists on his steadfast love for Gertrude. Gertrude claims she is not an angel and expresses discomfort with the conversation. Gertrude mentions having a headache and asks to be left alone. Mr. Erskine attempts to kiss Gertrude's hand but is rejected. Sir Charles discusses news about Miss Wylie and expresses frustration over a document he signed. Miss Lindsay has informed Jane that she must go home, causing tension among the characters.

The Countess does not take wine due to her medical issues. Jasper mentions that George has news about Marmaduke. Marmaduke has settled down in a mansion at West Kensington. The Countess expresses relief that Marmaduke is not married. Jasper doubts the seriousness of Marmaduke's intentions toward Constance. Lady Carbury asserts her perspective on societal issues regarding Marmaduke. The Rev. George believes it is not their place to interfere in Marmaduke's situation.

Cain proposes to tame men and women to work for them. Eve expresses contempt for Cain's idea, calling it a dream of creating unnatural monsters. Adam questions Eve's assertion that he is a fool. Cain claims that the Voice gave him the right to kill and that he is the first conqueror. Cain believes that he bears a mark that protects him from being slain. Adam challenges Cain's belief in divine justice. Cain states that danger and fear are necessary for courage and greatness.

The Male Figure is named Ozymandias. The Female Figure identifies herself as Cleopatra-Semiramis. Martellus created the Figures using material from Pygmalion. Pygmalion is found dead, prompting concern from the He-Ancient. The Female Figure denies responsibility for Pygmalion's death, blaming the Male Figure. The He-Ancient expresses disappointment over Pygmalion's death. The She-Ancient criticizes the Figures for being dangerous and disgusting.

The Envoy is the leader of the Potterbill party and is currently the Prime Minister. The Opposition, known as the Rotterjacks, has won every bye-election for the last six months. The Elderly Gentleman believes the Government should hold on until spring. The Envoy expresses concern that their majority will diminish by Easter due to bye-elections. Zoo states that there is no such thing as the future until it becomes the present. The oracle previously prophesied the victory of the Potterbill party at the General Election fifteen years ago. The oracle ultimately advises the Envoy to go home, and the atmosphere shifts to prosaic daylight.

Armande requested dinner as soon as possible. Marian expressed her opinion about the house, stating it was her idea of a comfortable modern home. Conolly and Marian discussed a novel that was read at Verona, mentioning disagreements about the characters. After dinner, the group returned to the drawing-room, which extended from the front to the back of the house. Marian opened a large window to access the garden and sat on a terrace with Elinor. Conolly asked if he could play the organ while Marian and Elinor talked. Marian revealed that she does not play the piano in Conolly's presence due to nervousness.

Susanna expresses indifference towards the opinions of others. The Rev. George visits the Electro-Motor Company to meet his father. The Rev. George describes a woman as abandoned and depraved but also not unattractive. The Rev. George is unable to persuade the woman to assist them. Mr. Lind questions the Rev. George about consulting Marian's wishes. Mr. Lind mentions receiving congratulatory letters regarding Marian's choice. The Rev. George feels a shift in his perception of his father and his own moral beliefs.

The text discusses the concept of spoliation and its implications for society. It suggests that if spoliation is not abandoned, society must either revert to Protection or face collapse. The Cobden Club is mentioned as preferring to reveal the truth about Protectionism rather than allow it to succeed. The text argues that collective ownership of England by its inhabitants would lead to socialism and eliminate artificial inequality. Trefusis and Erskine discuss the consequences of social unrest and the potential for violence against the wealthy. The conversation includes references to historical events, such as the aftermath of the Paris Commune in 1871. Donovan Brown, an artist, is mentioned as a Socialist, and his influence is noted in the context of recruiting others to the cause.

Wickens's boy accuses Smilash of inappropriate behavior with a lady. Smilash defends the lady's modesty and criticizes the boy's assumptions. Smilash describes a barge that is red and yellow with a green dragon figurehead. The bargee is depicted as a compassionate family man living with his wife and children. Smilash recounts traveling down the canal to Lyvern and mentions receiving sixpence from the lady. Smilash expresses grievances about being detained by police, referencing his rights. Mr. Jansenius recognizes Smilash and inquires about his wife.

Agatha Wylie is coming on Thursday. Trefusis expressed concern about not having the opportunity to see Agatha. Gertrude invited Trefusis to luncheon on Thursday. Sir Charles expressed anger towards Gertrude for inviting Trefusis. Agatha, Gertrude, and Jane met for the first time since parting at Alton College. Agatha felt anxious about the meeting with her friends. Gertrude had rejected matrimonial opportunities due to her pride in rank and exclusiveness.

The character is instructed about the situation regarding skates. The character admits to being a liar and expresses humility. Miss Wilson wishes to speak to the character before he leaves. The character encounters Jane, who perceives his pretense. The character is identified as Jeff Smilash when he enters Miss Wilson's study. Miss Wilson expresses disbelief regarding the character's claim of being a gentleman. The character acknowledges his common status and defends his actions.

The text compares various artists and their works across different periods, suggesting that a great religious movement is necessary for a great artistic one. Raphael is noted for his ability to paint a Transfiguration of the Son of Man, despite being disillusioned and unable to paint a queen of Heaven as earlier artists did. Michael Angelo is recognized for his portrayal of superhuman figures and is considered the greatest among modern painters and sculptors. Beethoven's last movement of the Hammerklavier Sonata, Opus 106, is described as a musical representation of physical movement, akin to atomic storms. The text contrasts the perception of art in Beethoven's time, which focused on the sublime and beautiful, with the contemporary view that emphasizes imitative and voluptuous art. Comedy is described as a critical art form that sustained the theatre after the decline of sublime tragedy, with playwrights like Molière and Oscar Wilde leading this movement.

Marmaduke expresses regret for his conduct towards Constance. Marian advises Marmaduke to leave matters as they are regarding Constance. Marmaduke acknowledges that he has not been clear about his intentions. Constance arrives at the summer-house while Marmaduke and Marian are talking. Marmaduke plans to take Constance to Bushy Copse that afternoon. Constance is described as being jealous and having previously reacted strongly to Marmaduke's actions. Marmaduke and Marian have a disagreement about Conolly's behavior.

Wylie and Trefusis discussed the idea of marriage and decided to marry before the end of next month. Lady Brandon expressed incredulity at Trefusis's announcement of his intention to marry Agatha. Trefusis stated that he and Agatha are not in love and that their marriage proposal was not premeditated. Gertrude left the room without speaking after Trefusis's announcement. Jane accused Trefusis of treating Gertrude poorly and expressed her belief that Agatha is double-faced. Trefusis planned to telegraph his solicitor about the marriage proposal. Jane was called to speak to Master Charles and Miss Fanny after Trefusis left.

The Irish race vanished from human knowledge after a certain generation passed away. The dispersed Jews also vanished to avoid being sent back to Palestine. The world has been described as dull without the presence of Jews and Irish. The elderly gentleman expresses confusion over the discussion about dust and civilization. The elderly gentleman asserts that his body is made of dust, but his soul is a living entity. The elderly gentleman dismisses scientific details about his body, focusing instead on the concept of the soul. The conversation ends with a disagreement about the nature of life and the subject at hand.

Adam expresses that if people choose to shorten their lives, they will continue to dig, fight, kill, and die. Eve questions the concept of being damned, which Adam defines as loving death more than life. Adam insists that Eve should continue her work or risk going without bread. Eve believes that there is something beyond bread that they will discover in the future. The setting shifts to a study where a clerical gentleman is writing. The clerical gentleman is described as being well-dressed and intellectual, but not a typical clergyman. A tweeded gentleman enters the study and reveals he has decided that the term of human life should be three hundred years.

Germany surrendered, but the blockade and famine against it continue. The Western Powers' alliances were based on opportunistic selection rather than intelligent selection. The Armistice and Treaty did not resolve the ongoing conflict. National debts remain unresolved due to the financial impact of the war. Russia is experiencing severe hardship and has shifted to Materialist Communism under new rulers. The Western Powers are struggling to find effective solutions and are facing potential collapse.

Elinor comments on the situation involving Marmaduke and a child. Marmaduke tells Marian to leave the child alone. Douglas expresses that it does not matter if the child bores him. Lucy does not respond to Marian's call and continues to play. Marmaduke chases Lucy, who avoids him while laughing. Marian expresses shock at Lucy's behavior, while Elinor defends the child's boldness. Marmaduke and Marian suggest various games to play after dinner.

The artist friends of Brown agreed to a transaction to prevent him from losing money. Brown and the narrator developed a friendship after the transaction. Brown's wife was angry with him for refusing fifteen hundred pounds. Trefusis believes that educating women about Socialism can help spread the movement. Trefusis has converted many young women to not fear or condemn Socialism. Trefusis presented a petition advocating for laborers' rights to Erskine and Sir Charles. Erskine declined to sign the petition presented by Trefusis.

Douglas expresses that he can still welcome Mr. Lind as Marian's husband despite her past. Douglas states that he is not bound to Mr. Lind's daughter in any way. Mr. Lind speaks to Douglas as a father and a gentleman regarding his daughter's situation. Douglas refuses to continue the conversation with Mr. Lind about Mrs. Conolly. Douglas asserts that he will have nothing to do with Mrs. Conolly in the future. Douglas claims that he has acted according to a higher standard of honor than ordinary men. Mr. Lind expresses concern for Marian's future if Douglas does not marry her.

The Parlor Maid expresses skepticism about living for several hundred years, especially in the context of marriage. Conrad suggests that the man the Parlor Maid is going to marry may live as long as she does. The Parlor Maid states she would not promise to live with the same man for several hundred years. Franklyn mentions a misunderstanding regarding his visit to Middlesborough, which has been misreported in the papers. Franklyn has a following and is believed to have the potential to contest a parliamentary seat. Conrad expresses disdain for party politicians and their behavior after the war. Savvy and Haslam enter the scene, with Savvy expressing disappointment about not being informed of Joyce Burge's arrival.

People could not conceive of a God who was not anthropomorphic. The Old Testament depicts a God with body parts and passions. The Church faced opposition from those who rejected this anthropomorphic view of God. The rejection of this idol led to the emergence of atheism as a response to perceived idolatry. The text describes the anthropomorphic idol as having negative traits such as cruelty and jealousy. The scientific community found the concept of a disorderly God intolerable. Charles Darwin is identified as a key figure in demonstrating that design could be explained without a personal designer.

Jane snatched the pen from Agatha and insisted on writing first. Agatha instructed Jane to write the date and an apology for sliding down the banisters. Gertrude took the pen and wrote about breaking the rules by sliding down the banisters. Agatha criticized Gertrude for shifting blame while confessing her own involvement. Agatha added to her confession, admitting to being persuaded by Gertrude and Jane. The three girls were interrupted by the sound of a gong, signaling mealtime. A young lady with an olive complexion arrived at a large mansion on Belsize Avenue.

Ecrasia and Arjillax discuss the value of sculptures, with Ecrasia expressing disdain for Arjillax's busts. Arjillax claims that his busts are part of a larger artistic design. The Newly Born expresses a desire to hear a story. Arjillax recounts a legend about the Archangel Michael, a sculptor and painter. The legend describes a temple dedicated to the goddess Mediterranea, filled with art that Ecrasia approves of. Arjillax asserts that the Archangel Michael's work was superior to that of other artists. Arjillax declares his intention to create art that satisfies Ecrasia's standards of beauty.

The Irrational Knot is a novel written by Bernard Shaw in 1880. The novel was not published by any London or American publishers at the time of its completion. Mrs. Annie Besant published The Irrational Knot as a serial in her magazine after it was rejected. Shaw states that he is no longer the same person who wrote The Irrational Knot due to the renewal of the body's substance over time. Shaw recalls the price of the paper used for writing The Irrational Knot as being inexpensive. Bizet's Carmen was a source of inspiration for Shaw while he was writing The Irrational Knot. The protagonist of The Irrational Knot is described as an Irish-American electrical engineer.

The elderly gentleman's name is Joseph Popham Bolge Bluebin Barlow. The elderly gentleman is fifty-six years old. The elderly gentleman was called Iddy Toodles by his mother during his childhood. He insisted on being called Joe at school and later Joseph at eighteen. The elderly gentleman claims to trace his family lineage back for more than a thousand years. He mentions ancestors Joyce Bolge and Hengist Horsa Bluebin who were involved in the prime ministership of the British Empire. The elderly gentleman expresses a sense of pride in his ancestry despite his current state of longevity.

The man spoke with a barbarous accent and propped his spade against the wall of the chalet. He stated that he came to house his spade, which he used to earn his living. Miss Wilson clarified that the young ladies were not her daughters. The man commented on the rarity of exceptional women, referencing a minister's sermon. Agatha inquired about the duration of the rain, to which the man humbly replied that only the Lord knows. The man offered an umbrella he had found, acknowledging it was not typical for someone of his status to carry it. Two gentlemen, Fairholme and Josephs, arrived at the chalet seeking shelter from the rain.

The characters Hetty and Sidney are engaged in a conversation about love and separation. Sidney expresses a desire to leave Hetty despite claiming to love her. Hetty insists that she does not want Sidney to leave her. Sidney describes himself as a pessimist and criticizes modern English polite society. Sidney reveals that his wealth is derived from stolen money, although legally obtained. Sidney's father was a successful businessman in the cotton trade. Sidney's father aimed to always be the gaining party in business transactions.

Marmaduke Lind and Susanna Conolly live at a villa called Laurel Grove in West Kensington. Susanna received a letter regarding a first rehearsal scheduled for the following Monday. The letter mentioned that the engagement could be renewable after Christmas. Marmaduke found an advertisement in the _Times_ for an adaptation of M. de Jongleur's opera bouffe titled _King Lewis on the Lewis_. Lalage Virtue is listed multiple times in the cast of the production, while Rose Stella is mentioned only once. Marmaduke received a bill from the West Kensington Wine Company indicating high champagne expenses. Susanna expressed a need for champagne to avoid feeling low.

Elinor expresses a desire to leave the house immediately. Miss McQuinch suggests staying and confronting the situation. Elinor and Miss McQuinch plan to go to Mrs. Toplis's in St. Mary's Terrace. Elinor mentions having thirty pounds of her own money. Miss McQuinch has nearly seventeen pounds in an old stocking. Marian warns Elinor about the implications of her decision on their future living arrangements. The Rev. George meets with his father for an hour before leaving the house.

The author reflects on the significant impact of his father, who was a prominent figure in the cotton industry. The father had the ability to influence various aspects of society, including business decisions and cultural production. The author expresses confusion over society's financial sacrifices made for his father's business acumen. The father's preferences determined the commercial success of various cultural and industrial products. The author discusses his marriage to Henrietta and the subsequent criticism of his actions following her death. He acknowledges his emotional response to Henrietta's death and explains his absence from her funeral. The author emphasizes the importance of respecting his father's legacy and contributions to industry.

Miss Wilson regretted not dismissing Sidney Trefusis summarily during their discussion. Sidney Trefusis stated that his marriage to Henrietta Jansenius was a result of her education. Henrietta Jansenius is now known as Henrietta Trefusis. Sidney Trefusis expressed that he fled from his marriage due to his inability to endure domestic bliss. Sidney Trefusis admitted that he and Henrietta have not communicated since their separation. The shepherd mentioned by Miss Wilson was assured to be comfortably settled in a lodging in Lyvern. The lodging shared by the shepherd and two other families was in poor repair and generated significant rent for the landlord.

Charles Darwin's doctrine of Circumstantial Selection reached the British public more effectively than Erasmus Darwin's concept of Evolution. The average British citizen is described as irreligious and unscientific, focusing on everyday topics rather than scientific theories. Circumstantial Selection is considered easier to understand and more concrete than Lamarckian evolution. Pigeon fanciers, dog fanciers, gardeners, and stock breeders can grasp the concept of Circumstantial Selection due to their practical experience. Darwin's popularity is attributed to his ability to present ideas that did not puzzle the general public. Many people have not read The Origin of Species in full because they accept its concepts before reaching the end of the book. Darwin's approach was characterized by extensive evidence and examples, which some found tedious.

The text discusses a process of transformation and modification related to natural history, categorized under the heading of Evolution. The author acknowledges that the process he discovered is not the sole method of evolution and does not exclude other methods. He demonstrates that some transformations previously considered functional adaptations may be due to Circumstantial Selection. The author is characterized as an honest naturalist who did not engage in theological speculation and maintained a simple demeanor throughout his life. Samuel Butler reacted against Darwin's theories, promoting Lamarckian ideas and criticizing Darwin's character. Butler's critiques were largely ignored by Darwin's supporters, who underestimated his intellectual contributions. The text critiques the intellectual community's acceptance of Darwinism, suggesting it led to a misunderstanding of the distinction between species modification and the emergence of new species.

He helped her to rise and commented on her weight. Miss Wilson insisted that the young ladies were not her daughters. Smilash claimed he had received excessive payment from the young lady. Fairholme advised Miss Wilson to take back the money given to Smilash. Smilash offered to perform odd jobs for Miss Wilson in the future. Miss Wilson expressed annoyance at Agatha's spending. Jane stated that Agatha only had threepence and could not have given Smilash a large sum.

Erskine was riding along a highway that swerved inland from a river. Trefusis was reading a book titled 'The Patriot Martyrs and other Poems' while lying in a meadow. Erskine felt disgusted and distracted by thoughts of Gertrude. Erskine lost his way while trying to return to Brandon Beeches and eventually found a railway station. Erskine caught a train that brought him within a mile of his destination. Trefusis expressed his contempt for Miss Lindsay and his hopes for Gertrude during a conversation. Gertrude identified herself as an unprotected girl during the exchange with Trefusis.

Marian and Edward Conolly discuss their engagement. Edward Conolly has multiple names, including Edoardo Sebastiano Conolly. Marian expresses a desire to inform Nelly about their engagement. Edward Conolly prefers to keep their engagement a secret for the time being. Miss McQuinch informs Marian that Mrs. Leith Fairfax will be arriving soon. Marian decides to face Sholto Douglas rather than avoid him. Edward Conolly plans to meet Marian at the Academy on Monday at half-past four.

Marmaduke informed Susanna that it was twenty minutes to five. Susanna expressed her intention to drive back to the theatre. Susanna confronted Marmaduke about his use of the name Sharp. Marmaduke admitted that Sharp was the name of a cousin. Susanna accused Marmaduke of lying about his identity. Susanna insisted that she would not accept dinners from strange men. Susanna paid the bill after Marmaduke was unable to find enough money.

The speaker is living in a two-roomed hovel instead of enjoying London society. The speaker is helping to liberate Manchester laborers who were enslaved by his father. The speaker believes in creating an international association of laborers to ensure fair work and wealth distribution. The speaker is currently propagating the principles of this labor association. The speaker prefers to spend his wealth on promoting labor rights rather than on personal luxuries. Henrietta expresses a desire to stay with the speaker and share in his work. The speaker feels that he cannot engage in a long idyllic life due to his commitment to labor issues.

Adam expresses despair about the inevitability of ceasing to exist. Eve notes that Adam frequently changes his mind about existence. Adam reveals that he struggles with self-acceptance and desires to change himself. Eve feels the need to care for Adam due to his neglect of himself. Eve points out the concept of death by referencing a dead fawn. Adam reacts with disgust to the dead fawn and decides to dispose of it. A serpent appears and reveals it has learned to speak by listening to Adam and Eve.

A paper was presented at the Society of Arts regarding an invention. Marian and the speaker attended the meeting together. Marian and Marmaduke were already acquainted before the introduction. Marmaduke has a daughter. Marian and Elinor visited Marmaduke at Hammersmith after encountering him on the river. Julia is a patroness of a Home for foundling girls. Julia wrote to Marmaduke offering to present his daughter to the Home.

Cain expresses disdain for a long life spent in labor, preferring a life of fighting and hunting. Adam accuses Cain of lying about the Voice that calls him to pay for Abel's life. Eve argues that Cain's actions stem from idleness and selfishness, contrasting the difficulty of creation with the ease of destruction. Cain believes he has a different relationship with the Voice than Adam, referring to Adam's Voice as the Devil. Adam claims his Voice represents Life, while Cain's represents Death. Cain envisions death as a transition to a more splendid and intense life of the soul.

The narrator has abandoned a project of living alone together with Sholto. The narrator hopes to gain a separation from Sholto without being accused of desertion. The narrator has experienced a grand passion, which they now consider a delusion. The narrator fears detection due to their past actions and the public interest in Ned's patents. American newspapers have published sensationalized accounts of the narrator's departure. The narrator describes a humorous incident involving Ned and an electrical experiment. Sholto is frustrated by the way he is portrayed in the newspapers.

Marmaduke's snuggery is located at the back of the house. Conolly has business to attend to in town and prefers not to enter Marmaduke's house. Lord Carbury is anxious about the relationship between Marmaduke and Lady Constance. Miss Lind believes Marmaduke should leave London immediately to avoid conflict with the Earl. Marmaduke has taken a villa, which has raised curiosity among the Carbury family. Conolly inquires about Susanna before leaving, and she appears confused upon encountering them. Susanna expresses frustration about Conolly's indifference towards her situation.

He became first accompanist, then chorus master, and finally trainer for the operatic stage. He speculated in an American tour, married, lost all his money, and came over to England to resume his business at Covent Garden. The speaker stayed in America and was apprenticed to an electrical engineer, working at the bench for six years. The speaker's father never gave him singing lessons and was known for teaching stage tricks and traditional operas. Marian and Conolly were engaged in a conversation about singing and personal experiences. Marmaduke and Miss McQuinch observed Marian and Conolly's interaction and expressed curiosity about their relationship. Elinor expressed her disdain for Marmaduke, leading to a brief conflict between them.

The protagonist poured a hot beverage into a large mug. Henrietta appeared at the door with frozen tears on her cheeks. The protagonist carried Henrietta to the fire to warm her. Henrietta expressed a desire to leave and not engage with the protagonist. Henrietta handed the protagonist a letter from Agatha. The protagonist recognized Agatha's involvement in the situation.

The inspector questioned Wickens's boy about what he saw in the canal meadow. Wickens's boy claimed to have seen a young woman and a man kissing. The boy stated that the man threatened him after giving him two pence. The boy answered questions affirmatively to appease his captors. The inspector expressed doubt about the boy's reliability as a witness. Smilash was brought in by two policemen and appeared to have an injury to his head. Smilash refused to provide information or go to the college when found by the police.

Douglas and Marmaduke have a conversation where Marmaduke expresses his intention to leave. Mr. Lind, referred to as Reginald, arrives to see Douglas after Marmaduke departs. Douglas expresses displeasure at Mr. Lind's visit and acknowledges the servant's announcement. Mr. Lind addresses Douglas about his disappointment regarding Marian's marriage and his recent actions. Douglas mentions a recent unpleasant meeting with Mr. Conolly, which Mr. Lind advises against repeating. Mr. Lind expresses his lack of satisfaction with Marian's marriage to Mr. Conolly. Mr. Lind reflects on the impact of Marian's marriage on their family dynamics.

The author expresses indifference to social status and material wealth. The author believes that a sufficient income is necessary for the practice of virtue. The text critiques the moral compromises made by those in pursuit of wealth. The author reflects on their past lack of understanding regarding social hierarchies. The author acknowledges their family's financial struggles and their choice to not contribute positively. The text discusses the relationship between the British peerage and American alliances. The author suggests that societal values prioritize wealth over moral integrity.

Sir Charles preferred songs that expressed melancholy and had a monotonous musical style. Agatha left the piano after Sir Charles's performance, which he felt was a failure. Erskine sat on a sofa with his head drooping while Agatha looked out the window. Agatha received a telegram stating that the sender had arrived safe and was happy. Erskine's telegram contained a message from Trefusis advising him to write to a woman and follow up in person. Sir Charles expressed relief that Trefusis was not as bad as he was thought to be. Gertrude found herself traveling with Trefusis against her resolution and felt uncomfortable.

Jane expresses a conviction that she will believe nobody from now on. Agatha questions Gertrude's perspective and suggests she is in the wrong. Gertrude accuses Agatha of self-conceit and recalls a past insult. Agatha claims to have repented for comparing Gertrude to a cat. Jane comments on Gertrude's tendency to focus on others' faults. Agatha argues that she has helped Gertrude and expresses frustration over their friendship. Gertrude feels that no one considers her feelings.

The author expresses a reluctance to participate in funerals and the practice of sepulture. The author allowed a funeral and a monument for Henrietta Jansenius despite personal objections. The author intervened to prevent Jansenius from being overcharged by a middleman for the funeral arrangements. The author disagrees with the portrayal of their involvement in the affair as self-serving. The author's wife disputes the accuracy of the account regarding their marriage. The author criticizes the use of economic concepts in a fictional narrative about personal relationships. The author reflects on the literary legacy of Shakespeare and expresses concern about contemporary novelists.

Smilash expresses a belief that the poor are becoming poorer and the rich richer. Miss Wilson suggests that Smilash should take the man home immediately. The man thanks Miss Wilson for Bess and the children before leaving. Agatha is seventeen years old and perceives the foibles of others without reverence for her seniors. Agatha believes she has a superior understanding of nature compared to her peers. Agatha laughs at her fellow students who idolize certain boys, thinking she is immune to such feelings. Agatha resolves to fall in love with Mr. Jefferson Smilash after a storm.

Erskine accused Trefusis of breaking his promise regarding a train journey with Miss Lindsay. Sir Charles informed Erskine that Miss Lindsay had given Trefusis permission to accompany her. Erskine expressed regret for causing a scene and went to his room. Agatha believed that Trefusis and she were the only sensible members of the party. Agatha resented Trefusis's journey with Gertrude, feeling it threatened her connection with him. The dinner was dull, with Lady Brandon speaking quietly and Erskine feeling depressed. After dinner, Agatha and Sir Charles performed songs by Schubert, which did not alleviate her feelings.

Weismann argued that animals, such as chicks and butterflies, act automatically without consciousness. Weismann claimed that butterflies do not learn from experience and are not conscious of their actions. The text compares the behavior of cats to that of butterflies, suggesting that cats also act with purpose and consciousness. The author critiques the Weismannite perspective, suggesting it underestimates the consciousness of living beings. The text discusses the concept of Circumstantial Selection and its implications for understanding evolution. The author asserts that one cannot definitively disprove the idea of being a product of Circumstantial Selection. The text contrasts Circumstantial Selection with Lamarckian evolution, suggesting both are unprovable.

Franklyn states that the program aims to extend human life to three hundred years. The election cry is 'Back to Methuselah.' Franklyn claims that Lubin and Surge will be remembered as part of a group of statesmen who nearly destroyed European civilization. Burge argues that the loss of life was less than a million. Franklyn asserts that the political and social problems of civilization cannot be solved by short-lived leaders. Lubin expresses skepticism about the idea of extending human life. Surge suggests that a statesman who sees himself as an instrument of a higher power will succeed.

The house is a hollow square enclosing a courtyard with a bath and a fountain. The courtyard is roofed with dusty glass and contains a mutilated nymph statue. The bath is partly covered with loose boards and contains various items including coals and a broken canoe. The house was built in 11780 by an ancestor of Trefusis's mother. Trefusis possesses a library of valuable books and family heirlooms. The study is designed for banqueting and features life-size plaster statues and a variety of furnishings. The walls of the study are whitewashed and contain sketches and memoranda.

Enoch walks on the hills and hears the Voice continually. Enoch has given up his will to do the will of the Voice. Cain questions the invention of death and its role in life. Adam and Eve express concern over Cain's thoughts on death. Adam states that he and Eve invented death. Eve notes that many of their grandchildren die before they learn to live. Eve wonders if their descendants will have enough time to learn great things.

London was considered the mightiest city of antiquity. The nearest houses to the location mentioned are at a place called Strand-on-the-Green. A veiled and robed woman passes behind the columns of a temple. A man resembling Napoleon I enters the scene wearing a military uniform. The man claims to be the Man of Destiny and expresses a desire to consult the oracle. The veiled woman informs the man that he will need to wait for the Baghdad envoy and his party. The oracle states that she is the one on duty and offers to answer the man's questions.

Marmaduke found the Rev. George in a state of inebriation on High Street and brought him along. The Rev. George expressed concern about being seen in public with the intoxicated Marmaduke. Conolly informed the group that Marian has eloped with Douglas. The Rev. George reacted emotionally to the news of Marian's elopement. Conolly stated that he must divorce Marian due to her elopement. Marmaduke suggested Conolly pursue damages against Douglas for the elopement. Conolly explained that their marriage, conducted by a registrar, has no ecclesiastical validity.

Trefusis and his friend engaged in a quarrel about the role of artists and their relationship with the wealthy. The monument for Henrietta Jansenius was placed in Highgate Cemetery by unemployed workmen. The inscription on the monument included Henrietta Jansenius's birth date, marriage date to Sidney Trefusis, and date of death. Mr. Jansenius considered the size of the tombstone an insult to his daughter's memory. The mason who designed the tombstone faced backlash from his employers and the trades-union for taking the job. Trefusis attempted to advocate for the mason through letters to various parties, but faced threats of libel from employers. Agatha ended her school-life after learning the truth about Smilash and felt a sense of relief at Henrietta's death.

The subject was not skilled in his hereditary trade of territorial aristocrat. He expressed a desire to become a watchmaker at a young age, which led to his mother's contempt and dread of his moral superiority. He had a strong interest in mechanics and built a laboratory and workshop in his park. He collected various mechanical devices, including typewriters, bicycles, and patented inventions. He had a large collection of musical instruments but could not play them effectively. He initially struggled with practical tasks but eventually focused on electrical engineering, employing a skilled assistant. Towers Cottage, a Tudor mansion, served as the family's residence after Carbury Towers was destroyed.

Marian returned to Mrs. Myers's house after a period of seclusion. Susanna, a deceased individual, was no longer able to call for Marian. Marian disliked the presence of Susanna's body in the room above. Marian considered moving to a more luxurious lodging due to her income. Marian heard a noise from Susanna's death chamber and felt compelled to investigate. Marian found her husband sitting by Susanna's body when she opened the door. Marian's husband expressed a desire for honesty in their relationship, rejecting previous conventions.

Mrs. Leith Fairfax and Mr. Lind discuss their differing views on human nature. Mrs. Fairfax claims to be an expert in analyzing character and believes human beings are shallow. A young gentleman with a banjo interrupts the conversation to inquire about a specific piece of music. Mrs. Fairfax expresses concern about the lack of music for the concert. Conolly offers to play the accompaniment for Marian, who is unsure about his ability. The Rev. Mr. Lind introduces Conolly to the group, stating he will help with the music. Miss Lind expresses curiosity about Conolly and asks to be introduced to him.

ECRASIA expresses regret over the death of a man who could have shared stories of the Golden Age. PYGMALION describes the man as a dangerous beast who attempted to attack him. MARTELLUS questions why a woman was not created alongside a man. PYGMALION explains that he intended to create a woman but abandoned the idea after his experience with the man. PYGMALION has been working on creating a digestive system and reproductive system for new beings. MARTELLUS claims that PYGMALION's artificial men are automata with no self-control. PYGMALION argues that his creations are conscious and capable of communication, despite MARTELLUS's assertions.

Sir Charles expressed disapproval of his wife's taste. Gertrude received a letter from her father, C.B. Lindsay, regarding a bill from Madame Smith for her dresses. C.B. Lindsay stated that he cannot afford to support Gertrude's extravagant spending on dresses. C.B. Lindsay mentioned that he had to raise L500 last month and expressed concern over Gertrude's financial demands. C.B. Lindsay commented on young Erskine's lack of prospects and criticized Trefusis for his political stance. Gertrude wrote a reply to her father addressing his concerns about her spending. Gertrude noted that it had been over three years since her father last paid Madame Smith.

Sholto offered the doctor a guinea for his attendance on the narrator. The doctor responded to Sholto's offer in a prompt manner. The narrator observed that Sholto has no sense of humor and is always grumbling. The narrator flirted with the doctor for amusement during the trip. Sholto pretended to know about a piece of machinery on the ship but did not. The narrator feels that their relationship with Sholto will not last long. The narrator experiences aversion and disgust towards Sholto at times.

John Metcalf informed the speaker that Sir James Hooker is the president of the Society for Naturalizing the Bread Fruit Tree in Britain. The speaker wrote an article on the Conolly electro-motor, which will be published in the Dynamic Statistician next week. The Conolly electro-motor is currently generating over fifty pounds an hour for the Company, with expectations of a thousand pounds a day next year. The speaker recalls Mr. Conolly as a common workman who fitted an electric bell in their study four years ago. Marian expresses concern about Sholto Douglas potentially holding a grudge against her. Elinor suggests that Marian should be kind to Sholto Douglas and that an éclaircissement may be necessary. Mrs. Fairfax leads the way to the Academy, while Elinor decides to explore the pictures independently.

The conversation involves two individuals discussing the topic of drinking and its consequences. One individual expresses disbelief in the other's ability to stop drinking. The other individual mentions a child named Lucy and her whereabouts. The first individual suggests that Lucy is better off with her Aunt Marian. There is a discussion about the child's observations and comments regarding drinking. One individual expresses a desire to get drunk to alleviate misery. The conversation concludes with a proposal to part ways and discuss custody of the child.

Mr. Conly is disengaged and requests Mr. Lind to come to his room. Mr. Lind instructs the clerk to ask Mr. Conly to come to him instead. Mr. Lind visits Conolly's room to discuss a matter regarding his daughter. Mr. Lind informs Conolly that his daughter is engaged to Mr. Sholto Douglas. Conolly asserts that he is engaged to Mr. Lind's daughter. Mr. Lind expresses his objections to the engagement based on social status. Conolly responds by criticizing Mr. Lind's perception of a workman.

Mr. Conolly has assured that Marian can withdraw from their engagement if she wishes. Marian believes Mr. Conolly is an eminent man and respects him. Mr. Lind opposes Marian's desire to marry Mr. Conolly, stating he is not a gentleman. Mr. Lind defines a gentleman as someone who is well born and well bred. Marian expresses her disagreement with her father's views and refuses to obey him regarding her marriage. Marian feels that her father is being unfair and that she cannot stay in her current living situation. Elinor suggests that Marian can talk to her despite the tension with Uncle Reginald.

Gertrude was presented at court and accepted invitations from those she deemed worthy. Gertrude's father was a retired admiral with limited financial means. Gertrude remained single despite her father's pressure to marry. The admiral could not afford to provide Gertrude with a dowry. Gertrude was invited to Brandon Beeches by Lady Brandon to escape her home life. Gertrude felt unhappy and somewhat broken in spirit during her reunion with Agatha and Jane. Agatha had become bolder and stronger since their school days, despite Gertrude's perception of her loss of youth.

Thinkers oppressed by the disorders of the living world find happiness in the contemplation of crystals and magnets. Materialism, as expressed by Lucretius and Tyndall, contains a nobility that can inspire poetry. John Davidson found his highest inspiration in Materialism. The Darwinian reaction against Bible fetichism contributed to the degradation of religion. The absence of a divine order led to a sense of chaos and initial exhilaration among people. William Blake criticized the concept of God, referring to it as Old Nobodaddy. In politics, it is easier to do without God than to do without his viceroys and lieutenants.

Burge-Lubin is identified as the President. Mrs. Lutestring expresses a view that Burge-Lubin is immature and childlike. Barnabas points out that Mrs. Lutestring receives a pension for three hundred years while they owe her only seventy-eight. Mrs. Lutestring contrasts the blessings received by Burge-Lubin's generation with the hardships faced by her own. Burge-Lubin defends the happiness and work of Chinese and colored individuals. The Archbishop questions the capabilities of Burge-Lubin and his generation. Burge-Lubin denies having met the Minister of Health and protests against perceived color prejudice.

The Elderly Gentleman expresses a desire to stay rather than return to a place he finds distasteful. The Oracle warns the Elderly Gentleman that staying will lead to his discouragement. The Elderly Gentleman believes that returning will result in his disgust and despair. The Oracle has been present for one hundred and seventy years and indicates that the Elderly Gentleman's death does not hold the same significance for her. The Elderly Gentleman ultimately chooses to stay, believing it to be the nobler risk. The Elderly Gentleman dies shortly after grasping the Oracle's hands. The scene shifts to a summer afternoon in the year 31,920 A.D., where a dance is taking place in a sunlit glade.

The text discusses the concept of self-control and its importance for survival in changing circumstances. Self-control is described as a highly developed vital sense that regulates appetites. The author criticizes Neo-Darwinians for overlooking the significance of self-control in the context of Evolutionary Selection. Nietzsche is mentioned as a philosopher who recognized the importance of power over self as opposed to power over others. The text reflects on the decline of the prestige of early Darwinian thinkers like Huxley, Tyndall, Spencer, and Darwin. The author expresses disdain for Neo-Darwinian interpretations of evolution, labeling them as lacking imagination and moral significance. Humanitarians initially embraced Darwinism but struggled with the Problem of Evil and the implications of attributing cruelty in nature to a benevolent God.

The narrator has taken measures to prevent a woman from drinking alcohol, including firing staff and stopping his own drinking at home. The woman has a history of defying the narrator's attempts to control her drinking and has expressed both a desire to stop and a willingness to continue drinking. Despite her struggles with alcohol, the woman continues to perform at the theatre, relying on her familiarity with old roles. The quality of the theatre has declined, with experienced actors leaving and being replaced by less skilled performers. The narrator has taken lodgings in town to distance himself from the woman but continues to visit her due to concerns for their child, Lucy. The woman has sent the narrator a letter claiming she has stopped drinking, despite her previous behavior and the narrator's doubts about her honesty. The woman accuses the narrator of encouraging her drinking and abandoning her after realizing the consequences.

The speaker expresses a belief that halving an income would make it tighter. The speaker states that if they left Bob, both would face disgrace. The speaker questions the difference in position between their situation and that of their sister when she marries Ned. The speaker asserts that Ned will not marry in a church but through a registrar. The speaker claims to be independent and able to leave Bob if they choose. The speaker refuses to make love a matter of money and declined Bob's previous marriage proposal. The speaker indicates they can attract clever people to their home and expresses a preference for their company over societal expectations.

Agatha danced in the room while Mrs. Wylie expressed concern for her mother. Miss Wilson and Mr. Jansenius entered the room, causing Agatha to become motionless. Agatha brusquely asked Henrietta about her husband, who had mysteriously disappeared. Henrietta shared her feelings about her marriage and her husband's disappearance with Agatha. Agatha suggested that Henrietta should search for her husband in rivers, but Henrietta believed he was not in danger. Agatha expressed skepticism about the permanence of love and marriage. Henrietta insisted that her love was different and that they were not like other couples.

The narrator expresses a preference for not having meals privately with Sholto. The narrator fears that their secret identity as Mrs. Conolly may be revealed. The narrator feels burdened by attention from others due to Sholto's appearance and their own past. Mrs. Crawford, a guest at the hotel, becomes determined to know the narrator. The narrator declines Mrs. Crawford's invitation to her mansion due to concerns about their identity. The narrator reflects on their past selfishness and the realization of their own folly. The narrator mentions the ease of obtaining a divorce under American law.

The text discusses the implications of a hypothetical elixir that could extend human life. The population of the country is assumed to be forty million people. Each person is estimated to consume five ounces of the elixir daily. This consumption would result in a total annual demand of approximately two million tons of the elixir. The characters express skepticism about the feasibility of producing such an elixir. Conrad identifies himself as a biologist and not a quack, indicating he does not possess the elixir. Franklyn argues that the will to live longer is not merely a wish but requires a deep conviction of necessity.

A laborer earned thirteen shillings a week before the war and now earns thirty when he can get it. Dr. Barnabas assures that his daughter shall marry the man of her choice, regardless of social status. Savvy expresses frustration about the political discussions and the lack of engagement from the guests. Franklyn mentions that he and his brother have a program of their own. Burge expresses a desire to learn and gather opinions from others. Lubin states that any new plank in the party platform must go through the National Liberal Federation. Franklyn indicates that he believes their program would not interest Burge.

Trefusis directed a cabman to drive after touching Gertrude's hand. Gertrude reacted by shrinking back into a corner of the vehicle as it departed. Trefusis expressed his opinion about Gertrude to Mr. Jansenius after she left. Trefusis stated that he is going to marry Agatha. Mr. Sidney Trefusis wrote a letter to the author regarding the portrayal of his friends in the novel 'An Unsocial Socialist.' Trefusis believes that actions in novels are judged by a romantic system of morals. Trefusis commented on the differences in the struggles for personal liberty between men and women.

Jeff Smilash initially resisted being taken against his will but later agreed to accompany the officers. A boy identified Smilash as the man who was kissed by a lady and claimed he threatened to drown him. The inspector warned Smilash that anything he said could be used against him. Smilash admitted to having a tendency to lie and described himself as lazy and self-indulgent. Agatha asked Smilash what he had done with the lady last seen in his company. Smilash claimed that the lady fainted upon seeing him and asked him to bring her water. Smilash stated that he carried the lady to the canal but found the water unsuitable for her.

Smilash was taken by a policeman and directed towards the gate. Agatha observed Henrietta embracing Smilash but did not hear their conversation. Henrietta expressed her desire for Sidney not to leave her again. Sidney lifted Henrietta onto his shoulder and ran away from the scene. Sidney and Henrietta reached a grassy area by the canal after navigating a ditch. Sidney expressed his longing for Henrietta since he left her. Henrietta sensed that Sidney intended to leave her again.

The speaker fled the country and returned with the ruins of a temple. The temple was rebuilt in one hour and illuminated more brightly than before. The rebuilt temple was subsequently destroyed again. The speaker expresses a belief that men should not be overly hard-hearted. The speaker argues that sentimental young men are undesirable. A discussion occurs about the futility of regret and the nature of sympathy. The characters engage in a game of chess before deciding to end it for the night.

The text discusses the impact of science on religion and the perception of religious stories as literal truths. An English village lad who learns that certain religious stories cannot be literally true may become indifferent or hostile to religion. The professional classes are increasingly rejecting the Bible and exposing their children to Ethical and Rationalist tracts. The text argues that indifference to religion is not a viable path for guiding nations towards civilization. Statesmen are urged to adopt a religion that can resonate with the general populace due to the commitment to Adult Suffrage. The text warns against the danger of reverting to old superstitions in response to the perceived failures of current beliefs. It emphasizes that the rejection of Darwinism does not imply a return to traditional religious beliefs.

The author attempted to earn an honest living from the age of fifteen to twenty-three. The author's last attempt to earn an honest living was in 1879 with a company formed in London to exploit an invention by Thomas Alva Edison. The Edison Telephone Company was merged into the National Telephone Company after a short period. The Edison Telephone Company employed American workers who had a strong work ethic and a disdain for British workers. The American workers admired Thomas Alva Edison and disliked Graham Bell, the inventor of a competing telephone. The author had knowledge of telephony and often assisted the official lecturer at the Edison Telephone Company. The author had connections with English peers who were interested in scientific expertise.

The conversation involves two characters discussing the nature of happiness in marriage. One character expresses dissatisfaction with her husband's behavior and communication style. The character feels jealousy towards her husband's interactions with other people, including women. She compares herself unfavorably to other women, noting their confidence and ease in social situations. The discussion touches on the idea that marriage may be fundamentally flawed if the characters cannot find happiness. The character expresses a desire for a different life, including the possibility of having children.

Henrietta has decided not to speak to Agatha again due to perceived shameful behavior. Smilash promised his wife Henrietta that he would behave towards Agatha as if no offense had occurred. Henrietta returned to London by the twelve o'clock express after pleading for a return to their domestic state. Smilash experienced feelings of disgust and remorse after sending Henrietta away. Smilash went to Wickens's pond to skate and found it crowded with Alton students and visitors. Farmer Wickens defended Smilash's presence on the pond against Fairholme's objections. Agatha recognized Smilash's voice while skating and approached him after he mentioned having something funny to tell her.

The speaker expresses amazement at the destructiveness of their creations. The speaker identifies as Lilith and claims to have brought life into existence. Lilith states that she has allowed humanity to live due to her hope and faith in them. Lilith believes that humanity is striving for redemption from physical existence. The speaker acknowledges that they will not interfere with humanity's progress until they achieve a certain state. Lilith reflects on the potential for humanity to surpass her and become one with her essence. The speaker asserts that life is eternal and will eventually fill the vast domain of existence.

The characters discuss the challenges of civilization and the failures of past attempts at civilization. Flinders Petrie is mentioned as having counted nine attempts at civilization that failed. The characters express concerns about the impact of Democracy, Socialism, and Votes for Women on society. Lubin states that he is patient but questions the usefulness of conclusions that cannot be realized. Conrad expresses doubt that people want to live longer than usual. Burge asks if Conrad has discovered the elixir of life. The conversation includes skepticism about the effectiveness of various health remedies.

The speaker expresses a desire to maintain their current living situation despite potential financial implications. The speaker indicates that they do not wish to visit or be visited by another individual. The speaker's father is described as wealthy and willing to provide financial compensation for the speaker's separation from Marmaduke. The speaker questions how Marmaduke would be compensated for the loss of income resulting from their separation. The speaker details various expenses and debts incurred during their time with Marmaduke. The speaker asserts that they are financially responsible for maintaining their household and that their earnings are insufficient. The clergyman expresses surprise at the speaker's financial situation and suggests separation, to which the speaker disagrees.

The Serpent claims to be wise and can talk about many things. Eve expresses discomfort when reminded of death. The Serpent explains that death can be conquered through birth. The Serpent describes renewal as being born again with a new skin. Eve learns that life is what differentiates the dead from the living. The Serpent states that it performed a miracle by creating a new snake from a part of its life. Eve expresses concern about the potential for only snakes to exist if Adam and others perish.

The text discusses the importance of money in personal and national morality. It states that money controls morality and criticizes the United States for its approach to morality and money. The author reflects on his father's financial situation in Ireland, describing him as poor but not homeless or hungry. The author mentions that his father's income was at least three figures, which was insufficient for the social position he aspired to maintain. The concept of 'rent of ability' is introduced, suggesting that social opportunity can exist independently of income. The author shares personal experiences of walking in fashionable areas while being financially constrained. The text includes a recollection of an encounter with a beggar, highlighting the author's own financial struggles.

Marian is in conversation with Duke Marmaduke about his need to write home due to his governor's illness. Marmaduke requests that Marian keep Lucy for another week and suggests discipline if necessary. Conolly and Elinor observe a moment between Marian and Douglas as they say farewell. Conolly informs Marian that Douglas is in love with her, which causes her to reconsider inviting him again. Marian reveals to Conolly that Douglas confessed his love for her earlier that day. Conolly expresses that he believes it is beneficial for men to fall in love with Marian. In October, Marian is on holiday at the house of Hardy McQuinch's brother, while Conolly works in a laboratory at their home.

ZOO expresses a feeling of anger and a desire to injure THE ELDERLY GENTLEMAN. THE ELDERLY GENTLEMAN claims to have made ZOO blush with shame. ZOO accuses THE ELDERLY GENTLEMAN of being an evil child and warns him of potential violence. THE ELDERLY GENTLEMAN apologizes to ZOO for hurting her feelings. ZOO states that she has recognized a violent instinct within herself due to THE ELDERLY GENTLEMAN's actions. ZOO declares a change in her political stance, stating she is no longer a Conservative. ZOO critiques the ineffectiveness of advice given to her by others, including the Prime Minister.

The conversation involves two characters discussing emotional responses and personal responsibility. One character suggests that a kiss can make a woman happy for a week. The other character expresses a lack of skill in kissing. The discussion shifts to the topic of divorce and its implications for a character named Marian. Elinor expresses dismay at the mention of divorce. The characters acknowledge that the situation will soon become public knowledge. Elinor indicates a desire for clarity regarding communication with Marian about her financial independence.

Agatha is facing expulsion from the college due to a disagreement with Miss Wilson and Mrs. Miller. Mrs. Miller mistook Agatha for her cat, which Agatha claims is not her fault. Agatha argues that she should be allowed to stay until the end of the term. Miss Wilson states that the fault book is meant for self-reproach and not for accusations against others. Agatha believes that her actions were justified and that she should have made an entry in the fault book regarding Miss Wilson's loss of moral force. Miss Wilson expresses reluctance to expel Agatha but emphasizes the need for order. Agatha promises to behave better in the future and informs her mother that she will stay at the college.

Agatha states that she is not in love with the man. The man suggests that Agatha must marry him. Agatha expresses that she does not care for the man and was only joking about marriage. The man insists that he wants Agatha to keep her word about marriage. Agatha refuses to promise to marry the man. The man expresses frustration with Agatha's indecision. Agatha advises the man to remain a bachelor.

The Ancient expresses a reluctance to dance, stating it would be painful to return to youthful rhythms. The Youth criticizes the Ancients for being unhappy and not engaging in joyful activities. The Ancient claims that the Youth are living a 'dog's life' by being carefree and unaware of deeper experiences. The Maiden expresses fatigue with dances and partners, suggesting a desire for more meaningful enjoyment. The Ancient observes that the Maiden is showing signs of maturity by acknowledging the tiresomeness of childish games. The Maiden indicates she is older than the Youth and questions how the Ancient knows this. The Youth suggests they should continue dancing despite the Ancient's departure.

Sholto proposed marriage to Marian. Marian refused Sholto's proposal. Marian expressed distress after Sholto left. Elinor believed Sholto was courting Marian. Marmaduke entered the room feeling low-spirited. Marmaduke stated he was leaving London. Marmaduke mentioned he was packing clothes he left behind.

The Newly Born expresses a desire for clean air. The He-Ancient states that the air will be clean soon. The She-Ancient advises against making living toys from children. Strephon expresses a desire to kill himself at four years old. Martellus returns from the grove after completing a task. Ecrasia refuses to allow the creation of more automata. The He-Ancient explains that children have played with dolls since the existence of men.

Douglas dined alone at a restaurant after parting with a friend. Mrs. Leith Fairfax recognized Douglas while in a cab and called to the cabman to stop. Mrs. Leith Fairfax expressed concern about Douglas's presence in London. Douglas stated he had no intention of leaving London at present. Mrs. Leith Fairfax suggested that Douglas should leave London for at least a year. Douglas's servant informed him that his mother had called and wished to see him. Douglas decided to go to Brussels that night and instructed his servant to repack his luggage.

Marmaduke expresses annoyance and states he intends never to speak to Susanna again. Conolly informs Marmaduke that it is not his duty to take care of Susanna. Conolly suggests postponing supper due to the current mood between him and Marmaduke. Conolly waits for his sister, Susanna, at the stage door after Marmaduke leaves. Susanna prefers taking a hansom cab over a brougham for comfort and cost reasons. Conolly shares that he performed at a concert with Master Lind, who is upset with Susanna. Marian Lind lives at Westbourne Terrace, Paddington, with her father, Mr. Reginald Harrington Lind.

Marmaduke left the table to fetch Marian for lunch. Lady Carbury expressed displeasure at Marmaduke's behavior. Elinor suggested that Marmaduke had his reasons for leaving. Marmaduke found Marian in the summer-house reading. Marmaduke confronted Marian about sending Conolly to inform him of his disgrace. Marian explained that she had no other means to warn Marmaduke. Marmaduke expressed disbelief at Marian's claim of him being under bad influence.

Nelly's book has a colonial edition that has just appeared. The advertisement for 'The Waters of Marah' by Elinor McQuinch is featured in a newspaper. Douglas reads positive reviews of Elinor McQuinch's book from various publications. Marmaduke expresses relief about being rid of the child's mother. Marmaduke offered the child's mother five hundred pounds to leave, but she refused. Marian appears happy when Marmaduke is away, suggesting tension in their relationship. Douglas expresses concern about Marmaduke's treatment of Marian.

Rousseau is mentioned as a Deist like Burge. Professor Barnabas has made an important communication. Joyce Burge believes Professor Barnabas is the greatest politician in the kingdom. Burge claims that the Liberal Party will be in power for the next thirty years due to Conrad's influence. Burge discusses the impact of a return to biblical principles on the Nonconformist vote. Lubin suggests that advocating for the extension of human life to three hundred years could benefit the Liberal Party. Conrad states that scientific opinion has been converging on the concept of Creative Evolution.

The speaker identifies as a Colonizer and an Exterminator. The Elderly Gentleman expresses concern about the treatment of natives during colonization. ZOO states that prolonging the existence of the elderly would lead to their slow demise. ZOO mentions that they weed out individuals who do not meet their standards. The Elderly Gentleman inquires about the fate of those deemed undesirable by ZOO. ZOO admits that undesirable individuals are killed. ZOO informs The Elderly Gentleman that there are no cities in their territory, only a temple.

Every king in Europe has been shot at in the streets. Trefusis expressed that kings are not accountable for the evils in their realms. Erskine admired a photograph of a woman in a rich gold and coral frame. Trefusis revealed that the woman in the portrait was his deceased wife, Hetty. Trefusis stated he keeps Hetty's portrait to correct his natural amativeness. Trefusis showed a collection of photographs, including one of his father's house that cost seventy-five thousand pounds. Sir Charles expressed secret disgust at being invited to admire a photograph of a country house.

Sir Charles and Jane have a disagreement regarding his singing duets with Miss Wylie. Jane expresses that she does not object to Sir Charles's singing but is frustrated that he interrupted Miss Wylie while she was going to write a letter. Agatha Wylie offers to write the letter first before singing duets with Sir Charles. Agatha goes to the library to write the letter and returns to find the drawing-room empty except for Sir Charles. Sir Charles claims that Jane is jealous and expresses his frustrations about her behavior. Jane returns to the drawing-room while Agatha and Sir Charles are singing, and her presence disrupts them. Agatha suggests that Gertrude is likely playing billiards with Mr. Erskine to avoid a potential argument between Jane and Sir Charles.

The letter was dated the 17th of December and sent from New York. Marian and her cousin Nelly had previously used affectionate modes of address in their correspondence. Marian expressed concern about how her actions might affect her father and George. Marian stated that she felt disgraced and worried about the scandal affecting George's prospects. Marian requested Nelly to contradict any rumors suggesting that Ned was at fault for her departure. Marian reflected on her misjudgment of Sholto's character during their voyage. Marian noted that Sholto's behavior changed negatively when they were isolated on the ship.

Lady Brandon expresses frustration about people trampling on her grounds without permission. Sir Charles is unable to take action until he consults his solicitor. Trefusis informs that a public meeting is planned at the crossroads. Chester questions Trefusis's right to be a capitalist and landlord. Trefusis recognizes Chester as the author of a tragedy titled 'The Patriot Martyrs.' Lady Brandon refuses to support Trefusis's request for funds for their demonstration. Lady Brandon mentions that Gertrude Lindsay is staying with them.

The author claims to have understood the concept of evolution before the age of ten. The text discusses the kinship of all forms of life as a basis for the theory of evolution. Darwin's ideas were welcomed by various groups, including Humanitarians, Militarists, Socialists, and Capitalists. The Socialists were particularly encouraged by Darwin's emphasis on the influence of environment on individuals. Robert Owen argued that criminals and the uneducated are victims of circumstance, advocating for a moralized society. The text critiques the belief that circumstances govern character, citing examples of individuals from similar backgrounds who differ greatly. The author references Lamarckian evolution to suggest that character can be developed through will and effort.

Lindsay is more amiable under the influence of hemlock than under the social system. Gertrude expresses outrage at Trefusis's comments about her unhappiness. Trefusis claims Gertrude's countenance and voice indicate her unhappiness. Gertrude asserts she is particularly attached to her friends. Trefusis describes Gertrude as cold, mistrustful, and fearful of judgment. Gertrude thanks Trefusis for his offer to find her basket and fill it. Trefusis notes Gertrude's appearance and makes a memorandum about her.

Divinity is associated with honor and public spirit rather than belief in Nobodaddy. The fitness of a man for public trust was historically assessed by his belief in Nobodaddy. Darwin's ideas led to the abandonment of the belief test for public trust. The absence of a belief test allowed individuals with self-serving interests to gain public trust. The British public was misled into believing they had a strong public opinion that would resist government overreach. Political reform was difficult to achieve, but once passed, it was unlikely to be reversed by the government. The loss of sanctity of Public Opinion allowed politicians to manipulate the public for personal gain.

Miss Carpenter expressed concern about her light shoes in the rain. Agatha suggested seeking shelter under the veranda of an old chalet. Miss Wilson initially hesitated due to concerns about trespassing. The group decided to go to the old chalet as the rain intensified. They found the gate to the chalet rehung and fastened. A young laborer emerged from the chalet as the group sought shelter. The laborer was dressed in new clothing and held a silk umbrella.

Ecrasia expresses indignation towards Martellus. Martellus reveals he once created busts of ancients but destroyed them. Arjillax is excited about Martellus's busts and wants to display them. Martellus claims that a live ancient is better than a dead statue. Martellus believes that art is false and life alone is true. Martellus introduces a new artist named Pygmalion, claiming he surpasses both himself and Arjillax. Ecrasia and Arjillax express skepticism about Pygmalion's artistic abilities.

The text discusses the aptitude for shorthand and keyboard manipulation, suggesting that these skills may be older or more easily assimilated than previously thought. It states that the evolutionary process is hereditary and that human life is continuous and immortal. The belief in heredity was prevalent, with people expecting sons to mentally inherit from their fathers. Intentional Selection was practiced in human marriage and in the cultivation of plants and animals. The author mentions that there are nearly two hundred different sorts of dogs capable of breeding with one another. The text references Lorenz Oken's contributions to the concept of Evolution, particularly his definition of protoplasm as the original substance of life. Oken's ideas were noted to have anticipated modern cell morphology before the advent of advanced scientific tools.

Lamarck proposed that giraffes evolved long necks by wanting to reach high leaves. An alternative explanation suggests that prehistoric stockbreeders selectively bred long-necked animals. Darwin introduced a third explanation that does not involve will or purpose, stating that survival depends on the ability to reach food. According to Darwin, animals that are shorter than the average will die of starvation, while taller animals will thrive and reproduce. This process of natural selection continues until the giraffe's neck is long enough to reach food, at which point it stabilizes. Darwin's theory operates without the need for human or divine intervention and does not rely on conscious intent. The text critiques the concept of Natural Selection as a reduction of beauty and intelligence to random changes.

Miss Wilson held classes in gymnastics, dancing, elocution, and drawing on Saturday mornings at Alton College. The afternoon at Alton College was spent playing lawn tennis, with lady guests allowed to bring male relatives. On a Saturday in late October, Miss Wilson went outside after luncheon and found a group of girls watching Agatha and Jane. Smilash emerged from the shrubbery carrying a ball and claimed he had feelings like anyone else. Miss Wilson questioned Smilash about a five shilling payment he claimed to have received from Agatha. Agatha denied giving Smilash five shillings, stating she only had threepence in her purse. Smilash argued that it was unreasonable for him to give up money he never received.

Miss Wilson forbids communication between Smilash and the young ladies in her charge. Smilash claims to take pleasure in personating his alter ego. Miss Wilson states that no one is admitted without a trustworthy introduction or recommendation. Smilash argues that disguises are generally used to conceal crime. Miss Wilson asserts that she reserves the right to exclude students from her college if she disapproves of their behavior. Smilash compares Miss Wilson's system to coercion and argues against it. Miss Wilson insists that her system is fundamentally different from traditional coercive systems.

The characters discuss the sacrifices made for the country during difficult times. Burge expresses his opinion about Lubin, stating he is not a real statesman and is lazy. Lubin enters the scene, described as a man in his sixties with Yorkshire origins. Lubin greets Franklyn and recalls a past meeting related to America. Savvy is introduced as Franklyn's daughter. Burge attempts to enlist Franklyn's support for the Liberal Party. Lubin shows a calm demeanor and engages with Burge and Franklyn.
