Mrs. Cave experienced a nervous condition during the emotional discussion about the missing crystal. Mr. Cave left the house in frustration after a painful supper scene related to the crystal's disappearance. The next day, Mrs. Cave received two customers in distress and shared a garbled account of the situation. Mr. Cave was aware of the crystal's location, which was in the possession of Mr. Jacoby Wace at St. Catherine's Hospital. Mr. Wace agreed to keep the crystal for Mr. Cave after considering the circumstances surrounding its disappearance. Mr. Cave claimed the crystal had come into his possession from a forced sale and had been unsold at ten shillings for months.

source.author: Herbert George Wells
source.title: The Country of the Blind, And Other Stories

text: The couple has spent nearly a thousand pounds over their intended budget of four hundred pounds. Marjorie expresses excitement about furnishing an empty room upstairs. The arrival of their child transforms Trafford and Marjorie's perspective on life. Trafford had been preparing to discuss the impact of Marjorie's spending on his research. Trafford realizes that his passion for research is less important than his new role as a father. He acknowledges that he had previously viewed Marjorie as an accessory to his career. Trafford decides that he must find a way to supplement his income.

Marjorie has conflicting thoughts about love and societal expectations. Mr. Magnet is characterized as good, kind, brave, modest, well-off, famous, and in love with Marjorie. Marjorie feels a duty to love Mr. Magnet but questions her feelings due to his physical appearance. She experiences a deep craving for beauty, excitement, and passion in her life. Marjorie struggles with the idea that Mr. Magnet may not be a suitable partner for her desires. Mr. Magnet proposed to Marjorie three days after visiting her twice for tea and supper. During his visits, Mr. Magnet engaged in various activities, including playing croquet and discussing social reform.

Aunt Plessington specialized in intellectual philanthropy and evolved her Movement with the help of Uncle Hubert. The Movement aimed to implement restrictions on the sale of meat, groceries, and tobacco, and to limit the consumption of sweets. Aunt Plessington believed that lower strata of society could not be trusted with their dietary choices. She proposed changes to the Truck Act to allow employers to provide housing, clothing, and other necessities instead of wages. Aunt Plessington's Movement attracted supporters from all classes in society. She recounted the growth of her Movement and the respect she and Hubert received in the world of politico-social reform. Marjorie expressed uncertainty about her future plans when asked by Aunt Plessington.

Hapley was tied down to a bed due to violent behavior caused by an imaginary moth. The doctor attending Hapley dismissed the existence of the moth and lacked knowledge of mental science. Hapley experienced the moth crawling over him while awake and in his dreams. Hapley is now in a padded room, troubled by the hallucination of the moth. The asylum doctor diagnosed Hapley's condition as a hallucination. Hapley believes the moth is the ghost of Pawkins and considers it a unique specimen. Two men in a canoe are searching for a location marked on a worn map that includes a river and a reef.

source.author: Herbert George Wells
source.title: The Country of the Blind, And Other Stories

text: The man was described as forcible, hard, and tactless. The narrator had the ability to control and soften the man. Gresham's reckless speech caused concern among the others. The narrator considered returning to the north but realized it would require separation from his lady. The narrator expressed a desire to remain a private man and not engage in political matters. The lady expressed doubt about the situation and the possibility of war. The narrator reassured the lady that there would be no war and emphasized his right to choose his life.

source.author: Herbert George Wells
source.title: The Country of the Blind, And Other Stories

text: The characters are planning a trip to Labrador. The trip to Labrador is described as a way to escape their current situation. The duration of the trip is expected to be the better part of a year. The characters express concerns about their responsibilities to their children. One character suggests that separating may be necessary if they cannot resolve their issues together. They ultimately decide to go to Labrador together.

Marjorie was to share a room with Daffy due to the unavailability of another room. Mr. Pope had secured the other room for his morning routines. Mrs. Pope mentioned that Marjorie would not have to move when Aunt Plessington arrives. Marjorie's father was in the vicar's study writing a letter to the Times. Marjorie and her family examined the vicarage's bedrooms and furniture after tea. The Popes had not met any of the vicarage residents prior to this visit. Marjorie felt a lack of understanding regarding the decoration and style of the vicarage.

Trafford's antecedents were not objected to by the narrator. Marjorie was described as the favorite daughter of the narrator. The narrator expressed hope that Syd and Rom would achieve as much as their elder sisters. Mrs. Pope maintained a fixed smile and refused to worry over a financial disappointment. Marjorie felt empowered to host dinners and aimed for a blend of simplicity and quality in her gatherings. The first dinner hosted by Marjorie included notable guests such as Sir Roderick Dover and Edward Crampton. Marjorie was regarded as a successful hostess by her guests.

The Batemo River has been occupied for nearly sixty miles. The occupying species has driven men out, occupied plantations, and captured at least one ship. They are believed to have bridged the Capuarana arm and advanced towards the Amazon. This species is organized into a single nation and uses poison against larger enemies. The poison is similar to snake venom and may be manufactured by the species. Legends about their capabilities, including engineering feats and communication methods, are prevalent in the Upper Amazon region. The species is rapidly increasing in numbers and is expected to expand their territory significantly by 1950 or 1960.

source.author: Herbert George Wells
source.title: The Country of the Blind, And Other Stories

text: The scene takes place at the cliff of the Leas. Gibberne holds a dog that appears stiff and lifeless. The narrator expresses concern about Gibberne's speed and the heat. Gibberne throws the dog away, which spins upward and hangs over a group of people. The effects of the New Accelerator drug cease suddenly. The world around the narrator and Gibberne comes alive again after the drug's effects wear off. The dog falls through a lady's parasol during the transition back to normal speed.

source.author: Herbert George Wells
source.title: The Country of the Blind, And Other Stories

text: Rubber sales are affected by a widespread depression in the market of plantation shares. Solomonson consulted Trafford about the unsoundness of Behrens' claim and Trafford's plans to publish a demonstration of it. Trafford proposed to publish an exposition on making synthetic rubber indistinguishable from natural rubber. Solomonson expressed concern about Trafford's intention to publicly share the synthesis of rubber. Solomonson has a strong friendship and admiration for Trafford and desires business cooperation. Trafford possesses a unique ability to find novel solutions to problems that others cannot solve. Sir Rupert was initially incredulous about Trafford's change of purpose but eventually considered a scheme of cooperation.

Marjorie and Trafford meet at a gate in a garden. Mr. Pope, Marjorie's father, discovers them together. Mr. Pope expresses anger and confusion upon seeing Marjorie with Trafford. Mr. Pope attempts to strike Trafford with a stick. Trafford states that he asked Marjorie to meet him. Marjorie insists that nothing shall keep her apart from Trafford. Mr. Pope demands that Marjorie go indoors.

The narrator believes they are Eden in Elvesham's body. The narrator experiences confusion and frustration regarding their identity. The narrator dresses in an evening suit and later finds more ordinary clothes. The narrator's study contains a writing-desk, a revolving bookcase, and many books. The writing-desk and its revolving top are locked, and the narrator cannot find the keys. The narrator attempts to break into the desk in a fit of rage. The butler and two women-servants find the narrator in the study after the destruction.

source.author: Herbert George Wells
source.title: The Country of the Blind, And Other Stories

text: The discussion took place after the last lecture in the introductory course in zoology. The lecturer stated that the goal of higher vertebrata is 'from ovum to ovum.' Hill expressed that science is systematic knowledge and questioned the validity of ideas that do not fit into this system. The hunchback questioned whether Hill is a materialist. The fair-haired student challenged Hill's views on aspirations and social concerns. Brooks, the laboratory attendant, entered with freshly killed guinea-pigs for dissection. The discussion ended abruptly as students rushed to secure specimens.

source.author: Herbert George Wells
source.title: The Country of the Blind, And Other Stories

text: A serious affair involved a list of humorists and prominent people associated with their industry at the _Literati_. Marjorie read the Chairman's introduction and her destined husband's speech with a sense of hostility. Mr. Magnet began his speech with modest disavowals and referenced a story involving a bluebottle and two Scotsmen. Mr. Magnet expressed concern about tempering hospitality with a demand for a speech and noted he was to introduce a debate. He discussed various types of humor, including American humor characterized by exaggeration and the humor of form and expression. Marjorie became distracted while reading and noted that the pun had become démodé. Her attention shifted from the speech to her father's hand taking possession of the _Times_, leading her to forget the discussion.

The laboratory telephone had a habit of disconnecting itself early in the afternoon. Trafford's bank account was overdrawn by three hundred and thirteen pounds. Trafford initially believed he had a surplus of one hundred and fifty pounds in his account. Marjorie had been ailing and irritable for two weeks prior to Trafford's discovery. Marjorie had spent nearly seven hundred and fifty pounds, including debts to Oxbridge tradesmen. Trafford was astonished to find that Marjorie had written several cheques carelessly. Marjorie initiated a conversation about her spending habits with Trafford.

Mrs. Pope expresses a desire to know more about Professor Trafford. Marjorie expresses distrust towards what her father says about Mr. Trafford. Mrs. Pope emphasizes the good qualities of Mr. Magnet and her concern for Marjorie's happiness. Mrs. Pope reveals that her husband may have to eat into his capital due to financial troubles. Marjorie declares her love for Mr. Trafford and her lack of feelings for Mr. Magnet. Mrs. Pope asks Marjorie to wait before making any commitments regarding Mr. Trafford. Marjorie agrees to promise her mother to wait until she is one-and-twenty before making decisions about Mr. Trafford.

Sir Galahad is described as a fair, tenoring person with an Arthurian moustache and a preference for long frock coats. He is characterized as dressing and behaving more like a gentleman than is typical. Sir Galahad is an orthodox Churchman who holds all doctrines with a flattened and slightly obliterated breadth. He is known for his profuse thoughtfulness, which extends to his journalistic and literary work, as well as his discussions. Trafford reflects on the nature of Talks, noting their fluidity and lack of substantial discussion. He compares the Talkers to dogs, suggesting they engage in superficial conversation without depth or sincerity. Trafford criticizes much of contemporary literature and philosophical discussion as being similar to the superficiality he observes in social Talks.

Trafford was noted as an authority in his field, sometimes having his name quoted without mention of Durgan. Trafford's renewed punctuality in the laboratory helped to revive Durgan's spirits. Trafford began to work late at night to compete with Behren's productivity. Trafford's preoccupation with work negatively affected his domestic life and relationship with Marjorie. The Traffords faced challenges in their marriage as they transitioned from passionate love to a more mundane reality. Trafford felt the burden of financial anxieties and trivial duties, which detracted from his research ambitions. Trafford recognized a growing conflict between his family responsibilities and his desire for scientific research.

The protagonist signed his name in the hall of the College with cold, stiff fingers. He observed a crowd at the notice-board, which likely displayed the biology list. The biology list included H. J. Somers and Wedderburn in Class I. The protagonist felt a mix of pride and disappointment regarding Wedderburn's success. The zoological demonstrator congratulated the protagonist on his achievement. The protagonist noticed Wedderburn interacting with five girl students in the laboratory. Miss Haysman discussed socialism and Browning with the protagonist in the museum.

source.author: Herbert George Wells
source.title: The Country of the Blind, And Other Stories

text: Trafford had limited experience of London, knowing only certain areas such as Chelsea, Kensington, and parts of the Strand. He had never visited significant locations like Hampstead Heath, the Botanical Gardens, or Epping Forest. Trafford was aware of the existence of poorer areas in London but had not experienced them directly. He had read about slums and discussed their issues but did not fully understand the reasons for their existence. Upon exploring unfamiliar regions of London, Trafford encountered a vast and densely populated industrial landscape. The areas he discovered were characterized by factories, public houses, and poorly maintained housing. The population in these areas appeared to be in a state of neglect, with little access to sunlight and wearing cheap, worn clothing.

Marjorie had won Mrs. Trafford's approval regarding a situation involving her daughter. Mrs. Pope was aware of the situation and had suspicions about Marjorie's actions. Cousin Susan Pendexter sent a letter inviting Marjorie to Plymouth. Marjorie returned to London from Plymouth after a week, having lied about her reasons for the trip. Marjorie was determined to secure her relationship with Trafford and was in a state of intense impatience. Marjorie and Trafford went to the registrar's office after meeting at Paddington. They traveled together to France after their marriage, with Marjorie expressing excitement about the journey.

The protagonist holds an unbroken medicine bottle containing green powder. He is sitting on a boulder covered with velvety moss near the crest of a hill. The environment is silent and dark, with a cold wind blowing. A green glow in the sky grows in extent and intensity as he observes the dawn. He sees faint images of schoolmates preparing their evening tasks while sitting in mid-air. A green sun rises over the hills, illuminating the surroundings in green light and deep shadows. The protagonist notes the extinction of his world as the green sun rises in the other universe.

source.author: Herbert George Wells
source.title: The Country of the Blind, And Other Stories

text: Marjorie and her world are described as moving and competing with muted cries for beauty, delight, and freedom. Trafford observes his children in the schoolroom, which has recently been promoted from a day nursery. Margharita, aged eight, is dressed as Becket, while Godwin, nearly seven, is dressed as an assassin knight. Edward, aged two, and the governess are also part of the children's play, with the governess disguised with a Union Jack. Trafford reflects on the upbringing of his children and the sacrifices he has made for their pleasant environment. He contemplates the potential future challenges his children may face, including societal pressures and the loss of deeper values. Trafford's wife enters the drawing-room, and he notes her change from the girl he once knew.

The narrator describes having a yielding disposition and being sensitive to vivid impressions. The narrator experienced a stammer acquired from a schoolfellow in youth. The narrator attended a theatre for the first time and was profoundly amazed and alarmed by the acting. The narrator initially believed the actors were trying to represent human beings. The narrator had difficulty sleeping after the theatre experience and dreamt of actors performing various exaggerated actions. The narrator realized they had not unpacked their razor and made an unusual gesture while thinking about it. The narrator began to notice changes in their behavior, such as bowing and performing nervous gestures.

source.author: Herbert George Wells
source.title: The Country of the Blind, And Other Stories

text: Marjorie felt restless and avoided Daffy while rebuking Theodore for not washing behind his ears. Marjorie attempted to play tennis but stopped after losing two sets. She picked a large bunch of flowers and left them on the piano until reminded by her mother. Marjorie was reluctant to meet Mr. Magnet at the station but ultimately went as her mother wished. Mr. Magnet arrived by the 2.27 train and appeared pleased with his recent press coverage. Mr. Magnet presented Marjorie with a sapphire he had bought in London, hoping for her approval. Marjorie felt a sense of meanness when she hesitated to express her true feelings about the sapphire.

Noyes was the last to leave the group and waved letters intended for England before following the others into the trees. Marjorie and Trafford walked back to their hut, discussing the tasks they needed to complete before the weather changed. They had been busy for nearly four weeks and were exhausted by the end of each day. The hut was constructed from a double framework filled with earth and twigs, as they could not use logs due to limited resources. The hut's floor was made of hammered earth and balsam twigs, and it was heated by a sheet-iron stove. A tent was set up near the hut to serve as a scullery and outhouse, and a thatched roof was built to protect their supplies. Trafford worked diligently to accumulate a wood pile for winter, gathering wood from the nearby thickets.

Mr. Cave observed bird-like creatures during his visions. Mr. Cave initially thought the creatures might be a diurnal species of bat or cherubs. The creatures had broad, silvery wings and a small body with prehensile organs under the mouth. The buildings in the valley had no doors, only circular windows for the creatures to enter and exit. Mr. Cave noticed glittering objects on masts that resembled the crystal he was observing. Observations suggested that the crystal in Mr. Cave's world was connected to a similar crystal in another world. The relationship between the two crystals remains unexplained.

source.author: Herbert George Wells
source.title: The Country of the Blind, And Other Stories

text: Pyecraft crawls on his ceiling and clambers around his doors. The narrator suggests that Pyecraft use lead underclothing to regain his ability to travel. Pyecraft expresses emotional relief at the idea of being able to return to the club. The narrator describes Pyecraft as weighing practically nothing and being a mere mass of assimilatory matter. The narrator observes Pyecraft eating buttered teacake while waiting to speak with him. The narrator recounts an experience of being taken to a Magic Shop by Gip. Gip points out various magical items in the shop window, expressing a desire to buy them.

source.author: Herbert George Wells
source.title: The Country of the Blind, And Other Stories

text: Medina-saroté and Nunez were in love. There was great opposition to the marriage of Nunez and Medina-saroté. Old Yacob had a liking for Nunez but believed he was incompetent. Nunez was struck by a young man but retaliated, leading to a change in how others treated him. Old Yacob and the elders discussed the possibility of curing Nunez's peculiarities. The blind doctor suggested that Nunez's eye condition affected his brain and proposed a surgical operation. Medina-saroté encouraged Nunez to consider the surgery despite his concerns about losing his sight.

source.author: Herbert George Wells
source.title: The Country of the Blind, And Other Stories

text: The narrator wrote down his memories of an explosion that occurred in a classroom. He experienced a backward flight during the explosion and thought he was killed. After the explosion, he was initially confused and believed he was still in the classroom. He perceived figures moving around him but felt disconnected, as if he were not part of the world. The narrator attempted to communicate with others but found an invisible barrier preventing interaction. He described the environment as profoundly dark with faint greenish light in the sky. He felt a sensation of being in the world but not being a part of it.

source.author: Herbert George Wells
source.title: The Country of the Blind, And Other Stories

text: The narrator encountered a man carrying a drawn sword near old temples. The man had a narrow face, dull grey eyes, a black moustache, and a scar on his upper lip. The narrator attempted to explain to the man that a woman was dead, but the man interrupted him. The man thrust his sword into the narrator's heart, which the narrator felt with astonishment but no pain. The scene shifted to a train station, where the narrator heard sounds of doors slamming and cab-horses. The narrator's conversation with a porter revealed that he could not reach the woman he mentioned. The three pursuers arrived at a broad valley after tracking fugitives along a difficult trail.

source.author: Herbert George Wells
source.title: The Country of the Blind, And Other Stories

text: The narrator expresses uncertainty about their location after drinking alcohol. The narrator describes their room as initially unfamiliar but recognizes personal belongings. The narrator experiences a sensation of being in two places at once. The narrator takes a powder that effervesces and falls asleep shortly after. Upon waking, the narrator feels discomfort and a sense of strangeness. The narrator perceives dim shapes in the room and suspects someone may have entered. The narrator realizes they are in a strange room after attempting to interact with familiar objects.

source.author: Herbert George Wells
source.title: The Country of the Blind, And Other Stories

text: Sydney and Rom are two sisters next in succession to Marjorie. Rom is short for Romola, named after one of their mother's favorite fictional heroines. Marjorie has a forbidden nickname, 'Old Gargoo,' which is short for gargoyle. The vicarage is described as a long and low house with two disconnected staircases and various outbuildings. The property includes a neglected orchard, a lawn area, and a vegetable and flower garden. Marjorie is introduced to the vicarage and its surroundings by Sydney and Rom. Mrs. Pope is described as a fine-featured, anxious-looking woman who resembles her children.

The little man felt momentary pleasure seeing a purple black flash turn into a snake. The group had ridden four days into a desolate place with limited resources. The journey was undertaken for a girl whom the little man considered a mere wilful child. A big wild dog approached the horsemen, running with purpose and not noticing them. The little man drew his sword as the dog passed by without foam. The little man reflected on the nature of obedience and the authority of his master. The little man observed that the horses did not like the wind.

source.author: Herbert George Wells
source.title: The Country of the Blind, And Other Stories

text: The motion of Mars in its orbit was perceived clearly. The time between thoughts appeared to grow longer, with a thousand years feeling like a moment. The constellations appeared to change, with Hercules and the Scorpion contracting and Orion and Aldebaran scattering. Saturn was observed growing larger and larger as it approached. The planet Saturn was described as having a flattened body, a disc-like belt, and seven satellites. The solar system became less visible as the observer moved into the outer Universe. The surrounding space became increasingly black and empty as the observer moved away from the stars.

source.author: Herbert George Wells
source.title: The Country of the Blind, And Other Stories

text: The protagonist experiences the city as a vibrant and enchanting place filled with lights and movement. He spends the evening at his club, studying geography and marriage laws using various reference books. After leaving the library, he decides to walk home through Baker Street, Oxford Street, and Hyde Park. Upon returning home, he finds his mother reading 'The Old Wives' Tale' by the fire. He expresses to his mother his intention to bring home a wife, which surprises her. His mother responds positively, saying she would be glad if he loved her. The protagonist shares details about his love for Marjorie with his mother, who encourages him to explain more.

Marjorie and her sister left the house after putting away the apparatus. Daffy mentioned that croquet had not yet been played. Mr. Pope was a coach-builder and inherited a family business. The Pope family had a long history in the coach-building industry, with Mr. Pope's great-grandfather founding the business. Mr. Pope's business faced competition from a varnish supplier who expanded into complete coach-building. Mr. Pope was known for his firm temper and admiration for historical figures like Cato and Washington. Mr. Pope decided to resist the trend towards lighter carriages and automobiles.

Mrs. Pope commented on a bird's-egg blue dress that suited a young woman. Mr. Magnet expressed his feelings for the young woman and mentioned that he asked her to marry him. The young woman, who is twenty years old, refused Mr. Magnet's proposal. Mr. Magnet planned to leave the following day after the proposal. Mrs. Pope expressed concern about the young woman's age and emotional maturity. Mr. Magnet described the young woman as sweet, easy, and graceful. Mrs. Pope believed she could sense the young woman's feelings and reassured Mr. Magnet about her intuition.

The speaker spent seven years in the rubber market. The speaker expresses frustration with Behrens, suggesting he has a flawed perspective. The speaker believes in a collective mind and a growing general consciousness. The speaker has not discussed religion with Marjorie in their nine years together. The speaker describes Marjorie as the essence of life and expresses deep affection for her. The birth of the speaker's first child was a significant event in his life. The speaker feels that his work was overshadowed by his relationship with Marjorie.

The boy learned to talk at an abnormally early age. His mother died when he was two years old. He was under the care of a nursery governess after his mother's death. His father was a stern lawyer who expected great things from him. The boy wandered away from home and encountered a green door. He felt an attraction to the door but also a conviction that it was unwise to enter. Upon entering the garden through the door, he experienced a sense of exhilaration and encountered two spotted panthers.

source.author: Herbert George Wells
source.title: The Country of the Blind, And Other Stories

text: Trafford experienced a range of emotions during the two months of separation from Marjorie. Initially, Trafford's passion for Marjorie overshadowed his other thoughts and responsibilities. Upon returning to London, Trafford's habitual interests and research began to regain prominence in his mind. Trafford consistently thought of Marjorie, recalling her physical presence and their moments together. As autumn progressed, Trafford's memories of Marjorie remained tied to the warmth of summer in Surrey. Trafford was surprised to find Marjorie in London in November when she called him at the college. Marjorie's voice on the phone reminded Trafford of her presence in his life.

Marjorie expressed a desire to go down to Mr. Magnet. Mr. Pope was reading an epitaph in the churchyard. Marjorie felt overwhelmed and caught in a trap after her interaction with Mr. Magnet. Mr. Pope demonstrated his approval of Marjorie's engagement with Mr. Magnet. Marjorie submitted to Mr. Magnet's embrace before returning to her room without saying goodnight. Daffy noticed Marjorie was upset and tried to comfort her. Mr. Magnet observed Marjorie from outside her window, feeling a sense of hope.

Marjorie has promised not to communicate with Mr. Trafford until she turns twenty-one. Mr. Pope confirms that Marjorie is still engaged to Mr. Magnet. Marjorie has not seen Mr. Magnet since the previous night. Mr. Trafford and Mr. Pope engage in a formal conversation regarding Marjorie's engagement. Marjorie begins the process of ending her engagement with Mr. Magnet. Mr. Magnet continues to pursue Marjorie despite the formal end of their engagement. Mr. Pope expresses his displeasure towards Marjorie after the engagement is broken.

Mr. Fotheringay possesses a powerful gift for working miracles. Mr. Maydig believes that Mr. Fotheringay is a man of astonishing possibilities. On November 10, 1896, Mr. Fotheringay began to work miracles in the study of a house behind the Congregational Chapel. Initially, the miracles performed by Mr. Fotheringay were small and timid. Mr. Maydig encouraged Mr. Fotheringay to test his powers despite his concerns about the Winch situation. The first larger enterprise undertaken by Mr. Fotheringay and Mr. Maydig was motivated by hunger. Mrs. Minchin is identified as Mr. Maydig's housekeeper.

source.author: Herbert George Wells
source.title: The Country of the Blind, And Other Stories

text: Sir Rupert was receiving attention after an incident. Marjorie expressed a desire to move Sir Rupert into the shade. Solomonson was wet but no longer bloody and claimed to be comfortable. The twins declined to fetch the doctor, preferring to stay with Theodore. Mrs. Pope instructed the maids to prepare tea. Trafford and the others were managing the situation while waiting for the doctor. Mr. Magnet and others were observing the wreckage of the monoplane.

The plant had green leaves with deep red splashes and was placed on a low bench near a thermometer. The individual spent afternoons meditating on the flowering of the plant. The orchid produced a rich, intensely sweet scent when it bloomed. The flowers of the orchid were white with streaks of golden orange and had a heavy labellum. The individual was found lying face upward at the foot of the orchid with tentacle-like aerial rootlets attached to him. The cousin attempted to rescue the individual by breaking the tentacles and smashing the windows of the greenhouse. The individual was bleeding from multiple patches when he was finally dragged out into the open air.

source.author: Herbert George Wells
source.title: The Country of the Blind, And Other Stories

text: Trafford and Mr. Pope engage in a heated argument. Trafford expresses his frustration about Mr. Pope's domestic control. Mr. Pope demands that Trafford leave his house. Trafford feels ashamed and perplexed after the argument. Marjorie plans to elope instead of having a traditional marriage. Trafford obtains a marriage license for Marjorie. Marjorie prepares a new outfit for the elopement.

Marjorie is a dignified woman who controls her house and life with skill. Marjorie is wearing a simple walking dress of brownish fawn color and a hat with a steely blue touch. Marjorie has been looking at a house near Berkeley Square, as suggested by Alice Carmel. Aunt Plessington and Uncle Hubert visit the Traffords after a five-year absence from advising Marjorie. Aunt Plessington's Movement has faced challenges, including a loss of voice and association with a new cult. Aunt Plessington has become snappy with Uncle Hubert, blaming him for the Movement's decline. Uncle Hubert has developed nervous movements and has changed in appearance over the years.

The garden features a moat. The furniture in the study is described as impressive and contains texts and books about the Scarlet Woman. The piano is identified as a Broadwood. The Dad is involved in a dispute regarding the tennis net. Toupee, a pet, initially refuses to enter the governess cart but attempts to secure the best seat. The village has a High Street with notable features including chestnut trees, cottages with thatch, and a public house. A drinking fountain commemorates the Diamond Jubilee of Queen Victoria.

Marjorie Pope had a clear, rapid memory that helped her excel in school and college. Marjorie was impressionable and attracted diverse influences from people around her. Her aunt Plessington was devoted to social and political work and sought to influence Marjorie. The Good Habits Movement, led by her aunt, aimed at legislative changes affecting lower classes. Marjorie experienced competing dreams about her future, including various ambitious roles. Marjorie was perceived as pretty, and some might consider her beautiful, but love was necessary for absolute beauty. Marjorie often daydreamed about beautiful things and enjoyed the idea of a carefree life.

The narrator and a woman run down a slope, attracting the attention of two men. Flying war machines resembling spear-heads are described, which have never fought. The war machines are made from a common alloy, not steel or aluminum. These machines are equipped with small guns that fire high explosive shells. The narrator foresees the inevitability of war due to the actions of a character named Gresham. The woman urges the narrator to return to his duty, expressing that his current life is akin to death. The narrator declares his commitment to love, stating he would choose to live for the woman, even in the face of death.

source.author: Herbert George Wells
source.title: The Country of the Blind, And Other Stories

text: Trafford experienced a growing desire for solitude to think clearly. He felt that he needed to physically and mentally remove himself from London and Marjorie's influence. Trafford considered a retreat to the Himalaya Mountains for sustained thinking. The idea of Labrador came to Trafford while he was at lunch in the Liberal Union Club. He was irritated by the superficial conversations of his fellow members at the club. Trafford questioned whether his associates had ever desired to escape the world as he did.

The protagonist considered using a bale of blankets and bent sticks to create a sleeping tent for herself and Trafford. She aimed to bring Trafford closer to the log hut to access supplies. The protagonist planned to construct a sledge from a flat piece of wood to drag Trafford. She discovered that the camping area was covered in drifted snow and that a wolverine had damaged supplies in the hut. As it began to snow again, she struggled to carry her improvised sledge through the trees. The protagonist used a compass on her watch chain to maintain her direction while navigating through the snow. She experienced physical discomfort and anxiety as she attempted to move uphill while the snow continued to fall.

Marjorie was compelled to address a meeting inaugurating a new phase in the Movement's history. Trafford left the room unnoticed while Marjorie was engaged with Aunt Plessington. Trafford considered going to Labrador for a year to confirm a new resolution. Mrs. Trafford's appearance had changed little in ten years, except for her grey hair and brighter eyes. Mrs. Trafford had observed a growing distance between herself and her son, Trafford. Mrs. Trafford sought to understand the new insurrectionary movement of women through study and discussion. Mrs. Trafford became a confidant to an increasing number of people despite losing confidences with her son and daughter-in-law.

The narrator reflects on the stress and anguish caused by war and misrule. The narrator and another character are above the Pleasure City, near the summit of Monte Solaro, looking towards the bay. The view includes Ischia, Naples, Vesuvius, Torre dell' Annunziata, and Castellammare. The narrator mentions the presence of floating palaces and aeroplanes bringing pleasure-seekers to Capri. Five war aeroplanes are seen manoeuvring in the eastward sky, produced by Gresham. Gresham is described as energetic but lacking imagination and relying on luck. The narrator contemplates the possibility of returning to fulfill responsibilities but ultimately chooses to pursue personal happiness.

source.author: Herbert George Wells
source.title: The Country of the Blind, And Other Stories

text: The characters discuss the need to clarify their thought processes and let go of material desires. They express a desire to return to England and embrace pure science, untainted literature, and sincere philosophy. Marjorie reflects on the possibility of failing again upon returning to London. Trafford reassures Marjorie that they have both changed since their time away. Marjorie acknowledges her tendency to be extravagant and suggests that they may revert to old habits. Trafford mentions that nothing ever heals completely and that they are fundamentally different now. Marjorie concludes that people do not change fundamentally without extreme circumstances.

Mr. Magnet ordered a lunch in London and had it sent down with waiters. The lunch featured pie-crusts and a cake with the name 'Theodore' written on them. Mr. Magnet initiated the lunch and insisted on its provision. Mr. Pope made a comment about melon with pepper and salt. Mr. Magnet offered a special twelve-year-old claret cup for Theodore. Marjorie felt anxious about Mr. Magnet's intention to propose on the church tower. There was awkwardness in dispersing after lunch, with various guests wanting to engage with Mr. Magnet.

The characters are planning to ration their supplies. Trafford expresses admiration for Marjorie's capable demeanor. Marjorie feels she has only truly loved Trafford in their current situation. Marjorie reflects on their past relationship and acknowledges their previous shallow love. Marjorie believes she has been selfish and has caused discord in their relationship. Marjorie recognizes the responsibilities of being a woman and the sacrifices required. Trafford and Marjorie discuss the dynamics of their relationship and the roles of men and women.

Marjorie observed a stark contrast between the dead earth and the vibrant sky. She felt a sense of insignificance regarding human existence in the vastness of nature. Marjorie and Trafford were in a remote wilderness, far from civilization. Trafford's condition worsened overnight, and he refused food, expressing a desire to die. Marjorie worked diligently to care for Trafford's wounds and prepare for their survival. She faced challenges navigating back to the hut due to snow and wind obscuring their tracks. Marjorie planned to gather essential supplies for Trafford's care.

Mr. Fotheringay was in the bar of the Long Dragon with Toddy Beamish, a dusty cyclist, landlord Cox, and Miss Maybridge. Miss Maybridge was washing glasses with her back to Mr. Fotheringay while the others watched him. Mr. Fotheringay attempted to define a miracle and received a reluctant concession from Mr. Beamish. Mr. Fotheringay demonstrated his definition of a miracle by making a lamp burn upside down. The lamp remained inverted for nearly three seconds before it fell, smashed, and went out. Mr. Cox accused Mr. Fotheringay of being a fool after the incident. Mr. Fotheringay returned home confused and troubled by the events that occurred in the bar.

source.author: Herbert George Wells
source.title: The Country of the Blind, And Other Stories

text: Scotland has one Holyrood, and Linlithgow is noted for its historical significance. Bothwellhaugh fired the shot that killed Regent Murray from a house that has since been taken down. The current structure at the site is a small house occupied by a tailor named Steele. The High Street in Linlithgow is narrow and features old stone houses with worn staircases. The area has a noticeable filth and odor, with a lively population during the summer evenings. The palace grounds at Linlithgow were visited, and the exterior of the palace was viewed. The journey from Linlithgow to Edinburgh took half an hour, and the first stop in Edinburgh was Addison's Alma Hotel.

The text describes various historical relics associated with Charlemagne and French kings. Included among the relics are a golden sceptre, a magnificent sword, suits of armor, and a religious book belonging to St. Louis. Catherine de' Medici's dressing-glass, set with precious stones, is also mentioned. Napoleon's personal belongings, such as his coat, hats, and camp-desk, are noted as part of the collection. Mr. Fezaudie discusses the current Emperor's power compared to that of the first Napoleon. The narrator mentions a visit from Miss ------, an astronomical lady, who seeks to join their party to Rome. The narrator describes a walk down Rue St. Honore and its crowded nature, as well as its historical significance related to Henry IV.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The only account of the events in Marseilles was a public despatch from the Syndic of Paris to the chief authority of Marseilles. A banner was hoisted half-mast in front of a hotel as a token of sympathy for the General and others slain in a treasonable attempt. The streets of Marseilles are described as narrow and steep, bordered by high houses that have never had sunlight. The cleanliness of Marseilles is noted to be poor, with dirt present in the hotel and elsewhere. An elevated walk provided a view of the Mediterranean Sea, described as blue and bright with sunshine. The landscape behind Marseilles includes mountains that are not clearly visible due to intervening buildings. The narrator expresses doubt about the significance of recording the peculiarities of Marseilles after the initial novelty has worn off.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: A blast was heard in a hotel corridor all night, unrelated to the wind outside. The narrator left Radicofani before sunrise and observed the ceremony from a vettura. The departure from Radicofani was described as dreary, with discomfort in dressing and searching for breakfast. At Ponte Centino, the narrator's passport was examined by a papal custom-house officer. The custom-house officer requested a fee of fifteen pauls to pass the luggage without examination. The narrator experienced potential corruption among the custom-house officials and noted a system of evasion of regulations. The landscape became fertile and picturesque as the journey continued, with mules and donkeys carrying grapes.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The tombs in the north transept include one of a modern archbishop and one of an ancient archbishop. An insane person hid behind the ancient archbishop's tomb before setting fire to the church a few years ago. The chapter-house is an octagonal hall with a vaulted roof, a tessellated floor, and seven arched windows of old painted glass. The great east window in the choir is seventy-five feet high and features old painted glass with Scriptural designs. The choir was draped in black as a token of mourning for a canon who died on Saturday night. The vestry contained various historical items, including wooden figures in knightly armor and an old iron helmet. Two banners of a Yorkshire regiment, tattered in the Peninsular wars, were hung over the door of the vestry.

The text describes a Gothic monument of Pope Benedict XII. made of white marble. The narrator and a companion attempted to locate the Church of San Pietro in Martire but were unsuccessful. Many people they asked for directions directed them to another Church of San Pietro, which is not of interest. The correct church is believed to contain a celebrated picture by Perugino. The narrator and a companion explored the city of Perugia on market day, finding the principal piazza crowded. They followed a descending street and exited through a city gate, observing the surrounding mountains and valleys. The narrator describes a beggar-man by the gate who received a small donation and expressed gratitude.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The narrator interacted with a woman who felt as if she were of high rank, similar to an Earl's daughter. Mr. J-----'s daughters, two pale and handsome girls, were present at the dinner. One of Mr. J-----'s daughters is to be married to a grandson of Mr. ------. The only man of cognizable rank present, besides Mr. ------ and the Mayor of Liverpool, was Sir Thomas Birch, a Baronet. The narrator attended the funeral services of Mrs. G------, a young American lady who died suddenly. Mr. G------, the husband of the deceased, appeared pale and overcome with grief during the funeral. Mr. Steele showed the narrator a pencil-case that formerly belonged to Dr. Johnson.

The last sleeping-place of condemned prisoners was hewn in solid rock. A beam was present where condemned prisoners were hanged. A stone staircase was used to bring condemned prisoners to their execution. Bonnivard's prison features seven massive pillars supporting groined arches. Byron's name is inscribed on one of the pillars in Bonnivard's prison. An iron ring remains on Bonnivard's pillar, to which his chain was fastened. The Duke of Savoy's kitchen features a fireplace that is at least twelve feet long.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The Corso was illuminated with moccoli as twilight arrived. The street was filled with voices shouting 'SENZA MOCCOLO'. Mr. Motley mentioned that a mock funeral of harlequin was formerly part of the Carnival. The current tradition of moccoli emerged from the previous mock funeral custom. The Catacomb of St. Calixtus is located alongside the Appian Way, near the tomb of Cecilia Metella. Visitors used wax tapers to navigate the intricate passages of the Catacomb. Cecilia Metella's tomb was inspected, revealing a round, vacant space inside.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The voyage to Marseilles was completed in three days. The steamer remained in the harbor of Leghorn without moving for an entire day. French cavalry horses were disembarked from steamers into gondolas or lighters. The steamer was detained by the French government to take on board despatches. The steamer weighed anchor for Genoa and arrived at seven in the afternoon. Genoa is situated at the foot of a semicircle of lofty hills and features the Doria Palace and a cathedral. Lord and Lady J------ boarded the steamer at Genoa.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: Mr. Monckton Milnes proposed the author's name at the event. The author's neighbors at the banquet were Colonel Campbell of the Artillery and Mr. Picton of the Library Committee. Lord ------ responded to the toast 'The House of Stanley' during the ceremony. The family of Lord ------ has been connected with the town of Liverpool for five hundred years. Monckton Milnes made a speech that the author could not hear clearly due to distance. The author's speech received more applause than any other at the event. The next morning, newspapers published reports about the banquet.

The keeper attempted to make the monkey eat, resulting in a struggle that overturned tea onto the straw bed. The monkey expressed a sense of injury through loud chatter and reached out to spectators for sympathy. The keeper called the monkey in a gentler tone, and they ended the interaction by hugging each other. The Aquarium contained specimens of both marine and freshwater life but was not considered perfect. Many well-dressed people and children visited the gardens on Saturday, where they fed bears with biscuits and cakes. One bear climbed a pole to receive food, while another sat on the ground groaning, and the third took food without performing tricks. The narrator observed the architecture along Portland Place and noted a lack of admirable design compared to older timber houses.

The servant ushered the visitors through a hall with family pictures by Lely, Vandyke, and Kneller. The library contained volumes that John Evelyn used to read and had a barren aspect with no carpet or luxurious furniture. A single volume of English history in the library was valued at two or three hundred pounds due to its rarity. A magnolia tree, at least fifty years old, grew against one of the library windows. Mr. ------ was making extensive alterations to the house, contributing to its ungenial meagreness. Mr. ------ is a young-looking man with a mustache and has the manners of someone who has seen the world. The three books brought by Mr. ------ included a manuscript in John Evelyn's hand and a prayer-book used by King Charles at his execution.

The Piazza Navona is a busy marketplace in Rome, offering various goods for sale. Items sold in the piazza include rusty iron, vegetables, fruits, fish, cigars, and bread. The marketplace is characterized by a shabby crowd and a lack of picturesque costumes. The Church of St. Agnes is located on one side of the piazza and is said to be on the site of a significant historical event. The interior of the Church of St. Agnes features rich marble columns and bas-reliefs. The Pantheon has a circular opening that allows views of the sky and clouds. Sunlight beams down into the Pantheon, illuminating dust motes and creating a serene atmosphere.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The custode showed an ancient manuscript of the Decameron and a volume containing portraits of Petrarch and Laura. The portraits of Petrarch and Laura are authentic and depict Laura as a fair-haired beauty. The exhibition of old editions of books was limited due to the volumes being in shut bookcases and modern bindings. On September 21st, the Val d'Arno was filled with thick fog that dissipated, leading to a bright and warm day. Mosaic brooches are a characteristic commodity of the town, primarily displayed on the Ponte Vecchio. The principal designs of the mosaics include flowers and birds, often made with precious materials. The Uffizi gallery was crowded with middle and lower class Italians and a notable number of English tourists.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The cavern described is a series of narrow passages and crevices with a low roof and is associated with lead mining by the Romans. Derbyshire spar is extracted from the cavern, with Blue John being the most valuable type found in a limited location. The guide's cottage displays various ornaments and toys made from Derbyshire spar and other materials. The Romantic Rocks are crags that stand isolated from the hillside, accessible for viewing at a cost of two pence. J----- and his mother went fishing near the railway and caught three minnows. The village has shops selling spar products, including a table valued at sixty guineas and another at three hundred guineas owned by the Marquis of Westminster. The total amount spent on souvenirs in Matlock was twenty shillings.

The narrator describes a visit to the Balbi Palace in Genoa, noting its painted ceilings and marble walls. The floors of the royal palace were made of various woods and inlaid by an English artist. The narrator expresses fatigue from viewing numerous artworks and sights. The group visited a pleasure-garden that offered seven different views of Genoa. A large yellow house in the outskirts of Genoa was formerly inhabited by Charles Dickens. In Leghorn, the group intended to visit Pisa but was delayed by banking and passport formalities. The narrator visited the tomb of Smollett in Leghorn, marked by a white marble obelisk.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The palace is entirely roofless from the first floor upwards. Mary, Queen of Scots, was born in a roofless chamber within the palace. The bedchamber of several Scottish Jameses is located in the same range as the chamber where Mary was born. A narrow, winding staircase in the bedchamber is said to have been used by King James III. to escape from conspirators. Queen Margaret's bower is a turret at the top of the palace that offers a view of Linlithgow town and the surrounding landscape. The most recent part of the palace was built by James I. of England and bears the figures 1620 on its central tower. In Robert Bruce's time, a castle existed at the site of the palace.

The author expresses weariness from hotel life in England. The author feels that hotel staff are focused on extracting money from guests. Dining options at English hotels are described as lacking variety, primarily consisting of joints and mutton. The author traveled from Grasmere to Windermere by stage-coach, which was heavily overloaded with passengers and luggage. The author felt apprehensive about the safety of the stage-coach due to the uneven road and the driver's condition. Upon arrival at Windermere, the author received a mail packet addressed to someone named William. The author engaged in conversation about the war with a gentleman in the coffee-room at Windermere.

The narrator went to Birch's eating-house with Mr. Bowman for turtle-soup. Mr. J. B. Davis, a former Secretary of Legation, invited the narrator to dinner at Vermont House in Camden Town. The host of the dinner is a Vermonter and a Yale College graduate who runs a book brokerage. Mr. Peabody, who is connected to the Salem Peabodys, also attended the dinner. Mr. Tom Taylor, a well-known wit and satirist, was expected at the dinner but arrived late. The host showed rare old books from his collection, including a black-letter edition of Chaucer and a collection of Bibles. The host possesses manuscripts, including a Spanish document signed by the son of Columbus and original songs by Burns.

The travelers left the Hotel des Colonies at about three o'clock. The Hotel des Colonies is described as very comfortable but expensive. The travelers' railroad carriage was comfortable and included two Frenchwomen and two nuns. The nuns were engaged in devotional activities and did not pay much attention to the scenery. At the station in Marseilles, the traveler bought two volumes of 'Livre des Merveilles' translated into French. The travelers arrived at the Hotel de l'Europe in Avignon in the evening. The gallery of their suite of rooms overlooks an enclosed court with various plants and decorations.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: J----- and the narrator walked in the shrubbery and took refuge from a shower beneath a rock overhang. The narrator's mother had a difficult excursion to Roslin, where she walked a long distance and was caught in the rain. The narrator and J----- left Edinburgh and stayed at the George hotel in Melrose. They visited Melrose Abbey and were guided by an old man who spoke the Scotch dialect intelligibly. The guide demonstrated a fondness for the Abbey, picking up withered leaves and showing knowledge of its history. The narrator noted the historical significance of King David the First in founding Melrose Abbey and other churches. After visiting the Abbey, the narrator and J----- walked to the Tweed River, where they observed people angling.

The achievements of English painters are considered inferior to those of English poets. Painting became an English art after the epochs of the greatest poets. Haydon is respected for his rejection of what he and his countrymen could achieve. Copley is acknowledged for his realistic portrayal of a slain man. Danby's painting 'The Evening Gun' is described as beautiful and effective. The works of Hunt and some Pre-Raphaelite painters are noted for their deeper value despite being disagreeable. A painting by Hunt depicting lost sheep is highlighted for its emotional truth.

Pierce has experienced little change and appears happier than in previous years. Pierce has achieved the highest success in public life and seems more like his early self. The author believes that Pierce would have been unhappy without attaining the Presidency. The author describes Pierce's tact as subtle and partially unrecognized by him. The author and Pierce maintain a close friendship, similar to their relationship in college. The author visited the Barberini picture-gallery to see the Beatrice Cenci for a farewell look. The author finds the Beatrice Cenci indescribable and notes its unique, elusive expression.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The child is loved entirely by Mr. Kirkup, who considers her his own. The child inherits her mother's gift of communication with the spiritual world. Mr. Kirkup lives in an ancient Knight Templar palace near the Arno River. Miss Blagden advised Mr. Kirkup to take the child to the seaside or countryside for her health. Catharine Fleeting, an Englishwoman and friend of Mr. Kirkup, has agreed to take charge of the child after his death. Mr. Kirkup declined a gift of half of Trelawny's family estate, as he was not destitute. The child's name is Imogen, and she has a history that adds to the romance of her situation.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The author made an after-dinner speech that was well received despite feeling unpracticed in oratory. The author took a walk with family through rural England, observing hedge-rows, grassy fields, and old stone cottages. On August 20th, a large number of factory workers arrived at Rock Ferry, brought by railways and steamers from distant locations. The factory workers were accompanied by music bands and banners representing their mills. A group of little girls from workhouses, dressed in coarse blue gowns, arrived at the dock and formed a procession. The girls had been educated at a charity school and were to be apprenticed as servants. On August 22nd, the author inventoryed the effects of Captain Auld, an American who had died, in a boarding house located in a mean street.

The apartment contains various curiosities and historical items, including a coal-grate used by Archbishop Sharpe. A glass case in the hall displays the suit of clothes last worn by Sir Walter Scott, including a short green coat and gray tartan trousers. The hall also features walking-sticks used by Scott and a hatchet he used for lopping branches. The study is small, lined with books, and contains volumes of the Moniteur that Scott used while writing about Napoleon. The library is of respectable size and contains many books, including a compartment full of volumes on ghosts and witchcraft. The drawing-room features an ebony cabinet presented to Scott by George IV and several portraits, including one of Scott at thirty-five. A notable painting of Mary, Queen of Scots, depicts her head cut off and lying on a dish, said to be created shortly after her death.

The castle features eight large round towers, with four of them having smaller towers that once contained winding staircases. The stairs in at least one of the towers are described as perfect and high aloft, while others are broken and inaccessible. There is no roof in any part of the castle, including the towers, hall, and kitchen, all of which are open to the sky. The railway passes at the base of the castle and goes into the town through an arch opened in the castle wall. One tower, said to have been the residence of Queen Eleanor, contains an oriel-window and traces of ornamental sculpture. All traces of wood-work and iron-work in the castle have been removed, reportedly by a Lord Conway during the reign of Charles II. There is a grassy space under the windows of Queen Eleanor's tower, which may have been used by the Queen for open-air leisure.

The Palace of Holyrood is located in Edinburgh. The author traveled to Edinburgh by train and stayed at Queen's Hotel on Prince's Street. The monument to Sir Walter Scott is situated in front of a hotel on Prince's Street. The Palace of Holyrood features Queen Mary's apartments and a noble hall hung with pictures of ancient Scottish kings. The blood-stain from the murder of Rizzio is located at the threshold of a door in Queen Mary's apartments. Holyrood Abbey is a roofless ruin that once served as a magnificent Gothic church. Holyrood Abbey contains tombstones of old Scottish nobility and monuments to illustrious Scotch families.

The early faces of the Madonna are described as a single type, characterized as heavy and sulky. This dull representation of the Madonna persists despite the beauty of surrounding saints and angels. Sodoma is identified as a prominent representative of the Sienese school of painting. A notable fresco by Sodoma depicts Christ bound to a pillar after being scourged, which is praised for its expression. The author observes a laborer in Siena performing a physically demanding task of carrying a large tree trunk. The author notes that Italians may exhibit strength in isolated efforts but are perceived to have less endurance than English or Americans. The author's walk in the countryside includes views of vineyards, olive trees, and various rural landscapes.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: On May 11th, a sailor came to complain of cruelty from his captain and mate, bearing visible injuries. The sailor was left behind when the ship sailed and was admitted to the hospital. The surgeon at the hospital indicated that the sailor was dying and likely unable to communicate. The hospital was often crowded, sometimes requiring patients to be placed on the floor. The sailor was found to have a tattoo of nautical emblems, suggesting he may have been a seaman despite claiming to be a farmer. Other patients gathered near the sailor's bed as he lay in a state of distress and insensibility. The nurse attending to the sailor was described as sharp-eyed and intelligent, managing the situation with calmness.

The cathedral features architectural elements such as chevrons and zigzag carvings around the arches of doors and windows. The cathedral service is lengthy, and the choral part is described as pleasant. There is an old knocker on the cathedral door in the form of a monstrous face, historically used for fugitives seeking sanctuary. The exterior of the cathedral is large and grand, with a central tower and two western towers, lacking intricate details found in other cathedrals. A notable sculpture depicts a cow, a milk-maid, and a monk, linked to a legend about the cathedral's site. The churchyard contains several horizontal slabs as monuments, with some appearing aged but mostly dating from the present century. A weather-worn marble slab commemorates Robert Dodsley, a bookseller and acquaintance of Samuel Johnson.

The Bodleian Library was closed for cleaning during the visit. Visitors were only admitted to the Picture Gallery of the Bodleian Library. The Picture Gallery features bookcases that extend more than four hundred feet. A brass statue of Earl Pembroke stands in the Picture Gallery. The lantern of Guy Fawkes, now rusty and partly broken, is displayed in the Picture Gallery. The Taylor Institute was also closed, but the curator allowed entry after persuasion. The Taylor Institute contains original models of Chantrey's works and a collection of drawings by Raphael and Michael Angelo.

The cathedral is constructed of black and white marble, with an intermixture of red and other colors. The architecture of the cathedral is primarily in the pointed Gothic style, featuring carved arches over doors and windows. There is a large round window at the front of the cathedral that casts colored light into the nave. The facade of the cathedral is richly ornamented with arches, statues of saints, busts, and stone lions. The Palazzo Publico contains a chapel with an altar and frescos, which is accessible to the public. The chapel at the Palazzo Publico is adorned with bouquets of fresh flowers and has a lamp burning before the crucifix. The cathedral features a tall tower and a dome, both constructed from layers of black and white marble.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: J----- sketched part of a broken wall that appeared thinner than the walls of English castles. The narrator and J----- drank from a deep well near the square tower of Philip le Bel. They left Avignon on Tuesday, June 7th, and traveled by rail to Valence. In Valence, they stayed at the Hotel de la Poste, which had dirty floors but was otherwise comfortable. Valence features a cathedral with a high interior supported by tall pillars and arches. They observed a large monument near the cathedral, which was a tomb of unknown antiquity. They arrived in Lyons at five o'clock and stayed at the Hotel de l'Univers.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The subject is described as delicate, with white and small hands, and manners resembling those of a gentleman. The subject is very deaf, which affected the interview experience. The subject has a collection of books, including works of magic and occult sciences, and manuscript copies of Dante from the early fourteenth century. Mr. Kirkup possesses a plaster cast of Dante's face, believed to be taken after his death, and a tracing from Giotto's fresco of Dante. The fresco of Dante was discovered by Mr. Kirkup, and the tracing is valuable due to the original's damage. Mr. Kirkup has a variety of artworks, including a picture of Savonarola and a fragment of a drawing by Rubens. A four-year-old girl, described as bright and merry, follows the subject, and her mother, Regina, is depicted in a portrait and was a spiritual medium.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The church door rang with a bell at the announcement of peace reported by the London papers. The church has been modernized and whitewashed, affecting its appearance. A marble tomb in the chancel features statues of Sir Anthony Browne and his lady, who were the Lord and Lady of Battle Abbey during Henry VIII's reign. The chancel and aisles are paved with tombstones, some of which have engraved brasses depicting knights and churchmen. The Webster family has the best pew in the church, which is furnished like a parlor and includes a bricked-up fireplace. An old woman living in the Abbey's wall described her room as a former prison and pointed out a beam where criminals were hanged. The mansion within the Abbey grounds is secluded and accessed through a principal door under a deep arch.

London stone is described as a rudely shaped and unhewn post. Jack Cade's sword is said to have made one or two long cuts or indentations in the top of London stone. The narrator traveled from London Bridge station to Greenwich, which is approximately five miles away. A fair has been held at Greenwich during the first three days of Easter for many years. Mr. Bennoch's house is described as pretty and comfortable, adorned with works of art. Mr. Newton Crosland is introduced as the husband of a literary lady and a believer in spiritual manifestations. The narrator visited the National Gallery for the first time and expressed a desire to acquire a taste for art.

The open space before the White Tower resembles a town square with gabled houses and various edifices. The White Tower is described as now more black than white and is the most prominent object in the scene. There are soldiers exercising in the open space, and numerous cannons and mortars are located at the base of the White Tower. Some of the cannons are of Turkish manufacture, while others belonged to the ship Great Harry and some are East-Indian. The warder indicated the spot where Anne Boleyn and Catharine Parr were beheaded, located on a line with one of the angles of the White Tower. The Beauchamp Tower is noted for being a prison for historical figures, with inscriptions left by former occupants on its walls. The visit included passing St. Paul's Cathedral, which is described as magnificent and beautiful despite its darkened appearance.

Bergere is a location where the narrator and J----- sought Hottinguer et Co., the bankers. The rest of the party proceeded along the Boulevards towards the Church of the Madeleine. The Boulevards are described as broad walks through broad streets that were crowded with people. The Church of the Madeleine is noted for its beautiful architecture, including magnificent pillars. The church was adorned with black cloth and a mourning-coach was present at its steps. Inside the church, there were numerous wax lights burning and a significant display of black velvet. The narrator observed a funeral service taking place, noting the attire of the priests and the overall ceremony.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The saloons feature gilded cornices, arches, and compartments with painted frescos. White marble sculptures, including winged cupids and allegoric shapes, are present in the saloons. The walls are adorned with scarlet damask and rich picture frames that glimmer in gold. A mighty wind raised a cloud of dust in the square before the palace, obscuring visibility. Rain eventually fell, allowing for a clearer view of paintings, including works by Rubens, Salvator Rosa, and Titian. Titian's painting 'Magdalen' depicts a sensual figure with golden hair and is described as splendid. Michael Angelo's Fates are described as an impressive group with varying expressions among the three sisters.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The Mayor and Council hold their meetings in a building constructed by an old guild of merchants and tradesmen. St. John's Church is located near a quadrangle of gabled houses, which includes Bond's Hospital and Bablake School. Bond's Hospital is designed for the reception of ten poor men. Bablake School was founded in 1563 by Thomas Whealby, Mayor of Coventry. The school admits children of the working classes at eleven years old and provides for them until they are apprenticed for seven years. The schoolroom features seven desks, an arched fireplace, and a gallery that overlooks the room. The revenue of Bablake School is approximately 900 pounds.

Powers believes in the validity of spiritual communications but finds it difficult to identify the spirits involved. Powers is a Swedenborgian and is open to many spiritual phenomena. Powers considers Home to be a knave but acknowledges him as a good medium for spiritual communications. The author expresses skepticism about receiving messages from spirits through unreliable mediums. The author has received written communications from several spirits, including family members and a spirit named Mary Hall. The author perceives a lack of substance in the communications from spirits, suggesting they may originate from earthly minds. Mary Runnel is often blamed for inaccuracies in the communications, despite the spirits claiming responsibility for their statements.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The narrator describes the experience of winter in St. Peter's and the behavior of local children around the church. The narrator observes that native Romans do not keep fires in their homes during winter, except for cooking. The Pantheon is mentioned as a location where the narrator felt uncomfortable passing between a devotee and a saint. The narrator notes that people who appear decent can unexpectedly become beggars as one approaches them. The weather in early February is described as cloudy and rainy, affecting the Carnival festivities. The narrator finds refuge in St. Peter's during inclement weather and describes the church's interior as having its own brilliance. A mosaic copy of Raphael's Transfiguration is noted as being preserved better than the original painting due to its material.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: Miss M------ reported hearing about a considerable number of troops gathered at Lyons due to recent disaffection. The hotel is located near the Place de Louis le Grand, which features a bronze equestrian statue of Louis XIV. The square surrounding the statue has barracks for soldiers and a soldier was on guard at the statue. The hotel is named HOTEL DE PROVENCE ET DES AMBASSADEURS and is characterized by faded pomp and a large dining room. A carpet-bag was missing and was replaced by Miss M------'s trunk, leading to difficulties with the railway officials. The journey included picturesque scenery with hills, a river described as the 'arrowy Rhone,' and vineyards along the track. The area featured old feudal towers, villages, and churches with spires shaped like extinguishers.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The pope sent his blessing to Lord Clifford, who died the next day. The little oratory connected with U----'s chamber contains a life-sized skull. U----'s apartment features a vaulted ceiling and a large saloon with a cushioned divan. The apartment above the saloon is decorated with engraved portraits of Roman emperors, popes, kings of Europe, doges of Venice, and sultans of Turkey. The engravings date from 1685 to about 1715 and were executed in Rome. Mr. Kirkup is an antiquarian living in Florence, known for his interest in spirit-rappings. Mr. Kirkup resides in an old house that was formerly a residence of the Knights Templars.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: There is a marble statue of Newton in the chapter-house, which has been damaged by weather. The statue was placed there by a former Earl of Buchan. The monuments of Sir Walter Scott and his family are located within an arched recess on one side of the church. The Pringle family is buried in a twin arched recess adjacent to the Scott burial-place. The Eildon Hills are visible from the direction of Melrose and have three distinct summits. Abbotsford is located three miles from Melrose and is described as a compact villa. The current owner of Abbotsford is adding a wing to the house.

The woman described uses an ear-trumpet to communicate with others. She is characterized as lively, sensible, and cheerful, discussing her own affairs without egotism. The woman identifies as an Atheist and believes that life ceases to exist after death. The narrator's family traveled to Rhyl, where they stayed in lodging houses and hotels. Rhyl is described as uninteresting, with a long sand beach and heavy walking conditions. The narrator experienced discomfort from heat and dust while walking towards Rhyddlan Castle. The village near Rhyddlan Castle is depicted as compact, with narrow streets and a squalid appearance.

The piazza features several statues and ancient sculptures, including a statue of Julius Caesar and a statue of Augustus in middle age. The statue of Julius Caesar is said to be the only authentic one and aligns more with his character than other depictions. There are also gigantic heads, hands, and feet in marble and bronze, as well as a stone lion and horse that were repaired by Michel Angelo. The narrator inquired about the picture-gallery from French soldiers, who were not knowledgeable about their surroundings. A soldier of the Papal Guard assisted the narrator in finding the entrance to the picture-rooms. The narrator notes that Italian galleries are at a disadvantage compared to English ones in terms of picture presentation. The narrator observed several noteworthy bas-reliefs, including an ancient one of Curtius plunging on horseback into the chasm in the Forum.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The narrator and their wife visited the picture and sculpture galleries of the Capitol. The narrator admired a painting by Vandyke featuring a beautiful face of a man. The narrator expressed admiration for Paul Veronese's painting 'Rape of Europa'. The narrator found charm in the Faun of Praxiteles in the sculpture gallery. The narrator suggested a story idea involving fauns intermingling with the human race. The narrator mentioned Mr. Gibson's colored statues and a claim about staining them with tobacco juice. The narrator and their wife took a moonlight walk in Rome, heading towards the Coliseum.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: Visitors today include H. A. B. and Monsieur H., the French Consul. H. A. B. is to dine at Rock Ferry and take the narrator on board the Great Britain. Monsieur H. speaks hardly any English and is described as a polite, gray-haired gentleman. The Church of St. Nicholas is considered the oldest sacred site in Liverpool. The current church structure has little of the original edifice remaining. The churchyard is paved with flat tombstones, many of which have effaced inscriptions. The Great Britain is noted for its convenient arrangement and adaptation for passengers.

The rector sent a messenger to inform the group about the church. St. Andrew's Church in Lower Bebbington was built in 1100. The group observed graves located between the church's buttresses. The group encountered little girls who expressed discontent about being reported to the sexton. The group got lost in a green lane while returning home. The Rock Ferry Hotel was their accommodation for nearly four weeks. The parlor of the hotel provided a view of the river and Liverpool.

The attendees at the event included individuals in gold-embroidered court-dresses and military uniforms adorned with medals. A trumpet sounded and a series of royal equipages appeared, each drawn by six horses and accompanied by a postilion, coachman, and three footmen. The Noble Guard was positioned on horseback opposite the loggia, and there was minimal ceremony observed by the populace.
