The narrator and J----- visited the Uffizi gallery, where J----- expressed strong disapproval of most artworks except for a few specific items in Dutch paintings. The Church of Or San Michele was originally a market and has undergone significant architectural transformations over the centuries. A picture of the Virgin was venerated in the market, leading to the consecration of a chapel due to the miracles attributed to it. The Palazzo Buonarotti, Michael Angelo's ancestral home, is located on Via Ghibellina and is described as an ordinary three-story house.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: Wordsworth's grave has a simple headstone and grass growing over it. Most monuments in the area are made of black slate and some are recently erected. The Enchanted Castle is located midway down a ridge in the valley of St. John. The castle appears dilapidated and resembles a Gothic castle that has decayed over time. Upon closer inspection, the Enchanted Castle is revealed to be a large ledge of rock. The vale of St. John is surrounded by Blencathra to the north and has steep crags on either side. The King's Head is a primitive inn located about a mile beyond the castle.

A bird flew into a small opening between two petrified flowers, behind which was its nest. The narrator and companions attempted to find the verger before returning to the hotel. The narrator's wife and J----- visited the interior of the cathedral the following morning. The narrator explored the town, passing the castle site and finding portions of the city wall. It was market-day in Carlisle, and the principal streets were crowded with people. A marble statue of the Earl of Lonsdale, who died about twenty years ago, stands in a busy street. The narrator described the cathedral in Glasgow as a fine old church with rich architectural details.

The narrator had breakfast with Mr. Milnes at a time named as a little after ten. The narrator walked over London Bridge and into the city, intending to take a cab from Charing Cross. The narrator visited the Guildhall, which is a spacious hall about one hundred and fifty feet long and half as broad. The Guildhall features a vast window with painted glass and several marble monuments, including those to the Earl of Chatham and his son, William Pitt. The hall contains statues of Beckford, Lord Nelson, and mediaeval kings, as well as painted wooden figures of Gog and Magog. There is an annual banquet at the Guildhall given by the Lord Mayor and sheriffs. The narrator experienced difficulty finding a cab and arrived at Upper Brook Street shortly before eleven.

The cathedral has a crypt and cloisters that are entire but not particularly interesting. The cathedral is described as grand and beautiful in one aspect. The river Wear flows through the center of the town and is characterized as pleasant and tranquil. An old mill is located on the shore of the river Wear, dating back to the times of the Abbey. The town has an irregular layout typical of ancient settlements, with upward and downward undulations. The narrator and a companion walked along the bank opposite the cathedral and found the paths delightful. The situation of Durham Cathedral is noted to be noble and visually striking.

The castle is in excellent repair and not crumbly. The yew-tree near the castle is estimated to be eight hundred years old. A stream flows along the base of the castle, which the housekeeper referred to as a 'wash.' The town of Skipton had a lively market-place with butchers displaying meat. The escutcheon of the Cliffords or the Thanets is carved in stone over the castle portal. There is a large old church at the extremity of the village below the castle. The scenery along the road to Bolton Priory is described as generally hard with long slopes and few trees.

A crowd gathered on the pavement of flat tombstones to witness a bride's departure. The bride and groom left in a post-chaise that had crimson curtains. Three post-chaises with postilions in scarlet were present at the event. The same cathedral hosted a dozen couples married in May. An old merchant discussed the negative impact of the electric telegraph on receiving bad news. The author visited an Exhibition and viewed pencil sketches and paintings, including a spring landscape by John Linnell the younger. The Exhibition featured ornamental art, including precious metals, glass, and historical jewels.

The American ambassador visited the author and stayed for one to two hours. The ambassador is staying at Mr. William Browne's residence at Richmond Hill. The ambassador plans to retire from public life next October at the age of sixty-four. The ambassador expressed that he would not be a candidate for the Presidency. The author dined at Mr. William Browne's with a large party, where the table service was made of silver. Mr. ------ mentioned a story about Shakespeare's death involving a revel at Stratford. Miss L---- is described as having an English appearance and being self-possessed.

The narrator visited Croce and noted its spaciousness due to less massive pillars. The narrator also visited the Duomo but felt content to leave it. The narrator lost their way while returning home and wandered through vineyards and olive trees. The narrator observed the gray battlements from a distance and had to retrace their steps. The narrator spent the evening star-gazing from a tower and saw a comet in the sky. The narrator viewed a model of the statue of America in Powers's studio, which embodies ideals of youth and freedom. Powers expressed a desire to return to America, but the narrator felt he lacked a definite purpose to do so.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The text discusses the challenges historians face in idealizing events. It mentions that full-length portraits often do not emphasize the face as much as the figure and drapery. Vandyke's portraits of Charles I. are noted for their focus on the face. The author expresses skepticism about the usefulness of viewing portraits due to various factors such as fading and height placement. The author recounts an encounter with Mr. J------, who informs him that Tennyson is present at the Exhibition. The author observes Tennyson in the company of Mr. Woolner and expresses admiration for him. The author reflects on Tennyson's un-English qualities and contrasts them with typical English characteristics.

A door intended for access to a gallery is never opened. The narrator, U----, and J----- climbed into a copper ball that was very hot. There is a circular balcony at the top of the dome of St. Peter's. The group visited the mosaic copy of the 'Transfiguration' before seeing the original in the Vatican. The manufactory of mosaics had artists working on medallions of saints for St. Paul's church. The Vatican picture-gallery consists of three rooms lined with red velvet and contains about fifty pictures. The 'Transfiguration' is noted for its detail and preservation, while the mosaic copy is considered less expressive.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: There are flights of stone stairs ascending through a natural avenue in the cleft of a double-summited rock. An arched doorway with a portcullis used to exist midway up the stairs to protect the upper fortress from enemies. The remains of several old buildings are located where the cleft of the rock widens into a gorge, but they do not belong to the ancient castle, which has mostly disappeared. The foundation of a tower dating back to the fifth century is located at the loftiest point on the right summit. The ancient castle's principal parts were on the lower summit of the hill, where the outline of its wall can still be traced. The armory contains some tattered banners, curiosities, and historical weapons, including the sword of William Wallace. The sword of William Wallace is described as formidable, two-edged, and rusted, with about nine inches broken off the point.

The text discusses the presence of bones and ashes on the pavement. Mr. Silsbee visited and discussed art, drawing from his three years of travel on the Continent. Mr. Silsbee left a manuscript describing a visit to Berlin. The narrator and Mr. Silsbee visited the Crystal Palace, purchasing return tickets for half a crown each. The architecture of the Crystal Palace is described as lacking beauty despite its vastness. The atmosphere inside the Crystal Palace was described as chill and comfortless. The narrator observed a statue of a nude mother with two babies, which evoked a sense of pathos.

The lower town has been appropriated as the back wall of a range of houses. Windows have been pierced through the lower town wall, and upper chambers and loggie have been built upon it. The old castle with its towers is located at one end of the upper town. Viterbo is described as a large, disagreeable town built at the foot of a mountain. Viterbo has more fountains than any other city of its size, many of which are well designed. A crippled postilion in Viterbo wears a green jacket faced with red and begs from travelers. There is little provision for poverty and age in Italy, leading to earnest entreaties for aid from beggars.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The original Roman paving-stone has been removed and replaced with a fac-simile engraved in marble. General Pierce visited during dinner, and the narrator noted changes in his appearance. General Pierce expressed melancholy about not having children. The narrator accompanied General Pierce to St. Peter's and observed he was less changed than previously thought. General Pierce is not planning to run for the Presidency again but would consider it if the party demanded it. The narrator visited Miss Hosmer's studio to see her statue of Zenobia. Miss Hosmer's statue of Zenobia is described as unfinished but notable for its dignity and beauty.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: Cotton was sent to America from the Bahama Islands in 1786 by royalist refugees. The inferior short-stapled cotton had been previously cultivated in America for domestic purposes. The variety of cotton now grown in America was first introduced into Georgia. Captain J------ saw a vessel commanded by an Englishman with his wife and thirteen children during his voyage to Australia and India. The thirteen children had all been born and raised on board the ship and knew little of dry land. The two past days have been Whitsuntide holidays celebrated at Tranmere in a manner similar to the old 'Election' in Massachusetts. The crowd at the Whitsuntide celebration in Tranmere appeared grimy and did not wear holiday suits.

The plan for the day included visiting Westminster Abbey and the National Gallery. Visibility decreased due to fog while walking down Regent Street. The Duke of York's Column and Nelson's Pillar were barely visible. Poets' Corner was entered, which appeared dusky and grim. The painted windows of Westminster Abbey were described as rich and beautiful. Somerset House was noted for its Grecian facades and sculptured bas-reliefs. The Temple Gardens contained green grass and blooming chrysanthemums, but no roses.

The church features a double row of Norman arches made of light freestone that support the roof. There is a stained-glass window of modern manufacture and a five hundred-year-old piece depicting St. Anthony. Marble slabs with inscriptions are affixed along the walls between the arched windows. The chancel contains a monument for the Ratcliffe family, consisting of a stone slab on four small pillars. The church has an antique font with bas-reliefs of Scriptural subjects, sculpted by an artist from a thousand years ago. The sexton has a personal connection to Robert Southey and has known him since his early manhood. Southey's grave is marked by a large block of slate, which is described as not fitting for a poet.

The superintendent of the Armory is a practical armorer and an old soldier. The Armory contains a helmet, a bomb, a grenade from the Crimea, and muskets from the same region. The collection includes Minie rifles, old-fashioned Brown Bess muskets, and swords used at the battle of Sheriffmuir. Two tattered banners from the Peninsular battles and a piece of old oak from the Douglas Tower are displayed in the Armory. The pulpit and communion-table of John Knox are also present, with the pulpit dating back to 1500. A child's toy-gun belonging to the armorer's son was found among the weapons. The garrison consists mostly of a Highland regiment, and musicians were practicing near the castle during the visit.

The group visited a petrifying cave where the process of petrifaction can take months to years. Articles placed in the cave under drippings from the roof develop a hard deposit. A horse's head was in the process of petrifaction, and a broken eggshell was purchased for a penny. Specimens of petrified oak were observed, showing that the stony substance was incorporated with the wood. The group traveled from Matlock to Manchester and then to Liverpool for an engagement. Southport was crowded with Whitsuntide visitors, primarily from factory towns. The town offers various amusements, including donkey-riding, a theatre, and street performers.

King Arthur is said to have beheaded one of his enemies on a stone in the market-place. The villages were lively, likely due to market-day activities involving Welsh people. Welsh was spoken universally and familiarly among the people, with the omnibus-driver speaking imperfect English. The remains of a castle were few, with only part of the external wall still visible. A modern castellated mansion has been built within the castle's original site, made of red freestone. The ancient walls of the castle are of immense thickness, with a passage measuring fifteen feet wide on one side. The excursion included a visit to the valley of the Clwyd and a walk along the beach.

The Tower has a significant amount of ground within its outer precincts, including streets, houses, inhabitants, and a church. The White Tower, which contains the armory, is located at the center of the fortress and is a square, battlemented structure with a turret at each angle. The gallery of mounted knights and men at arms includes notable figures such as Henry VIII and Charles Brandon, Duke of Suffolk. A splendid suit of armor, gilded all over, was presented by the city of London to Charles I. John of Gaunt's suit of armor indicates he was seven feet high and shows signs of wear. The cloak worn by General Wolfe when he fell on the Plains of Abraham is displayed under a glass case. Sir Walter Raleigh's apartment in the Tower was where he wrote the History of the World.

A little boy with a broken thigh was observed by a surgeon who noted that children generally recover well from accidents. Two American sailors in the surgical ward had recently been stabbed and were doing well despite their severe injuries. The surgeon believed that having several patients together could positively influence their spirits. Gervase Elwes, son of Sir Gervase Elwes, married Isabella, daughter of Sir Thomas Hervey. Gervase Elwes died before his father and left a son named Henry who succeeded to the Baronetcy. Barry Cornwall, also known as Mr. Procter, is the Commissioner of Lunacy and makes periodical circuits through the country. The author and his family are experiencing hooping-cough during a season characterized by cold east winds.

The narrator and Bennoch entered the town of Hastings, which is described as modern and consisting of lodging-houses, shops, hotels, and parades. The narrator took a warm bath in Hastings and felt rejuvenated afterward. The narrator visited the lodgings of Mr. Martin and his wife, Helen Faucett, who are friends of Bennoch. Mr. Martin is identified as the author of Bon Gaultier's ballads and a barrister. The narrator had a pleasant lunch with Mr. Martin and Helen Faucett, and they walked to the railway station together. The narrator attended a dinner at the Milton Club on Ludgate Hill, which is for dissenters and nonconformists. The dinner included sixteen guests, mostly authors or people connected with the press, and featured an abundance of wine.

The Chamber of Peers is ninety feet long and half as broad and high. The Chamber of Commons is larger than the Chamber of Peers. Westminster Hall is accessed through a lofty archway and has a stone pavement. Westminster Hall features a roof with carved beams and rafters of chestnut. Westminster Hall measures about eighty paces in length and twenty-seven paces in width. The cloisters of Westminster Abbey are in excellent preservation and feature flat tombstone pavements. The walls of the cloisters bear marble tablets inscribed with the virtues of the deceased.

The narrator observes a poor family with a motherly figure and children displaying endurance and intelligence. The narrator expresses a desire to give more money to the poor family instead of to a begging subscriptionist. The narrator has received visitors at the Consulate from the United States, including Mr. D. D. Barnard and Mr. Sickles. Judge Douglas is described as very short but possessing dignity and sociability. The narrator notes that incidents in the streets of the city differ from those in American cities. A dinner-party at Mr. Holland's featured a discussion about Charles Dickens's energy during theatrical performances. Moore's diary mentions a Guernsey lily that originated from a shipwreck on the coast of Japan.

The breastplate and helmet of Henry of Navarre are made of steel and have engraved designs that are partially obliterated. A breastplate belonging to an Elector of Saxony has a bullet-hole through it, which caused his mortal wound, leading to his death two days later, three hundred years ago. The Exhibition had a large crowd of visitors, primarily from the middling class, making it difficult to view the objects. The author visited the Exhibition with R----- and Fanny, while J----- went to the Botanical Gardens. The historical portraits in the Exhibition include images of Richard II., Henry IV., Edward IV., and Jane Shore, which are described as lacking artistic merit. Vandyke is noted for bringing portrait-painting into fashion during the time of Charles I. and the Commonwealth. The author expresses doubt about the value of portrait-painting in accurately representing the individuals depicted.

Laburnum plants are abundant. There is a traditional prophecy regarding the ivy reaching the top of Bebbington spire. Mr. Turner states that the current font is inside the church, while the outside font is of unknown antiquity. A ten-year-old boy plays the accordion on the Rock Ferry steamer. The boy is described as clean, neatly dressed, and unlike other street children in Liverpool. The journey from Rock Ferry to Leamington began on a rainy day, and the scenery was not striking. The Clarendon Hotel in Leamington is described as spacious and stately, with a courteous landlady.

Mrs. Jameson visited a basilica with a spacious nave and a flat ceiling that is frescoed and gilded. The basilica contains a chapel with the tomb of St. Sebastian, which includes a sarcophagus and a recumbent statue of the saint. The statue of St. Sebastian is designed in the style of Bernini and is considered to be of better taste than most of his works. Franciscan monks were arranging benches in the basilica while people gathered for a catechism examination. A monk at the door requested a contribution for the church or a religious purpose. The Appian Way features numerous large tombs, including the tomb of Cecilia Metella, which is made of travertine and has a battlemented wall built by the Caetanis. Mrs. Jameson expressed a negative opinion about American sculptors in Rome, while previously praising William Story's work.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The captain has not drunk wine for the last seventeen years. The captain believes that a crew can best be governed by kindness. There is a cage in the inner closet containing two land-birds that the captain has cared for. The narrator expresses a sense of disgust at dining in a house with a small entrance-hall and narrow staircase. The bill of fare at the dinner included broiled soles, half of a roast pig, and stewed oysters. The weather on December 11th was foggy, cold, and gloomy. On Christmas Eve, mistletoe was hung in various parts of the house, and maids attempted to kiss the gentlemen boarders.

J----- was assaulted and fought vigorously, receiving scratches during the conflict. The mistletoe has white, wax-looking berries and dull green leaves with a parasitical stem. On Christmas day, music and a woman's powerful voice singing a Christmas hymn were heard in the street. The market-houses during the season displayed various heavy food items, including prize oxen, fat sheep, and adorned pigs. The narrator feels a distinction between English and American people while in a foreign land. On January 1st, 1856, the narrator participated in a New Year celebration at Mrs. Blodgett's but did not stay for the ceremony of letting the Old Year out. The narrator has been suffering from low spirits, attributing it to his bachelor condition.

Mr. ------ experienced a ghostly encounter with an apparition of his uncle at the moment of the uncle's death. A tomb with a Latin inscription for William Bentley, a doctor who died in 1680, was discovered beneath a summer-house in a garden near Chester. Musicians often perform in public spaces, such as on ferries, to collect contributions from passersby. Children are frequently seen barefoot and barelegged on wet sidewalks during the dismal November weather. Graves of individuals believed to have died from the plague are located near stone crosses in Cheshire. Hawthorne Hall, located in Cheshire, has a history involving the Lathoms, Leighs, and Pages families. Small trade continues in open-air markets despite the cold weather, with various goods being sold on the streets.

Mary Runnel is a character that represents skepticism and a sense of unreality in dreams. Miss ------ writes communications with a pencil held loosely, moving rapidly regardless of her focus on the paper. The handwriting produced by Miss ------ is more free than her own. Miss ------ sometimes perceives each word before it is written, while at other times she is unaware of what will come next. The Uffizi gallery contains a collection of approximately twenty thousand drawings, with one to two hundred displayed in three rooms. The drawings in the Uffizi gallery are often rough and discolored, yet they are considered to possess a unique charm. The first sketches of a picture are viewed as more suggestive and inspiring than the finished works.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The building has a roof made of oak and features a flat design resembling a spacious old garret. There are alcoves on each side with simple benches and reading-desks, and the books appear to be very old. Some valuable books were formerly chained to the bookcases, and a few remain chained. Mr. E------ displayed an old copy of the Bible and a vellum manuscript of the works of Duns Scotus. The chapel has been partially renewed and features ecclesiastical decorations and encaustic tiles. The college gardens offer views of Christ Church meadows and the river. The RATCLIFFE LIBRARY is a circular building with a lower story of arches and primarily contains scientific works.

The small ponds serve as mirrors for the surrounding scenery. The hills around Rydal Water are craggier and less wooded than others previously seen. A modern house overgrown with ivy near the lake is identified as Mr. Wordsworth's residence. Mrs. Wordsworth is still residing at the house identified as Mr. Wordsworth's. The narrator and companions planned to return to inspect Wordsworth's residence after staying at Brown's Hotel in Grasmere. A gardener informed the narrator that the house they were inspecting actually belongs to Mr. Ball, a Quaker gentleman. Wordsworth's ornamental garden is adjacent to Mr. Ball's grounds, separated only by a wire fence.

The narrator went to bed at eleven and slept unquietly. The narrator intended to rise early to see the town of Lancaster before breakfast. The breakfast was delayed by half an hour, affecting the narrator's schedule. Lancaster is described as a not very remarkable town built of stone with taller houses and narrow streets. The castle in Lancaster is renovated, with a fine old front featuring a statue of a warrior. The narrator traveled from Lancaster to Liverpool by train, which took from half past nine to twelve. The narrator attended the launch of a ship near Chester, which was affected by heavy rain.

Several individuals knelt in the church during the narrator's visit. The church features a long nave with six pointed arches on each side and multiple chapels. The walls of the church are adorned with pictures and gilded virgins. The castle of St. Andre was built by Philip le Bel to restrain the people of Avignon. The castle is located on a bold hill above the Rhone, opposite Avignon. The castle's ramparts are mostly intact, and it has two large round towers at the entrance. The area within the castle contains old stone houses that appear to be the dwellings of peasants.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The narrator found ------ in better spirits than their last meeting, despite their misfortune. The fog in London was described as dense and black, resembling a distillation of mud. Gas was lit in all shop windows due to the heavy gloom caused by the fog. The narrator has been in London for at least a month longer than expected during a dreary season. The narrator attended an evening at Dr. ------'s house, who had been treating children with measles. Dr. ------ is a homoeopathist and a believer in modern spiritualism. Dr. ------ discussed Mr. Harris, an American poet of spiritualism, and his works, which he considered to have light and splendor.

The British Museum contains the Townley Gallery, which features ancient sculpture. The sculptures in the Townley Gallery include headless and legless forms, as well as broken-nosed faces. The frieze of the Parthenon depicts horses that resemble ponies more than modern fine horses. The Assyrian room in the museum features marble slabs sculptured in bas-relief with scenes from the life of Senmacherib. The museum houses relics and fragments excavated by Layard, including pieces of broken glass with iridescent colors. The museum includes halls of fossil remains, mineralogical specimens, and a fac-simile of the Koh-i-noor diamond. One piece of pure iron in the museum weighs about fourteen hundred pounds and is speculated to be an aerolite.

The gray pyramid of Caius Cestius is enclosed by a parapet and features a high, unbroken slope and peak. The blocks of marble on the pyramid fit closely together, with some crevices allowing plants to grow. The marble of the pyramid has turned gray due to two thousand years of atmospheric action. The narrator visited the Coliseum and described the afternoon weather as delightful and unique. General Pierce discussed his presidential life with the narrator, indicating he has no desire to renew it. Pierce was recognized as the master-mind of his Cabinet, which consisted of men of great ability. Caleb Cushing was described as intellectually fickle, needing stable judgment to maintain consistency.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: Two armed figures, one in brass mail and the other in bright steel, stood on a raised dais underneath a great picture. The hall contained a gallery located a third of the way up towards the roof. The items in the hall were in perfect condition, without rust or decay, but appeared to belong to a past age. Battle Abbey was first granted to Sir Anthony Browne, who was seen asleep with his first wife in the church. The property was sold to the Websters in 1719, and the current proprietor is Sir Augustus Webster. The gardener guided visitors through the ruined portions of the Abbey, including two ivied towers and an old refectory. Hastings is a famous watering and sea-bathing place located about seven miles from Battle.

The room described is wainscoted with carved oak and features a coved ceiling painted with planetary symbols. The room contains frescoes by Perugino and was noted for its magnificence and beauty. The chapel visited is similar in size and construction to the previous room and is also wainscoted with old oak. The chapel's walls are entirely frescoed and retain more original brightness than the previous room. One of the frescoes in the chapel depicts the decapitation of John the Baptist. The narrator and companions explored narrow, ancient passages in the upper city that may have been inhabited by Etruscan princes. The Tiber River was crossed shortly before reaching Perugia and is described as broad, rapid, and turbid.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: Southey did not keep a gardener as a regular part of his establishment. The current occupant of Southey's residence is referred to as Mr. Radday. The house was closed during the visit, but the gardener showed the visitors around the grounds. Southey's library and the room where he died were visible from the windows. Southey's residence is surrounded by trees, most of which were planted by him over fifty years ago. The Greta river is audible around the house and was a place where Southey used to walk. The visitors ordered a one-horse fly for a drive to Lodore after leaving the grounds.

The meadow at the bottom of the valley has produced three crops of grass during the present season and will produce another. The lawn around Poulton Hall requires care and is shorn every three or four days. Mr. B. stated that three oaks on his lawn are the largest in the county. The lawn and Poulton Hall contribute to the perception of English life. Mr. B. and his sisters invited the narrator to visit the house during their absence in Scotland. There is an attic chamber called the Martyr's chamber, associated with a lady who was imprisoned there for her religion. The river Mersey has a muddy color and is not crowded with ships due to many being in the docks.

Holborn features antique-looking houses that are not particularly remarkable. St. Paul's Cathedral has a dome and pinnacles that are visible from various avenues. The lower part of St. Paul's Cathedral is more affected by smoke than its loftier portions. There is a statue of Queen Anne in front of St. Paul's Cathedral. St. Paul's churchyard includes a street running around the base of the church and an enclosure with tombstones. The Zoological Gardens are located at the end of Regent's Park and are extensive but not as impressive as expected. The hippopotamus is noted as the chief treasure of the collection at the Zoological Gardens.

There are six round towers, one on each side of two gateways. The castle has been significantly damaged, requiring extensive use of gunpowder for its ruin. The walls are made of agglomerated small stones and mortar, with a casing of red freestone. Each round tower contained a small room approximately twelve to fifteen feet across and had three stories. The inner courtyard is a nearly square parallelogram, about forty-five paces across, and is grass-grown with a few recently planted trees. There is a moat around three sides of the fortress, approximately sixty feet wide and now mostly filled with earth. No wooden structures remain in the castle, only bare stone and some plaster.

The narrator visited Routledge's bookshop to discuss Miss Bacon's business but found the partners absent. The narrator and J----- visited St. Paul's Cathedral to escape the heat of the city. The narrator pointed out monuments to three British generals who were slain in America during the last war. At Guildhall, J----- showed no interest in Gog and Magog. The narrator observed a monument to the officers of the Coldstream Guards who were slain in the Crimea. The narrator met with a member of Routledge's firm, who expressed willingness to assist with Miss Bacon's work but suggested their firm may not be the best fit for publication. The narrator visited the Picture Gallery at the British Institution, which contained paintings by first masters.

Mr. Powers demonstrated the efficiency of his invention by punching a hole through an iron bar with a force equivalent to ten thousand pounds. The author expresses enjoyment in the company and conversation of Mr. Powers. The author visited the Pitti Palace and spent several hours viewing its collection of paintings. The gallery features notable works, including a Judith by Allori and two peasant Madonnas by Murillo. Miss Howorth states that copying pictures, especially those of Raphael, is a regular profession that may hinder the progress of modern painting. The weather is described as very hot, with warm nights and active wildlife in the garden. The author feels a desire to work but is hindered by a sense of being unsettled due to frequent relocations.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The palace has separate portions for its residents and a common area for their servants. The library contains about eight thousand volumes and is associated with the Barberini household. An ecclesiastic from the Barberini household showed a very old Bible and some poems of Tasso in the library. The group visited the Palazzo Galitzin, where they lunched with the Misses Weston and met a French abbe. The Castle of St. Angelo features an outer wall and is accessed by drawbridges. The ancient entrance to Hadrian's tomb has been walled up and is not accessible. The mausoleum has been used as a fortress for nearly twelve centuries.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The narrator was introduced to various notable individuals, including Sir Emerson Tennent and Mr. Samuel Lover. Miss Jewsbury is known in literature and had a conversation with the narrator about Emerson. Miss Jewsbury mentioned that Miss Martineau had given Emerson a lock of hair from a mummy. Miss Jewsbury is currently involved in a literary project with Lady Morgan. The narrator attended an event where ices and jellies were served, and some guests performed music. After supper, Mr. Lover sang Irish songs, contributing to the entertainment of the evening. Mrs. Heywood hosted a dinner that included notable guests such as Mr. Monckton Milnes and the Bishop of Lichfield.

The hotel accommodations include breakfast, lunch, and dinner with various food items and wine. The hotel is described as having a gloomy front, an enclosed court, and galleries connecting the rooms. The hotel appears old and dingy, with signs of former magnificence in the bedroom decor. There are no chambermaids, and the hotel lacks the comfort and cleanliness typical of English and American hotels. The hotel has a significant number of English and American travelers, indicating its popularity among tourists. The streets of Terni are narrow, paved, and intricate, leading to difficulties in navigation. The travelers left Terni in a vettura at six o'clock in the morning.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The narrator describes a sunset and the visibility of a comet during their return to the house. Mr. and Mrs. B------, Scotch people from the next villa, visited the Storys. William Story entertained guests by drawing caricatures, including one of a Presidential candidate. The narrator describes the streets of old Siena as looking grim at night. The narrator visited the cathedral, noting its interior is made of alternating black and white marble. The cathedral features various ornaments, including gilding, frescos, and a magnificent wheel-window of painted glass. The Institute of the Fine Arts contains works of Sienese painters, with a dispute between Florence and Siena regarding the origins of modern painting.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: Numerous specimens of Venetian glass are described as fragile. The glass was used to test poison by shattering at its touch. Palissy ware is characterized by its embossed designs of vegetables and sea creatures. Sevres china is noted for its inestimable value due to artwork from master painters. The author visited an exhibition on two consecutive days and found enjoyment in the experience. Mr. C S------- is a poet who lives in a semi-detached suburban residence in Manchester. Mr. C S------- received various tokens of esteem, including a presentation copy of Southey's works.

Gothic architecture is characterized by intricate details that create a moral charm. Classic architecture is described as an outline without small points for emotional connection. The Campanile's grandeur is enhanced by its height, while the Pantheon's design retains its sublimity regardless of scale. The Museum of Natural History in Florence contains rooms dedicated to Galileo. A colossal statue of Galileo stands beneath a frescoed dome in the museum. One niche in the museum preserves a shriveled forefinger of Galileo, while another contains two telescopes used for his discoveries. The Palazzo Vecchio is noted for being the loftiest and most picturesque tower in Florence.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: Coventry features many modern fronts that conceal antique arrangements, including old rafters and intricate passages. The hotels in Coventry are old buildings with new exteriors and have archways for vehicle access. The streets of Coventry were crowded and busy during a fair day, with various merchandise for sale in the open air. St. Michael's Church is noted for its magnificent Gothic architecture, intricate details, and a steeple that is three hundred and three feet high. Trinity Church, located near St. Michael's, has a tall spire but did not attract as much interest. St. Mary's Hall is open to the public and is currently owned by the Corporation of Coventry.

The Duttons of Dutton retained power for many hundreds of years. On midsummer-day, the Duttons rode through Chester to the Church of St. John to renew their licenses. In the time of Henry VII, the Duttons claimed that Cheshire minstrels should deliver them four bottles of wine and a lance at the feast of St. John. An Irish family consisting of a gray-haired man, his pale wife, and three daughters was found in a ferry-house. The Irish family was traveling to Liverpool to seek a passage back to Ireland due to extreme poverty. The children of the Irish family appeared to be patient and endured their circumstances. The narrator observed the family's situation and reflected on the struggles of poor people.

The Isis is a narrow stream with a sluggish current. The Roebuck Hotel has an entrance through an arch from High Street and features a paved court. The court of the Roebuck Hotel is surrounded by flowers in pots and vases. Students from the University of Oxford were observed discussing horses and boats at the Roebuck Hotel. The Castle Hotel is located within fifty yards of the water-side in Southampton. Mrs. ------ is an instructress of young ladies and is willing to host the narrator and companions for a few weeks. Southampton is described as a pretty town with a High Street that resembles American streets.

Old villages are frequently scattered along the track, characterized by peacefulness and rural verdure. Old country-seats resembling English halls or manor houses are present on the hillsides, surrounded by park scenery. Gray churches are located in the midst of small towns in the area. On June 30th, the author and his wife took a cab from Southampton to Netley Abbey, which is about three to four miles away. Netley Abbey is described as a picturesque and ivy-grown ruin with large trees and abundant weeds and grass on its walls. The Abbey has been private property since it was taken from the monks, and remnants of a residence built from its materials have mostly disappeared. The author purchased a basket from a woman identified as the gypsy of Netley Abbey, who claimed to have lived among the ruins for thirty years.

Ulverton and other villages are characterized by antique appearances and close clusters of houses. The houses along the road are generally old, built of stone, and covered with light gray plaster. Furness Abbey is located near a railway station and has a new hotel within its grounds. The ruins of Furness Abbey cover a space of sixty-five acres and include remnants of a roofless church. The nave and choir of the abbey were nearly three hundred feet long, with the transept being more than half that length. The material of the abbey is a soft red stone, now overgrown with lichen and moss. The arches of the nave and transept are described as noble and immense, with some still partially intact.

The church has a great cloister with a walk of intersecting arches and a pavement of flat tombstones. Frescos on the walls of the cloister depict incidents in the lives of the seven founders of the church. The lower part of the cloister walls is covered with marble inscriptions commemorating deceased individuals. A stone octagonal structure in the center of the cloister is a well, not a tomb. Mr. Powers discussed the impossibility of flying using current motive power and anticipated future advancements in flying technology. Powers shared a method for treating chest complaints through inhalation of nitric acid and a remedy for burns using wet wash-leather. Powers informed about the failure of the electric cable attempt between England and America and proposed an alternative method for laying the cable.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The cathedral features a mid-partition that divides the choir and nave. The interior of the cathedral has a cold and bare atmosphere with very few monuments. The walls of the cathedral are grayish, and many windows contain ancient painted glass. Some modern windows are brighter in color and material beauty than the ancient ones but are considered less authentic. The screen between the nave and choir has eleven carved figures representing kings. Admission to the Minster is free, and several old vergers were present during the visit.

There has been a great deal of fog on the river, causing boats to navigate cautiously while ringing their bells. On December 13th, the weather was chill and frosty, with some foreboding of snow in New England. A barefooted young woman was observed, with her feet having a red complexion due to exposure to cold air. At the ferry-room, various women and a middle-aged man were present, with one young lady reading a shilling volume of James's 'Arabella Stuart.' Different social classes in England seem to interact more easily than in America, with less palpable shock in their encounters. A gentleman on the Rock Ferry steamer demonstrated English caution by not responding until he recognized the voice of the speaker. Among the beggars of Liverpool, a man without legs and arms was noted for his intelligent countenance and fixed gaze.

The Times's articles are characterized by breadth rather than high moral standards. Dr. ------ recounted a conversation with Sir Lytton Bulwer about the feelings experienced before public speaking. Canning expressed that he would give one of his best speeches when feeling nervous before speaking in the House of Commons. President Pierce is noted to have oratorical power but also experiences reluctance before speaking. Dr. ------ dined at the Reform Club on April 5th. The Reform Club features a large reading-room with an extensive library and various amenities for bachelors. Mr. Douglas Jerrold, introduced by Dr. ------, is described as a short man with a bent back and a lively demeanor.

Christ Church has produced notable figures such as Archbishops, Prime Ministers, and poets. The college dinners at Christ Church cost students one shilling and eleven pence each. Breakfast and supper are not provided in commons at Christ Church, but can be ordered from the buttery. Merton College is one of the oldest colleges in Oxford and has a venerable appearance. Merton College features a Norman archway used by the Queen of Charles I and a thirteenth-century building with a stone roof. The stone used in Oxford colleges decays quickly when exposed to the weather, affecting their appearance. Merton College's library is located in an old building and has a pleasant fragrance of ancient books.

The Rhone river passes near Avignon and appears to double upon itself. The Durance river joins the Rhone a few miles below Avignon but is not visible at that location. The Duomo of the popes was visited on June 2nd, where a custode showed various curiosities. The Gothic tomb of Pope John XXII features a recumbent statue beneath a stone canopy. The sacristy contains jewels and sacred treasures, including an ivory figure of Christ on an ebony cross. The church features a high stone chair with grotesque sculptures and a massively picturesque interior. Several chapels within the church contain pictures, sculptures, and monuments from various historical periods.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: Wordsworth's residence is an old stone house with a plastered exterior. The house is situated in a secluded area surrounded by shrubbery and flowers. There is a circular terrace in front of the house, which Wordsworth helped to construct. The terrace offers a view down the valley of the Rothay, with Windermere visible in the distance. The gardener mentioned that 'little Barbara Lewthwaite' had recently passed away, leaving grown-up children. Wordsworth did not own the house; it is the property of Lady Fleming, and Mrs. Wordsworth still resides there. The weather during the day was cloudy and showery, with occasional thunder.

The distance to the city gate is estimated to be two or three miles. Perugia is situated on a hill and is described as picturesque. The Grand Hotel de France is located near the city gate. Gaetano is identified as an inhabitant of Perugia. The travelers initially declined the services of a cicerone. They visited the church of San Luigi, which has stained and painted windows. The Cambio or Exchange was located near the church they visited.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The railway carriage windows were frosted with ice upon arrival in France. The journey included views of distant chateaus, churches, and towns, but the scene was bleak. The travelers arrived in Paris at five o'clock and took a carriage to the hotel de Louvre without luggage examination. They chose to dine at the restaurant within the hotel de Louvre instead of the table d'hote. The Rue St. Honore is one of the old streets in Paris, known for the assassination of Henry IV. The travelers walked along the Rue de Rivoli and noted their proximity to famous landmarks like the Louvre and the Champs Elysees. They found the Restaurant des Echelles, which was frequented by English and Americans and had a menu printed in both English and French.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The garden features a refreshment-room with drinks, cakes, and pastry, but no substantial food. There is a small dwelling-house in the center of the garden, likely for the overlookers of the place. A little girl, simply dressed, appears to live within the garden grounds. A daguerreotypist operates a business in a shanty within the garden, accompanied by his wife and family. The garden includes a maze where individuals may wander while still being able to see the exterior garden. The author visited the Isle of Man and spent time with S----- and the children, who stayed for a fortnight. The church of Kirk Madden is described as picturesque, surrounded by shadowy trees and an overflowing churchyard.

The house is probably timber-framed and overlaid with plaster. The wing of the house is a chapel. Mr. ------ has a clergyman and a bishop in his diocese. The entrance-hall opens onto a quadrangular court and contains old oak furniture. The house features a historical element known as 'The Bloody Footstep.' George Marsh, a Protestant clergyman, was burned at the stake during the time of Bloody Mary. The footprint is a dark brown stain in the stone and has a shallow cavity.

The street is described as commonplace, hot, dusty, and disagreeable. Surrounding the street are green hills, woods, villas, cottages, and castles. Beyond the river, there is a line of crags approximately three hundred feet high, with varying vegetation. The narrator stayed at the old Bath Hotel, which has extensive passages and a beautifully arranged garden. During the stay at Matlock, there was consistent brilliant sunshine and lush grass and foliage. The narrator visited a church, likely associated with the Arkwright family, but did not enter it. The next day, the narrator visited a grand cavern with a guide who provided candles.

The English Notebooks of Nathaniel Hawthorne, Volume I, is dedicated to Francis Bennoch, Esq. The Editor states that the private journals of Mr. Hawthorne were originally intended for his own reference. There was a demand for a biography of Mr. Hawthorne, but the Editor refused due to the delicacy of the subject. Mr. Hawthorne expressed a desire that no one write his biography, leading the Editor to publish his private records instead. The Editor transcribed the manuscripts without altering their sequence, omitting some passages for various reasons. The Editor hopes that the volumes of notes will counter the perception of Mr. Hawthorne as gloomy and morbid. Mr. Hawthorne is described as possessing a cheerful mood and a healthful mind, despite his deep sympathies.

One altar was used for acts of devotion without a priest, with participants alternating in prayer. An old woman was selling rosaries, religious books, and medals of the Immaculate Virgin near the church. The popes' palace is located adjacent to the church and is currently used as barracks by soldiers. The architecture of the palace is described as a confused mass with no regular description due to modern alterations. The palace contains a chapel with two floors, one of which is occupied by soldiers' beds. The interior of the palace features defaced frescos and large, gloomy halls that were once ornate. The top of one of the towers offers views of the surrounding landscapes, including the Rhone River.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: R------ was present at the battle of New Orleans. R------ fired twenty-four times during the battle. General Carroll ordered R------ to stop firing when the British were in retreat. R------ hit a British officer with one of his shots. R------ kept the sword of the British officer he shot as a memento. The British General Pakenham was killed during the battle. R------ reported the death of General Pakenham after the battle.

The Irwell river empties into the Mersey. The narrator visited the Arts' Exhibition and described the building as more convenient than showy. The interior of the exhibition featured long vaulted vistas and a variety of artworks including pictures, statues, and vases. The narrator expressed difficulty in enjoying the exhibition due to the overwhelming number of artworks. The Gallery of British Painters contained hundreds of pictures that the narrator found interesting but could not focus on. The narrator noted the presence of individual relics of antiquity, including a dagger associated with Felton and a target of Emperor Charles V. Wolsey's portrait and his cardinal's hat were displayed in a glass case, which had been purchased by Charles Kean.

The surgeon who attends the court was present in the private room with the coroner. The American captain involved in the case was approximately thirty years old and displayed a rude demeanor. The case concerned a man who died from natural causes after being frost-bitten, leading to no blame for the captain. The jury initially suspected boiling water caused the man's injuries but changed their opinion after the surgeon's explanation. The coroner's influence was significant in guiding the jury's verdict. The court-room contained police officers, officials, and a few spectators and witnesses. Mr. B. and the narrator visited the residence of Sir Thomas Birch, which is a large brick mansion with notable landscaping.

The narrator walked into the city after breakfast to explore its appearance and churches. The heat caused the narrator to return home after initially planning to stay in the city. The interior of the Duomo was cool and dim compared to the outside heat. Street merchants in Florence display various wares on movable counters during the morning. Cherries are abundant in the markets and streets, with some being very large. Mr. and Mrs. Powers visited the narrator, and Mr. Powers shared stories and ideas. Mr. Powers recounted an incident involving a servant who stole oil to maintain a shrine to the Virgin.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The cathedral features a statue of Gothic sculpture in the nave. There are sitting statues of popes of Sienese nativity throughout the cathedral. Shrines and chapels built by noble families are located along the aisles and transepts of the cathedral. The gravestone of a person who fell in the battle of Monte Aperto is located in the cathedral's pavement. The surrounding countryside of Siena is described as beautiful, with a stream and a bridge resembling a Roman aqueduct. The streets of Siena are paved with bricks set edgewise in steep areas and broad flag-stones in level areas. The walls of Siena are primarily made of brick, with some fragments of ancient stone-work.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: Loch Achray is located near the Trosachs and is less than a quarter of a mile wide. The area features dwarf oaks, birches, and firs that do not grow tall. Visitors can take omnibuses through the pass of the Trosachs to a hotel built by Lord Willoughby d'Eresby. The hotel has a parlor within a round tower with four narrow windows. A path along the right shore of Loch Achray offers picturesque views and leads to Ellen's Isle. The path becomes wilder and more shadowy with overhanging foliage as one travels further. Rain can affect the experience, but shelter can be found under trees along the path.

The church was built over a thousand years ago, with parts of it worn away by time. Several broken niches in the church once held statues, most of which have fallen or crumbled away. There are many gravestones around the church, but none are of any antiquity. The clergyman's house is closely connected to the church and is described as a comfortable-looking residence. The sexton, a jolly-looking man, was found in the churchyard and accompanied the visitors to the ruins. The church contains a nave supported by two rows of Saxon pillars, which are covered with plaster. An ancient wooden coffin and a piece of a statue were discovered in the ruins, but their ages are unknown.

The mountain of Radicofani is described as wide, dreary, and barren. A mountain tempest of wind, rain, and hail occurred while climbing Radicofani. The castle on the summit of Radicofani is associated with the robber-knight Ghino di Tacco from Boccaccio's Decameron. The hillside above the castle is covered with numerous large fragments of stone. The town near the castle is built on an unusual foundation and is thought to be inhabited by dependants of the knight. The hotel where the narrator stayed was originally a hunting-palace built by the Grand Dukes of Tuscany. The town of Radicofani is located a quarter of a mile above the hotel and is accessible by a steep road.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The text discusses the nature of Note-Books as reflections rather than definitive conclusions. The author expresses concern about the accuracy of printed sentences in the Note-Books. The author began his services in Liverpool on August 1st, 1853. The author received eight sovereigns, four half-crowns, and a shilling as receipts for the previous day. The author has had two non-business calls from an American captain and Mr. H---- B----. The author suspects a young woman who asked for money may not be trustworthy. The author received an invitation from the Mayor to dine at the Town Hall on the following Friday.

The narrator inquired at various livery-stables for a conveyance to Stonehenge and took a fly from the Lamb Hotel. The drive to Stonehenge included seven miles over a turnpike and two miles across Salisbury Plain. During the drive, the narrator observed a group of men in uniform, identified by the driver as lunatics from a neighboring asylum. Salisbury Plain is described as a vast, treeless, and houseless area with gentle swells and views extending to the horizon. The narrator noted large flocks of black-faced sheep being watched by shepherds and dogs. Upon reaching Stonehenge, the narrator found a picnic-party and an artist painting the scene. A clergyman named Mr. Hinchman approached the narrator's group while they were at Stonehenge.

Castagno assassinated Domenico to obtain the secret of painting in oils. Domenico, unaware of Castagno's treachery, requested to be taken to him while dying. Castagno lived to be seventy-four years old and revealed his crime on his death-bed. Domenico died in Castagno's arms. The narrator spent time in Florence planning and sketching a romance. The narrator attended a tea reception at Miss Blagden's on August 28th. Mr. Powers described an apparition of hands during a spiritual session at his house.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: Gerard Dow is noted as a master among painters for his realistic depictions. A straw mat and a dented metal vase in Dow's paintings are described as exceptionally realistic. The text discusses the spiritual representation of common household items by Dutch painters. The author expresses an increasing appreciation for the works of old masters and English painters. Etty is criticized for his portrayal of women, which the author finds unappealing. Hogarth's painting March to Finchley is highlighted for its expression of English nature and emotion. The author observes a crowd at Manchester Cathedral during a wedding, noting the emotional impact of the bells.

There was a game of Vingt-et-un and a game of whist in the dining-room. Mrs. Halton drove off in a pony-chaise after the card games. Prayers were held in the oak dining-room before breakfast, with all the servants present. A parrot named Poll was praised for being silent during prayers but was vociferous during breakfast. The dining-room features carvings of coats of arms from successive possessors of the house. The group traveled from Rock Ferry to Shrewsbury, arriving between three and four o'clock. Shrewsbury is described as being situated on an eminence surrounded by the Severn River.

A tall column surmounted by a statue of Sir Walter Scott is located in an enclosed green space. There is a bronze equestrian statue of the Queen in one of the streets. The University is situated in High Street, in a dense and old part of Glasgow. St. Mungo's Cathedral is a large and fine old church located near a public green. The price of a ticket for St. Mungo's Cathedral is two pence. The crypts of St. Mungo's Cathedral contain massive arches supporting the structure above. The narrator took a steamer up the Clyde and later traveled by railway to Balloch.

Public speaking can create a strong connection between the orator and the audience. The act of speaking in public can sharpen and invigorate the mind. There is skepticism about whether public speaking elevates the orator intellectually or morally. The Mayor toasted various professions during an event, with attendees standing to show assent. The worst orator mentioned was a major of Artillery who spoke nervously. The winter weather on the Irish Sea is described as bleak and windy. Christmas time included singing by children and expectations for Christmas-boxes.

The region described is characterized by a lack of comfort and the presence of beggars. The narrator arrived at Spoleto before noon and observed a busy street from the inn window. The gateway of Spoleto is traditionally associated with Hannibal's attempt to enter the city after the battle of Thrasymene. The Duomo, or cathedral, in Spoleto was described as small and uninteresting. The narrator traveled through the valley of the Clitumnus, which was overcast and chilly. A small temple, possibly described by Byron and associated with Pliny, was observed in the valley. Beggars in the region were noted for their urgent and fervent requests for alms.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The narrator and J----- ascended a distance along a cascade before parting ways, with J----- going up the hill and the narrator taking a path along the side of the hill. The narrator considers the stretch of Loch Lomond in front of Inversnaid to be the most beautiful lake and mountain view he has ever seen. The glen of Invernglass is located directly opposite the narrator's viewpoint and winds among the feet of Ben Crook, Ben Ein, Ben Vain, and Ben Voirlich. The narrator's wife joined him to enjoy the view until a steamer arrived to land passengers before continuing on the loch. A Highlander wearing dark tartan and displaying his legs passed by the narrator and his wife, who was later identified as a manufacturer with a shooting-box on the hill. The narrator and his wife hired a boat to visit Rob Roy's cave, which is located about half a mile up the lake. During their return from the cave, J----- attempted to catch a fish but it escaped, with the boatman suggesting it might have been a pike.

The doctor became acquainted with one of Prince Albert's attaches during his tour in Scotland. The attaché invited the doctor to join Prince Albert's shooting party, offering him a gun, a keeper, dogs, cigars, and wine. The attaché noted that Prince Albert enjoys having Americans in his shooting parties due to their shooting skills. The doctor mentioned that Louis Napoleon had returned his bow on multiple occasions and made remarks about him to the Empress. The doctor has been told in France that he resembles the Emperor and is trying to enhance this resemblance by training his mustache. The doctor expressed the opinion that English people do not understand comfort in their domestic arrangements as well as Americans do. The author noted that an unfinished opera based on The Scarlet Letter had been performed successfully in New York.

The conversation included topics about art and fleas. Miss Bremer expressed her fondness for the long and severe winters in Sweden. Two young ladies, one German and one French, visited Miss Bremer after a walk. Miss Bremer gave a bunch of roses to Miss Shepard for her six sisters. The group visited the edge of the Tarpeian Rock, which is about the height of a four-story house. Miss Bremer bid farewell to the group with affectionate gestures. The narrator and their companion are searching for lodgings for the next winter.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The lid of the tomb was found to be decayed or broken when it was opened about a year ago. The grandmother's coffin contained beautiful, glossy, living chestnut ringlets, which had grown over half a century. Madam ------ was once carried to the grave in Barbary, where her husband was Consul-General. Madam ------ revived after being thought dead and later believed the funeral procession to have been a dream. Mr. ------, her son, was born on shipboard off the coast of Spain and claims four nationalities. Mr. ------ has hereditary claims to a Spanish countship and spent his infancy in Barbary. The hospital visited was a large edifice of red freestone, where a mate was being treated for a severe accident.

London is poorly lighted outside the principal thoroughfares. The narrator arrived at lodgings that appeared cheerful with a fire. Fanny brought unhappy news about an unspecified situation. The narrator visited the British Museum and found it wearisome and depressing. The Egyptian remains at the museum were noted for their size and ponderosity. The narrator and J----- sought their luggage at a railway station and then explored London. They encountered boys from Christ's Hospital playing during their visit.

The hall retains a significant amount of freshness and brightness. Ancient statues and busts in the hall have corroded surfaces due to long burial. There are two cabinets in the entrance room, one adorned with precious stones and the other with ivory carvings of Michael Angelo's Last Judgment and Raphael's Loggie. A large piece is broken out of one of the marble steps leading to an elevated apartment in the hall. The Academy of St. Luke is located in the Via Bonella, close to the Forum in Rome. The collection at the Academy includes works by Vandyke, Titian, and Guido. San Pietro in Vincoli is situated on or near the summit of the Esquiline mount.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: Douglas Jerrold expressed pain and emotion after being described as 'acrid.' A second bottle of Burgundy was opened during the conversation. Jerrold felt hurt that someone he considered a friend shared the world's negative opinion of him. The narrator attempted to comfort Jerrold by comparing him to the Burgundy wine. The group attended a ballet at the Haymarket Theatre after their conversation. On April 8th, the narrator attended a supper-party at Mr. D------'s with several notable individuals. The narrator visited Mr. and Mrs. Hall's home, which was described as pretty and well-arranged.

Women in Marseilles wash linen in streams and collect water for household purposes. Women in Marseilles often gather in public spaces to socialize and enjoy the sunshine. The climate in Marseilles is described as keen and cutting, with ice observed along rivulets in midwinter. Public squares in Marseilles are adorned with statues, fountains, and trees, serving as gathering places for the populace. The atmosphere in Marseilles is characterized by lively conversation among the crowd, contrasting with the silence often found in English crowds. A juggler performed in a public square in Marseilles, with his wife assisting him during the act. The narrator left Marseilles on the Neapolitan steamer Calabrese, which was clean and comfortable despite the cool air.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The narrator and his wife visited the palace of Breadalbane during the queen's residence. They observed portraits and paintings by Vandyke, Sir Peter Lely, Sir Godfrey Kneller, and Rubens. The narrator felt a sense of weariness during the visit, which was shared by his wife. After leaving the palace, they walked through the Canongate and observed the conditions of Edinburgh's population. The narrator noted the presence of many children in the area. They later visited an ornamental garden between the old town and the new town, where they saw a picturesque sunset. The next morning, they took a cab to explore Edinburgh, passing notable sites including the University and Arthur's Seat.

On February 24th, the author crossed the Ponte Sisto and explored the area opposite the Capitoline Hill. Several schooners and barks, each weighing two or three hundred tons, were moored at a quay near the Capitoline Hill. A steamer armed with a large gun and two brass swivels was also present at the quay. The author crossed the river via the island of St. Bartholomew, which is densely covered with buildings. The ruins of the theatre of Marcellus were observed, featuring a circular edifice with Ionic and Doric columns. The author passed between the Circus Maximus and the Palace of the Caesars, near the Baths of Caracalla. The author encountered the remains of Columbaria and the tomb of the Scipios before entering the Campagna through the gate of San Sebastiano.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The girls played a game where they chased one another within and outside a ring, which opened to let a fugitive pass and closed to impede a pursuer. Another game involved several girls being blinded and pursuing a single girl who rang a hand-bell to indicate her location. The narrator walked from the Park to Rock Ferry, a distance of three or four miles, along a foot-path through fields with mown grass and ongoing wheat harvest. Laborers paused to observe the narrator and appeared more willing to rest than American laborers. The narrator visited an alehouse in Tranmere, where the entry and tap-room floor were chalked with corkscrew lines. The alehouse featured decorations including sea-shells, an earthenware figure, and advertisements for Allsop's ale and the Ancient Order of Foresters. Smithell's Hall, located two or three miles from Bolton, is one of the oldest residences in England and retains much of its historical appearance.

Mr. ------ displayed a homely and plain manner with old-fashioned dignity when addressing Mrs. Browning. Mrs. Browning is a believer in spiritual communications, while her husband, Robert Browning, is an infidel. Mr. ------ recounted a story about a successful spiritual communication involving Cooper the novelist and his deceased sister. Robert Browning expressed skepticism about the spiritual session he attended with his wife and Mr. Hume. Mrs. Browning's health limits her to early hours, prompting the gathering to conclude around ten o'clock. Mr. ------ indicated that it may be too late for him to revisit Europe. Little Pennini assisted with serving cake and strawberries during the evening gathering.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: One wall of the unfinished nave remains standing and has been incorporated into a palace. The family visited the Villa Belvedere with Mr. and Mrs. Story. The vicinity of Siena is described as cooler and breezier than Florence. The Villa Belvedere was built by an Englishman who left it to his butler. The villa features lawns and shrubbery that have an English character. Mr. Story is considering purchasing the Villa Belvedere. The family observed vineyards and interacted with local peasants during their visit.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The Madeira is a ship that accommodates about seventy passengers. The narrator and their companion drove to the dock after shopping in town. The narrator's wife, S-----, and their children were on board the ship. The narrator and J----- left Southampton at three o'clock. They arrived in Worcester after traveling on multiple railway lines. In Worcester, they stayed at the Crown Hotel, which has an entrance through an arched passage. The Guildhall in Worcester features statues of Queen Anne, Charles I, and Charles II.

The narrator had previously met Mr. ------ at a dinner at Mrs. H------'s. Mr. ------ has an extensive domain with winding walks, dells, hillocks, and rustic bridges. The grounds contain a thick growth of ferns that serve as cover for game. The narrator's room is called 'The Beam Chamber' and features a large rough-hewn cross-beam. Dinner was served in a room panelled with old carved oak, believed to be from the era of Henry the Seventh. The dining room has a Gothic cornice and furniture of Gothic patterns. Candles were used for lighting during dinner due to the overcast day.

George Marsh underwent an examination at Smithell's Hall. The examination and martyrdom of George Marsh are detailed in the eleventh section of Fox's Book of Martyrs. A stone at Smithell's Hall is believed to bear the mark of George Marsh's footprint. The stone was once removed from the pavement and is cracked across at one end. The examination room at Smithell's Hall opens into a Chapel that can accommodate a large congregation. The estate has changed ownership several times since the Conquest. The oak framework of the house is believed to be over a thousand years old.

The interior of Notre Dame features painted roofs, gilded capitals, and illuminated frescoes. Workmen's boards, timber, and ladders currently occupy the center of Notre Dame, obstructing its grandeur. The front of Notre Dame has twin towers and three deep-pointed arches, with intricate carvings and statues. The narrator visited the consul's office located at 51 Rue Caumartin. The vice-consul introduced the narrator to a gentleman described as courteous and well-suited for the consul position. The vice-consul advised the narrator to obtain necessary vises in Paris for better validity. There is a charge of five francs for the consul's vise, which surprised the narrator.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The text describes a scene in a painting featuring a pool of water and figures that appear to project from the canvas. The face of Jesus is described as resembling human flesh and blood, which contrasts with the celestial aspect of the figure. The composition of the painting is criticized for having two distinct parts that do not interact with each other. The text mentions a visit to the studio of Mr. Wilde, an artist from Boston known for his vibrant paintings of Venice. Mr. Wilde's paintings are noted for their bright colors, but the text suggests they do not surpass the beauty found in nature. The text also describes a visit to the studio of an elderly Swiss artist named Mueller, who created detailed water-color and crayon drawings. The author expresses admiration for the works of Mr. Brown, Mr. Wilde, and Mr. Mueller, while feeling disappointed by the landscapes of famous old masters.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The narrator's wife left to find another chapel with decorations by Cimabue or Giotto. The narrator found the church unimpressive despite its antiquity, size, architecture, and tombs. The Bargello was formerly the palace of the Podesta of Florence and is now a prison. The Bargello is described as an immense square edifice of dark stone with a tall tower. The Church of Or San Michele was once a market and is now a church with statues by Donatello. The Riccardi Palace was built by Cosmo de' Medici over four centuries ago and remains well-preserved. The Riccardi Palace features a pillared arcade and displays statues, bas-reliefs, and sarcophagi.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The city of Genoa is characterized by its bold, barren, and brown islands with snow on their summits. Upon landing in Genoa, the party encountered a crowd of cab-drivers, hotel-runners, and commissionaires speaking multiple languages. The commissionaire named Salvator Rosa guided the party through narrow streets to an old church with a magnificent interior made of polished marble. The Cathedral of San Lorenzo features an exterior of black and white marble slabs, some of which were sourced from Jerusalem. Inside the Cathedral of San Lorenzo, there are rich decorations including precious marbles, a pillar from Solomon's Temple, and artworks by old masters. The party visited another church built by a pirate, which is noted for its interior adorned with burnished gold and precious stones. Throughout the visit, priests and worshippers were observed kneeling in devotion in the cathedral and other churches.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The landscape in Lincolnshire is described as level. Little Byforth is a village with twenty or thirty stone and thatch dwellings, all over a hundred years old. Grantham is a town where the route branches off from the main railway line. The marketplace in Grantham features an ancient cross and the Angel Inn, which has antique architecture. The church in Grantham has a fine tower and spire adorned with Gothic ornaments. Nottingham is described as an unlovely and uninteresting town. The narrator decided to take a fly to Newstead Abbey after breakfast.

The Porta San Frediano is a tall, square structure of stone or brick in Florence. The arch of the Porta San Frediano is about half the height of the structure externally. The church of the Annunziata is described as magnificent and was decorated with scarlet silk and gold-embroidery. The Fair in Florence features cloth as the chief commodity, including coarse linen and cotton prints. The attendees of the fair are described as having a rustic appearance with sunburnt faces and thin frames. The crowd at the fair is characterized as dull and lacking warmth or cohesion. Italian crowds are noted for their civility and native courtesy.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: Hadrian's tomb is located beneath a modern structure. The vaults that served as a prison are situated above the ancient structure. Beatrice Cenci was confined in a small, vaulted room for a year before her execution. Benvenuto Cellini was also imprisoned in the same area for an assassination. An oubliette, a dungeon where prisoners could be buried alive, is present in the castle. The Archangel Michael statue has stood in bronze at the castle for many centuries. The castle includes a hall with frescos and modern furniture, indicating recent occupancy.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The narrator and J----- returned to their hotel after navigating irregular streets. The hotel is described as uncheerful, dark, musty, and staffed by a formal waiter.
