The narrator and J----- visited a castle located above the railway station, which is private property. The castle was built at various times, with the keep constructed by Edward I., and is currently owned by the Duke of Cleveland. St. Mary's Church, estimated to be eight hundred to a thousand years old, features a tall spire that is undergoing repairs. Bishop Butler, the author of the Analogy, is buried in the churchyard, which contains a heavy gray tombstone with a Latin inscription. The Council House, built in 1501, was used by councillors for the Welsh marches and hosted Charles I. and James II. during their reigns.

The narrator encountered village children who begged for money but returned to play when nothing was given. The village is located far from Liverpool and has not been significantly affected by cockney residences. A steamer landing-place is situated about a mile from the village, where a large new hotel has been built. The narrator observed the 18th Regiment, the Connaught Rangers, marching to embark for the East. A piece of marble sculpture representing St. George and the Dragon was found in a cottage near Rock Ferry. Good Friday is considered a day for planting by the English and Irish due to its religious significance. Mrs. ------ mentioned the origin of Benjamin Franklin's customary civil dress when attending court.

The church contains tombs and sarcophagi of the Corsini family. A marble Pieta is located within the church. The Torlonia Chapel is described as rich and gilded. The table at which the Last Supper was eaten is preserved in the church. Several sacred relics are preserved in the church, including the staircase of Pilate's house. The church has a porta santa that is opened by the pope during a jubilee. The Carnival scene in the Corso is described as jolly, while nearby streets exhibit ordinary Roman gravity.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The narrator visited the Church of the Capuchins and saw Guido's Archangel for the first time. The narrator had previously seen a mosaic copy of the Archangel at St. Peter's. The narrator described the original Archangel as having a beauty that surpasses the mosaic copy. The narrator expressed a strong familiarity and emotional connection to Rome. The narrator and companions traveled from Rome to Civita Vecchia, experiencing a desolate countryside. The narrator and companions faced various troubles while at Civita Vecchia regarding their passport. The narrator arrived at Leghorn early and considered spending time there for health benefits.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: A piece manufactured in Brussels for the Count de Burgh dates to 1632 and is a relic of the battle of Worcester lost by Charles. Worcester Cathedral has been renewed and repaired, with ongoing work by stone-cutters and masons on the exterior. The interior of Worcester Cathedral features a light-colored paint and has very little stained glass. The cathedral's plan includes a nave and side aisles with great clustered pillars and intersecting arches. Two tombs with recumbent figures and several mural monuments are located within the cathedral. The tomb of King John is located in Worcester Cathedral. The Museum of the Worcester Natural History Society has a well-arranged collection of natural history specimens and is open to the public on certain days.

Reformers do not include Republican simplicity of manners in their system. The dinner included turbot, lambs' feet, cutlets, and ptarmigan, along with bottles of Chateau Margaux and Chambertin. Mr. Douglas Jerrold is described as having a wise and humorously absurd nature, with a warm heart beneath a thin crust of outward acerbity. The conversation included discussions about Bulwer and Dickens, with differing opinions on their literary positions. Douglas Jerrold expressed admiration for the Duke of Devonshire, describing him as a true, honest, and kind-hearted man. Jerrold spoke highly of Emerson, Longfellow, and Lowell during the evening. The narrator proposed sending Thoreau's works to Dr. ------, but hesitated about Jerrold's judgment on them.

The festival featured a variety of sports and games, including wooden horses, swinging cars, and shooting targets. Admission to the theatres at the festival was priced at twopence for one and a penny for the other. The festival included booths where men and women were drinking and smoking pipes. Orange-girls were selling poor quality oranges that appeared to have been boiled for freshness. Brewers' draymen in England are allowed to drink as much of their master's beverage as they like. The note of the cuckoo was first heard on May 31st, described as soft and pleasant. The English women of the lower classes possess a unique grace not found in their American counterparts.

The text describes a sculpture of Apollo overtaking Daphne, highlighting the transformation of Daphne into a tree. The narrator expresses a lack of enthusiasm for the sculpture compared to its description. The narrator visits a large fountain surrounded by old trees and various works of art. Mr. Brown, an American landscape painter, is described as unpolished but confident in his art. Mr. Brown's paintings depict Swiss and Italian scenery, with one moonlight picture described as magical. The narrator prefers Mr. Brown's landscapes over those of old masters, citing a belief in the evanescent charm of art. The text mentions a visit to another studio where various sculptures, including an Eve and William Story's Cleopatra, are observed.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The landscape described is bleak, barren, brown, and bare, resembling wintry New England before snow. The houses in the area have roofs that are not very sloping and are typically covered with white plaster. Farmhouses are connected to their outbuildings, forming a quadrangle on three sides. The travelers arrived in Marseilles at about eleven o'clock after a long journey and a cold dinner in Avignon. A bronze statue of an archbishop, who was notable for his humanity during the plague of 1720, is located in a public square in Marseilles. The public square was crowded with people who appeared to be loitering in the sunshine, with a mix of gentlemen and peasants present. There were reports of unsuccessful attempts on the Emperor's life, which attracted a large crowd to the telegraph office.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The narrator expresses weariness with fine scenery after a short tour of mountains and lakes. The narrator reflects on the beauty of England and its variety within a small area. The journey included views of Blencathra, Skiddaw, and the vale of Grasmere. The group traveled from Ambleside to Newby Bridge along the eastern shore of Windermere. Hawkshead is described as a small, whitewashed old town with a Norman church. The narrator notes that attempts to describe scenery are often inadequate. The group has experienced rainy weather while staying at Newby Bridge.

The narrator's wife visited a museum while the narrator chose to walk in the sun. The narrator walked through the Forum and under the Arch of Titus towards the Coliseum. French drummers and trumpeters were performing near the Coliseum and the Arch of Constantine. The narrator walked along the Appian Way to the Baths of Caracalla. The Palace of the Caesars is located near the Baths of Caracalla and is topped by a convent. The narrator noted the destruction of Roman ruins by early Christians and the conversion of pagan temples into churches. On March 3rd, the narrator's family celebrated U----'s birthday by driving to the tomb of Cecilia Metella.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The town of Bolsena is described as having refuse strewn throughout its streets. The upper town of Bolsena was originally an Etruscan city known as Volsinii. The Romans destroyed Volsinii and built a town on its site, which includes the lower city. The streets of the upper town are narrow and winding, resembling paths rather than proper streets. The architecture of the upper town includes a mix of black houses and remnants of ancient structures. The narrator mentions having a midday meal that included fish from the nearby lake.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The text describes a beggar who moves on his hands and knees, using wooden shoes for support. The beggar receives alms from three individuals, including a young woman and two gentlemen, likely English or American. The beggar is not persistent in his demands for alms, and a simple shake of the head can deter him. The author notes that the Pincian is crowded with people and carriages despite the rainy weather. The author took a sitting for a bust in a studio formerly occupied by Canova, which lacked furniture and warmth. The text mentions that the Carnival continues despite the rain, with reports of fatalities during the event. The church of San Luigi de' Francesi is described as dirty and lacking care, with many tombs and monuments of French individuals.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The vagabond musicians in town are numerous from May to November. Musicians on steam ferry-boats earn very little, approximately a shilling a day per man. Some musicians include older men and women playing instruments, often with younger associates. Street performers can attract crowds, but they do not typically receive donations from onlookers. The common people observe street performances without criticism or unkindness. A person may be remembered as a ghost if the circumstances of their death are unknown. The author traveled to North Wales, visiting Chester, Bangor, and Beaumaris, where they saw an old castle.

Radicofani features a square tower with an arched gateway in its basement story. The town is densely populated and has both ancient and unattractive characteristics. The street in Radicofani is narrow and paved with flagstones that are not as smooth as those in Florence. The houses in Radicofani are tall and have multiple stories, but they appear dingy and shabby. The town contains shops, cafes, and churches that are crowded closely together. The pathway leading to the old castle is steep, winding, and becomes rough as it ascends. There is a farmhouse within the castle's wall, with signs of agricultural products but no visible life.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The narrator followed the footsteps of cows and met two boys from Ormskirk who were mounted on donkeys. The boys had empty panniers that they used to carry vegetables to market. The narrator saw the tower of Ormskirk Church and entered the town, directing steps to the church. Ormskirk Church is situated on a gentle eminence and has a pavement of flat gravestones in front. The church is the burial-place of the Earls of Derby but was closed at the time of the narrator's visit. The market-place was busy with various wares and a crowd of men and women on market-day. Ormskirk is known for its gingerbread, which is sold to railway passengers.

The journey included a stop at Callender, where Ben Ledi was visible behind the town. The travelers changed horses at Doune, an old town that they did not have time to explore. They mistakenly alighted at the Brig of Allan, which is three miles short of Stirling. The Brig of Allan is noted as the principal Spa of Scotland. After tea, the travelers explored the village street and enjoyed views from a nearby eminence. Stirling Castle is located on a height that resembles a hound, lion, or sphinx. The travelers took a train to Stirling early in the morning and visited the post-office and a bookseller's shop.

The Crystal Palace features mediaeval statues, arches, and doorways that are vividly presented. Benvenuto Cellini's statue of Perseus and a sitting statue by Michel Angelo of a Medici are notable artworks in the Crystal Palace. The bronze gate of a baptistery in Florence is intricately carved with lifelike Scripture subjects. The House of Diomed is described as a dismal abode with cold iron benches. The Tropical Saloon contains banyan trees, water-plants, and birds, but has a faint and sickish atmosphere. A California pine-tree trunk in the Tropical Saloon is large enough to contain fifty people. Mr. Silsbee assisted in searching for a lost sable tippet but was unsuccessful.

The area described has a plain, business-like atmosphere and has been a center for tradesmen for hundreds of years. Sign-boards indicate long-established businesses, including silk-mercers and hosiers, with some dating back to 1109. The narrator crossed the Thames over a bridge near Charing Cross and later visited London Bridge, which was crowded. The Thames is described as narrower than expected and less majestic compared to the Mersey. The narrator encountered Mr. Clarke, whom he had met previously during a ship launch on the Dee. In Regent Street, the narrator observed a company of dragoons in polished brass helmets and steel cuirasses. The narrator visited St. James's Park, where they saw various waterfowl and Buckingham Palace, which appeared deserted.

The narrator describes a lofty elevation of ground with picturesque old buildings. The narrator finds the cathedral's Gothic architecture impressive, more so than the ruins of Rome. The narrator notes the effective but complex business methods in France. The narrator left Lyons at four o'clock and arrived in Geneva at nearly ten o'clock. Geneva is situated on low, flat ground by the lake, with steep streets behind it. The town features new edifices and quaint gray buildings, with high red roofs and towers. The color of the Rhone river in Geneva is described as intensely blue and beautiful.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The Colonel was a veteran of the Peninsula with a medal for three battles in addition to Waterloo. The regimental band played during dinner but did not perform 'Hail Columbia' due to its absence from their repertoire. The band played a series of negro melodies as a compliment to a white countryman. After dinner, whist was played, followed by supper, and the group returned to their huts around four o'clock. The camp-beds were described as comfortless, providing little warmth or sound sleep. The regiment participated in a general review on a bright day with a strong east wind. The Duke of Cambridge was observed riding on a white horse during the review.

The Arch of Septimius Severus features bas-reliefs of Eastern wars. The Column of Phocas has a series of steps ascending on four sides to its pedestal. The Basilica of Julia has a floor made of beautiful and precious marbles, many of which are cracked and have been removed. Excavations in the area are approximately fifteen feet below the current street level. The Colonna Palace is currently occupied by the French Ambassador. The hall of the Colonna Palace is fifty-five paces in length and features giallo antico pillars and pilasters. The ceiling of the hall is adorned with frescoes depicting scenes from the history of the Colonna family.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: Forms and appliances of human life are not conducive to happiness until they are repurposed for new uses. Monks likely did not enjoy their edifices as much as current inhabitants do due to the change in use. The narrator visited an old church with a musty odor and ancient architecture, including side aisles and pointed arches. The cathedral visited had hospitable open doors and was free to enter, which was noted as a kindness not experienced elsewhere in England. The narrator observed significant architectural features in the Lady Chapel, including majestic arches approximately eighty feet high. A procession of men-at-arms on horseback was seen in the market-place, preparing for jousting. The narrator expressed reluctance to leave Peterborough but was glad to depart from an uncomfortable hotel.

The narrator traveled by train to London, getting out only once at Rugby. The train journey lasted for about seventy or eighty miles without stopping. Upon arrival in London, the narrator met S----- who was expecting him. S----- and the narrator visited Kensington Gardens after the children went to the Zoological Gardens. Kensington Gardens is described as an artificial woodland and park scenery with a palace inhabited by the Duchess of Inverness. The Serpentine River, located partly within Kensington Gardens, is larger than some world-celebrated lakes. The gardens were populated by well-dressed individuals, including families and children.

The text describes frescos by Fra Angelico located in a large cloister. The cloister features a picture of St. Dominic kneeling at the Cross and other works by various artists. The cloister is surrounded by a square open to the sky and paved with gray stones, likely over graves. The chapter-house contains a fresco of the Crucifixion by Fra Angelico, surrounded by images of saints and prophets. A shrine near the entrance of the church features a wooden image of the Saviour, adorned with offerings. The opposite arch of the entrance contains a wax-work representation of the Nativity, with the Virgin dressed in elaborate attire. The narrator visited the Academy of Fine Arts for the second time on July 13th.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The market-house in Shrewsbury was erected in 1595. The statue of Richard Plantagenet, Duke of York, was moved to the market-house from a demolished tower in 1795. Shrewsbury was a metropolis for the surrounding country, attracting neighboring gentry to build town-houses there. The Ireland mansion in Shrewsbury is a four-story timber house with projecting towers and embowered windows. The Severn River is described as the largest river encountered in England, approximately a stone's throw across. The English Bridge is a notable bridge in Shrewsbury with several arches. An old tower of red freestone is the only remaining tower from the town wall that once stood at intervals along its course.

BORROW, author of the Bible in Spain, is supposed to be of gypsy descent by the mother's side. Mr. Martineau mentioned that he had been a schoolfellow of Borrow and thought it probable that Borrow had gypsy blood. The Captain is a Marblehead man by birth and is nearly sixty years old. Oakum, the Captain's wife, is described as being at least six feet tall and well-proportioned. The Captain and Oakum have no children and Oakum has accompanied her husband on his voyages. On June 9th, a telegraphic message announced the arrival of the narrator's wife at Southampton. The narrator and J----- traveled from Birmingham to Leamington and then to Oxford, where they made stops.

The author observed the behavior of people facing starvation, noting their patience and meekness. The author visited Otterpool and Larkhill with Mr. Bright to see skaters on private waters. The author described the comfortable living conditions of Englishmen, including well-kept grounds and secure access. The skaters at Otterpool were treated well with hot luncheons, and their skating skills were noted to be superior to those of New England skaters. A beggar-woman was seen at Otterpool, but no one gave her assistance. On February 21st, two groups of unemployed work-people visited the author's house in Rock Park seeking charity. The author reflected on the connection between their feelings as an American and the public sentiment in their home country.

The site visited was an ancient Columbarium located near the Appian Way. The Columbarium featured a large, square chamber sunk beneath the ground with a narrow, steep staircase leading down to it. The walls of the chamber contained nine rows of semicircular niches, with nine niches in each row, resembling entrances to a pigeon-house. Each niche contained two round holes covered with earthen plates, which held ashes and fragments of bones of the deceased. The names of the deceased were inscribed in Roman capitals on marble slabs above each niche. Another similar chamber containing the ashes of Pompey's household was discovered a few years ago. The Columbarium was estimated to hold the remains of at least seven or eight hundred persons.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The Corso is described as a stately and palatial street. The author visited St. Peter's twice and felt a sense of breadth and loftiness. The Museum of the Capitol was visited, and the statues were perceived as more beautiful than before. The Corsini Palace is located in Trastevere and features a grand staircase and picture-rooms. A portrait by Vandyke and a portrait of Pope Julius II. by Raphael were notable artworks observed in the Corsini Palace. The palace contains old furniture and a marble curule chair, believed to be Etruscan. The author's accommodations in Rome consist of seven rooms, including an antechamber, with a view of a quiet piazza.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The old mansion of the Argyle family has towers at the corners and is now occupied as a military hospital. The castle parade includes an outer rampart of Queen Anne and an old round gate-tower. The old palace and the old Parliament House are located in the inner region of the castle. The great hall of the palace is now partitioned into multiple rooms and serves as barracks. The tower where King James stabbed the Earl of Douglas has been renewed, leaving only the mullions of the historic window. The Carse of Stirling is surrounded by the Highlands and is noted for its fertile and beautiful landscape. The battle of Bannockburn and Wallace's victory were fought on the Carse of Stirling.

The text describes a meditative and philosophic man who feels that being at the summit of human greatness is not worthwhile. It discusses the decline of artistic skill during the dynasty of the Caesars, culminating in poor representations of prominent figures. The 'Dying Gladiator' is highlighted as a significant statue that evokes deep emotion and requires the spectator's engagement. The narrator expresses a preference for the 'Dying Gladiator' over other famous works, including a statue of Antinous. The museum is described as being very cold, which the narrator attributes to the presence of numerous marble statues. The narrator and companions seek the prison of the apostles Peter and Paul, indicated by an inscription near the Forum. They descend into a dark chamber where they hear voices and see light through an iron-grated hole, indicating the presence of visitors being shown St. Peter's dungeon.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The church entrance was undergoing improvement when the Reformation occurred and has remained unfinished. The body of the church is of much earlier date, with the oaken roof believed to have been renewed in Henry VIII's time. The nave of the church has a one-sided aspect with a single aisle and sturdy pillars. The pavement is covered with old oak pews, and there are modern stained glass windows on the opposite side of the aisle. A small square chapel, once separated from the chancel, had its pavement taken up for burial purposes, revealing upright corpses. The Clapham family and the Morley family were buried upright in the chapel. The narrator traveled from Skipton to Leeds, passing the ruined Abbey of Kirkstall, and later stayed at the Black Swan in York.

Skiddaw is located at the head of a long ridge of mountains with several peaks. The eastern side of Skiddaw features many noble eminences. The western side has a lovely wood and a range of lofty cliffs that descend steeply. The cliffs have a declivity at their base that is sometimes covered with trees or shrubs. The area has a variety of mountain shapes and an abundance of water prospects. There is a country inn at Lodore that has been enlarged to accommodate guests. The cascade near the inn is audible from a distance of four miles.

The traveler describes various souvenirs available in Geneva, including wood and ivory carvings, jewelry, and watches. Watches in Geneva are priced significantly lower than in England. Cigars are a principal article of commerce in Geneva, with numerous cigar shops and no duties on imported goods. The traveler left Geneva by steamer on June 12th, starting from a quay near their hotel. The scenery of Lake Geneva improved during the voyage, particularly along the southern shore. Coppet is a picturesque village mentioned by the traveler, associated with Madame de Stael. The traveler notes the presence of historic buildings and natural beauty along the lake, including old churches and castles.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The text describes a Carnival event in which Americans and English were advised not to throw confetti at non-combatants. Participants in the Carnival engaged in throwing confetti and bouquets, often from open carriages manned by youths. The narrator mentions an encounter with Mrs. T------, who threw lime at them during the event. The narrator's companion, J-----, wore a black mask that attracted more confetti than they might have otherwise received. The day of the events was referred to as masking-day, although most attendees did not wear masks. The narrator and their wife visited the church of Santa Maria Maggiore and the Piazza di Monte Cavallo to see ancient statues. They also visited the Barberini Palace, where William Story was residing, and made calls in the neighborhood of the Piazza de' Spagna.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: Vale of Terni features fertile land with vines, olive groves, and fields of grain. The area is characterized by numerous shrines located in various settings. The landscape includes steep hills that create a winding passage for travelers. Ruined castles and convents are visible on hillsides, indicating historical significance. Some villages in the region appear wretched and lack signs of prosperity. At Strettura, two oxen were added to the horses for the ascent of Monte Somma. The landscape includes a mix of agricultural fields and dense shrubbery, with houses generally appearing dismal.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The palace features several quadrangles paved with stone and surrounded by brick walls. Soldiers stand sentinel at the exterior gateways and various doors of the palace, allowing entry without question or fee. Wolsey's great Hall is over a hundred feet long and sixty feet high and broad, with walls and ceiling covered by a fresco by Verrio. The great Hall contains stained or painted glass windows and antique tapestry depicting Scripture subjects, interwoven with threads of gold. The roof of the great Hall is intricately carved oak and appears to be in perfect condition. The withdrawing-room next to the great Hall is more than seventy feet long and twenty-five feet high, featuring ancient tapestry and a stained-glass window. The suite of apartments extends for half a mile or more, containing rooms of state, royal bedchambers, and numerous artworks.

The narrator arrived at Hotel Wheeler in Havre from Paris on June 22nd. The hotel is located near the Petit Quay Notre Dame with views of steamers and dock activities. The hotel decor includes lithographs and colored views of New York, reflecting American preferences. The food at the hotel is described as abundant compared to French and Italian meals. The narrator plans to depart for Southampton by steamer and then travel to London, Liverpool, Boston, and Concord. The narrator spent more than four months writing 'The Marble Faun' while in England. On November 14th, 1859, the narrator noted renovations at Lillington's church and modernizations in Warwick.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The narrator left Shrewsbury at half past ten and arrived in London at about four in the afternoon. The narrator's lodgings are located at No. 21 George Street, Hanover Square. St. George's Church is situated a short distance below the narrator's lodgings. The narrator visited various landmarks in London, including Hyde Park, Regent's Park, and St. Paul's Cathedral. The narrator describes St. Paul's Cathedral as grand and noble, contrasting its serene presence with the surrounding bustle. The streets in the old city of London are described as sufficiently broad and not as narrow and irregular as expected. The narrator notes that the buildings in London are generally of a dark hue and have become blackened by smoke over time.

The crypts of the cathedral were built to maintain a level floor due to the site's declivity. Glasgow is described as a stately city with magnificent public buildings and shops, particularly in Buchanan Street. The predominant building material in Glasgow is dark gray granite, contributing to a stern and grim atmosphere. Argyle Street, Trongate, and Salt-Market were once the principal business streets of Glasgow. High Street and Salt-Market are now crowded with lower orders, creating an unpleasant atmosphere. The University features a broad stone staircase leading to a large hall adorned with dark oak paneling and carved cornices. The Principal of the University, aged eighty-six, welcomed visitors to inspect the College.

The pope prayed at the chapel of the Holy Sacrament. A detachment of the Swiss Guard was on duty before the chapel. The pope was scheduled to appear at twelve but arrived nearly half an hour late. A procession of cardinals and attendants preceded the pope's entrance. The pope knelt at the prie-dieu and spent three or four minutes in prayer. After praying, the pope kissed St. Peter's toe and directed his devotions towards the high altar. The pope left the church through a side door, making a short passage into the Vatican.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The narrator left Viterbo on October 15th and traveled through Monterosi to Sette Verse. At Sette Verse, the only notable feature was an old Roman bridge with a single arch that has existed for two or more thousand years. The narrator drove along the Cassian Way towards Rome the following day, describing the atmosphere as delightful. The narrator expressed a sense of comfort and pleasure approaching Rome, contrasting it with a previous cold and weary arrival. The narrator encountered the custom-house at the Porta del Popolo, where a scudo helped facilitate their passage. Upon arriving at 68 Piazza Poli, the narrator found their new home to be comfortable and cozy. The narrator praised their vetturino, Constantino Bacci, for his excellent service and kindness during their travels.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The group left their shawls and carpet-bags in the salle a manger of the Hotel Faucon. The cathedral in Lausanne has a prominent pinnacled tower that is visible from a distance. Lausanne is built on a hill with steep streets and long stairs, making navigation difficult. The cathedral stands on a higher site than any other building in Lausanne. The interior of the cathedral is well-maintained but lacks the majesty and mystery typical of old churches. The church contains a French version of the Bible printed at Lille about fifty years ago. There are arrangements for collecting contributions in the church, including a strong box and boxes on poles.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: Mr. ------ had a claim to five francs. The author visited Notre Dame and observed its rich front and sculptures. Notre Dame is located near the Seine River on an island formed by two branches of the river. The area around Notre Dame appears old and is inhabited by poor people. The author noted the excessive mud on the pavements of Paris. The author walked through the gardens of the Tuileries, which have wide walks, fountains, and statues. The author stayed at the Hotel d'Angleterre in Marseilles after departing from the Hotel de Louvre.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The narrator had a sense of an impending presidential nomination before it occurred. The narrator observed a shop selling cotton or linen cloth near a tower in the Via Portoghese. A fritter establishment was opened in a piazza, featuring a wooden booth covered with red canvas. The fritter shop operated with a stove, frying pan, dry sticks, flour, and oil, and was busy during its operation. The fritters produced were described as resembling a bad doughnut and were sour due to the fermentation process preferred by Romans. The fritter shop was dismantled after three days of operation, leaving only charcoal on the pavement. A statue of Venus was discovered outside the Porta Portese, found in an excavation resembling an ancient bathroom.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The narrator and J----- walked across a foot-bridge spanning the Tweed River. The narrator expressed skepticism about William of Deloraine's difficulty in swimming a horse across the river. The narrator and J----- visited Abbotsford, located about three miles from Melrose. The landscape between Melrose and Abbotsford is described as not beautiful or noteworthy. The entrance to Abbotsford has been altered since the narrator's last visit. The narrator observed various historical items during the visit, including Sir Walter's study and an armory. The narrator and J----- decided not to visit Dryburgh Abbey due to threatening rain.

Bath is a city located in a valley surrounded by hills. The older part of Bath is on a level area, while modern developments extend up the hillside. The houses in Bath are primarily constructed from Bath stone, which darkens over time. Bath's architecture features elements reminiscent of Parisian design, with decorative roofs and pillars. The streets in Bath are clean and paved with large stone blocks, providing comfortable walking conditions. Bath has a population of approximately eighty thousand people and offers various social advantages. The abbey is the only notable antiquity in Bath, and Beau Nash's former residence is now part of an ale-merchant establishment.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The church has a pew across the aisle from the pulpit that is optimal for seeing and hearing the clergyman. Lady Fleming's pew is located beneath the pulpit and is one of the curtained pews in the church. The chancel walls feature monuments to the Flemings and painted escutcheons of their arms. There is a poor-box made of oak with the date 1648 and the name of the church, St. Oswald's, on it. The interior of the church is described as plain and simple, with a buff color applied to it by church authorities. The Rothay river is noted to be clear and approximately twenty yards wide at the bridge. The Swan Inn, where Scott used to visit, is a small whitewashed house with a painted sign of a swan.

The narrator describes the walls of an abbey as gray and rough, having endured for a thousand years. The narrator and their companions crossed the river Tweed via a foot-bridge. They returned to their inn for tea and spent a quiet evening by the fireside. Breakfast included broiled salmon, likely sourced from the Tweed. A coarse-looking man at the inn claimed to own the best horse around the Eildon Hills and boasted about his fishing skills. The narrator observed that drunkenness among the Scots occurs at early hours, noting a difference from their experiences in England. The group traveled to Dryburgh Abbey by a drosky, encountering a young girl who served as the ferryman.

The text discusses a statue made of Daniel Webster. The author suggests that future generations may find Webster's costume absurd. Webster had other costumes that he wore in private, which the author believes represent his real life. The author expresses uncertainty about their perception of the real Webster based on his public attire. Powers comments on the distinction between a taste for art and moral character. The author visited the Uffizi gallery and observed various artworks and a collection of goldsmiths' work. The author and their wife visited the Academy of Fine Arts and the Duomo, noting its cool atmosphere and stained glass windows.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: Mr. Powers objected to Mr. Gibson's practice of coloring his statues. Mr. Powers stated that he had made wax figures in his earlier days but no longer does so. A letter by Mr. Powers on the subject of color in sculpture was published in the London 'Athenaeum' and offended some of Mr. Gibson's friends. Mr. Powers believes that everything in intellect or feeling can be expressed in colorless marble as well as by a painter. Mr. Powers claimed he could model a blush in marble if an artist could express it in a picture. Mr. Powers brought a bunch of roses and appreciated their delicate blush. The Uffizi gallery is located in the upper story of the palace and features busts of the Medici family.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The sculptor's work was crafted with skill and care, intended for a tomb rather than a public display. The tombs were richly adorned and furnished with exquisite art, yet were placed in darkness. The walls of another tomb were decorated with medallions in stucco, created quickly while the plaster was wet. The artist demonstrated rapidity and accuracy in creating designs that would have suited a festive hall. A thigh-bone was handled and measured in the tomb, among many relics of the deceased. Modern Romans have practices of disposing of the dead that involve stripping bodies and placing them in trenches. Italians have a strong fear of corpses and a particular dread of sudden death, especially apoplexy.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: Mr. ------ is described as a large man of the world, dignified and experienced in handling difficult circumstances. Despite his public life and significant positions, Mr. ------ is perceived to lack innate force to prevent insults. Mr. ------ is characterized as having shrewdness and tact, allowing him to take advantage of circumstances. He is accompanied by his son, who serves as Secretary of Legation, described as a small young man with a little mustache. The narrator traveled from Liverpool to London, arriving after ten o'clock and staying at a lodging-house secured by Mr. B------. The journey to London was described as dull and monotonous, with few passengers in the carriage. The narrator found Mr. ------ to be an agreeable companion with a self-respecting character.

Nathaniel Hawthorne traveled from England to France on January 6th, 1858. Hawthorne and his companions packed their luggage and left for London Bridge station at seven in the morning. They took a train to Folkestone and then boarded a steamer to cross the English Channel. The weather was cold and inclement during their journey. Upon arrival in Boulogne, they underwent a brief examination by customs officers. The majority of their luggage was registered through to Paris for later examination.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: On August 31st, the narrator traveled by rail from London to Oxford. The narrator and their companions were expected guests of Mr. Spiers, the Ex-Mayor of Oxford. Mr. S. C. Hall met the group at the Oxford station and guided them to their lodgings on St. Giles Street. Durham, the sculptor, was part of the group visiting Oxford. The narrator found Oxford to be picturesque and rich in beauty, contrasting with their previous impressions. Mr. Hall pointed out notable sites in Oxford, including Maudlin College and the Crown Inn, associated with Shakespeare. The Ex-Mayor hosted a dinner for the group, showcasing his collection of art and gifts received during his mayoralty.

The narrator attended a dinner where Mrs. M------ discussed Tennyson's poetry. Tennyson considers 'Maud' his best poem and lives in the Isle of Wight. Mr. Tom Taylor entertained the ladies during dinner. The narrator took leave after making apologies to Mrs. Heywood and traveled to London Bridge station. At the station, the narrator met Mr. Bennoch, who had dined with the Lord Mayor. Mr. Jerdan visited the narrator and discussed a potential degree or diploma for the narrator. The narrator expressed a desire to meet Dickens before leaving England.

The colony of rooks was driven away and settled in a grove behind a house. No rooks have built in the ancient grove since the colony was removed. William Fitch Arnold, born in 1794, possesses the estate of Little Messenden Abbey in Bucks County and is a magistrate. William Fitch Arnold was formerly Captain of the 19th Lancers and has two sons and four daughters. Eastham is a village located five or six miles from Rock Ferry and features many antique houses. The village of Eastham has a church made of red freestone that appears old and beautiful. The village inn in Eastham has a neat parlor with a cheerful fire and portraits on the walls.

The pictures are contained in three contiguous rooms of the lower piano. One notable picture is 'Christ disputing with the Doctors' by Albert Duerer. The collection includes Raphael's Fornarina and Guido's portrait of Beatrice Cenci. The Rospigliosi Palace is located in the Piazza di Monte Cavallo. The garden at the Rospigliosi Palace features a fish-pond and eight marble statues. The Casino at the end of the garden is richly ornamented with bas-reliefs and statues. Guido's Aurora is located in a large room on the ground-floor of the Casino.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: Cavalier and his wife are depicted in excellent preservation, with prominent noses and no signs of wear. The Cavalier died in 1637, and his statue was likely sculptured after the Restoration. Cromwell is said to have stabled his horses and damaged monuments in churches across England. The Lady's Chapel is ninety feet long and serves as a church with various monuments and inscriptions. The crypts below the church are believed to be older than the upper building and contain many buried individuals. The cloisters are in a perfect state and form an unbroken square around a green grass-plot. The cathedral was constructed over three hundred years, beginning in 1188 and finishing in 1498.

The Arno river is between one hundred and one hundred fifty yards wide between the Ponte alle Grazie and the Ponte Vecchio. The right bank of the Arno has a broad margin of mud and gravel where water-weeds grow. The color of the Arno river is described as yellow, similar to the Tiber, but not perceived as polluted by city sewerage. There is a gravel island in the Arno river from the Ponte alle Grazie downward, allowing men and horses to wade through shallow areas. The buildings along the river's edge include a broad paved way with a parapet on the right shore and structures supported by arches on the opposite shore. The Ponte Vecchio features a continuous street of ancient houses and is home to a community of goldsmiths selling various jewelry and ornaments. The area around Bellosguardo consists of narrow zigzag lanes with scattered villas and houses, leading to a view of Florence.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The narrator expresses doubt about a site they were supposed to visit. The narrator regrets not seeing the grotto due to a companion's enthusiasm. The visits to sepulchral places concluded with Scipio's tomb. On March 10th, the narrator visited the Sciarra Palace on a rainy day. The Sciarra Palace is located on the Corso, opposite the Piazza Colonna. The narrator recalls several famous paintings seen at the Sciarra Palace, including works by Raphael, Leonardo da Vinci, and Titian. The narrator visited the sculpture-gallery of the Vatican for three hours.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The text describes little brooks flowing across a road in Yorkshire. The Devonshire House is an ancient inn associated with the Duke of Devonshire. The narrator visits the ruins of a Priory located in a valley near the river Wharfe. The nave of the old church at the Priory is still in good repair and serves as a worshipping place for the neighborhood. The remains of the Priory include a roofless choir with broken arches, which is less impressive than other abbeys. The grounds around the church and ruins are used for burial, featuring modern tombstones with crosiers. There is a large, old stone farm-house near the ruins, believed to be built on the site of part of the Priory.

The author visited the gallery of the Pitti Palace. The gallery contains many works by Andrea del Sarto. The author observed a respectable-looking man in new pantaloons at the gallery. The author found amber cups in a cabinet of curiosities to be particularly pleasing. The author wandered through the Boboli Gardens after leaving the palace. The author has heard about spirit matters related to Mr. Home's visit to Florence. Mrs. Powers reported a seance where spirits of twenty-seven monks were said to have disturbed the gathering.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The landscape includes both rural and city life set against a backdrop of mountains. The city features ancient houses built with large stones and solid arches. The streets are narrow and made of stone or ancient brick, making it difficult for carriages to navigate. Assisi was historically significant as a center for art, supported primarily by ecclesiastics. The Church of St. Mary of the Angels is a modern structure built on the site of a church destroyed by an earthquake. The chapel within the church is where St. Francis founded his order and is one of the few parts not destroyed by the earthquake. The ascent to Perugia requires assistance from oxen due to the steepness of the hill.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: Mr. ------ expressed concern that S------'s shock had affected his intellect. Mr. ------ believed S------ should retire from public life but felt no one would tell him. S------ was described as a capable individual who should have lived in good fellowship. S------ was not emotionally engaged in discussions and displayed a calm demeanor. Miss Bremer lived in a small and humble chamber in Rome, which was modestly furnished. Miss Bremer welcomed guests with cordiality and simplicity, without acknowledging her living conditions. Miss Bremer spoke English with a unique accent, making her difficult to understand, yet her listeners felt she conveyed good sense.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: An American lady has been in the Liverpool almshouse for three years and is in a state of insanity. The lady calls herself Jenny Lind and has not revealed her true identity or connections. Mr. ------ was unable to pay his bill at an inn, leading the landlord to take possession of his luggage. The Governor of the Lunatic Asylum stated that Mr. ------ is in need of a change of clothes. The American Hotel is described as a small, respectable, and clean establishment. The landlady of the American Hotel confirmed that Mr. ------ had left without paying his bill. Mrs. Blodgett knows Mr. ------ and his mother, who has recently remarried and is currently in Italy.

Mr. Thompson is an artist whose pictures are noted for their beauty that comes from deep within. Mr. Thompson's studio is located in the Via Sistina. William Story is working on a sitting statue of Cleopatra in his studio, which is located on the same street as Mr. Thompson's. William Story has a variety of talents, including being a poet, prose writer, lawyer, painter, musician, and sculptor. William Story has completed a statue of Goethe's Margaret, which depicts her pulling a flower apart to determine if Faust loves her. The basilica of St. John Lateran is the second-ranking basilica after St. Peter's and has certain sacred privileges. The facade of St. John Lateran is described as lofty and grand, possibly more so than that of St. Peter's.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The group initially disappeared while picking and eating blackberries in a moat. The castle walls were covered with ivy. The village was described as old and ugly with small, irregular streets and mean houses. The parliament house in the village was where Edward I. granted rights to his Welsh subjects. The travelers became lost on Rhyddlan moor due to ditches and streams. They took shelter under a cart-shed at a large farmhouse that was dirty and ill-kept. They encountered a civil man who guided them along paths to Rhyl.

The figure described represents a man who suggested to Pope Paul III. that the nudities of the 'Last Judgment' ought to be draped. Michael Angelo consigned this man to hell for his suggestion. The picture's effect is diminished by the high altar and its canopy, which obstructs part of the artwork. The author visited the Via Portoghese with Mr. Thompson and saw an old palace with a tall, battlemented tower. The palace was once inhabited by a nobleman whose son was rescued from a monkey that took him to the tower. The nobleman vowed to build a shrine at the tower's summit if his son was safely returned, which he did. The Spada Palace is described as a dark and massive old edifice with a great gloomy hall and a statue of Pompey.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The castle features several round towers built of gray stone, which are crumbling and covered in ivy. The castle was the first built by Edward I. in Wales, where he resided during the construction of Conway Castle. Queen Eleanor gave birth to a princess at this castle. A meeting of Welsh bards was held at the castle a few years ago. The castle is located near an arched stone bridge over the river Clwyd. Rhyddlan marsh, located across the river, was the site of a battle between the Welsh and Saxons a thousand years ago. Conway Castle is described as a perfect specimen of a ruinous old castle, with the town built in what was once the castle-yard.

The text describes a collection of humming-birds, strange fishes, and a large pike from the river Avon. A young lady prepared a bunch of skeleton leaves and flowers that resembled fine lace-work. The collection included minerals, shells, and fossils, including remains of antediluvian creatures. Historical curiosities featured two locks of hair from Edward IV, authenticated by a manuscript letter from 1739. The collection also included a seal of the Earl of Warwick and a sword from Bosworth Field. The narrator traveled from Leamington to London, leaving most of their luggage behind due to a van breakdown. The narrator expressed feelings of restlessness and discomfort while walking in London, describing the city as dull and unpicturesque.

The narrator left the Castle Hotel after paying a bill of twenty pounds for a little more than a week's board. The Castle Hotel was once an old Roman castle, although it has been modernized and painted white. There is a dungeon beneath the Castle Hotel where the landlord keeps his wine. The narrator and J----- walked towards Shinley along the water-side, leaving the rest of the family to follow in a fly. The shore near Southampton has traces of ancient fortifications, possibly dating back to Roman times. On June 28th, the narrator left Liverpool from the Lime Street station on a hot day. The narrator arrived in Gloucester and stayed at the Wellington Hotel, which is near the station.

The Scottish border is located eight or nine miles from Carlisle Castle. Carlisle Castle has experienced many sieges and battles. The castle currently has about six old-fashioned guns on its ramparts. The garrison at Carlisle Castle consists of approximately twenty men, all of whom served in the Crimea. The castle's ramparts include a place where soldiers used to drop down at night, which is now boarded up. The cathedral near the castle has ancient foundations and features a recently constructed east window. The exterior of the cathedral has been largely renewed with red freestone in recent years.

The square is surrounded by old buildings that have been modernized while retaining their historical character. The Church of the Holy Cross is made of red freestone and is part of the Abbey of St. Peter and St. John. The Abbey of St. Peter and St. John originally covered ten acres of ground. A stone pulpit from the abbey is now located in a garden and is overgrown with ivy. The battlefield of Hotspur and Falstaff is located four miles from Shrewsbury. The Butter Cross is a public building that serves as a market for butter, eggs, and poultry. The Raven Inn is where Farquhar wrote his comedy 'The Recruiting Officer' in 1701.

A plumed hearse transported the coffin to the Necropolis. The coffin was placed in a chapel where another coffin and mourners were present. A clergyman conducted the service in a black-silk gown. One of the bearers stumbled while carrying the coffin, but they managed to prevent it from falling. Captain Auld's grave was dug nine feet deep and is reserved for twelve months. The undertaker and grave-digger expressed pride in the grave's depth and site. A dispute arose between the clergyman and the undertaker regarding burial fees after the service.

The hall features a richly painted roof with historic subjects and extensive ornamentation. The Peers' seats consist of four rows of long sofas covered with red morocco. The woolsack is a large square seat covered with scarlet, positioned between the rows of sofas. The throne is located near the entrance of the hall and is richly carved and gilded. The House of Commons is larger than the House of Lords but less richly ornamented. The speaker's chair in the House of Commons is loftier and statelier than the throne in the House of Lords. The hall and chambers are described as having limited physical space for the significant roles of the Lords and Commons.

The house has complicated fastenings on the door and separate barricades on the iron-barred windows. There are bolts and shutters for every window in the house. The Count Montanto lets his country seat and resides in the city during the hot months. The Count obtained three dollars more than the initial offer for the rental of his property. Signor del Bello haggled for compensation for cracked crockery and received fifty cents. William Story is spending the summer with his family in Siena and has sketched another subject for sculpture. Italians universally believe in the influence of the evil eye, which is often associated with monks.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The town of Acquapendente is situated on a height that descends to the valley below. French soldiers were stationed at the gate of Acquapendente and checked passports. Acquapendente features a narrow street with tall, aged stone houses. San Lorenzo Nuovo was built by Pius VI as a refuge for people displaced by malaria. San Lorenzo Nuovo has classic architecture, a spacious piazza, and straight rectangular streets. The lake of Bolsena is located beneath a hill, surrounded by depopulated shores. The old town of San Lorenzo is situated on a precipitous bluff and has Etruscan tombs.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: Byron planted an oak tree that is now a vigorous young tree. Byron erected a monument to his Newfoundland dog, which is larger than most Christian tombs. The monument is composed of a marble, altar-shaped tomb surrounded by a circular area of steps, twenty feet in diameter. The gardener stated that Byron intended the monument as a burial place for himself and his sister as well. The Abbey church, which was once present, measured sixty-four yards in length and has now been removed except for one ivy-grown western wall. The landlady mentioned that the current descendants of Byron and Lovelace have a reputation for being wicked, mad, and miserable. The narrator and companions left Nottingham and traveled to Derby, where they waited at a crowded railway station during the Whitsuntide holidays.

Mr. W. J------ is an Irish-American merchant in good standing. Mr. W. J------ was acquainted with General Jackson and witnessed a street fight involving him and Colonel Benton. Colonel Benton shot at General Jackson from behind, but it was Jesse Benton's bullet that broke Jackson's arm. The Mayor's dinners are considered agreeable, although the author finds speaking to a toast somewhat annoying. The Mayors are expected to spend more than their salary of 2,000 pounds on these dinners. The dinner attended by the author had about fifty guests, including two bishops and two officers in blue uniforms. The author observed a large crowd waiting for soup-tickets after the dinner.

The remains of the ancient Capitol form the foundation of the present edifice. The architecture surrounding the piazza with the equestrian statue of Marcus Aurelius is described as ineffective. The dome of St. Peter's is set with mosaic-work, with pieces approximately half an inch square. The roof of St. Peter's offers a view of Rome and the Mediterranean Sea in the distance. There is a small house on the roof of St. Peter's where the custodes likely reside. The ascent to the dome includes steep and narrow staircases and a perpendicular iron ladder to reach the copper ball.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The journey to London was without any remarkable incident. At Waterloo station, the group found one of Mr. Bennoch's clerks who guided them to take two cabs to East Kent station at London Bridge. The group traveled to Blackheath and arrived in the afternoon. On Thursday, the narrator visited the Royal Academy Exhibition, Westminster Abbey, and St. Paul's. On Friday, the narrator walked over the heath and through the Park to Greenwich, spending hours in the Hospital. The narrator attended a conversazione at Mrs. Newton Crosland's, where they met Mr. Bailey, the author of Festus. The narrator visited the wine vaults of the London Docks, which were extensive and filled with port-wine and sherry-wine.

York is an exceedingly old city, founded about a thousand years before the Christian era. The Emperor Severus died in York, and Constantine the Great was born there. York is partly surrounded by a wall and has several gates that the city authorities maintain. A local resident provided directions to the railway station by walking along the city walls. The fee for crossing the Ouse by ferry is a halfpenny. The narrator traveled westward across England to Liverpool after parting with Mr. Bowman. York contains many old churches with weather-worn stones and stained glass windows.

Nearly three hundred artifacts were removed to Paris by Napoleon, and except for the Antinous, none returned. There is a painting by Perugino in one of the rooms, featuring a devout St. Michael. A small bronze Apollo, believed by Winckelmann to be an original of Praxiteles, is located in one of the rooms. The coffee-house is situated a hundred yards from the casino and features an ornamental garden. The Villa Albani is a separate building from both the coffee-house and casino and is not open to strangers. The Count of Castelbarco, the current proprietor of the Villa Albani, resides in Milan. The grounds of the Villa Albani include straight paths, alleys, shrubberies, and a variety of flowers and trees.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: Monte Testaccio is a natural hill near Rome, with a height of two or three hundred feet. The base of Monte Testaccio is surrounded by small farm buildings. A large iron cross is located at the summit of Monte Testaccio. Monte Testaccio is composed entirely of broken crockery, including urns and teacups. The Protestant burial-ground is located near the pyramid of Caius Cestius. The pyramid of Caius Cestius is partially built into the city wall constructed by Emperor Aurelian. The pyramid is in perfect condition and has remained largely unchanged for twenty centuries.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The Southport inspector wears a green and silver uniform and greets local residents with an air of equality. The superintendent of the district, who may have been an army officer, was present during the examination of the thieves. The thieves, James and John Macdonald, were brought from Liverpool and are described as shabby and dirty but intelligent. Witnesses identified the thieves through various testimonies, including a railway boy and a pawnbroker. The case against the prisoners included evidence of stolen property found in their possession. The prisoners were committed for trial at the Liverpool assizes scheduled for the current month. The narrator and his wife left Southport for a tour to York, arriving in Skipton after a journey of about sixty miles.

The services of Easter Sunday included singing, chanting, prayers, and reading of Scriptures for nearly an hour and a half. A canon delivered a sermon lasting about twenty minutes during the Easter service. The author expressed a preference for longer sermons without elaborate ceremonies, reflecting Puritan values. The author encountered a young gentleman, presumed to be American, during a wait in the nave after the service. The author and his wife took a promenade along the wall and explored the crooked streets of York. The author observed a procession of about fifty charity-school boys in flat caps and green collars. The ruins of St. Mary's Abbey were noted as extensive and located in the midst of the city.

The scene included a bottle of English ale poured into a glass, resembling English bitter ale. The narrator and companions crossed the Ponte di Santa Trinita over the Arno River. The river was calm, reflecting the palaces and bridges along its shores. The Italian sky was described as bluer and brighter than the American sky. Mr. Powers visited and discussed Italian food, including poultry, mutton, beef, and a dish made from acacia blossoms. Powers expressed a critical view of classic busts, except for the bust of Caracalla. Mr. Harte was mentioned as the best contemporary sculptor for making busts.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The English people experienced a sudden change in their perception of religious externals without losing their religion. The French Revolution led to a loss of both religious substance and externals. The interior arrangement of the choir and chancel has been modernized and differs from other examples seen. The nave has no stained glass, while the chancel contains some recent stained glass and fragments of antique glass. Mary, Queen of Scots, was originally buried beneath a plain marble slab in the southern aisle for a quarter of a century. A Saxon monument dating to 870 commemorates Abbot Hedda, who was killed by the Danes. The ancient font in the nave has been repaired recently but retains its individuality despite past damage.

The narrator requested a photograph of their party during a visit to Oxford. The group included Mr. and Mrs. Spiers, their eldest son, Mr. and Mrs. Hall, Fanny, Mr. Addison, the narrator's wife, and the narrator. Not all individuals participated in the photograph, as S----- turned away and Mrs. Hall refused to be included. Mr. Spiers was noted for his hospitality during lunch. The narrator planned to send Mr. Spiers a set of their Tales and Romances as a gesture of gratitude. The narrator visited Hampton Court after returning to Blackheath and was impressed by Wolsey's great Hall. The grounds of Hampton Court appeared beautiful but were viewed only briefly from the palace windows.

The route included plains and lower hillsides that were fertile, particularly for olives and vines. Numerous shrines and crosses were observed along the way, with many crosses adorned with wooden symbols of the crucifixion. Mists indicated rain in certain areas, and light rain began to fall while sunshine was visible in parts of the valley. A rainbow appeared and remained visible for an extended period. The travelers reached Assisi, which is situated on a mountain and features a gray castle and wall. In the Piazza Grande, the travelers saw a temple of Minerva, which has been converted into a Catholic church. The travelers experienced strong winds while exploring the city, which amused the local people.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The church is built with black and white marble that has turned brown and yellow over five centuries. A long colonnade of arches extends alongside the facade of the church, with a tomb beneath each arch. The Chiostro Verde is an enclosed green space within a four-sided colonnade, adorned with frescos. The cloister of Santa Maria is open to the public square and is frequented by local residents. The chapter-house features a groined roof with two great pointed arches and is covered with frescos. The chapter-house is currently used for public worship and contains confessionals and chapels. A priest performed mass in the chapter-house while visitors engaged in personal devotion.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The road from Ambleside ascends steeply, leading to a pass with bare hills and little vegetation. The pass is described as having a gorge of steep hills, with gray stones covering many areas. An old stone building at the highest point of the pass is identified as the highest inhabitable house in England. The Kirkstone, which gives the pass its name, is initially not easily recognizable until descending towards Brothers' Water. A view of Brothers' Water is visible while descending Kirkstone Pass. At Patterdale, at the foot of Ullswater, the travelers took luncheon at a hotel characterized as very good. The hotel staff included a black-coated waiter and a mistress in lady-like attire, with a custom of tipping all service staff.

The travelers felt a stronger emotional connection to Rome than to London. The countryside along the journey was undulating but lacked significant elevation and trees. The travelers stopped at Castel Nuovo di Porta for a meal, which included beefsteak, an omelette, and red wine. The locanda where they dined featured an old Roman altar and a shrine. The afternoon drive included views of Soracte, a prominent rock formation. The road followed the ancient Flaminian Way, which was well-paved with large flag-stones. The travelers passed through a town called Rignano during their journey.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: An old triptych painted on wood is hanging in a chapel beside the high altar. The church has two doors with round arches and deep carvings, one featuring pillars formed of a peculiar knot in stone-work. The pillars of one door rest on two nondescript animals resembling walruses, while the other door's pillars consist of figures standing on carved lions. The town has a tall, square tower said to be of Roman origin. The immediate neighborhood of the town is fertile, with an olive-orchard and olive-trees along the city wall. A stately old palace of the Piccolomini is located close to the church, built in the style of Roman palaces. A team of poor vettura-horses stopped at the door of the albergo, and an ancient gentleman and lady, identified as the Prefect of Florence and his wife, alighted from the carriage.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The text describes a misty and dreamlike quality of certain artworks that are difficult to comprehend. The author expresses an intention to buy Ruskin's pamphlet to better understand the artworks. Marlborough House is described as a potential residence for the young Prince of Wales, featuring a large central hall and fine architectural details. The mantel-pieces in Marlborough House are adorned with classical designs and sculptures in high relief. The author visited the National Gallery and viewed works by Turner and Claude, expressing a preference for Claude's paintings. The author experiences a sense of weariness from frequently seeing certain paintings, preferring the works of Murillo. The text describes the author's journey through a dense fog towards St. Paul's Cathedral, which becomes obscured by smoke.

The narrator experiences poor appetite and insomnia, often thinking sad thoughts. The narrator feels a sense of dread when going to the office, anticipating bad news from Lisbon. The narrator attended a dinner at Mr. B------'s featuring various American dishes. The dinner included New York oysters, American partridges, terrapin soup, and a thirty-one-pound turkey. The narrator read St. Luke's account of Christ's agony, trial, crucifixion, and resurrection. Mr. H------, a shipwright from Boston, visited the narrator and has traveled in the East. Mr. H------ has brought back curiosities, including a gold coin of Vespasian and a piece of a mummy.

Mr. ------ is a small, slender young man with black, curly hair and a thin, dark visage. Mr. ------ engaged to identify the narrator at the Bank of England. The bank clerk informed them that the bank post-bill was not yet due. Mr. ------ offered to cash the bank post-bill for the narrator. Mr. ------ resides in Greenwich and invited the narrator to visit him. The narrator attended an afternoon service at St. Paul's Cathedral. St. Paul's Cathedral is characterized by its light, white walls, and marble pavement.

At the corner of a grass-plot around Queen Eleanor's tower, there is a trunk of a tree of ivy with a strong stem and vigorous branches. The narrator and O'Sullivan climbed to the top of one of the towers of the castle and observed a photographist preparing to take a view of the castle. The narrator noted the presence of streets, kitchen-gardens, and dwellings within the precincts of the castle, indicating a blend of modern life with historical architecture. The narrator and O'Sullivan took a train back to Rhyl, arriving around four o'clock, and later traveled to Chester and Rock Park, reaching home at about eleven o'clock. On September 13th, the narrator began wearing a watch from Bennet's, 65 Cheapside, London, which is warranted as the best watch they can produce. The narrator returned to Rhyl by steamer on September 20th, arriving at nearly four o'clock and walking to their lodgings at 18 West Parade. The narrator made an excursion to Ruthin, passing through ancient places such as Rhyddlan, St. Asaph, and Denbigh, and noted the steep streets and architectural features of these towns.

The Colonel and Major are both over sixty years old and have spent thirty and twenty-seven years in India, respectively. The Major is the younger of the two and has a perfectly white head of hair. The Major expressed a strong appreciation for his father's legacy as a poet and sang several of Robert Burns's songs. The Major is the son of Robert Burns and spent an evening at Abbotsford with Sir Walter Scott. Mrs. ------, the mother of an insane young man, traveled from Naples with three small children to discuss her son's condition. The young man had a previous attack of insanity lasting three months three years prior to the current incident. The Governor of the Asylum informed Mrs. ------ that her son had experienced a relapse and was not doing as well as before.

The mansion was the family residence of the Medici for nearly two centuries. The mansion has hosted an emperor, a pope, and a king as guests. The mansion was sold to the Riccardis and later bought by the government. The mansion is currently occupied by public offices and societies. The chapel within the mansion features frescos painted by Gozzoli. The grand gallery of the mansion has a frescoed ceiling depicting members of the Medici family. The final horse-race of the Feast of St. John took place on June 30th at three o'clock P.M.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The narrator is engaged in sketching a romance titled The Marble Faun. A wedding party departed from the narrator's door, with the bride being the daughter of an English lady, the Countess of ------. The bridegroom is a young man of English birth, son of the Countess of St. G------. A swarm of beggars, primarily women and some blind people, gathered in the street during the wedding. The wedding party distributed small amounts of money to the beggars, who reacted by struggling for the coins. The wedding guests included the Pope's Nuncio, who was accompanied by two priests. The narrator visited the gallery of the Pitti Palace and observed a Madonna by Raphael.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: There is a public library in Grasmere that is accessible to the inhabitants. The author observed the weather changing from rain to clearer skies before reaching the hotel. The author and their companions left Grasmere after breakfast on July 21st. They traveled to Ambleside along the border of Grasmere Lake. Nab Scaur is located behind Wordsworth's house and has a grand appearance. De Quincey and Hartley Coleridge lived in a cottage near Rydal Water. The author reflects on the beauty of England, particularly in summer, and its impact on human life.

The text discusses the condition of modern Rome, particularly in relation to cleanliness and the juxtaposition of beauty and ugliness. Visitors to the Forum are advised to be cautious of their steps due to the unclean state of the area. The author notes that locals exhibit a disregard for cleanliness in sacred spaces, such as St. Peter's and the Pantheon. The author and his wife set out to find the Baths of Diocletian and the church of Santa Maria degl' Angeli. They encountered the Fountain of the Termini, which features a statue of Moses striking the rock. The exterior of Santa Maria degl' Angeli is described as lacking architectural merit and resembling a pile of ruined brickwork. The interior of the church, transformed from Diocletian's Baths, is noted for its lofty and airy space, attributed to Michael Angelo.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The great bell of St. Peter's tolled during twilight. U---- expressed her love for Rome and regret at leaving. The journey to Florence began on May 24th after leaving Rome. There was a dispute with Lalla, the female servant, and her mother. The travelers encountered military music and a French regiment marching into the city. The regiment consisted of young men in excellent uniform and equipment. The travelers passed through the Porta del Popolo after a passport examination.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The Arno River is populated by goldfish and minnows. The garden paths are shaded by high walls of box. The view from the esplanade includes Florence and the Apennines. The Duomo and Palazzo Vecchio are notable landmarks in Florence. U---- sketched the tower of the Palazzo Vecchio, attracting the attention of passersby. The Pitti Palace was visited on a sultry morning with darkening clouds. The atmosphere in the picture-rooms of the palace was obscured, affecting the appearance of the artwork.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: A woman begged for bread near the Abbey, claiming hunger was hard to bear. The narrator perceived the woman as an impostor and chose not to give her anything. The narrator and his companions sought shelter in Westminster Abbey as it began to rain. Westminster Abbey is described as preferable to St. Paul's in terms of variety and interest of monuments. The narrator visited Mr. B------ to leave a watch for examination and repair. Mr. B------ mentioned that he and his brother had a ground-rent income of two thousand pounds per annum from land at Blackheath. The narrator walked through various streets, including Fleet Street and the Strand, and observed bookshops and stalls.

The narrator and their companions arrived in Florence without luggage examination at the gate. They initially drove to the Casa del Bello but found the rental agreement was not finalized. The narrator visited Mr. Powers's studio but was unable to meet him due to his engagement. The narrator and their companions stayed at the Albergo della Fontana hotel. Mr. Powers visited the narrator in the evening and was described as a plain person with strong simplicity and warm kindliness. The next day, through Mr. Powers's assistance, the narrator engaged the Casa del Bello for fifty dollars a month. During a visit to Powers's studio, the narrator observed various sculptures and noted Powers's opinions on other artists' works.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The text discusses equestrian statues in London, including those of various kings at Charing Cross and the Duke of Wellington opposite Apsley House.
