The author finds the idea of placing a man on a horse in a public space absurd due to safety concerns. English sculptors have attempted to mitigate this absurdity by depicting horses in a calm manner. The statue of Wellington at the Piccadilly corner of the Park has a stately effect when viewed from a distance. The author had a visit from Mr. Coventry Patmore, who was introduced by Dr. Wilkinson. Mr. Patmore is described as youthful in appearance, slender, and possessing a refined mind. The author is preparing for departure to Italy and has arranged for a passport with the American Minister.

Mr. Mueller's studio is contiguous to that of a young German artist who is not well known and seldom receives visitors. The young artist's studio contains a bed, a dressing-table, an easel, and sketches of Italian scenes and figures. Miss Shepard spoke a few kind words to the young artist in German, which seemed to win his heart. The jeweller Castellani specializes in reproducing ornaments in the old Roman and Etruscan fashion. The author observed a modern imitation of an Etruscan lady's toilet-case in Castellani's shop, along with other jewelry items. The author visited the sculpture-gallery of the Capitol and looked at busts of illustrious men and emperors. The weather during the author's visit was warm in the sun but cool with a breeze.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The journey began at eleven o'clock and continued until after dark. The travelers arrived in Dijon and halted for twenty-five minutes for dinner. They reached Lyons at about ten o'clock and left their luggage at the railway station. The group took an omnibus to the Hotel de Provence, which was chosen at random. The hotel was located off the direct route of the omnibus, requiring the driver to drop them at a corner. The hotel featured old and worn staircases, a long corridor, and spacious sleeping rooms. In the morning, soldiers were observed as sentinels in various locations around the hotel.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The text discusses a concept for a story involving a ring that symbolizes the complexities of a second marriage. The tombs mentioned may have originally been above ground, similar to the tomb of Cecilia Metella. Mrs. Jameson invited the narrator to visit her and take a drive around Rome. Mrs. Jameson appears to be suffering from a condition resembling gout in one foot. The narrator describes Mrs. Jameson as having once been a beautiful woman with blue or gray eyes and fair hair. The drive included notable locations such as the theatre of Marcellus, the Palatine Hill, and the Baths of Caracalla. At the Church of 'Domine, quo vadis?', Mrs. Jameson pointed out a stone with supposed miraculous prints of the Saviour's feet.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The gallery contains specimens of antique sculptures including Apollos, Bacchuses, Venuses, Mercurys, and Fauns. The Venus de' Medici was not found in the gallery during the visit. The ceiling of the gallery is covered with frescos and the floor is paved with a polished stone composition. The final piece of sculpture in the gallery is a copy of the Laocoon. There is a series of rooms parallel to the gallery that are primarily devoted to pictures, with some containing statues and bas-reliefs. The collection includes works by French, Dutch, and Flemish masters, which were found to be more interesting than the Italian works. The Venus de' Medici was eventually glimpsed in an octagonal room, which is described as the best room of the series.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The narrator describes an old man as a good-tempered, upright, and bold individual with dogmatic opinions. The old man has a rough background but is pleasant in social interactions. The narrator contrasts the old man with an Englishman who has spent his life in Liverpool and works as an Inspector of Nuisances. The Englishman is described as gracious and affable but has a narrower range of ideas compared to the old man. The Englishman recounts a story about discovering a dead body in Liverpool, which he describes in detail. The narrator dined with the new Mayor of Liverpool at the Town Hall, where characteristic municipal traditions were observed. About fifty gentlemen attended the dinner, and the Mayor toasted various countries before the Republic.

The hat described has a high crown and was originally bright red but is now mottled gray with cracks. The signet-ring mentioned belonged to a Pharaoh who reigned over Egypt during Joseph's prime ministry and is made of massive gold with Hebrew-like inscriptions. The collection includes a golden and enamelled George worn by Sir Thomas More and an embroidered shirt of Charles I. The shirt of Charles I is washed and folded, with no blood-marks, and the linen is coarser than modern peasant wear. The Cavalier General Sir Jacob Astley's buff-coat is made of thick leather and is adorned with silver-lace on the sleeves. The exhibition features works by British painters, including Hogarth's pictures such as the Sigismunda and the March to Finchley. The author plans to revisit the exhibition multiple times to gain further understanding and improvement from the displayed items.

The general costume of the inhabitants includes frocks or sacks, often worn with shirt-sleeves or a coat hung over one shoulder. People of respectability prefer cylinder hats and broadcloth frock-coats, but they also appear somewhat shabby. Almost all women wear shawls, and some ladies wear swelling petticoats and gilded fans. The vehicle commonly used for driving is a little gig without a top, which is seldom seen. The vicinity of Siena features pleasant country lanes, a verdant outlook, and a wide prospect of purple mountains. On October 8th, a visit was made to the Palazzo Publico, which contains fine old halls and chapels adorned with ancient frescos and pictures. The cathedral in Siena has a pavement covered with life-size figures depicting Gothic or Scriptural scenes.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The great hall has a vaulted ceiling and is followed by a series of noble rooms with rich frescos and mosaic floors. The rooms contain antique cabinets inlaid with precious stones and Florentine mosaics, each highly valuable. Many rooms are adorned with arras depicting landscapes, hunting scenes, and historical subjects. Some rooms feature mosaic floors made of stone and marble, while others are covered with carpets. The picture gallery is accessed by ascending several narrow flights of stairs and contains a large collection of well-preserved paintings. Raphael's 'Madonna della Seggiola' is highlighted as the most beautiful picture, with an artist copying it during the visit. The overall aesthetic of the rooms and gallery is described as grand yet soft, with a subdued splendor.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The narrator holds the title of Honorable in their own country. The narrator and their companion found a comfortable hotel but chose not to spend excessively. They experienced the English custom of lodgings, which requires immediate responsibility for housekeeping. On July 1st, the narrator traveled to Coventry with J----- on a warm day. Coventry is located approximately nine or ten miles from Leamington. The streets of Coventry are described as crooked and narrow, with some houses jutting over one another. Coventry houses are noted to be larger than similar styles seen elsewhere, with architectural similarities to Boston.

The author experienced a heavy cold and fever during the week of June 27th. The Feast of St. John took place on the Thursday prior to June 27th. Mr. Powers visited the author and discussed the expression of human eyes. Powers suggested that the expression of eyes depends on the surrounding muscles rather than their color or light. Powers commented on Michael Angelo's statue of Lorenzo de' Medici, attributing its effect to shadow rather than the sculptor's skill. Powers shared anecdotes from his early life as a clerk in Cincinnati, including drawing caricatures of a museum proprietor. Powers became so familiar with the museum proprietor's face that he could draw it in the dark.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The view of the German Ocean was described as blue, sunny, and breezy. The narrator and J----- waited at Berwick for over an hour and took a walk into the town. Berwick is characterized by rough houses, some of which are thatched, and there is evidence of a former wall around the town. The river Tweed offers a fine view both above and below the railway bridge. The narrator reached Durham around eight o'clock and wandered along a path by the river in the evening dusk. Durham Cathedral has no organ-screen or partition between the choir and nave, allowing for a clear view of its length. The pillars of Durham Cathedral are described as immensely thick and support round Norman arches.

O---- P------ is described as a short, black-haired, dark-complexioned man with an unrefined appearance. O---- P------ has been residing in Liverpool for about six months and requested a letter of introduction to visit the British Museum. On March 1st, 1857, a robbery occurred at the narrator's house, where thieves entered through a broken window. The thieves stole silver cups and other items from the sideboard, leaving the house ransacked but some items behind. The police were informed of the robbery, and an inspector and constable conducted an investigation. The thieves were later caught in Liverpool, and some stolen property was recovered from them and a pawnbroker. The police-office in Southport contains numerous advertisements of various crimes, including the narrator's own robbery.

The statue described is a representation of Venus, which has suffered significant damage over time. The statue's legs are broken into fragments, its arms are severed, its body is broken at the waist, and its head is detached. Despite the injuries, the statue's restoration is skillful, allowing it to maintain its overall effect. The room containing the Venus statue is noted as a treasure-place of the Uffizi Palace, housing many famous artworks. Mr. Robert Browning visited the narrator's group and extended an invitation to see them that evening. Mr. Browning appeared younger and more handsome than previously seen two years ago in London. The Brownings are planning to leave Florence soon for Normandy.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The Prince Borghese opens his collection to the public for viewing and for artists to study. The collection is open every day except Saturday and Sunday, with a fee required for entry. The collection contains between eight and nine hundred pictures, many of which are considered masterpieces. The author expresses difficulty in fully appreciating the art due to external weariness and the overwhelming number of works. The author notes a preference for Dutch and Flemish paintings over Italian masters. On March 1st, the author intended to visit the Colonna Palace but found it closed due to the custode's illness. The author visited Il Gesu church, where a priest was preaching to a large audience.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: A sailor aboard a ship exhibited visible signs of abuse and ill treatment. The text describes a dire situation on ships, comparing it to hell. The author suggests that legalizing flogging on ships could improve discipline among crew members. The captain of the Assyria plans to cover the funeral expenses of a deceased sailor. The author visited the ship William Lapscott to take depositions regarding a homicide in New York. The cabin of the ship is described as elaborately furnished with fine materials. Witnesses to a homicide on the ship claimed they were too intoxicated to remember the events clearly.

Mr. Archer is a surgeon associated with a prison or house of correction in Liverpool. An attorney who committed forgery took prussic acid but later recovered and became wealthy in New South Wales. Mr. Robertson Gladstone mentioned a magistrate named Sir John who paid a fine for being drunk in public. The narrator visited the North Hospital to take a deposition from a dying man regarding his ill treatment on the ship Assyria. The dying man described being beaten and ill-treated during his voyage from New Orleans. The dying man expressed a desire to return to America and mentioned a sum of four dollars and a half he wanted to retrieve. The deposition taken from the dying man is unlikely to result in punishment for those involved in his ill treatment.

The narrator and companions visited Liverpool to see an American circus company. The narrator had previously visited the circus with another companion and felt a sense of patriotism. On May 27th, the group left Boston by railway and arrived in Peterborough in about an hour and a quarter. The group stayed at the Railway Hotel in Peterborough and visited the cathedral after dinner. The cathedral in Peterborough features three lofty arches and is in perfect repair, though it has lost many statues and sculptures. The interior of the cathedral includes a nave with clustered pillars and Norman arches, but much of it is covered in plaster and whitewash. The cathedral suffered damage from Cromwell's soldiers, resulting in the loss of much of its original wood and marble.

The text describes a scriptural altar-piece copied from Rubens and a picture of St. Michael and the Dragon. The location mentioned has been repaired and is entirely new, having never been inhabited by the family. The author notes that the newness of the house makes it less effective compared to a lived-in space. The rooms were not presented at their best, with carpets not down and furniture covered. The gardens contain noble conservatories and hot-houses with rare flowers and tropical fruits. The author mentions a kind and intelligent under-gardener who gave a purple everlasting flower as a memento. The author reflects on past affairs and people from America while observing Miss Martineau, who is described as a large, robust, elderly woman.

Many carriages and visitors are present at the construction site in Rome. The site of the basilica has been uncovered, revealing several tombs and artifacts. Excavations have brought to light precious marbles, pillars, a statue, and elaborately wrought sarcophagi. The tombs are accessible by long flights of steps and are frequented by many visitors. One tomb is believed to be a burial place constructed by early Christians, while the adjacent tomb is from pagan Rome. The inner tomb was found without any earth and features a square room with a mosaic pavement and beautifully ornamented walls. The smaller sarcophagi in the inner tomb are covered with intricate bas-reliefs depicting various figures.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The promenade in England is lively around nine o'clock after sundown. Sick and infirm people are seen in bath-chairs or sitting on benches. The Town Crier in Southport is described as a meek-looking old man with a doleful tone. The war-steamer Niagara arrived in the Mersey recently. Captain Hudson visited the office of the narrator with his purser, Mr. Eldredge. Mrs. Blodgett and her family planned to visit the ship Niagara the following day. The officers of the ship are described as gentlemanly but not polished.

The text describes a collection of off-hand sketches that resulted in disappointment for the artist. There is a collection of miniatures in the same suite of apartments, some of which are described as exquisite and lifelike. Two miniatures of Benjamin Franklin are noted, with one being particularly picturesque. The crowd of Sunday visitors is described as generally being of a lower class compared to weekday visitors. Many of the Sunday visitors are private soldiers in various uniforms, some wearing medals denoting Crimean service. The galleries of sculpture in the Louvre are described as having astounding extent and featuring antique statues and various marble shapes. The arrangement of the sculptures is noted to be skillful and ingenious, although the author did not feel particularly impressed by the sculptures themselves.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The speaker demonstrated fluency and engaged earnestly with the audience during his speech. His views on England's position and the war were pessimistic, and his speech was practical and straightforward. The audience reacted positively to his speech, which concluded with great cheering. Mr. Layard is characterized as a true Englishman with moral strength and common sense. An old seaman, aged sixty, provided testimony in a case of alleged ill-usage by ship officers. The old seaman had a dignified presence despite admitting to past drunkenness and mischief-making. The weather changed to rain after a prolonged dry period characterized by east winds.

There is a wide, deep well made of solid red freestone with steps leading down to it. The well likely supplied water to the old cotters and retainers of Tranmere Hall five hundred years ago. Tranmere Hall is an old gray stone building with multiple gables and windows, some of which have been built up. The Hall has two sun-dials made of stone, one of which has worn-off figures and the other lacks a gnomon. Tranmere Hall has been converted into a farm-house, surrounded by a village and modern dwellings. On March 27th, the author attended court at St. George's Hall, where Mr. Justice Cresswell presided. The author dined at Mr. J. P. Heywood's on April 7th and learned about a bloody footstep tradition at Smithell's Hall.

The narrator visited a hotel in Newcastle that is described as better than any hotel seen in the South of England and almost as good as those in Scotland. The coffee-room of the hotel is spacious and features a full-length portrait of Wellington. There were many American guests in Newcastle and the North of England. The narrator observed two Newcastle gentlemen drinking hot whiskey-toddy in the smoking-room. On May 8th, the narrator left Newcastle early in the morning by rail, while Mr. Bowman stayed behind for business. The narrator noted a station called 'Washington' along the railway route, linked to the Washington family. Upon arriving in York, the narrator found York Cathedral impressive but noted its rectangular outline and lack of complexity compared to other Gothic buildings.

The narrator describes a sensible and courteous man who has a melancholy demeanor. On October 19th, the narrator notes a custom among people in distressed circumstances to seek help from neighbors with the support of a friend. A grocer, who became security for a friend, visits the narrator's office accompanied by another grocer for support. The grocer seeking help is described as elderly and somewhat sickly in appearance. The narrator observes that the custom of seeking public assistance is foreign to American habits. On November 2nd, a young Frenchman enters the narrator's office, dressed in a grayish cloak and well-fitted trousers. The Frenchman claims to be a naturalized American citizen seeking employment after leaving America for health reasons.

The sun set near eight o'clock on the evening described. Northern lights appeared before darkness fell over Arroquhar. The narrator and companions stayed in a new hotel with excellent accommodations. Mr. Macregor, the hotel host, drove the group to Loch Lomond's shore. The group signaled for a ferryman to cross Loch Lomond to Inversnaid. Rob Roy's cave is located about a mile from Inversnaid along the lake shore. The journey to Aberfoyle involved a steep ascent from the inn.

The text discusses various artworks, including those by Cimabue, Giotto, Bonamico Buffalmacco, Gentile da Fabriano, Perugino, Andrea del Sarto, and Carlo Dolce. Bonamico Buffalmacco is noted as having produced a better picture than Cimabue and Giotto. The 'Adoration of the Magi' by Gentile da Fabriano is described as a splendid work with noble figures. Three pictures by Perugino are mentioned, with one depicting the Virgin holding the dead Christ noted for its deep expression of woe. The text states that after Perugino, the interest in paintings declines despite improvements in technique. Carlo Dolce's portrait of the Eternal Father is described as a masterpiece of absurdity. The text mentions a statue of St. Matthew by Michael Angelo, which appears to be in a state of incomplete creation.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The statue represents Daniel Webster holding the written roll of the Constitution in his right hand. Webster is depicted as a strong figure, symbolizing him as the preserver of the Union. The statue's surface is wrought to a sort of roughness, which the sculptor Powers noted took great effort. The statue is intended to be placed in the open air in Boston. The text describes various specimens of castings, including delicate flower baskets and lifelike hands. The market in Florence is described as noisy and crowded, featuring various fruits and vegetables. The people in Florence have a preference for unripe foods, including fruits and meats.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The narrator has been assigned a pleasant room for study in Florence. The weather in Florence is described as delightful and warm. The narrator plans to write daily and visit pictures and statues. The narrator observes that Florence has both antique and massive buildings. The streets of Florence are enjoyable to walk on compared to those in Rome. The Baptistery in Florence is octagonal and covered with black and white marble. The interior of the Duomo is noted for its dim grandeur and painted windows.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: U---- and R----- have been riding between fields and barn in a hay-cart. The roads provide beautiful walks along the river-side and among gentle hills. The hedges and stone fences are adorned with flowers, moss, and ivy. Mr. W------, the landlord, has lent a work illustrating the antiquities of Furness Abbey. The hotel may have been rebuilt from an old manor-house erected by a family of Prestons after the Reformation. The Earl of Burlington is the current proprietor of Furness Abbey. On July 16th, the narrator traveled by steamboat from Newby Bridge to Lowwood Hotel on Windermere Lake.

The area around the lake is described as too marshy for agricultural use. Flocks of sheep are observed, tended by men and boys who appear unhealthy. The lake is less visually appealing upon closer inspection, lacking rocky margins and sandy beaches. Two islands are visible from a distance, one associated with the murder of an empress. The town of Bolsena is located nearly a mile from the lake on higher ground. Bolsena features a striking entrance with a view of a castle that has three towers. The streets of Bolsena are described as narrow, dirty, and filled with signs of poverty despite fertile land.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The portal arch may never have been closed since the Reformation. The establishment is now called 'The College' and is let in rooms and small tenements to poor people. St. William's College was founded in Henry VI.'s time for the residence of the parsons and priests of the cathedral. Easter Sunday service at the cathedral commenced at half past ten. The choir of the cathedral has been recently renovated after being destroyed by fire. The choir was filled with a congregation that included officers in full dress and white-robed choristers. An enormous organ in the choir is clad in rich oaken carving.

The author visited the Sistine Chapel for the first time on May 15th. The Sistine Chapel features a partition of white marble that divides the room. The walls and ceiling of the chapel are covered with fresco paintings, except for a ten-foot high section intended for tapestries by Raphael. The ceiling is painted by Michelangelo, depicting the progress of the world and mankind. The wall behind the altar is dominated by Michelangelo's 'Last Judgment'. The author describes the current state of the chapel as dusky and dim, requiring sunlight for visibility of the designs. The author expresses a personal reaction to the depiction of Jesus in 'Last Judgment', finding it undesirable.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: Mr. Milnes introduced the narrator to the Marquis of Lansdowne, who was dressed in a blue coat and gray pantaloons. The Marquis of Lansdowne had his right hand wrapped in a black-silk handkerchief and greeted the narrator with his left hand. Mrs. Browning was introduced to the narrator by Mr. Milnes and was described as a small, delicate woman with dark hair and a pleasant face. The breakfast-room was decorated with pictures and featured a large round table. The narrator discovered that an elderly lady at the table was the mother of Florence Nightingale. During breakfast, Mrs. Browning discussed her interest in spiritualism and mentioned that her husband, Mr. Browning, rejects the subject. Mrs. Nightingale spoke to the narrator about London smoke and characterized Lady Byron as an excellent and exemplary person.

The text discusses the evolution of art over a period of at least two hundred years, mentioning early painters such as Giotto and Cimabue. The paintings from this period are characterized by great care and detail, but lack lifelike illusion, with conventional backgrounds and accessories. The effect of these paintings, when new and freshly gilded, was described as exceedingly brilliant, similar to rich illuminations in old monkish missals. Fabriana Gentile's painting of the Adoration of the Magi is noted for its life, action, and vivid representation of the three kings' magnificence. Fra Angelico is recognized for his delicate execution, particularly in his depictions of Christ and the Virgin, despite the author's lack of personal enjoyment of his works. Perugino is identified as the first painter whose works possess genuine merit worthy of preservation, with a notable depiction of the Virgin. Carlo Dolce's painting of the Eternal Father is criticized as inadequate, despite being finely painted.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The street features two or three peaked gables and a low arched entrance leading to a small paved quadrangle. The quadrangle is a few paces wide and approximately twenty paces long, with a glimpse of a garden visible through a half-closed doorway. Inside the Hospital, there are neat apartments for the Matron and several small rooms for destitute widows, each containing basic furnishings. Each widow has a small room for sleeping and cooking, and receives three and sixpence a week for sustenance. The widows contribute twopence each towards the funeral costs when one of them dies. Market-day in Coventry features booths and stalls selling various goods, including Twice-Told Tales and country produce. The autumn season is characterized by green foliage, with many flowers still blooming despite the presence of withered leaves.

The narrator gave all the pennies they had to the children before continuing their journey. The narrator and their companions were driven into a small tavern due to rain before arriving at Rhyl. After dinner, the narrator traveled to Chester and Rock Park, while S----- and the children followed the next day. On September 22nd, the narrator dined at Mr. John Heywood's in Norris Green, where Mr. Mouckton Mimes and his wife were present. Mr. Milnes mentioned that he owns land in Yorkshire associated with the pilgrims of the Mayflower and that Elder Brewster was the Postmaster of the village. On September 26th, the narrator attended a soiree at the Town Hall hosted by the Mayor and Mrs. Lloyd to receive the Earl of Harrowby. On October 5th, the narrator attended a dejeuner on board the James Barnes, a vessel built by Donald McKay of Boston.

The church had been covered with frescos by Giotto, assisted by Cimabue, which were mostly obliterated. A one-legged attendant followed the group into the church and continued to accompany them as they moved through the streets. A sickly-looking beggar approached the group and asked for help, but was dismissed by a boy in the group. The one-legged attendant did not offer to guide the group but kept pace with them as they navigated the streets. The group left Foligno in the morning, which was described as bleak, chill, and threatening. The group drove through the Umbrian valley and passed the old town of Spello, which is noted for its steep streets and ancient pictorial art.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The hills in the area are generally bare of trees but have strong and striking outlines. Many older Welsh women wear high-crowned black beaver hats similar to men's hats. Welsh is the prevalent language spoken by many inhabitants in the area. An old stone image of a warrior, believed to be the natural son of David, Prince of Wales, was seen in a church. The church contained a stone coffin that was open and empty, previously holding a person of rank. The town features monumental brasses engraved with portraits from Elizabeth's time. The author visited the Zoological Gardens in Liverpool, which includes various animal enclosures and a theatre.

Giuliano de' Medici is sculptured by Michael Angelo and is located in a niche. At the feet of Giuliano are two allegorical statues, Day and Night. On the opposite side of the chapel are two similar statues representing Morning and Evening. The statue above Morning and Evening is considered worthy of Michael Angelo's reputation. The statue features a sitting figure with a helmet, one hand supporting the chin and the other resting on the thigh. The Medicean Chapel was built over two centuries ago for the reception of the Holy Sepulchre. The chapel is octagonal in shape and features a series of frescos painted within the last thirty years.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The narrator and children intended to walk to Charing Cross but missed their way. They encountered St. James's Palace, which has a clock-tower and is guarded by sentinels. The interior of St. James's Palace consists of large, paved courts with dark brick walls and no greenery. The palace is extensive and features a carriage-drive that likely accommodates carriages during events. The narrator and children passed Marlborough House and a long range of stone edifices on their way. They reached Charing Cross and Trafalgar Square, which has numerous architectural monuments and fountains. The afternoon plan included attending divine service at Westminster Abbey.

The Palazzo Vecchio features a bronze equestrian statue of Cosmo de' Medici, the first Grand Duke. There are marble statues, including one of David by Michelangelo, located at each side of the palace door. The Loggia di Lanzi has three large arches and serves as a shelter for people from sun and rain. Benvenuto Cellini's Perseus is displayed in the Loggia di Lanzi. An edict from the Grand Duke regarding a water project was posted in the Loggia di Lanzi. The Duomo's facade is described as a bare, ugly space with rough plaster and visible brickwork. The campanile, or bell-tower, stands near the Duomo and rises to a height of nearly three hundred feet.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: There was an old woman and some children visible near a stagnant ditch full of water-weeds. Men and women were harvesting carrots and digging potatoes along the roadside. The narrator intended to go to Ormskirk but got lost and found a picturesque hamlet. The narrator entered a public-house with a large sign representing a dance around a Maypole. The coffee-room of the public-house smelled of bad tobacco-smoke and was shabbily furnished. The narrator had a meal that included hot chops, household bread, rich cheese, and home-brewed ale. The estate owner was identified as Mr. Scarisbrick by a boy the narrator inquired.

The narrator met R----- and a servant while exploring a large house. The house has multiple rooms, including a dressing-room, a vaulted saloon, and a writing-study with fresco decorations. There are numerous saloons, anterooms, and sleeping-chambers on both the basement and upper floors, as well as a subterranean area. The house contains a locked chapel and an oratory with religious artifacts, including a wax representation of a boy holding a heart. The lower floor is furnished and decorated with frescos, but the bare pavements create an impression of discomfort. The grounds around the house feature gravel-walks, shrubbery, and a podere, or cultivated tract, that appears fertile. The rural laborers observed by the narrator dress in shirt-sleeves and resemble sunburnt individuals from the United States.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The casino has a basement floor that contains a suite of beautiful rooms filled with statuary. The entrance hall of the casino is brightly frescoed and paved with ancient mosaics depicting combats with beasts and gladiators. The gallery on the basement floor is sixty feet long and features rich marble flooring and walls adorned with various types of marble. The hall is decorated with pillars of Oriental alabaster and frescoed with arabesque ornaments. Canova's statue of Pauline, sister of Bonaparte, is located in the upper rooms and represents her as Venus holding an apple. The upper rooms also contain works by Bernini, including statues of Aeneas and Anchises, and David. The overall effect of the casino's decoration is described as rich and magnificent.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The Mersey River is visible with green fields on the opposite side and a densely populated shore leading to the city center. The city center features the dome of the Custom House, steeples, towers, and the spire of St. Nicholas, along with coal-smoke in the air. The Albert dock and Queen's tobacco warehouses are located along the bank, along with several shipyards. The author moved into a new house in Rock Park, which has three apartments, a kitchen, a pantry, and four chambers on each of its three stories. The rent for the house is one hundred pounds unfurnished and one hundred sixty pounds furnished. Rock Park is a private property area populated by professional people and merchants, with quiet streets and a police station at the entrance. The previous occupants of the house cultivated a garden with many rare flower varieties that bloom throughout the year.

Katrine and J----- examined an old stone fortress erected in a mountain pass after the rebellion of 1745. The fortress is built of rough stones in the form of a parallelogram and measures between thirty and forty paces long. The two remaining sides of the fortress are about twenty feet high and have little port-holes for defense. A small Highland cabin has been built against the wall of the fortress, with a dog in the doorway and hens nearby. The length of Loch Katrine is ten miles, and it meets the pass of the Trosachs at its termination. The steamer Rob Roy was boarded at the head of Loch Katrine around five o'clock. The scenery along Loch Katrine is described as not being as rich and lovely as that of Loch Lomond.

The group traveled in a coach towards Newby Bridge, arriving at the Swan Hotel. The Swan Hotel is described as an agreeable place with a pleasant rural aspect. A stone bridge of five arches crosses the river Severn near the hotel. The hotel provides various meals including trout, cold beef, ham, toast, muffins, and excellent wine. The stage-coach passes from Milnethorpe to Ulverton twice a day, and a steamer operates between the hotel and the head of the lake. The group climbed a steep hill to a tower, offering a wide view of mountain scenery and Windermere Lake. On July 12th, the group took a phaeton to Furness Abbey, a drive of about sixteen miles.

The scene includes a paved courtyard and a small piazza with a figure of a man dressed in a blue coat and buff breeches. A large dog is sitting on its hind legs in a kennel beside the porch, and another man is seated in an arbor near the gateway. The village dwelling is described as castellated and contains wooden images, suggesting it may have been created by a whimsical individual now buried in Bebbington churchyard. The old church bell was ringing as people and children dressed neatly moved towards it. The church of Bebbington is a large edifice built in the form of a cross, with a date inscribed in stone that is approximately from the year 1300. The church features an ivy-covered steeple and has a significant appearance of age, despite some portions being renewed. There are monuments in the churchyard, some recent and some dating back to 1684 and 1686, with most looking antique due to the effects of the climate.

The author describes a man in England as physically impressive compared to English noblemen. The author reflects on his emotional response while reading the last scene of The Scarlet Letter to his wife. The streets of London have numerous vagrant entertainers, including tumblers and puppet-showmen. The author observes a tumbler performing on a pole in Fleet Street and describes the crowd's reaction. The author notes the presence of beggars and street performers seeking small change in London. The author visits Clement's Inn and sees a garden with a bronze figure, recalling Justice Shallow's connection to it. The author expresses confusion about the Inns of Court and their purpose while navigating the area around St. Paul's.

Englishmen tend to avoid eloquence in after-dinner speeches and prefer plain speaking. The audience of an Englishman speaking plainly is generally satisfied and may be prejudiced against overly glib speakers. On October 6th, there was widespread anxiety and subsequent exultation in England regarding Sebastopol, which was later revealed to be incorrect. The Times had begun to issue threats against America based on the mistaken belief that the war was nearing a prosperous conclusion. An Englishman in adversity maintains his dignity and is viewed as a respectable character. On October 16th, news arrived of the loss of the Arctic and the deaths of Captain Luce and his son due to a collision with a French steamer. Captain Luce chose to stay with his son during the sinking of the ship rather than risk sending him away in a lifeboat.

On October 2nd, the narrator went to 67 Grace Church Street to cash a bank post-note with Mr. Oakford. The narrator visited the offices of two lines of steamers located in Moorgate Street and Leadenhall Street. The city was described as being very crowded, with many people engaged in business activities out of public view. The narrator took a boat from London Bridge to Chelsea, with departures every ten minutes and a voyage duration of forty minutes. The narrator observed the river-front of the Houses of Parliament from Westminster Bridge, noting its noble appearance. On October 3rd, the narrator returned to the city to arrange passages to Lisbon, accompanied by J-----. The Surrey Zoological Gardens were described as a poor suburban amusement location, with a menagerie that was scanty.

The group rented a suburban villa for two months and arrived there yesterday morning. The villa is located on a hill called Bellosguardo, about a mile beyond the Porta Romana. Upon arrival, the group found the iron gate of the villa shut and locked. J----- and B. P------ had previously entered the house but were unable to re-enter due to the door's springlock. B. P------ enlisted the help of local contadini to retrieve the keys from inside the house. The group climbed to the top of the tower of the villa, which is made of decayed wood and is not very high. The landscape surrounding the villa included the convent of Monte Olivetto and various white villas, including Galileo's tower and the duke's villa.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The narrator passed through Vevay and Clarens during their journey. Clarens is noted for its picturesque scenery, with hills close to the water and a rocky cliff resembling a rounded pyramid. The narrator has a personal connection to Clarens due to its association with the love story of St. Preux and Julie from Rousseau's romance. The Castle of Chillon is described as an ancient-looking group of towers situated on the water's edge. The narrator was disappointed by the appearance of the Castle of Chillon, which did not match their expectations of it being elevated above the lake. The narrator arrived at the Hotel Byron at nearly eight o'clock after a mile walk. A rainbow appeared across the lake during the latter part of the voyage, which the narrator viewed as a good omen.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The Rows in Chester are narrow passages that connect shops and houses. A woman living in one of the houses has resided there for twenty-one years and described her living conditions as dismal. During cholera times, she witnessed multiple coffins being carried out of her passage. The Rows are popular business locations in Chester, providing shelter from rain and dim lighting for displaying goods. Many buildings in the Rows are modern, but some have ancient oaken frames visible on the exterior. An inscription on one building claims, 'GOD'S PROVIDENCE IS MINE INHERITANCE,' placed there two hundred years ago. The narrator dined at the Royal Hotel after considering local taverns, which appeared dingy and unclean.

The expedition was to the Temple of Vesta. The Arch of Janus Quadrifrons is located in the Forum Boarium. The Temple of Vesta is a well-preserved Roman ruin situated on the bank of the Tiber. The Temple of Vesta is surrounded by a circle of Corinthian marble pillars. The Temple of Fortuna Virilis retains its antique form and is in better preservation than many Roman ruins. The Ponto Rotto is the old Pons Emilius, which has been recently connected to a suspension bridge. The interior of the Temple of Vesta is a plain cylinder of marble fitted up as a chapel.

text: The weather in France was colder than expected, with frost on the carriage windows. The landscape resembled the December aspect of the narrator's native land, featuring broad, bare fields and streaks of snow. The journey to Amiens took three to four hours and was described as disagreeable. The narrator experienced difficulties understanding the French railway officials due to their rapid speech. Upon arrival in Amiens, the narrator was taken to the Hotel du Rhin, which was cold and uncomfortable. The town of Amiens featured a cathedral that appeared different from English cathedrals, being taller and more slender. The exterior of the Amiens cathedral was described as venerable, with well-preserved statues and elaborately wrought doors.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: Albert was charged with assaulting, beating, and stabbing the chief mate. The chief mate has been hospitalized since the assault and appeared in court to give evidence. The chief mate is described as a thirty-year-old man with black hair, black eyes, and a dark complexion. The second mate is characterized as a youth with long sandy hair and an intelligent appearance. Paraman, one of the prisoners, is identified as the individual who allegedly delivered the first blow to the chief mate. The magistrate dismissed all prisoners except Paraman, who is to be sent to America for trial. The magistrate, Mr. Mansfield, engaged in informal conversation during the proceedings.

The author expresses a lack of interest in spiritualism and skepticism towards its validity. The author has visited picture galleries and is beginning to appreciate Turner's artwork more than before. The shops in London are starting to display decorations and items for the Christmas season. The author feels weary of London and England, comparing their feelings to those of old Loyalists after the Revolution. The author enjoys walking through London streets, finding pleasure in them similar to that experienced in their hometown. The author visited Westminster Abbey and noted the splendor of the tombs and monuments on a sunny December day. The author has a particular impression of Murillo's St. John, describing it as having a mischievous intelligence.

French soldiers are present in the city, creating a significant amount of noise with drums, fifes, and trumpets. The presence of French soldiers contributes to the safety of Rome, making it as safe as London. The Carnival is currently taking place in Rome, but local interest appears limited. Foreigners, particularly English and Americans, occupy the balconies along the Corso during the Carnival. Individuals are seen attempting to retrieve driftwood from the Tiber River, which has a muddy appearance after recent rains. The Tiber River is described as broad and rapid, with clayey banks that appear to have been eroded over time. The Basilica of Santa Maria Maggiore, founded in A.D. 342 by Pope Liberius, features a grand nave with Ionic columns and a gilded roof.

text: The Rosetta Stone features a Greek inscription and Egyptian characters. Visitors to the British Museum included people from poorer classes and children. Figures of Indian Thugs have been removed from public display in the British Museum. The Chaplain of Newgate stated that representations of Indian Thugs suggested garroting to English thieves. On December 8th, there was dense fog in London, affecting visibility. The author visited Marlborough House to view English pictures. The author expressed difficulty in understanding many of Turner's pictures and drawings.

The subject has a small, brisk, wide-awake figure and wears a man's sack of purple or plum-colored broadcloth. She greeted the narrator and his wife without waiting for an introduction. Her attire includes a shirt-front, collar, cravat, and a brooch of Etruscan gold, along with a black velvet cap. Miss ------ has a collection of works displayed in her studio, including a piece titled Beatrice Cenci and a monumental design of a female figure in quiet sleep. She is associated with the artist Gibson, which benefits her exposure to potential audiences. The narrator observed pilgrims in Rome during holy week and encountered a woman begging for money. The narrator has not made journal entries recently due to laziness and indisposition.

text: The footstep is a slight cavity in the stone, shaped like a man's foot with a peaked shoe. George Marsh was a martyr and a curate who was burnt. Mrs. ------ invited the narrator to see the Hall and the footmark in Lancashire. The Earl of ------ has a pale, thin face that appears short and compressed. S----- attended court during the Hapgood trial and has a different opinion of the Earl of ------ than the narrator. The narrator attended a dejeuner on board the Donald McKay, where Mr. Layard, M. P. was the principal guest. Mr. Layard is described as a man of middle stature with an open, intelligent, and kindly face.

The street was decorated with foliage and a triumphal arch honoring a member of the Massimi family. The occasion for the feast was Whitsuntide. The town was crowded with peasants dressed in their best attire. Civita Castellana is located on a high, flat table-land above a deep valley with the Treja river. A modern road leads down from Civita Castellana to a narrow stone bridge crossing the river. The travelers stayed at a hotel with sleeping chambers beneath an arcade, separate from the rest of the hotel population. The group encountered laborers returning from the fields, with women commonly participating in agricultural work.

text: The hall is enclosed by oaken panelling carved with escutcheons of society members who have held the office of reader. A large window in the hall is emblazoned with the arms of Templars who have been Chief Justices. Other windows display coats of arms of local dignitaries connected with the Temple. The screen at the lower end of the hall is made of carved oak and dates back to Queen Elizabeth's time. Two oaken tables are set for law students to dine upon, with a cross-table for society leaders at the upper end. The cost of dinners in the hall is two shillings per gentleman, which includes ale and wine. The Temple Church features a circular vestibule and well-preserved monumental knights in chain armor.

An angler was catching chubs and dace under the walls of the bishop's palace by the river. The Severn river appears sluggish but has enough movement to carry the angler's float quickly. Two vessels, comparable in size to small schooners, were lying at the bridge. The narrator and companions ordered luncheon at their hotel, which included cold chicken, cold ham, and ale. They took a fly to the railway after paying a bill of about fifteen shillings, plus an additional five shillings for service. They traveled from Worcester to Wolverhampton and then to Birkenhead, arriving in the rain and darkness. The streets were crowded with people and illuminated for the celebration of the taking of Sebastopol and the visit of the Duke of Cambridge.

The miniature of Anne of Cleves is part of the Exhibition, which Henry VIII. used as a basis for marrying her. The picture of the Infanta of Spain was brought to Charles I. by Buckingham. The Refreshment-room at the Exhibition has ample space for both first and second classes. John Ball and his wife were observed consuming cold boiled beef and porter in the Refreshment-room. The narrator met Judge Pollock of Liverpool and was introduced to Mr. Du Val, an artist from Manchester. Mr. Du Val invited the narrator to dinner at his residence, which featured a lawn and shrubbery. The cab driver who took the narrator home was found to be drunk but managed to drive without incident.

The author visited the Isle of Man and recorded impressions of a church in Eastham. The author sat on a tombstone under the Great Tree of Eastham in the churchyard. An old woman warned the author not to let the sexton see him during sacrament-time. The author observed two upright stones in memory of old servants of the Stanley family. The author visited Birkenhead Park, which features a large ornamental gateway and neatly laid out grounds. The author attended a session in the Crown Court, where Baron ------ was the judge. The author visited St. John's Church in Chester, which is built of red freestone.

The broad stone staircase ascends externally from the court to the iron-grated door in the second story. Two officials informed that the Bargello only exhibits an old chapel with frescos by Giotto, viewable by appointment with the custode. The Church of the Badia is built in the form of a Greek cross with a flat roof and has a brick pavement and dark stone walls. The church contains several Gothic tombs and a few pictures that are difficult to see due to low light conditions. In the chapel of the Bianco family, there is an oil painting by Fra Filippo Lippi that is poorly lit and hard to discern. The Uffizi gallery was reinspected, including the cabinet of bronzes featuring works by John of Bologna and Benvenuto Cellini. The cabinet of gems displayed crystal cups with engraved devices and enamelled gold covers by Benvenuto Cellini.

text: The wire-work screen before many shrines displayed offerings of roses and other flowers, both fresh and artificial. Women and girls were seen carrying large bundles of twigs, shrubs, and flowers, sometimes obscuring their figures. Country houses observed had open galleries or arcades on the upper stories for domestic labor. The houses varied in appearance, with some being ancient and time-stained, while others featured cheerful colors or frescoed designs. Grass was spread to dry on the road, likely cut by peasants for winter forage. Vines were observed growing on trees, potentially fig-trees, and were described as picturesque in their natural growth. Mist was present among the hills in the morning, described as cheerful with sunlight.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The narrator parted with a strong handshake and was promised a visit soon. The narrator visited Truebner's in Pater Noster Row and met Charles Reade. The narrator has been walking the streets of London during dull November days. The narrator describes the experience of being in busy areas of London as a mix of enjoyment and heaviness. The narrator notes the lack of splendor in London, with some exceptions in Regent Street. The narrator's wife has been unwell, leading to mostly solitary excursions. The narrator and his wife visited Lincoln's Inn Fields and admired its modern yet antique-style Hall.

The monument features a cross-legged knight in armor and several battered warriors with square helmets. The burial-place of the old Barons of Kendal is located in the chancel below the high altar. Stone seats with richly carved canopies, used by priests during mass, are preserved against the wall of the choir. The ruins include a church, a better-preserved Chapter-house, a kitchen, and a meeting room for monks. There is a school-house for the children of the tenantry or villeins of the abbey, with a stone bench and a master's seat. The ruins also include remnants of a mill and a mill-stream that flows under old bridges.

Cromwell's artillery battered the city, which retains its height and strength. The garden of the College features semicircular recesses with iron garden-seats and round towers on the exterior. The wall of the College is about six feet thick and has loop-holes for archers and musketeers. The Oxford plant, which bears a small blue flower, is unique to the area and difficult to introduce elsewhere. New College chapel contains old brasses inlaid into tombstones and antique busts, indicating its historical significance. The crosier of William of Wickham, made of silver gilt and richly decorated, is displayed in the chancel of the chapel. The Cherwell is a narrow, sluggish stream that joins the Isis to form the Thames, and is navigable by various types of boats.

Mrs. Jameson expressed a favorable opinion of Mr. Thompson's pictures. The discussion included the relevance of modern costume in sculpture. Mrs. Jameson objected to modern costume elements like buttons and breeches. The narrator and Mrs. Jameson mutually decided to end their evening engagement. The narrator visited the Villa Albani with a ticket obtained through Mr. Cass. The villa features a large hall lined with a variety of beautiful marbles. A notable sculpture at the villa is a colossal bas-relief of Antinous.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The architectural splendor of Paris is characterized by stately edifices and grand monuments. The Place de la Concorde is a large square bordered by the Tuileries, the Champs Elysees, and the Seine. The Champs Elysees has bare earth beneath its trees, lacking grassy soil. The current Emperor has significantly changed the appearance of Paris in recent years. The Louvre is a vast and beautiful edifice that contains Egyptian, Greek, and Roman antiquities. Many artists, including young men and elderly individuals, were observed copying paintings in the Louvre. The French maintain memorials of their history and the achievements of their forefathers.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: Peterborough Cathedral is described as a delightful and serene location. The Bishop's secretary's residence is located behind the cathedral and near the churchyard. The Falcon Inn is an old-fashioned inn in Peterborough, possibly dating back to Queen Elizabeth's time. The Guildhall in the market-place has an open basement story and connects to a large old house. Henry VIII preserved the abbey church by converting it into a cathedral during the Reformation. The grounds of Peterborough Cathedral feature old houses adapted from monkish residences. The atmosphere of Peterborough Cathedral's grounds is described as domestic and conducive to a natural life.

Fra Angelico is known for creating principal figures in his artwork, which includes predellas and triptychs on wood. The wood used in Fra Angelico's pictures is worm-eaten, and the colors have often faded or changed over time. One of Fra Angelico's works depicts the Last Judgment, featuring Jesus and devils tormenting damned souls. The Church of St. Lorenzo was built over four centuries ago and stands on the site of an ancient basilica. The interior of the Church of St. Lorenzo features a nave with a flat roof, Corinthian pillars, and a mosaic pavement of black and white marble. The high altar of the Church of St. Lorenzo is flanked by two bronze pulpits adorned with medieval bas-reliefs. The new sacristy, known as the Capella dei Depositi, was built by Michael Angelo to house two monuments of the Medici family.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The graveyard appeared neglected and contained a few tombstones, including one for Mr. George Gibson. St. Katharine's Dock is located along the Thames and was crowded with great ships. The area around the Tower featured draymen, dock-laborers, sailors, and various vendors. The shops near the Tower sold items related to ships, sailors, and commerce, including nautical instruments and clothing. The neighborhood had old gabled houses and retained some architectural antiquity due to escaping the Great Fire. The group visited St. Paul's Cathedral, where they rested beneath the dome and heard the sounds of the city. Smithfield is still occupied with pens for cattle, although it has ceased to be a cattle-market.

Browning has celebrated the exterior of Casa Guidi Windows in song. The palace features a spacious staircase and a hall that opens onto a balcony. Browning mentioned that the nearby church was the first to perform an oratorio. Robert Browning, nicknamed Pennini, is nine years old and was born in Florence. Mrs. Browning is described as a pale, small person with a slender voice. Mr. and Mrs. E------, Miss F. H------, and Mr. ------ with his daughter were also guests. Mr. Browning was active in maintaining conversation with all guests.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne

text: The Piazza del Campo is the principal place of Siena and resembles an amphitheatre. The Palazzo Publico is a Gothic structure located on one side of the Piazza del Campo. The Palazzo Publico features a long battlemented front and a tower that rises high into the air. The Piazza del Campo serves as the market-place of Siena, filled with booths and stalls in the morning. An antique fountain, adorned with statues and bas-reliefs, is located on the side opposite the Palazzo Publico. The cathedral is situated in the highest part of the city and is a common destination for visitors. The baptistery, designed to be part of the cathedral, features a rich interior with clustered columns and frescos.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The text describes a profile visible in solid rock, which can be touched and seen. The custode led the narrator down steps to the lower cell of the Mamertine Prison. The Mamertine Prison is one of the few remains from the kingly period of Rome and served as a state prison for hundreds of years before the Christian era. Notable historical figures associated with the prison include Jugurtha and Catiline's adherents. The custode showed a stone post where St. Peter's chain was said to have been fastened and a spring of water believed to have miraculously appeared. The staircase to the lower dungeon is modern, while an ancient flight of stairs leading from the Capitol is now built into the wall. The narrator visited Mr. J. P. K------ at the Hotel d'Europe, who discussed various topics including the Kansas difficulty and St. Peter's character in the Church.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The Carleton Club building is constructed from buff-colored or yellowish stone and features polished Aberdeen granite pillars. The building has a running border of sculptured figures and various ornamental details. The bronze equestrian statue of Charles I. is located at the head of Whitehall, where the Regicides were executed. The Banqueting-House, built by Inigo Jones, is situated across the street from the Horse-Guards. Westminster Abbey has undergone significant repairs and lacks visible signs of age. The Houses of Parliament are described as an immense structure made of warm-colored stone with elaborate finishes. The Tower of London operates as a show-place, charging sixpence for entry, which includes viewing armory and crown jewels.

Sir Thomas Birch proposed to accompany the group to Knowsley Park for admittance. The gate-warden of Knowsley Park was an old woman who granted access at Sir Thomas Birch's request. The family of the Earl of Derby was not present at Knowsley Park during the visit. The mansion of Knowsley is described as exceedingly vast with a front and two wings. The oldest part of the mansion dates back to the time of Henry VII. The mansion of Croxteth, the seat of Lord Sefton, is located near the public road. Rooks were observed in the trees near Sir Thomas Birch's house during their visit.

The purpose was to purify her apartments from traces of an evil spirit. The church of St. Lorenzo was visited on September 17th. The famous Medici statues of Michael Angelo were seen during the visit. The library had a long and wide gallery or hall with windows painted with the arms of the Medici. Rare manuscripts were preserved under glass and books were fastened to desks by iron chains. A vellum manuscript of the Bible with illumination by Ghirlandaio was shown. The ancient reader experienced a luxury that the modern reader lacks.

text: Mr. ------, the sculptor, criticized Powers, stating he is not an artist despite acknowledging his skill in bust-making. Mr. ------ claims that Powers has sold parts of the Greek Slave statue separately. Mr. ------ believes that Powers lacks scientific knowledge of the human frame. Mr. ------ mentioned Powers's disappointment regarding a twenty-five-thousand-dollar appropriation from Congress. The tomb of the baker Eurysaces is located outside the Porta Maggiore and features symbols of his trade. The Claudian aqueduct is still in use to bring the Acqua Felice into Rome. The narrator expresses discomfort with the Roman atmosphere and a sense of languor in the city.

text: Popolo intended to spend the forenoon in the Campagna. The Tiber River appeared muddy and was flowing between deep banks of clay. The French proposed to draw off the Tiber to recover sunken statues and relics, but Romans objected due to malaria concerns. A man fishing on the river caught nothing during the observer's stay. The banks of the Tiber were described as bare and uninviting, with a rough aspect and shabbiness in visible houses. The Pantheon contains seven deep, pillared recesses that serve as chapels, along with shrines of saints. The Church of St. Ignazio, belonging to the College of the Jesuits, features a wide nave supported by marble columns and a dome.
