text: The journey started between five and six in the morning to reach Terni in time to see the falls. Borghetto is located on a bluff with a valley surrounding it, through which the Tiber flows. The road featured various medieval fortresses and ruins, which were described as more beautiful than Roman remains. The landscape included diverse trees, vines, and fig-trees, contributing to the scenery. Otricoli is a village situated on a promontory above the valley, characterized by a few gray houses and one brightly painted building. The travelers used six horses to ascend the hills, accompanied by a boy with club feet who was active and cheerful. The boy did not beg for alms but requested a small payment for his assistance, contrasting with other children who begged along the road.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The narrator observed a half-ruinous tower with cracks in its walls while passing through a village. Children from the village accompanied the narrator and others, begging for money. The narrator and the group arrived at the Lake of Thrasymene between five and six o'clock. The landscape around the lake included high hills and a mountain, with fertile land covered in wheat-fields, vines, and olives. The town of Passignano had a narrow street along the shore of the lake, described as dirty and ugly. The narrator encountered a large number of beggar-children during a walk through the village. The villagers, including old and young women, were observed asking for alms.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The text describes a visit to Llandudno, a watering-village at the base of the Great Orme's Head. An omnibus was taken to Llandudno, which is four miles away from the starting point. The group encountered two girls speaking Welsh on the omnibus, one of whom was reading Tupper's 'Proverbial Philosophy.' The group ascended the Great Orme's Head, where they found an old mine shaft and observed the view from the hill. Visitors were seen riding donkeys to ascend the hill, and the area was noted for its yellow gorse and harebells. After descending, the group had lunch at a confectioner's shop and visited a village bazaar. The group returned to Conway to visit the interior of Conway Castle, which is described as perfect in its style and purpose.

An attendant accompanied the travelers instead of the host, who showed them a picture of Rienzi, a former prisoner. A vase containing silver coins was placed beneath the picture, suggesting a customary fee deposit. The travelers stayed at Hotel de l'Europe and visited the Rocher des Dons daily. The old church at Rocher des Dons features heavy arches and a vaulted roof. Old women regularly pray together at the church, sometimes making a pilgrimage from chapel to chapel. A race day in Avignon attracted a large crowd, including a young man with a wooden leg. The streets of Avignon are crooked and paved with round pebbles, contributing to uncomfortable walking.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The text describes a visit to a museum where various historical artifacts and specimens were observed. The narrator expresses a preference for scattering ashes of the deceased over land rather than storing them in urns. The narrator reflects on the idea of leaving a clean world for future generations. The narrator visits St. John's Wood, a suburb inhabited by the middling class. The narrator discusses perceived financial meanness among the English with Mrs. Oakford and Miss Clinch. Mr. Oakford arrives after being caught in a heavy rain shower while traveling by omnibus. The narrator visits the Houses of Parliament, noting its immense size and unfinished exterior.

The text describes a public promenade near a cathedral. The narrator searched for Petrarch's house, which is located nearby. Petrarch's house is two stories high, covered with light-colored stucco, and lacks an appearance of antiquity. A well, mentioned by Boccaccio, is located opposite Petrarch's house and is octagonal in shape. The narrator found the cathedral to be stately with great arches and beautiful painted windows. The narrator and companions lost their way while returning to the hotel and had to return to the cathedral for a fresh start. The painted windows of the cathedral are described as more brilliant than those seen in England.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The subject of the text has an oil painting and a crayon sketch of himself displayed in his parlor and drawing-room, respectively. The government has awarded him a pension of fifty pounds for his poetic merit. He has received favorable notices of his poems from American newspapers following a recent publication. The Exhibition contains about a third of the good pictures available in England, with contributions from Tory nobility and gentry. Certain painters, such as Vandyke, Rembrandt, and Rubens, are well represented in the Exhibition. The author dined with Mr. F. Heywood and met Mr. Adolphus, who has written a critical work on the Waverley Novels. The author expresses a desire to leave England and seek another environment.

The river mentioned is the St. Lawrence, which flows through several English lakes and carries off their excess waters. The church of Grasmere is a plain structure with a low body and a small porch with a pointed arch. The churchyard contains the grave of William Wordsworth, which is marked by a simple slate slab. Hartley Coleridge is buried near Wordsworth, with his grave marked by a marble stone. The churchyard is small and contains mostly slate headstones, with grass recently mowed. The graves of Wordsworth and his family are closely situated together in the churchyard. The narrator and a companion searched for the post-office in the town of Grasmere without success.

The text describes a visit to Hampton Court, highlighting various artworks and historical artifacts. Vandyke's picture of Charles I. made a significant impression on the observer. The observer mentions seeing works by Sir Peter Lely, Kneller, Titian, Rubens, and West in the galleries. The observer recalls a humorous depiction of the Resurrection and Last Judgment. The funeral canopy of the Duke of Wellington and the state bed of Queen Anne are noted as impressive artifacts. Raphael's cartoons are described as faded and not particularly appealing to the observer. The visit concluded with a walk through Bushy Park and passing through villages, including Twickenham.

On August 27th, steamboats to Rock Ferry were crowded with large parties of people from Liverpool. Two bands of music in uniform were playing in competition in the hotel coach-yard. The attendees were drinking coffee from blue earthen mugs that they brought with them. The weather included rain at the time of arrival, but the sun later shone intermittently. The men were generally dressed in dark clothes, while the women wore shabbily dressed cotton gowns and bonnets. On August 29th, a walk to Bebbington took place on a fine afternoon with bright sunshine. The walk included views of a centuries-old cottage and a village with narrow streets and a notable almshouse.

The author describes their experience with various fruits in Italy, including grapes, figs, pears, and peaches. The figs initially lacked sweetness and resembled decaying squash, but later varieties became sweeter as they ripened. The author notes that the fruit quality in Italy does not surpass that of New England summers and autumns, except for figs and grapes. The author expresses discomfort with mosquitoes in Italy, describing them as larger and more aggressive than American mosquitoes. The author recounts an incident where a mosquito flew into their mouth and stung their throat. The author visited the Uffizi gallery and expressed a preference for it over the Pitti Palace gallery. The author finds the combination of painting, sculpture, gems, and bronzes in the Uffizi gallery particularly appealing.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: Raleigh was asleep when the narrator and others entered a dark room without windows. The room contained instruments of torture brought by the Spaniards during the Armada and a depiction of Queen Elizabeth on horseback. A headsman's block used for the execution of the Scotch Lords Kilmarnock and Lovat was present in the room. The White Tower housed the Regalia, including Edward the Confessor's golden staff, under glass and in an iron cage. The Beauchamp Tower contained inscriptions and sculptures made by state prisoners, illuminated by small lancet windows. The ancient moat surrounding the fortress has been drained and now forms a hollow space with grassy banks. The narrator and others traveled along Thames Street towards London Bridge, passing through a fish market.

The guide provided information about the cathedral based on knowledge acquired from archaeologists. The Yacht Inn was the principal inn of Chester and hosted Jonathan Swift during his travels. The landlord of the Yacht Inn described the affable nature of Chester residents towards visitors. The Yacht Tavern is an old house built in the gabled style with sound timbers and framework. The Bishop's house in the same street features curious sculptures depicting Scriptural scenes. An antique staircase leads to a gallery in the county court, which is described as ancient and dusky. A Kentucky man, over seventy years old, has been visiting and is involved in coal and iron mining.

The Cambridge men beat the Oxonians in this year's trial. Christ Church is the most considerable college of the University of Oxford in terms of student numbers. Dr. Pusey is a canon at Christ Church. The cross on the pavement is supposed to mark the spot where bishops were martyred, but this has been disputed. St. John's College has beautiful gardens with ancient trees and sunny glimpses through leafy branches. The hall at Christ Church is over a hundred feet long and features a carved oaken roof. The hall contains portraits of illustrious personages who were members of the college, with specific rules regarding their admission.

Lord Belhaven is depicted reclining with a bruised nose. The vault near the high altar in Westminster Abbey is empty of remains. The old Scottish kings were likely removed from their burial site during the Revolutionary movements at the accession of William III. High Street in Edinburgh features tall houses that are seven stories high. The house of John Knox is among the antique houses in Edinburgh that are still in good repair. The Grass-Market is the site of the Porteous Mob, marked by a cross in the pavement. Edinburgh Castle is accessible to any peaceable person and contains dwellings for officers and accommodations for soldiers.

The text describes a visit to Kenilworth Castle, where schoolboys were present and the atmosphere was cheerful due to shouts and sunshine. The author notes that a castle, such as Kenilworth, is less interesting as a ruin compared to an abbey, which was built for beauty and has a more graceful decay. The ruins of Kenilworth Castle are extensive but have been diminished by the removal of structures for building houses and roads. During the visit, the author and companions identified various parts of the castle using a guide-book and observed the remains of the moat and Lin's Tower. The author mentions visiting a church with a venerable exterior that has been modernized and lost its original beauty, along with the uninteresting remains of a Priory. The author traveled from Rugby to Liverpool and describes Mr. T------, a young man with extensive travel experience and a recently published book. Mr. T------ is characterized as a fluent speaker with a tendency to discuss political matters and revolutions, and he is considering settling in London.

The author expresses a heightened interest in watching the stars on September 29th. Mr. Powers discussed his treatment by the government regarding a $25,000 appropriation for a statue. The payment and purchase of the statue were left to the discretion of the President. The author criticizes the government's approach to art and public commissions, suggesting it is influenced by political connections. Mr. ------, an artist from Florence, described Home as a knave but acknowledged his perplexity at Home's performances. Mr. Powers invited the author to visit the Grand Duke's new foundry to see a bronze statue of Webster. The statue of Webster is eight feet high and was noted for its perfect likeness and natural costume.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: Dr. ------ received flowers and a potted plant. The narrator attended a dinner hosted by the Lord Mayor. The narrator observed a young lady with a unique complexion and raven-black hair at the dinner. The narrator felt a simultaneous admiration and repugnance towards the young lady, whom he perceived to be a Jewess. The next day, the narrator had lunch with Bennoch and accompanied him to a government office in Downing Street. Bennoch was involved in a matter related to a monument for Miss Mitford, which lacked public enthusiasm. The narrator visited the House of Commons and noted the appearance of its members, finding them less impressive than expected.

A woman was observed confessing for nearly an hour before a priest exited the confessional looking weary. Another woman was seen confessing for a long time, with the priest barely listening behind the curtain of the confessional. The act of confession is described as tedious for priests, who often hear minute and commonplace sins. After her confession, a woman sat on a bench with a straw hat and appeared comforted by receiving absolution. An old woman in the cathedral asked for a donation from the observer after speaking to the woman who had just confessed. The observer noted that many people attended the cathedral, some in their best attire and others in simple work clothes. A father was seen teaching his young sons how to use holy water at the cathedral.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: There are two dead pine-trees in front of the hotel, which appear to be alive due to ivy-vines growing around them. The trunks of the ivy-vines are more than a foot in circumference. On July 19th, S----- took U----, baby, and nurse to Newby Bridge by steamboat. J----- and the narrator walked to Bowness, passing through woods and hills. Bowness is described as a bustling harbor with an old church and several large hotels. The narrator met Miss Charlotte Cushman at the Lowwood Hotel. The road to Rydal passed through Ambleside, where Miss Martineau's residence, 'The Knoll,' is located.

The cardinals entered the chapel with a page holding up each of their purple trains. Singing and chanting were heard from within the chapel. A bulky old lady in black, identified as the Queen of Spain, entered the chapel. The narrator attempted to exit through the Scala Santa but was turned back by a sentinel. The narrator found themselves in a long gallery with numerous inscriptions in Greek and Latin. A French gentleman informed the narrator that the custode would admit them to the sculpture department of the Vatican. The narrator observed the extent and beauty of the Vatican, including its courts and views of Rome.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The event took place in Liverpool on a fine, sunny day with dry streets. The procession consisted mainly of ordinary-looking individuals in great-coats and umbrellas. The Bishop of Chester and Sir Henry Smith were the only individuals in distinctive attire. Mr. Browne, the central figure of the ceremony, was described as a plain and unpretentious man. The corner-stone of the projected edifice was a large square of red freestone with a brass plate inscription. The ceremony included a prayer from the Bishop of Chester and speeches from several distinguished guests. The banquet that followed was a cold collation served to approximately nine hundred people.

The factory described has four or five stories with rows of machines producing delicate ribbons. A manufacturer pays 500 pounds annually to French artists for new ribbon patterns. The English struggle to produce tasteful ribbon designs compared to the French. Coventry is a town of considerable size that is rapidly increasing. Trinity Church has undergone renovation, restoring some of its beauty but impairing its ancient character. The churches visited had worn tombstones and faded frescoes, with little impressed by their renovations compared to Italian churches. Mr. B------'s house is located on the outskirts of the city in a windy area.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The lodgings at Chorlton Road were described as small, mean, uncomfortable, and unbeautiful. The view from the parlor windows was of a large mud-puddle on a vacant building-lot. The air quality in Manchester negatively affected the narrator's wife's throat. The narrator and his family left Manchester for Leamington, where Fanny had secured lodgings. Leamington was described as clean and well-structured, contrasting sharply with Manchester. Kenilworth is located less than five miles from Leamington and has between three and four thousand inhabitants. The entrance to Kenilworth Castle was historically beneath an arch that has since been converted into a residence.

The text describes various objects including old earthen jugs, flasks, a brass kettle, and old books being examined. The representation of these objects is noted for its fidelity and boldness, contrasting with the work of other Dutch masters. The author visits the convent of San Miniato, located on a hill outside of the Porta San Gallo. The convent features a high wall that is ancient and covered in ivy, resembling a fortress. Inside the church, there are masons working on the pavement, and the interior includes Gothic monuments and ancient carvings. The author expresses a sense of weariness towards famous artworks like Raphael's canvases and the Venus de' Medici. The text describes the beauty of the moonlight and the Val d'Arno, emphasizing the mist that enhances the valley's appearance.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The street features a church or basilica on one side and a fountain in the center. Fountains in the city are often large and elaborately designed, constructed under the orders of various popes. Fragments of antiquity can be seen built into walls, including churches that were once Roman temples. The sixteenth century appears close in time compared to older antiquities in Rome. Egyptian obelisks in the piazzas are considered more impressive than Augustan or Republican antiquities. The Corso street is narrow, averaging about nine paces from sidewalk to sidewalk, lined with palaces. St. Peter's Basilica has a warm atmosphere due to the heat retained within its massive walls.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: Mr. and Mrs. Story accompanied the narrator to look for lodgings in Siena. Siena is located on the site of an extinct volcano and features narrow streets and tall ancient palaces. The city of Siena is described as picturesque, with Gothic architecture and old stone balconies. The narrator and a companion visited the cathedral and the Piazza del Campo in Siena. The narrator's lodging is in a palace with a frescoed ballroom and spacious accommodations. The narrator observed that public officials in Siena are courteous and willing to assist. The narrator noted that the city is not extensive and that the interest in its old town may be limited for travelers.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: A round block of marble was found and placed upon the neck of the Venus de' Medici statue, revealing a nearly complete head and face. The newly discovered head is described as superior to the existing head of the Venus de' Medici statue. The eyes of the newly discovered head are well opened, contrasting with the smaller eyes of the Venus de' Medici. The proprietor of the vineyard where the statue was found is optimistic about making a fortune from it and is awaiting a bid from the Papal government. The statue is made of Greek marble and was first found about eight days prior to the inspection. A wine shop has opened on the premises to accommodate the influx of visitors to see the statue. General Pierce left Rome for Venice on April 19th, while the narrator had to remain due to a friend's illness.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The narrator followed a road around the exterior of the city wall. The city wall is described as fifty feet high with towers and buttresses. The gate of San Giovanni is located near the Basilica of St. John Lateran. A French sentinel was present at the gate of San Giovanni. The Palazzo Borghese was built around 1590 and is situated near the Corso. The picture-gallery in the Palazzo Borghese occupies part of the ground-floor. Visitors and artists were present in the Palazzo Borghese, with some making copies of famous paintings.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The chapel contains painted windows from the time of James I, featuring large, expressive figures of Scriptural people. Gray's Inn is located near Holborn and features multiple quadrangles and a large area of greensward. Staple Inn has a front with four or five ancient gables and leads to a paved quadrangle. The crowd near Charing Cross was composed mostly of well-dressed people, largely women, due to the opening of Parliament by the Queen. The Horse Guards were drawn up outside the Whitehall Gateway, featuring a regiment of black horses and burnished cuirasses. An open carriage, belonging to the Queen, was seen passing through the Whitehall Gateway. The author visited the British Museum on a muddy day and has become more familiar with its collection over time.

The island experiences a variety of weather conditions that are more common than in America. The landscape near Oxford features green hedges and golden grain-fields. Mr. Frank Scott Haydon discovered a historical figure named Henry Atte Hawthorne in a record from the first Edward III. On August 21st, the narrator took a steamer from the pier-head to Runcorn. The river Mersey is characterized by a persistent northeast breeze. The shores of the river near Runcorn are described as level and monotonous, with few notable features. Runcorn is depicted as a shabby town with manufacturing chimneys and irregular streets.

The narrator wandered about the city and became lost near Holborn. The narrator attended a performance of Louis XI at the Princess's Theatre featuring Charles Kean. On April 1st, the narrator visited the National Gallery before traveling to Aldershott Camp. Lieutenant Shaw of the North Cork Rifles received the narrator and Bennoch at Tamborough and escorted them to his quarters. Aldershott Camp consists of numerous wooden barracks arranged in regular streets on a bleak heath. The narrator dined with the officers of the North Cork at the regimental mess, which was described as the most endurable place in camp. All officers of the regiment were Irishmen, and the narrator noted their hospitality and camaraderie despite their limited intellectual interests.

The church has a nave divided from side aisles by columns and features a wide interior. A statue of Moses is located in a niche in one of the side aisles on the right, near the high altar. The statue of Moses has two small horns on its forehead and is described as a majestic figure. The church contains pictorial attractions, including a notable picture of Hope by Guido in the sacristy. Visitors observed French drummers performing in public grounds near the Coliseum. The weather during the visit was clear, bright, and warm, with a refreshing air. The family visited the Villa Borghese, which is located just outside the Porta del Popolo.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The ship has good ventilation, providing ample air for passengers in lower berths. Four to five hundred Liverpool merchants and their wives were invited to a dejeuner on the ship. The tables for the dejeuner were set between decks, where passenger berths had not yet been installed. The day was overcast, affecting the overall cheerfulness of the scene. The meal included cold fowl, rich foreign pies, and plenty of champagne and other wines. The narrator expressed annoyance at the prospect of giving a toast but found comfort in conversation with Mrs. ------. Rev. Dr. ------ made a speech expressing his positive feelings towards America and Cambridge University.

The old gateway in Southampton stands across High Street and is a notable historical feature of the town. On June 16th, the narrator traveled to Salisbury by train with S----- and Mrs. ------. Salisbury Cathedral has a spire that is four hundred feet high and is located in the center of the city. Salisbury is described as an antique city with more regular streets and more picturesque houses than Oxford. A clear stream runs through one or more streets in Salisbury, bordered with stone. Salisbury Cathedral is made of gray stone and is noted for its beauty and historical significance. The interior of Salisbury Cathedral lacks painted glass and has a light hue, differing from its original ornate design.

Dumbarton Castle has a long history and was first besieged by the Danes. Mary, Queen of Scots, was brought to Dumbarton Castle as a child before going to France. A large stone sun-dial in the fortress was made by a French officer during the Peninsular war. Dumbarton is a town of considerable size with commerce and manufacturing. The view of Dumbarton Castle from a bridge over the Clyde shows its two summits, one shaped like a pyramid. Loch Lomond is a narrow lake surrounded by steep and lofty mountains, extending thirty miles in length. The scenery of the Highlands is described as stern and impressive, with hard outlines and minimal foliage.

Several artists attempted to copy a picture but failed in essential points. The narrator's memory of the picture is somewhat enlivened but not distinctly clear. The narrator and their companion saw pictures by Domenichino, Rubens, and other famous painters in the Casino. In the garden, they examined statues and observed fish at the stone margin of the pool. They saw two infants of the Rospigliosi family, one playing and another sleeping on a nurse's bosom. The narrator visited the Church of St. Andrea, which belongs to a convent of Jesuits. The Church of St. Andrea is described as having an oval shape, two domes, and richly decorated interiors.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The narrator returned to the library with an older man who insisted on taking precedence. The older man is described as a kind old man, and the narrator expresses a belief in the kindness of the English aristocracy. Mr. Palfrey is in England to conduct research at the State Paper Office for a work he is preparing. Mr. Palfrey mentioned a letter from New England during the time of Charles II, which refers to Governor Bellingham and the narrator's ancestor. The narrator visited the Record Office and met Mr. Joseph Hunter, who provided old records for the narrator's family research. The narrator found the old records difficult to read and eventually gave up the search for their family name. The narrator traveled from Blackheath to London and then to Birkenhead, where they were received by Mrs. Blodgett.

The hotel is located in Edinburgh, a city known for its splendid scenery. St. Giles's Cathedral has been divided into three interior sections by the Covenanters. Short's Observatory is located near the entrance of Edinburgh Castle. The narrator observed a camera-obscura and a solar microscope at Short's Observatory. The narrator purchased a golden and amethyst-bodied cairngorm beetle with a ruby head as a gift. The old town of Edinburgh is situated on a ridge that rises to a castle rock. The valley between the old town and the new town contains various public spaces, including ornamental gardens.

The villagers had access to food from their gardens, including pigs, chickens, olives, and wine. The children appeared to be in good health, while some old women showed signs of distress. Three policemen intervened to disperse a group of beggars bothering the family during their walk. The inn of Passignano was described as a tall, dark old house with a brick-paved dining room. Dinner at the inn was plentiful, exceeding the family's expectations for food availability. The view from the window included Lake Thrasymene, illuminated by the moonlight. The surrounding countryside was fertile, featuring vines, wheat-fields, and olives.

source.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
source.title: Passages from the French and Italian Notebooks, Complete

text: The bargaining for a camel took place between Dick and the sheik. Dick insisted on a good Bisharin camel and refused to accept a baggage-camel. The driver expressed reluctance to waste a good camel for a blind man. Dick identified the camel by feeling its branded mark, confirming it was a Biharin. The camel was released and ran into the desert with its driver following. Dick mounted the camel and instructed the driver to proceed quickly. During the ride, Dick struggled with fatigue and attempted to stay alert.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The narrator describes a conversation with Dr. Heatherlegh regarding his health, focusing on the importance of the stomach. While traveling on the Blessington lower road, a landslide occurs, blocking the road. The narrator and Dr. Heatherlegh avoid potential danger from the landslide by stopping their rickshaw. Dr. Heatherlegh begins treatment for the narrator's ailments, which includes liver pills, cold-water baths, and exercise. After a week of treatment, Dr. Heatherlegh dismisses the narrator, stating he has cured most of his bodily ailments. The narrator expresses gratitude to Dr. Heatherlegh, who refuses payment and encourages him to pursue a relationship with Miss Kitty. The narrator feels revitalized and proposes a ride with Kitty after his recovery.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The warship Clampherdown experienced mechanical failures during battle. The crew of Clampherdown engaged in combat with a cruiser. Clampherdown was armed with an armor-belt but had vulnerable areas at the stern and bow. The crew of Clampherdown fought fiercely, reminiscent of naval battles from earlier times. The sinking Clampherdown carried a significant amount of steel before going down. The crew of Clampherdown successfully boarded and cleared the enemy cruiser. Seven men from the Bolivar returned to Sunderland after a challenging voyage.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The text discusses the moral implications of Indian racing. Shackles is described as a horse with unique physical characteristics and temperament. Shackles was sold raw and out of condition at Calcutta for Rs. 275. Brunt, a riding-boy from Perth, West Australia, learned to ride Shackles by sitting still. Shackles achieved fame across various locations, including Ajmir and Chedputter. The Chedputter racecourse has a peculiar echo effect due to its brick mounds. The mare named 'The Lady Regula Baddun' is mentioned as a competitor in the racing context.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Subadar Prag Tewarri placed the head of the Boh on top of a mound of trophies. The head of Subadar Prag Tewarri's son was placed below the head of the Boh. The First Shikaris returned to camp after the event. A widow in Chester mourns for her only son. There is a grave on the Pabeng River that the Burmans avoid. The Overland Mail is a service that operates in the name of the Empress of India. The Overland Mail must be delivered regardless of obstacles such as weather or terrain.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Dumoise received a telegram from Simla ordering him to go to Nuddea on special duty. There was an outbreak of cholera at Nuddea, prompting the Bengal Government to borrow a Surgeon from the Punjab. Dumoise expressed a desire to live and stated he had things to do. Ram Dass, a servant, pleaded with Dumoise not to go to Nuddea and expressed fear for his life. Dumoise went to Nuddea alone after giving Ram Dass his wages. Eleven days later, Dumoise joined his Memsahib, and the Bengal Government had to borrow another Doctor for the epidemic. The first Doctor sent to Nuddea died in Chooadanga Dak-Bungalow.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Mrs. Bent and her baby were brought to a house before she realized it. Bent was thankful for the move due to concerns about infection. Mrs. Hauksbee offered Mrs. Bent good milk and proximity to the Doctor. Mrs. Bent expressed bitterness about her friend Mrs. Waddy leaving her. The Doctor visited the house three times a day due to the child's illness. Mrs. Hauksbee took on the responsibility of caring for Dora Bent. Mrs. Bent panicked when Dora showed signs of choking.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Mrs. Mallowe confirmed that her relationship with a man is absolutely Platonic. Mrs. Mallowe indicated that she was responsible for the man's last promotion. Mrs. Mallowe warned the man against the Topsham girl and informed him of a private memo about him. Mrs. Hauksbee expressed interest in managing a mature, unattached man without flirtation. Mrs. Hauksbee claimed to have successfully caught the attention of Otis Yeere. Mrs. Hauksbee met Otis Yeere at a social event after their previous discussion. Mrs. Hauksbee stated that she found Otis Yeere lonely and unbefriended before their interaction.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Dick is tasked with delivering mules to the A. C. G. at Tanai-el-Hassan. An English subaltern inquires about Dick's actions while he is with George. Dick expresses concern about loading the mules for the train that departs at six o'clock. The subaltern mentions that the area has been experiencing disturbances from the Fuzzies. Dick has a touch of ophthalmia and is unable to see well. The subaltern observes that Dick appears to be down on his luck. Dick requests to ride in the fore-truck of the armoured train as a non-combatant.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Dick experienced a sense of urgency and anxiety about his creative work. He felt unable to paint soldiers due to the emotional weight of the subject matter. Dick expressed a desire for divine assistance during his time of waiting. He reflected on his artistic ideas, deciding to incorporate elements of Melancolia into his work. Dick wrote a letter to Maisie, focusing on her health while downplaying his own situation. He became absorbed in his creative process, forgetting his worries and the people around him. Dick aimed to evoke strong emotions in his artwork, particularly through the character of Bessie.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: There was a row in Silver Street near Dublin Quay between an Irish regiment and English cavalry. The conflict started at Reveille and lasted until dark. The first man dropped at Harrison's and the last in front of the Park. The English were too drunk to know what was happening, while the Irish did not care. The altercation escalated when someone drew a side-arm, resulting in a fatality. After the incident, many participants faced punishments while some were under guard. The text includes a section about the young British soldier and the challenges faced by recruits.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Blayne dined at the Judge's house. Anthony was called out during dinner. Mingle experienced stomach pain. Markyn is fresh from Simla and is described as fit. Gadsby is reportedly engaged to Minnie Threegan, daughter of a Colonel. Minnie Threegan is remembered as a small girl with red hair. Jervoise recalls meeting the Threegans and describes Minnie as having called him the 'Tick Tack Sahib.'

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Dick reflected on people he had previously exposed for his craft. He remembered Binat, an artist who spoke about degradation. Maisie accidentally smudged a wet sketch that fell into the ashes of the studio stove. Dick felt a mix of hatred and gratitude towards the red-haired girl. Dick had been working for three months on his art, which he felt cost him ten years of effort. Maisie followed Dick's advice to focus on her own work but showed no interest in his art. Torpenhow expressed disappointment in Dick's lack of productivity.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The Bisara is described as the only regularly working, trustworthy love-charm in the country, with one exception. The other love-charm is in the possession of a trooper of the Nizam's Horse, located at Tuprani, due north of Hyderabad. If the Bisara is not stolen but given, bought, or found, it will turn against its owner in three years, leading to ruin or death. The Bisara is currently safe on an ekka-pony's neck, inside a blue bead-necklace that protects against the Evil-eye. A dirty hill-cooly woman with goitre owned the Bisara in Theog in 1884 before it was sold to Churton, an Assistant Commissioner. Churton's collection of curiosities included the Bisara, which was sold for three times its silver-value. Pack, a disliked and small man, was hopelessly in love with Miss Hollis, who did not reciprocate his feelings.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: There were two pink Dominoes and one of them cloaked the spouse of Sir Julian House. Sir Julian House is described as old with gold hair and blue cerulean eyes. Boanerges Blitzen is a servant of the Queen who aspired to rise through writing. Blitzen's writing led to reprimands and a lack of promotion over seven years. Binks of Hezabad inquired about the low death rate in his district, attributing it to drains and sewage-outfalls. An incident involving a Commissariat elephant caused Binks to flee in fear. Binks successfully sought the City Elders to address a blocked drain after his encounter with the elephant.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Bishen Singh is a wood-carver who has a petition to make to Orde. Bishen Singh has a strong prejudice against Bengalis, which he expresses in Punjabi. Orde discusses the various racial and class prejudices present in India. Bishen Singh has worked in Calcutta and had Bengali carpenters as assistants. Orde points out that race-hatred is a significant issue in India. Bishen Singh is described as a poor man with no concern for political matters. Bishen Singh promised to execute a carved wooden doorway for Pagett to be sent to England.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Maisie and Dick had a conversation about a threepenny piece. Maisie expressed a desire for the day to be like it was always. Dick reflected on his feelings for Maisie and the hope for their future. Dick threw a piece of silver into the river as a prayer for Maisie's safety. Torpenhow was working on a manuscript while the Nilghai commented on it. Dick returned to his chambers feeling self-conscious but in a good mood. Torpenhow criticized Dick for not having written anything in several days.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The Boy experienced a transition from a sheltered life under his father's roof to a more chaotic and lively environment in India. He engaged in activities such as whist and gymkhanas, which he took seriously despite his inexperience. The Boy faced financial losses due to his naivety in gambling and betting on races. His emotional sensitivity led him to take his losses and experiences more seriously than others might. A remark from a woman affected The Boy deeply, contributing to his feelings of despair. He requested leave to go shooting near a Canal Engineer's Rest House, claiming he would hunt big game. The Major, concerned for The Boy, sought to check on him after hearing about his expedition.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Mrs. G. is in bed and appears to be very ill. Ayah expresses distress over Mrs. G.'s condition and urges Capt. G. to call the doctor. The doctor enters and assesses Mrs. G.'s condition, indicating there is a chance for recovery. Capt. G. is visibly affected by the situation and appears dazed. Capt. M. observes that Capt. G. has aged significantly in a short period. After five weeks, Mrs. G. is recovering and expresses relief at being back in her room. Capt. G. shows concern for Mrs. G.'s health and encourages her to regain her strength.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Moti Guj is an elephant who is deeply cherished by Chihun. Moti Guj lifted Chihun's brown baby into the air, prompting Chihun to offer food as a reward. Moti Guj requires only four to five hours of sleep each night. Moti Guj searched for Deesa throughout the night, fearing for his safety. Deesa returned to the plantation at dawn after being drunk and reported himself to the planter. Moti Guj responded to Deesa's call and quickly arrived at the planter's door. Deesa and Moti Guj expressed joy upon reuniting and proceeded to work together.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Tomlinson is confronted by a Spirit who grips him by the hair. They travel to the belt of Naughty Stars that rim the mouth of Hell. The Devil questions Tomlinson about his worthiness for Hell. Tomlinson reflects on his past sins and his love on earth. The Devil dismisses Tomlinson's claims of bravery and worth. Tomlinson admits to borrowing his neighbor's wife to commit a sin. The Devil orders his minions to deal with Tomlinson's presence.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Otis Yeere is encouraged by Mrs. Hauksbee to assert himself and seek opportunities beyond his current situation. Mrs. Hauksbee believes in Otis Yeere's potential despite his self-doubt. Otis Yeere has gained self-confidence and is recognized for his accomplishments in the wilds. He has successfully managed a Municipality and saved lives through his actions. Otis Yeere is knowledgeable about the Gullals, a tribe of hillmen near Sikkim. Mrs. Hauksbee has shared Otis Yeere's experiences and achievements with others, potentially exaggerating them. The narrative suggests that a man with the support of a knowledgeable woman can navigate social interactions effectively.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Dick established himself in quarters in Port Said. He spent his evenings on the quay and boarded many ships. Dick interacted with various individuals, including Englishwomen and army officers. He sought to document his experiences through sketches and writings. Dick received a telegram from Torpenhow in England urging him to return. He deposited half of his funds with Monsieur and Madame Binat. A dance was held at Madame Binat's house featuring Zanzibari girls.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The speaker expresses a desire to be in a cleaner, greener land rather than where they currently are. The speaker mentions the old Moulmein Pagoda and the sea in relation to Mandalay. The speaker refers to the ship Malabar in harbor with the Jumner. The speaker indicates that they are returning home after a period of service. The speaker reflects on the conditions faced by soldiers, including cold and pneumonia. The speaker recalls a mate left by the ford of the Kabul river. The speaker describes Kabul town as a difficult place and expresses a strong emotional connection to a fallen comrade.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Mr. Beeton expresses concern for Dick's situation and suggests his son Alf could read to him. Dick agrees to let Alf read the newspapers to him and sing a song. Alf is described as a proud child with school-board certificates for good conduct. After reading to Dick, Alf returns home looking pale and scared. Alf reports that Dick praised his reading but expressed dislike for the newspaper content. Mr. Beeton speculates that Dick's discontent may be related to financial losses. Dick reflects on his mental state and contemplates the seriousness of his situation.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Capt. G. expresses a desire to help Minnie and states he would die for her. A voice, presumably Minnie's, mentions that there is enough death already and pleads for Pip not to die. The voice reflects on their marriage and expresses regret, asking for forgiveness. Capt. G. reassures the voice that there is nothing to forgive. The voice expresses a desire to be remembered and loved until the end. The voice questions the truth of the phrase 'Till Death do us part' and expresses confusion. The voice indicates a sense of impending departure and mentions feeling choked.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Miss T. and Miss D. discuss the placement of a string and the appearance of May Olger. Captain Gadsby is referred to as the Captain Sahib and is going for a ride with Mamma. Miss T. is instructed to bring Captain Gadsby some tea and is concerned about her appearance. Captain Gadsby is described as a big yellow man with an enormous moustache. Miss D. mentions that May Olger said being kissed by a man without a waxed moustache is undesirable. Miss T. expresses disdain for May Olger and prepares to meet Captain Gadsby. Captain Gadsby and Miss T. engage in a conversation where both struggle to find topics to discuss.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Henry Augustus Ramsay Faizanne is referred to as 'The Worm'. The 'Shikarris' is a high-caste regiment that requires members to have specific skills. The Worm struggled to fit in with the 'Shikarris' and did not excel in their activities. The Senior Subaltern was critical of The Worm and made his life difficult. The Worm made a bet with the Senior Subaltern, promising to pull a memorable prank. The Senior Subaltern was engaged to a girl who was in love with him. The Worm preferred to write letters home rather than socialize with the Mess.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Carnehan presented the dried head of Daniel Dravot to the narrator. Daniel Dravot was once referred to as the King of Kafiristan. Carnehan expressed a desire to go to the Deputy Commissioner for assistance. Carnehan was described as a crooked man crawling along the roadside. Carnehan was admitted to the Asylum suffering from sunstroke and died shortly after. Charlie Mears was a twenty-year-old bank worker from north London. Charlie Mears was the only son of a widow.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Lispeth played with an old puzzle-map of the World in the House when she was a child. Lispeth attempted to imagine where her Englishman was and made daily pilgrimages to Narkunda to see if he was coming. The Englishman had no intention of returning to marry Lispeth and forgot about her while butterfly-hunting in Assam. The Chaplain's wife informed Lispeth that the Englishman had only promised his love to keep her quiet and was engaged to a girl of his own people. Lispeth rejected the Chaplain's wife's explanation and decided to return to her own people, stating that Lispeth had been killed. Lispeth married a wood-cutter who beat her, and her beauty faded over time. Lispeth was an old woman when she died and could sometimes recount the story of her first love-affair when drunk.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The conversation involves two characters, referred to as HE and SHE. SHE expresses a desire for russet gowns and questions HE about future gifts. HE mentions spending two days and two nights on a train to meet SHE. SHE refers to a past location called Shaifazehat and questions its current state. Captain Congleton is mentioned as someone SHE dances with and considers for escort. SHE expresses concern about HE's trust and confidence in her. The dialogue touches on themes of trust, jealousy, and past relationships.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: There is a gathering of correspondents in Torpenhow's room to discuss military operations. Torpenhow, the Keneu, and the Nilghai invited all the men they had worked with to the gathering. Dick is feeling perplexed by the noise from the gathering and prefers to be alone. Dick's dog, Binkie, enters the studio and settles on Dick's lap. Torpenhow informs Dick that he will be leaving for Brindisi the day after tomorrow. Dick expresses relief at Torpenhow's departure, indicating a desire for solitude.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: There are approximately sixty thousand individuals in the province described as criminal or vagabond. The youth, Mr. Dma Nath, is a second-year student at Mission College. Mr. Dma Nath's father is a writer at Shershah and is seeking promotion. Mr. Dma Nath believes the National Congress movement is significant and involves educated individuals. Mr. Dma Nath's mother does not have strong political ideas, and his father is of the Kayeth caste. Mr. Dma Nath expresses a desire for advancements in sciences, arts, and industrial development. The college has a debating club where they elect a Mr. Speaker.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The Regiment was ordered to water their horses at the squadron troughs located behind the stables. There were four troughs arranged in a line, allowing the entire Regiment to water in ten minutes. The Band played while the squadrons watered their horses, which typically took seventeen minutes. A horse carrying a skeleton and kettle-drums approached the Band, causing panic among the troops. The horses reacted to the fear of their riders, leading to a chaotic stampede away from the troughs. The Colonel and most officers were unaware of the situation until they heard disturbances from the Mess. The panic lasted until the moon rose, after which the men returned to Cantonments feeling ashamed.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Mrs. G. asks Capt. G. about 'farcybuds'. Capt. G. provides a detailed and unpleasant description of glanders and farcy. Mrs. G. expresses discomfort and accuses Capt. G. of being horrid. Mrs. G. inquires about a letter she found with a big grey envelope. Capt. G. identifies the letter's sender as Mrs. Herriott, a former acquaintance. Mrs. G. recalls a conversation about Mrs. Herriott at a tennis event. The letter contains a congratulatory message regarding Capt. G.'s marriage.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Mrs. G expresses frustration about a letter from Harriet Herriott. Capt. G defends the letter, suggesting it shows motherly interest. Mrs. G believes Harriet Herriott is an interfering old woman. Capt. G asks Mrs. G to stop reading the letter aloud. Mrs. G becomes emotional and apologizes to Capt. G. Capt. G reassures Mrs. G that he is not angry with her. Mrs. G requests to go to her own room while seeking reassurance from Capt. G.

text: Pasha referred to himself as king and had witnessed the harsh conditions around Suakin. Torpenhow, wearing a flannel shirt, represented the Central Southern Syndicate during the campaign. The Central Southern Syndicate focused on providing detailed and picturesque accounts rather than addressing criticisms. Torpenhow encountered a young man sketching bodies on the battlefield, who claimed to be doing nothing specific. The young man, later identified as Heldar, produced various sketches of war scenes. Torpenhow arranged for Heldar to work with the Central Southern Agency on a trial basis. Heldar was accepted into the fraternity of war correspondents after completing financial and political arrangements.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: God has granted dominion and power. The ploughman is concerned with the wheat and believes the rest is the will of God. The Mahratta spear was sent by God and was broken in a fated year. The Ploughman acknowledges that God provides both good years and dearth. To-tschin-shu is condemned to death. The Undertaker's Horse is described as professional and placid. Jock Gillespie returned home after dinner and engaged in activities at the Club.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The narrator was aroused by their syce taking the Waler's bridle and inquiring about their health. The narrator entered Peliti's for a glass of cherry-brandy and engaged in conversation with others present. Kitty entered the shop and expressed concern for the narrator's well-being, prompting the narrator to lie about their condition. The narrator left Kitty to finish the ride alone and returned to their hotel to reflect on their experience. The narrator experienced a vision of a woman who had been dead for eight months, which caused them distress. The narrator sent a note to Kitty the next morning to apologize for their behavior and explained it as a health issue. The narrator and Kitty rode out together the following afternoon, with tension remaining between them due to the previous day's events.

source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The speaker identifies as a young Pagan who does not worship The Goddess. The speaker references The Rupaiyat of Omar Kal'vin and discusses financial issues related to debt and income. The speaker expresses a desire for charity and promises retrenchment in exchange for assistance. The speaker reflects on the nature of revenue and expenses, indicating a struggle with financial management. The speaker describes a surreal experience involving various bizarre observations and hallucinations. The speaker mentions being treated for a condition by a medical doctor and expresses a desire for a different treatment. The speaker concludes with a description of a chaotic experience involving the heavens and an incomprehensible voice.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Mrs. Hauksbee disliked Mrs. Reiver and viewed the situation as a trial of strength. Pluffles was initially loyal to Mrs. Reiver but gradually shifted his allegiance to Mrs. Hauksbee. Mrs. Hauksbee treated Pluffles well to gain his trust and confidence. Pluffles discussed his engagement to a girl at Home with Mrs. Hauksbee, referring to it as a 'piece of boyish folly.' Mrs. Hauksbee used a soothing tone to critique Pluffles' judgment and behavior. She suggested that marriage would improve Pluffles and painted an idealized picture of his future. Mrs. Hauksbee discouraged Pluffles from traveling to Bombay to get married.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Corporal Slane was engaged to be married to Miss Jhansi M'Kenna. Slane had his Colonel's permission for the marriage and was popular with the men. The wedding was planned to take place during the hot weather, after which Slane and his bride would go to the Hills. The other men in the barracks were generally miserable despite having free time after their morning work. The temperature in the barracks often reached 96 to 103 degrees, making it difficult for the men to engage in activities. Losson and Simmons had a contentious relationship, with Losson often bothering Simmons. Losson bought a parrot and taught it to insult Simmons.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Capt. M. and Capt. G. are discussing the behavior of a Captain of the Pink Hussars. Capt. G. expresses fear of being perceived as cowardly by his peers. Capt. M. suggests that Capt. G. should send his wife home for the hot weather and join him in Kashmir. Capt. G. acknowledges that his wife, Mrs. Gadsby, is well-regarded by the men of the Pink Hussars. Capt. M. implies that Capt. G. may have to sacrifice his military career for his wife's sake. Capt. G. feels that he is not entitled to expect more from his friend, Capt. M. Capt. M. predicts a mundane future for Capt. G. if he leaves the service.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The captain received credit for saving approximately twenty-five thousand pigs when a steamer collided with a timber-junk. The Nilghai is the chief and youngest of the war correspondents, with experiences dating from the birth of the needle-gun. Torpenhow expressed concern about Dick's growing reputation and the need to keep him humble. The Nilghai criticized a piece of Dick's work, calling it a chromo-litholeomargarine fake. Torpenhow mentioned that Dick has left war work and believes he is his own master. The Nilghai noted that some individuals respond differently to discipline, comparing it to horses. Torpenhow and the Nilghai discussed their past experiences with Dick and his behavior.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The text features a narrative involving a Rajpoot lord and a Thakur's sword. The character Abdhur Rahman is identified as the Durani Chief. The story describes Abdhur Rahman's mercy and justice in the Khyber hills. Yar Khan is mentioned as the Captain of the Guard and a bastard of the Blood. The narrative includes a scene where a hound of Hindustan is led out to die. The King of Kabul expresses his authority over the Afghan race. The story concludes with a warning from the King to Yar Khan regarding jesting with Kings.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Tods is a child who claims to know about Ryotwari. Ditta Mull is a character mentioned by Tods who expresses concerns about land tenure. Ditta Mull believes that the current land policy requires him to renew his papers every five years, which he finds troublesome. Tods translates Ditta Mull's thoughts from vernacular to English during his conversation with the Legal Member. The Legal Member acknowledges Tods' insights and considers them significant. Tods mentions that Ditta Mull has one daughter and expects to have a son soon. The Legal Member reflects on Tods' comments and concludes that the short tenure is a weak point in the land policy.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The Colonel was upset and felt mocked by his men. The Regimental Sergeant-Major reported to the Colonel and reassured him about the horses. The Colonel instructed the Sergeant to put the men to bed and prevent them from waking up at night. During a Commanding Officer's parade, the Colonel addressed the White Hussars and criticized their behavior. The White Hussars responded positively to the Colonel's speech, cheering for him but not for Lieutenant Hogan-Yale. Hogan-Yale received a letter from someone claiming to be the 'Secretary Charity and Zeal' regarding a skeleton. Bronckhorst was described as a middle-aged man in the Army with a coarse manner towards his wife, Mrs. Bronckhorst.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Daniel is in the calf of the leg and realizes the situation. Daniel sees the Army and recognizes them as Englishmen. Billy Fish decides to stay with Daniel and Carnehan despite the danger. The Bashkai fellows flee when Daniel and his companions approach the Army. Billy Fish is killed by the Army without any sound being made. Daniel is taken to a rope bridge over a ravine and is ultimately killed. Peachey is crucified between two pine trees but survives the ordeal.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Maisie plans to return to Kami's for a month to complete her picture. Dick expresses doubt about Maisie's artistic abilities and her commitment to her work. Maisie believes that a successful picture could draw attention to her other works. Dick is frustrated with his situation and feels undervalued in relation to Maisie. Dick intends to create his own version of a Melancolia to prove his artistic capabilities. Maisie and her companion discuss Dick's departure and her desire to talk about her picture. Dick is allowed to see Maisie and her companion off as they leave by the Dover night-boat.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Grish Chunder expressed excitement about a man he believed could see things through an ink-pool. Grish Chunder suggested pouring ink into the man's hand to reveal visions. The narrator declined Grish Chunder's suggestion, expressing concern for the past rather than the future. Charlie commented negatively on Grish Chunder's character after the narrator returned to him. Charlie shared a poem with the narrator, who preferred to read it silently. Charlie had been reading a book and was not pleased with the narrator's feedback on his poetry. Charlie explained that a scrawl on the back of the paper was not poetry but a form of blank verse.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Mrs. Boulte fainted after a conversation about her feelings for Captain Kurrell. Mrs. Vansuythen expressed anger towards Boulte and Kurrell during the incident. Boulte carried his wife into Mrs. Vansuythen's bedroom. Kurrell made a comment about his relationship with Mrs. Vansuythen. Boulte accused Kurrell of lying about his feelings for Mrs. Vansuythen. Mrs. Boulte had informed Boulte about Kurrell's statements regarding Mrs. Vansuythen. Boulte stated that his wife told him she hated him.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Dravot refused to stop singing and whistling despite warnings about avalanches. The group killed their mules due to a lack of food. Ten men with bows and arrows chased twenty men in a valley. Dravot shot at the twenty men, hitting one at a distance of two hundred yards. Dravot interacted with the ten men, eventually gaining their friendship. Dravot laid a rifle and cartridge at the feet of a stone idol named Imbra. Dravot was recognized as a king by the villagers and commanded their worship.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Hannasyde adored Alice Chisane and admired Mrs. Landys-Haggert for her resemblance to Alice. Alice Chisane and Mrs. Landys-Haggert were both married. Hannasyde felt conflicted about his feelings for Mrs. Landys-Haggert. Mrs. Landys-Haggert acknowledged Hannasyde's kindness and resemblance to Alice Chisane. Hannasyde expressed a desire to never see Mrs. Landys-Haggert again. A half-caste clerk believed that his work was crucial to the Treasury payments. Wressley was a man in the Foreign Office known for his extensive knowledge of treaties.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The characters are referred to as HE and SHE. SHE is sixteen years old and HE is twenty years old. HE has been waiting outside the school for two hours. SHE expresses fear about their relationship and the potential for mistrust. HE insists that he will not tire of SHE. SHE expresses a desire for time to think about their situation. MRS. BUZGAGO is rehearsing a solo for the Fancy Ball.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The Boy died of cholera while the narrator and the Major were with him. The narrator and the Major created a false letter to comfort The Boy's family. The letter described The Boy as virtuous and beloved by his regiment. The Major and the narrator consumed whiskey while writing the letter. They included personal items of The Boy, such as a watch, locket, and rings, in the packet. The Major cut off a piece of his hair to include in the packet as a substitute for The Boy's hair. They worked for four hours to dig a grave and performed a private prayer for The Boy.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The narrator experiences a feeling of being trapped in quicksand after stepping onto the sand. Gunga Dass, who speaks English, advises the narrator to return to his house due to the unhealthy conditions. Gunga Dass informs the narrator that the boat is only available during the daytime. The narrator awakens to the sound of a horse in pain and discovers his horse, Pornic, dead. Gunga Dass explains that the horse is considered better than a crow and mentions a political maxim about the greatest good. The body of Pornic is divided among the group, and Gunga Dass prepares a meal for the narrator. Gunga Dass indicates that another Sahib died in a burrow nearby, suggesting a grim fate for the narrator.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The text references a character named Snarleyow, who is a horse involved in a military action. The Driver's Brother is injured during the action and requests to be put out of pain. The Driver's Brother is ultimately run over by a limber after sustaining mortal wounds. The narrative suggests that serving the Queen requires soldiers to disregard personal ties and family. The Widow at Windsor is depicted as a powerful figure with wealth and influence over military forces. The soldiers are referred to as 'poor beggars in red,' indicating their status and sacrifices. The text emphasizes the importance of the military and the consequences of war on soldiers.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The Copleigh girls, Saumarez, and the narrator returned to the tomb after a storm. Saumarez appeared anxious and kissed Miss Copleigh in front of the picnic attendees. The picnic attendees were described as dust-white, ghostly-looking men and women under orange trees. Saumarez suggested that everyone should return home to avoid being searched for by the Station. The group rode home in pairs, with Saumarez accompanying Edith Copleigh. The narrator felt a sense of fatigue and shame after the events of the picnic. Pluffles was a subaltern in the 'Unmentionables' and was financially supported by his wealthy parents.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Mrs. Landys-Haggert is a woman of the world who does not understand Hannasyde's admiration. Hannasyde is a selfish man who takes trouble to meet Mrs. Landys-Haggert's wishes. Hannasyde enjoys Mrs. Landys-Haggert's company when she discusses trivial matters. Hannasyde is uninterested in Mrs. Landys-Haggert's personal views and experiences. Mrs. Landys-Haggert questions Hannasyde's motives for being her cavalier servente. Hannasyde admits he does not care for Mrs. Landys-Haggert, which amuses her. Haggert's Department orders him to move from Dindigul to the Frontier with little notice.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The narrator met Charley in a public billiard-saloon. Charley expressed a desire to pursue a literary career, focusing on poetry and stories. Charley had never fallen in love but was eager to experience it. Charley often visited the narrator instead of socializing with his fellow clerks. Charley struggled with his writing, expressing frustration over his inability to produce a satisfactory story. The narrator provided Charley with a space to write when he requested it. Charley believed his writing was better when read aloud than in written form.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Strickland participated in the Painting of the Death Bull at Jagadhri. Strickland spent eleven days as a faquir in the gardens of Baba Atal at Amritsar. Strickland was involved in the Nasiban Murder Case but did not gain departmental recognition for it. Strickland fell in love with Miss Youghal, who eventually reciprocated his feelings. Mrs. Youghal opposed Strickland's relationship with her daughter due to his job. Strickland took three months' leave for personal reasons and was later found working as a sais for the Youghals. Strickland's time as a sais was described as a period of rigid mental discipline.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The conversation involves a discussion about creating a story with a hero who saves a girl and marries her. The hero is described as a low political man with black hair who hides during fighting. There is a disagreement about the hero's hair color, with one character insisting he is red-haired while the other insists he is black-haired. The characters discuss the design of the ship, with one insisting it is open or half-decked. One character expresses a desire to submit an essay to Tit-Bits for a prize, while the other suggests focusing on the galley story instead. The narrator reflects on the limitations of their notes and the originality of their story ideas. The narrator concludes that the Lords of Life and Death would prevent any knowledge that could simplify the understanding of the past.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Mrs. Mallowe mentions that The Dancing Master has been spreading rumors about a woman's love for him. Mrs. Bent believes the rumors about The Dancing Master's relationship more than anyone else. Mrs. Hauksbee expresses her frustration until bedtime. Bobby Wick passes an examination at Sandhurst and is posted as Second Lieutenant to the Tyneside Tail Twisters. Papa Wick was a Commissioner in the Chota-Buldana Division and is proud of Bobby's achievements. Papa Wick advises Bobby to stick to his Regiment and avoid distractions from other duties. The narrative includes a reference to the social dynamics in a village where young men go to India for opportunities.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Moriarty expressed his feelings about Mrs. Reiver and his own troubles in a low whisper. Moriarty felt a significant influence from Mrs. Reiver and reflected on his own mistakes. After recovering from a bad attack of jungle-fever, Moriarty continued to spend time with Mrs. Reiver. Moriarty managed to control his drinking habits and did not drink alone. Moriarty believes that Mrs. Reiver saved him from ruin, despite her not being aware of his weaknesses. Reggie Burke was the manager of an up-country branch of the Sind and Sialkote Bank and was involved in a significant fraud. Reggie Burke was known for his ability to balance work with the frivolities of ordinary life.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: A woman attempted to poison a man with arsenic after he rejected her advances. The man had to control his emotions while witnessing flirtations involving Miss Youghal. He gained significant knowledge about the behaviors of saises and their thefts. He became a skilled player of knuckle-bones, a game played by jhampanis and saises. The man experienced frustration and amusement during his time in Simla. An incident occurred involving an old General flirting with Miss Youghal, leading to a confrontation. The General reacted humorously to the situation after learning the full story.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: McIntosh Jellaludin bequeathed his papers to a person referred to as 'the sahib.' McIntosh expressed a desire for his book to not die in its current form. He claimed that the book would make the recipient famous. McIntosh was in a deteriorating condition but continued to speak until he died. A native woman present was emotionally affected by McIntosh's death. Strickland assisted in sorting McIntosh's papers and suggested the writer was either a liar or a remarkable person. The bundle of papers contained disorganized content and required significant editing.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Dick was leaning over the Embankment wall, watching the Thames. Dick was reflecting on Torpenhow's advice while observing the faces of people passing by. Dick believed he could learn from the suffering of the poor and the wealth of the rich. Dick encountered Maisie, who had grown from a child into a woman. Maisie informed Dick that Amomma had died from over-eating. Maisie was busy painting and mentioned working under Kami in Vitry-sur-Marne. Maisie had a girl living with her and was not selling much of her artwork.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Moriarty had a sound constitution and a great brain. The government ordered Moriarty to Simla after he came out of the desert. Mrs. Reiver was in a position of power during the season Moriarty arrived in Simla. Moriarty was heavily-built, handsome, and nervous, often anxious to please others. Moriarty admired Mrs. Reiver, attributing virtues to her that she did not possess. Moriarty struggled with a personal vice that he kept secret from others. Moriarty experienced a severe episode of delirium tremens after a period of drinking.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Lispeth found a young Englishman who had sustained a head injury and brought him inside for care. The Chaplain attended to the Englishman, while Lispeth expressed her intention to marry him. The Englishman was a traveler from Dehra Dun who had fallen while searching for plants and butterflies. The Englishman was engaged to another woman in England and did not intend to pursue a relationship with Lispeth. Lispeth was emotionally invested in the Englishman, while he found their interactions pleasant but inconsequential. The Chaplain's wife advised the Englishman to tell Lispeth he would return to marry her. After two months, Lispeth learned that the Englishman had returned to England.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Maisie expresses concern about the nature of their relationship and work. Dick reflects on the challenges of an average man's life. Maisie believes Dick is better than she is in terms of patience and work ethic. Dick acknowledges that he could not have seen certain truths without Maisie's influence. Maisie shares her feelings of loneliness and past fears of poverty. Dick advises Maisie to keep her money safe and not to lend it to others. Dick's past experiences with poverty have deeply affected him.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Dick experiences a gray haze in his vision and attributes it to indigestion. Dick visits a local doctor who suggests he see an oculist for his vision problems. Dick believes the local doctor lacks expertise and seeks the best oculist in London. While waiting at the oculist's office, Dick recognizes a reproduction of one of his own sketches. Dick reads a verse from a Christmas-carol book while waiting for his appointment. During the examination, the oculist discusses Dick's condition using medical terminology. Dick concludes that the oculist's diagnosis indicates decay of the optic nerve and is likely hopeless.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Dick recognizes Cassavetti's voice and realizes there is a conflict somewhere. The Nilghai informs Dick that the trouble is in the Soudan. The group discusses various aspects of the impending war in the Soudan. Cassavetti reads an inaccurate list of troops amid interruptions. The Keneu introduces a new war artist to Dick. The conversation includes questions about troop deployments and logistics. Dick expresses a desire to join the others in the conflict.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Imray was last seen at his club in India, where he was alive and well. Imray did not appear at his office or on the public roads, leading to a search for him. The Indian Empire conducted inquiries into Imray's disappearance, including dragging ponds and plumping wells. Imray's possessions were sold after he was declared missing for several months. Strickland, a member of the police force, rented Imray's empty bungalow after several months. Strickland had a dog named Tietjens, who was believed by locals to be a familiar spirit. Tietjens played a significant role in protecting Strickland, including preventing an attack on him.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
