text: A blind beggar in the Punjab had a method of communication using a knotted twig and string. The blind man reduced the alphabet to eleven primitive sounds. Carnehan sent a letter to Dravot asking him to return due to the growing size of their Kingdom. Carnehan observed the priests at the village of Er-Heb, which had pending land cases and issues with men firing arrows at night. Dravot returned with an army and claimed to have conquered the surrounding area, wearing a gold crown. Dravot stated that he and Carnehan were gods and had established a connection with local chiefs and priests. Carnehan noted that the local chiefs and priests could perform a Fellow-craft Lodge but did not know the Third Degree.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The Colonel's son and Kamal engage in a conversation about the value of life and the consequences of their actions. Kamal expresses a desire to not speak of dogs when facing a greater threat. The Colonel's son insists on the importance of his father's mare and offers to fight for it. Kamal agrees to give the mare to the Colonel's son along with additional gifts. Kamal introduces his son to the Colonel's son, assigning him the duty of protecting him. Both men take an oath of brotherhood, solidifying their bond. They return to Fort Bukloh together, despite the tensions between their backgrounds.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The Colonel returned home late after his carriage driver got lost due to intoxication. Mrs. Larkyn found the Colonel's watch on her lawn after hearing a crash at two o'clock in the morning. Mrs. Larkyn decided to send the watch back to the Colonel's Wife without revealing the truth. The Colonel's Wife harbored strong negative feelings towards Mrs. Larkyn. The Colonel's Wife confronted her husband about the watch, but he denied any wrongdoing. The Colonel's Wife experienced jealousy and mistrust during her confrontation with her husband. The Colonel's Wife sought ways to influence her husband's behavior after their argument.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Trades, manufactures, and industrial arts are neglected and regarded with contempt by new literary figures. A young individual expressed a desire to manage steam-engines and factories without engaging in manual labor. Opposition arose against a proposal to establish an elementary technical school for workmen's sons, led by an individual with a college education. The Indian workman is expected to rise in social status despite opposition from the literary caste. New railway and factory workers in India are forming separate hereditary castes. The traditional habit of Indian people is to form self-contained family groups focused on their own interests. There are concerns about the size of the Indian army and its ability to manage various powerful minorities.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The scene takes place in the GADSBYS' bungalow in the Plains at 11 A.M. on a Sunday morning. Captain GADSBY is examining a complete set of Hussar's equipment spread over the floor of his study. Mrs. G. enters with her hand bound in a cloth, stating that she has scalded it over Tiparee jam. Captain GADSBY expresses indifference towards sweets and suggests that Hyder should look after the jam. Mrs. G. expresses disappointment that the jam did not set properly. Captain GADSBY is preoccupied with his work and asks Mrs. G. to leave him alone.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: A subaltern indicated that they had been trapped and expressed concern about the camel guns not firing. The men positioned themselves against the sides of the square to avoid being left outside during the fighting. The camel guns at one corner of the square began firing as the square moved forward to secure higher ground. An attack was launched by three thousand men armed with spears and swords against the square. The right flank of the square was identified as the weakest point by the attacking forces. The infantry fire was held until the right moment, resulting in significant casualties among the attackers. Dick, Torpenhow, and a young doctor moved towards the weakest side of the square as the fighting intensified.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The narrator experienced a period of emotional turmoil for seven days. On May 15th, the narrator left Heatherlegh's house at eleven o'clock in the morning. The narrator visited the Club where he learned that other men were aware of his story as told by Heatherlegh. The narrator felt a sense of alienation from his peers and envied the coolies on the Mall. While wandering down the Mall, the narrator encountered Kitty and a man on horseback. The narrator saw Mrs. Wessington, who appeared as she did when she was alive, carrying a cardcase. The narrator struggled to maintain his grip on reality by reciting the multiplication table.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Torpenhow entered the studio looking guilty. A girl was asleep on Torpenhow's sofa. The girl was in a poor condition, with a cheap sailor-hat and muddy dress. Torpenhow brought the girl to his rooms after she collapsed from starvation. The girl had previously worked as a general servant. The girl expressed fear of being harmed when Dick looked at her. Dick offered to call a policeman to help the girl.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Charlie Mears described a redheaded man who captured a galley. The redheaded man came from the north and sought free men as rowers. Charlie mentioned that the man had been to Furdurstrandi. Charlie referenced a poem by Longfellow about Othere, an old sea captain. The narrator speculated that Charlie might be recalling past adventures of the Vikings. The narrator expressed frustration over Charlie's selective memory and reluctance to share information. The narrator encountered Charlie again in Gracechurch Street, where he was focused on a billbook.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The administrative hierarchy in India includes the Viceroy at the top, followed by the Lieutenant-Governor, Commissioner, Deputy, and Assistant. The Secretary of State is responsible to the Empress, who is implied to have a higher authority. Aurelian is described as a young man who is considered an intellectual nuisance at the Club. McGoggin is portrayed as a diligent worker who struggles with his beliefs and the expectations of his role. The climate and work environment in India are said to discourage intellectual pretensions. McGoggin's excessive dedication to his work leads to warnings about his health from a doctor. The narrative suggests that McGoggin's efforts to improve upon orders may be counterproductive.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Mrs. G. expresses feelings of loneliness and a desire for more involvement in Capt. G.'s life. Capt. G. acknowledges Mrs. G.'s feelings and suggests inviting nice people to dinner. Mrs. G. feels that she is not a companion to Capt. G. and believes he prefers it that way. Capt. G. discusses the importance of lighter saddlery for cavalry equipment. Mrs. G. questions why Capt. G. is concerned about saddlery when he is not a trooper. Capt. G. explains that he commands troopers and is interested in improving their equipment. Capt. G. states that if they develop a lighter saddlery, it could be adopted by all regiments.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The tribes are positioned both behind and in front. Tommy experiences difficulties during the march. The camel is described as lying in the water-cut. Looting is referenced as a common practice among soldiers. The song discusses the challenges and rules of looting. Working in pairs while looting is advised for safety. The narrator shares experiences and advice on acquiring loot.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Dick experienced trouble with his eyes and visited an oculist. The oculist informed Dick that he was going blind due to a scar on his head and damage to his optic nerve. Dick claimed he could see better when he was drunk and expressed a need to complete his work before losing his sight. Torpenhow returned after a period of absence, and Dick felt joy and grief upon seeing him. Bessie observed Torpenhow and Dick walking together and expressed her disapproval of their interaction. Dick requested three more days to finish his painting, Melancolia, while struggling with his alcohol dependency. Torpenhow agreed to give Dick three more days to work on the painting but expressed concern for his well-being.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The text references a Russian post and a gray-coat guard on the Helmund ford. Mahbub Ali expresses uncertainty about warning a King of his enemies. Wali Dad is mentioned as a character who sought favor at the Kabul court. Wali Dad traveled to the gray-coat squadrons but did not find success. The King held a discussion with his Chief in War during a durbar in Kabul. Gholam Hyder, referred to as the Red Chief, reacts to Wali Dad's warnings with a smile. The ballad of Boh Da Thone describes a warrior who faced his fate at the hands of Harendra Mukerji.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Bessie expressed her preference for warmth, comfort, and freedom from fear of physical pain. Dick made two or three monochrome studies of Bessie's head. Bessie discovered disreputable socks in Torpenhow's room and planned to mend some of them. Bessie spent her time at home doing nothing and avoided interaction with other girls. Bessie preferred to stay in the studio with Dick rather than go out into the streets. Bessie was careful with Torpenhow's linen and occasionally spoke with him on the landing. Bessie made a supplication to Torpenhow, asking him to live with her until he found someone else.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: A girl was being prepared to marry the King in a temple halfway down a hill. Dan expressed his desire to take his own wife instead of participating in the marriage customs. The priest informed Dan that the girl was afraid and being comforted in the temple. Billy Fish advised that if the King could abandon the marriage, it would benefit all involved. Dravot, the King, insisted on proceeding with the marriage and called for the girl. The girl, adorned with silver and turquoises, appeared frightened and hesitant. During the interaction, the girl bit Dan, causing him to bleed.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Michele D'Cruze worked as a Telegraph Signaller earning Rs. 35 a month. Miss Vezzis's family valued their English origin and traced their descent from a mythical plate-layer. Mrs. Vezzis initially opposed the marriage of her daughter to Michele due to his family's background. Mrs. Vezzis eventually consented to the marriage on the condition that Michele earn at least fifty rupees a month. Michele was transferred to Tibasu, where he sent messages and thought of Miss Vezzis. A riot occurred in Tibasu involving local Hindus and Mohamedans due to a lack of authority presence.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The characters discuss the need for Mr. Heldar to improve his appearance. Bessie expresses regret for how she treated Mr. Heldar in the past. Mr. Heldar acknowledges that he looks unkempt and needs new clothes. Bessie offers to help Mr. Heldar by brushing and keeping his new suit clean. Mr. Heldar feels a sense of gratitude towards Bessie for her concern. After their meeting, Mr. Heldar decides to shave and buy new clothes. Mr. Heldar contemplates the possibility of paying Bessie to care for him.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: George and a group of assistants loaded mules onto a narrow-gauge armoured train. The train was plated with three-eighths inch boiler-plate and had two bogie trucks covered in plating. The leading bogie truck was equipped with a machine-gun muzzle, while the second had openings for lateral fire. Dick boarded the train as it departed, and the subaltern noted that they often faced attacks from the desert inhabitants. The train encountered an obstruction caused by sand and gravel on the tracks, resulting in a twenty-minute delay. The train eventually reached the camp at Tanai-el-Hassan after overcoming various difficulties. Dick expressed a desire to find food and was in search of George after disembarking from the train.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Kamartha stayed with Polder of Kumaon for six weeks due to rheumatic fever. Polder sends a box of presents and toys to the Ricketts every year. Heatherlegh, the Doctor, runs a hospital for incurables in addition to his regular practice. Heatherlegh believes that overwork is a significant cause of illness and death. Pansay died after suffering from overwork and a feverish chill. Pansay was engaged to Miss Mannering, but she broke off the engagement. Pansay wrote a manuscript about his experiences while he was in a high fever.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Namgay Doola is a villager who has been accused of conspiracy against the king. The king judges his subjects daily between eleven and three o'clock. A villager who conspired with Namgay Doola sought the king's favor after confessing. Namgay Doola has bound half his village by an oath of treason. Namgay Doola cut off the tail of a cow belonging to the villager who betrayed him. The kingdom was in an uproar over the sacrilege against the holy cow. Namgay Doola barricaded himself in his hut and defied the king's authority.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: A man receives a fatal bullet wound and experiences agony before redoubled firing occurs. Dick expresses a desire to be at the forefront of the battle despite warnings from Torpenhow. Torpenhow observes that Dick has gray hair at the temples and appears old. Dick falls from the Bisharin's saddle and dies from a bullet wound to the head. Torpenhow holds Dick's body under the protection of a camel. The text includes a preface addressed to Captain J. Mafflin by Rudyard Kipling. Miss Minnie Threegan and Miss Emma Deercourt are in a bedroom in Simla discussing a dance.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Dick was preparing for an expedition and was concerned about his appearance. Madame expressed mixed emotions about Dick's readiness for the expedition. The lighthouse boat took six days to reach Suakin, with two days wasted in the Canal. George was worried about the safety of his loved one and took Dick under his wing upon arrival. The new railway runs to Tanai-el-Hassan, seven miles from Suakin, where a camp is located. Dick expressed a desire to hear Englishmen talk, as he was known in the area a long time ago. George mentioned that only those who need to go to the camp would travel with the armoured train.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Dravot plans to run the country with the support of forty Chiefs. Dravot and Peachey establish a Lodge in the temple of Imbra. Dravot claims to be a God and a Passed Grand Master in the Craft during a levee. The priests and Chiefs are given names based on men known in India. An old priest discovers a Master's Mark on the stone used for Dravot's chair. Dravot declares himself Grand Master of all Freemasonry in Kafiristan. Peachey and Dravot raise high priests and Chiefs in a Lodge ceremony.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The characters are planning a trip from Tonga to Rome, with stops in Kalka and Umballa. The duration of their relationship is seven months and fourteen days. The characters express concern about the potential fallout from a scandal. One character feels that their social connections will amplify the impact of the scandal. The conversation touches on themes of love, societal judgment, and personal sacrifice. The characters discuss a recent wedding and the gifts exchanged. The setting includes references to weather conditions and locations such as Sanjaoli and the Mall.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Imray Sahib has returned from a long journey and is in the next room. Bahadur Khan killed Imray Sahib after believing he bewitched his child, who died of fever. Strickland witnesses Bahadur Khan's confession of the murder. Bahadur Khan expresses that he feels trapped and believes he will be hanged. Strickland orders policemen to take Bahadur Khan to the station. Bahadur Khan dies after being bitten by a snake. Strickland reflects on the situation, noting that Imray made a mistake.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The battle in India extended from the Dockyard Gates to the slums of Longport. Bobby Wick had an ugly bruise on his nose and was responsible for the comfort of fifty females. The Tail Twisters were described as a particular Regiment with a reputation for being protective. The Colonel commanding the Tail Twisters had previously questioned the competence of subalterns applying to the Staff Corps. Bobby Wick was taught that the Regiment was akin to family and that bringing shame upon it was a serious offense. The Regiment was noted for its excellence in shooting, drilling, and bravery. Bobby participated in a review with the Tail Twisters, which consisted of one thousand and eighty soldiers.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Torpenhow is a character who informs Maisie that Dick Heldar has gone blind. Maisie expresses disbelief upon hearing that Dick is blind. Maisie decides to go see Dick after learning about his condition. The narrative includes a red-haired girl who encourages Maisie to visit Dick. Torpenhow assists Maisie during her journey to Calais. A legend circulates in Vitry-sur-Marne about an Englishman and a girl eloping. Torpenhow reflects on Maisie's previous authority over Dick during their journey.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The narrator meets a wanderer who shares stories of his adventures in the Empire. The wanderer expresses a belief that if more people were like him and the narrator, India's revenue would be significantly higher. The narrator and the wanderer discuss politics and postal arrangements. The wanderer has eight annas for dinner and the narrator has no money due to a budget issue. The wanderer needs to send a telegram to Ajmir but cannot afford to do so. The wanderer asks the narrator to deliver a message to a friend at Marwar Junction. The narrator agrees to deliver the message for the sake of the wanderer's mother.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: A soldier's equipment is important for the soldiers. Capt. G. and Jack have been thinking about improving soldier equipment for two or three years. Mrs. G. expresses a desire to help Capt. G. with his work. Capt. G. prefers to work by rule of thumb rather than using a written list. Capt. G. has some involvement with sick horses. Mrs. G. is curious about Capt. G.'s papers and equipment. Capt. G. warns Mrs. G. not to investigate certain papers.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The text describes a conversation between two characters about a nightmare involving a galley ship. One character recalls being chained to an oar on the upper deck during a fight with another ship. The character describes the chaos of the battle, including being pinned down by other men and the breaking of oars. He mentions hearing the water sizzle as their rowers yelled and attempted to back water. The character describes a galley coming to ram their ship and the resulting crash that caused oars to shoot up through the deck. He recalls the sensation of water crashing down on them from the bulwarks during the fight. The conversation touches on the visual perception of water before it crashes, comparing it to a banjo-string drawn tight.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Three weeks passed without a sign from Bisesa. Trejago visited Amir Nath's Gully for the fifth time, hoping for a response. Bisesa emerged from the darkness with both hands cut off at the wrists. Trejago was attacked and sustained a wound to his groin. Trejago left Amir Nath's Gully and went home bareheaded as dawn broke. Trejago remains uncertain about the fate of Bisesa and the circumstances surrounding her situation. Moriarty, a Civil Engineer, developed a habit of secret drinking while working alone in an out-district.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The narrator agrees to the first terms proposed by Gunga Dass but refuses to give up his boots. The narrator believes that there is no law in the settlement except for the law of the strongest. The narrator resolves to maintain his health and strength until his release from the settlement. The narrator describes his sleeping conditions in a narrow den that smells abominably. The narrator experiences intense nervous terror during the night. The narrator considers the possibility of escaping by running past rifle shots. The narrator discovers that the boat is not present, providing him an opportunity for escape.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Miss Venner could not understand a copy of a text in Central India. Dumoise was the Civil Surgeon at Meridki and was nicknamed 'Dormouse' due to his sleepy appearance. Dumoise married Miss Hillardyce, the daughter of 'Squash' Hillardyce. Dumoise and his wife lived a secluded life after their marriage, rarely making friends. An epidemic of typhoid broke out in the Station during the cold weather, affecting multiple households. Dumoise delayed seeking help for his wife, who was suffering from typhoid, leading to criticism from Mrs. Shute. Mrs. Dumoise ultimately died from a relapse after the typhoid outbreak was initially managed.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The king lived on the road to Thibet in the Himalaya Mountains at an elevation of 11,000 feet. His kingdom measured four miles square, with most of the land being steep. The king's annual revenues were less than 400 pounds, which were used to maintain one elephant and a standing army of five men. He was tributary to the Indian government and received funds for road maintenance. The king sold timber from his forest to railway companies, using the deodar trees for railway ties. The king would ride to Simlatown to meet with the lieutenant-governor and viceroy regarding state matters. The king's palace was a four-roomed, white-washed mud-and-timber house.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The narrator hears sounds resembling a billiards game coming from the next room. The next room is too small to accommodate a billiard table. The narrator experiences intense fear and dread while listening to the game. The khansamah informs the narrator that the building was previously a billiard room for the Sahibs. The billiard room was used by the Sahibs who built the Railway. The khansamah recalls a fat, angry Sahib who requested brandy while playing billiards. The Sahibs who used the billiard room are all deceased.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The Vansuythens held a ceremony on the platform near Narkarra Road, which granted them freedom from the Station's rights and privileges. After settling down, the Vansuythens hosted a housewarming for Kashima, which made Kashima free of their house according to tradition. The Rains caused the Narkarra Road to wash away and resulted in cattle wading knee-deep in the pastures of Kashima. Boulte's behavior towards his wife changed to become more affectionate after the Rains, which startled Mrs. Boulte. Mrs. Boulte suspected her husband was being influenced by the Vansuythen Woman and felt troubled about her property, Kurrell. During a conversation, Mrs. Boulte expressed her feelings to Boulte, who responded with indifference and suggested she could leave with Kurrell. Mrs. Boulte remained in deep thought after Boulte left the room, reflecting on her actions and the state of her marriage.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: A woman is cleaning a samovar near a well in the center of the Serai. McIntosh Jellaludin has a native woman who assists him and has been with him since they met three years ago in Jullundur. McIntosh Jellaludin is described as a scholar and a gentleman when sober, but more of a scholar than a gentleman when drunk. He tends to get drunk about once a week for two days, during which the native woman cares for him. McIntosh Jellaludin has recited poetry in various languages while intoxicated. He expresses a sense of detachment from his drunken state, claiming he feels no consequences from his actions. McIntosh Jellaludin reflects on the nature of degradation and the relationship between the highest and lowest states of being.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Mrs. Bremmil mourned deeply after the death of her child. Bremmil attempted to comfort Mrs. Bremmil but it increased her grief. Mrs. Hauksbee, known as the 'Stormy Petrel,' arrived in Simla and became involved with Bremmil. Mrs. Hauksbee publicly spent time with Bremmil, causing gossip among others. Mrs. Bremmil chose to remain at home, grieving and reflecting on her child's belongings. Mrs. Bremmil decided to allow Bremmil to attend a social event without her. Mrs. Bremmil received a new dress from Phelps' shortly after making her plans.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Otis Yeere works in a swampy district with a native Assistant, native Doctor, and native Magistrate. Life in the district is described as cheap and characterized by high mortality and rapid population turnover. Otis Yeere feels thankful to take a break from his work in the district. Mrs. Hauksbee has developed a friendship with Otis Yeere and learns about his past life and aspirations. Mrs. Mallowe comments on Otis Yeere's relationship with Mrs. Hauksbee, suggesting that he has attracted attention. Otis Yeere feels a sense of vanity and self-worth due to his association with Mrs. Hauksbee. Otis Yeere gains self-confidence after receiving new clothes, which changes his demeanor.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Wressley was regarded as the foremost expert on the Central Indian States during his time. The Foreign Office and Heads of Departments often echoed Wressley's statements without contributing original thoughts. Wressley was recognized as a crucial member of the Foreign Office, receiving praise from his superiors. The Viceroy of India at the time was skilled at managing relationships among his team, including Wressley. Wressley's name and position were well-known in India, but few understood his personal life or contributions. Wressley fell in love with a girl named Tillie Venner, who was known for her lively personality. Wressley struggled to balance his work with his feelings for Miss Venner, which affected his performance.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: A man in tattered riding-breeches was sewing a square of coarse canvas over an open space. Twenty whale-boats were near a sand-bank with English soldiers bathing or washing clothes. A regimental carpenter was attempting to repair a whale-boat with insufficient white lead. The Nile was falling, making navigation difficult for the whale-boats. British troops were present in the desert, with more columns waiting to embark on the river. The river-column's duty was to keep the whale-boats afloat and avoid damaging villagers' crops. Correspondents of newspapers were present with the soldiers, often unaware of the overall situation.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Dick is concerned about a potential health issue that may lead to blindness within a year. Binkie is a dog that accompanies Dick and provides him with comfort. Dick reflects on the suddenness of his situation, comparing it to being shot. Torp is in the south of England inspecting dockyards and is unable to assist Dick. Dick feels he must face his challenges alone and cannot rely on others for support. Dick recalls a memory of a soldier in the Soudan who experienced a moment of comic bewilderment before dying. Dick expresses a desire to remain calm despite his fears about his future.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: A voice asked for the Senior Subaltern, Lionel. Four men reacted suddenly to the voice, three of whom were married. A woman entered the light, reaching for Lionel and sobbing. The woman claimed to be Lionel's wife and expressed distress over his letters. Lionel denied ever having a wife. The Colonel suggested they clarify the situation in the Mess. The woman accused Lionel of marrying her during his leave eighteen months prior.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Torpenhow expressed concern about the beginning of strife. Dick requested the return of his sketches from a man representing the syndicate. The man was surprised by Dick's assertiveness as an ex-employee. Dick accused the man of theft and expressed a desire not to harm him. Dick instructed the man to write a note to his office to return the sketches. Torpenhow confirmed that he retrieved one hundred and forty-seven sketches. Dick expressed satisfaction with the quality of his sketches after reviewing them.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Torpenhow shows Dick a large room that will serve as his studio. The room is located in the top story of rickety chambers overlooking the Thames. Dick observes the room has a skylight and a bedroom beyond. A middle-aged gentleman enters, introducing himself as the head of the Central Southern Syndicate. The gentleman claims that the syndicate played a significant role in promoting Dick's work. Dick requests to retrieve his sketches, which he believes belong to him. The gentleman informs Dick that the sketches are considered the property of the syndicate.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: A man expressed to Reggie that he believed he was going to die and requested his salary for September to be sent to his mother. The man reflected on his life, stating he had not committed serious sins and felt he had been preserved from them. The man died after speaking to Reggie, who then covered his face with a sheet. Reggie carried a letter of condolence from the Directors but did not use it. Tods was a six-year-old boy known in Simla for his fearless behavior and interactions with adults. Tods once disrupted a meeting of the Legislative Council while chasing his pet kid onto the Viceregal Lodge lawn. Tods was well-liked by the servants and had a significant influence in his household.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The text describes a march over the Grand Trunk Road in India. The march involves a regiment of eight hundred Englishmen. The march occurs around Christmas-time and just after the rains. The soldiers experience discomfort from marching and blistered heels. The narrative includes references to Indian temples, peacocks, and monkeys. The soldiers reflect on their friends in England during the march. The text mentions the camaraderie among soldiers and their activities during downtime.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The narrator experienced exhaustion and agitation from a previous day's events and the violent ride. The narrator attempted to escape the situation by running around the base of the crater and crawling to the riverfront. The narrator was shot at by rifle bullets and felt a sense of dread about facing death. Gunga Dass threw water over the narrator's head while laughing, showing a lack of concern for the narrator's condition. The narrator felt hungry and offered Gunga Dass four annas, which Gunga Dass insisted on taking. The narrator ultimately gave Gunga Dass all the money he had, totaling Rs. 9-8-5. The villagers showed indifference towards the narrator, and Gunga Dass provided him with food that included a chapatti and foul well-water.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The conversation involves characters discussing a woman who wore a lace tucker into her riding habit. The woman was seen riding with The Dancing Master and was described as looking unkempt. Mrs. Hauksbee ordered the Hawley Boy not to call on the woman, but he did so anyway. During the visit, the woman appeared lazy and unengaged, sitting on a couch and grunting. The Hawley Boy was noted to have giggled during the encounter, which Mrs. Hauksbee found inappropriate. The Dancing Master arrived shortly after Mrs. Hauksbee and the Hawley Boy left the woman's residence.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Janoo and Azizun informed that the jadoo-work was taking place in their rooms due to more space. Janoo expressed skepticism about the jadoo, suggesting it was a scheme to extract money from Suddhoo. Suddhoo exhibited signs of distress, repeatedly calling his son's name and questioning Azizun about the seal-cutter's actions. The seal-cutter entered the room after Suddhoo was instructed to extinguish the lamp, leaving the space in darkness. The seal-cutter was described as having a blue-gray face, rolled-back eyes, and a demonic appearance. A brass basin with a pale blue-green light was present in the center of the room during the seal-cutter's performance. The seal-cutter performed a crawling motion on the floor for ten minutes, causing distress among the observers.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The characters in the text include Bessie Broke, Dick, and Torpenhow. Bessie is offered three quid a week to sit for a drawing. Bessie lives in a one-room place that costs five and sixpence a week. Dick and Torpenhow discuss Bessie's potential transformation after being fed and cared for. Dick expresses a desire to use Bessie as a model for his work titled Melancolia. Bessie arrives for her appointment unpainted and begins to feel calmer as she sits still.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The Man's Wife received four-hundred-rupee bracelets and inexpensive luxuries from her husband. The Man's Wife and the Tertium Quid wrote to each other daily and rode to the Post Office together. Simla has peculiar customs that affect social relationships and friendships. The Man's Wife was perceived as kittenish and innocent but was also described as learned and evil-instructed. Women in Simla accused the Man's Wife of stealing their husbands, leading her to feel misjudged. The Man's Wife expressed concern about rumors regarding her relationship with the Tertium Quid. The Man's Wife's husband earned two hundred rupees a month and allowed her eight hundred and fifty.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Danny Deever is being hanged in the morning. Files-on-Parade and the Colour-Sergeant discuss Danny Deever's fate. Danny Deever shot a comrade while he was sleeping. The regiment is marching away after the hanging of Danny Deever. Tommy is denied service at a public house because he is a red-coat. Tommy is treated poorly in public spaces but is celebrated when the band plays. The poem reflects on the treatment of soldiers and their experiences.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Torpenhow suggested that Dick should pray to be delivered from arrogance. Dick expressed satisfaction with his recent success and desire for more. Torpenhow returned to his chambers after a holiday in the country. Dick sold all the canvases he wanted at his exhibition, referred to as the 'Wild Work Show.' Dick studied under Kami for two years in Paris, who taught by personal magnetism. Dick recalled vibrant colors from his time in the Soudan, describing them in detail.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The narrative involves characters named Torpenhow and Dick. Dick recalls a journey from Lima to Auckland on a condemned passenger-ship converted to a cargo-boat. The ship was owned by a second-hand Italian firm and was in poor condition. Dick describes the ship as having been previously used in the China passenger trade. There was only one other passenger on the ship, a woman who watched Dick paint. Dick's painting was inspired by the sea and the woman, and he used limited colors. The painting was large, measuring seven by fourteen feet, and was influenced by a poem by Poe.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Dick and Torpenhow worked closely together while traveling in Egypt. Dick obtained exclusive information from a telegraph-clerk while he was intoxicated. Torpenhow used the information to write a descriptive article. Dick and Torpenhow faced various challenges, including fear of being shot and dealing with difficult travel conditions. The camel-corps and infantry were alerted to a potential enemy presence while on the bank. The camel-corps did not engage in combat but waited for a square to form. Torpenhow noted the large number of armed men, suspecting they were associated with the Mahdi.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The character Dick expresses a realization about the presence of too much Ego in his life. Dick engages in various artistic activities before deciding to end his work for the day. Torpenhow observes that Dick has broken his usual routine and speculates about the reasons for this change. The housekeeper Beeton informs Torpenhow that Dick has not dined out while he was away. Beeton describes Dick's late-night activities and interactions with other young men. Dick reflects on his memories with Maisie while walking in the Park. Dick feels a sense of happiness and peace as he thinks about his time with Maisie.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Kitty prefers the company of Cubbon, a young man in a Dragoon Regiment at Umballa, over Barr-Saggott. Barr-Saggott organizes an archery tournament for ladies with a diamond-studded bracelet as the prize. The tournament is held at Annandale and is attended by the residents of Simla. Miss Beighton, Kitty, is anxious to compete in the archery tournament. During the tournament, Kitty performs well but engages in unconventional shooting techniques. Cubbon appears troubled during the competition, while Barr-Saggott is nervous and dressed elaborately. Kitty's shooting performance includes hitting the target multiple times, but she also aims at less valuable points.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The conversation involves two individuals discussing the nature of success and work. One individual expresses a desire for success and questions the validity of their work. The other individual advises that good work is influenced by external factors rather than personal effort. They discuss the importance of mastering one's craft and not focusing on success. The conversation highlights the idea that worrying about success can diminish one's creative power. The speaker reflects on their own experiences with the pressures of seeking recognition for their work. They suggest that true work should be done without the expectation of external validation.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The text includes a poem titled 'Victorian Ode' that addresses the Lord God of Hosts. The poem reflects on themes of power, humility, and the need for divine guidance. The text also features a poem titled 'The Vampire' that discusses the folly of unreciprocated love. The poem 'The Vampire' describes a fool who invests emotionally in a woman who does not care. Another poem titled 'To the Unknown Goddess' expresses longing and desire for an unknown woman. The speaker in 'To the Unknown Goddess' contemplates the possibility of meeting the woman and the impact she may have on his life. The text references Philip Burne Jones, who exhibited a painting in London in 1897 that inspired 'The Vampire'.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Pinecoffin is a Civilian and a farmer. Nafferton is interested in agricultural information and has a reputation for being earnest. Nafferton proposed a scheme to feed the British Army in India using Pig. The Government instructed Pinecoffin to provide Nafferton with information regarding Pig. Pinecoffin began researching various aspects of Pig, including its mythology and distribution. Nafferton requested additional information from Pinecoffin about swineherds and Pig in the Cis-Sutlej states. The Government eventually forgot their initial instructions to Pinecoffin.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The average age of marriage is seven, with many girls married even earlier. Girls as young as twelve and thirteen often become wives and mothers, leading to high mortality rates for both mothers and children. Consequences of early marriage include pauperism, domestic unhappiness, and poor health. Widows of boy-husbands face severe social stigma and may not remarry, leading to a life of seclusion or worse outcomes. The advanced political parties in India do not advocate for social reforms related to women's issues. Funds for medical aid to women in India are often redirected towards scholarships for men. The Punjab province contributed only about seven thousand rupees to the maintenance of civil dispensaries last year.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Bimi is described as being mad with jealousy. Bertran claims that Bimi is not mad and that he obeys and loves his wife. Bertran's wife is described as a very pretty girl. Bertran left his wife alone with Bimi in the garden. Bertran found his wife's bedroom door locked and broke it down. Inside the room, Bertran found no sign of his wife, only scattered items. Bertran eventually killed Bimi after making him drunk.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Phil was living comfortably and satisfied with his life in India. Phil decided to marry Dunmaya, a Hill girl, and they were married by the forms of the English Church. Dunmaya was described as an honest girl who adapted to English customs within six months. Agnes, Phil's former love, received a large income after her husband's death in Bombay. Agnes decided to find Phil and offer him her hand and wealth after her husband's death. Phil was working as an Assistant on a tea plantation near Kangra at the time Agnes sought him out. Dunmaya was making efforts to improve Phil's character, which was viewed as unfair by the narrator.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Capt. G. is working with leather equipment in the house. Mrs. G. expresses interest in what Capt. G. is doing. Capt. G. has a scar on his arm from a knife wound received in Afghanistan. Mrs. G. is concerned about the scar and asks how it happened. Capt. G. explains that he was attacked by a man while he was unable to run. Mafflin intervened during the attack and killed the assailant. Mrs. G. reacts with shock upon learning the details of the incident.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: The text references screw-guns and their association with the Army. The narrator describes walking with a mule and a group of seventy gunners. The narrator mentions climbing difficult terrains and engaging with various groups such as the Naga and Looshai. Gunga Din is identified as a regimental bhisti who served the narrator and his troop. The text describes the hardships faced by soldiers in India, including the need for water. The narrator recalls the treatment of Gunga Din by the soldiers, highlighting their reliance on him.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Captain Gadsby is introduced in a conversation with Miss T. Miss T. expresses her thoughts about Captain Gadsby and her mother. Captain Gadsby observes Miss T. interacting with her horse, Vermillion. Miss T. forgets about Captain Gadsby while attending to her horse. Gilded Youth interacts with Captain Gadsby, leading to a lecture on discretion. Miss Threegan and Miss Deercourt meet at the New Simla Library. Miss T. confirms her engagement and discusses plans with Miss Deercourt.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Riley was ill and expressed concern about the Bank's future without his presence. Reggie attended to Riley's needs and communicated with the Directors on his behalf. Riley received sympathetic letters from the Directors during his illness. Reggie paid Riley's salary out of his own pocket while he was unable to work. Riley's condition worsened over three months, but he remained mentally engaged. The Directors granted Riley a 25-percent salary increase as a form of mental stimulation. Riley continued to worry about the Bank and lectured Reggie on various topics until the end of September.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Maisie was busy packing her canvases and stripping a small house across the Park. Dick went to Dover and spent a day fretting over the possibility of getting a kiss from Maisie. Maisie arrived at the pier in a gray waterproof and a gray cloth travelling-cap. Dick and Maisie discussed their relationship, acknowledging that one of them would have to be broken. Maisie allowed Dick to kiss her, which turned out to be a long kiss despite her initial anger. Dick advised Maisie to be careful about drinking water in France and to write to him if she needed anything. The red-haired girl expressed her disapproval of Maisie allowing Dick to kiss her.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Strickland changed into decent clothes and prepared to confront Mr. Youghal. A sais at the Club requested decent clothes from the men he knew. Strickland managed to gather various clothing items and rode to the house of old Youghal. Strickland received moderate civility from Youghal and kindness from Mrs. Youghal. Strickland and Miss Youghal were married with the condition that he would adhere to Departmental routine. Miss Agnes Laiter cried as the Gravesend tender left for Bombay, feeling sorrow over her love for a man going to India. Phil Garron was sent to India for a position related to 'tea' and hoped to reform his ways and marry Agnes Laiter.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Saumarez was moving off to the habit when the narrator intervened. The narrator intended to fetch Edith Copleigh back after pushing Saumarez back. Edith Copleigh galloped away when she saw the narrator approaching. The narrator rode after Edith Copleigh through difficult terrain during a storm. Edith Copleigh expressed a desire to go home while crying and covered in dust. The narrator informed Edith Copleigh that Saumarez had something to say to her. Edith Copleigh had been present when Saumarez proposed to her sister.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: In Simla, 'Young' Gayerson and 'Very Young' Gayerson discussed the behavior of 'Very Young' Gayerson. 'Very Young' Gayerson expressed feelings of wretchedness and unhappiness. 'Young' Gayerson suggested that 'Very Young' Gayerson should cut his leave short and return to his duties. 'Young' Gayerson and 'Very Young' Gayerson visited the Venus Annodomini, who introduced her daughter to them. 'Very Young' Gayerson felt uncomfortable during the visit with the daughter of the Venus Annodomini. The Bisara of Pooree is described as a tiny, square box of silver containing a carved eyeless fish. The Bisara of Pooree is believed to have been stolen and passed through various hands before reaching its current location.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Gunga Din is depicted as a brave and selfless water-bearer during a battle. Gunga Din provides water to a wounded soldier despite the danger of gunfire. The soldier expresses gratitude for the water given to him by Gunga Din. Gunga Din is fatally wounded while helping the soldier to safety. The soldier reflects on Gunga Din's character and acknowledges his superiority. The poem also describes the challenges faced by soldiers waiting for supplies from the commissariat camels. The commissariat camel is portrayed as troublesome and difficult to manage during military operations.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Doone expresses feelings of physical and emotional distress. Blayne suggests that Doone should take leave from his duties. Anthony reports that Mingle is in poor health and frightened. Mingle has a bad stomach and is anxious about his condition. Anthony believes Mingle's anxiety could worsen his health. The group discusses raising money to help Mingle. Jervoise agrees to contribute one hundred rupees for Mingle's situation.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Sleary's fits is a poem that discusses themes of corruption and incompetence in railway management. Exeter Battleby Tring is portrayed as a knowledgeable railway engineer who is overlooked for a position due to not being from Chatham. The Little Tin Gods are depicted as corrupt officials who prefer to appoint a Colonel from Chatham over a qualified candidate. Delilah Aberyswith is introduced as a lady with a taste for fashion and a thirst for information, connected to powerful individuals. Ulysses Gunne is characterized as a writer who flatters Delilah and engages in questionable financial dealings. The poem suggests that Delilah learns a secret related to appointments from an Aged Councillor, which is implied to be treasonous. The narrative concludes with Ulysses and Delilah in a romantic setting, where Delilah reveals the secret.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Dick did not work for the rest of the week after a particular Sunday. Maisie ignored Dick's suggestions about line-work for her art. Maisie planned to send her new picture to the Salon with Kami's permission. Dick expressed frustration over Maisie's decision to pursue a new idea. The red-haired girl referenced a poem from The City of Dreadful Night while discussing art. Dick criticized Maisie's choice to base her work on existing art and literature. Maisie believed she could create a unique interpretation of Melancolia despite Dick's doubts.

source.author: Rudyard Kipling
source.title: The Works of Rudyard Kipling One Volume Edition

text: Shemus returns from the woods after half a day without bringing any food. Teig mentions that there is only a bit of mouldy bread in the house. Mary states that there is enough flour to make another loaf. Shemus expresses frustration towards the beggars who would not share their alms. Cathleen, Oona, and Aleel enter and Cathleen identifies herself as Countess Cathleen. Cathleen recalls living in an old grey castle with a kitchen garden during her childhood. Mary offers to guide Cathleen and her companions on the path to the market.

The text discusses the conflict between inspiration and a 'masculine portion' or 'spectre' of nature that kills creativity. It critiques the tendency to generalize forms and reduce art to uniformity, contrasting it with the pursuit of variety and freedom. The author emphasizes that wisdom and happiness are found in particulars rather than general knowledge. The text argues that both art and life should avoid tepid moderation and embrace excess for true vitality. Samuel Palmer's diary from 1824 states that excess is essential for great art, and medium should only enhance this excess. The author insists on three commands for art: to seek a determinate outline, avoid generalized treatment, and desire abundance. The text concludes with the idea that spiritual labor can transform mere sensation into new inspiration.

The speaker did not meet anyone who considered Wilde innocent. An old enemy praised Wilde's audacity and self-possession. Lionel Johnson changed his opinion about Wilde's imitators. Wilde was described as a martyr by some individuals. Willie Redmond recounted Wilde mocking actors at a theatrical society event. Wilde's brother had a strained relationship with him during the trials. Gleeson White stated that Wilde would never regain his reputation.

The text discusses the concept of death and its influence on the living. Adonais is described as having fled to a state of eternal existence after death. The deceased are said to remain present in nature and influence the living. Mrs. Shelley reflects on Shelley's speculations regarding the fate of the spirit after death. The text suggests that love, beauty, and delight are eternal and do not change with death. Shelley's poetry incorporates elements of mysticism and idealism. Intellectual Beauty is associated with both the happy dead and various spiritual entities.

The subject of the text is an artist who experiences visions that influence his work. The artist decides to leave the Art schools due to a perceived weakness in his will. The artist interacts with elder students, including John Hughes and Oliver Sheppard, who are recognized Irish sculptors. A girl in the modeling class is stone deaf, and the male students use profanity towards her while she works diligently. The students lack formal scholarship and critical knowledge of art history, primarily influenced by French art. The narrator has some knowledge of English poetry, particularly the works of Browning, which contrasts with the other students' knowledge. The narrator expresses a desire for a different artistic style, influenced by pre-Raphaelitism and personal memories of their father's lost designs.

An old man signaled for fire to light his pipe. Bridget expressed concern about bringing evil upon the house. Mary expressed her dissatisfaction with her current life and wished for freedom. Father Hart advised Mary to take Shawn's hand, emphasizing love's importance. Shawn expressed a desire to create a perfect world for Mary. Maurteen heard a child singing a strange song about the lonely of heart. The voice in the song described faeries dancing and the wind's laughter.

The princess was brought to the shore to see the serpent that was coming to take her away. Jack used a suit of clothes from the third giant and spoke with the princess without her recognizing him. The princess cut off a piece of Jack's hair and took one of his shoes to identify him later. Jack killed the serpent with a sword he obtained from the giant, preventing it from taking any more king's daughters. The bully claimed to have saved the princess and was favored by the king after the incident. The princess declared she would marry only the man whose hair matched the piece she had and whose foot fit the shoe she had taken. Jack's shoe fit him and his hair matched the piece cut by the princess, leading to their marriage and a three-day feast.

The narrator trained horses for their uncle. The uncle discussed England and mentioned meeting two lords who exchanged wives while on holiday. The uncle had a moment of temptation involving a woman but was deterred by a vision of an angel. The narrator met a girl driving a pony-carriage who was engaged and became her confidant. The girl often quarreled with her fiancé, leading to multiple breakups and reconciliations. The narrator experienced supernatural events while staying with cousins at Avena house in Ballisodare. The narrator and their cousin heard unexplained sounds and witnessed strange occurrences in the house.

The text discusses the distinction between the world of imagination and the perishable world created by memory and whim. It emphasizes the importance of purifying one's mind through the study of great masters to access the unfallen world. The author expresses a struggle to differentiate between two schools of thought in art, favoring the Florentine approach. The author experienced a significant change after returning to London from Felpham in 1804, overcoming temptations that threatened his imaginative power. The spirit of Titian is mentioned as a source of doubt regarding the execution of art without a model, which affected the author's imagination. The author claims to have regained the intellectual vision he had in his youth after visiting the Truchsessian Gallery of pictures. Following this experience, the author began to write extensively about the principles of art in clear prose and rhyme.

The text discusses the influence of sensory experiences on art and the human body. It contrasts the works of Canaletto and Franz Francken to illustrate different emotional responses to art. The author argues that art should evoke physical sensations and memories rather than abstract thoughts. The text states that all art is sensuous and that contemplative art can become broken and uncertain. It emphasizes the need for a consistent emotional world in art for it to resonate with the soul. The author references the _Divine Comedy_ as an example of ordered images that relate emotions. The text mentions that visionaries and ideal art often rely on trance-like states for their creation.

Leonardo da Vinci warned against pre-occupation with arts that cannot survive one's death. Carleton predicted in 1870 that there would be no developments in Irish Literature for twenty years. The land war in Ireland contributed to a period of bitterness that affected literary output. The author and Lady Gregory founded an Irish Theatre eight or nine years after Carleton's prediction. Dr. Douglas Hyde was an undergraduate when the author first met him in Dublin. Dr. Hyde gained considerable popularity as a Gaelic poet despite being unknown in intellectual Dublin. The author contributed to the London publication of Dr. Hyde's book _Beside the Fire_, which used a unique expression of emotion and romance.

Goethe, Balzac, Flaubert, and Count Tolstoy are mentioned as significant writers. William Blake believed that imagination was the first emanation of divinity. Blake argued that the imaginative arts are the greatest of Divine revelations. He claimed that everything that lives is holy, while lethargies and cruelties are unholy. Blake's philosophy allowed him to express beautiful feelings without concern for their utility. He was a symbolist who created his own symbols and sought a mythology. Blake's works include the _Songs of Innocence_ and various 'Prophetic Works.'

The text discusses the evolution of poetry and its relationship with beauty and rhythm. It contrasts contemporary poetry with the works of poets like Smart, Blake, and Keats. The author notes that modern poetry has shifted away from traditional marching rhythms. The text highlights the fading of the sanguineous temperament in poetry. It states that poetry has become more spiritual but has lost weight and measure. The author compares _Laon and Cythna_ and _Endymion_ to _Faerie Queene_ in terms of complexity and attention required. William Morris is mentioned as having a smooth and unexacting musical style.

The subject of the text critiques the influence of Venice and Holland on art. The subject believes that inspiration reveals eternal existences and divine essences. The subject values distinct and sharp boundary lines in art as essential for perfection. The subject argues that true beauty in art is derived from form and outline rather than mere color. The subject emphasizes that the greatest beauty is found in forms that change least from youth to old age. The subject expresses a preference for severe art over the styles popular in his time. The subject warns against the dangers of being captivated by nature's softness, which can obscure true artistic vision.

The text discusses the concept of mind as existence, with water serving as a symbol of existence. The Witch travels along the Nile and observes human life reflected in its waters. Alastor compares the river he follows to his mind and contemplates the uncertainty of thought after death. In the poem _Mont Blanc_, Shelley likens the flow of thoughts to the flow of the Arne river. Cythna describes her mind as a cave that reveals its secrets and reflects a universal mind. The text references various caves as symbols of life, mystery, and the human experience. Shelley uses towers as symbols of thought and knowledge, contrasting them with caves.

The text discusses the importance of new legends for the imagination of the world. It notes a reaction against the rationalism of the eighteenth century and the materialism of the nineteenth century. The symbolical movement has reached its peak in Germany with Wagner, in England with the Pre-Raphaelites, and in France with Villiers De l'Isle Adam, Mallarmé, and Maeterlinck. The arts are described as seeking to create a sacred book through legends. The text mentions various legends, including Sclavonic, Finnish, Scandinavian, Welsh, and Irish legends. The author reflects on a personal change in writing style from descriptive to spiritual and unemphatic. The struggle against externality in literature is noted as a significant trend among writers in Europe.

The narrator observes a shift in color perception in a room filled with red and blue objects. A Martinist approaches the narrator with a drawing of a circle and a dot, expressing excitement. A lean man shows the narrator his horoscope, highlighting its negative aspects with melancholy. A poet discusses the effects of Indian hemp, noting a three-month adjustment period. A woman in evening dress enters the room after attending a students' ball, unaware of her husband's presence. The narrator reflects on the nature of drama and its criticism by journalists, emphasizing the importance of historical context. The writer argues that drama should not be limited to modern experiences but can draw from ancient themes.

One woman near Gort claimed to have seen the fool, describing him as a big strong man who was half naked. The wife of the old miller stated that the stroke of the fool, known as the Amadan-na-Breena, has no cure. An old woman from the Bog of Kiltartan confirmed that there is no cure for the stroke of the Amadan-na-Breena. A man with a tape claimed that June is the worst month because that is when the Amadan gives his stroke. A boy experienced a fright when he saw a lamb with a beard, which he believed was the Amadan in June. A certain Regan mentioned that those who receive the touch of the Amadan-na-Breena are doomed. An old woman in a Galway workhouse noted that the Amadan-na-Breena changes his shape every two days.

The room described has curtains of grey corduroy and walls covered with brown paper. There is a portrait of Cardinal Newman and a religious picture by Simeon Solomon in the room. Johnson quoted imaginary conversations with famous individuals, including Gladstone and Newman, throughout his life. Johnson's favorite quotations were from Cardinal Newman, whom he likely never met. Johnson objected to the public quotation of private conversations even after the individuals had died. He claimed to have had a conversation with Gladstone that was later proven impossible due to Gladstone's absence from Oxford on that date. Johnson's knowledge of languages and literature is questioned, particularly regarding his claims about Welsh.

The text discusses the perceptions of Shakespeare's character Richard II among German critics and Professor Dowden. Professor Dowden believed that England's success was due to the perfection of character, contrasting it with the failures in Ireland. Dowden viewed Henry V as the typical Anglo-Saxon and a model presented by Shakespeare, despite his commonplace vices. The text mentions a reputation of a writer who claimed Shakespeare admired only one character from his works. The author argues that Shakespeare had a sympathetic view of Richard II, recognizing his unfitness for kingship but also his lovable qualities. Shakespeare's portrayal of Richard II reflects the conflict between artistic ideals and the practical demands of leadership. The text concludes that Shakespeare cared little for the state beyond its external appearances and believed in the importance of peace over civil war.

The Return of Ulysses is noted for its classical gravity of speech and lyrical beauty. The unity of place and time in the late acts of The Return of Ulysses compels a logical procession of incidents. Mr. Bridges' poetry is characterized by pale colors and delicate silence reminiscent of cloudy country days. Interest in the arts has declined over generations, with fewer people engaging in them. People increasingly prioritize business and entertainment over the appreciation of the arts. Those who care about the arts view themselves as a priesthood of a nearly forgotten faith. Historically, the arts were closely linked to religion, but they have become more independent and proud.

Mary Hynes was considered the handsomest girl in Ireland and died young. It is believed that those who are admired may be taken by the Sidhe. An old man from Duras remembers Mary Hynes attending a pattern festival. Raftery, a poet, is said to have admired Mary Hynes despite being blind. The old beliefs suggest that beauty is linked to the gods and the Sidhe. People who admired Mary Hynes are thought to have failed to bless her, which may have contributed to her fate. The old men and women discussing Mary Hynes express a gentleness reminiscent of ancient Greek traditions.

MARY urges the merchants to give food or money to the starving poor. FIRST MERCHANT expresses uncertainty about finding deserving poor. SECOND MERCHANT suggests that if each person brings merchandise, they will offer a good price. MARY points out that the starving have already sold their livestock and fields. FIRST MERCHANT claims that not everything has been sold and mentions a concept of an 'immortal' self. SHEMUS and TEIG express skepticism about the merchants' intentions and the value of their souls. FIRST MERCHANT instructs to announce that they buy men's souls for a good price.

John O'Leary hoped for an Irish literature of the greatest kind. Lionel Johnson, Katharine Tynan, and the author aimed to reform Irish poetry. The group sought to create a more subtle rhythm and organic form in poetry. Lionel Johnson had a gift for expressing political thought in verse. The author was influenced by William Morris and aimed to cultivate a passionate patriotism in Ireland. Madame Maud Gonne was able to draw large crowds and speak about 'Mother Ireland.' The political movement associated with Gonne struggled to build lasting achievements.

The wind blows over the lonely of heart. Mary hears faint music and small steps when the child approaches. Maurteen offers ribbons to the child to tie up her wild hair. The child claims to be much older than the eagle cock on Ballygawley Hill. Father Hart identifies the child as being of the faery people. The child asserts her power to prevent anyone from passing unless she wills it. Father Hart prepares to confront the child with the support of holy figures.

Potter died from the effects of semi-starvation after living on bread and tea. Farrar attended Potter's funeral and observed a woman who had previously managed his finances. An actor mimicked Michael Moran's sayings, songs, and appearance on stage. A dispute arose among friends about the actor's mimicry, leading to a wager of a forty-shilling supper. Mr. Benson did not play the scene in _Richard III._ where the ghosts walk as Shakespeare wrote it. Goethe stated that art is art because it is not nature. The subject experienced disturbances at night from entities that communicated in Irish and played pipes. Joseph, your mother's uncle, married and began building a house for his wife near the Lough. The narrator's father was a weaver who set up his looms in a nearby cottage. In 1812, Percy Bysshe Shelley traveled to the Continent with Godwin's daughter. Shelley described his experiences of sailing down rivers in the preface to _Laon and Cythna_. Shelley's poetry frequently features rivers, streams, and wells, often associated with caves. The poem _Alastor_ includes a scene where the protagonist travels along a river in a cave. Caves and fountains are recurring symbols in Shelley's works, including _Cythna_ and _Prometheus Unbound_. Shelley may have drawn inspiration from Plato's cave allegory and Porphyry's writings on caves. The text references a cave in Ithaca described by Homer, which is associated with nymphs.

The narrator visited a house in Leinster Road where several middle-aged women were playing cards. The narrator was offered a glass of sherry by the women and lost sixpence as a result. Ellen O'Leary was the hostess and kept house for her brother John O'Leary, a Fenian who had been sentenced to twenty years of penal servitude. John O'Leary was released after five years on the condition that he would not return to Ireland for fifteen years. Ellen O'Leary shared stories about her brother's life, including his involvement with the Fenian movement and his views on politics. John O'Leary had a collection of second-hand books and encouraged the narrator to read works by Davis and the Young Irelanders. John O'Leary spoke of his prison life without mentioning hardship, stating he did not come to complain.

A woman appeared before the eyes of a man on a cross. An evoker of spirits reported seeing spirits, one of which had arms without hands. The narrator recalled two gravestones seen by a knight in chain mail. The evoker of spirits suggested the knight might be undergoing penance for violence. The narrator experienced visions that were related to dominant moods and events in life. The narrator had a vision while staying with friends in Paris and later encountered a servant who had seen his imagined injury. The narrator received a letter from a fellow student shortly after thinking intently about that student.

The narrator experienced feelings of indignation and curiosity about a group of people before entering a museum. The narrator had ambitions of living a solitary life inspired by Thoreau on Innisfree. The poem _Innisfree_ was inspired by a memory of lake water and a fountain seen in a shop window. The narrator reflected on the oppressive nature of urban architecture while passing the new Law Courts. The narrator spent time at Oxford copying out texts for a publisher and returned home feeling unwell. The narrator believed that achieving literary success required significant effort and time. The narrator observed the faces of people in London and recalled Ruskin's negative views on societal decline.

Oona bandages Aleel's wound and expresses a sense of insignificance. The scene takes place in the house of Countess Cathleen. Cathleen is kneeling in front of an altar in the oratory. Aleel enters and urges Cathleen to leave the castle and the woods. Cathleen questions the existence of evil in the woods compared to the rest of the world. Aleel describes a dream involving a figure with birds around his head. Cathleen refuses to leave, stating her commitment to pray at the altar.

The text describes a vision seen from Rosses Point, where a woman is observed traveling from Knocknarea. According to local folklore, Queen Maeve is buried under a great heap of stones at Knocknarea. The woman observed is described as strong, handsome, and appearing to be about thirty years old. The Master Pilot recounts a vision of a procession of women in costumes from another age. The seer, a girl of twenty-five, experiences a vision of Diana and her dogs while in a trance. The narrator reflects on the interconnectedness of personal and folk imagery in dreams and visions.

A Mayo woman reported that something bad had entered a house opposite her. Two friends of the Mayo woman encountered a figure they believed to be the devil. One friend was approached by the figure on horseback, who vanished when she refused to ride with him. The other friend encountered a flapping object that resembled a newspaper, which transformed into a young man who also vanished when she declined his invitation. An old man on the slopes of Ben Bulben found the devil ringing a bell under his bed. A Mayo woman recounted a story of a servant girl who hung herself for the love of God and was buried with Christian rites. The Mayo woman described her visions of holy things and the beauty of the Virgin and the lily of the valley.

The author created a map of Sligo on the ceiling of their study using pastels. The author wrote a couple of Sligo stories and finished 'Wanderings of Oisin.' The author planned to create a theatre and set words to music. The author believed that personal utterance could be a valuable form of expression in literature. The author's father insisted that personal utterance was egotism and preferred drama.

Florence Farr lived in lodgings at Brook Green, approximately twenty minutes' walk away. Farr possessed three notable gifts: tranquil beauty, an incomparable sense of rhythm, and a beautiful voice. Farr expressed her artistic genius through an unfashionable art that has rarely existed since the seventeenth century. The narrator formed a friendship with Farr that was characterized by both enduring connection and exasperation. Miss Maud Gonne visited the narrator's home and brought an introduction to his father from John O'Leary. Gonne's views on war caused tension between her and the narrator's father. The narrator observed Gonne's beauty and presence, comparing her to a classical embodiment of Spring.

The narrator describes a body that has characteristics reminiscent of the American Indian. The narrator expresses fear of other boys and doubts about their own courage. The narrator's grandfather is mentioned as someone who was not afraid of danger. The narrator allowed a friend to take punishment in class before admitting to their own actions. The narrator returned home the next day after walking approximately thirty miles. The uncle's general servant found the narrator's walk amusing and laughed at the mention of it.

The text discusses the impact of a certain individual's genius on modern Irish literature. The individual is described as having an uncritical folk-genius and an imitative sympathy. He aimed to revive old Irish heroes in his unfinished _History of Ireland_, drawing from historical texts.

William Pollexfen was the narrator's grandfather. William Pollexfen had a reputation for physical strength and was known for his silence. He owned many sailing ships and had a violent temper. The narrator confused his grandfather with God and prayed for punishment for his sins. An incident occurred where a cousin suggested to William Pollexfen that he should give a doll to her if roles were reversed.

Countess Cathleen gives the larder and dairy keys to Oona. Countess Cathleen instructs the Porter to take a key that opens a small room for herbs. Shemus Rua reflects on his wife's refusal to accept money from their master.

The text describes a setting with cages full of birds, dogs, a parrot, and a hawk from Donegal. W. E. Henley lived a quarter of an hour's walk from Bedford Park on the high road to Richmond. The text discusses the perception of creativity and inspiration in relation to poets and their experiences. It contrasts descriptions in the Iliad and the Odyssey with those in the Æneid and modern writings. The text suggests that the blind man in ancient times became a poet due to being driven away from other activities. It posits that poets of the silver ages do not need to refuse life, as they live in a time of shattered ideals. The text mentions that general praise can be detrimental to poets, as it may lead to enslavement by public opinion. It describes the irregular nature of creative energy and its connection to deep emotional experiences. The text includes an anecdote about an old man who had many imaginations despite limited observations in his life.

The text discusses the shape of theatres and the need for a larger theatre to be built. It criticizes the half-round theatre design, suggesting it is outdated and not suitable for modern stage art. Decorative scene-painting is suggested as a new art form that would enhance the theatrical experience without overwhelming the performance. Mr. Gordon Craig's use of decorative scenery at a recent performance is noted as a significant advancement in theatrical scenery.
